en: Preface to the New Commentary on the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma:
That the *Lotus Sutra* is the king among all sutras is something even a child at the breast can say.
Yet, when it comes to explaining why it is the king, even those of great talent and vast wisdom cannot do so. Why is this? It is because the *Lotus Sutra*...
This is the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*). The Buddha Vehicle is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*). The Buddha’s knowledge and vision is the Buddha’s realm (*viṣaya*).
It is impossible for ordinary intelligence to explain the Buddha’s realm. Among the various masters of Zhendan (China), there have been dozens of schools that have commented upon it;
yet only the Great Master of Tiantai has attained the correct understanding. This Great Master was among the assembly who heard the teaching together on Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*), and as for his...
This refers to those of diminished virtue who act as messengers for the Tathāgata. Having attained his teaching, is it not indeed appropriate?

After the Great Master, there have been many who selected and excerpted from his commentaries; however, as in the case of the *Yirushi* (If-Only) commentary, one should adopt them by taking only the essential points.
Extending what was drawn forth, he attained a fitting appropriateness in his moderation. He was once titled Ichian (One Hut);

during the Yongle era of the Ming dynasty, he served as a monk official in the Sengluosi and resided at Upper Tianzhu Temple. He once received an imperial decree to investigate the Tripitaka and compiled the *Sanzang Fashu* (Numerical Categories of the Tripitaka).
During the Eikyō era of our own [Japan], he came to this country on an official mission; at that time, I traveled together with him across the sea to Tsushima. And so, in harmony...
The poem he composed in response to the imperial decree allows one to know his character. I once obtained a copy of a new commentary; I held it and read it repeatedly, never tiring of it.
Regretting that I could not share it with others, I disregarded my own meager learning and ventured to annotate the margins. I then entrusted it to the carver.
Indeed, the wondrous essence of the single mind disperses into speech and coalesces into written characters; such is the nature of both speech and writing.

These characters are merely the wondrous manifestation of the single mind. Those of superior capacity understand them through spiritual intuition (*śraddhā-vimukti*), while those of inferior roots enter through faith.
However, as for those of middling intelligence and the foolish, they perceive and discriminate them.

As for those who understand through spiritual intuition and enter through faith, they do not grasp at the signs of language and written words; they may simply hear the scriptural text and [attain realization].

I have taken charge of it. As for those who possess discerning awareness and discrimination, they would not be further deluded by what is obscure, nor would they find it difficult to be guided by instruction.
Should they seek its textual meaning and happen to produce a single phrase of understanding or a single thought of faith that permeates their spirit, the benefit thereof would be immeasurable;
this is my aspiration for its circulation.
Written by the monk Fukashi on the fifteenth day of the final month of autumn in the year of Dingwei during the Kwanmei era, at the western hermitage of the Gakoku Aranya.

Preface to the Re-engraved Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* When using a leaden awl to bore a well, even if the well is situated upon high ground, not only will the water of principle be difficult to bring forth, but even when reaching the damp mud, it remains far removed.
How does this compare to using a sharp spade to dig into the earth, penetrating straight through the diamond-hard bedrock? It is without obstruction.
Previously, the Dharma-spring overflowed and surged forth. Formerly at Gṛdhrakūṭa, the Sūtra was preached for eight years;

it was compiled in Western India and spread continuously for eight *li* before reaching China, where it was translated into seven fascicles. Thus, the flavor of the true principle remained hidden within the layered mountains.
As for the various masters of the Six Dynasties who eventually produced commentaries and sub-commentaries, they can be counted on one's fingers at seventy-odd schools.

If one seeks those whose principles are profound and whose prose is extensive, then Guangzhai (Jingying Huiyuan) is the foremost. Was this not like digging a well on high ground? Were his lead and iron chisels not sharp?
When Zhiyi appeared and expounded the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), he first refuted Master Yun of Guangzhai, and the others surrendered to him upon hearing of it.
[The text] ceases. Does his sharp axe cleave the earth? Does the fountain of Dharma overflow?

Yet the people of the world merely know that the stream is long and the branches are luxuriant, without tracing back to the fact that the source is distant and the roots are deep. Indeed, our Wise One, formerly at Vulture Peak, attended the assembly and heard [the teaching] in person;
he contemplated the Great Sameness and listened with focused attention, directly receiving the seal of transmission. At the Great Suo Daochang, he perfectly realized samādhi, and even—

With unimpeded eloquence, he proclaimed the teachings in accordance with their true nature; moreover, his compilation at Zhang’an cannot be compared to mere literary composition, and Jingxi’s commentaries and exegeses provide documented evidence of their authenticity.
Since the former sages have already submitted themselves in this manner, why should later students trouble themselves with further deliberation?
It would be no different from the fireflies vying for light against the two luminaries, or the puddles in a cow's hoofprint attempting to match the measure of the four oceans. How much more so!
I see that they do not know their own measure. One must know that for the wise, the marvel of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* lies in its *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning);
the *Wenju* (Textual Phrases) comes next; and as for the various modern commentaries (*kezhu*), they are yet further below.

If a student first studies the commentaries, then the *Wenju*, and finally the *Xuanyi*, it is like looking at water in a river, then in a river, and then in the sea—it cannot avoid [the error of mistaking the source for the flow].

Gazing across the vast ocean toward the Spirit of the Sea (Ruo), he sighed. [This work] first presents the profound meaning (*xuan-yi*), followed by the textual analysis (*wen-ju*), and finally the topical outline and commentary (*ke-zhu*).
It is like felling a tree: starting from the roots, then the trunk, and then the branches; it may be said to be like pulling up the thatch-grass by its roots so that the entire clump is removed.

This was carved into woodblocks at the Upper Tianzhu Monastery by the Dharma Master Yiran, a native of the Hongwu era of our present dynasty. The year [of publication] was when it was printed in the Former Capital.
The old blocks were discarded. I previously obtained a printed edition from a Sanskrit manuscript at Siming. I subsequently searched for it diligently and found the carved blocks at Shouning in Min.
Later, because it was inconvenient for students to obtain them, I commissioned Master Gaopeng of Baofeng, the head of the Siming assembly, to raise funds for their re-engraving.
The version currently preserved at Longshu Hermitage in Wulin is this one. Recently...

Li Cao Rong, a descendant in the fourth generation from the East of the Sun (the lineage of the Eastern Ocean), has considered that carrying these Buddhist scriptures (*brahmapustaka*) is inconvenient; moreover, as his eyes grow old, he finds it difficult to read the minute script.

Therefore, he has reformed them into bound volumes (*pustaka*) with characters written slightly larger. He has solicited funds for carving the woodblocks so that they may be widely circulated. Thus, he is profoundly devoted to the Dharma.

This may indeed be called diligent. He further commanded that my own *Xuan-yi ji-lüe* (Abridged Compendium of Profound Meaning) be engraved before it, so that students, though unable yet to survey the vast ocean of its meaning, might first dip their fingers into it to know its flavor. When the work was completed, he questioned me regarding it;
therefore, I did not decline this humble task and have ventured to compose this preface. At the time...
In the seventh year of the Ming Tianqi era, when the year was Jiayu (Jiangyu) and the branch was Danyue (Danye), on the seventy-fifth day of the seventh month of summer,
the seventy-fourth old monk Chuan Deng, a transmitter of the Tiantai teachings and contemplations, recorded this in the Buxun Hall to the east of the Lengyan Altar.
Preface to the Sub-commentary on the Sectional Annotations of the Lotus Sūtra:
Although the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for forty-nine years—comprising the five periods and four teachings—the ultimate intent lies in the Perfect [Teaching].

Thus, while the *Avataṃsaka* belongs to the "combined" [teachings] and the *Prajñāpāramitā* still carries vestiges [of the provisional], it is only upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that he directly abandons expedient means and speaks solely of the Unsurpassed [Truth]. This is...
It is for this reason that [the Lotus Sūtra] is praised with such earnestness as the king among sūtras.

When the teachings spread to the Eastern Land (China), those who propagated the *Avataṃsaka* like Xianshou or those who propagated the *Prajñāpāramitā* like the Chan school were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

yet those who propagated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* have numbered no more than ten or so generations since Tiantai. What is the reason for this? It is likely because the partial and expedient are easy to accept, whereas the perfect and real are difficult to shoulder.
Regarding that principle of the insentient and the discourse on the inherent evil of nature, even the Venerable Kāśyapa harbored doubts as to whether it were the teaching of Māra;
how much more so for one who, with a countenance like gold, conceals his personal color and directly grasps the meaning of what was then a source of wonder and doubt for devas and humans?
Is this not as rare an encounter as the feathers of a phoenix or the hooves of a qilin? Through this, I further believe that the propagation of the Lotus Sūtra is difficult indeed. All Buddhas...

He appeared in the world, yet did not encounter those of great faculties; there were those who entered *nirvāṇa* without the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* being preached, which demonstrates the difficulty of encountering such a vessel.
Guangzhai was the first to proclaim [the teachings] in Hebei, followed by dozens of schools, concerning the meanings of the provisional and the real, and the fundamental and the manifested.
It is only upon reaching ultimate wisdom that one can finally achieve certainty; thus, the Four Reliances (catvāri pratisaraṇāni) are difficult to encounter.
From their compilation at Mount Tiantai until the Five Dynasties period, barely four hundred years had passed, yet within China there was no one capable of articulating their meaning.

It was only by seeking them in Goguryeo that they were first recovered; thus, the continuity of their transmission is difficult to maintain. From the Song dynasty down to the Ming, the sublime purport was once again severed. Its flourishing—
Ten thousand chambers were restored by Dharma Master Miaofeng. He transmitted them first to Master Wujinding and secondly to Master Hanyoulu.

As they alone upheld the complete vehicle against those of narrow-minded and partial-secrecy, resentment and jealousy filled the roads; thus, the difficulty of maintaining such independent standing is evident.
Viewed from this perspective, even grasping at empty space with one's hands and treading upon Mount Sumeru with one's feet would be considered an easy matter.
Yet, while the *Dantideva* [commentary] is complete and superior, it does not fall into the trap of conflating the general and the specific, making it difficult for others to supplement further.
Master Cao and Master Rong, descendants of Master Lu, lamenting that the lineage of the Buddha’s seed was difficult to purify, consequently took up the annotated version and re-edited it.
Together with my fellow practitioners—Mr. Mingyu Wang, Mr. Qikai Zhang, Mr. Zhimeng Chen, Mr. Jihuang Deng, Mr. Zhenfu Ma, Mr.
Yinghua Jiang, Mr. Yangfeng Chen, Mr. Daoru Lin, Mr. Guojin Gai, Mr. Yinghua Gong, Mr. Ruhua Gao, and Mr.
Ye—we have planned to publish this work for posterity. For the Lotus Sūtra...
The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) serves as the entrance gate; the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) serves as the hall; and the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) serves as the inner chamber.

The *Kezhu* (Sectional Commentary) is an abridgment of the *Wenju*. To propagate the *Lotus Sūtra* without knowing the *Kezhu* is already a flawed approach—even the *Yanjing Yaoyie* (Essential Explanations of the Yanling Edition) still retains such shortcomings.

How much more so for those who falsely interpret the scriptural text and merely extend their own arbitrary speculations? Their engagement with the *Lotus Sūtra* is like driving a carriage toward the north when one intends to go south.
Master [Zhiyi] was refined in the profound meaning of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. How could he not have been capable of innovating something new and extraordinary?

Yet his reason for strictly adhering to what was falsely transmitted was precisely because, apart from the teachings of Master Zhi (Zhizhe), all others were a confused mixture of the provisional and the ultimate.

Having already galloped across the world where sheep and deer prances side by side—driving the white ox-chariot—he had long since transcended them. Why must one insist on creating a pretense of understanding, merely to delude those who do not know?

How lamentable! This is yet another difficulty faced by Master Xuezhong. I have thus issued this wind-announcement to all quarters: based on the sub-commentary (*ke-zhu*), one reaches the *Xuan-yi*; based on the *Xuan-yi*, one reaches the *Zhi-guan*.
As for the profound, solid, and remote depths of the *Dharmapada-nidāna* (the Lotus Treasury), one may now enter them directly.
Be careful not to fall into the confusion of the general and specific [teachings], thereby defiling the seeds of the Perfect [Vehicle]. Then the Tathāgata will be deeply indebted to you.
How fortunate! This serves as the preface.
Written with palms joined in reverent devotion by Shao Jiance of Yongjia, a Jinshi degree holder and Imperial Envoy of the Office of Attendant Gentlemen, under the auspices of the Imperial Grant.
Preface to the New Commentary on the Lotus Sutra:
The Sutra says, "The treasury of the Lotus Sutra is profound, firm, and remote; no one can reach it.
If this is so, how could verbal explanations possibly aspire to equal it? This is precisely...

Although the World-Honored One Śākyamuni taught the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm—non-dual and undifferentiated—during the twenty-one days [following his enlightenment], even one as wise as Śāriputra could not avoid being startled and doubtful;
how much more so for the rest of the assembly? This is truly a gate of great liberation that is difficult to believe, difficult to understand, and inconceivable.
During the Chen and Sui dynasties, at Tiantai...
The Great Master Zhizhe, the Venerable Gao, personally received the teachings at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and attained profound awakening through the "Great Enlightenment" (Dàsū).

He realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra and obtained the *dhāraṇī* of revolving. Subsequently, while residing in Jiangling, he expounded the ten fascicles of the *Xuan-yi* (Profound Meaning) for his disciples, including Zhang’an;
this work alone explained the title of the sūtra, which is what is known as the "Ninety-Day Discourse on the Profound. Later, while residing at Waguan Temple, he again [expounded] for Zhang...

Zhiyi and his colleagues separately explained the scriptural text according to the principles of the provisional and the real, the original and the manifested, titling their work *Wenju* (Words and Phrases), which also consists of ten fascicles.
Previously, the commentary produced at Guangzhai Monastery was not free from errors; the Great Master eliminated these entirely to rectify the teachings.
Later, during the Tang dynasty, the Venerable Jingxi further expanded upon the Great Master’s explanations and composed the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Words and Phrases) in ten fascicles.

The *Xuanyi Miaoyue* (Exegesis on the Profound Meaning) in ten fascicles and the *Shiwenju* (Commentary on the Textual Phrases) comprise the entirety of this sutra’s subtle essence, complete and without remainder.
Nevertheless, as the phrasing is vast and the principles are profound and mysterious, none but those scholars who have long served as lecturers could enter them.
Thereupon, one named Huiyugu of Yuan, relying solely upon the established words of the Great Master, [composed...]
Annotations were added beneath the lines of the text to inspire and enlighten beginners; it is a pity that, due to the passage of time, the woodblocks no longer exist.
The former abbot of Upper Tianzhu, Master Yiguan Ru, was a disciple of the eminent monk of former times, Master Guangan.

Having received the authentic transmission from him, he was extensively versed in the doctrines and teachings, and his expositions were so proficient that today, among those who have mastered both aspects [of the teachings], he stands as a peerless figure.
In his leisure time while residing at the Great Baoen Temple in Nanjing, he reflected upon the desolation of the ancestral Way and the imminent collapse of the Great Teaching.
Consequently, he took the Master’s established words as the basis for his commentary on this sutra, not daring to arbitrarily add his own views to muddle the discourse and mislead future students.
He edited the text with greater detail than the *Huìyùgǔ* (Wisdom Valley) edition, compiling it into seven fascicles. [End of] Wu.

Gu Daozhen transcribed this with the utmost care and precision. Together with his fellow Buddhist practitioners Guan Shuchun, Feng Juecheng, Gu Daosheng, Gu Xiran, Jiang Menggui, and others, he raised funds from the public to carve the woodblocks for its publication and circulation.
One day, Shuchun and his companions arrived at my residence bearing incense to request a preface. At that time, I was eight [years old].

At fourteen years of age, I have been confined to my home by illness; how could I possibly set pen to paper? Nevertheless, beholding such an act of sublime virtue, I ought to join in the joy of its accomplishment.
Although the treasury of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is profound, solid, and remote, such that no one can reach it, how could it ever be fully attained through mere words?
For now, I shall select one or two points to compose a preface to mark the beginning; you should know this.
The sūtra’s inconceivable retribution is likewise inconceivable;

it is sufficient above to repay the profound kindness of one's sovereign and parents, and sufficient below to sustain the subtle interests of all that flies and swims. Like the great void, how could it have any measure?
Therefore, for those who read this preface hereafter, they should seek the meaning beyond the words.

Preface by Yao Guangxiao, Grand Master for the Cultivation of Goodness and Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince of Wu Commandery, on the Fifteenth Day of the First Month in the sixteenth year of the Yongle era;
Fascicle One of the Annotated Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Compiled by the Bhikṣu Yirú, Abbot of Shang Tianzhu Jǎngsì Temple.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the profoundly deep and secret treasury of the original ground; it is the root source of a single transformation and the ultimate teaching of the five periods.
The Tathāgata’s intent in appearing in the world was precisely to preach this sutra in order to reveal and instruct all beings.
Because this text directly points to the fundamental source of birth—the treasury of original enlightenment—and leads to seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood, the Sūtra says:
"The Buddhas appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition; that is to say, to open, reveal, awaken, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Alas, those of inferior capacity are not yet able to hear this; if they were to hear it, they would give rise to slander and fall into suffering.
The Sūtra says: "If one were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would slander the Dharma and, out of lack of faith, fall into the three evil realms.
Having no choice, the Tathāgata established provisional teachings for them;

first, he employed the Great Teaching of the Avataṃsaka to accommodate those inclined toward the Lesser Vehicle, yet as they were unable to believe and accept it, he remained unmoved at the site of enlightenment and traveled abroad to transform beings."
At the Deer Park, he preached the Tripiṭaka teachings for them and further guaranteed the ultimate emptiness;

therefore, he had to use the Vaipulya sūtras to censure and rebuke them, causing them to feel shame for their Lesser Vehicle views and to aspire toward the Great Vehicle. Although they aspired to the Great Vehicle, their attachment to the reality [of the Lesser Vehicle] was not yet forgotten;
thus, he entrusted Śāriputra with the task of turning the wheel of teaching, extensively expounding the Dharma of the wisdom of emptiness to refine and purify them.
Those who cling to their emotions have already destroyed what is established; yet they still take the real to cover the provisional, and the provisional obscures the real.

The roots of the Two Vehicles have not yet opened, their capacity for Buddhahood remains ruined, and the fact that the Tathāgata attained Buddhahood long ago has not yet been revealed. It is here, at this great assembly on Vulture Peak, that the secret essentials are discussed intensely:
the provisional gate of skillful means is opened, the wondrous principle of reality is demonstrated, and the provisional capacities of all sages are brought forth.
Because it skillfully reveals the profound subtleties of the fundamental stage, the Sūtra says: "Directly abandoning expedient means, he speaks only of the Unsurpassed Way.
As for its teaching, the three vehicles all converge in the One Vehicle; the nine realms alike return to the Buddha-realm.
Only now is his long-lasting lifespan revealed, and only now is his original intent for appearing in the world fully expressed. This is what is called the "Marvelous."

This is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This scripture consists of twenty-eight chapters; the wondrous Dharma discussed therein does not transcend the provisional and the real, the fundamental and the manifested, and the provisional and the real.
"Provisional" refers to the nine realms and the three vehicles; "real" refers to the Buddha-realm and the perfect vehicle. "Fundamental" refers to attaining Buddhahood long ago;

"manifested" refers to the transformation through teaching after the fruit [of enlightenment]. The first fourteen chapters constitute the Gate of the Manifested, which opens up the provisional and reveals the real.
The fourteen chapters following the "Expedient Means" (Hōben) constitute the "Root Gate" (Honmon), which reveals the fundamental by opening up the traces.

Since the revelation of both the traces and the fundamental occurs according to the varying capacities of sentient beings—whether sharp or dull—there are three cycles and seven parables. Regarding the three cycles:
the first, the Cycle of the Dharma-Explanation, was taught for those of superior capacity as the doctrine of the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle; Śāriputra alone attained awakening therein.
That which is discussed in the "Expedient Means" chapter is this: the second cycle of parables, consisting of the three carts and the one cart, was taught for those of middle capacity;
that Kāśyapa and the other four great disciples attained understanding is precisely what is explained in the "Parable" chapter.
The third cycle of causes and conditions was taught for those of inferior capacity, explaining the causal connections of past lives regarding the twelve hundred followers.

The Śrāvakas receiving their predictions refers precisely to what is elucidated in the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter; the provisional teachings of the Trace Gate (jimen) culminate in these three cycles (*trivartman*).

A cycle implies a beginning, and since an end must correspond to a start, those of superior capacity began at the Deer Park by receiving the Lesser Vehicle and concluded at the Lotus Sūtra by obtaining their prediction.

By analogy, one should know that those of middling capacity likewise [began with the Lesser Vehicle], while those of inferior capacity first planted the seeds during the Mahābhijñājñāna-buddha period.
Because the conditions for the assembly have finally opened, it is said that there are "three turnings. Regarding the seven parables:
first, the Parable of the Burning House, which illustrates how the three realms are not secure, as clarified in the *Puyi-pin* (Parable Chapter);

second, the Parable of the Poor Son, which illustrates how the followers of the Lesser Vehicle lack the merit and wealth of the Great Vehicle, as clarified in the *Xinjie-pin* (Understanding Chapter). Third...
The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs illustrates that while all conditioned wholesome dharmas are capable of eliminating evil, unconditioned wholesome dharmas are supreme,

as clarified in the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter. Fourth, the Parable of the Phantom City illustrates how the true emptiness and *nirvāṇa* of the Two Vehicles can prevent the errors of views and afflictions and repel the enemy of birth-and-death, as explained in the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter.
The fifth, the parable of the jewel in the garment, illustrates the prince’s formation of karmic conditions;
it refers to the seed of the wisdom-jewel of the One Vehicle, which is the "enabling cause" (*jñāna-hetu*), as explained in the "Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples.

The sixth, the parable of the jewel in the topknot, illustrates the Middle Way and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) that is the primary object of veneration for the ultimate fruit, as explained in the "Chapter on the Peaceful Practices" (*Anraku-gyō-bon*).
This clarifies the preceding point. The six metaphors above all illustrate the Trace Gate (*jimen*), which reveals the Real by opening up the Provisional.

The metaphor of the seven physician’s sons illustrates how the Buddha is like a great king of physicians who universally cures the illnesses of all sentient beings, as explained in the "Life Span" chapter (*Shòuliàng pǐn*);
this single metaphor illustrates the Fundamental Gate (*běnmén*), which reveals the Fundamental by opening up the Trace.

First, explaining the primary title to clarify the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-vidha-gambhīrārtha*): 1. The name as both dharma and metaphor; 2. The true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as the essence (*śarīra*); 3.

The One Vehicle’s cause and fruit as the thesis (*abhiprāya*); 4. Severing doubt and engendering faith as the function (*karman*); 5. The unsurpassed *amṛta* (nectar) as the character of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding "the name as both dharma and metaphor": "dharma" refers to the wondrous Dharma, and "metaphor" refers to the lotus flower. As for what is said...

"Exquisite" (myō) refers to the name "inconceivable," which is a term of praise. What is called the "Dharma" consists of the ten realms, the ten suchnesses, and the teachings of provisional and real, and manifest and original.
This is because the Exquisite Dharma is difficult to understand, whereas metaphors make it easy to clarify.

Just as with the lotus flower, where the blossom and the fruit exist simultaneously, so too in the Exquisite Dharma, the provisional and the real are of one essence; therefore, there is the Gate of the Trace.

The three parables of the Original Gate (Honmon) and the three parables of the Trace Gate (Jimon). Regarding the three parables [of the Trace Gate]: first, the metaphor of the flower blooming for the sake of the lotus, which represents establishing the provisional for the sake of the real;

second, the metaphor of the flower opening and the lotus appearing, which represents opening the provisional to reveal the real; third, the metaphor of the flower falling and the lotus being perfected, which represents abolishing the provisional to establish the real.
Regarding the three parables of the Original Gate: first, the metaphor of the flower blooming for the sake of the lotus, which represents descending from the fundamental to manifest the trace.

The metaphor of the lotus appearing as the flowers bloom illustrates the opening of the traces to reveal the fundamental; the metaphor of the lotus forming once the flowers have fallen illustrates the abolition of the traces to establish the fundamental.
Thus, the single metaphor of the "Lotus" in this primary title serves as the general metaphor, whereas the seven metaphors in the body of the sutra, such as the burning house, are specific metaphors.
Therefore, the *Miaoxuan* states: "The seven parables are the specific; the lotus is the general."

Because the general encompasses the particular, it is placed at the beginning of the chapter. Although the general and the particular differ, they are all intended to reveal the dharma of provisional and real, and of origin and trace.

"Sūtra" means "dharma" and "permanence. That which serves as the common track for the ten realms is called "dharma," and that which does not change across the three periods of time is called "permanent.
Thus, using "dharma" as a metaphor constitutes the title of this sūtra. As for its essence being the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*):
This means that because each and every phenomenon of the ten realms and ten suchnesses is free from false appearances, it is called the "true aspect" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, Nāgārjuna said: "Except for the true aspect of all phenomena, everything else is the work of Māra.

This wondrous essence is referred to as the "true aspect of all phenomena" in the Trace Gate (*śeṣamukha*), whereas in the Origin Gate (*mūlamukha*) it is referred to as "neither thusness nor difference. Although the origin and the trace differ, the wondrous essence remains the same.
Because its essence is one, the true mark (*dharmatā*) constitutes the essence of this sutra. Regarding the "One Vehicle cause and effect" as the thesis (*artha*):
the thesis refers to the essential meaning, namely that the Buddha’s own practice of cause and effect is the thesis. Why is it the essential?
Because when speaking of "cause," it encompasses immeasurable wholesome qualities; when speaking of "fruit," it encompasses immeasurable realizations. Therefore, by means of this one...

The vehicle of cause and effect constitutes the central doctrine (*mūla*) of this sutra; the severing of doubt and the engendering of faith constitute its function (*prayojana*). "Function" refers to its efficacious power.

In the Trace Gate (*jiaomen*), the provisional is revealed and the provisional is severed, while real faith is engendered; in the Origin Gate (*benmen*), the distant is revealed and the near is severed, while far-reaching faith is engendered.
Therefore, the severing of doubt and the engendering of faith constitute the function of this sutra. It is the unsurpassed *amṛta* (nectar) of *sarpirmaṇḍa*.
Regarding the "characteristics of the teaching" (*jiao-xiang*): "teaching" refers to the words spoken by the Sage for those below;
"characteristics" refer to the discernment of similarities and differences. This sutra is pure and perfect, differing from partial and inferior teachings.

It is likened to the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter), which differs from the flavors of milk, curd, and fresh or processed butter; therefore, the unsurpassed *amṛta* is taken as the characteristic of the teaching of this sutra.
However, these five layers of profound meaning are all the essential tenets elucidated within the sutra;

the Patriarch pre-emptively took them to explain the title because he wished for those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it to be able to comprehend the great purport of the entire sutra through the title alone.
Preface to the Propagation of the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma.
Regarding the five characters of the title, they are explained as before. "Propagation" (*hongchuan*) means to broaden and expand;

"to propagate" means to transmit and circulate. "Preface" (*xu*) refers to sequence. The *Erya* states: "The walls on the east and west are called *xu*," with the commentary noting: [the term denotes the boundary between inner and outer spaces].
Thus, the distinction between the internal and external is made: by observing the walls, one distinguishes the interior and exterior of a residence;

by examining the preface, one comes to understand the origins and significance of this sutra. The Vinaya Master’s composition of this preface was intended to ensure that the great principles of this sutra would be widely disseminated to future generations, transmitted from one to another without interruption.
Narrated by Shi Daoxuan of Zhongnan Mountain.
The name Zhongnan Mountain is derived from its distance of eighty *li* from Chang’an, located in Wugong County of Fufeng. To the east it adjoins Mount Li and Mount Taibai;
to the west it connects with Mount Taibai and the Longshan range. Because the mountain’s northern extension culminates toward the south, it is so named.
The *Zhongnan Guanzhong Ji* states: "Zhongnan" is also called "Zhongnan" (Central South), for it lies in the center of the heavens and to the south of the capital;
thus it is called Zhongnan. Regarding "Śākya," the Sanskrit term is fully rendered as Śākya, which in this [Chinese] context means "Capable Benevolence" (*Néngrén*);
it is the clan name of the Buddha. Therefore, all who renounce the world to join the Buddha take "Śākya" as their surname. The *Āgama Sūtra* states: "Four..."

Just as rivers entering the sea all share the same salty taste, so too do those of the four castes who leave the household life all come to be called Śākyas; this is what is meant. The Vinaya Master’s name was Daoxuan;
he was born into the Qian family of Jingzhao. His father was the Minister of Personnel (Lishi Shangshu).

His mother dreamed that a lunar disc pierced her womb before she conceived, and she further dreamed of a Brahman monk who said to her, "The one you carry is the Vinaya Master You of Liang. Upon [waking],...

The Master Chang Shiyen (styled Yunkong), at the age of twenty, left the household life and shaved his head; he then relied upon his preceptor to receive full ordination and further studied the Vinaya.
In the seventh year of the Wude era of the Tang Gaozu (the Jiashen year), he moved his residence to the Zhuma Aranya on Mount Zhongnan, where he composed the *Xingshichao*.
He frequently practiced the Pratyutpanna Samādhi, conducting it in a total of twenty sessions over time.
He was constantly moved by the fact that devas and humans would bring him food and serve as his attendants.

Later, while practicing the Way at Ximing Monastery, he stumbled and fell against the steps during the middle of the night. A youth in armor and helmet appeared to protect him. The Vinaya Master asked, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am Zhang Qiong, a prince of the Baxia Heaven. Because of your virtue in the precepts, Master, I have come to provide you with protection."

He then presented the Buddha’s tooth relic to his master; the master carried it in his hands at night while practicing the Way and concealed it in an underground pit during the day, with only his disciple Wen Gang knowing of it.
He also transmitted to him the formula for compounding medicinal elixirs, which is the present-day Tianwang Buchin Wan (Tianwang Supplementing the Heart Pill).
When the master questioned him regarding events from when the World-Honored One was in the world until after his parinirvāṇa, Liangqiong recounted them one by one in detail.

Question: Regarding the *Sui lu ji wei gan tian shi ying zhuan* (One Scroll on the Record of Following the Collection to Invoke the Response of Celestial Attendants), on the third day of the tenth month in the winter of the second year of the Qiánfēng era of Emperor Gāozōng (the Dīngmǎo year), the Master entered nirvana.
When the assembly heard that celestial beings and humans had spoken with one voice, requesting the Master to return to Maitreya’s Inner Court, Emperor Mùzōng praised him, saying:
"In each generation there are awakened beings who act as the Tathāgata’s envoys; dragons and ghosts submit to them, and they are received by Heaven."

His reputation spread throughout the Five Heavens as people served him, and his fame reached ten thousand *li* as he traveled afar. When the golden crow fell in the west, the Buddha-sun rose in the east.
I prostrate myself in refuge at the feet of the founder of the Vinaya school, whose posthumous title during the Yizong era was Chengzhao.

"Shu" refers to one who transmits; such a person is called a worthy (*xian*). "Zuo" refers to one who creates; such a person is called a sage (*sheng*). As the Confucian classics state: "I transmit but do not create. This is the definition of a Vinaya Master.
It is called a "narration" (shu) because it is spoken with self-effacement.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the comprehensive essence of all Buddhas' descent of their numinous spirit.

"Comprehensive" (tong)—pronounced as in the rhyme of "zong"—means to unify; "descent of the numinous" (jiangling) is equivalent to the descent of the spirit; and "essence" (chi) refers to the ultimate goal. All Buddhas [descend] from Tuṣita...
The fundamental intent behind the descent of their spirits and appearance in the world is nothing other than to cause all sentient beings to open,
show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and to grant them the prediction of attaining Buddhahood before finally coming to rest. Since this sutra now reveals and clarifies this—
having opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for sentient beings and granted them the prediction of Buddhahood— it serves as a comprehensive record of the appearance of all Buddhas in the world.
For this reason, it is said that [this work] unifies the fundamental purpose of the descent of all Buddhas.
It was preserved and developed in the Great Xia (China) for a thousand years before being transmitted eastward to Zhendan (China) for more than three hundred years.
"Accumulation" (*skandha*) refers to gathering and binding together; "compilation" (*saṃgīti*) is the same as this. "Great Xia" (*Daxia*) is an elegant appellation for the land of Zhuguo (India).

The Tathāgata was born in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, the *jiayin* year, and entered *parinirvāṇa* on the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Mu of the Zhou dynasty, the *renshen* year.
After his *parinirvāṇa*, the disciples, including Ānanda and others, [proceeded as follows].

From the initial compilation of the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma Piṭakas of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna until the seventh year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han, approximately one thousand years had elapsed;
thus it is said, "having emerged after those thousand ages," where *líng* (age) refers to *nián* (year).

In that year, the Emperor dreamed of a golden man of great stature with a halo of light around his neck, who flew into the imperial court. At dawn, he questioned his ministers and the scholars of the Imperial Academy.
Fu Yi submitted a memorial, saying: "During the reign of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, a Buddha appeared in the Western Regions;
his form was sixteen feet tall and of golden hue. Might that which Your Majesty dreamed of not be this very being?

The *Dras* Wang Zun supported this by citing the *Yiji* (Records of Anomalies) from the *Zhou Shu*. Thereupon, the Emperor dispatched the General of the Household Cai Yin, the *Dras* Qin Jing, and others.
Eighteen men were dispatched to the Western Regions to seek the Buddha-dharma.

Cai Yin and his companions reached the kingdom of Yuezhi, a border state of India, where they encountered the two Indian monks Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna. These two, carrying Buddhist scriptures and images, came to China (Zhendan) and subsequently returned east together.
In the tenth year of Yongping, they entered the palace to present the scriptures and images; the Emperor was greatly pleased. At the Yong Gate, the Emperor...

Outside [the capital], the temples were established where Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna resided; having arrived with the scriptures carried upon white horses, they subsequently named the site Baima Temple (White Horse Temple).
In the fourteenth year of the Yongping era, the Daoist masters of the Five Peaks, Fei Shucaí and Chǔ Shànxìn, grew envious and disparaged them as being deceptive and false.
Mātanga and Ratna reported this to the Emperor, saying: "Our Buddha has appeared in the world; his Dharma cannot be destroyed by water or fire."
The Emperor requested that the practitioners of the Daoist arts verify this.

He commanded Wang Shucai and others to bring forth all their marvelous scriptures and secret manuals to be burned together with the sutras and images brought by Dharmaratna and Kālayasas. On the fifteenth day of the first month, the fire was lit;

yet the various scriptures of Dharmaratna and Kālayasas remained entirely unburnt. The practitioners bowed their heads in respectful submission, and the Emperor marveled at them even more because of this.
Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna studied the Chinese language for a long time and translated five scriptures:

the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*, the *Ten Stages*, the *Severing the Bonds*, the *Buddha’s Previous Births*, and the *Treasury of the Dharma Ocean*. From this point on, the Buddha-dharma began to flow into the Eastern Land;
therefore, it is said that the teaching was transmitted to Zhendan (China). Zhendan is also called Zhandan. Master Lin stated that the eastern direction belongs to...
Since *Zhèn* (Vibration) is the direction where the sun rises, it is called *Zhèndàn*. The *Huáyán yīnyì* (Phonology and Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) translates this as "the land of Hán.
The *Lóutàn jīng* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra) states that the area east of the Onion River (*Gonghé*) is named *Zhèndàn*, so called because the sun first rises and shines upon the eastern corner.
According to this, *Zhèndàn* is not a Sanskrit term. From the seventh year of the Yongping era of the Han dynasty...
Up to Emperor Xian, a total of one hundred and fifty-five years had passed before the territory was returned to Wei;
during the Wei dynasty, there were five emperors for a total of forty-five years before it was returned to Western Jin;

during the Western Jin, there were four emperors for a total of fifty-two years until the second year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of Eastern Jin, when Kumārajīva translated this sūtra—by that time, eighty-nine years had elapsed, totaling three hundred and four years.

Eleven years [had passed], hence it is said "over three hundred *car*"; *car* refers to a year. The *Erya* states that for the dynasties of Tang and Yu, a year was called a *car*, taking its meaning from the completion of one cycle of things and the beginning of another.
During the Yongkang era of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin, there was the Dharma-protecting Bodhisattva Zhu Fahu from Dunhuang at the Qing Gate in Chang'an.
When this sutra was first translated, it was titled *Zhengfahua* (The Lotus of the True Dharma).
Emperor Wu of the Western Jin, surnamed Sima, named Yan and styled Anshi, was the son of Emperor Zhao of the Wen dynasty.

Having received the abdication from the Wei dynasty, he ascended the imperial throne; in the year of Yiyou, he changed the era name to Taishi and established the state as Jin, with its capital at Luoyang. Therefore—
It is said that the Western Jin dynasty began with Emperor Wu, followed by Emperor Hui, then Emperor Huai, and ended with Emperor Min.

Emperor Hui’s personal name was Zhong and his courtesy name was Zhengdu; he was the second son of Emperor Wu. He ascended the throne in the fourth month of the gengxu year and changed the era name to Yongxi.
Subsequently, it was changed to Yongkang in the gengshen year, and then again to Yongchang for only one year. Chang’an was anciently called Xianyang.
During the reign of Emperor Gaozu of the Han, the name was changed to Chang’an. The Qing Gate (Qingmen) is located to the east of the city of Chang’an;

it is the place where Shao Ping once grew melons. Dunhuang is the present-day Sha-zhou Road in Gansu Province; it was the ancient land of the Flowing Sands (Liusha), within the domain of Yongzhou as described in the *Yugong* section of the *Shujing*.
During the Han dynasty, it was the commandery of Dunhuang, where the Yang Pass, the Yumen Pass, and the Wa Water were situated. [Zhú]...
Dharmarakṣa (translated as Fahu) was a native of the Yuezhi people who thoroughly mastered the arts and doctrines of thirty-six countries and was proficient in their languages.
In the second year of the Taishi era (the Bingxu year), he arrived at Yumen from India and subsequently resided in Dunhuang, where he became known in the world as the "Dunhuang Bodhisattva.
Later, he entered Chang’an and settled at the Qing Gate. (From the *Da Zhou mulu*).
It says that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was translated in the seventh year of Taikang;
however, since Taikang was actually the reign title of Emperor Wu, and the preface states it was during the reign of Emperor Hui, one should take Yongkang as the correct date.
During the Long’an era of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin dynasty, the Dharma Master Kumārajīva of Quci translated this sūtra under the Later Qin Hongshi era,
naming it the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The Eastern Jin dynasty of the Sima clan was established in Jiankang, beginning with Emperor Yuan and ending with Emperor Gong, who abdicated to the Song.

There were eleven sovereigns in total, for a combined duration of one hundred and three years. Emperor Yuan’s personal name was Rui; he was the son of Prince Jin of Langya and the great-grandson of Emperor Xuan.
At the age of fifteen, he succeeded to the title of Prince of Langya, and subsequently served as General Who Pacifies the East.

He was appointed as Protector of Jiankang during the fourth year of the Jianxing era (Bingzi) of Emperor Min of the Western Jin. By imperial decree, he acted as regent for the myriad affairs of state;
the following year, he ascended the throne as Prince and changed the era name to Jianwu. The year after that, in Wuyin, he first ascended the imperial throne and changed the era name to Daxing.
Regarding the translations of the *Kumārajīva* within the territories of Later Qin, the prefaces invariably record the events of Eastern Jin first.
This preserves the orthodox lineage. The tenth sovereign was Emperor An (An-di), whose personal name was Dezong. He was the Crown Prince of Xiaowu;
on the *bingshen* day, he succeeded Xiaowu and ascended the imperial throne. In the following year, *dingyou*, he changed the era name to Long’an, which lasted for five years.
He then changed it to Yongxing, which lasted for three years. Finally, he changed it to Yixi, which lasted for fourteen years. The ruler of Later Qin was surnamed Yao and named Chang.
His courtesy name was Jingmao, and he was a Qiang person from Chiting.

During the eighth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty (the Guiwei year), Former Qin’s Fu Jian attacked the Jin; Yao Chang was appointed as General Longxiao of the Yanzhou Governor.
Later, he was further appointed as Commandant to suppress慕容泓 (Murong Hong) and others. When Yao Chang’s army suffered a great defeat, he fled in fear toward the north bank of the Wei River.
Ma Muzhi and others incited the Qiang chieftains to lead their households—some fifty thousand families—in allegiance to Yao Chang. They enthroned him as their盟主 (overlord).
In the fourth month of the Bingxu year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, Yao Chang entered Chang’an from the Shaanxi region and ascended the throne.
He changed the era name to Jianchu and established the state title of Da Qin (Great Qin); later historians distinguished this as the Later Qin. This was Yao Chang.
He dispatched General Wu Zhong to capture Fu Jian at Wujiang; Jian’s son Fu Pi was subsequently killed by Feng Gai.

Fu Deng, Prince of Nanyang, ascended the throne in the twelfth month of the eighteenth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty (the *guisi* year). In this year, Fu Chang died, and his son Fu Xing succeeded him.
Leading his forces, he attacked the Former Qin; the Qin ruler Deng suffered a great defeat. In the following year, the *jiawu* year, Xing assumed the imperial title.
The reign title was changed to Huangchu, marking the fifth year; it was then changed again to Hongshi, corresponding to the third year of Long’an of the Jin dynasty, the Jihai year.
Quci is the name of a country identical to Kucha, located to the southwest of Yanqi.
*Śramaṇa* is translated here as "diligent cessation," meaning to diligently cultivate all forms of goodness and to cease all evils. *Kumārajīva* is translated here as "Child."

Śrīmitra was a native of Kucha. During the Former Qin dynasty, Fu Jian dispatched the General of the Light Cavalry, Lü Guang, leading seventy thousand troops to invade the Kingdom of Kucha and capture Kumārajīva.
In the seventh year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, the *Renwu* year (352 CE), Lü Guang returned with Kumārajīva to Liangzhou.
Hearing that Fu Jian had already passed away, Lü Guang subsequently seized control of Liangzhou and established himself as the King of the Three Rivers.
He ascended the throne and changed the state’s name to Dali, altering the era name to Tai’an; this was the eleventh year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty.
Upon the death of Guang, his son Shao succeeded him but was assassinated by Lü Zuan, who then established himself as Duke of Taiyuan. Lü Zuan was subsequently deposed by Lü Chao.
Later, in the third year of Hongshi of Yao Xing of the Later Qin, he dispatched an army to invade Long, who then submitted a memorial.
Lung-xing (Hui-lung) subsequently welcomed Kumārajīva to Chang’an; this was the *xin-chou* year, the fifth year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty.
In the eighth year of Hongshi, Kumārajīva translated the present sutra at Caotang Temple into seven fascicles;

this was the *bing-wu* year, the second year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty. Regarding the preface, the Vinaya Master stated that the "Long’an years" refers to the time when Kumārajīva first arrived.
The year "Cháng'ān" (Chang'an) is not the year in which Kumārajīva translated this sutra. The *Fahua wenju* states:
"Kumārajīva finished translating the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* at the Xiaoyao Garden in Chang'an on the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the fifth year of the Hongshi era of the Later Qin;
then, in the summer of the eighth year, he translated this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at Cūtang Monastery."

In his youth, Kumārajīva could recite thirty-two thousand words from the *Lotus Sūtra* daily. Following his mother, he left the household life and traveled extensively throughout the Western Regions, where he mastered a vast array of scriptures.

He was particularly adept at the Mahāyāna teachings. During his time in Kucha, whenever the kings gathered for assemblies, they would invariably invite the Master to preach the Dharma, listening with profound reverence as they knelt and prostrated themselves.
Later, while residing in the kingdom of Qin, he extensively expounded upon the sūtras and śāstras; the following is a record of what he translated.
He produced three hundred and eighty fascicles. The ruler of Qin treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher, honoring him with exceptional favor.
On the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the fifteenth year of Hongshi, he entered nirvana at the age of seventy;
this was the ninth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, the *guichou* year.
The version translated later by the Śramaṇa from North India, Jñānagupta, at Daixingshan Monastery during the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, bears the same title, *Miaofa* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka).
Emperor Gaozu Wen of the Sui, surnamed Yang and named Jian, was a native of Huayin in Hongnong; he was a descendant of Yang Zhen, the Grand Marshal of the Han dynasty.
The fourteenth-generation descendant, Yuwen Jin, served the Wei dynasty and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhou. His son, Jue, received the abdication of Wei, and the state name became Zhou.
Jian, the father of Zhong, had previously served the Zhou dynasty with merit and held the office of Grand Tutor (Taifu) and the title of Duke of Sui;

Jian inherited this fief. In the thirteenth year of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty, the year of Xinchou, Jian received the abdication of Zhou and established his capital at Chang'an. The state name was Zhou.
The dynasty was named Sui, spanning three reigns from Emperor Wen to Emperor Gong for a total of thirty-seven years;
it is referred to here by its dynastic name as "the House of Sui. "Renshou" was the era name of Emperor Wen. Regarding its etymology:
the Indic term has been subject to much dispute and confusion. Formerly it was called Shendu, or alternatively Xiandou; however, following the correct phonetics, it should be rendered as India.
It is called "Cloud-Moon Canopy" because the sages and saints of that land succeed one another in guiding ordinary beings and governing all things, just as the moon shines down upon them.
The territory of the five Indias spans over ninety thousand *li*; what is here called Northern India is one of the five kingdoms of India.
As for the two Dharma Masters, Jñānagupta and [Śīladhara], the name Jñāna is fully transcribed as...
Jñānagupta (translated as Zhìdé, "Virtue of Resolve") was a person from Northern India of the Kṣatriya caste;
he traveled abroad to propagate the teachings and arrived at this realm. Dharmagupta (fully named Damo Jueduo, translated as Fàmì, "Dharma-Secret") was a person from Southern India.
The omission of his preface indicates it is missing. According to the preface to the *Supplemented Sūtra*, it states: "The first year of Renshòu of the Great Sui."

In the year of Xinyou, the śramaṇa Shangxing of Puyao Monastery invited the two Dharma Masters Jñānagupta and Dharmagupta to Daixingshan Monastery to retranslate this sūtra in eight fascicles, titled the *Addition-Text Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Thus, we know that Jñāna and Gupta were two individuals. This is recorded in Master Sheng’s catalogue.
Regarding the term "added sections" (*tiānpǐn*): this refers to five instances where verses were added, combined, or rearranged within the two translations of the Jin and Qin periods.

First, the addition of the concluding verses of the *Pumen pin* (Universal Gate Chapter) after the Jin and Qin versions; second, the supplementation of the full text of the *Rìguāng yù* (Sunlight Simile) after the Qin version’s *Yàowáng pin* (Medicine King Chapter);
third, the merging of the *Tiānshòu pin* (Devadatta Chapter) into the *Bǎotǎ pin* (Treasure Stupa Chapter); and fourth... [the fourth point].

The *Zhūlèi pǐn* (Chapter on Entrustment) has been moved to follow the *Púxián pǐn* (Chapter on Samantabhadra), and the *Wǔhuí tuóluóní pǐn* (Chapter on the Fivefold Dhāraṇī) has been moved to follow the *Shénlì pǐn* (Chapter on Supernatural Powers).

Furthermore, the *Fǎhuá guǐyí* (Ritual Procedures for the Lotus Sutra) translated by Amoghavajra of the Tang dynasty is entirely identical to these alterations made to the *Tiānpǐn fǎhuá jīng* (Expanded Version of the Lotus Sutra);
this greatly deviates from Master Kumārajīva’s original arrangement of the chapter sequence.
Regarding the three scriptures that are repetitive in their textual structure and present their themes alternately, those esteemed by the world at the time all propagated the Qin translations.

Because one scripture has three translations, they are said to be "repetitive" (*chóngtà*); their phrasing and purport are presented interchangeably, such as the "Ten Suchnesses," which are absent in the Jin translation but present in the Qin translation.
Furthermore, regarding the latter half of the chapter on the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs in the Jin [translation]...

What exists in the two translations from the Sui dynasty but is absent from the translation of the Qin dynasty, and what is placed in the twenty-second fascicle in the Qin translation but is moved to the end of the volume in the Sui translation—thus it is said that "the textual principles are presented interchangeably. "Zong" (宗) means honored;

"shang" (尚) means esteemed as supreme. Although this sutra underwent three translations, that which has been honored and esteemed throughout antiquity and the present is transmitted solely through the Master Shi (Kumārajīva).
Regarding the texts translated herein:
as for the remaining chapters, individual verses, and other such works, they are not absent; their full details are provided in the preface and catalog, and thus are not recounted here.
Beyond these three translations, as stated in the *Nanyue Yinyi* (Explanations of Terms), Dharmamati [translated] during the Yongping era of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty.
One fascicle of the *Devadatta-parivarta-sūtra* was translated [by Dharmarakṣa], and one fascicle of the *Samantamukha-parivarta-sūtra* was translated by Jīmūtavāhana during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
As this master’s name and meaning are not recorded [in the standard catalogues] and his portions differ from others, they are called "separate chapters" (*zhīpǐn*).
Furthermore, Jñānagupta translated the *Samantamukha-parivarta* again at Longyuan Monastery in Yizhou, Xichuan.
The verses consist of one fascicle; therefore, they are called "Separate Verses" (*bieji*).

Although the verses of such chapters differ in their structural divisions, each possesses its own source and tradition, as fully recorded in the prefaces and chronicles of those respective sutras; thus, I shall not describe them here.

Furthermore, "flow" (*liu*) refers to a category or type; for instance, when items are grouped according to their common characteristics and designated as a "chapter" (*pin*), this is what is meant. [This concludes] the chronological account.
The character "xiàng" (象) is also interchangeable with "lì" (歷). Another interpretation is that it means "redundant" (*yáo*), where "redundant" carries the sense of "abundant.
This implies that within the original text of the Qin [translation], there were already numerous branches and distinct categories of verses;

the origins and lineages of these chapters and verses are fully detailed within each respective chapter and verse, as can be seen from the prefaces contained therein. Therefore, they are not [included here].

In my private opinion, while it is certainly true that the previous interpretation identifies only the *Geya* (repeated verses) of the "Universal Gate" chapter as the "separate verses," if one examines the meaning of the text closely, it seems that the intent does not merely refer to the separately translated *Dharmarakṣa* version of the "Universal Gate" and its two chapters as being auxiliary;
rather, it refers to all the chapters within this single sutra as being auxiliary. Furthermore, the Vinaya Master composed...
The Preface: To establish the correct [text], how could the edition from the Qin dynasty have indiscriminately included works translated by others? Let the reader examine this carefully.

Indeed, as for the descent of spiritual power upon the Sacred Mountain, it could not have been brought about through transformation were it not for a Great Sage; and as for the reach of such transformative influence, it is never apart from past conditions.
There is no need to guide the mind further.

Regarding the phrase "the numinous mountain descends its spirit," this is borrowed from the Confucian classics, specifically the intent of the passage "The mountain has descended its spirit, giving birth to Shen and Fu.
It means that those who are transformed by the numinous mountain all possess the refinement of heroic spirits and thus descend into birth.
Were it not for our Buddha, the Great Sage, whose supernatural powers cause awe and whose wisdom and eloquence proclaim the truth, by what means could they be guided and delivered?
This statement refers to the suitability [of the teaching] to the capacity [of the listener]. "Appropriateness" (*shì*) refers to that which is suited to the scope of the transformation;
it is also termed "suitability. This means that although the Buddha is a Great Sage, he cannot transform those who lack the karmic affinity, as was the case at Vulture Peak.

Those who were to be converted had all, in the past during the era of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, planted the seeds of the One Vehicle while listening to the Prince’s re-exposition of the Lotus Sutra.
Although they subsequently regressed from the Great Vehicle and were gradually disciplined over time, it is only now that they have attained wondrous awakening.
Were it not for the seeds of past affinity, there would have been no cause for their minds to be opened and guided.
These words mean that the capacity of the recipient corresponds to the response of the teacher.

Thus, when the Immortal Garden (Lumbinī) was completed, the capacities were distinguished as Great and Small; when the Golden River (the Nirvāṇa Sūtra) delivered its final charge, the teachings differed according to the categories of Half and Full.
Is this not because the teaching is bestowed in accordance with the timing of the vehicle, such that there is no need to scrutinize its sublime assembly?

In Sanskrit, it is called Vārāṇasī; formerly it was called Pārāṇa. It is translated as "City Encircled by Rivers," or because it was inhabited by a herd of deer, it is also named "Deer Park" (Mṛgadāva);
because it was the dwelling place of ancient seers, it is also named "Seers' Park" (Ṛṣivadana).
Regarding its completion: after the Tathāgata had practiced austerities for six years, he attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree.

Once the Buddha had attained enlightenment, he necessarily taught the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings. Since these capacities vary—being either sharp or dull—the teachings differ as Great or Small.
This is illustrated by the fact that at the beginning, the *Avataṃsaka* was separated from the Deer Park, while the Small [Vehicle] was separated from the Great Vaipulya;
yet both Great and Small were heard together. These two phrases state that the response must accord with the capacity. In the Sanskrit language, this is *śrāvakavati*.
The "River" (河) here is translated as the Golden River (金河), which is the place where Jambūnada gold is produced. On the riverbank stands a Śāla grove outside the city of Kuśinagara.

Regarding the term "final instructions" (顧命), the Confucian classic *Shangshu* contains a chapter titled "Guming" (*Guming pian*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary states: "Because one issues instructions while facing death, it is called 'gu' (to look back);
'gu' signifies the intention of one who is about to depart. As the Buddha was on the verge of entering parinirvāṇa, he bestowed [these instructions].
The sūtras that teach the Nirvāṇa are like the *Ruling Testament* (*Gulim*) composed by King Cheng when he was about to pass away.

The teaching of the four vehicles in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* corresponds to the Vaipulya Piṭaka; the "half-syllable" teachings consist of the *Tong* (Shared), *Bie* (Distinct), and *Yuan* (Perfect) [teachings], while the "full-syllable" teachings consist of the *Yuan* alone.
Therefore, it is said: "The paths differ according to the categories of half and full. These two phrases refer to the capacities [of sentient beings].
Regarding the sequence in which the teaching is received— first mentioning the Immortal Garden (Sandalwood Grove) and later the Golden River (Nairañjanā)—
this is because the beginning and end of a single transformation are cited to encompass the intermediate periods of the Vaipulya and Prajñā teachings.

Thus, the summary states that "the teaching covers the vehicles and the times," just as the *Avataṃsaka* was taught for those of great capacity during its specific time and vehicle, while at the Deer Park, the complete *Sūtra* teachings were expounded.
When beings of small capacity were to be guided, he taught the Tripitaka;
when beings of both small and large capacities were to be guided, he taught the four teachings of the Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect. Even in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it was likewise so.

Although these four periods of teaching were established to accommodate various capacities, if one speaks in terms of their respective scriptural divisions (*piṭaka*), they all belong to the provisional (*upāya*) and are insufficient [as ultimate truth].
Upon examining the facts, it is clear that the Great Assembly of the Lotus Sūtra discusses nothing but the single reality;

the merit of the Lotus Sūtra is supreme within this entire transformation, its principles surpassing those of all other scriptures. This is already evident from the words of the foremost Vinaya Master, who stated that it is "the most excellent.
These words are sufficient as evidence.

Thus we know that the five thousand who withdrew from their seats were those whose pride had increased, while the five hundred who received predictions of enlightenment were those who together honored the traces of the secret transformation.

At the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, the Tathāgata has already praised the two wisdoms of all Buddhas— the provisional and the ultimate— as being profoundly deep, immeasurable, and difficult to fathom.
When Śāriputra resolved his doubts and presented his request, and the Tathāgata granted permission to preach, five thousand people rose from their seats and departed.
The Tathāgata then rebuked them, saying, "The roots of these people's offenses are deep and heavy, and they are possessed of overweening pride.
He further remarked that it would be well for them to withdraw. Although this was a rebuke of others, its underlying intent was to spur them toward progress.
Among those present, there were those with overweening pride who did not feel the inclination to withdraw from their seats.
Pūrṇa and the other five hundred disciples were originally bodhisattvas of profound rank; they now secretly conceal their true status while outwardly manifesting the traces of śrāvakas.
Upon reaching the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, they were again granted the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood. This was because their secret manifestation was honored as an aid to the Buddha.
The traces of his transformative activities are sublime; this signifies the principle that while the traces are high, the foundation remains below.
Thus, he emitted light and manifested auspicious omens to reveal the source of the teachings for those who request them.

In the "Introduction Chapter," it is stated that after the Tathāgata had preached the *Ananta-artha-sūtra*, he entered meditative concentration and emitted light from the white tuft between his brows, fully manifesting the six auspicious omens.
Consequently, Maitreya conceived doubts and requested Mañjuśrī to provide a definitive answer.
Thus, we know that the emission of light and the manifestation of auspicious signs constitute the fundamental source for initiating inquiries and expounding the teachings.
Emerging from meditative absorption, he extols his virtues and elucidates the grand strategy of the Buddha’s wisdom.
In the "Expedient Means" chapter, the Tathāgata rises calmly from samādhi and praises the virtuous intent of the two kinds of wisdom—provisional and ultimate—of all Buddhas;
he causes sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, which is the Buddha’s wisdom.
Only then will the grand and far-reaching strategies be fully realized. The two types of wisdom and the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are all merely different names for the Buddha-wisdom.
The dilapidated house is the gateway through which one enters the great system of the Dharma.
In the "Parable Chapter," at the outset, the three carts are used to entice the children out of the burning house; subsequently, great carts are bestowed equally upon them.

This serves as a metaphor for how, at the Deer Park, the Buddha initially provided provisional teachings on the Truths, the Causal Links, and the Path for the three vehicles of the Śrāvakas and others, leading them to practice and escape the triple world.
Upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he opened up these provisional means to reveal the ultimate reality, speaking only of the One Vehicle.
Because the Dharma of the One Vehicle’s perfect reality causes all beings to open, realize, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgata first guides sentient beings by means of the Three Vehicles, and subsequently delivers them solely by means of the Great Vehicle.
This is like a time when the empire is in great order: the written characters are unified, the carriage ruts follow the same tracks, and the laws are harmonized into a single circle.
The text teaching the single reality is concise, yet its metaphors are identical to those of the Great Vehicle; how could it be otherwise?

The parable of the dilapidated burning house is precisely the teaching that leads from the Small Vehicle toward the Great; therefore, it is said that this text provides a path for universal entry into the Great Vehicle.
The "Parable of the Phantom City" preserves the continuity of past causes so that they do not fall into oblivion.
A "phantom city" (*nirmita-pura*) is something non-existent that suddenly acquires a name; it is called a "city" because it prevents wrongdoing and wards off enemies.

It serves as a metaphor for the emptiness and *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), which prevents the wrongs of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and wards off the enemy of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). This is the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter.
At first, for the sake of the weary multitude, he manifested a city as a place of rest, and only then led them to the place of jewels;
this is like how, in the past, when the Tathāgata was a prince, he planted the seeds of the Mahāyāna for them, yet they later regressed from the Great Vehicle toward the Small.

Just as they stopped at the manifested city, now that they have reached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he again preaches the Great Vehicle and bestows upon them the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
To become a Buddha is surely not unlike the parable of the illusory city; it is the non-forgetting of the conditions from former lives that guide one forward.
The "tied jewel" illustrates that the rational nature is ever-present.
In the "Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples," after Cunda and the others had received their prophecies, they repented and reproached themselves.
They then used the metaphor of the tied jewel to express their realization; the jewel is likened to the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is the causal seed for the Mahāyāna.

This is because, in the past during the era of the Buddha Mahāvairocana (Great Pervasive), the Buddha had previously taught them the Great Dharma and caused them to resolve their minds [for enlightenment].
The seeds of the One Vehicle have been neglected and forgotten for many kalpas; unaware and unconscious of them, one only now realizes they were never lost upon receiving this prediction.
The rational nature [of these seeds] is ever-present, just as when a person stays at the house of a close friend and the friend ties a jewel inside their garment;
though the person falls into a drunken sleep and remains unaware, they immediately recognize it when the friend points it out to them later.
The jewel within the garment not being lost serves as a metaphor for the eternal presence of the fundamental nature (li-xing).
The act of digging a well illustrates the manifold methods for awakening.

In the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," the Buddha said: "For example, suppose there is a person who, parched with thirst, requires water; he digs into the high plateau and still sees [the signs of it]..."

When one encounters dry soil, one knows that water is still far off; yet by applying effort without ceasing, one eventually encounters moist soil, and with a mind of certainty, one knows that water must be near.
This serves as a metaphor for those, whether householders or renunciants, who have not yet heard, understood, contemplated, or practiced this sutra:
such persons are still far from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. However, if they do hear, understand, contemplate, and practice it...
One must know that this sutra indicates that such a person has drawn near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;

it is only through the Buddha’s various skillful means (*upāya*) of teaching and transformation that they finally attain awakening and entry. Therefore, it is said that there are manifold methods for "showing" and "awakening."
The phrasing and meaning are perfectly clear, yet the metaphors presented are exceedingly profound.

The literary expressions and underlying principles correspond exactly; when further elaborated through the various analogies mentioned above, the purport of this single sutra is uniquely subtle and far-reaching.
Were it not for Great Compassion that universally rescues those submerged in the stagnant currents, and a singular heart of pity that saves those whose natures have become deluded;
were it not for the Tathāgata’s arising, sentient beings would remain mired in the various realms of existence, drowning in the river of craving. It is for such as these that he appears.
With great compassion, you extensively provide a ferry for salvation; how could you otherwise uproot the suffering of birth and death and cause them to attain the bliss of Nirvana?
Furthermore, sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance, mired in delusion and confusion;
were it not for the Tathāgata’s singular and ultimate heart of pity, how could you rescue them from the darkness of their stupor and restore them to their original nature?
This is its brilliance.
From the Han to the Tang dynasties, spanning over six hundred years, among the total of more than four thousand fascicles of all the scriptures that have been received and upheld,
none surpasses this sūtra.

From the tenth year of the Yongping era of the Han dynasty, when Buddhism first began to flow into the Eastern Land, until the time of Emperor Gaozu of the Tang, three hundred and fifty-two years had passed during the Eastern Jin;
furthermore, fifty-nine years under the Song; twenty-three years under the Qi; fifty-five years under the Liang;
thirty-three years under the Chen; and thirty-seven years under the Sui. Then, from the reign of Tang Gaozu—
In the second year of the Qiánfēng era of Emperor Gāozōng, the Vinaya Master entered nirvana; thus, including his fifty years of life, the total duration was six hundred and nine years.
Hence it is said that "more than six hundred years" have passed. However, it remains unexamined at what specific year during the Táng dynasty the Vinaya Master composed this preface.
Within these more than six hundred years, although the catalogs of the various sūtras translated in their entirety number four thousand, [the text continues].
Among the many thousands of fascicles that have been widely upheld throughout past and present, none surpasses the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* translated by Master Kumārajīva.

It is surely because the capacities of beings and the teachings have met in resonance, and because it is a lingering trace of the wisdom of the Victorious One (Mañjuśrī), that upon hearing it, one feels profound reverence, as if encountering the majesty of King Bimbisāra himself.
Regarding the remaining achievements:

"The capacity and the teaching strike one another" means that "capacity" (*ji*) refers to the capacity of those to be transformed, while "teaching" (*jiao*) refers to the teaching that can transform them; "striking" (*kou*) signifies the act of impact.

This means that the capacity must receive the teaching, and the teaching must reach the capacity; thus, the capacity and the teaching mutually strike and move one another. Furthermore, as for receiving...

The capacities of those to be taught were all alike; having together planted the seeds of the One Vehicle under the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū in the past, those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom had already attained the Way during the initial, middle, and final periods of his teaching.

As for those of duller faculties who regressed from the Great Vehicle during the intermediate period, the Buddha has gradually guided and sustained them until now, in this royal city, where they too have finally attained the Way. Hereafter, [the same shall apply].
Those who receive and uphold this sutra were likely not the most dull-witted among those who planted seeds in the past;
compared to the many of former times, they are as few as a stray mote of dust. Thus it is said that they are like the "stray motes of the Victorious in Wisdom.
Furthermore, those who hear this sutra and believe and revere it without doubt are precisely those whom the Buddha King Majestic Sound did not slight.
This is because he sought to utilize the remaining merit from his prior cultivation of the Mahāyāna conditions and seeds.
He has therefore briefly composed a preface at the beginning of this scripture to synthesize its contents.
"Briefly" (*zhé*) means exclusively; "synthesizing" (*zōng*) refers to one who holds the threads and weaves them into a fabric—here, the Vinaya Master who is exclusively devoted to this scripture.
I have composed this preface at the outset to synthesize the great purport of the entire sutra,

so that those who recite and uphold it may know where the meaning and intent converge and how the Dharma and its metaphors mutually clarify one another— just as a loom and thread hold the silk and weave the cloth,
ensuring that everything is orderly and systematic without confusion.

May I thereby quickly purify the six sense faculties, look up to the auspicious assembly of the Compassionate Honored One, swiftly accomplish the four virtues, and hasten toward the profound path to the Land of Bliss.
This means that those who recite and uphold this scripture, provided they understand its great purpose, should follow it in every thought through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.
