By establishing practice based on understanding, one naturally attains the purification of the six sense faculties; thus, one is able to see the Buddha as ever-present at Mount Grdhrakūṭa.

This was like the Great Master Zhiyi of the Sui dynasty, who, while practicing the *Lotus Samādhi* and reciting the sutra until reaching the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," suddenly attained great enlightenment and beheld Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Because the first assembly remains solemnly undispersed, the Sūtra states:

"If there are those with profound resolve and faith-understanding, they shall see the Buddha always present on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa," or it is said that the Compassionate Honored One refers to Maitreya. The *Samantabhadra-ādhyeṣaṇā-parivarta* says:
"If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and understand its meaning and purport... and so on, up to: "...they shall immediately go to Tuṣita Heaven above."

Regarding the two teachings spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva, both lead to the swift accomplishment of the four virtues, namely: permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*).
That which does not shift or change is called "permanence"; that which is free from the suffering of the two deaths is called "bliss"; that which possesses the eight great masteries is called "self";
and that in which the three delusions are completely exhausted is called "purity. Once these four virtues are accomplished, one will certainly attain rebirth [in the Pure Land].
The *Gujing* (Ancient Scripture) on the Land of Ultimate Bliss states:
"If one practices as taught, at the end of life here, one will immediately proceed toward the dwelling place of Amitābha Buddha, surrounded by a multitude of great bodhisattvas;
this is the path (*dao*). 'Path' carries the meaning of 'that which enables passage,' signifying that by means of this profound and wondrous path, one is able to pass through to the Pure Land."
It is for the sake of the state. To "promote extensively" (弘贊) means without limit; to "bequeath forever" (永貽) means to hand down to posterity.

Such is the intent of the Vinaya Master in composing this preface: namely, that he wishes to assist and promote this sutra so that it may endure forever. "Assist" (贊助) means to support; "bequeath" (貽) means to leave as a legacy. The Vinaya Master’s purpose in writing the preface is, in essence, to provide such assistance to this scripture and ensure its eternal transmission.
This is left for future generations in the hope that it may be transmitted and circulated endlessly and without limit. Someone asked:

"Regarding the two gates of the *Lotus Sūtra*—the provisional (*jia*) and the real (*ben*)—why did the Vinaya Master [Zhiyi] only introduce the provisional and not speak of the real? Now, I shall answer:

If one knows that the provisional is manifested from the real, then one also knows that the real is revealed through the provisional. Therefore, the Venerable Jingxi [Zhanran] said: "If one understands the wondrousness of the provisional..."
The Fundamental is wondrous and not distant; though the fundamental and the manifested differ, they are inconceivably one.
*The Preface to the Propagation of the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma*, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Preface to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter One: The Introduction.
The meaning of "introduction" (*nidāna*) has three aspects: sequence, cause, and narration. These five factors—beginning with "Thus" (*evam*)—are placed at the head of the sutra.
The "Preface" (序) serves as the introductory sequence that initiates the manifestation of the six auspicious omens through the emission of light;
it is the preface that poses questions and answers to resolve doubts, acting as a prologue to the main exposition. Because it possesses these three meanings, it is called the "Preface Chapter" (序品).

The Sanskrit term for "chapter" is *varga*, which is translated here as "pin" (品). A "pin" is so named because items of similar meaning and category are gathered together within a single section. Only...

The "Chapter on the Former Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva" is designated as the first because it was personally proclaimed by the Buddha, whereas other chapters were either arranged by the compilers or added by the translators;
thus, it is called the first. Furthermore, there are both general and specific prefaces.
From the words "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) up to "sat down to one side" constitutes the general preface, as this formula appears at the beginning of all sutras.

Because of these five matters, from the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One" until the end of the chapter constitutes the separate introduction (*pṛthag-nidāna*), as this is a single sutra with a separate introduction.
Next, the explanation of the sutra text has two parts: first, the Trace [Teaching], and second, the Fundamental [Teaching].

Regarding the *Fahua Wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra), the ancestral master Zhiyi of Tiantai said: "I divide the text into three parts: the first chapter is the Introduction; the [subsequent] chapters are the Expedient Means (*upāya*)."
The section on the "Analysis of Merits" concludes with nineteen lines of verse; these constitute fifteen chapters and a half, titled the "Proper [Section]" (*zhèng*).
Following the verses, up to the end of the sutra, there are eleven chapters and a half, titled the "Circulation" (*liútōng*). Furthermore, when divided according to time, there are two parts:

from the Preface to the "Peaceful Conduct" (*Ān-lè-xíng*), comprising fourteen chapters, which reveals the provisional through the manifesting of the real based on the traces (*jì*); from the "Emergence from the Earth" (*Yǒngchū*) to the end of the sutra constitutes the second part.

The four chapters consist of the exposition of the provisional to reveal the real based on the fundamental [teaching], with the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination for both the original and the trace aspects respectively. The first chapter serves as the introduction;

the section from the end of the "Expedient Means" chapter to the "Bestowal of Prophecy upon Learners and Non-learners" constitutes the main body; the section from the end of the "Dharma Master" chapter to the "Peaceful Practices" constitutes the dissemination;
and the section from the end of the "Emergence" chapter to where Maitreya has already asked about this matter constitutes the introduction to the Buddha’s present response, comprising half a chapter.
From the passage "The Buddha addressed Ajita" down to the nineteenth verse of the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit," this section is titled the "Correct [Teaching].

From here until the end of the sutra constitutes the "Circulation. Now, I shall record the analysis of the text from the preceding three sections. First, regarding the Trace Gate (Ji-men), there are three parts;
the first is the first chapter, the Introductory Section (Xufen). Second, within that, the Common Preface (Tongxu) has six parts; the first is the essence of the Dharma heard.
"Thus, thus.
This phrase raises the essence of the Dharma as it was heard. "Thus" (yathā) means not different; "thus" (tathā) means non-erroneous.
Because it is "thus" with respect to the three truths, it is called "thus, thus" (evam). If explained according to the teachings, the various sūtras are not uniform in their "thusness" (yathā).

This is also different from the Buddha’s clarification that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) possesses words while ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is without words. Ānanda transmitted the words of the Buddha’s conventional truth;
because these do not differ from what the Buddha spoke, they are called "Thus" (*tathā*). Because one realizes the principle of ultimate truth through these conventional words, it is called "This.
Thus, the beginning of the Tripiṭaka sūtras is "Thus have I heard. The Buddha’s clarification is that form itself is [emptiness].

Emptiness-emptiness is precisely form; form and emptiness are empty, and form and emptiness are non-dual and without distinction. That emptiness and form are not different is the suchness (tathatā); that reality is present within phenomena is the truth.

Ānanda transmits the Buddha’s words of definitive expression (*vyañjana*), which are not different from suchness; that the definitive expression is identical to the definitive meaning (*artha*) is the truth.
This is the "Thus" at the beginning of the sutra according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). The Buddha clarifies birth and death.
"There is this nirvana; there is this non-arising; there is exiting saṃsāra; there is entering nirvana; there is neither exiting nor entering nirvana.
This middle way—Ānanda, transmitting this "exiting existence, entering non-existence, exiting non-existence, entering the middle"—is no different from what the Buddha taught.
It is like proceeding from the shallow to the deep, where everything is affirmed as "this"; such is the beginning of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao).

Furthermore, the Buddha clarifies that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa*, which is also the Middle Way, the true nature of the *dharmadhātu*, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) pervading all places;
there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma. Ānanda transmitted this, and it is no different from what the Buddha taught;
therefore, it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*). Because it is unmoving, it is called "This Text. It accords with principle and is the ultimate accomplishment. This then—
The "Thus" at the beginning of a sutra in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is precisely the "Thus" of the present sutra. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
When the Buddha was about to enter nirvana, Ānanda asked the Buddha what words should be placed at the beginning of all sutras. The Buddha said: "One should say: 'Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in such-and-such a region, in such-and-such a country, together with such-and-such a great assembly. This is the general introduction (tongxu)."

It is also called the "Preface Refuting the Heterodox," because it refutes the *āgama* of the non-Buddhists; it is also called the "Preface of Verified Faith," because it is intended to ensure that those who hear it have no doubts.
△ Second, the person capable of upholding [the teaching].
"I have heard.
"I have heard" means that Ānanda heard such a Dharma from the Buddha. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Ānanda recounted the Buddha’s final instructions to the assembly; because he personally received them without error, it is said, 'I have heard. △ Third: The Hearing.
"Maintaining harmony at one time.
"At one time" means that hearing and maintaining [the teaching] are in harmony and not at different times; it also refers to the unification of the causes and conditions of response and resonance.
It is the time. △ Fourth, hearing from the Buddha at the proper time.
"Buddha" is a Sanskrit term; *buddha* here means "the Knower. He is the knower of the past, present, and future, as well as of sentient beings and non-sentient beings.
He is called Buddha because he has awakened to all phenomena, such as birth, number, permanence, and impermanence. Furthermore, "the Awakened One" (Jue-zhe) carries three meanings:
first, self-awakening, which is the realization that one's own nature is truly eternal and the understanding that delusions are empty and false;

second, awakening others, which is the exercise of unconditional compassion to deliver the realm of sentient beings; and third, the perfection of awakening-practice, which is therefore termed "Sublime Awakening" (Miaojue). Thus it is named.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The nature of all phenomena is neither born nor extinguished. How marvelous!

The Great Teacher has awakened by himself and is able to awaken others. If this is explained according to the teachings (*śāsana*), it means that beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment, he realized the awakening of the mundane and the supramundane.

Awakening to the mundane refers to suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*); awakening to the supramundane refers to the path and its cessation (*mārga-nirodha*). Furthermore, he is able to awaken others as well.

When the fourteen minds have exhausted both the active afflictions and their latent tendencies, and he manifests a body sixteen feet tall to preach the Dharma of the Truths, the Causal Links, and the Degrees for those of the Three Vehicles, this is the Buddha of the Tripitaka Teaching.

When he manifests a body that combines the inferior and superior responses, and under the tree, through a single moment of mental correspondence, severs the remaining residual habits, this is the Buddha of the Shared Teaching.
When he manifests solely the sublime and extraordinary marks while seated upon a lotus pedestal, [this is the Buddha of the Distinct Teaching].

The Buddha who assumes office is the Buddha of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-bhūmi*); he conceals the previous three marks and manifests only the inconceivable mark like empty space—this is the Buddha of the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*).

This present sutra precisely clarifies the revelation, opening up the Buddhas at the stage of fruition of the previous three teachings to reveal them as the Dharma-body Buddha of the Perfect Teaching, as it is said: "Within the soiled garment, the true body [is real]."
Because this layman Ratnaguṇasaṃcaya possesses the thirty-two marks, each mark being boundless, he is both the *vairocana* (the majestic special form) and the *dharmakāya*.
Thus, the Dragon Girl praised him, saying: "The subtle and pure *dharmakāya* is endowed with the thirty-two marks.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "The *vairocana* manifests in four places, but the *Lotus Sūtra* alone is the most supreme. △ Fifth, the power of hearing and retaining.
He was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
"Dwelling" means being able to abide; that which abides and that in which one abides—this is precisely the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. That which is dwelt upon is...
Regarding this "King's House City" (Rājagṛha) in the Sahā world: King Śarabha, together with a thousand kings, established the capital city among the Five Mountains to form a great kingdom;
thus it is called Rājagṛha. The etymological origin of this account appears in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Gṛdhrakūṭa is translated as "Spiritual Vulture Peak" (Língjiù) or "Vulture Head Mountain" (Jiùtóu Shān); it is named so because its peaks resemble vultures, and it is also called "Wolf Tracks" (Lángjì).
The Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the present all dwell upon this mountain. After the passing of a Buddha, Arhats reside here;
after the Dharma has perished, Pratyekabuddhas, spirits, and deities dwell here. Since it is the abode of such holy beings, it is called Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak).
When the Buddha preached this sutra, there were three assemblies: the middle assembly was held within the Many-Jeweled Stupa, while the first and last assemblies were both held on this mountain.
"Middle" means that the Buddha abides in the Middle Way; now, dwelling in the mountains, he teaches the Middle Way. △ Sixth, the companions who hear and uphold [the teaching], in two parts:
first, the listing of the assembly; second, the specific groups. First, the assembly of Śrāvakas, in two parts: first, the assembly of Bhikṣus, in six parts.
First, the category of those with great renown. First, the general enumeration.
"Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.

"Together with" (*sārdham*) carries the sense of being in company. "Great" (*mahat*) refers to one whose capacity and measure are venerable, who is honored by great beings such as celestial kings, and who possesses the Great Path, the Great Function, and Great Wisdom;
for these reasons, he is called a "great bhikṣu"—this is the meaning of *Vimalakīrti*.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Some say there is a translation, while others say there is no translation. As for 'having a translation,' it is translated as 'one who removes scarcity' (*pindapāta*).

Sentient beings with meager merit, while in the causal stage, lack the means to sustain themselves and thus receive retribution characterized by great scarcity and want. The monastic practice of the precepts is a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) that can produce wholesome qualities;
because it removes the scarcity of cause and effect, one is called 'one who removes scarcity. Others say there is no translation..."
The translation of the term [Bhikṣu] contains three meanings: first, destroying evil; second, terrifying Māras; and third, mendicant.

As for the precepts that guard against physical misconduct, they certainly eliminate mental confusion. Because wisdom awakens one to the emptiness of perceptions, it is able to destroy the evils of views and afflictions;
thus it is called "destroying evil. Since it can destroy evil, the Māras think: "Now that he has left the realm, he will further transform others so that they all leave the triple world together."

Because he acts contrary to the Māra’s intentions, the Māra becomes sorrowful and fearful; therefore, he is called "Terrifier of Māras" (*bhīṣmamāra*). As for householders, there are three lawful ways to sustain their lives and livelihoods:

first, agriculture; second, commerce; and third, government service. However, for those who have left the home life, the Buddha does not permit these; rather, they sustain themselves solely through alms-seeking.

Thus, with their bodies at peace and the Path preserved, they bring benefit and merit to their donors; for this reason, they are called "Alms-seekers" (*bhikṣu*). As for the term "Assembly" (*saṃgha*):

In the Sanskrit language, *saṃgha* means "harmonious assembly. This refers to the harmony of affairs such that there is no division among the members, and the harmony of the Dharma such that there is no divergence from principle.
△ Second, the explanation of the number:
together with twelve thousand people.
△ Third, the stage of the three knowledges (*vidyā*).
These are all *arhats*.

In the Sanskrit language, *arhat* was formerly translated as "the unattached" (*aśakta*), "the non-reborn" (*ajanman*), or "the worthy recipient of offerings" (*arha-pūjā*); alternatively, it is said that there is no direct equivalent, as the name contains multiple meanings.
Because the husks of ignorance have been shed through these three meanings, he will not receive the retribution of birth and death in the fields of future lives;
thus, he is called "Unborn" (*anutpāda*). Because he has severed the ninety-eight latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), he is called "Slayer of Thieves" (*arhat*).

Because he possesses the merits of both wisdom and abandonment (*prahāṇa*) and is worthy of being a field of merit for humans and devas, he is called "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*). △ Fourth, the praise of his virtues.
"All outflows are exhausted and there are no further afflictions; having attained one's own benefit, all fetters of existence are ended, and the mind has attained mastery.
These two phrases praise the aforementioned "slayer of thieves," wherein "outflows" (āsrava) refers to the three outflows:

first, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), which refers to all afflictions of the desire realm with the exception of ignorance; second, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), which refers to [the afflictions] of the upper realms...

The afflictions (*kleśa*) of the two realms [the form and formless realms], excluding ignorance; the third, the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), refers to the ignorance of the three realms—ignorance being precisely delusion (*moha*).
The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Because one loses the Path, it is called an outflow (*āsrava*). The *Vinaya* states: "A deluded person creates karma, opening the gates of all outflows.

The *Abhidharma* states: "One falls into birth and death (*saṃsāra*). The meaning of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* applies to both cause and effect, whereas the *Vinaya* focuses exclusively on [the result].
According to the Abhidharma, it is solely because of the fruit that [suffering arises]: through delusion one creates karma, which leads to the suffering of birth and death;

the Dharma-body perishes, the life of wisdom is lost, and these precious treasures are all stolen by the enemy. "Afflictions" (*kleśa*) refer to the dharma of turbid vexation that agitates the mind and spirit—namely, the ninety-eight *anuśayas*.
Afflictions are that which moisten, while outflows (*āsrava*) are what is moistened. When both the agent (the affliction) and the object (the outflow) are exhausted, [liberation is attained].
The phrase "this is the meaning of slaying the thief" refers to attaining one's own benefit. This single line is a praise of the *Arhat* (Worthy One):

all causes and effects within the three realms are termed "others," while the merit of wisdom and abandonment is termed "one's own benefit. Because one is fully endowed with this own benefit, one becomes an *Arhat*.
The two phrases "exhausting all fetters of existence" and "attaining self-mastery of mind" are a praise of non-birth in the various realms of existence; these constitute the second [pair].
The "fifteen" refers to the places of birth; their "bondage" (*saṃyojana*) is precisely the twenty-five causes for birth.
Because cause and effect do not perish, it is called "existence. When the cause is exhausted and the effect perishes, this is "non-arising.

One who attains mastery over the mind is said to be "perfected in concentration" (*samādhi*), while one perfected in wisdom (*prajñā*) is said to be "perfected in wisdom. Mastery of wisdom does not necessarily entail mastery of the mind.
"Having mastery over the mind necessarily means that wisdom is present now; what is here called 'mastery over the mind' is the perfection of both concentration and wisdom.
△ Fifth, the listing of names:
Their names were Ājñātakauṇḍinya.

*Ājñāta* is his name; this translates as "one who has known" (*wu zhi*). This "having known" does not mean having no knowledge at all, but rather knowing that there is nothing [ultimately] to be known.
If one relies on the two truths, it refers to knowing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and thus he is named for the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
*Kauṇḍinya* is his clan name; this translates as "fire-vessel. He belonged to the Brahmin caste; because his ancestors served fire, they were named after it.

There are two meanings: illumination and burning. Because illumination prevents darkness from arising and burning prevents material things from arising, he takes "Non-arising" (Ajita) as his clan name.
Alternatively, he is called Śākyamuni because he was the very first among all humans, devas, and arhats to hear the Dharma and attain the Way;
thus, he is described as the Buddha’s eldest son, namely Ajñāta-kauṇḍinya.
Furthermore, Mahākāśyapa is translated as "Great Kauruṣya.
His ancestors practiced the Way, and a numinous tortoise bore the chart of the immortals in response to their virtue.
He was named Mahākāśyapa (Great Kāśyapa) because his clan was that of the tortoises; at that time, people commonly addressed him by his surname.

He was also called Piṇḍola because his parents had prayed to a tree deity for his birth. He was further called Kāśyapa because the radiance of his body could outshine all other lights so that they did not appear.
He was also called Prabhasa because the flames of his bodily light surged forth. He was a disciple of the Buddha.
Among them, Mahākāśyapa is preeminent; because he was the eldest among those of the same clan as the Three Kāśyapas and others who possessed the Ten Powers, he is called Mahākāśyapa.

The Sanskrit term *mahat* contains three meanings—great (*bahu*), much (*prabhūta*), and superior (*viśiṣṭa*)—which corresponds to the "non-translation due to multiple meanings" (*bahvartha-avyaya*) among the five types of non-translation.
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma was entrusted to him so that the Teaching might endure for a long time.
He then transmitted the golden-threaded *saṃghāṭī* robe to dwell upon Mount Kukkuṭapāda until the future appearance of Maitreya;
only after the dharma has been entrusted and the robe passed on will he finally enter parinirvāṇa.
[The others were] Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Nadīkāśyapa.
Kāśyapa explained as before: *Uruvilvā* means "Pumpkin Grove," *Gayā* means "City," and *Nadī* means "River.
These three men, in the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, together erected a sacrificial pillar;
by this cause and condition, they were reborn as brothers. The elder brother served as the preceptor to King Bimbisāra and had five hundred disciples.
The two younger brothers likewise each had two hundred and fifty followers; they all practiced according to their elder brother’s methods and were unwilling to return to the Buddha.
Consequently, the Buddha performed ten kinds of supernatural transformations, such as being immune to dragon venom, unburnable by dragon fire, and unfathomable by the waters of the Ganges.

The elder brother and his two younger brothers, along with their disciples, were all subdued and entered the monastic life under the Buddha. These events are recorded in the *Cīvaravastu* (Sūtra on the Auspicious Responses).
Śāriputra. "Śāri" is translated here as *śālika*, a water-bird resembling a heron; "putra" is translated as "son.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the wife of King Vaidarbha gave birth to a daughter whose eyes resembled those of a śārika bird; thus, this girl was named Śāri.
Because he was born from a *śarīra* (relic), he is named Śāriputra;

it is also translated as "Son of the Body" (*Śarīraputra*), for this woman possessed a beautiful form and he was born from her body, hence he is called "Son of the Body. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Within my Buddha-dharma, Śāriputra is foremost in possessing infinite wisdom and resolving all doubts."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana. "Maudgalyāyana" is the Brahmin clan name; this is translated as "Praise and Recitation. His personal name is Kauṣṭhila. "Kauṣṭhila" is the name of a tree;
because he was born through praying to the deity of that tree, the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* translates it as "radish," according to Paramārtha.
*Muṅga* is translated as "hemp beans" (*mung bean*); both items were favored by ancient seers, and thus they named their clans after them.
The correct term is *Mahāmuṅgalyāyana*, which is translated as "Master of Hemp Beans"; *śu* (菽) also refers to beans. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Among my disciples, he who possesses supernatural powers and can fly light and swift to the ten directions is Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
First: Mahākātyāyana.
Kātyāyana is the gotra (clan) of the Brahmin;
this is translated as "Ornament" (*wen-shi*), because he was skilled in discussing the meaning of the *Āgamas*. Thus it is said in the *Āgama Sūtras*.
Regarding those who are foremost in skillfully discerning the meaning and expounding the teachings of the Dharma,
Kātyāyana is the first. Aniruddha—
alternatively called Aniruddha, which means "Free from Poverty," or Aniruddha, which means "As [the Buddha]"— is also foremost.

"Intention" (*manas*) is a name for "wish-fulfilling. In the past, during a time of famine, he offered millet-rice to a Pratyekabuddha and thereby obtained the enjoyment of his wishes among gods and humans for ninety-one kalpas;
thus it is called "Wish-fulfilling" (*cintāmaṇi*). Since that time, he has lacked nothing, and thus it is called "Without Poverty" (*apariśeṣa*).
Furthermore, having received the precepts and left the household life under the Buddha, through his diligence, for seven days and seven nights, his eyelashes...
Because he did not engage in [proper practice], his vital essence was lost and his physical eyes were impaired; the Buddha therefore instructed him to seek the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

By fixing his mindfulness upon the object, a pure form derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) arose within half his head, penetrating both internally and externally so that he could see all light and darkness throughout the trichiliocosm as clearly as looking at a fruit in the palm of his hand.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "In my Buddha-dharma, the divine eye possesses penetrating vision."
Among them, the Bhikṣu Aniruddha was foremost.
Kapphiṇa—here translated as "Housing Star"—was so named because his parents prayed to the constellation Gṛhakṣetrā (the Housing Star) when he was born; furthermore, at first...
At the time of his renunciation, while traveling to see the Buddha, he encountered rain at night and took shelter in a potter’s house, using straw as a seat.
Later, another bhikṣu also came to stay the night; Kapphiṇa immediately pushed his straw aside and gave it to him.
At midnight, the later-arrived bhikṣu asked where he was going, and he replied, "I wish to see the Buddha. Thereupon, the later bhikṣu...
Having heard the Dharma, he attained the Way with sudden clarity; the bhikṣu was none other than the Buddha himself.

Because he stayed overnight in the room of the Master Táo (the Star of the Dipper), the room was named after the place where he attained the Way, hence it is called "Fángsù" (Dipper). Furthermore, he was skilled in calculating the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) and clearly understood celestial diagrams;
he derived his name from this mastery. As the *Āgama Sūtra* says: "In my Buddha-dharma, those who well know the lunar mansions, the sun, and the moon [are rare]."
The bhikṣu Kapphiṇa was foremost.
Gavāmpati—translated here as "the rumination ox" or "ox-track"—was formerly a king of oxen for five hundred lifetimes. When an ox has eaten...

Thereafter, he constantly engaged in empty panting; as the residual retribution had not yet been eliminated, he perpetually chewed and gnawed. Consequently, people of the time called him "the Ox-chewer" (*go-mukha*).
To avoid being ridiculed by others, he always resided in the heavens, unaware that the Buddha had entered *parinirvāṇa*.

Kāśyapa convened a council of a thousand *arhats* and dispatched a junior monk to summon Gavāmpati. When Gavāmpati questioned the Buddha’s messenger, the messenger replied: "The Buddha has already entered *parinirvāṇa*."
He immediately said, "When the Buddha appeared, I appeared; when the Buddha remained, I remained; when the Buddha passed away, I passed away. He then entered parinirvāṇa.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states that he delighted in dwelling in the heavens and did not delight in being among humans, and that the Cow-Track Bhikṣu was the foremost.
Revata, also called Revatī;
this is translated as "Constellation Parent," as he was requested for a son from the constellations and thus named after them.
Although he attained renunciation, he still followed his original name. The *Āgama Sūtra* states that while sitting in meditation and entering samādhi, his mind did not falter.
The foremost among those who crossed over amidst chaos and disorder was Pilindavatsa (the *pi* being pronounced with the "qie" of *qihe*).
This means "Residual Habit. For five hundred lifetimes he had been a Brahmin, and his residual influence remained such that he was still haughty when crossing the Ganges River.
He rebuked the River Spirit, saying, "You petty maid! Stop the flow! The River Spirit was thus split into two branches.
Having been rebuked, the spirit went to complain to the Buddha. The Buddha ordered him to offer a formal apology. Thereupon, the spirit joined his palms and said, "Petty maid, do not be angry.
The great assembly laughed at this. The River Spirit said, "I have apologized, yet you still scold me. The Buddha said, "This is merely my habitual way of speaking; truly, I have no haughty mind."
Bakkula—here translated as "Good Appearance"—is so called because his countenance is upright and handsome. At the age of one hundred and sixty, he has been free from illness and untimely death;
this is due to his observance of the precept against killing in the past. For ninety-one kalpas, his life was not cut short prematurely. Formerly, he gave a single... to the Sangha.
Because of the *harītakī* fruit, his body was always free from illness; the *Ekottarika Āgama* states that his lifespan was extremely long and he never met an untimely death;
he always delighted in dwelling in seclusion and did not remain among the crowds—Bakkula was foremost in these respects.
Mahākoṣṭhila—translated here as "Great Thigh"—is so called because his knee bones were large and thick. He was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra;
when he could not surpass Śāriputra in debate with his sister, he reflected to himself: "This is not my sister's power; it must be that a person of wisdom is dwelling within her."
His mother said, "If you were not born from my mouth, this would be one thing; but now that you have grown up, what will you do?

He immediately left home and went to South India to study the eighteen scriptures. People of the time ridiculed him, saying, "It has been difficult to master these for generations, and it is no hope for a single lifetime.
He sighed and said, "At home I was surpassed by my sister; abroad I am slighted by others. I swear I shall not stop until I have mastered them."

Because he had no leisure time to clip his nails, people called him the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail). Later, he went forth as a monk under the Buddha and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Nanda.
He is also called Gopāla Nanda, which means "Good Joy" or "Exquisite Delight. He was named "Joy" because he first aspired to the Way;
he is called "Good" because his joy was superior among the joyful.
Sundarananda—
Sundarī is the name for "a beautiful and beloved wife"; Nanda is translated as "Joy," which is his own name.
He specifies the name of his wife to distinguish him from Nanda the cowherd.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: "Pūrṇa" translates as "Fulfilling the Vow," which is the father's name; "Maitrāyaṇī" translates as "Compassion," which is the mother's name;
"Putra" (Ni) is a common suffix for Indian women's names. He is named after his parents, hence he is called the Son of Pūrṇa-Maitrāyaṇī. [From the Āgama.]
The Sūtra says: "My father's name was Pūrṇa and my mother's name was Maitrāyaṇī; thus, my fellow practitioners of the holy life have come to call me Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti."
He is called Kūṭadanta, also Śāriputra, and also Kalyāṇakārin. On the day of his birth, all the storehouses in his home became empty;
thus he was named Kūṭadanta (Empty-born). Because the storehouses were empty, his parents were struck with wonder and consulted a diviner.
The diviner declared it auspicious, and for that reason he was named Śāriputra (Good Fortune). Furthermore, upon leaving the household life, he perceived emptiness and attained the Way.

By cultivating a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he attained the Samādhi of Non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*); thus, because he was always able to protect the minds of sentient beings, he was named the Buddha of Wholesome Karma.
When the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, people from all over the land flocked together, vying with one another to prostrate in worship;

however, Subhūti alone sat upright in his stone chamber, contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), and suddenly awakened to the Way. Therefore, he is regarded as the foremost among those who understand emptiness.
Ānanda, he is called "Joy" (Nanda), or "Rejoicing" (Pramudita), or "Untainted" (Anāsakta). He was born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment;
because the entire kingdom celebrated with great joy, he is named Joy, and also Rejoicing. Ānanda followed the Buddha into the palaces of devas, humans, and nāgas.
Because his mind was free from attachment when he beheld devas, humans, nāgas, and goddesses, he was named Anāsakta (The Unstained).
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the great assembly of Kāśyapa praised him, saying: "His face is like the pure full moon; his eyes are like blue lotuses.
The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma flows into the heart of Ānanda. When he entered parinirvāṇa, he entered the Vāyu-pracala-samādhi (the Samādhi of the Swift Wind) within the Ganges River.
He divided his body into four parts: one remained in heaven, one in the dragon palace, one in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, and one with King Ajātaśatru.

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Knowing the proper time, clearly understanding the destination of things without doubt, remembering what he has learned without forgetting, possessing vast and profound erudition, and being capable of upholding [the Dharma]—Ānanda is foremost."
Rāhula; this is translated as "Obstruction.
He was the biological son of the Buddha. Because he once blocked a mouse hole in a past life and furthermore did not look after a Brahmin for six days, he remained in the womb for six years;
thus his name is "Obstruction. Initially, when the Buddha was a prince, he sought... [text fragment ends]
When the King, his father, did not permit his renunciation, he said, "If you have a son, I shall allow you to leave the household life.
The Prince then pointed with his finger at the Queen’s belly and said, "Six years from now, you shall give birth to a son.
Once the Prince had departed for the homeless life, Yaśodharā became pregnant. All the Śākyas were incensed and suspected her of being unchaste; consequently, Yaśodharā prepared a pit of fire.
He made a vow, saying: "If I have done wrong, may both mother and son perish; if these are truly my offspring, let Heaven be their witness.
He then took his son and threw them into a pit, which miraculously transformed into a pond where lotus flowers supported their bodies.

Only then did the King and the people cease to doubt. Thereupon, the father king said with joy: "Though I have lost my son, I have gained a grandson; this grandson shall be a Golden Wheel-turning Monarch."
"What regret could I have if the Buddha later sought to have me leave the household life, yet my father the King would not permit it? Yaśodharā then ascended a high tower;
Maudgalyāyana flew through the air and took her away. The Buddha ordained her, and she became a disciple of Śāriputra, becoming foremost among those who practice in secret.
△ Sixth, the concluding verse.
Such great arhats as these are those widely known to the multitude;
this refers to a group of many acquaintances. "Acquaintance" (jñātaka) means to know by hearing their names and to recognize by seeing their forms;
alternatively, it means to know by seeing their forms and to recognize by perceiving their minds. Because they are known to many, they are said to be "widely known to the multitude."
△ Second, those of limited knowledge:
furthermore, there were two thousand persons, both learners (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Those who are learners—namely, those in the first three fruits—who investigate the truth and sever delusions are called learners; the fourth fruit, the Arhat...
When one has truly exhausted all delusions, they are called "one beyond training" (aśaikṣa). This merely cites their status to clarify the number [of categories] and does not extol their virtues;

therefore, they are termed the "assembly of those with little knowledge. The holy and the mundane have severed ties, and there is no distinction made between those with much knowledge and those with little.
Specifically, those who aspire to the lofty and admire the distant are led by means of "much knowledge," while those who conceal their names and hide their virtues are drawn by the opposite.
Those who retreat do so because they are led by limited understanding; however, one must not lose sight of the fundamental principle due to the mere traces of quantity.
△ Second, the Bhikṣuṇīs:
The Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī was present together with her retinue of six thousand.
Mahāprajāpatī is translated here as "Great Path of Love" (Dà Àidào) and also as "Gautamī," which means "Leader of the Assembly.
She is called "Great Path of Love" because she possessed wisdom and was thus able to love the Path; she is called "Leader of the Assembly" because she served as the head of the community of nuns.
She was the Buddha’s maternal aunt. According to the *Huìzhèngjì* (Records of the Correct Verification), ten years after the Buddha attained enlightenment...

In the fourth year, her maternal aunt requested to leave the household life, but the Buddha did not grant permission. Ānanda made three requests on her behalf, and the Buddha instructed Ānanda to convey the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*).
He said, "If you can practice these, I will allow you to go forth. She replied that she could practice them, and he subsequently ordained her. As for the Eight Rules of Respect:
when a *bhikṣuṇī* who is one hundred years old sees a *bhikṣu* who has only recently received the precepts, she must rise to welcome him.
1. One must pay obeisance and invite [the preceptor] to sit; 2. one must not revile or slander a bhikṣu; 3.
one must not expose the faults of a bhikṣu, though a bhikṣu may speak of a bhikṣuṇī’s faults; 4. one must seek to receive the full ordination within the Saṃgha; 5.
if one commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, one must perform *mānatva* before the Saṃgha for half a month; 6. one must seek an instructor from within the Saṃgha.

Seventh, one should not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) where there are no bhikṣus. Eighth, when the summer retreat has concluded, one should go before the Saṃgha and request a person to perform the invitation for criticism (pravāraṇā).
The bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, was also present together with her retinue.
Yaśodharā is translated here as "Flower-Colored" (Huá-sè) and is also called "Renowned" (Míng-wén).

While at home, she was the wife of the Bodhisattva and a renowned figure among devas and humans; after renouncing the world, she became the leader of the community of nuns and attained the stage of *aśaikṣa*—thus she is "Renowned.
The *Sūtra on the Twelve Years of Wandering* lists three principal wives: first, Gopī; second, Yaśodharā; and third, Mṛgajā.
The *Cezeng jing* (Sutra on Past Occurrences) and the *Ruixing jing* (Sutra on Auspicious Responses) both state that Rāhula was the son of Gopī;
however, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Lotus Sūtra* both state that he was the son of Yaśodharā. How can these two interpretations be reconciled?

It may be that those sutras refer to the mother-in-law (the Great Mother), while this sutra refers to the biological mother. The *Śāstra* states: "Gopitā was a precious woman who was barren; she is none other than Gopī."
By reversing the order of the characters for "woman" (nǚ), it is known that she is the daughter of Yaśodharā. △ Second, the assembly of Bodhisattvas, in six parts: first, their class.
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
To be fully expressed, one should say *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*; here, the two characters *sattva* are abbreviated.

"Bodhi" (菩提) here means "the Way" (道); "sattva" (薩埵) here means "mind" (心). According to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, "bodhi" refers to the Buddha-way, and "sattva" refers to the accomplishment of sentient beings.
Because one uses the way of all Buddhas to accomplish sentient beings, one is called a "bodhisattva.
Furthermore, "bodhi" refers to one's own practice, while "sattva" refers to transforming others; that is, practicing the Buddha-way for oneself and transforming others. △
Second, regarding the number:
eighty thousand.
In other sutras, the assembly of bodhisattvas is very large; why is it so small in this sutra? Perhaps this refers to their primary number, or...
It is like a king discussing secret matters; they cannot be deliberated upon by the entire realm, yet for now, let us speak of eighty thousand.
△ Third, the stages and positions: all are non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated here as "Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment. There is nothing greater than it; it is unsurpassed.
Its Way is true and correct, such that there is no dharma it does not know—this is "Perfectly Complete Knowledge" (*saṃyak-saṃbodhi*).
Master Yuan says: *An* translates as "no" (*an-*); *uttara* translates as "above" (*-uttara*); *samyak* translates as "correct," "equal," or "complete"; and *bodhi* [translates as] "enlightenment."
On the contrary, one realizes that the Sanskrit term *avaivartika-bhūmi* is translated here as "the stage of non-retrogression. There are three types of non-retrogression:

first, non-retrogression in position; second, non-retrogression in practice; and third, non-retrogression in mindfulness. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies that upon attaining the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), one obtains the Tathāgata’s single body which is an infinite body, endowed with these three non-retrogressions.
If one were to explain this by correlating it with a sequential order where there is no fixed sequence, then:

The seventh stage of faith is called non-retrogression in position; from the eighth stage of faith onward, it is called non-retrogression in practice; and from the first dwelling (bhūmi) onward, it is called non-retrogression in mindfulness.

Furthermore, entering emptiness is called non-retrogression in position; entering the provisional is called non-retrogression in practice; and entering the Middle Way is called non-retrogression in mindfulness.
What is now termed the "first dwelling" is said to fully possess the three virtues, hence it is called the "three non-retrogresions"; among these, prajñā is the position.
Because one does not regress and is free from the two deaths, liberation is the non-regression of practice; because all practices are complete, the Dharma-body is the non-regression of mindfulness;
and because the realized realm is attained, this stage of non-retrogression possesses both meanings.
What precedes this clarifies the stages, while what follows praises its virtues; now, by means of non-retrogression, one proceeds to the capacity for universal deliverance below.

The passage concerning "a hundred thousand sentient beings" consists of thirteen phrases, which may be interpreted through both vertical and horizontal arrangements. First, the vertical interpretation concerns the meaning of the ten stages (*bhūmi*):

it praises the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), because one rejoices that there is no longer falling back into the two extremes and entering the Middle Way, thereby attaining the three kinds of non-retrogression. Thus it should be understood. Second, the horizontal interpretation concerns the meaning of the first dwelling (*vihāra*): it refers to those who have attained non-retrogression.

This is a vertical discourse praising the initial Stage of Joy, rejoicing that they do not fall back into the two extremes and enter the Middle Way, having obtained the three non-regressions. Therefore, this should be known.
This praises the first stage (*bhūmi*). Discussing it from a horizontal perspective, it praises the initial dwelling of the resolve for enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*):

by giving rise to all [virtues] with a single emergence, one transcends the two extremes, transforms the ordinary person, and surpasses the sages, abiding in the Middle Way; because the mind is in every thought-moment tranquil and extinguished (*śānta*), it is said that one has attained non-retrogression.
△ Fourth, praising the virtues.
All have attained *dhāraṇī*.
*Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "total retention" (*saṃgraha*) and also as "obstructive retention" (*vāraṇa*). To explain it vertically, this is a praise of the second stage.

This stage is named "Free from Defilement" (*vimalā*), also called "Free from Obscuration" (*vigata-āvaraṇa*). It is free from all evils and attains the maintenance of all virtues; this is precisely *dhāraṇī*.
Because it explains the meaning of "joy," it is known that this refers to the second stage (*bhūmi*). Discussed crosswise, this is a praise of the first dwelling (*prathamavihāra*);

it praises the attainment of *dhāraṇī* because it obstructs and distances the obstacles of grasping at signs, ignorance, and nescience, while sustaining and realizing virtues such as prajñā, liberation, and the Dharma-body.
Thus, it is said that one "attains *dhāraṇī*."
"Skill in eloquent exposition" (*pratibhāna*)— that is,
skill in eloquent exposition being one of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)— is the vertical discourse that praises the third stage,

the Radiant Ground (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*), also called the Luminous Ground (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). This is because the internal wisdom and the external eloquence of exposition are such that one who wishes to know the wisdom must rely upon its exposition.

Because it is said that the various forms of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) are most supreme, we know this praises the third stage (*bhūmi*). Discussing it crosswise, this is a praise of the first dwelling (*vihāra*):
even those with the semblance-understanding of the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) can already pervade the trichiliocosm with a single wondrous voice;

how much more so, then, the merit of the secret of speech (*vāgguhya*) of the true understanding of the first dwelling? Therefore, it is called the "eloquence of joyful speech" (*pratibhāna-pratibhāna*).
He turns the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
"Irreversible" means that, as previously explained regarding the wheel of Śakra, it possesses the sense of turning and the sense of crushing;

for when one turns the wheel of Dharma, one is able to crush and destroy the afflictions and karma of sentient beings. In terms of vertical exposition, this is a praise of the fourth stage, the Flaming Wisdom (Arciṣmatī).
It can destroy darkness and also burn the wick; it turns the wheel of Dharma. It destroys its own delusions as the wick is burned, and dispels the confusion of others as darkness is removed.
Thus, we know this praises the fourth stage (*bhūmi*). In terms of horizontal progression, this is praising the first dwelling (*vihāra*):
being able to manifest as a Buddha in a hundred worlds and teaching the Dharma to transform sentient beings, one is said to be able to turn the irreversible wheel.
The Wheel of Dharma.

Having made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, the "Erecting of Discourse" is precisely the praise of the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā bhūmi*). On this stage, one attains profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and employs supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Because its power is difficult to surpass and difficult to equal, reaching everywhere throughout the ten directions in a single thought-moment to make offerings to all Buddhas, one knows that this praises the fifth stage.

From a horizontal perspective, this is precisely praising the attainment of inconceivable spiritual power in the first dwelling (bhūmi), whereby one is universally able to serve all Buddhas of the Dharma-realm;
thus it says, "making offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas."

Regarding the phrase "planting the roots of all virtues in the presence of the Buddhas," this establishes the discussion as a praise of the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*). Because one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one is able to make offerings to the Buddhas;

thus, the merit that serves as the seed for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the root of virtue. Since this wisdom of presence manifests like planting seeds in the earth, it is known [as such].

This praises the sixth stage. In terms of a horizontal exposition, it is a praise for the first dwelling (bhūmi) wherein one attains the true reality (dharmatā) and is thus able to plant all roots of virtue.
One is constantly praised by all Buddhas.

The vertical interpretation praises the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṃgamā*), because the two types of wisdom and skillful means therein transcend all extensive cultivation of benefit and accord with the Buddha-mind;
thus it is known that this praises the seventh stage. The horizontal interpretation praises the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) for opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*);
because one’s own dharma and knowledge and vision are identical to those of all Buddhas, one becomes [an heir] of all Buddhas.
That which is praised:
cultivating the body through loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

To speak of this vertically is to praise the eighth stage, the Immovable (*Acalā*), wherein right gnosis (*samyagjñāna*) is immovable and does not emerge from the triple world (*traidhātuka*). However...
Pervading the body with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one should enter the five destinies; pervading the mouth, one preaches the Dharma; pervading the mind, one establishes skillful means (*upāya*).
Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* fully pervades the three karmas, we know this praises the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).

From a horizontal perspective, it is a praise of the first dwelling (*vihāra*), for through unconditioned loving-kindness (*anālambana-maitrī*), the form-body (*rūpakāya*) manifests universally, responding throughout the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, it says "cultivating through loving-kindness."
The body.
Skillfully entering the Buddha’s wisdom.

This "vertical discourse" is a praise of the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), which profoundly penetrates the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and thoroughly reaches the wondrous source.
Because the name and its meaning correspond most perfectly, we know this praises the ninth stage. Discussed crosswise, it is precisely a praise of the first dwelling for entering the secret treasury;
thus it says, "skillfully entering the Buddha’s wisdom" and "penetrating great knowledge."

The vertical discourse (*ūrdhva-vāda*) praises the tenth stage, the Dharma-Cloud Ground (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*): its *dharmakāya* is like space, its meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is like a great cloud, and its wisdom (*prajñā*) is like a heavy rain;
it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*) for skillfully entering the Buddha-dharma and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) for skillfully employing the Buddha-dharma;

thus, one knows this praises the tenth ground. The horizontal discourse (*tiryag-vāda*) praises the single mind of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), which possesses the threefold wisdom (*trividha-jñāna*) that is without equal.
Because it transcends all obstacles, it is called the "penetration of great wisdom" and the "reaching of the other shore.
This vertical discourse is a praise of the internal virtues within the tenth stage; it describes reaching the other shore of the three truths while still within the causal state.

Furthermore, it will not be long before he reaches [the goal]. This incidental discussion is intended to praise the fact that the matters and principles of the first stage (prathamabhūmi) have reached their ultimate consummation;
therefore, it is said that he has "reached the other shore.
His fame is heard throughout immeasurable worlds.

The vertical exposition (*ūrdhva-vyākhyāna*) praises the external virtues of the tenth stage; because its internal virtues are profound and vast, its fame spreads universally, such that its inner qualities and outer reputation correspond.

If one posits the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) following the ten stages, the two phrases—"having reached the other shore" and "now its name is heard throughout immeasurable worlds"—are applied to it as a horizontal exposition (*tiryag-vyākhyāna*).
This is a praise of the true, perfect virtue of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), which accords with its name;
thus it is said that "its fame is heard throughout immeasurable worlds" and that "it can deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings."

The "Vertical Discussion" (*vṛtti*) is precisely a praise of the tenth stage (*bhūmi*). While the other stages are called "able to deliver beings" when referring to one realm up to nine realms, this tenth stage is not so named because it excels those preceding it;
thus, it is specifically termed "able to deliver. One must understand that all stages are fully endowed with the aforementioned merits;
however, the reasons for their appearance or omission in the explanation are due to the human tendency to prefer variety, and thus they are presented according to the ten stages.
Furthermore, because the meaning of the names is established vertically and is easy to understand, this single path is composed to explain the text.

To discuss it horizontally, this is a praise of the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), which is able to serve as the basis for the ten realms of existence (*daśadhātu*) and establishes protection and refuge;

therefore, it says it "can deliver hundreds of thousands of sentient beings. This perfectly praises what virtues of the First Stage are not encompassed [by other stages]. Briefly stated, there are thirteen phrases. Part One.

If this is so even for those dwelling [in the first stage], how much more so for the subsequent stages? As for "sentient beings" (*sattva*): at the beginning of the eon, male and female beings arise together in the world;
furthermore, the aggregates (*skandha*) arise together; and because they receive birth in various places, they are called sentient beings. △ Fifth, the enumeration of names.
Their names were Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and others. "Mañjuśrī" translates here as "Wondrous Virtue.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "To see the Buddha-nature clearly is like [the state of] Wondrous Virtue.
The *Saṃghāṭasūtra* (Siyi jing) states: "Although he speaks of all dharmas, he does not give rise to the mark of dharmas, nor does he give rise to the mark of non-dharmas."
He is so named because of his marks; the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that Mañjuśrī means "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (*Miaojixiang*).
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that in the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, he became a Buddha named Nāga-uttara-rāja (Dragon Race Supreme Honored King).
The *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* states that in the present, in the world-system of Joy to the north, he becomes a Buddha named Joy (*Huanxi*).
The *Sūtra on the Compassionate Grace of the Buddha Ratnakūṭa Muni’s Rebirth Above* states that in the future he will attain Buddhahood under the name Puxian (Universally Manifesting).
This refers to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
In the Sanskrit language, *avalokiteśvara* means "One Who Observes the Sounds of the World.

Because he perfectly unifies the subject and object of perception and thoroughly elucidates both existence and non-existence, he illuminates and exhaustively penetrates the true nature (*dharmatā*), examining both its origin and its manifestation; thus, he is called "Observation" (*avalokita*).

"The sounds of the world" (*loka-svara*) refers to the objects of observation. As the myriad phenomena flow and change, they are distinct and diverse; though beings utter various cries, all alike receive his grace and are freed from suffering.
Because the Bodhisattva’s vast compassion universally rescues all beings at once, causing them to attain liberation, he is called Avalokiteśvara.

The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "If there are sentient beings suffering who invoke my name and mind me, yet are not seen or heard by my divine ear and divine eye and do not escape their suffering, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. At that time, the Buddha Ratnagarbha said to him: [May you...]
Observing all sentient beings, he gives rise to great compassion; you shall now be named Avalokiteśvara—this will be explained in detail in the relevant chapter.
As for the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta:
In the Sanskrit language, *Mahāsthāmaprāpta* means "One Who Has Attained Great Power. The *Sīsapuṣpa-sūtra* states:
"Wherever I set my foot, the trichiliocosm and the palaces of Māra tremble; therefore, you are named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Buddha Ratnagarbha said: "Because of your vow to take hold of the great trichiliocosm, I shall now name you Mahāsthāmaprāpta."
Regarding the Bodhisattva Nityodyukta (Ever-Vigorous), the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "This bodhisattva follows after a single sentient being for immeasurable kalpas without abandoning them;
even if they do not yet receive transformation, he does not forsake them for a single thought-moment. Because of his physical and mental diligence, he is named Ever-Vigorous."
Regarding the Bodhisattva Anikṣiptadhura, the *Suyāmasūtra* states:
"A period of Ganges-sand kalpas constitutes one day and night; thirty such days constitute a month; twelve such months constitute a year.
After passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, one encounters a single Buddha. In this manner, one encounters Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi is named "Unresting" because he practices all pure conducts, cultivates meritorious virtues,
and subsequently receives his prediction [of enlightenment] with a mind that never ceases.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "For what reason is he called 'Jewel-Palmed' (*Ratnapāṇi*)?

It means that when this bodhisattva transforms sentient beings in various buddha-fields, if he wishes to touch as many buddha-worlds as he desires with his right hand, he is able to accomplish it according to his wish;
from his hand there issues forth the sounds of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, as well as the sounds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity."
Regarding the sound of his relinquishing, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi produces the seven treasures from his hands to bestow upon all sentient beings;
furthermore, he causes them to rejoice and attain nirvāṇa, and is therefore named Ratnapāṇi."
Regarding Medicine King Bodhisattva, the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states:
"In the past, when he was named Starlight, he heard the Venerable Sūryagarbha preach the Buddha’s wisdom.

He offered medicinal herbs from the Snow Mountains to the assembly of monks, vowing that in the future he would be able to cure the two types of illness—those of body and mind—for all sentient beings. Thus it is said.
World-Honored One, he is hailed as the Medicine King; hereafter he shall become a Buddha named Loushi Tathāgata.
[From] the Bodhisattva Courageous Bestowal (Yongshi) up to the Bodhisattva Transcending the Three Realms (Yue Sanjie).
Regarding these seven bodhisattvas, the commentary lacks an explanation; thus, this brief supplement sets forth their meaning:
because he universally bestows the world-transcending Dharma-treasure upon sentient beings without weariness, he is named *Vīradatta* (Courageous Giver);

because the three truths he realizes are venerable like jewels and the three wisdoms he realizes can illuminate perfectly like the moon, he is named *Ratnacandra* (Jewel Moon); [and] because the perfect and wondrous three wisdoms can eliminate... [afflictions].
Because it dispels the darkness of delusion, affliction, and feverish distress with a clarity as cool as moonlight, it is called "Moonlight.

Because its three wisdoms are perfectly luminous and without deficiency, like the full moon, it is called "Full Moon. Because it possesses great power and function through the profound union of object and wisdom, it is called "Great Power.
Because it universally responds to all conditions and universally uproots all sufferings by means of that great power and function, [it is so named].
He is named "Immeasurable Power" because he has transcended the two kinds of birth and death— those of the fragmented and those of transformation— and thus has surpassed the three realms.
This is the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla.

Bhadrapāla means "Good Protector" (Shànshǒu) in this language. The *Sīyì jīng* (*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*) states that because sentient beings who hear his name will certainly attain *samyak-saṃbodhi*, he is named "Good Protector.
Alternatively, he is called "Worthy Head" (Xiánshǒu), as his rank is equal to that of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), making him the foremost among the worthy ones.

Regarding Maitreya Bodhisattva, the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that "Melifiya" is the Chinese translation for "Cishi" (Maitreya), which refers to his clan name. In the past, he was a king named Dharmaruci;
because he nurtured the people with compassion, he has been known as Cishi from that time until the present. This is recorded in the *Siyi jing* (Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra).
It is said that if sentient beings see him, they immediately attain the Samādhi of the Compassionate Mind; therefore, he is named Maitreya,
also known as Ajita, which means "Invincible," and as Ratnakūṭa Bodhisattva.
Master Kumārajīva’s commentary on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Because he accumulates the treasure of wisdom, he is named Ratnakūṭa (Treasure Accumulation).

Regarding the Bodhisattva Śāstṛ (Teacher), the *Saṃgharakṣitabhikṣuṇī-sūtra* states: "He gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings who have fallen into deviant paths, causing them to enter the right path."
Because he seeks to bestow grace and requite [benefits], he is called the "Guide. △ Sixth, the concluding statement:
"Thus, together with eighty thousand Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
△ Third, the eight groups of followers; first, the assembly of devas of the Desire Realm.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra was together with his retinue of twenty thousand devaputras.
"Śakra Devānām-indra" (釋提桓因) is translated as "Indra," meaning "The Able One," for he is the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The *Yingluo jing* (瓔珞經) states: "After two thousand twenty-four kalpas beyond the Bhadrakalpa, he will become a Buddha named Aśoka."
"Venerable One, there are also the devaputras Moon, Universal Fragrance, and Jewel Light.
These three devaputras are the inner ministers of Śakra, like high ministers; they are the very ones known as the Three Luminaries."
Candra was the Devaputra Ratnaśrīcandra; Samantagandha was the Devaputra Tārakadeva; and Ratnaprabha was the Devaputra Ratnamati-sūrya.
The Four Great Kings were present together with their retinues of ten thousand devas.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings are the external ministers of Śakra, like military generals residing on the four sides of the belly of Mount Sumeru.
In the east is Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which means "Holder of the Nation" (*Ciguó*); because he protects and sustains the land, he is also called "Abider of the People.
He presides over the golden terrace and leads the gandharvas and bhūtas. In the south is Virūḍhaka, which means "Increase."
Because he causes the roots of goodness in others to increase, he dwells upon the lapis lazuli terrace; he presides over the *pīlita* and *kumbhāṇḍas*.
To the west is Vaiśravaṇa—translated as "Broad Eye" (*viśāla-locana*) or "Diverse Speech"—who is able to produce all kinds of speech;
he dwells upon the silver terrace and presides over the venomous *nāgas* and *piśācas*. To the north is Vaiśravaṇa—translated as "Much Hearing" (*bahu-śruta*)—who possesses great merit.
The fame of his virtue resounds in the four directions; thus, he formerly presided over the Vidyutprabha terrace and led the rākṣasas and yakṣas.
These four heavenly kings each lead two classes of spirits to prevent them from troubling human beings, which is why they are called the "World Protectors" (Lokapālas).
Above these, there are the three heavens of Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, and Tuṣita, but they are not listed here because the text is abbreviated.
The Devaputra Īśvara and the Devaputra Maheśvara were together with their retinue of thirty thousand devas.
Īśvara is the fifth heaven, Nirmāṇarati, so called because its inhabitants create their own transformations within the five sensory realms to enjoy themselves.
Maheśvara is the sixth heaven, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, so called because when its inhabitants desire the five sensory realms, other devas [provide them].
Because they transform what is falsely created by others to achieve their own pleasure, they are none other than the Māra kings. △ Second, the assembly of devas from the Form Realm:
the Brahmā King, Lord of the Sahā World (up to) together with his retinue of twelve thousand sons of gods.
*Saha* is correctly transliterated as *Sokha*; this is translated as "Endurance" (*kṣānti*).

Because the sentient beings of that land abide in the ten non-virtues and are unwilling to renounce them, the land is named after its inhabitants and is thus called "Endurance. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* asks: "Why is it named Saha? It replies:
"Because these sentient beings endure the three poisons and all afflictions, it is therefore called the Land of Endurance. (From the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*)

"Brahmā" (Brahman) is a Western term; here it is translated as "Free from Desire. Because he abandons the fetters of the lower realms and ascends to the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu), he is called "Free from Desire.
"Śikhin" is translated here as "Crest" (or "Topknot").

Although the sutra mentions Brahmā first and then cites Śikhin as if they were two different persons, according to the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explanatory Treatise), Śikhin is actually the king and Brahmā is the title of his office; thus, "Brahmā" indicates his rank while "Śikhin" reveals his personal name.

The name "Terrifier" (Bhīṣma) refers to a single individual; this deity dwells in the intermediate stage of the First Dhyāna. Because there is *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) within, and speech without, he exercises sovereign authority as a king.
The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states that from the Second Dhyāna upward, the dharma of speech does not exist, and thus one cannot be a king.
If the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-vyākhyā* says that Maheśvara dwells at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), [it refers to a different context].
The Lord of the Great Thousandfold World takes the position of supreme honor as King;

if one says that there are words and commands capable of governing those above and crowning those below, it refers specifically to Śikhin as King, while the Radiant Heaven (Ābhāsvara) and others are equivalent to the heavens of the Second, Third, and Fourth Dhyānas.
△ Third, the assembly of Dragon Kings and others.
There were eight dragon kings, namely Nanda Dragon King and Upananda Dragon King.

"Nanda" is translated here as "Joy," and "Upananda" as "Excellent. These two brothers always protected the kingdom of Magadha by sending rain at the proper times, so that there were no years of famine.
King Bimbisāra held a great assembly once every year to repay their kindness.
When the common people heard this, they were all filled with joy; from this time forth, he was known by the name of the one subdued by Maudgalyāyana.
As for the Dragon King Sāgara—Sāgara here means "Salt Sea"—he received his name from the sea in which he dwells.
The Nāga King Vāsuki—
Vāsuki is here translated as "Many-Headed" (Duōtóu) and also as "Jewel Renown" (Bǎochēng)—
and the Nāga King Takṣaka.
Takṣaka— here translated as "Manifesting Poison" (xiàndú) or "Many-Tongued" (duōshé)—
and the Nāga King Anavatapta— also called Anotatta,
which translates as "Without Affliction" (wǎonǎo). The Āgama Sūtras state that there is a lake on Mount Himavat named Anavatapta.
Within the Anavatapta Lake there is a hall with five pillars where the dragon always resides; it is named after this lake.
The Dragon King Mānasa—*mānasa* here meaning "large-bodied" or also "great-power"—once pushed back the ocean waters to submerge the city of Sudarśana.
This city is encircled by a dragon coiling its body to block the seawater.
The Dragon King Utpala—also called *Utpala*, which translates as "dark-colored lotus"—dwells here; it is named after the lake upon which he relies.
Each was accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues.
△ Fourth, the assembly of *kiṃnaras*.
There were four *kiṃnara* kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues.
Kinnara (translated here as "Doubtful Deity") resembles a human but possesses a single horn; thus he is called a "Non-human. He is the deity of the Dharma-music of the Heavenly Emperor.
He dwells on the Ten Jewel Mountains (*daśa-ratna-parvata*). Whenever his body manifests extraordinary signs, he ascends to present music.
When the Buddha preaches the Dharma, the various devas play stringed instruments and sing songs to praise the Dharma-gates; this is precisely that deity. Formerly, he was called... [text ends].
The *Dharma-vīṇā* (Lute of Dharma) performs the wondrous melody of the Four Noble Truths; the *Mahā-vīṇā* (Great Lute) performs the great melody of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
and the *Dhāraṇī-vīṇā* (Lute of Retention) performs the collective melody of the preceding three. What is now called the "performance" (*tsū*) refers to the teaching method of these four.
Their fundamental abiding is inconceivable, yet their traces manifest through strings, pipes, and song to extol the Ten Powers. △ Fifth, the Gandharva Assembly.
There were four gandharva kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
"Gandharva" is translated here as "Smeller of Fragrance," for they take fragrance as their food; they are also called "Fragrance-Body" because fragrance issues from their bodies.

They are the deities of the worldly music of the Heavenly Emperor. As for "music," it refers to the art of acrobatic performances involving tossing and tumbling around banners. [The text continues with] the sounds of music.
"Those" refers to the drums, cymbals, strings, and pipes; "beautiful" refers to those that are superior among the banners and canopies;
"beautiful sounds" refers to those that are superior among the strings and pipes. △ Sixth, the assembly of asuras.
There are four asura kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
"Asura" is correctly translated as *asu-lo*; this means "neither handsome men nor beautiful women," because the men are ugly while the women are beautiful.
It is also called "Non-Gods" (*fei-tian*). The *Jingming shu* states: "The retribution of these spirits is adjacent to that of the various devas, yet they are not devas. It is also said: [omitted].
There is no wine in the four continents; flowers are gathered and fermented in the great ocean, yet due to the karmic power of the fish and dragons, its flavor remains unchanged.
Because he has vowed to sever anger and envy, it is said that there is no wine. There are two kinds [of spirits]:

those categorized under the realm of ghosts (preta) dwell on the shores of the great ocean, while those categorized under the realm of animals (tiryagyoni) dwell at the bottom of the great ocean. *Bazi* (婆稚)—properly *Bajika* (跋稚迦)—is translated as "ball" (*tuán*).
Pāyāga was so named because he was released from bondage after making a vow while fighting with Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
Khara-karṇa means "Broad Shoulders" and is also called "Evil Shadow," for he is the one who causes the ocean waters to surge.
Vemacitra means "Pure Mind" and is also named "Various Doubts"; he is the father of Śacī. Rāhu... [text truncated]
The Cloud-Obstructing and Support-Obstructing [beings] are those who obstruct and support the sun and moon;
because the sunlight cannot reach the eyes when they block it, people consequently say there is a solar eclipse, and the same applies to the moon. △ Seventh, the Assembly of Garuḍas.
There were four Garuḍa kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
"Garuḍa" is translated here as "Golden Winged One"; their wings are golden in color, and the distance between the two wings is three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*.
They possess the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) upon their necks and take dragons as their food; they are those of great majestic power, whose majesty surpasses all others.
Furthermore, because he awes and subdues all the nāgas, he is called "Great Body" (Mahākāya); because his body is large and he leads a great multitude, he is called "Great Fullness" (Mahāpūrṇa);
because the nāgas he devours are always satisfied according to their desires, he is called "As He Wishes" (Yathāruci); and because this jewel is on his neck, he is so named.
△ Eighth, the King of Men and the Multitude.
King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, was accompanied by several hundred thousand followers.
"Vaidehī" is translated here as "Sīwéi" (思惟, *sīmā*); she was the mother of King Ajātaśatru. "Ajātaśatru" is translated as "Wèishēngyuàn" (未生怨, *Ajātaśatru*).
The *Commentary on the Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations* states: "On the day before he was born, a physiognomist divined that once this child was born, [his enmity] would be certain."
Because he intended to harm his father, he was named Ajātaśatru. *Myōraku* (妙樂) says that while his mother was pregnant, he already harbored an evil mind toward King Bimbisāra;
because he was evil even before birth, he was named Ajātaśatru. He is also called Vairōṭi, which means "Fingerless.
*Myōraku* says that according to the signs at his birth, the king ordered him to be placed on a tower and dashed down.
He was named "Immortal" (A-mi) simply because he lost one finger; the palace attendants who cared for him called him "Good Vision.
The *Puchao jing* (Sutra on Universal Transcendence) states that Ajātaśatru repented before Mañjuśrī and attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).

At the end of his life, he entered the Piṇḍala Hell, whereupon he immediately emerged and was reborn in a Buddha-land above, attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) under Maitreya.
When they departed, they returned to this realm; he is named Bodhisattva Acalā, who shall later become a Buddha titled Tathāgata Śuddhaloka.
△ Second, the summary:
each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.
△ Second, the specific introduction in five parts: First, the sequence of the assembly gathering; second, the majestic deportment of the initial gathering of the assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly.
"At that time" refers to the moment when he was about to manifest the six auspicious omens. In the Sanskrit language, this is *lokakāla*, which translates here as "the world."
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that one who possesses these nine titles is revered by all beings and honored alike by those in heaven and those among humans;

therefore, he is called the World-Honored One (*Bhagavat*). Regarding the "four assemblies" (*catasraḥ parṣadaḥ*), the traditional interpretation holds that there are two groups each for the ordained and the laity, totaling four assemblies.

This definition is narrow in its scope and limited in its meaning. Now, according to a single assembly, we further distinguish four types, namely: those who initiate [the teaching], those who are the appropriate recipients (*pratipannaka*), and so forth.

Those who influence and form karmic connections by employing skillful means and wisdom, discerning the opportune moment and timing to inspire, mobilize, and accomplish beneficial aims, are called the "Initiating Assembly" (*janaka-parṣad*).
