Those who, having planted roots of virtue in past lives, encounter the convergence of conditions when their potential has matured, and immediately attain the Way upon hearing [the teaching], are called the "Appropriate Audience" (*pratibhāga-parṣad*).
The "Influential Ones" (*anubhāva*) are the Buddhas of the past and the Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Concealing their ultimate perfection, they assist the Dharma King like a form has its shadow or a valley its echo; though they act without deliberate effort, they bring great benefit.
This group is called the "Echoes and Shadows. Regarding those who "form connections" (*karmic bonds*):

"connection" (*jie*) refers to the initial establishment of the karmic structure, while "condition" (*yuan*) refers to the supportive conditions that enable the completion of the end. Since they possess neither the power to strike nor the power to suppress, [they remain in this state].

Because their faculties were dull and shallow in the past, the three types of wisdom did not arise; thus, although they see the Buddha and hear the Dharma in the present life, there is no benefit from the four *siddhāntas*.
They merely serve as causes and conditions for attaining liberation in the future, and are called the "assembly for establishing a connection.
As it is with the assembly of bhikṣus, so it is with the other three assemblies; together these sixteen assemblies surround [the Buddha] as he performs the majestic deportment of circumambulation.
...and so forth. △ Second, the assembly gathers to make offerings.
They offer, revere, respect, and praise.

Regarding "making offerings," in general terms, all three types of action (the three karmas) constitute making offerings; in specific terms, the act of bestowing material requisites is called making offerings.

Nurturing those who are humble and cautious with reverent rites is called "veneration"; focusing the mind with utmost mindfulness is called "respect"; speaking words that extol [the virtues of others] is called "praise.
△ Second, the sequence of manifested auspicious omens, in two parts: first, the six omens in this land; sixth, the teaching of the Dharma.
For the sake of all bodhisattvas, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings*, which instructs bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.

Regarding this preaching of the Mahāyāna sūtra, the *Sūtra on Good Precepts* states that there are seven kinds of "greatness": first, greatness of the dharma, referring to the *Vaipulya* among the twelve divisions of the scriptures;
second, greatness of mind, referring to the seeking of bodhi; third, greatness of understanding, referring to the understanding of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; fourth...
The greatness of purity refers to the pure mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). The greatness of adornment refers to the five adornments of merit and wisdom.

The greatness of time refers to the practice of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. The greatness of fulfillment refers to attaining enlightenment by adorning oneself with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
The first six constitute the greatness of the cause, while the seventh is the greatness of the fruit. The combination of these great causes and great fruits constitutes the Mahāyāna.
The *Sūtra* takes "conveying" as its primary meaning, for it conveys [beings] back to the secret treasury of the three virtues.

Regarding the "Infinite Meanings," they arise from a single dharma; this single dharma is what is called the signless (*animitta*). This signlessness and non-signifying is termed the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
From this true mark arise infinite dharmas, namely: the two dharmas, the three paths, and the four fruits, and so forth.

All dharmas are called "immeasurable," and their true nature (*dharmatā*) is the locus of meaning (*artha-sthāna*). From this single locus of meaning, immeasurable dharmas emerge; thus they are attained as the "entrance into the immeasurable.

To bring these immeasurable dharmas back into the single locus of meaning is to establish the introduction (*nidāna*). It is like a mathematician who, from the number one, brings down all other numbers;
by subtracting all those numbers, they return to the number one. Because of this subtraction, the subtraction serves as the removal of the basis, and from that one, the flow proceeds.
The various gatherings and returns, when unified and opened as a single sequence, are likewise so;

therefore, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* is called "from one to many," while the present sūtra is called "gathering the many back to one. For this reason, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* serves as the prologue to the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Regarding the phrase "the teaching for bodhisattvas": the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* employs its teachings to instruct bodhisattvas.

The "locus of meaning" (*arthapada*) refers to the principle of the Truths (*satya*). That which is "protected and remembered by the Buddha" refers to the *Ananta-artha-pada*, which is that which the Buddha himself has realized;
therefore, it is that which the Tathāgata protects and remembers, as the Sūtra says: "The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states:
Because there is no characteristic of birth-and-death, it is called "formless Nirvāṇa"; because even this [Nirvāṇa] does not exist, it is called "non-characteristic."
The two dharmas refer to the sudden and gradual [teachings]; the three paths refer to the three vehicles; and the four fruits refer to the Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Buddha.
△ Second, entering samādhi:
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra (up to) his body and mind were unmoving.
Regarding those who sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), the Chan Gate says: "If it is the half-lotus, the left leg presses upon the right;

if it is the full lotus, one further crosses the right over to press upon the left, like a coiled dragon. All Buddhas of the past and their assemblies of disciples have practiced this method entirely.

Furthermore, if even when rising from the full-lotus posture one gives rise to unwholesome thoughts, others still feel a heart of reverence; how much more so when entering deep states of meditative realization?
It is not something that displeases devas and humans; nor is it a worldly object of enjoyment shared with non-Buddhists.

Because it can destroy the armies of Māra and the afflictions, this samādhi is here called *tiao-zhi-ding* (the Samādhi of Rectitude), also called *zheng-ding* (Right Concentration), and also called *zheng-shou* (Right Reception).
After the Buddha had preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, he again entered the *Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings*; this refers to the concentration of wisdom (*hui-ding*).
Mutually establishing one another, there is no dhyāna without wisdom and no wisdom without first entering samādhi; because there is no dhyāna without wisdom, he first expounds the Dharma.
Having finished preaching this *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, his re-entering [samādhi] serves as the prologue to the *Lotus Sūtra*.
As for "body and mind unmoving," it is the method of samādhi; because it is maintained within body and mind, they do not move. △ Third, the raining of flowers.
At that time, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers (up to) scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly.
*Māndārava* here means "pleasing" or "white flower"; *mañjūṣaka* means "soft" or "red flower.
The raining down of these four flowers symbolizes that one shall obtain the causes of Buddhahood; the causes of Buddhahood consist of abiding and practicing.

The light directed toward the ground represents the cause perfected through practice; the small white light symbolizes the nature-seed-nature (*gotra-bhūmi*) of the ten abidings (*bhūmi*), which opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The large white light symbolizes the nature-seed-nature of the ten practices (*caryā*), which reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The small red light symbolizes the path-seed-nature of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), which awakens to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The large red light symbolizes the noble seed-nature of the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), which enters into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, because there is the sense of scattering as an offering to the fruit [of Buddhahood], it is said that they were scattered over the Buddha.
△ Fourth, the earthquake: the worlds of all Buddhas shook in six ways.

The *Guangming ji* states: "The six ways consist of three types related to form—shaking (*kampa*), rising (*prakampa*), and surging (*samprakampa*)—and three types related to sound—thundering (*raṇa*), roaring (*praraṇa*), and crashing (*saṃpraraṇa*)."
Regarding these six kinds of sounds described as "wondrous music," there are differences between the new and old commentaries regarding their literal interpretation.

The new commentary explains them as: moving (*dong*), surging (*yong*), shaking (*zhen*), striking (*ji*), roaring (*hou*), and bursting (*bao*). For now, we shall follow the old interpretation: "moving" refers to being unsteady and swaying; "rising" refers to ascending from below;

"surging" refers to the unevenness of mounds and hollows; "shaking" refers to a deep, rumbling sound; and "striking" refers to the clashing of [objects]. *Peng* (pīng) and *ke* (kè) are the sounds of impact.

(Kèhé qiè) To emit a sound is called "roaring" (*ghoṣa*); to cause sentient beings to awaken is called "awakening" (*bodhana*). In the sūtras and śāstras, these are generally indicated by the term "shaking" (*kampita*).
This refers to designating one [aspect] each for both form and sound. Furthermore, within the six types of earthquakes, each has three further divisions:

namely, shaking (*calana*), universal shaking (*saṃpracalana*), and so forth; universal shaking (*saṃpracalana*) includes direct shaking (*pracaḷana*) and shaking the four continents (*cāturdvīpaka-kampita*), while shaking the great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu-kampita*) constitutes universal shaking.

When [the earth] shakes equally and universally, the other five types of shaking are likewise combined, making eighteen kinds of shaking in total. If categorized according to the *dharmas*, these represent the purification of the eighteen realms (*dhātu*).

Now, when this sutra speaks of the "six kinds of shaking," it signifies the six successive stages—of abiding, practice, and orientation (*vihāra*, *caryā*, *mukha*)—and the grounds (*bhūmi*), which break through ignorance (*avidyā*).
Since ignorance has been vast and pervasive, never before having been invaded or destroyed, it is now about to be demolished; therefore, there is shaking.
The earth manifests this; if ignorance is transformed, it immediately becomes clarity, which is why the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions shake in six ways.
Regarding these six ways, the *Guangji* (Record of Light) says "striking" (*jī*), while the present commentary says "awakening" (*jué*). "Striking" means to strike, beat, or pound;
"explosion" (*bào*) refers to the sound of fire. △ Fifth, the assembly rejoices.
At that time, the assembly of bhikṣus (through to) rejoiced, joined their palms, and with single-minded devotion gazed upon the Buddha.
"Bhikṣus" and "bhikṣuṇīs" refer to the two groups of the ordained; "upāsakas" and "upāsikās" refer to the two groups of the laity.
Upāsaka is correctly transliterated as *Upāsaka*, which translates as "male lay follower" (*jìnshì nán*); upāsikā [is the female counterpart].

The correct term is *upāsikā*, which is translated here as "female lay practitioner" (*jìnshì nǚ*). She is called a "lay practitioner" because she personally attends upon and practices the teachings of the Buddhas.
The Sanskrit word *deva* is translated as "heavenly being" (*tiān*). They are called "heavenly beings" because they are naturally and spontaneously joyful and possess superior bodies;
this refers to the various devas of the desire realm and so forth. The Sanskrit word *nāga* is translated as "dragon" (*lóng*). As for dragons...
There are four kinds: first, those who guard the celestial palaces and maintain them so they do not fall; second, those who raise clouds and bring rain to benefit the human realm;
third, those who command the earth-dragons to break through rivers and open canals; and fourth, those who guard the hidden treasures of the wheel-turning kings and those of great merit.
*Yakṣa* is the original term; it is translated as "swift" (*jiéjí*), also as "valiant" (*yǒngqián*), and also as... [text fragment].
The violent and wicked gandharvas and so forth are explained as before. Regarding the mahoragas—also called *mahoraga*—this is translated as "large-bellied crawler.
Kumārajīva said: "These are earth-dragons that crawl on their bellies.

As for "humans and non-humans," since among the eight classes there are humans, ghosts, and animals, the term "humans and non-humans" is used as a comprehensive summary. Dragons, ghosts, and the others obtain [their respective states].

Those who attended the Dharma assembly were characterized by an urgency regarding the Vehicle but a laxity regarding the precepts; thus, while they heard the Dharma due to their urgency regarding the Vehicle, they fell among dragons and spirits due to their laxity regarding the precepts.

As for the Wheel-Turning Kings, the *Āgama Sūtras* state that when the human lifespan increases to twenty thousand years, an Iron Wheel-Turning King appears to rule exclusively over Jambudvīpa; when it increases to forty thousand years, a Copper Wheel-Turning King appears.
When the lifespan in the two continents of the southeast increases to sixty thousand years, a silver-wheel-turning king appears to rule over three continents—east, south, and west.
When the lifespan increases to eighty thousand years, a gold-wheel-turning king appears to rule over the four continents.
A golden wheel-treasure suddenly manifests before him, and the king says, "Go toward the east and turn the wheel according to the Dharma. Thereupon, it turns toward the east.
The King, leading his fourfold army, followed behind him as he traveled to tour the various kingdoms in the south, west, and north; it was likewise so in all directions.

Therefore, it is called a Wheel-Turning Sage King. When the multitude beheld the auspicious signs of falling flowers and the trembling of the earth—omens of an extraordinary nature—they knew that the nectar of immortality was about to descend.
Joy overflowed within them, manifesting the arousal of great spiritual capacity and their resonance with this supreme response; thus, they rejoiced.
With joy, they joined their palms and gazed at the Buddha with single-minded devotion. △ Sixth, the Emission of Light:
At that time, the Buddha emitted from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows a light (extending until) there was nowhere it did not pervade.
Regarding the *ūrṇā-kośa*, the *Foshanhaiguan Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Ocean of Buddhas) states: When the Buddha was first born, the hair-tuft was five feet long;
during his time of ascetic practice, it was one zhang and four chi long; upon attaining Buddhahood, it was one zhang and five chi long.
The interior and exterior of this hair-tuft are both empty, like a tube of white beryl, pure within and without, extending from the initial state of doubt through the intervening stages of practice.
All various marks and characteristics, up to and including all merits of entering *nirvāṇa*, are manifested within the *ūrṇā-kośa*.
This *ūrṇā* is located between the two eyebrows, which symbolizes the Middle Way and the virtue of permanence (*nityatā*). Its soft texture symbolizes the virtue of bliss (*sukha*).

Its ability to contract and expand with mastery symbolizes the virtue of self (*ātman*). Its white color symbolizes the virtue of purity (*śubha*). Its light illuminating this land and other lands symbolizes self-awakening (*svasaṃbodhi*).
"Awakening others by illuminating the east" means that the east is the beginning of the four directions, signifying that the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are the commencement of all positions.

Regarding the "eighteen thousand," this is discussed in terms of the eighteen realms (*dhātu*): when one hundred dharma-realms and a thousand natures and characteristics are combined, they total eighteen thousand.
These states have not yet been opened by the Buddha-wisdom; now they ought to be opened, and thus these numbers are used.

This merely indicates the traces of his manifestation. In the teaching of the Trace Gate (*jijumon*), Bodhisattvas of the birth-body (*shōshin*) clearly perceive the principle and enter the ten stages (*jūjū*) up to the tenth ground (*jūji*).
In the teaching of the Root Gate (*honmon*), Bodhisattvas of the dharma-body (*hosshin*) increase their path and diminish their births;

because they likewise progress through the four stages of growth, it is said that "there is nowhere it does not pervade. △ Second, the six auspicious omens in other lands. Part one: seeing the six realms of existence.
Sentient beings—from those as low as the Avīci Hell up to the very end—behold all the beings of the six destinies in that land.

"Avīci" is translated here as "Uninterrupted" (wu-jian); according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, regarding the fruit of the destinies, there are five aspects in which [the suffering] is uninterrupted: time, sensation, life-span, and physical form.
Regarding "Avīci" (the Uninterrupted) and "hell" (*naraka*): the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states that the name is established according to its meaning;
because it is a prison beneath the earth, it is called a "hell. Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "Five hundred *yojanas* below Jambudvīpa, there is this hell.
*Akaniṣṭha* is translated as "Ultimate of Obstruction," which refers to the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Ārūpyadhātu*).
The "six destinies" (ṣadgati) are those of devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
"Destiny" (gati) has the meaning of "direction," referring to how one proceeds toward rebirth within the six realms according to the karma one has created. △ Second, seeing the Buddhas of that land.
Furthermore, one sees the Buddhas currently residing in those lands.
This demonstrates that those Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the five turbidities, which is the same intent as the appearance of the Buddha in this land.
△ Third, hearing the Dharma preached by the Buddhas.

Furthermore, hearing the sutras and dharmas preached by those Buddhas represents that those Buddhas initially [taught] from the single dharma of formlessness; this is not gradual, but sudden, and its intent is the same as when the Buddha of this land first taught the *Avataṃsaka*.
△ Fourth, seeing the fourfold assembly attain the Way.
Furthermore, one sees those various bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs (up to) those practitioners who have attained the Way.
This manifestation of that Buddha is not gradual, yet it is gradual; its intent is the same as that of the Buddha of this land in sequentially expounding the Tripiṭaka.

"Practitioners" refers to those who cultivate the practices of the Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Pāramitās across the Three Vehicles. "Those who have attained the Way" refers to those who have realized the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga).
This is the cultivation of the Way. △ Fifth, seeing the practices of the bodhisattvas:
Furthermore, one sees the various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas (up to) practicing the bodhisattva path with their various characteristics and appearances.
This demonstrates that the intent of the various Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā sūtras preached by that Buddha is the same as what was taught by the Buddha of this land following the Tripiṭaka.
Regarding "various causes and conditions": planting wholesome roots in the past serves as the cause, while receiving the teachings now serves as the condition.
Because Bodhisattvas penetrate all four teachings, they are said to have "various causes and conditions"; each of the four teachings possesses its own four gates.
Because there are various appearances, one knows that the appearances of causes and conditions are of infinite distinct varieties;

all of these are the same as that and this in their wondrous joy. It is said that "causes and conditions" refers to the distinctions between response and stimulus, while "faith and understanding" refers to the different capacities for such stimulation.
"Appearances" refers to the differences in practice following faith. Because there are these differences, it is called "various," even though the paths diverge.
It does not exceed two flavors. △ Sixth, seeing all Buddhas enter nirvana:
furthermore, seeing all Buddhas pass into parinirvāṇa (up to) erecting stupas made of the seven treasures with the relics of the Buddhas.

This is the manifestation of that Buddha’s *prajñā* (wisdom), followed by the provisional opening of the way to reveal the ultimate reality (*śūnyatā*), whereby immeasurable dharmas are gathered back into the single dharma;

his proclamation of entering *nirvāṇa*, the cessation of his transformative activity, and the erection of stupas is identical in intent to the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* by the Buddha of this land.
"Parinirvāṇa" is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term; in its full form, it should be called *mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Regarding "Mahāparinirvāṇa": *mahā* means the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), *nirvāṇa* means liberation (*vimukti*), and *pari* means wisdom (*prajñā*;
here rendered as *du*). It is thus the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*). *Śarīra* is also called *śilāra* or *śarīra*;
it is translated as "sacred relics" (*linggu*) or "bone-body. In Sanskrit, *stūpa* is also called *sodubuo*, which is translated as "square mound" (*fangfen*).
Alternatively, it is translated as "round mound" (*vartula-stūpa*) or "lofty and manifest," referring to the place where the bodily relics are enshrined.
Although the characteristics of the stupa’s construction represent the two sūtras, the specific marks of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* remain hidden.

If, within what is perceived, one also sees the bestowal of predictions upon the śrāvakas and the teaching on the long duration of their lifespans, then the core meaning of the orthodox tradition has already been disclosed; thus, [the current section] would not constitute the introduction. Even now...
Seeing that the single mark of nirvāṇa encompasses the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Commentary states, "opening up the provisional," and so forth.
△ Third, the sequence of the narrative of doubt and reflection, in two parts: first, Maitreya’s doubt and reflection; third, first, the correct recollection of the six auspicious omens.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought: [omitted] "By what causes and conditions does this auspicious omen arise?

Regarding 'spiritual transformations' (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*): 'spirit' (*ṛddhi*) refers to the celestial mind, which is innate wisdom; 'transformation' (*prātihārya*) refers to shifting and changing, which is the manifestation of the six auspicious omens.
The Dharma-king’s power of the Dharma surpasses and benefits all. Maitreya could not fathom these external transformations."

Because he did not know his own inner wisdom, doubt arose; furthermore, since Maitreya had encountered Buddhas and planted many roots of goodness, how could it be that he did not have some vague perception?
It must be that he concealed what was clear and revealed what was obscure, speaking expediently of his ignorance. △ Second, the question of who asked and who answered.

The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "Oldly called *gē*; this is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term. Alternatively, it is called *gētā*, which is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound.

After explaining the sequence of this land, there are two further points: first, according to differences in inclination, some prefer discursive explanations while others prefer metrical verses;
second, according to differences in the arising of understanding, some gain understanding from discursive explanations while others gain it from metrical verses;
third, according to differences in acuity, those who are sharp awaken upon hearing once, whereas those who are dull awaken only after a second explanation.
Wu (悟) further explains that the Buddha spoke with such earnestness and repetition because the assembly had gathered both before and after [the teaching], and thus there are verses [to summarize it].
From "Mañjuśrī, O Guide, for what reason... up to "...his body and mind were refreshed, attaining what he had never experienced before."

The first line of verse describes the auspicious omen of emitting light; the "Guide" refers to the Buddha, for it is precisely because he can lead others through preaching the Dharma and entering meditative absorption that he is called the Guide.
The next one and a half lines describe the auspicious omen of raining flowers. In Sanskrit, this is *candana*;

some say it is not translated here because it does not exist in this land, while others say it is translated according to its meaning as "medicine," because it can eliminate illness. Thus, it is called *candan*.

Regarding "sandalwood-scented wind": wind originally has no fragrance, yet this fragrance is extraordinary; fragrance fundamentally belongs to flowers, and the fragrance of flowers is like that of sandalwood.
Therefore, it is called "sandalwood-scented wind. Now, celestial flowers are supremely wondrous; how could they possess color without fragrance?
This symbolizes that as one proceeds from cause to fruit, it is like a flower possessing fragrance. Once the flowers and the wind have gathered, every stage (bhūmi) is then adorned.
The first half-verse describes how the causes of this manifestation are purified, such that when they reach their fruition, the result is majestic purity.

The next half-verse describes the auspicious omen of the earth’s trembling, and the following verse describes the auspicious omen of the assembly’s joy. △ Second, the verses on questioning the six auspicious omens in other lands;
first, the question concerning sentient beings of the six realms.
The radiance from between his eyebrows shines upon the eastern direction (extending as far as... so that the beauty or ugliness of the retribution received is seen here in its entirety.
Sentient beings are those who go; birth and death are the place to which they go; the conditions of good and evil karma are the causes by which they go;
and the retribution received, whether beautiful or ugly, is the fruit of that which is gone to. △ Second, the verse:
That Buddha preached the Dharma;
furthermore, he beheld the various Buddhas, the Holy Sovereign Lions, who illuminate the Buddha-dharma and awaken sentient beings.
These four lines of verse refer to that Buddha’s teaching of the sudden doctrine (sudden teaching) to suit those of great capacity. "Holy Sovereign" (shèngzhǔ) means holy...
This refers to the "Lord of Lords," meaning that among the retinue of all bodhisattvas, he is the lord; thus he is called the "Noble Lord.
In the Sanskrit language, this is *upasaṃhā*, which is translated as "Lion" (*siṃha*), or alternatively as "Śarabha. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:

"The lion lets out a roar and bellows with a thunderous cry to destroy false lions, to test his own power, and so forth"—this serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s ability to subdue [all adversaries].
Subduing the Army of Māra, he addresses the assembly: because he possesses the ten powers and other such qualities, he is called the Holy Lord, the Lion.

Furthermore, "lion’s roar" refers to definitive teaching; the two previous Lords did not roar like a lion, for their teachings were not definitive and did not discourse upon the true primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
To expound the subtle and supreme Dharma is, as in this land, first [to establish the foundation].
Zhao Gao-shan explains that although the Huayan teaching is said to encompass the Separate (Bie) [Vehicle], it is called "the first" because it is purely Great (Mahāyāna) from the outset.
The two preceding teachings are still mixed with afflictions and are therefore not pure; because they do not reach all capacities, they are not called "gentle and supple.
Since that [teaching] expounds both the Separate and Complete (Yuan) [Vehicles], it is termed "pure and gentle. It instructs all bodhisattvas...

"Sakyamuni" (Sa) refers to the fact that in this land, such as the seven assemblies and so forth, there are no śrāvakas; because both the Separate and Perfect [teachings] equally expound the Middle Way, it is called "the profound and subtle Brahma-sound";
because it accords with principle and is appropriate to the capacities of the listeners, it is said to "cause people to delight in hearing it.

Regarding "each in their own world," there are two meanings of "each": first, the eighteen thousand [worlds] are each distinct; second, the primary and attendant [buddhas] are different, and thus they are each distinct.
The two teachings of Separate and Perfect each have four gates, which are called the "various illuminations of the Buddha-dharma that awaken sentient beings.
This refers to "first seeing my body in this land and entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states:
"Because there are no matters of the three vehicles, it is called 'Buddha-dharma. △ Third, the question regarding the fourfold assembly in other lands. Part one: Opening the sound.
Regarding the hearing of the Hīnayāna:
if a person encounters suffering and, weary of old age, illness, and death, is taught nirvāṇa as the exhaustion of the limits of all suffering—this verse fully elucidates the Four Noble Truths.
"If a person encounters suffering"—where "suffering" encompasses both cause and effect—refers to the two truths of Suffering and its Origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*).
To feel weary of old age, sickness, and death is the Truth of the Path; to preach Nirvana for them is the Truth of Cessation.

If a person encounters suffering yet creates evil karma, their suffering will not come to an end. If a person encounters suffering yet creates wholesome karma, their suffering likewise will not come to an end.
If a person encounters suffering and seeks liberation through the teachings of non-Buddhist paths, they merely increase their views and attachments, which is not the cessation of suffering.

Furthermore, if a person encounters suffering and grows weary of it, and further grows weary of its accumulation, such that they respond to the Buddha’s teaching on *nirvāṇa*, this person will then be able to reach the ultimate end of all suffering.
Regarding *nirvāṇa*, Master Sengzhao’s *Nirvāṇa Treatise* states: "This is called 'extinction and transcendence' (*mie-du*).
It signifies that the great afflictions are forever extinguished and one has transcended the four currents [of existence]. This is the true emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle."
This is *nirvāṇa*. △ Second, opening the path for the Middle Vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas:
If there is a person with merit who has previously made offerings to the Buddha and aspires to seek the supreme Dharma, one should preach the Pratyekabuddha vehicle for them.

"If there is a person with merit" means that while a Śrāvaka plants the seeds of merit over three lifetimes, a Pratyekabuddha plants the seeds of merit over a hundred kalpas; this is what distinguishes them.

Because they are *śrāvakas*, it is said that they possess merit; this means they have cultivated much merit. Because they have made offerings to the Buddhas, this means they have made many offerings to the Buddhas.
Those who "aspire to the supreme Dharma" refer to those who deeply seek the sublime principle of dependent origination; this means they have heard much of the Dharma.

In the Sanskrit language, *pratyekabuddha* is translated here as "Pratyekajñāna" (Solitary Realizer); because they awaken through contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, they are called "Pratyekabuddhas."

Because this is the true principle of reality, it is said that the Pratyekabuddhas have a distinct practice. The *Jì* (Record) states: "The cultivation of the Pratyekabuddhas does not establish intermediate fruits;

they deeply contemplate dependent origination and have long cultivated the three types of merit and wisdom. Since these are flourishing, they preemptively subdue the two habits, and thus they rank above the Śrāvakas.
△ Third, the opening of the Mahāyāna of the Six Perfections.
If there are sons of the Buddha who cultivate various practices to seek unsurpassed wisdom, for their sake the pure path is taught.

Because they are able to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas through true compassion, they are called "sons of the Buddha. Because they cultivate the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), they are said to engage in "various practices.
Because they are resolute in seeking the path of the Buddha, it is called "unsurpassed wisdom. Within the six perfections, there are no six obscurations, just as medicine [removes] illness.
Because there is no illness within it, it is called the "pure path," yet it is not ultimate purity. Miaole (Miaole) says:

"The cultivation of various practices and supreme wisdom is common to all teachings; now, even those of the ordinary and small vehicles obtain the names 'various' and 'supreme,' yet these are not ultimate.
This is spoken provisionally regarding the Three Baskets and the Six Perfections. It is called "the medicine without illness" because there is no illness within the medicine.
Purifying the ears. △ Fourth, concluding the preceding section and opening the subsequent one:
"Mañjuśrī, I abide here... (up to) such a multitude; I shall now briefly explain them."
"To see and hear such as this" refers to seeing the Buddha’s sons and so forth, which constitutes "seeing";
to expound the sutras and preach for them and so forth constitutes "hearing. Because the general outline is roughly sufficient, it says "such as this," which serves to conclude what preceded.
Furthermore, the phrase "and thousands of billions of matters" and so forth opens up what follows; because it continues the subsequent discourse, it says "now."

The Sītā River flows out from each [lake], encircling it once before entering one of the four oceans.
Its sands are finer and more numerous than those of the Gaṅgā; outsiders consider it a river of merit, washing away sins upon entry.
The Buddha also followed worldly convention by frequently pointing to it, and because he often taught the Dharma near this river, he used it as a metaphor. △ Second, the sequential questions.
Sixth, regarding the initial inquiry on *dāna* (giving), there are three parts; first is the inquiry on the relinquishing of wealth. It says:

Again, one sees the Bodhisattva giving his own flesh, hands, feet, wife, and children, seeking the Unsurpassed Way.
One's own flesh and so forth constitute the internal body; one's wife, children, and so forth constitute the external body. △ Third, the question regarding the relinquishing of life:
Furthermore, one sees the Bodhisattva joyfully giving away his head, eyes, and body to seek the wisdom of a Buddha.
To sacrifice one’s head and eyes, and even to sacrifice one’s life, yet not speak of the Dharma, is to defer to the *prajñāpāramitā* hereafter.
△ Second, the inquiry concerning *śīla*.
Mañjuśrī, I see various kings (up to) shaving off their hair and beards and donning the dharma-robes.

Regarding the passage "the various kings shaved off their hair and beards," the commentary states that the inquiry into the precepts (*śīla*) specifically concerns the observance of the precepts by *bhikṣus*.

Because it is easy for householders to practice giving but difficult to observe the precepts, whereas it is difficult for those who have left the home life to practice giving but easy to observe the precepts, the discussion of the precepts is framed here in relation to the *bhikṣu*.

The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary explains that the phrase "went to" (*wang yi*) indicates that he went to no one else; thus, it points to the Buddha's dwelling as the place where the honored one was questioned.

Because it is the unsurpassed path that is utterly supreme, it is called "abandoned" (*atyakta*); because it is not treated with contempt, it is called a "land of bliss" (*sukhāvatī*). Because both body and mind are detached from worldly attachments, it is called "shaving the head.
As for the "Dharma robes," these are the *kāṣāya*. The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) states:

"If the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, engage in strife, they should contemplate this *kāṣāya*, which gives rise to a mind of compassion. This causes the *bhikṣu* to remain peaceful; how could one not endure [this power]? Furthermore, regarding the nāgas...
Obtaining a single strand of gold, he does not swallow it, possessing clarity as described in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. △ Third, the inquiry regarding patience:
"Suppose one sees a bodhisattva who has become a bhikṣu, dwelling alone in a secluded and quiet place, delighting in the recitation of the sūtras."
There are three kinds of patience (*kṣānti*): enduring wicked people and ferocious beasts in secluded groves and deep valleys without harboring anger is the patience of birth;
restraining oneself and maintaining one's resolve is the patience of ascetic practice (*duṣkaracaryā*); and seeking the Buddha-way is the patience of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Furthermore, being a bhikṣu is the patience of ascetic practice; dwelling alone in quietude is the patience of birth; and delighting in the recitation of the sūtras is [the patience of the ultimate truth].
This is the patience regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*). △ Fourth, the inquiry into diligence:
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas who, with courageous diligence, enter deep mountains to contemplate the Buddha-way.
Now, deep mountains are fearsome and are not the dwelling place of those who are indolent or timid; only those of courageous progress can find peace therein. Beside...
If there is no [conceptual] object, one contemplates and cultivates the true mark (*dharmatā*), never ceasing for a single thought-moment, as they advance in their quest for the Buddha-way.
△ Fifth, the inquiry regarding meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), in two parts: first, the inquiry regarding fundamental dhyāna.

Furthermore, one sees those who, having detached from desire, constantly dwell in seclusion and deeply cultivate meditative concentration, thereby attaining the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

Those who have detached from desire practice the fundamental *pṛṣṭhābhimukha-vimokṣa* (back-turning deliverances) according to both the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) Teachings, as well as meditations such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to detach from the desires of the desire realm.

The *Bie* (Distinct) Teaching further includes detachment from the desires of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). The *Yuan* (Perfect) Teaching, moreover, involves detachment from the desire for the "Dharma-love" that accords with the Path.

Those who deeply cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) may give rise to a single grade of the first dhyāna; this concentration is not yet profound, and so on up to the ninth grade, transmitted in succession.

According to tradition, one who has deeply mastered this samādhi possesses mastery over transformation and is able to manifest the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Ordinary beings possess only five of these powers;

those of the Two Vehicles possess all six. In the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), even though Bodhisattvas share in the portion of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states belonging to the Buddha, they are still said to possess only the five supernormal powers.

In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), which is based on principle, both the beginning and the end possess all six supernormal powers. If speaking according to reality, from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) onward, they likewise [possess them].
They merely attain the untainted supernormal powers (*anāsrava-abhijñā*). Regarding the six supernormal powers: first, the divine eye; second, the divine ear; third, knowledge of others' minds;

fourth, recollection of past lives; fifth, mastery over bodily form; and sixth, the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). What is here called the attainment of the five supernormal powers refers to not yet having attained the ultimate power of the exhaustion of outflows.
Although those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who have exhausted both views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are said to possess all six, if one looks toward [the goal of] Bodhi...

The Bodhisattvas likewise have only five [faculties], because their ignorance of the Separate and Perfect Teachings (*vyavasthāna-vibhūti* and *pariniṣpanna*) has not yet been exhausted, and they have only partially realized the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
△ Second, the question regarding supramundane dhyāna:
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas sitting in peaceful meditation (*samādhi*), joining their palms, and praising the Kings of Dharma with ten million verses.

This is the meditation of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], wherein stillness and distraction do not obstruct one another; one does not arise from the meditative concentration of cessation yet manifests all manner of dignified conduct.
Like the lute of the asuras, which produces melody without being struck, it manifests form through resonance despite being without conditions or thought.
Therefore, one is able to dwell peacefully in dhyāna while praising the Buddha. △ Sixth: Questions on Prajñā, Part One: First, the question regarding self-cultivation.
Furthermore, one sees that the Bodhisattvas possess profound wisdom and firm resolve, such that they are able to question the Buddhas and, having heard [the teachings], receive and uphold them all.
"Profound wisdom" means that their insight exhausts the fundamental principles; "firm resolve" means that their vows are vast and great.
These two types of adornment enable them both to question and to maintain [the Dharma]. △ Second, questioning for the sake of transforming others.
Furthermore, one sees the sons of the Buddha endowed with both meditative concentration and wisdom (up to) shattering the hosts of Māra and beating the Dharma drum.
"Endowed with both meditative concentration and wisdom" refers to those dwelling on the stages of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings] who are then fully possessed of them.
"Immeasurable metaphors" refers to the various skillful means within the various teachings that employ countless analogies to assist in revealing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the vanquishing of the hosts of Māra: the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) vanquishes the four Māras; the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*) successively vanquishes the eight Māras; and the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama*) perfectly vanquishes the eight Māras.
In the Sanskrit language, *māra* means "one who can take away life. The Māra of Death (*mṛtyu-māra*) truly can take away life.

The remaining—the Māra of Afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the Māra of the Five Aggregates (*pañca-skandha-māra*), and the Māra of the Lord of Heaven (*devaputra-māra*)—can create the causes and conditions for taking away life, and they can also take it away themselves.

Because it is the life-force of wisdom, all four Māras are said to be able to snatch away that life. It is also translated as "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*), because they act as hindrances for those practicing the Way;
the first three Māras can thus be understood accordingly. Regarding the Heavenly Lord Māra (*devaputra-māra*), the *Chuiyu ji* states:

"On the sixth heaven there is a separate abode for Māra, which is subsumed under the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*). Since one has already defeated Māra, [the following] should..."

Regarding the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, it is said that "beating the Dharma drum" means that upon the initial stage of the Bodhisattva path (the Stage of Initial Resolve), one attains perfect enlightenment and acts as a Buddha within a hundred Buddha-worlds, awakening sentient beings with the true and wondrous Brahma-voice; this is precisely the complete beating of the Brahma-wheel Dharma drum.

As for the "eight māras" mentioned in the *Fuxing* (Subsidiary Practices): these refer to the four [māras] beginning with the *skandha-māra*, along with the four beginning with impermanence (*anitya*). This is according to the ancient translations.

In the sutras and śāstras, the character for *māra* (魔) was written with the "stone" radical (*shí*) since the time of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty; however, it is argued that because *māra* can afflict and disturb people, the character should properly have the "ghost" radical (*guǐ*).
