Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas dwelling in forests emitting light to rescue those in the hells from suffering and lead them into the Buddha-way.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "It is easy to cultivate compassion in the first dhyāna, joy in the second dhyāna, and loving-kindness in the third dhyāna."

In the cultivation of equanimity (*upekṣā*) within the four dhyānas, since it is said that the dhyāna of compassion (*karuṇā*) therein is for the sake of transforming others, it cannot be the case that this applies solely to the first dhyāna.
Thus we know that for each and every dhyāna, one should speak of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) up to sympathetic joy (*muditā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*). △ Third, the question on diligence (*vīrya*).
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha who never sleep, walking in meditation groves and diligently seeking the Buddha-way.
"Never sleeping" refers to such dharma-gates as the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* (Banzhou Nianfo). Regarding sleep, the *Zhiguan* states:
"The mind and spirit being murky and dark is 'sleep'; the six consciousnesses being obscured and blocked while the four great elements become lax and unrestrained is 'slumber. △ Three.
Questioning on *śīla*:
Furthermore, one sees those who possess the precepts and whose majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) is flawless, as pure as a precious gem, seeking the path to Buddhahood.
That their majestic deportment is flawless is the first, the "unimpaired precept"; that they are pure like a precious gem is the tenth, the "ultimate."

Regarding the ultimate precepts (*atyanta-śīla*), it suffices to cite the beginning and the end, as the middle can be understood by implication. The *Mahā-śāstra* clarifies the ten aspects of the precepts:

first, being unimpaired; second, being unbroken; third, being unpierced; fourth, being unmixed; fifth, following the Path; sixth, being unattached; seventh, being praised by the wise; eighth, being sovereign;
ninth, following meditative concentration; and tenth, being complete—this is precisely the ultimate. Now, these ten from beginning to end are all the Bodhi...
Therefore, they all seek the Buddha-way. △ Fourth, the inquiry on patience:
Furthermore, one sees the sons of the Buddha abiding in the power of patience (until) being able to endure everything in order to seek the Buddha-way.
Regarding patience (*kṣānti*), the *Dharmadhātu-krama* states that it is so named because the inner mind is able to endure external offenses.
There are two types: first, patience toward sentient beings (*sattva-kṣānti*); second, patience regarding phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*). Patience toward sentient beings has two aspects:
first, being able to endure without attachment when receiving respect and offerings, such that pride and negligence do not arise; second, [enduring] anger, abuse, beating, and harm.

Furthermore, being able to endure mosquitoes, gnats, and the like, such that no anger or affliction arises, constitutes the practice of patience toward living beings (*sattva-kṣānti*) and patience toward phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*). This patience is also twofold:
first, those not consisting of mental factors (*acaitasika-dharma*), namely cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, thirst, old age, and illness;

second, those consisting of mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), namely anger, sorrow, desire, pride, and various false views. To be able to endure these two types of phenomena without being moved is called [patience].
Regarding the power of the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), the *Āgama* Sūtras state that there are six kinds of powers: the crying of a child is its power; the anger of a woman is her power;
the arrogance of a king is his power; the advancement of an Arhat is his power; the compassion of the Buddhas is their power; and the forbearance of a bhikṣu is his power.
The *Śāriputra-śīla-sūtra* (Yijiao jing) states: "If one cannot endure the poison of malicious abuse, it is like drinking [poison]."
Regarding "ambrosia" (amṛta), it is not merely called the wisdom of one who has entered the Path. *Miaole* says: "The first half-verse refers to the person capable of endurance;
the next half-verse refers to the objects of endurance; and the final half-verse refers to the application of the intent of endurance. △ Fifth, further questioning on dhyāna.
Furthermore, he saw Bodhisattvas who, for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, remained free from all frivolous laughter in their pursuit of the Buddha-way.
Being free from frivolous laughter dispels the hindrance of restlessness and regret; being free from the company of delusion dispels the hindrance of hatred;

associating with the wise dispels the hindrance of doubt; single-mindedness dispels confusion and removes the hindrance of greed; and withdrawing the mind to dwell in mountain forests removes [the hindrance of sensual desire].
Regarding the "Exquisite Joy of the Sleep-Covering," the first one and a half lines clarify what is abandoned; the subsequent half line clarifies the intent of abandoning it.
According to various teachings on dhyāna, all abandon the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) with the intent of [attaining] the Buddha-way. As Kāśyapa says in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*:
"There are four things that must be swiftly abandoned and fled from beyond a hundred yojanas: first, gain and honor; second, evil friends; third, evil... [evil speech].

The multitude of those living together in the fourfold community engage in much joking, laughter, anger, and quarreling. △ Six: Questions on Dāna (Giving). First, regarding the four matters of giving:
seeing a bodhisattva [offering] delicacies, food, and drink (up to) flowing springs and bathing pools as gifts to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "The first line refers to two things, namely food and drink and medicinal decoctions; the next line refers to clothing;
the following two lines refer to bedding, dwellings, and so forth—'yāo-zū' means side dishes, and 'shàn' refers to fine delicacies. △ Second, the conclusion of the giving.
Thus, through such various kinds of giving, they experience subtle and wondrous joy without weariness, seeking the unsurpassed path.
△ Seventh: Inquiry into Prajñā. Part One: Prajñā that is Ineffable yet Spoken.
There may be bodhisattvas who preach the dharma of quiescence, providing various instructions for countless sentient beings.

Although the ultimate principle of quiescence is fundamentally inexpressible, because there are causes and conditions, it can also be expressed; thus they provide instruction through refined and elegant terminology to guide and transform others.
△ Second, contemplating the *prajñā* that cannot be contemplated.
Alternatively, one may see the Bodhisattva contemplating the nature of all phenomena as being without dual characteristics, just like empty space.
Although the nature of all phenomena is empty and fundamentally cannot be contemplated, it can be contemplated by practicing in accordance with that nature.
△ Third, explaining and contemplating the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha whose minds are unattached, seeking the unsurpassed path through this wondrous wisdom.

This non-attachment of the mind is precisely the cessation of the mind’s sphere of activity; because the mind is unattached, it is necessarily free from verbal expression—that is, the path of language is severed.
When the path of language is severed, the preceding initial practices are obliterated; thus, that which is unspeakable is spoken of as "mind."
The sphere of practice is extinguished and merged; the preceding and succeeding practices cannot be observed, yet they are observed. Although both are merged, there is speech and illumination.
△ Sixth: Questioning the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa. Part One: Marking the Buddha’s Extinction and the Erection of Stūpas.
Mañjuśrī, furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, make offerings to his relics.
Second, regarding the number of stupas:
they further see sons of the Buddha constructing countless *sāgara-nidhi* (Ganges-sand) numbers of stupas and temples, adorning the realms.
△ Third, the dimensions of the stūpa:
The precious stūpa is five thousand yojanas in height and its length and breadth are both exactly two thousand yojanas.
△ Fourth, the adornments of the stūpa’s appearance.
Each stupa and temple had a thousand banners and streamers, with jeweled lattices and canopies from which precious bells chimed harmoniously.
"Màn" (mò yáng qiè) refers to a curtain; "jiāo" means interlaced, and "lù" means manifest or exposed. △ Fifth, the explanation of the various implements for making offerings.
The devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans constantly made offerings with incense, flowers, and music.
△ Sixth, the conclusion on making offerings to stūpas and temples:
"Mañjuśrī and the sons of the Buddhas... [up to] ...like the king of celestial trees, its flowers in full bloom."
The Heavenly King of Trees is the Pārijātaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, translated here as "Perfectly Round" (Yuánshēng).
A major sūtra states that the tree is one hundred yojanas high, with roots fifty yojanas deep and branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas wide;
its floral fragrance pervades fifty yojanas, and its radiance illuminates eighty yojanas. △ Second, the verse requesting an answer.
Second, first raising a doubt and stating a request: Third, first raising the matter of what was seen in this land.
When the Buddha emitted a single ray of light, I and the assembly saw this world-realm in all its various wonders and excellences.
△ Second, citing the matter of seeing other lands:
The supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) of all Buddhas are rare and marvelous; they emit a single pure light that illuminates immeasurable lands.
The first two phrases praise the source of this light, which is precisely their supernatural power and wisdom. The mention of "all Buddhas" is used to illustrate through the many the one.
The first phrase specifically points to Śākyamuni’s rarity; it is precisely because he was not so before that he is called "rare.
The third phrase praises the essence of the light, which is pure due to two factors. The fourth phrase praises the function of the light, namely the lands it illuminates;
since they exceed eighteen thousand, they are called "immeasurable," and the previous establishment of a specific number was merely for the sake of convenience.
That which is signified. △ Third, requesting an answer to resolve the doubts of the assembly:
"We have seen this, which we have never before encountered; O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, we pray that you resolve the doubts of the assembly.

"To see this" refers to seeing the auspicious signs in the two lands; because these differ from those of a single transformation [land], they are called "unprecedented. "O Sons of the Buddha" [is addressed to] all the Bodhisattvas.
Because these matters of doubt are not trivial, I respectfully submit them again; it is not solely for my own sake that I speak of "the assembly.
△ Second, the explanation of the four underlying difficulties, part one: the direct explanation.
"The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy, gazing upon both you and me... [until] ...and seeing the various Buddhas; this is no small cause."

These four lines of verse explain the resolution of anticipated objections (*pūrvapakṣa*). Regarding "anticipated objections," Mañjuśrī internally formulated these difficulties and was unwilling to answer immediately;
his intention had three aspects: first, this auspicious omen is rare and extraordinary, and it cannot be hastily or lightly adjudicated;

second, the assembly of the wise is as vast as the ocean, and he humbly defers to their superior brilliance; third, he is hesitant and reticent, giving rise to the yearning and admiration of the multitude.
Therefore, he suppressed his objections and rejected them in secret. Maitreya’s manifest explanation of the intent behind these objections also has three points:
first, when omens are great and doubts are profound, if one does not resolve them, anxiety will linger in the heart, obstructing the hearing of the true teaching;

second, the assembly is as vast as the ocean, and their capacities rest upon you, O Benevolent One; third, the entire multitude looks up to you, and thus we know that they have focused their sincerity with profound earnestness. This is why—
Manifesting the Words to Resolve Difficulties and Requesting an Immediate Response: First, Subduing the Objections. These objections arise because of the formal request. The request says:
"O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, please resolve the doubts of the assembly. Mañjuśrī then first subdues the objection:

"You say there are doubts in the assembly, yet the assembly has never doubted. If they were in doubt, they should ask; since the assembly does not doubt, what is there for me to resolve? Maitreya then [responds].
The first verse explains: "The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy, both for me and for those like me;
they wish for me to question you, desiring that you grant them an answer. Mañjuśrī, based on this, raises the second objection: "The assembly shares the same doubt, which is not easily answered;
wait until the Buddha emerges from meditative absorption, and then the doubt shall be resolved. Maitreya then employs the second verse.

Śāriputra, if there is doubt lingering in your breast or anxiety that prevents you from being at ease, you should answer at the proper time; furthermore, you should know when the Tathāgata will emerge from his meditative absorption.
Therefore it is said: "O Son of the Buddha, answer in due time to resolve doubts and bring joy. Because of this, Mañjuśrī raised the third objection:
"I and you both dwell on the stage of training; we wish to fathom the subtle intent of the Buddha and deliberate upon it together in private."
When [Mañjuśrī] asked me to respond, it was logically impossible for me to do so; Maitreya then explained this with the third verse.
My mind also reflected deeply and hesitated between two poles: whether he would preach the wondrous Dharma or whether he would bestow a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

Therefore, he said that the wondrous Dharma attained by the Buddha while sitting at the site of enlightenment—whether he intended to preach this or to bestow a prediction—was the reason Mañjuśrī rose from his seat for the third time.
The four objections: "If it is as you say, this is already a resolution of doubts; why trouble yourself to answer? Maitreya then used the fourth verse to explain:
'How could one with a mind of hesitation judge such a great matter? He said, 'He reveals the various Buddha-lands; this is no small cause.
Once Wen-shu’s (Mañjuśrī) challenges were exhausted, his modesty and humility also ceased; thus he raised these questions."
In the preface, Mañjuśrī’s subduing of the four difficulties represents the hidden [aspect], while Maitreya’s explanation through the four verses represents the manifest [aspect].

Mañjuśrī acts as the guest and Maitreya as the host. Regarding these four hidden difficulties, Guangzhai received them from his immediate predecessor, who in turn received them from Master Zhao of the North of the River.
Since these were the former sages, their ingenious insights beyond the literal text were truly celestial.

In the "Preface to the Questions and Answers" (*Xia dawen xu*), Tiantai states that if Maitreya remains subdued by the four doubts, he is "latent," whereas Manjusri’s explanation through the four verses is "manifest.
Here, Maitreya acts as the guest and Manjusri as the host;
this is a subtle insight beyond the literal text originating from Tiantai, not a transmission of another commentary. △ Second, the conclusion of the request.
Mañjuśrī, you should know that the fourfold assembly, the nāgas, and the spirits are all gazing upon you, wondering what you will preach.
△ Section Five: The Introduction to the Answers to the Questions, Part Two: The Extended Prose (Gadya), Subsection Four: First, Self-Reflection on the Answer, Part One: Indicating the Chapters.
At that time, Mañjuśrī said to Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: “...as I contemplate (*vitarka*).

‘Contemplate’ means to think; ‘contemplate’ means to deliberate. To contemplate now as it was in the past, and to deliberate on the past as it is now—how could Mañjuśrī, an ancient Buddha, not know [this], yet manifest such contemplation as a trace? △ Second, the actual contemplation.
Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, desires to preach the Great Dharma (up to: to beat the great Dharma drum and expound the meaning of the Great Dharma.

As for "desiring to preach the Great Dharma," it refers to how in the past all Buddhas, after preaching the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, then opened up the provisional to reveal the real, gathering the immeasurable back into the one.
Considering that the present Buddha has already preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, he likewise ought to [proceed accordingly].
To open up the provisional and reveal the real, and to bring the immeasurable back to the one—this is the Great Dharma.

As for the raining down of the rain of the Great Dharma, it was only after the ancient Buddhas rained the four flowers that all were moistened by this single rain and universally entered the perfect causes of the stages of abiding, practice, transference, and realization;
by analogy with the present Buddha’s raining of flowers, it should likewise be that all are moistened by this single rain.

Because all have attained the causes for Buddhahood through the stages of abiding, practice, and penetration (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*), it is said that "the great rain of Dharma falls. Regarding "blowing the great conch of Dharma":
blowing the conch signifies a change in designation. Just as in the past, when the fourfold assembly beheld this auspicious omen, they rejoiced;

their obstructions were removed, their faculties were activated, and they were immediately transformed—such that both the teaching and the practice-principle became one—so too should the present assembly rejoice, for their obstructions must likewise be removed, their faculties activated, and they transformed by the teaching.
The principles of practice are all one; since the transformation has already become profound, it is said that he "blows the great Dharma-conch.
As for "beating the great Dharma-drum," this is like sounding the drum to warn the soldiers; it is a metaphor for destroying ignorance.

Considering that in the past, immediately after the earth shook, there were six occasions of destroying the thieves of ignorance, I infer that now, following the Buddha’s shaking of the earth, there should likewise be six occasions of destroying ignorance.
Because the sound of the teachings is most sublime, it is said that he "beats the great Dharma drum. Regarding the "expounding of the great Dharma meaning":

since the Buddhas of the past emitted light from the white tuft between their brows and immediately thereafter preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one should infer that after the present Buddha has likewise emitted light, he too must immediately preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
thus, it is said that he "expounds the great Dharma meaning. These five phrases are all [as follows].
"Reflecting on the past, I now infer the present by analogy with the past. △ Second, a brief answer based on what was previously seen:
"O sons of good family, regarding my [encounters] with the Buddhas of the past... (up to)... therefore I manifest this auspicious sign."
Initially, I deliberated with my own wisdom; now, I respond based on what I have briefly observed. This is intended so that all sentient beings may hear and know it.

"Hearing" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), and "knowing" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). By condensing the immeasurable into a single transformation, this reconciles the doctrines and principles of the Three Vehicles.
Through the sixfold destruction of ignorance and so forth, it reveals, awakens, and causes entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, it is called "all."
This is a teaching difficult for the world to believe. △ Third, the detailed response concerning what was previously seen, in three parts.
First, citing the initial Buddha, identical in three respects; first, the time period:
"O sons of good family, as in the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago..."
In the Sanskrit language, *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* means "an incalculable period of time. △ Second, the designation of the name:
At that time there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp Brightness) [up to] Teacher of Gods and Humans, the World-Honored One.

*Śālendrarāja-prabhāsa* (Sun-Moon-Lamp-Illumination) is a specific epithet, while *Tathāgata* and the others are general epithets. Since every Buddha’s *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) possesses these ten, they are called general epithets.
To provide a concise summary of the meaning of these ten titles: "Tathāgata" means one who is free from falsehood; "Arhat" means a worthy field of merit;
"Samyak-saṃbuddha" means one who knows the *dharmadhātu*; and "Vidyācaraṇa-sampanna" means one who is endowed with the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
One who is perfected in knowledge and conduct and does not return again is named the Well-Gone (Sugata); one who knows the realms of sentient beings is named the Knower of the World (Lokavid);

one who is without equal is named the Unsurpassed One (Anuttara); one who tames the minds of others is named the Tamer of Men (Puruṣadamyasārathi); one who serves as the eye for sentient beings is named the Teacher of Gods and Humans (Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām);
one who knows the three groups [of beings] is named the Buddha. Possessing these ten virtues, he is named the Honored One of the World (Lokaguru). These are the ten titles.
Regarding the differences in how the titles of the sūtras and śāstras are expanded or condensed: the *Mahā-saṃnipāta-sūtra* commentary explains [the epithets] as eleven phrases;

the third chapter of the *Mahā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* combines "Unsurpassed Being" (*anuttara-puruṣa*) and "Tamer of Men" (*sārathi-sattvānām*) into a single phrase, making "World-Honored One" (*bhagavān*) the tenth phrase. The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states:
"First is the Tathāgata, and so on up to the tenth, the Buddha; being fully endowed with these ten titles, he is named the Honored One among the World."
△ Third, the exposition of the Dharma. Part one: clarifying that the initial teaching is identical to the Sudden Teaching.
He expounded the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, and is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy Brahma-conduct.
The three excellences of beginning, middle, and end refer to the three sections of the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Circulation of the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*);

these are called the "excellence of timing. Their meaning is profound and far-reaching; this refers to the definitive principle (*nītārtha*) of the Sudden Teaching, which the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot fathom to its limits or depths, and is thus called "profound and far-reaching"—this is the "excellence of meaning.
Its phrasing is skillful and subtle; this refers to the [Sudden Teaching]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content available up to that point.*
The eight tones of speech that expound the convergence of principles and speak directly to gladden the minds of Bodhisattvas are called "excellence of speech.
Being pure and without admixture, not shared with those of the Two Vehicles, it constitutes the sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*).

That which is uniquely and fully endowed with excellence clarifies the dharmas of both the internal and external realms through the *pūrṇa* (full) syllables; this is the perfect excellence of the sudden teaching, pure and non-dual.
That "marginal flaws and impurities" refers to the characteristics of the sudden teaching’s harmonious and well-cultivated pure conduct;

that "sudden teaching’s unconditioned benevolence and compassion" means that this Mañjuśrī’s citation of the seven excellences (*saptakuśala*) of the ancient Buddhas’ sudden teaching is identical to the seven excellences now taught by the present Buddha in the sudden manner.
△ Second, the identity with the gradual teachings opened after the sudden.
For those seeking the state of a Śrāvaka (up to) for the sake of all Bodhisattvas, he taught that they should practice the six pāramitās.

Because they hear the Buddha’s voice and teachings, they are called Śrāvakas. Since the four—suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—are all examined as true and not false, they are named the Four Noble Truths.
Regarding śamatha and vipaśyanā: "Suffering" refers to the shifting of the three characteristics (arising, changing, and ceasing); "origin" refers to the flowing of the four minds.
When the path (consisting of the divisions of greed, anger, and delusion) moves, its antidote is easily usurped (as enlightenment and afflictions tilt against one another);

when it ceases, existence is extinguished and returns to non-existence (extinguishing the twenty-five states of existence and returning to *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*). This *nirvāṇa* is precisely the *śūnyatā-nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). Previously, it was asked:
"If a person encounters suffering, for whom do you preach *nirvāṇa*? Now, Mañjuśrī cites the sequence of the ancient Buddhas following the Sudden Teaching.
This Śrāvaka vehicle is opened in order to answer this question. In Sanskrit, *pratyekabuddha* means "solitary enlightened one" (*yuanjue*);

because they awaken to the principle of ultimate truth by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, they are called "solitary enlightened ones. The twelve links of dependent origination are:

first, ignorance (*avidyā*)—so called because there is nothing clearly understood; this refers to all afflictions of the past. Second, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)—the act of conditioning is called "formations"; this refers to karma of the past.

3. Consciousness (*vijñāna*): Since there are afflictions and karma, the deluded thoughts of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) enter and take up residence in the mother’s womb; this is termed "consciousness. 4. Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): "Name" refers to the mind; "form" refers to physical substance. 5. Six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*): The six faculties are formed within this womb;

because these faculties have the meaning of "entering" toward sensory objects, they are termed "bases. 6. Contact (*sparśa*): After emerging from the womb, contact occurs through the faculties encountering their respective objects; this is termed "contact. 7. Feeling (*vedanā*): Due to the contact between the six objects and the six faculties, one experiences the preceding realm;

this is termed "feeling. 8. Craving (*tṛṣṇā*): Greed for the five desires is termed "craving. 9. Grasping (*upādāna*): Giving rise to a mind of attachment toward the realms of the five sensory objects is termed "grasping."

This is called "grasping" (upādāna). Tenth is "existence" (bhava): the essence of this is karma; because past formations, through wholesome or unwholesome karma, lead to rebirth within the three realms of existence, it is called "existence.

Eleventh is "birth" (jāti): from existence, one again receives the body of the five aggregates in a future life; this is called "birth. Twelfth is "aging and death" (jarāmaraṇa): the maturation and decay of the body of the five aggregates resulting from birth is called "death.

Because ignorance, formations, and so forth, successively induce results as causes and mutually depend upon one another as conditions, they are called the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda).
The Emperor asked: "If there are people with merit who seek the supreme Dharma, how should they proceed?
Now, Mañjuśrī, following the sequence of the ancient Buddhas, also opens this intermediate vehicle (*madhyama-yāna*) to answer this question.

As for the six *pāramitās*—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—these are the six *pāramitās*. This is translated as "reaching the other shore" (*pāra-gata*).
Taking birth and death as this shore and nirvana as the other shore—this is because by practicing these six perfections, one is able to reach nirvana.
It is also said that "the task is completed," meaning that the Bodhisattva universally cultivates all modes of practice for the sake of sentient beings until they are fully perfected.
The previous question asked about the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of various practices; now, Mañjuśrī cites the ancient Buddhas in succession.
Following the Sudden [teaching], the Bodhisattva Vehicle of the Six Perfections was also opened to answer this question.

As with the three vehicles mentioned above, it is clear that the ancient Buddhas taught the gradual after the sudden, which is the same as the present Buddha’s teaching of the gradual. △ Third, the identity of the revelation of reality following the sudden and gradual.
It causes them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieve the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Regarding this "knowledge of all modes," the *Guanyin xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of Avalokiteśvara) states:

"The ability, within a single mode of knowledge, to know all paths and know all modes—the single mark of quiescent extinction (*ekalakṣaṇa-nirvāṇa-lakṣaṇa*)—and to be able to know and understand the various categories of practices, is called 'one [mode of knowledge]'."
The knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) is precisely the Buddha-wisdom. △ Second, citing that twenty thousand Buddhas were likewise [so named].
Next, there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa... (up to) the Dharma he preached was good in the beginning, middle, and end.
First, citing one Buddha, it fully enumerates both the sudden and gradual teachings as being identical to those of the present Buddha;

then, citing twenty thousand Buddhas, it mentions only the teaching of the sudden [Dharma] as being identical to that of the present Buddha; therefore, it is said that the Dharma they preach is "good in the beginning, middle, and end.

Finally, citing one Buddha, it mentions only the opening of the gradual [teachings] as being identical to those of the present Buddha; therefore, it is said that he preaches Mahāyāna sūtras named "The Nameless."
The reason why the meanings of the measures are thus is that when Mañjuśrī saw them, they all possessed the five flavors;

however, because Mañjuśrī skillfully explained them to avoid prolixity, he pointed only to the first Buddha, from which the others can be known. Thus, the middle and final [Buddhas] are cited by analogy, merely being mentioned alternately.
*Phalada* means "swift" here, and is also called "sharp-rooted. △ Third, citing the final Buddha.
The events witnessed at the beginning of the third [eon] are identical to those of the present.
That final Buddha, before he had gone forth into homelessness, had already planted the roots of all manner of goodness under tens of millions of Buddhas.

In the past, the Buddha had eight sons; now, this Buddha has one son. Although their numbers are unequal, they both appeared in the same land of cohabitation and both manifested the possession of sons.
The birth of one son represents the singular purity of the One Way, while the birth of eight sons represents the Eightfold Noble Path.
Though their numbers differ, we take up the fact that they both possessed sons as being identical. Thus it is said:

To give rise to the Mahāyāna mind is precisely the Four Great Vows. The *brahmacarya* (pure conduct) consists of the practices of compassion, joy, and equanimity, which are acts for transforming others during the stage of causal cultivation.
△ Second, the past events and the present are identical; this has two parts: first, the similarity of the manifest signs, with a further division into two:
first, clarifying the six auspicious omens in this land.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa [shone] throughout eighteen thousand buddha-lands in the eastern direction, leaving no place unilluminated.

This light [indicates] that the six auspicious omens in the Buddha’s own land were identical to those of the present; first, his arrival at the site of the Buddha and being protected by his mindfulness corresponds to the preaching of this Dharma;
second, from the conclusion of preaching this sutra until the point where body and mind become immovable corresponds to entering meditative concentration.
From "At this time" up to "and the great assembly," the rain of flowers is identical to the fourth [section];

from "the earth shook in six ways" up to "this earthquake is identical to the fifth"; from "at that time, within the assembly" up to "with one mind contemplating the Buddha," the joy of the multitude is identical to the sixth;
from "at that time, the Tathāgata" up to "there was nowhere it did not pervade," the emission of light is identical [to the seventh]. △ Second.
This clarifies the six auspicious omens in other lands.

Just as we see these various Buddha-lands now, it is said in general that by seeing what is seen now, one knows that the six auspicious omens in the other lands of past Buddhas were also identical to those of the present. △
Second, the doubt is the same.

Maitreya, you should know that the doubts in the assembly at that time—up to the desire to know the causes and conditions for which this light was manifested—are identical to the doubts of Maitreya now. △ Second, [the section on] having previously seen it.
The events are identical to those of the present; the first six points concern the identity of the person.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Prabhāsa who had eight hundred disciples.

Just as the Buddha of the past entered meditative concentration and caused Prabhāsa to preach the sutra, so too does the Buddha of the present enter meditative concentration and cause Śāriputra to preach the sutra. This is precisely the case.

The basis for this is that the persons involved were the same: in the past, the eight sons of the Buddha studied under the Tathāgata Wonderful Light (*Prabhāsa*), and upon emerging from meditative absorption, the Buddha addressed Wonderful Light and entrusted [the teaching] to him;
now, the Buddha’s son Rāhula also studied under Śāriputra, and upon emerging from meditative absorption, the Buddha likewise addressed Śāriputra and entrusted [the teaching] to him.
Thus, the sequence of the Trace Gate (*jijimon*) is concluded. Therefore, they are the same. This is what those who harbor doubts [ask].
It is said that Wuliangguang (Prabhāsa) was a bodhisattva while Śāriputra was a śrāvaka; how can these two be the same?

Past events have already been revealed, yet while he was called a bodhisattva, his present activity had not yet emerged, so he was merely referred to as a śrāvaka. When the time comes for his true identity to be disclosed, Śāriputra will be seen as a great bodhisattva and no longer the same [as before].
As for the past manifestation of Wuliangguang, why must he not have acted as a śrāvaka? It is simply a matter of expediency.
This is because Mañjuśrī skillfully employs the expedient means of concealment and manifestation. Regarding the "disciple," the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā* states:

"The teacher possesses the capacity to mold and perfect, while the student possesses the virtue of being a worthy recipient. 'Worthy recipient' means that one leaves one's father to follow the teacher and honors the teacher as a father;
yet the teacher, in his humility, treats the student as a younger brother. △ Second, the sameness of preaching the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa [taught] the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas.
△ Third, the duration of time is the same:
for sixty intermediate kalpas he did not rise from his seat, [and] neither in body nor mind did he give rise to weariness or fatigue.
In the past, when the Buddha preached the sutra, he did not rise from his seat for sixty small kalpas; now, when the Buddha preaches the sutra, fifty small kalpas are said to be like half a day.

Thus, the duration of time is the same. The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states that although the numbers sixty and fifty, as well as "a meal's time" and "half a day," appear slightly different, they are all instances of the long being perceived as short; therefore, it is said they are the same. One must understand this.
Believing that the scriptural account of sixty minor *kalpas* is not false, his resolve to hear the Dharma was further strengthened by the Buddha’s majestic power;
thus, he sat for the duration of that time, forgetting its length. In the Sanskrit language, *kalpa* means "the differentiation of time.
At the beginning of a *kalpa*, when the human lifespan was ten years, a son’s age was twice that of his father’s; in this manner, it increased until the lifespan reached eighty-four thousand years.
After the first hundred years, it decreases by one year; thus it continues to decrease until it reaches ten years. One such period of increase and decrease constitutes a small kalpa (*antarakalpa*).

Twenty such cycles of increase and decrease constitute a medium kalpa (*madhyakalpa*). The periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness each consist of twenty such cycles of increase and decrease, thereby forming a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).
As for the statement that the kalpa of emptiness also consists of twenty cycles of increase and decrease, this is merely a conventional designation.
Speaking in terms of the duration of a *kalpa*, the present appearance of Śākyamuni in the world falls precisely within the ninth *antarakalpa* of decrease among the twenty minor *kalpas*.
△ Third, the proclamation of his parinirvāṇa is the same.
The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa [will remain] for sixty intermediate kalpas until he enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Previously, when that Buddha preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he announced his entry into extinction; this was just as Kāśyapa Buddha, because the land was pure, announced his extinction within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and then entered extinction.
Now, in the "Jeweled Stūpa" chapter (*Ratnakoṭi-parivarta*), it is clarified that the Tathāgata does not...
It has been long since he was destined to enter *nirvāṇa*; his transformation through the Way is complete, and he has proclaimed the cessation of his worldly activities.
Regarding Brahmā and Māra: Brahmā is the lord of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and is also the lord of the three realms; Māra is the lord of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

"Śramaṇa" is translated here as "diligent in cessation," for one diligently practices various virtues and brings all evils to rest. "Brāhmaṇa" is translated here as "pure conduct"; [this refers to] non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*).
In the middle [section], it says "those who have left the household life" (zhong chujia), meaning those of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
△ Fifth, the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is the same. At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakośa... [up to] ...an Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Regarding the "bestowal of a prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*): the holy word states that to bestow [a prediction] means to grant it; to "predict" (*vyākaroti*) means to record the aspiration of the mind regarding the fruit.
In the past, the Buddha bestowed a prediction upon the Bodhisattva Guṇasaṃbhava; how could the prediction bestowed upon the Śrāvakas in this present sutra be the same?

Since the work of transformation was already accomplished in the past, the statement that he "bestowed a prediction upon a Bodhisattva" was precisely to bring together the three vehicles and return them to the One Vehicle. As for the Śrāvakas obtaining a prediction—if one were to say...

Regarding the passage where the Buddha, having previously bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon the śrāvakas, arose from samādhi: why did he not speak further on the matter? It is because Mañjuśrī’s skillful discourse rendered such a teaching unnecessary;
thus, he merely mentioned the bestowal of the śrāvaka predictions. *Tathāgata* is translated here as "Thus-Come One" (*Rulai*); *Arhat* as "Worthy of Offerings" (*Yinggong*);
and *Samyaksaṃbuddha* as "Perfectly All-Knowing" (*Zhengbianzhi*). These are cited here as an abbreviated enumeration from among the ten titles [of a Buddha].
This is the third section. △ Sixth, the general account of the sutra after the extinction [of the Buddha], which is the same as the first part of the fifth [section]. First, it clarifies the time:
After the Buddha had bestowed his prophecy, he entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) during the middle watch of the night.
When the fuel of shared conditions for transcending the world is exhausted and the fire is extinguished, this is ultimate *nirvāṇa*. △ Second, identifying the person:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light (*Prabhāketu*) upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

he taught the Dharma for humans for a full eighty minor eons (*antara-kalpa*).

The eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa (up to) the last among them to attain Buddhahood, named Dīpaṃkara.

The reason for citing these eight sons and eight hundred [disciples] is that, on the proximate level, it resolves doubts; and on the secret level, it reveals the *āyus-pramāṇa* (lifespan). As for resolving doubts:
some might say that Maitreya, as the Regent (*abhiṣikta*), is the Great Mañjuśrī, whereas one who is not a Regent is merely "small" and "unworthy."
Answer: Because it would be improper for Mahākāśyapa to ask [such questions], Maitreya is cited; as he was one of the eight hundred disciples of the past, it is fitting that he should have asked.

Furthermore, since [Maitreya] was formerly a disciple of Prabhāpāla who personally received instruction from the Buddha and subsequently became his teacher, he should resolve the doubts regarding the six auspicious omens now displayed by Maitreya. As for the secret revelation of the lifespan, Prabhāpāla is Śākyamuni.
The ninth-generation patriarch’s grandson has now become a Buddha, while the patriarch becomes his disciple; thus, the relationship between teacher and disciple is not fixed.
This conveys the meaning that the esoteric and the manifest are neither arising nor ceasing. Miaole states:

"If one discusses how the eight sons all take Miaoguang as their teacher, then the eight sons all have Miaoguang as their father-teacher. Since it is said that the eight sons are successive, [the point is established].

Although the predictions were received simultaneously, the Master Miaoguang (Prabhāpāla) should have been predicted first for his eldest son; the others followed in succession as they became teachers one after another.
Thus, Miaoguang occupies the headship of the eight generations, while the last of the eight sons was named Rendra (Dīpaṃkara).
Since Rendra became the teacher of Śākyamuni, Miaoguang is therefore the ninth-generation ancestor of Śākyamuni. He was born...

Regarding those who are not "born" (Ajita) and so forth: since master and disciple are mutually related, one should know that while the birth of the master and disciple is real, it is not [ultimately] birth;
likewise, their previous cessation was not [ultimately] cessation. As for the name "Dīpaṃkara" (Lamp-Maker), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"When the Prince was born, the light from his entire body was like a lamp. Therefore he is called Dīpaṃkara; even upon attaining Buddhahood, Śākyamuni Buddha is also named Dīpaṃkara.
When practicing as the youth Mañjuśrī, he fulfilled two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha, receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of his future enlightenment.
Second, by completing one-eighth of the final [third] *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, he now abides in the stage of the "Bodhisattva in the Final Birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
Among his eight hundred disciples, there was one person... [who] made offerings, paid respect, honored, and praised him.
△ Fifth, the comparison of past and present:
Maitreya, you should know that at that time, the monk named *Prabhāsa* (Wonderful Light)... [was] none other than you, the Bodhisattva *Yaśaskāma* (Seeker of Fame).

At that time, Mañjuśrī, wishing to reiterate this meaning within the great assembly, spoke these verses:

△ Second, the two verses on the identity between past and present. Part one: the verse on the six auspicious omens here and there being identical. Part one: the verse on the six auspicious omens in this land.
At that time, the Buddha was preaching a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Teaching of Infinite Meanings* (up to: manifesting various rare and wondrous events).
The first line of verse describes the preaching of the Dharma; the next line describes entering meditative absorption;

the following two lines describe the falling of flowers and the spontaneous sounding of celestial drums, signifying that this is a teaching spoken of its own accord without being requested; the next half-line describes the joy of the assembly;
the next half-line describes the trembling of the earth; and the final line, which describes the emission of light and the manifestation of various rare events, serves as the general summary.

These are the various auspicious omens. △ Second, the verse on the six auspicious omens in other lands, part five: first, the verse on seeing the sentient beings of the six realms of existence together.
This light shines upon eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction (up to) each making offerings to their respective Buddhas.
The first half-verse reiterates the general auspicious signs; the next line specifically enumerates the six destinies, hence it says "all.

Within the subsequent line, the causes and effects of birth and death, as well as the locus of birth and death, are explained in general. The two characters "locus" (*chu*) serve as a general heading.
"Karma" clarifies the cause of birth and death, while "retribution" clarifies its effect. "Locus" refers to the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). The next... [one line].

Regarding the "ground upon which the practice of vidyā relies," since neither the preceding long prose section nor the questions and answers mention its light and color, why would it not have been present before?
Some say it is *sphaṭika*, translated here as "water-jade";
others say it is *vaidūrya*, translated as "blue-colored gem" (*nīla-ratna*), or alternatively rendered as "not far away," referring to the west.
In this region there is a mountain not far from the city of Vārāṇasī; because this jewel emerges from that mountain, it is named accordingly.

The next line clarifies the offerings made in the various realms of existence: although these are called "offerings," they signify the maturation of the capacities [of sentient beings]; one should know that the previous [offerings] were likewise not without purpose.
△ Second, the verse on seeing the Buddhas of those lands who are identical.
Furthermore, one sees all Tathāgatas spontaneously attaining the Buddha-way (up to: the manifestation of a true golden image within.

"Spontaneously attaining the Buddha-way" means that while the path of skillful means involves the deliberate cultivation of the mind to give rise to the true Way, this spontaneity is the effortless accord with principle.
This spontaneous attainment of the Buddha-way is the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward-body), and the lapis lazuli is...
The Dharma-body is fundamentally pure; the golden image manifests its form in response to sentient beings. △ Third, a verse on hearing the Buddha preach the sudden teaching:
"The World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, expounded the profound meaning of the Dharma."
This indicates that the Dharma is being applied to the person; since the Dharma is profound and mysterious, one should know that it must accord with great capacities to reveal the Sudden Teaching.
Regarding the phrase "applying the Dharma to the person" in the *Miaole* commentary:
it simply says "profound Dharma" without mentioning "Bodhisattvas," for when applying the Dharma, such a specification is required. △ Fourth, the verse on hearing sounds.
Hearing the three vehicles and so forth is identical to the gradual teachings opened by the Buddhas of the past;
that in each and every Buddha-field there are countless assemblies of śrāvakas (up to this point) is due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light.

This refers to classifying persons according to the Dharma; since those of the Two Vehicles must necessarily know that the Three Piṭakas were taught for their sake, the first line of verse above concerns what was taught for the sake of Śrāvakas, such as the Four Noble Truths.
Although the Pratyekabuddhas are not explicitly mentioned in the verse, they are included therein by implication.
The next two lines of verse concern the Mahāyāna of the Six Pāramitās, such as the practice of giving, patience, and so forth.
The other [perfections] are merely included within the two perfections of dhyāna and prajñā;

yet, regarding the bhikṣu as a bodhisattva of the six perfections, since the verse of the preceding inquiry already states, "Furthermore, I see bodhisattvas acting as bhikṣus," there is no contradiction in designating such a bhikṣu as a bodhisattva.
Miaole (妙樂) says: "To speak of 'people' in terms of the Dharma means simply to refer to them as śrāvakas."
It is not said that the Four Truths are required only by persons; they may also be followed by some bhikṣus who go to where the Dharma is preached to seek the Buddha-way.
The general verse on the four practices is sufficient to encompass the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s six perfections:

the third practice corresponds to dhyāna (meditation), and the fourth practice corresponds to prajñā (wisdom). △ Fifth, the verse describes the various causes and conditions through which one sees the Bodhisattva. This is precisely...
The opening [of the sūtra] is identical to that of the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā teachings.
Furthermore, it is seen that various bodhisattvas have deeply entered various dhyānas and samādhis (up to) preaching the Dharma in pursuit of the Buddha-way.
△ Second, the verses on the doubts and reflections of the fourfold assembly are identical.
At that time, the fourfold assembly saw the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa... [and wondered] what the causes and conditions for this matter were.
△ Third, the verses on the identity of past and future [lives], consisting of six parts; first, the verse on the identity of the causal person.
The Honored One, revered by devas and humans, has just arisen from samādhi (up to) causing Miaoguang to rejoice.
Regarding "the world" (*loka*): it is called "world" because of separation; it is called "interval" (*antara*) because of differentiation;

"eye of the world" (*lokacakṣus*) refers to the Bodhisattva acting as the eye for both the mundane and supramundane worlds, transforming and guiding humanity. △ Second, the verse on the commonality of preaching the Dharma.
He preached this Lotus Sūtra.
△ Third, the verse on the duration of time:
For sixty full minor kalpas he did not rise from this seat (until) they were all able to receive and uphold it.
The Wonderful Light (Prabhāsa) received and upheld the Dharma of the former Buddha, just as Śāriputra received the entrustment of the present Buddha.
△ Fourth, the verse on the simultaneous entry into extinction:
After the Buddha had preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and caused the assembly to rejoice, [he declared] "I shall now enter into *nirvāṇa*."
This is the same as when the Buddhas of the past announced their parinirvāṇa;

you must now follow in their footsteps with single-minded diligence and abandon all negligence, for the appearance of the Buddhas is extremely rare, occurring but once in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
This was entrusted by the Buddhas of the past in the same manner as the present Buddha; as the *Śāriputra-prakaraṇa* (The Sutra of Bequeathed Teaching) says:
"O bhikṣus, after my parinirvāṇa, you should treasure and revere the *prātimokṣa*, as if encountering light in the darkness, or as if a poor man finding a treasure."
When the sons of the World-Honored One heard that the Buddha had entered nirvana, each harbored grief and distress, crying out, "How swift is the Buddha’s extinction!
At that time, the assembly, hearing of the Buddha’s entry into extinction, wept with sorrow just as they do now for the Buddha. As the Mahā-sūtra says:
"Tears filled their eyes, and blood appeared all over their bodies like *pārijātaka* flowers. This is the reverence for the Dharma and the longing for it.
This is the aspiration of humanity.
The Sage Lord, the Dharma-King, comforts the immeasurable multitudes, saying: "When I enter parinirvāṇa, you should not grieve or fear.
This was how the Buddhas of the past comforted the assemblies at that time, just as the present Buddha does now; as the *Śāsanānuśāsana Sūtra* says: "You all..."
"O Bhikṣus, do not harbor grief or distress. Even if I were to remain in the world for one kalpa or two kalpas, this assembly would still eventually pass away;

it is impossible for an assembly to exist without dissolution. I am fully endowed with the means to benefit myself and others through the Dharma; if I were to remain much longer, it would bring no further benefit. 5.
The verses on the bestowal of the prophecy are the same [as those previously given].
This Bodhisattva Guṇagañja, through the untainted true reality (*anāsrava-tathatā*), has also delivered immeasurable multitudes.
"Untainted true reality" refers to the dharma of the three perfectly wondrous truths. "Untainted" means that the three truths are gathered and subsumed without any loss or leakage.
"True reality" means being free from the marks of false conceptualization; thus it is named true reality. That is to say—

This is the mark of the markless. △ Sixth, the verse on the universal propagation of the sutra after his passing, identical to the five [sections] above; first, the verse on the time period and the benefit of the assembly after his passing:
"The Buddha entered parinirvāṇa this very night, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted... [until] ...to seek the unsurpassed path."
Regarding the analogy of "the fire being extinguished when the fuel is exhausted": in the Hinayana, the Buddha takes the body of retribution as the fuel and wisdom as the fire;
because the wisdom relies upon the body of retribution, when the body perishes, the wisdom ceases—hence it is said that "the fire is extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.

In the Mahayana, sentient beings' spiritual capacities are taken as the fuel and the manifested response as the fire; when the capacities of sentient beings are exhausted, the responsive form likewise perishes—hence it is said that "the fire is extinguished when the fuel is exhausted."
△ Second, two verses on the names of those who propagate the sutra:
This Dharma Master Wonderful Light reverently upholds the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma.
