Because it takes "deep-seated poison" as its meaning, it is called "deep-seated poison" due to the extreme severity of its affliction and destruction;
it is named "poison" because it can destroy the supramundane wholesome mind. △ This concludes the first section of the sixth hexad.
He teaches and transforms them so that they may attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Because the teaching can express the principle, and by investigating the principle one gives rise to practice and thereby attains bodhi, it is known that the teaching and the principle function together;

this corresponds to the preceding metaphor of there being only a single gate. △ Second, combining the individual metaphors into four; first, combining the metaphor of seeing the fire, which has four parts.
First, regarding "the eye that can see when joined":
this "eye that can see when joined" refers to the Tathāgata’s eye of tranquil illumination, which is able to see. △ Second.
Combining what has been seen regarding fire:
all sentient beings undergo various sufferings such as birth, old age, sickness, and death;
this corresponds to the fire seen arising from the four directions. Herein, the eight sufferings are clarified as being like fire.
Suffering is explained as before. The suffering of not obtaining what one seeks consists of the craving, attachment, and pursuit [of objects].

The subsequent experience of the hells, heavens, and the human realm constitutes the suffering of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The suffering of separation from the beloved arises from abandoning that which is cherished;

this is precisely the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). The suffering of encountering the hated and disliked is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), because the mind perceives an object of suffering. This—
Since the eight sufferings arise from the four inversions, the preceding text states that they "arise from the four directions. △ Third, a summary of what was previously seen in detail:
Sentient beings are submerged within them, joyfully playing (until: ...even when encountering great suffering, they do not regard it as a calamity).

The preceding analogy of fire corresponds to the sons' lack of awareness and realization, and so forth. Because they do not contemplate suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), they do not give rise to revulsion;
because they do not contemplate the path (*mārga*) and its cessation (*nirodha*), they do not seek liberation. Although they encounter great suffering, they do not regard it as a calamity;
this corresponds to the aforementioned state of mind where there is no revulsion or distress and no aspiration for deliverance. △ Fourth, the correspondence regarding the arousal of fear.
Śāriputra, having seen this, the Buddha then thought: "[... so that they may sport [in liberation].

This corresponds to the following: "Although I am able to lead them safely out through this burning gate, my intention is to uproot their suffering and hardship"—this refers to the power of Great Compassion uprooting the sufferings of the five turbidities and bestowing immeasurable bliss.
This is precisely the power of great compassion and its bestowal of great bliss. △ Second, combining the abandonment of the stool with the use of the carriage;
first, combining the abandonment of the stool; third, combining the preliminary suitability.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata again had this thought: [down to] "sentient beings cannot be delivered by means of this.

The preceding analogy contained both exhortation and admonition; now, however, it contains only exhortation and lacks admonition. This is because the exhortation to cultivate what is correct is primary, while the admonition against evil is secondary.
Now, as for the suitability of the middle [approach], that which is achieved solely through supernormal power corresponds to the aforementioned power of the body and the power of wisdom.
This is like joining the strength of one's hands to praise the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, or joining the strength of a robe-sack, or joining a desk;
yet when the Buddha first appeared, he employed these [methods] as a provisional fit for sentient beings, as they could not be saved by them.
△ Second, combining with those who lack the capacity.
Why is this so? Because these sentient beings—from [the point where they are described]—by what means could they understand the Buddha’s wisdom?
Śāriputra cannot attain liberation; he does not accept the exhortations and parables.

It is precisely because the obstructions of the five turbidities are heavy that they have not yet escaped the fires of birth and death, and thus cannot enter the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna. Therefore it is said: "By what means could they understand?"
The phrase "the Buddha’s wisdom" corresponds to the preceding statement that there is "only one gate," yet it is narrow and small;
therefore, one cannot understand the Buddha’s wisdom. △ Third, combining and ceasing the transformations, in two parts: first, restating the three previous parables;
third, the parable of being unable to save with one's own body and hands.
Śāriputra, although that elder possessed strength in his body and arms, he did not employ it;
rather, he combined these with relinquishment and skillful guidance for those who lacked the capacity, thereby ceasing his transformative activity.
Although this passage does not contain the explicit words "relinquishment," the intent to cease transformative activity is very clear. △ Second, citing the parable of bestowing the three vehicles.
He merely used earnest expedient means to strive to rescue his sons from the perils of the burning house.
△ Third, the analogy of the equal bestowal of great chariots:
subsequently, he gave each of them a precious, great chariot.
△ Second, the formal application of the parable of the burning house.
The Tathāgata is likewise; although he possesses power and fearlessness, he does not employ them.
△ Second, the formal application of the chariot parable, in four parts: first, the formal application of the three vehicles as appropriate.
He merely uses wisdom and skillful means to rescue sentient beings from the burning house of the triple world.
△ Second, he accords with his sons' previous inclinations by preaching the three vehicles:
the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddha-vehicle.
The "Three Vehicles" (triyāna) take "conveying" as their essential meaning:

the Śrāvaka takes the Four Noble Truths as his vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha takes the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination as his vehicle, and the Bodhisattva takes the Six Perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) as his vehicle; they transport beings out of the triple world and lead them back to Nirvāṇa.
Within this teaching, the Bodhisattva’s Six Perfections are also termed the "Great Vehicle" (Mahāyāna), which is now called the "Buddha Vehicle" (Buddhayāna).

This Bodhisattva’s thirty-four moments of mind suddenly sever the habitual tendencies of both *darśana-heya* (views) and *bhāvanā-heya* (thoughts), whereby he attains Buddhahood; therefore, it is called the Buddha Vehicle.
△ Third, the combined praise of the rarity of the vehicle, which has three parts: first, the combined demonstration of its transformation.

And he spoke these words: "You must not [settle for] the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; you should aim for the Buddha-vehicle. This triple world demonstrates the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya);
do not crave its coarse and wretched things, even to the point of giving rise to attachment. This demonstrates the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya).

'Form' refers to the physical appearances of men and women, as well as the various colors of the world—black, yellow, red, white, and so forth. 'Sound' refers to the music of strings and flutes, and the tinkling of bracelets and pendants."
These sounds include the voices of men and women singing and chanting; fragrances refer to the body odors of men and women as well as the scents of worldly food and drink;
flavors refer to the various delicious tastes of foods, meals, and delicacies; and tangibles refer to the softness, smoothness, and delicacy of the bodies of men and women.
These are called the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and also the five desires (*pañca-kāma*). One should quickly emerge from the three realms (*tridhātu*).
This indicates the two truths of Cessation and the Path; that is, it demonstrates that beyond the three realms there exist the fruits of the Three Vehicles attained through wisdom and abandonment.
Thus, it causes one to quickly exit the three realms so that one may obtain the Three Vehicles. The Three Vehicles properly take the Path and Cessation as their essence.
This corresponds to the previous three carts which are now outside the gate, where they can be used for play. △ Second, the correspondence with the realization.
[The text] turns.
"I now guarantee this matter for you" (up to) "by these means I entice and advance sentient beings.
This corresponds to the [previous section]: "In accordance with what you desire, I shall grant it all to you. △ Third, the combined exhortation to turn.
He further spoke these words: "You should know that [until] you shall obtain immeasurable peace and happiness. This concludes the exclamation of rarity.
These three vehicles are the ritual methods by which all Buddhas employ skillful means to guide sentient beings; thus they are praised by the multitude of sages.
To attain the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) is to achieve mastery; to attain the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) is to be unbound.

"Birth has been exhausted and there is no further existence" means that having nothing further upon which to rely, one has accomplished what was to be done and established the holy life (*brahmacarya*), meaning that through untainted diligence one cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
"Roots" refers to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*); "powers" refers to the five powers (*pañcabala*); "enlightenment" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*);
and "path" refers to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and so forth are as explained previously regarding their abiding.
Because it is true emptiness and nirvana, it is called "peaceful, secure, and blissful. △ Fourth, the suitability for the wishes of the sons has three parts;
first, the suitability of the sheep-drawn carts.
Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings who possess the nature of wisdom within (up to) seeking the sheep-drawn carts to exit the burning house.
Those who possess the nature of wisdom within have previously cultivated the aspiration for the Three Vehicles and seek to perfect the wisdom-nature of the Three Vehicles;

therefore, the Buddha bestows upon them the teachings of the Three Vehicles. "Possessing the nature of wisdom within" and so forth refers to hearing the Dharma from the Buddha and receiving it with faith.

This corresponds to the previous analogy of hearing about the rare treasures spoken of by the father, which satisfied their wishes—this is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). "With earnest diligence" corresponds to the previous analogy.
Each mind is courageous and sharp—this refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). "Diligence" (*vīrya*) combines with the preceding: "pushing and shoving. "Pushing" means reasoning; "shoving" means expelling evil.
Because evil is removed, the refined principle becomes clear; thus, one advances in the cultivation of wisdom. "Desiring to exit quickly" combines with the following:
they compete and race together. This is called the Śrāvaka Vehicle. It combines with the preceding: "striving to exit the burning house. A "Śrāvaka" (Hearer) is one who hears.
Because they follow the Buddha’s voice and teachings, they are called Śrāvakas (Voice-hearers).
Since Śrāvakas cannot transform others—just as a sheep does not look back at the flock behind them—the Śrāvaka-yāna is likened to a sheep-cart. △ Second, combining it with the deer-cart.
If there are sentient beings who, from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, [seek] the deer-cart to exit the burning house—

the term *pratyekabuddha* in the Sanskrit language means "solitary enlightened one," and those who speak of seeking "spontaneous wisdom" enter through the gate of the twelve links of dependent origination;
this gate exists inherently from the beginning and was not created by Buddhas, devas, or humans, and is thus called "spontaneous."
Wisdom that is not heard from another is also called "self-arisen wisdom" (*svayambhū-prajñā*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
A practitioner asked the Buddha, "Great Virtuous One, who created the twelve links of dependent origination? The Buddha replied, "I did not create them. He asked again, "Did someone else create them?
The Buddha replied, "Nor did anyone else create them. Whether a Buddha appears or not, their fundamental nature has always existed. [One who] deeply understands all these...

Regarding the "conditions of dharmas" (dharmapratyaya): because Pratyekabuddhas observe the conditions of causes and effects—both in direct and reverse order—through hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, it is said that they have "profound knowledge.
A Pratyekabuddha is a "Dharma-practitioner" (dharmanusārin) who hears little Dharma from others but extensively deduces its meaning for himself;
therefore, he is compared to a deer. As the *Biexing shu* states: "The Pratyekabuddha is likened to a deer. Because a deer does not rely on humans, this analogy is applied.
There is still the compassion of a transformative vow. △ Third, the bestowal of the ox-carts:
"If there are sentient beings who, from the Buddha, the World-Honored One... [until] for the sake of seeking ox-carts, emerge from the burning house."
The Bodhisattva is called an "All-Knowing One" (sarvajña), which differs from the two vehicles and is indeed Buddha-wisdom;
thus, when a Bodhisattva contemplates this while cultivating the causes, it carries the meaning of not "riding" [the vehicle] in a dualistic manner.

Because the Bodhisattva’s compassion transforms sentient beings—just as an ox patiently endures the burden of transport—the ox-cart is used as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva-vehicle. Furthermore, the ox-cart possesses water.

The ox and the white ox differ; the water-buffalo cart is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva Vehicle of the Six Perfections, while the great white ox cart is a metaphor for the One Buddha Vehicle of the Perfect Teaching.

[The author] privately comments: since the "all-knowing wisdom" (sarvajñatā) is not the same as that of the Two Vehicles, and "natural wisdom" (svayambhū-jñāna) and "teacherless wisdom" (anācārya-jñāna) are not the same as those of the Pratyekabuddhas.
△ Third, the equal bestowing of the great carts: Part One, the dual [explanation].
The second section consists of two parts; first, the citation of the parable regarding the escape from calamity:
"Śāriputra, it is just as that elder [leads his children] out of the burning house to a place of safety and fearlessness."

The preceding analogy had four points; now we merely combine two of them. Combining [the points on] escaping danger has the meaning of "seeking the vehicle," while combining [the points on] equal bestowal has the meaning of "joy.
△ Second, citing the section on equal bestowal:
"Reflecting that my wealth is immeasurable, I shall bestow great chariots upon all my sons."
△ Second, the combined application of the two parables. First, the combined application regarding escaping calamity:
"The Tathāgata is also like this" (up to) "...emerges from the perilous path of the three realms of suffering and fear to attain the bliss of nirvāṇa."
The "gate" (mén) has three meanings: the meaning of entry, the meaning of exit, and the meaning of distinction.

If the triple world is the dwelling and the five aggregates are the house, then by being deluded regarding a single form-and-mind, one enters that very same form-and-mind; this is the gate of birth-and-death for entering the dwelling.
If it is taken in the sense of "exit," it refers to departing from the triple world by means of a vehicle; this pertains to those who receive the teachings of the two vehicles—Tripitaka and Shared.

If we take the principle elucidated [by the teaching] as the gate, and consider it in its distinct sense, this refers to taking the principle elucidated under the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) as the gate.

What is now called the "gate of the Buddha's teaching" specifically refers to the principles under the teachings of both the Tripitaka (Zang) and Shared (Tong) Teachings acting together as the gate to exit the three realms and escape from suffering. Miaole states that all three meanings are based upon...
Regarding the meaning of "taking the principle that is expressed as the gate": this intends to clarify that the meaning of the *dujiao* (separate teaching) gate is not established [independently].

Although the sutra speaks of "teaching," it must necessarily be contrasted with "principle. Therefore, one knows that although the separate teaching expresses a distinct principle, it is not itself a "gate" or a "vehicle.

It is only by being contrasted with the *zang* (treasury/storehouse) and *tong* (common) teachings that the name "separate" is established; it is called "separate" because it takes a distinct principle as its object. The ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the separate teaching are [contrasted] with those of the treasury...
Those of penetrating wisdom all emerge from the burning house; since their emergence from the burning house is identical, they may likewise be called "those who have attained the ten stages.
Furthermore, as that which is realized is the same—the *nirvāṇa* of the two teachings—they may also be said to have "attained the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
△ Second, the equal bestowal of the five [vehicles], in five parts: First, the reason for providing the vehicles.
At that time, the Tathāgata thought thus: (up to) the treasury of all Buddha-dharmas, such as the powers and fearlessnesses.
"Immeasurable wisdom" corresponds above to "immeasurable wealth," meaning the overflowing of immeasurable treasuries.
△ Second, expanding his mind accordingly.
"All these sentient beings are my children" (up to) "I shall bring them all to extinction through the Tathāgata’s extinction.
This corresponds to the principle that my wealth and possessions are immeasurable, and thus I ought not to give inferior, small carts to my children.
"The Tathāgata’s extinction" refers to the Mahāyāna *triguṇa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of the three virtues). △ Third, the chapter heading on the equality of mind.
These sentient beings who have escaped the triple world are collectively granted the aforementioned equal distribution to all sons. △ Fourth, the chapter on the equality of the chariots:
they are provided with all the implements of entertainment, such as the meditative concentrations and liberations of the Buddhas.
△ Fifth, the analogy of the great carriage that is correct, vast, and expansive.
All are of one characteristic and one kind, praised by the sages, and capable of producing pure, wondrous, and supreme bliss.

This corresponds to the aforementioned analogies of the high and wide [carriage] up to the servants and so forth. "One characteristic" refers to the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). That is to say—
The single category of the Dharma-body is the seed-wisdom, which is precisely Prajñā; it can give rise to pure and wondrous bliss.
This bliss is the absence of suffering and is termed liberation. These three virtues are lofty and vast, fully endowed with adornment, and encompass all qualities;
thus it is called Mahāyāna. △ Fourth, the analogy for the non-existence of falsehood has two parts. First, restating the concession that the Small Vehicle is not different from the Great Vehicle.
Śāriputra, it is like that elder... [up to] ...that elder is not guilty of falsehood.
The three vehicles were used as inducements originally to eliminate the five turbidities; once the five turbidities are eliminated, great goodness is naturally preserved.
Therefore, he gives only the great vehicle. △ Second, showing that the result does not contradict the original intention. Part one: the combined explanation.
The Tathāgata is also like this, being without any falsehood... (omitted)... but he delivers and liberates them solely by means of the Mahāyāna.
This corresponds to the previous statement: "I use skillful means to enable my sons to escape. △ Second, combining the conclusion with the illustration.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable wisdom (up to: ...), he distinguishes and teaches three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
Combining the above [points], how much more so when the elder, knowing his own wealth to be immeasurable and wishing to benefit his children, grants them both the three and the one;
this is not false. This explanation differs slightly from the previous one; the intent of the former was to cause the children...

Having attained deliverance, the mind does not abide in the three realms; since it has emerged, it is neither withheld nor is it false. Now it is clarified that the Tathāgata’s original intent in appearing in the world was to preach the Mahāyāna;
however, because those of small wisdom delight in and are attached to the triple world, he used skillful means to entice and lead them.
Once they have attained deliverance, he returns the Mahāyāna to them; as this accords with their original aspiration, it is said that he is able to bestow the Great [Vehicle] upon sentient beings.

The Dharma of the *yāna* cannot be received in its entirety; however, if one can receive it as in the *Avataṃsaka*, it is already identical to the Great [Vehicle], and there is no need to open the One into Three.
As for those who cannot receive it, the Buddha uses the power of skillful means to differentiate and teach the Three within the Single Buddha-vehicle.
These three exist because of sentient beings and are not the Buddha’s original intent; by explaining it in this way, the teaching is established without contradicting the fundamental principle.
"The mind is not empty. Miaole (Miaole Daoshi) says this is slightly different from what preceded it;

previously it was said that "the intention does not reside in the three," whereas now it is said that "it is fundamentally intended for the Great [Vehicle]. Although there is a slight difference, the names differ while the meaning remains the same.

△ Second, the verse recitation, in two parts: first, the hundred-verse hymn which reiterates the preceding prose; second, the initial part, which reiterates the opening analogy, in two parts: first, the general summary.
To illustrate this with the first verse concerning the elder,
the Buddha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"It is like an elder."

The verse on his titles simultaneously conveys his name, conduct, virtue, and achievements. Since he possesses the virtue of leading others, it is known that his conduct is universally revered by the states and cities;

it is also known that both internally and externally, his age and virtue are equally eminent. This is a metaphor for the Buddha being fully endowed with wisdom, cessation, compassion, and all myriad virtues.
△ Second, the verse on the house, in two parts: first, the verse on the vastness of the house.
There was a great house.
△ Second, a detailed description of the nature of the house:
that house was ancient and had become suddenly dilapidated.

Question: If one speaks from the perspective of causes, they may indeed be without beginning;

Now, these following three lines extensively set forth the nature of the house to clarify the characteristics of what is being burned:
"The hall and house are high and perilous.

One interpretation states that the head is the palace (*prāsāda*), the belly is the hall (*sabhā*), and the back is the house (*gṛha*); their continuous succession from moment to moment, characterized by impermanence, constitutes "highness."

Regarding "perilous" (*wei*): one interpretation states that the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) is the hall and the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) is the house; since one cannot avoid falling [from them], it is called "perilously high.
Another interpretation, "Sublime Joy," explains "moment-to-moment" (*nien-nian*) as meaning continuity; thus, it is "high" because of continuity and "perilous" because of impermanence.

As for the phrase "the head is the palace and the belly is the hall," this is one explanation based on the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*). As for the phrase "the hall of form and the house of desire," etc., this is one explanation based on causes and conditions (*yin-yuan*).
This is an explanation.
The pillars at the base are crushed and rotten, the beams are selected for their leaning, and the foundations and steps have collapsed.

The life-faculty that supports [the body] is like these pillars; it is also said that the two feet are the "base of the pillars," yet they are subject to the three characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

The term "transmigration" (qiān) signifies the crushing of decay. Consciousness serves as the structural framework, acting as the beams and rafters; that which is destroyed by various sufferings is like a collapsing edifice.
Past karma constitutes the foundation and steps, while the time of senescence represents its ruin.
Regarding the phrase "the structural framework of consciousness," it governs the entire body, just as beams are selected and erected to establish a house.
The walls are crumbling and split; the plaster is peeling away; the thatched roof is falling into disorder; and the rafters and eaves are misaligned and detached.

Regarding the "walls," one explanation states that the four great elements constitute the walls and the skin constitutes the plaster; the lack of rectitude in the four modes of deportment constitutes the falling into disorder;

and the dullness of the five consciousnesses, which do not correspond to their respective objects, constitutes the misalignment and detachment. It is also said that these refer to the walls themselves.

The body is cracked and split like parched and withered skin; its once-vigorous complexion is now as fresh and clean as newly applied plaster, yet it decays toward old age and death like a crumbling wall.
The hair and beard fall away in decay and old age, just as thatching grass falls in disarray from a roof.
The limbs and joints are weak and frail, unable to support one another, like rafters and eaves that have become misaligned and fallen apart.
The surrounding barriers are winding and crooked, and they are filled everywhere with impurities.

"Surrounding barriers" refers to the six consciousnesses; "winding and crooked" refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), because the six consciousnesses rely upon the six organs to grasp objects, making them difficult passages—hence the term "winding and crooked.
Since the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) pervasively defile the six organs, it is said they are "filled everywhere with impurities. △ Third, the verse:
Five hundred people.
There are five hundred people dwelling therein.
The root-natures of the three vehicles are subsumed within the five destinies; this also serves as an analogy for the thirty sons. △ Fourth, the verse.

The fire breaking out in four places at the beginning clarifies the matters on the ground, which is a metaphor for the desire realm. The fire breaking out in four places at the beginning clarifies the categories of things burned, which is a metaphor for the ten *anuśayas* (latent proclivities) of sentient beings.
Regarding the first [of these two], the correct clarification of what is burned: the first part clarifies the burning of birds and beasts, which is a metaphor for the five dull *anuśayas*.
Regarding the first of these five: the first part is a metaphor for the *anuśaya* of pride (*māna*).

The hawk, the owl, the eagle, the vulture, the crow, the magpie, the pigeon, and the dove—because pride causes sentient beings to exalt themselves and disparage others, just as these birds are by nature inclined to soar high and look down, these eight birds are used as metaphors for the eight types of pride (*māna*).
To disparage others is "pride" (*māna*), while to esteem oneself is "arrogance" (*mada*); this is clarified in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
Pride is now illustrated by the analogy of eight birds: pride of physical vigor is like the owl; pride of nature is like the screech-owl; pride of wealth is like the eagle;
pride of sovereignty is like the vulture; pride of longevity is like the crow; pride of intelligence is like the magpie; pride of performing good deeds is like the pigeon;
and pride of physical form is like the dove. △ Second, the illustration of the latent tendency of anger.
Vipers, snakes, vipers, scorpions, centipedes, and millipedes—these are metaphors for the latent tendency of anger (*dveṣānuśaya*).
There are three types of anger: first, irrational anger, which means that without considering whether it is appropriate or not, one suddenly gives rise to a mind of anger;
second, anger in accordance with reason, which means that another person has actually harmed me; third, anger arising from dispute, which means being attached to one's own [position].
To understand this is called "others' actions are non-virtuous. A venomous snake whose poison is rampant does not need to touch its victim to suck it;
this is like anger arising from what is unreasonable (*ayoniśomanasikāra*). If a viper or a scorpion touches its victim, it stings; this is like anger based on grasping at principles (*dṛṣṭi*).

Centipedes and millipedes are metaphors for anger born of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). People of the world say that those with red necks are centipedes, while those that are not red are millipedes. *Vṛścika* (scorpion).

(Yīnyuán yòu wúguānqiè; it refers to a lizard and also to a venomous snake. *Fù* (fāngliùqiè; one gloss says: a *huǐ* [viper] with needles on its nose; the large ones reach seven or eight feet in length. *Xié* (xǔxiéqiè; also called *xiéhǔ*;
a venomous insect. *Yóuyán* (also a venomous insect). △ Third, an analogy for the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*).
Lizards, centipedes, weasels, badgers, mice, and so forth, down to dung beetles and various other insects, gather upon it.
This is a metaphor for delusion (*moha*): when the mental factor of delusion does not clearly comprehend its object, it is called "delusion," which is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*).

There are two types of ignorance: first, independent (*kevala*) ignorance; second, associated (*samprayukta*) ignorance. Lizards, centipedes, and the like, sitting motionless, represent independent ignorance. Weasels and badgers... [represent associated ignorance].
The "mice" are a metaphor for the various evil insects of associated ignorance; that they "arise fully from the root of delusion" refers to how all fetters (saṃyojana) originate.
That they "run about crosswise" clarifies that the characteristics of these fetters condition one another, or condition the three realms, arising as swiftly as they run about crosswise.
The mention of "excrement and urine" below clarifies that the objects to which the deluded mind becomes attached are all [impure].
Because it is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure, it is said to be a place of excrement and urine where foul odors overflow and impurities flow forth.

Because one is deluded and fails to understand this, reckoning it as permanent, pleasurable, self, and pure, one gives rise to defiled attachment; therefore, it is said that dung beetles and various insects gather upon it.

*Shou-gong* (the gecko, i.e., the *yanyan*; the *Bowu zhi* states that if one raises it in a vessel and feeds it cinnabar, it can prevent lewdness and dissipation, and for this reason it is called [by that name]).

The gecko; the centipede (the *Śāriputra-vinaya* states it is the dung beetle); the weasel (*shèjiù*—a wild mouse, reddish-yellow in color that eats mice); the mouse (*xī*—a small mouse); and the dung beetle (also called the *kělán*;
a black-shelled insect that rolls balls of soil and dung). △ Fourth, analogies for the latent tendencies of greed.
Foxes, wolves, and jackals gnaw, chew, trample, and tread [upon the remains] until they are emaciated with hunger; terrified and panicked, they seek food everywhere.
This is a metaphor for the latent tendency of greed (*lobha-anuśaya*). Greed is of two kinds: first, that which possesses power; second, that which lacks power.
That which possesses power takes by means of its majesty and authority, like the wolf and the fox; that which lacks power can only beg from others for coarse and inferior things, like the jackal.
The character *gan* (with the phonetic *zhu*, meaning "to savor") refers to chewing; it clarifies that greedily seizing an object and drawing it toward oneself is like chewing.

It is not done according to principle, but rather like treading upon something. Furthermore, when the greedy mind seizes an object, whether it be useful or useless, taking what is useful is like chewing, while taking what is useless is like treading.
Thus, the greedy mind seizes an object, perhaps taking only a single thing.
Or, taking many objects that have distinct boundaries, such as morsels of meat and bone scattered in disarray, they accumulate the five sensory objects without knowing contentment.
A pack of dogs comes rushing forward, seizing and clutching [bó-cuò, "to grasp with the hands"];
those with strength greedily seize and clutch those who are weak, while the hungry and emaciated are terrified and frantic—this is greed that knows no satisfaction, like one who is starving.
Seeking but unable to obtain what one desires is like a weak person who exhausts themselves in various ways to find it;

it is like a person of frantic desire who, despite being wealthy, remains greedy and scurries about seeking food—this is the pursuit of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). The *ya-jian* (wild jackal) resembles a fox but is smaller;
its coloration is bluish-yellow and its tail is large. Regarding the term "chì-niè" (to gnaw): some say it means to bite so hard that the teeth sink in.
"Seizing" means to gather and snatch away by force. "Panicked and terrified" means to be filled with fear.
△ Fifth, the parable of the suspicious dog: "Fighting, struggling, snarling, and barking."
This analogy refers to the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) and vacillation between two extremes; "doubt" means being undecided as to what is right or wrong.

"Contention" (*raṇa*) means regarding something as correct. "Tugging" (*cī*) means regarding it as incorrect. "Biting and snarling" (*caika*) and "howling and barking" refer to the act of speaking out to resolve the principles of right and wrong.
*Miaoyue* states that "tugging" (*cī*)—according to the *Shiming*—means "to cross" (*chā*), referring to the five [fingers].
"Seizing" (*ca*) means to grasp; "pulling" (*che*) means to drag. It is also said that seizing forward is called *ca* and pulling backward is called *che*.
"Gaping" (*jianshi*) refers to baring the teeth with pursed lips. "Barking" (*haofei*) refers to emitting a loud, roaring sound.
The *Zhiguan* states: "Doubt and indecision constitute gaping; intimidating others constitutes barking. It is like a watchdog that causes others to fear."
Therefore, it barks. △ Second, the conclusion:
"The state of that house being so terrifying and transformed" concludes the five dull afflictions (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
△ Second, the analogy of the ghosts and spirits being burned, representing the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-kleśa*); first:
This is a general explanation.
Everywhere there are *chimei* (goblins) and *wangliang* (sprites).

This is a general metaphor for the five views of self (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*), such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), which arise from contact with the five sense bases (*pañca-sparśāyatana*) and are constantly present even in moments of haste.
Because the driving force of gain and fame (*lābha-satkāra*) universally conditions the four truths and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), it is said that these exist everywhere.

Now, spirits and ghosts possess intelligence while birds and beasts do not; therefore, the driving force of gain is likened to spirits and ghosts, and the dull driving forces (*dauṣṭhulya*) are compared to birds and beasts.
The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) states: "Chimei are the essences of things. Secular texts say that the monsters of mountains and marshes are called chimei."
The "Western Metropolis Rhapsody" (*Xijing fu*) states that mountain spirits with tiger forms are called *chī*, while house spirits with pig heads and human bodies are called *mèi*.
As for *wǎnglǎng*, they are aberrant manifestations of wood and stone; the *Yupian* states they are water spirits. △ Second, specifically clarifying the five [categories], first:
an analogy for wrong views.
The yakṣas and evil spirits who devour human flesh (up to) the sounds of their quarreling are most terrifying.
This is an analogy for wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): because one reckons in terms of annihilationism or eternalism and does not believe in cause and effect, it is called "wrong view.
Yakṣa is also called *yakṣa*, which refers to a swift-moving spirit; this is an analogy for the person with wrong view who denies cause and effect. "Human" is an analogy for wholesome retribution.
The supramundane cause and effect, when one’s mind is not intermingled with afflictions and false views and yet denies this principle, is like eating human flesh.
The various species of venomous insects are the analogies for evil retribution;

the mundane cause and effect, when one’s mind is intermingled with various afflictions and false views and yet denies this principle, is like devouring those species of venomous insects. As for those that hatch from eggs, are born from wombs, or give birth through viviparity:
The phenomena of the world arise from causes of their own kind to produce effects of their own kind. That which "stores" (藏) refers to the cause having the capacity for the effect;
that which "protects" (護) refers to the certainty that it will not be lost. Furthermore, human flesh is wholesome while venomous insects are unwholesome.
A mind of false views denies the reality of wholesome and unwholesome causes and effects, just as a yakṣa devours human beings.

The "flesh-poisoning insects" (*vatsanābha*) that breed and give birth represent, in general, the coexistence of good and evil, wherein all things function through the principle of cause and effect producing one another.
That they have eaten their fill signifies the fulfillment of a mind of false views.

That their malevolent intent grows more intense signifies the expansion of that mind of false views. The sounds of fighting signify that what was accomplished within the inner mind is now manifested outwardly.
The teaching declares that the doctrine of no cause and no effect can cause those who hear it to fall into the three miserable realms;
therefore, it is said to be "most terrifying. Regarding the term *fú* (孚): the *Miaole Yupian* states that "to incubate eggs is called *fú*";
the *Tongsu Wén* states that "metamorphosis from an egg is called *fú*"; and the *Guǎngyá* states that "*fú* also means to give birth. As for *rǔ* (乳), it means to nourish.
Therefore, it is said that birds give birth by means of *fu* (incubation) and beasts give birth by means of *ru* (lactation).

As for "those of the same kind," this refers to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) which obtains an outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), because the offspring resembles the father; thus it is used as a metaphor. △ Second, the analogy for the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The *kumbhāṇḍa* spirits crouch upon earthen mounds (up to) wandering back and forth, sporting and frolicking at will.

This is a metaphor for the clinging to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which grasps what is false as the path; it is called "reckoning non-cause as cause," and the precepts of chickens, dogs, and so forth are termed *śīlavrataparāmarśa*.
*Kumbhāṇḍa* is translated here as "jar-shaped" (*píng xíng*) because their form resembles a jar; they are thus devils and ghosts.
The superior among ghosts is like one who cultivates tainted wholesome deeds (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and is thus able to overcome various insects.

Those crouching on earthen mounds represent the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who cultivate the ten wholesome precepts and are thereby able to be born in the six heavens of the desire realm; these six heavens are high places within the desire realm, just as earthen mounds are elevated spots.

Furthermore, when non-Buddhists maintain their precepts and are able to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they may first attain the concentration of the desire realm, or they may attain...
The future is fixed; the future is fixed. Not yet liberated from the desires of the desire realm, the summit of the desire realm is like a mound of earth.

Those who have detached by one or two feet obtain the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) samādhi, as if reaching one foot; those who have detached by two feet obtain the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) samādhi, as if reaching two feet.
To ascend to the higher realms is to go forth, while to fall back is to retreat. Holding the view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is like being heedless.

Regarding the *kumbhāṇḍas* who delight in playful pleasures: they are fearsome spirits. *Crouching* (*khu*) refers to sitting on the haunches; *squatting* (*ju*) refers to sitting with the feet flat on the ground.
They seize dogs by both hind legs and throw them down until they cry out, then place their own feet upon the necks of the dogs, terrifying them for their own amusement.
Just as one might grasp a dog’s paw, so too does one who slanders [the truth] do so; thus, there is no cause for suffering.
Just as grasping the dog’s paw, one further slanders that there is no fruit of suffering resulting from the cause of suffering.

Just as the pain added to the neck by the foot results in the fruit of suffering, so too does the person of false views deny it, saying that there is no principle by which a cause of suffering yields a fruit of suffering.

It is like striking someone until they lose their voice; having slandered [the truth] by claiming there is no cause for suffering and no fruit of suffering, one is like a dog that barks out of its own pleasure.
The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) states: "To slander by claiming there is no cause for suffering refers precisely to regarding what is not a cause as a cause—this itself is slander.
This is because it is originally a worldly cause, yet one claims it is a supramundane cause; since these two causes do not exist, it is likened to seizing a dog.
[This refers to] the two feet. △ Third, an analogy for the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*):
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose bodies are tall and large (up to) emitting great evil sounds, crying out and seeking food.
This is an analogy for the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), one falsely conceives of them as a self;

this is called the "view of a self-body. To reckon a self by entering vertically through the three periods of time is called "long"; to reckon a self by extending horizontally across the five aggregates is called "great.

Because one reckons the self as autonomous and fails to cultivate wholesome dharmas, there is a lack of shame and dread of blame; thus it is said that one is "naked," and because one is adorned with evil, it is said to be "black" and "without merit."
Because he lacks the resources of virtue, he is said to be "emaciated. Because those who calculate [him] do not transcend the triple world, he is said to "dwell permanently therein.
Because they calculate that the self resides in the heart and speak words proclaiming the characteristics of a self, he is said to "utter a great evil cry.
Hoping to attain the fruit of the Way through this speech, he is said to "shout for food. ○ "Nude" (lǔ; originally written as luò; bare-bodied).
(Also, "袒" means to bare the shoulder). △ Fourth, the simile for the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*):
Furthermore, there are various hungry ghosts whose throats are like needles.

This is a simile for the clinging to views; it means that because one relies on these views, one reaches as far as the Realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which is called the clinging to views regarding the non-permanence of the Realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.

Yet, calculating *nirvāṇa* to be like a narrow throat through which one’s life is perilously sustained, it is said that its throat is as thin as a needle. The *Myōraku-kyō* (Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra) states:

"Regarding those who grasp at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), they take what is not the fruit to be the fruit. They do not consider the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) to be the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, yet they calculate it to be eternal.
Being formless and consisting solely of mind, it is called the 'narrow throat'; the extreme limit of life within the three realms is called the 'perilous life'."
To calculate this as "constant" is termed "preserving life"; "preserving life" precisely corresponds to the meaning of calculating the fruit [of one's actions].
△ Fifth, the analogy for extreme views:
Furthermore, there are various ghosts with heads like oxen (omitted)... driven by hunger and thirst, they cry out and run about.
This analogy illustrates how, based upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one calculates a self and clings to the extremes of permanence and annihilation;

clinging to either permanence—rather than annihilation—or annihilation—rather than permanence—is called the "view of extremes" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). The two extremes of permanence and annihilation are like the two horns on a cow's head.
To consider the body as the self or the self as the body arises from the view of a self-identity, just as the two horns arise from the head. Thus it is calculated.
The faults of eternalism and nihilism sever the roots of supramundane goodness, just as eating human flesh severs the roots of mundane goodness.
Whether one calculates [existence] as eternal or calculates it as annihilated, these views revolve back and forth like tangled hair;
calculating eternity destroys annihilation, while calculating annihilation destroys eternity. They are as cruel and predatory as a savage beast.
There are those with wisdom who, like those driven by hunger and thirst seeking sustenance through food and drink, each present two views as they cry out and run about.
As the *Miaole* (Exquisite Joy) states: "If one calculates [the self] as permanent, the body is not the self; if the body is annihilated, the self is permanent.

If one calculates [the self] as annihilated, the body is annihilated and the self is annihilated; or both are permanent and both are annihilated," as detailed in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation). △ Second.
In summary, regarding the sharp and dull [faculties]:
from the yakṣas, hungry ghosts, and various evil birds and beasts, up to such immeasurable fears and perils—
these first two lines summarize the characteristics of afflictions in the desire realm and likewise summarize the sentient beings of sharp and dull faculties.

The first phrase refers to those of superior faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*) and the second to those of dull faculties (*mṛdu-indriya*); the following two phrases generally encompass both types of faculties.

Since both are driven by outflow-tainted minds (*sāsrava-citta*) and lack the food of the flavor of the Path (*mārga-rasa*), they are said to be "hungry. Because of this hunger, the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) proceeds with great rapidity; thus it is called "urgent.

Regarding the "four directions," although the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*) are numerous, they do not exceed these four categories. "Peering through windows" refers to looking through the openings.

I have privately clarified that his erroneous contemplation of the principle of emptiness and his yearning for the flavor of the Way, despite his observations, were characterized by a mind mired in attachment;
thus he failed to accord with the correct principle, much like looking through a window at the sky and failing to perceive its unimpeded nature.
The latter two phrases summarize this broad refutation of error. *Miaoyue* states: "Because of the partition of the window and door, one sees the sky, yet it is a partial sky."

There is no distinction between the biased and the correct because one peers into the principle through the window; there is no calculation of right or wrong, yet by forming attachments, one incurs faults, and through these faults one falls into evil states—thus the fear is immeasurable.
△ Second, clarifying the cause for the outbreak of fire as a metaphor for that which gives rise to the five turbidities.
This dilapidated old house belongs to a single person who has been away from it for no long time.

The three realms are the place where the Buddha manifests his transformative response; because he has, since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, vowed to deliver sentient beings, it is said to belong to this one person.
While the elder was in the house, he was able to ensure they were careful regarding the fire, but after he had departed, the sons remained ignorant.

Therefore, the arising of the fire within is precisely due to the Tathāgata’s constant instruction of these beings during his time as the Greatly Penetrating Buddha (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū), commanding them to subdue the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya) as if one were being cautioned against fire.
However, once the karmic resonance of sentient beings has been exhausted, the Tathāgata’s response also ceases;

thus, the five turbidities subsequently arise, like the fire breaking out. It is not that the Buddha fails to respond to conditions, for he proceeds to other lands to meet with those who have the necessary affinity.

Because [the fire] has departed forever, it is said that it has "recently emerged. △ Third, the analogy for the momentum of the fire’s ignition illustrates the actual onset of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
"Suddenly a fire breaks out in the house behind" (up to) "it crushes and shatters, causing the walls to collapse and fall."
The three realms are the dwelling, the five aggregates are the house; the four directions are its locations, namely body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (*kāya*, *vedanā*, *citta*, *dharma*).

Because one gives rise to the four inversions, the five turbidities, and the eight sufferings regarding body, sensation, mind, and phenomena, it is said that they "continuously succeed one another at once.

Because they gradually increase, it is said they are "simultaneously ablaze. The severance of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the "explosive wind," and the dismemberment of the body is the "rending"; furthermore, one undergoes suffering.
The sound of moaning in bitter grief is called "the bursting of the sense-faculties.

The breaking [of the body] is called "tearing," the severing of breath and the separation of bones from tendons is called "crushing and snapping," and the dissolution of the four great elements is called "the collapsing of walls and foundations.
This fourth section clarifies the signs of being burned, which serve as metaphors for the eight sufferings and the five turbidities.
The various ghosts and spirits raised their voices in a great cry (up to: they were so utterly terrified and panicked that they could not escape on their own.

This is analogous to the aforementioned ghosts and spirits, which represent those who follow the views of the "personality-belief" (sakkāya-diṭṭhi). Those who reckon things as eternal (sassata-vāda) claim that dharmas are fixedly eternal;

since what exists must eventually cease to exist, they argue that non-existence is itself eternal. Those who reckon things as annihilated (uccheda-vāda) claim that dharmas are fixedly annihilated, asserting that there is only this single death and nothing more.
Furthermore, they continued to cry out, shouting at the top of their voices because the matter had already been made manifest through their definitive discourse.
The vultures and eagles represent the dull afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), while the *kumbhāṇḍas* and others represent the sharp afflictions.

Among these, those with the dull affliction of attachment to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) originally did not conceive of annihilation; now, seeing impermanence, they merely give rise to doubt and fear, not knowing how to achieve liberation.

For this reason, it is said that they are "terrified and unable to escape on their own. *Miaole* (妙樂) states: "The first two phrases belong to the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); the next phrase belongs to the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*);
and the final three phrases clarify the reason for not escaping, which depends exclusively upon views;

therefore, it repeats the mention of the *kumbhāṇḍas* and so forth. *Zhouzhuang* (周慞). [Supplementary note: In the *Chuci* (楚辭), it says "soaring aloft and moving about" (*lian xiaoyang xi zhouchang*); Wang Yi’s commentary explains that "zhou" means to circulate. In some versions of the sutra, it is written as "zhuang" (慞).]

(Instruction: The correct title is "Chapter on Fear"). △ Second, explaining the events within the holes as a metaphor for the arising of fire in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu). Part one: The things being burned.
Malevolent beasts and venomous insects hide and scurry within the holes, and piśāca demons also dwell therein.
The concentration of the four dhyānas is like a hollow opening; although it does not reach the open expanse outside the gate, one can still escape the fierce flames.
Likewise, by entering the concentration of the four dhyānas, although one has not yet exited the realm [of form], one can still escape the coarse evils of the desire realm.
It also enables sentient beings with sharp faculties to attain dhyāna-concentration, just as the piśāca spirits also dwell therein.
The *Zhong fanyi mingyi* states: "Piśāca" means "one who devours vital essence," referring to those who consume the vital essence of humans and the five grains.

*Miaole* explains that the first two phrases refer to the dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*), while the subsequent two phrases refer to the sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*). △ Second, the cause for the outbreak of fire.
Because their merit is meager, and due to their scanty fortune, they encounter suffering by being close to evil. △ Third, as for the force of the fire’s arising:
they are oppressed by the fire.
Although there is no fierce flame within the hollows, there is still the affliction of heat;

this is like the fourth dhyāna, which, though devoid of the evils of the desire realm, still possesses the subtle suffering of the attachment to the flavor of joy and bliss, and is therefore said to be "oppressed by fire.
△ Fourth, the signs of being burned.
They mutually harm one another, drinking blood and devouring flesh, until foul smoke and blazing embers fill the four directions.
Just as sentient beings driven by sharp or dull afflictions may attain the same meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) yet hold differing views,
thereby engaging in mutual contention and mutual injury, so too, once various views arise within meditative concentration, one cannot give rise to outflow-free (*anāsrava*) concentration and wisdom.
To be attached to the flavor of dhyāna is like drinking blood; to be attached to the five factors such as *vitarka* and *vicāra* is like a jackal devouring meat.

This is a metaphor for the craving of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Since one has already abandoned this craving by cultivating the future concentration (*anāgāmya-samādhi*) within the desire realm, it is said that they have both already died previously.
This is also called "devouring the craving for meditative concentration," just as a great predatory beast can swallow the entire desire realm.
Because of this greed, it is said that they compete to come and devour [beings]. The four inversions and eight sufferings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are like a fierce flame;
the four inversions and eight sufferings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are like foul-smelling smoke. Because smoke surpasses flame, the form realm is likened to smoke.

Furthermore, the form realm encompasses body, sensation, mind, phenomena (*dharmas*), and the four great elements (*mahābhūtas*); as these are suffering on all four sides, it is said to be "pervasive."
△ Third, the analogy for phenomena in the air: the arising of formless fire. Part one: the things burned.
Centipedes, millipedes, and venomous snakes, being scorched by the fire, scramble to flee from their burrows.

Previously, in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the centipede was used as a metaphor for hatred (*dveṣa*); now, in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the centipede is likewise used as a metaphor for hatred.
Although the centipede is not explicitly mentioned in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the mention of "poisonous insects" includes the centipede;

thus, one knows that hatred pervades all three realms. Regarding "venomous snakes" and so forth: those who are weary of the realm of form attain liberation by proceeding toward the formless realm, being weary of form.
Contemplating coarse objects as formless dharmas is like [a snake] leaving its hole due to being scorched by fire; the "wonderful bliss" mentioned previously refers to this.

The previous mention of "hiding in a hole" was used as a metaphor for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), whereas now, because it has "left the hole," it is used as a metaphor for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The realm of form is like the hole;
aversion to the lower [realm] is like the burning, and aspiration for the higher [realm] is like leaving the hole. △ Second, the characteristics of that which is burned.
The kumbhāṇḍa ghosts seize and devour whatever they encounter (up to: ...), wandering about in agitation and distress due to the torment of hunger and thirst.
Because one who attains the formless concentration (*ārūpyasamādhi*) necessarily extinguishes the conditions of the lower realms, it is said that they "seize and devour whatever they encounter.

Even those dwelling at the summit, the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), cannot escape the various sufferings of perversion, which are like a fire burning upon the head. Thus, even in the Peak of Existence... [the state of] non-perception... is not exempt from suffering.
There are also the fires of the eight sufferings: the arising of divergent thoughts in the mind is the suffering of birth;

the non-abiding of mindfulness is the suffering of aging; the agitation of the mental faculty that obstructs concentration is the suffering of illness; the falling away from concentration is the suffering of death; the failure to attain concentration despite seeking it is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
and the presence of obstacles when seeking concentration—which is necessarily met—is the suffering of encountering those one hates. Thus, concentration is lost.
The suffering of separation from what is loved refers to the suffering of the four aggregates; the mind itself is the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
Because there is no support of untainted food and drink, one is afflicted by hunger and thirst; since this remains within the cycle of saṃsāra, one wanders about in agitation and distress.
△ Fourth, the summary: Thus the various perils within the three realms are not one.
Such is the house—extremely terrifying, with poisonous harms, fires, and manifold calamities.
The verse on the general analogy concludes. △ Second, the verse on the specific analogies (three parts); first, the verse on the elder seeing the fire (three parts). First:
The verse describes the one who is able to see.
At that time, the master of the house was standing outside the gate and heard someone say:
"The master of the house" refers to the elder, the one who is able to see; "standing outside the gate" precisely corresponds to the preceding line: "Although I..."

One is able to emerge safely through the gate of what is being burned. As for "standing," it means that the Tathāgata, abiding in the stage of the Dharma-body, constantly harbors great compassion and desires to save sentient beings;
because he does not remain seated upon the throne of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), he is said to be "standing.

Regarding the phrase "hearing someone say": previously it was said "seeing," whereas now it is said "hearing"; "hearing" is used here as a substitute for "seeing," for hearing necessarily follows from seeing.
"Other dharmas are the Teacher of the Buddha" refers to the dharma of samādhi. When this dharma acts as the teacher, it is "another person.
If one enters samādhi, one is able to perceive the capacities [of beings]; because samādhi enables the Buddha to see, it is said that "there is a person.
Furthermore, it is also said that great compassion is "another person. △ Second, the verse on what is seen.
"You sons, because of your former play, you entered this house; being young and ignorant, you took delight in it and became attached to it. Question:
"Regarding the sons' original departure, why did they enter again because of their play? Answer:

"It was during the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū that they once gave rise to the Great Mind, which is called 'leaving the triple world. Yet, they subsequently fell back, which is called 'entering,' just as when a person lifts [a load]..."
When the feet are about to exit and reach the side of the gate, yet turn back, this is called both "exiting" and "returning to enter.

Furthermore, the fundamental nature of reality is inherently pure and is not a phenomenon of the triple world; thus it is called "exiting. Because of ignorance, conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) arises, whereby there is birth and death;

thus it is called "entering. Therefore, it is said that one first came to enter due to playing in the realm of phenomena. In the past, the conditions for affinity were shallow, and the great goodness was slight.
Those who have not yet attained renown are called "infantile" because they have regressed from the Mahāyāna and subsequently transmigrate through the three realms, shrouded by ignorance;

this is what is meant by "lack of knowledge. Regarding the explanation according to phenomena (*dharma*), it refers to regressing from the Mahāyāna and subsequently engaging in play with the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*).
Regarding the explanation according to principle (*artha*), it refers to engaging in play with conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). As for what is called "conceptual proliferation":

That is, because the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of the triple world are themselves the principle (*li*), one “emerges”; because the principle is itself the views and afflictions, one “enters.
△ Third, the verse on alarm and fear:
Having heard this, the elder was startled and entered the burning house.

△ Second, two verses on the analogy of abandoning the small table and using the carriage. First, one verse on the analogy of abandoning the small table. 3. First, [the Buddha] must consider what is appropriate;
only then can he provide rescue so that there is no burning or harm. (Up to: "In this place of such suffering and difficulty, how much more so with a great fire!"

"Appropriate" (*fāngyí*) means to adapt the Great Teaching to suit [the capacity of the audience]. "Exhorting and instructing" (*gàoyù*) refers to the meaning of explaining various afflictions and hardships to provide admonitions and teachings.

*Miaole* says: "The first line clearly explains the adaptation; the second line begins with the first phrase, which generally establishes that which is to be burned—namely, view-delusions and affliction-delusions (*jìnsī*).
The next phrase generally clarifies the force of the burning, and the following two phrases are brief [explanations]."

This clarifies the characteristics of burning. Furthermore, the subsequent one and a half lines extensively clarify that which is burned; within this text, the two categories of *darśana-heya* (afflictions abandoned through insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (afflictions abandoned through cultivation) are listed intermingled rather than in their proper sequence.
Following that, one line provides an analogical conclusion. Within this, the first two phrases present the subject of the analogy, while the subsequent two phrases provide the formal analogy:
since there is no concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), hunger and thirst are already terrifying; how much more so [the suffering of the fires of hell].

Furthermore, they are again scorched by the fires of turbidity; just as when one attains the contaminated meditative concentrations (*sāsrava-samādhi*) of the upper realms, one is already scorched by a small fire because the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) is absent, how much more so when falling into the great fires of the lower desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
He specifically points to hunger and thirst as this very suffering. △ Second, the verse on not accepting [the gift].
The sons, being ignorant, although they heard their father’s instruction, still remained attached to their pleasures.

The preceding verse states that the sons were unwilling to believe and accept it; "not accepting" means they lacked the capacity [for understanding] (*anabhavyatā*), which is due to their childish ignorance.
Because the text is abbreviated, it simply says "ignorant," yet they "still remained attached to their pleasures."
Having neither great aspirations nor practicing the minor ones, and being devoid of both the great and the small, one further becomes attached to the triple world.
△ Third, the verse on the cessation of transformation:
"Amusing oneself without end."

The verse above says, "He merely looked at his father and played," which refers to the *dṛṣṭi-heya* (delusions abandoned through seeing) and *bhāvanā-heya* (delusions abandoned through cultivation). The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states:

"Because the delusions of seeing and cultivation did not cease, the Great Transformation was suspended. Even if the delusions of seeing and cultivation had not ceased, there would still have been those with great capacity; the Tathāgata, at that time, would likewise not have withheld the Great [Vehicle].

However, because both the Great and Small [vehicles] were lost, and there remained only the delusions of seeing and cultivation, he first caused them to emerge from the turbid world by bestowing [the Lesser Vehicle]."
[The Buddha said: "Listen closely. △ Second, the verse on the analogy of the chariots, in three parts. First, the verse on the provisional teaching of the three chariots:
At that time, the elder had this thought... (up to) he then contemplated and devised various skillful means.

The first line clarifies the intended purpose; the next line explains the reason for employing the "Small" [Vehicle]. Because they are attached to views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), only the Small [Vehicle] is bestowed.
The following half-line clarifies the intent of employing the Small: if the Small were not employed, then both the Great and the Small would perish;
thus it says, "it will be harmed by fire. Because of this harm, one loses the body; because one loses the body, one loses life. The subsequent half-line is the actual [explanation].

I contemplate bestowing the small gift of the teachings of the Three Vehicles. ○ *Dānmiǎn* (the first character is read as *dōu hán*, meaning "to delight excessively"; the second is read as *mí yuàn*, meaning "to be submerged").
△ Second, the verse praising the rarity of the vehicle has four parts; first, the verse exhorting [the Buddha] to turn the wheel.
He addressed his sons, saying: "I have various kinds of rare playthings and excellent chariots made of wondrous jewels.
These "wondrous jewels" still belong to the realm of skillful means; that is, they are the wondrous jewels within the teachings of skillful means.
If these wondrous jewels were so great, why did [the sons] all go to their father's place to request them? 2. The Verse Showing the Turning [of the Wheel].
"The goat carts, deer carts, and great ox carts are now outside the gate.
That they are outside the gate is like showing the Four Noble Truths to cause one to know the transcendence of the world. △ Third, the exhortation to turn [the wheel].
"Come forth, all of you!
△ Fourth, the verse on the proof of the turning [of the wheel]:
'I have fashioned these chariots for you; you may play and sport therein according to your pleasure.'"
The meaning of the sutra text is this: "I am skilled at constructing vehicles to provide for all; you shall verify for yourself that I will certainly not lack vehicles.
This citation is without error, and the testimony granted is not false. △ Third, the verse on fulfilling the sons' wishes.
When the sons heard it said that such chariots [would lead them] to an open space, free from all suffering and hardship, they ran toward it;

this verse praises those who have seen the Truth (*dṛṣṭasatya*), while the following verse praises those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). △ Third, the verse on the analogy of bestowing great chariots equally, in four parts:
first, the verse on rejoicing at being freed from danger; second, the verse on being freed from danger.
The Way-seeker sees that the sons have emerged from the burning house and are seated upon lion thrones at the crossroads.
Regarding these lion thrones, there are two interpretations: first, it is said that the sons sit upon these thrones because they have escaped the three realms and are therefore fearless;
second, it is said that the elder sits upon this throne, for when the elder sees his sons have been delivered from calamity, he immediately attains fearlessness.

Regarding "awe-inspiring," the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states that the "four crossroads" refers to the Four Noble Truths. Initially, while [the father] stood outside the gate, the son was still within;
thus, the father remained standing. Now that the son has emerged, the father sits peacefully. Furthermore, because the great capacity [of beings] had not yet been met, he is said to have stood;

because the transformation of those with small capacities was already complete, he sits peacefully. Thus, we know that "standing" signifies hidden benefit, while "sitting" signifies [manifested] peace.
Manifesting the benefit. △ Second, the verse on rejoicing.
He speaks of his own celebration, saying: "I am now happy" (up to) "therefore, O people, I am now happy.

Regarding the phrase "speaking of his own celebration," etc., it means that because he has obtained those to be converted (*vineya*), he rejoices and is glad; [this occurred] at the places of twenty thousand *koṭi* of Buddhas.

Because he instructs them in the great conditions, it is said they are "born"; because they undergo minor ripening in the interim, it is said they are "nurtured. Having passed through this long period, they are repeatedly matured;
since their sustenance and care are not easily obtained, it is said it is "extremely difficult. Because the great elements are subtle, the ignorant and small-minded give rise to the five turbidities;
because they invite results through causes due to ignorance, it is said they "enter the house. The latter two lines refer to the many [defilements] of the lower realms.

The first two lines describe the fire of the *dṛṣṭi-kleśa* (afflictions of views) and *jñeya-kleśa* (afflictions regarding the knowable) that has arisen; the next two lines describe the intensity of the flames that have scorched them;
the following two lines combine these aspects of the *dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *jñeya-kleśa*; the next two lines clarify the reason for their joy;
and the final two lines conclude with the intent of their rejoicing. △ Second, the verse on the sons requesting the vehicles.
At that time, the sons knew their father had taken his seat... (up to) "Now is precisely the right time; please deign to grant it.

The first two phrases clarify the occasion for requesting the chariots, through which one knows from the preceding text that the father is seated. From "All went to... and below, there are two lines concerning the actual request;
within these, the first line is the formal request and the second line describes the granting of permission. Now follows the actual [granting].
The final two lines conclude the description of the ropes. △ Third, the verse on the equal bestowal of the great chariots. First, the verse explaining the great chariots:
"The elder is immensely wealthy, with many treasuries containing gold, silver, lapis lazuli, tridacna shell, agate, and coral."

Wu Cheng states that "kū" (storehouse) refers to the ground, while "zàng" (treasury) refers to the functioning of all dharmas; thus, the name "zàng" signifies the six faculties, such as the eye, which possess all dharmas.
Regarding the statement that the functioning of all dharmas is called "zàng," this is based solely on the meaning of "containing and storing.
As for the six faculties possessing all [dharmas] being called "kū," it is because "zàng" is broad while "kū" is narrow. This is merely [the distinction].
The various treasuries for storage differ, just as the six sense organs are distinct;

yet because each organ possesses [all others], all practices are complete within each sense organ. Were it not for this single school, how could one hear of these roots and practices being treated as treasuries and storehouses, each containing all dharmas?
△ Second, the verse on the Great Vehicle.
With various precious objects, one constructs great chariots (extending to) with bells suspended on all four sides and entwined with golden cords.
All phenomena pertaining to cause and effect are collectively termed "various treasures. In terms of the provisional teachings, this refers to the meaning of attaining through cultivation;

as for the analogy of constructing them, because there are many offspring and many [components], the chariots are not singular. Therefore, what is constructed is manifold and moreover vast, and it is also necessary to indicate the directions.

Knowing that the arising of cultivation is termed "construction," one dissolves this construction through its inherent nature; thus, construction returns to what is originally possessed, which is the very body of the chariot.
The adornments below are the various means of deliverance, as explained previously.
A net of pearls is spread over it (until) it is surrounded on all sides by various colorful ornaments.
Regarding "pearls and so forth," this refers to the manifestation of the canopy of the various gates of loving-kindness (*maitrī-mukha*). These are not merely one;
rather, they are like the mesh of a net, with a single pearl within each individual mesh, just as the manifold gates of loving-kindness all accord with reality.

While the preceding text simply mentions "hanging garlands of flowers" to indicate that those who see them are made joyful, the present statement that they "hang down everywhere" clarifies the multitude [of these adornments].
The "mechanism" (jī) signifies universal joy; the various colored decorations symbolize that in the places where transformation is manifested, the appropriate responses are established differently;
and the fact that they surround it on all sides symbolizes that the suitability for gathering sentient beings is complete without any deficiency.
[He] uses soft silk and cotton wadding to make quilts and mattresses... (up to) many attendants and guards surrounding him.

Having obtained such a vehicle, he causes his sons and others (to reach) the point where they mount this precious vehicle and proceed directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Regarding "day and night": when one first attains the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the light of the wisdom of the Middle Way is like the division of day, while ignorance remains as night;

when one personally attains the wisdom of the Middle Way, it is like the sun, whereas entering into birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is like night. Because one constantly practices these two modes of existence, it is so called.

"Throughout many kalpas you have been scorched by manifold sufferings; I have rescued you all and caused you to emerge from the triple world.

The first line clarifies that although obstacles are removed and birth-and-death is exhausted, it is said "yet in reality it is not extinguished" because while the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-janma-maraṇa*) has been exhausted, the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-janma-maraṇa*) still remains.
