△ Second, explaining why they cannot be transformed [by the One Vehicle] and thus the three vehicles are taught.
If there are people of small wisdom who are deeply attached to craving and desire... [up to] "the Buddha taught that the Truth of Suffering is real and without difference.

From here below, it correctly clarifies the four truths with active effort (*saṃskṛta*). Because those of small wisdom have heavy obstructions and do not immediately believe and accept [the teaching], this is a skillful means (*upāya*) to provide guidance by opening up three paths;
for the sake of those of small wisdom, he speaks of the Truth of Suffering. Among the Three Vehicles, these are the Śrāvakas.
At the very least, one takes the Truth of Suffering as the initial gateway. "Suffering" has the meaning of oppression and affliction; "Truth" means that which is examined and verified as not false.

In summary, this does not go beyond the cycle of birth and death within the six realms. For those sentient beings whose minds find joy [in worldly things], if one accords with their original habits, they will rejoice;
yet, fundamentally, they loathe birth and death and seek nirvana for themselves. Now, upon hearing of renunciation, they immediately...
Because of the habitual tendencies from past lives, the mind finds joy in this truth; "truly without difference" means that the *Śāstrāṃśa-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Bequeathed Teachings) states:
"The Buddha taught that the Truth of Suffering is truly suffering and cannot be made into pleasure," hence it is said to be "truly without difference.
The two following phrases clarify the capacity of the sentient beings (*mārga*), while the two subsequent phrases clarify the response of the Buddha (*prati-saṃvid*).

If there are sentient beings who do not know the root of suffering—[extending] to the fact that all sufferings have craving as their root—the first line correctly clarifies the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), in the sense of "gathering" or "summoning"; since origination is the cause of suffering, it is called the "root of suffering.
Because sentient beings do not know this, they become deeply attached [to it], taking it to be real; these two phrases reveal that the Path (*mārga*) is able to cure this.
The two phrases beginning with "the accumulation of all sufferings" clarify the faults and afflictions of the origin (*samudaya*).
If craving is extinguished, there is no basis for support, and all sufferings are utterly extinguished; this is called the third truth, the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Herein, the first two phrases clarify the function of ceasing the origin: if the causes of the origin are extinguished, then suffering will not exist.
The latter two phrases of the basis clarify how the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) receives its name.
Because it is the Truth of Cessation, one practices the Path (*mārga*).
This clarifies the Truth of the Path; "path" carries the meaning of being able to lead through, as it can lead one to reach true emptiness and *nirvāṇa*. Briefly stated...
Thus, morality, concentration, and wisdom—when expanded—are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*).
To be free from all bonds of suffering is called attaining liberation (*vimukti*); [this continues] until: "merely being free from false delusion is called liberation."
The first two lines reiterate that attaining liberation from the *samudaya* (origin) is the binding agent and *duḥkha* (suffering) is that which is bound;

being free from this suffering and its origin is called attaining liberation. The following two lines pose a question: "Attaining liberation by contemplating the Truths—what kind of liberation is this?
The subsequent two lines provide the explanation: "It is merely being free from delusion," for ignorance is already unreal to perceive.
Because volition arises in attachment to ignorance, it is called "illusory existence. Regarding the four truths, if one merely eliminates these delusions, this is termed "liberation";

however, because one is liberated from the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) realm but not yet liberated from the *pariṇāma-vaśitā* (transformational) realm, it is not yet sovereign. △ Third, explaining the latter:
if one is capable [of further progress], one may return to that great [state].
In reality, it is not because [the Buddha] has attained all-encompassing liberation that he appears in the world, but rather to bring peace and security to sentient beings.

All-encompassing liberation is precisely the unconditioned Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and the Unsurpassed Path is the unconditioned Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). The Buddha’s original intent was to bestow all-encompassing liberation upon all;
yet now you have merely severed the cycle of birth and death through segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*), and what you have realized is not the True Emptiness.
Because they have not yet attained all-encompassing liberation, and because it ultimately does not accord with the Buddha’s original intent, it is said:
"It is not my wish that they reach extinction; this is merely the liberation of the Hīnayāna.
Now, by causing them instead to attain the Unsurpassed Way and enter Great Nirvāṇa, this is the ultimate fulfillment of the Buddha’s original intent—the Way of Non-action.
Having previously sought to expound this [teaching] on the cessation and destruction of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*) regarding suffering and its origin, sentient beings were unable to bear it;
now that their obstacles have been removed, he speaks of it again. As the Dharma King, the Buddha has attained mastery over both provisional and ultimate teachings;

having opened the three provisional gates to reveal the one ultimate reality, how could there be any falsehood? As the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "The first one and a half lines [refer to] the Unsurpassed Way."
The Dharma refutes [the preceding], and the next one and a half lines reveal the Buddha’s fundamental mind. △ Second, sixty-five lines of *gāthā* in isolation exhort faith;
this is also called the method for penetrating the sutra. Part two: first, the heading; second, the initial heading distinguishing what can be spoken from what cannot be spoken.

This refers to the skillful exposition for the sake of those who contemplate the future; it is as stated in the subsequent text:

If those who hear it are deluded and fail to understand, one should not preach it for them;
this explains the section on "preaching and not preaching. △ Second, explaining what is accessible and what is inaccessible:
first, clarifying that one should not preach to evil people out of great compassion.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, do not preach this sutra to those who are arrogant, indolent, or who harbor views of a self.
First, it is listed that those with arrogance, indolence, attachment to a self, and desire will inevitably give rise to evil slanders and obtain evil retributions;
therefore, out of great compassion, one must not preach it to such wicked ones.
Ordinary people of shallow understanding are deeply attached to the five desires (up to the point where they) sever all seeds of Buddhahood in the world.
Regarding the severing of the seeds of Buddhahood in the world, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* takes afflictions (*kleśa*) as the seeds of the Tathāgata;

this [text] takes the nature of objective spheres (*viṣaya*) as the seeds of Buddhahood (the natures of good and evil phenomena are different names for the nature of objective spheres). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* [teaches] that one studies the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

If one takes this grasping of the nature of the *tadyakti-hetu* (the cause of manifestation) as the seed of Buddhahood, it is the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* that applies the principle of the nature of the mind to ensure this grasping is not severed;
if one takes this grasping of the nature of the *mūlahetu* (the primary cause) as the seed of Buddhahood, it is the present sūtra that clarifies that even minor good roots lead to Buddhahood.
If one does not believe that minor good roots lead to Buddhahood, one severs the worldly seed of the Buddha.
Furthermore, some may frown and harbor doubts... (up to) because they sever the seeds of the Buddha, they undergo this retribution for their sins.

The *Miaole* commentary states that among the animals, those said to "sever the seeds of the Buddha" specifically refer to those who destroy the two causes: the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) and the direct cause (*upādāna-hetu*).
Lack of faith severs the direct cause of the Buddha-seed; failing to practice even minor good deeds severs the contributory cause of the Buddha-seed.
This sutra universally opens the Buddha-seed for all six realms of existence; if one slanders the meaning of this sutra, it is as if they have severed it.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Four: "The Stage of Faith and Understanding.

Indeed, faculties may be sharp or dull, delusions may be thick or thin, teachings may be expressed through both Dharma and parables, and awakenings may occur earlier or later—thus it is for the two vehicles.
Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they had merely contemplated emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet harbored not a single thought of joy or aspiration for the Bodhisattva Dharma.
At the beginning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly, those of superior faculties understood upon hearing the brief exposition, while those of middling faculties did not yet comprehend it;
their attachments were stirred and doubts arose. Although they heard extensively from the five Buddhas, they remained obscured and unenlightened; now, hearing the parables, they rejoice.

Because they leap with joy, faith is aroused, understanding arises, doubt is dispelled, and the principle is clarified, it is called the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (*śraddhādhimukti-parivarta*).

Furthermore, because those of middle capacity, upon hearing the teaching of parables, first shatter their doubts and enter the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) of the Mahāyāna, it is called "Entering by Faith" (*śraddhā-praveśa*);
and because they enter the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) of the Mahāyāna, it is called "Understanding. As the text says: "Today we are truly śrāvakas, for by the Buddha..."
The sound of the Way causes all to hear; because hearing the Perfect Teaching leads one to enter the Perfect Stage, it is called the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding.
△ Second, the Chapter on Faith and Understanding clarifies how those of medium capacity attain understanding. Part One: The Sūtra Master’s Narrative of Joy. Sub-part One: Narrating the Inner Mind.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti (up to: gave rise to a rare mind and leaped for joy.

"Subhūti" alone is called "Venerable Life" (*āyuṣmat*), while the three [others] are called "Great" (*mahat*); this is the general explanation. Generally speaking, they are all "great" and all possess "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
Specifically, Subhūti understands the wisdom of emptiness-of-emptiness as his life; among all those possessing wisdom, the Buddha’s wisdom is foremost. The Buddha, regarding...
Prajñā summons them and instructs them; because they are summoned by those possessed of wisdom, they are called "Wisdom-Life" (prajñājīvika).

The phrase "that which was heard from the Buddha," and so forth, refers to the causes for attaining joy. The preface states that I have recently heard a parable which speaks of the rare occurrence of the arousal of the bodhicitta. Because it is called "arousing," it is termed "faith" (*śraddhā*).

He further thinks: "If I were to obtain a son to whom I could entrust my wealth and property, I would be at ease and joyful, free from further anxiety.

When there is an opportunity for deliverance, it is called "obtaining a son"; when he bestows the prediction of Buddhahood upon him, it is called "entrusting the Dharma-wealth," which accords with his original aspiration and is thus termed "joyful.
This concludes the general analogy of the preceding section. 2. The Analogy of the Father and Son Meeting. (Part Two)
First, regarding the son’s initial sight of his father, there are four points concerning the manner of that first encounter.
World-Honored One, at that time, the impoverished son, wandering about in search of employment, happened to come upon his father’s house.

Through his weariness with suffering and his aspiration for joy, he sought out the flavor of principle; by gradually accumulating such practice, he eventually established supramundane roots of goodness.
Therefore, it is said that by means of this root of goodness, accumulated through successive acts of service, one is able to strike upon the Buddha’s compassion;
hence it is said that one "encounters" the father’s house. The father is a metaphor for the Dharma-body after the Path; the house is a metaphor for unconditional compassion (*nirālambana-karuṇā*).

Because both the Great and Small capacities strike upon this house simultaneously, and because there is a great capacity within this house, it is said that one "sees the father from afar"; yet because there is also a small capacity, it is likewise said.
If he were to stand by the gate as only a small being and not a great one, the son would not see the body of the Honored One with its distinctive marks,
nor would the father say, "I now have something to entrust to you regarding my wealth and treasuries. If he were only a great being and not a small one,
the son would not be standing by the gate, nor would he say, "This place of exquisite bliss is not where I obtained goods through hired labor."
Regarding the method of labor for hire: exchanging one's strength for wealth originally arises from a false view, yet it still holds the hope of escaping suffering.

Although this is a wrong pursuit, it secretly provides support for the Right Path; thus, it causes those in the world who weary of suffering to eventually form the karmic conditions for transcendence.

Because the worldly can easily lead to the supramundane, it is said that labor for hire proceeds "from one to one," and because it moves from stage to stage, it is said to be "successive," meeting [the goal] without prior expectation.
Therefore, it is called "encountering by chance": through worldly phenomena, one suddenly feels the compassion of the supramundane;

furthermore, through unexpected worldly false reasoning, one gives rise to right view and encounters the Buddha. Moreover, unexpectedly, within a small act of merit, one secretly enters the perfect gate of the Mahāyāna.
When both the capacities for the Great and Small Vehicles strike this dwelling together, if the capacity for the Great Vehicle has not yet matured, right view [remains incomplete].
Yet, with a slight sense of resonance, he gradually drew closer to the side of the gate. △ Second, the place where he saw his father:
Standing by the side of the gate, he gazed from afar at his father.

"By the side of the gate" is a metaphor for the two contemplations (*dvividha-vipaśyanā*) as skillful means; that is, the practitioner who possesses the capacity for the perfect center stands at the gate.
Because right view in the Two Vehicles pertains only to partial truth, it is called "beside the gate";

because the Samādhi of Emptiness alone and the Wisdom-Eye of partial truth only glance sideways at the Dharma-body, it is said that one "sees his father from afar. This means that while the great capacity has just begun to be aroused, the act of knocking and summoning is still distant;
hence, it is said "from afar. △ Third, the appearance of seeing the father.
"Seated upon a lion throne with a precious footstool supporting his feet.

This refers to the time when the Tathāgata preached the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. "Seated upon a lion throne" means that the perfect retribution Dharma-body dwells securely within the principle of emptiness;
because there are no longer the two types of delusion (the pervasive and the specific) nor the fear of the eight māras, it is said he is "seated upon a lion throne."

Furthermore, regarding the precious footstool that supports the feet: meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) serve as the feet, while the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) serves as the stool.

This signifies that the concentration and wisdom of non-arising rely upon the realm of *tathatā* (suchness). As the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states: "Sitting upon the lion throne" is explained as having a symbolic meaning;
although the actual lion throne lacks the physical form of a lion, it exists only to represent something. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The Buddha is the foremost among men..."
Because it is where the Buddha, the Lion, sits, it is called the lion throne; what the Buddha speaks is called the lion’s roar. Regarding the "perfect reward body" (*pūrṇa-vipāka-kāya*):
although its categories include both the general and the particular, it is called the perfect reward because it follows what is preeminent and fundamental.

As for the "jeweled lecterns" and so forth: a single lectern supports two feet, which are the basis for concentration and wisdom; since there is no distinction between them, they are adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom. The Dharma [is thus revealed].
Because the body is capable of being designated [as such], it is said that concentration and wisdom are unarisen.
Various Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and householders (up to) stood in attendance at his left and right, holding white fly-whisks in their hands.
The Brahmin named Pure Conduct (Viśuddhacārin), noble and of high integrity, is the Bodhisattva Equanimity (Samatā) Free from Defilement.
The Kṣatriya refers to those of the royal lineage, namely the Bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi up to the ninth bhūmi.
The Householder, wealthy but not noble, refers to the thirty minds [of the stage of practice]. The pearl necklace refers to the dhāraṇīs of morality, concentration, and wisdom.
The "three samādhis of the bhikṣuṇīs" are the four *ratnābharaṇas* (necklaces). That which is worth ten million refers to the merits of the forty stages (*bhūmi*) used to adorn the Dharma-body.

Regarding the "officials, commoners, servants, and attendants": those who clarify the meaning through other gates—that is, those who receive the two teachings of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and the *Śrāvaka* (Shared)—and have severed the delusions of the shared [vehicle], are called "commoners.
Those who receive the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-śāsana*) and have severed the delusions of the shared [vehicle] are called... [the term for officials follows].
If an official is one who clarifies the meaning [of the Dharma] alongside the gate, this is still the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya*). Internally, it accords with true wisdom;
externally, it accords with the conditions of sentient beings. This is analogous to the principle of officials and commoners having the duty of internal service and external labor.
The white fly-whisk is the function of provisional wisdom (*prajñā*). As for "left and right," "right" refers to the function of the wisdom that enters emptiness, which sweeps away [delusions].

Regarding the fourth dwelling, "Dust on the Left": one enters the provisional wisdom (*prajñā*) to sweep away the dust and sand of delusions. These two constitute the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Middle Way;

thus it is said that they attend and stand by [the Buddha]. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "Previously, officials and subjects were contrasted with the ten dwellings and ten practices of the Perfect Teaching;

now, officials and subjects are contrasted with those who have severed the pervasive delusions through the three preceding teachings. Furthermore, because they are listed together with servants and attendants, this is clearly understood.
Names are established according to their meanings and cannot be fixed definitively; fundamentally, how can one adhere to a single "stump" when both principle and phenomena vary?

Therefore, while previously the officials and commoners were treated as substantial entities, here the officials and commoners are subsumed under the provisional (upāya). Thus, within the two gates of identity and difference, they are treated as identical across different stages, yet must be distinguished as distinct.
Difference refers to the application of the provisional, while identity refers to the revelation of the ultimate; these are merely the officials and commoners themselves.
In meaning, it should belong to both.
It is covered with jeweled canopies and hung with various flower banners (extending to) all manner of magnificent adornments, its majestic virtue being exceptionally sublime.
"Covered with jeweled canopies" refers to true compassion; "hung with various flower banners" means that the flowers are the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).

The banners are supernormal powers; the sprinkling of fragrant water upon the ground signifies the pouring down of the Dharma-water to moisten the minds of the bodhisattvas, thereby subduing the dust of delusion—this is also the water of meditative concentration sprinkled upon the mind-ground.
The scattering of various named flowers signifies the arrangement of the seven kinds of pure flowers:
namely, the purity of precepts, concentration, wisdom, the severance of doubt, the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path, and the purity of final knowledge.
"Precepts" refers to the three types of precepts, such as the restraint of moral discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*). "Concentration" refers to samādhis such as Śūraṅgama.
"Wisdom" refers to true wisdom (*prajñā*). "Elimination of Doubt" means having already transcended doubts regarding the two truths.

"Purity of the Path and Non-Path" means practicing through non-paths while attaining penetration into the Buddha-way. "Purity of Knowledge and Vision" means the perfection of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).
"Clearly seeing the Buddha-nature" means that the perfection of the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-sampad*) has been achieved and ignorance is forever exhausted.
"Arranging precious objects" means arranging the true merits of the various stages (*bhūmi*). "Taking out and putting in" has the same meaning as the previous "entering and exiting.
Taking for oneself is "taking," while transforming others is "giving. Its majestic power is preeminent, and its radiance is boundless.
The physical form and marks are boundless, like a vast ocean of sublime characteristics; this principle must refer to the Buddha Vairocana—how could it possibly refer to any other Śākyamuni?

(The character "chū" [出] is pronounced with the first tone when things emerge spontaneously, but with the fourth tone when one causes something to emerge. (The character "nèi" [內] is often read by the secular as *níu* [儒], which is incorrect;
it should be read as *nà* [納], meaning "to enter. The ancient character for "nà" was interchangeable with this. △ Fourth, the arising of a mind of fear and avoidance.
The impoverished son saw that his father possessed great power and influence (up to the point where he realized), "This is not a place where I can obtain wealth through hired labor.

"Great power and influence" means that because his wisdom is vast, it is called "great power," and because his spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*) are vast, it is called "great influence"—this has the same meaning as the aforementioned physical strength of hand and arm.
"Terror" refers to one of inferior capacity who, being weak and frail, feels fear and dread toward the Great Way; this is "regret."
As for those who have come here, the Buddha originally intended to present them with the Great Dharma;
however, as it did not accord with their capacities, they harbored a desire to retreat from the Great [Vehicle], and thus it is said that they "regret having come here.

Regarding the phrase "privately forming this thought," this refers to something secretly and subtly present within their faculties, occurring in the hidden realm rather than being manifest before them upon seeing the Exalted Response Body (nirmāṇakāya); hence it is called a "private thought. Alternatively, it may refer to the King.
Regarding the phrase "the King and his peers": Pāpīyān is the King, and his followers are his peers.

Those of inferior capacity who have severed the seeds of existence and attained the state of silence—whose path transcends all forms and appearances—behold the image of the Supreme Response-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), which is beyond the reach of gods and men.

Because the Dharma they preach is utterly distinct from that of the Two Vehicles, those of meager virtue who have never before seen or heard it immediately declare, "This is Māra; this is the work of Māra."
Furthermore, it is said that the Dharma-body is like a king and the Reward-body is like a king;
this refers to the Mahāyāna Dharma-recompense and is not a place where one gains benefit according to the Small Vehicle.

Therefore, I privately reflect that these may indeed be kings and the like, and not places where I, a hired laborer, can obtain wealth—this is because those of small capacity cannot receive the Great Transformation.
"It would be better to go to the poor quarters and exert one's strength where there is ground for it. Having formed this thought, he ran off quickly.

Regarding the phrase "it would be better to go to the poor quarters," the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "One is able to use the dharmas obtained from the poor to deliver those who are base and inferior.
However, because the principle of emptiness alone does not encompass the myriad virtues and is therefore not the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is referred to as "poor."
Because the village is situated in a remote wilderness, it is said that those of small wisdom exert their efforts there;
"exerting effort" means to rely upon this small wisdom to attain *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. The untainted robes and food are called "robes" and "food," respectively;
thus it is said that robes and food are easily obtained. If one dwells here for a long time, one must traverse the path of the Mahāyāna through immeasurable eons.

Because it has been for kalpas, it is said that [the father] has long dwelt [there]. Since I originally loathed and feared birth and death (*saṃsāra*), yet practicing the Mahāyāna necessarily involves entering *saṃsāra* to extensively study the myriad practices (*pāramitās*), it is said that he "presses me.

Because I originally delighted in the Small Vehicle, yet now causes me to give rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna—this is like being forced to abandon the Great and take up the Small—it is said that he "runs swiftly. △ Second, the father sees his son.
Fourth, regarding the place where the father first saw his son:
at that time, the wealthy elder was upon the lion throne;
the lion throne is the place where he saw his son. The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata dwells in the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) of fearlessness.
This is to illuminate the capacities [of beings] through their environment. △ Second, "Recognizing the child upon seeing him.
Regarding "recognizing the child upon seeing him":
the Tathāgata, having discerned the capacity, knew that this was a sentient being with whom he had established a karmic connection in the past. △
Third, seeing his son, he rejoices;
his heart is filled with great joy.
That his heart is filled with great joy means that the Buddha constantly observes his son's capacity, and now that this capacity has arisen in accordance with his compassion, he therefore rejoices.

This refers to the arising of the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) within the "Exposition of the Dharma" (the *dharmadeśanā*) concerning the acquisition [of the child], which corresponds to the "Great Terror" in the parable.

That passage speaks of "terror" because it clarifies that great compassion extracts suffering; this passage speaks of "joy" because it clarifies that great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) bestows happiness.
△ Fourth, the child’s wish is fulfilled.
He then had this thought: "Regarding my wealth and storehouses... although I am now old, I still harbor greed and attachment.

In the past, seeing sentient beings decline from the Great Vehicle to take up the Small, seeking food in impoverished quarters and struggling for their livelihoods, I constantly wished to give them wealth;
yet finding no opportunity, I could not do so. Today, the opportunity has arrived, coinciding with my heart of great compassion; therefore, I say that the storehouses are now available."
That which I have been constantly mindful of as entrusted to me is clarified as follows: it is not merely because [the beings] are poor and lack great wealth;
rather, because they are oppressed by the manifold sufferings of saṃsāra and are objects of my great compassion, I am constantly mindful of them.

Yet, although I wish to rescue them, because they lack the capacity (indriya) for salvation and cannot be saved, I said, "I have no means to see them. Now, however, because the capacity for deliverance has arisen, I say, "And suddenly..."
"Because he has long been called one who possesses a great compassionate heart, it is said that this deeply accords with my wishes.
As for why he says "I am old," it is because his period of transformation in this world has come to an end; thus he speaks of being "old.

Furthermore, as he has not yet encountered those of great capacity (*mahā-indriya*) to whom the Dharma may be entrusted, from whom could those yet to be delivered find liberation? Therefore, he says, "I still cherish [this Dharma] despite my age."
It is said that because the present opportunity will come of its own accord and there is no need for such anxiety regarding stinginess, my wish is fulfilled.

△ Third, the parable of the father’s command to pursue and entice [the son], in two parts: first, dispatching an attendant to pursue him; third, first, acknowledging the previous gate of exhortation and assessing the suitability of the lack of opportunity, in two parts:
first, the assessment of suitability.

He immediately dispatched an attendant to pursue and bring [the person] back. At that time, the messenger ran swiftly to seize him. This refers to leading [the practitioner] through the *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra];
here, leading them through the "Exhortation Gate" (*kuan-men*) above is the intended application.

Regarding "dispatching an attendant": wisdom is that which dispatches, and the teaching is that which is dispatched; the principle is the primary, while the teaching is the secondary. From the Buddha, the twelve divisions of scripture (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) emerge.
It is intended that sentient beings who lack the capacity will not receive [the teaching], just as they would not accept milk;
therefore, it is said that "a bystander is sent away. Furthermore, regarding the "bystander," "bystander" refers to ministers and assistants;

this means that Dharma-body Bodhisattvas are dispatched to preach the Mahāyāna, such as when the four Bodhisattvas are made to explain the forty stages (*bhūmi*) within the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*—this is what is meant by "sending away the bystander."
Regarding "hastily pursuing to bring back": this refers directly to the Great Teaching being adapted for those of limited capacity;

thus it is said they are "hastily pursued. Because they possess the great seeds from the past, it is said they are "brought back. Regarding "running swiftly to seize them": the clear meaning of the Mahāyāna is manifest and straightforward;
by employing this to meet the needs of sentient beings, one causes them to hasten toward Bodhi. Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Vehicle) Sūtra says: "Its speed is like the wind."

If one takes a bodhisattva as a bystander, that bodhisattva, possessing their own supernatural powers and further empowered by the Buddha, can also cause that person to swiftly enter into Bodhi. △ Second, those lacking the karmic affinity.
The impoverished son was startled and alarmed, crying out in resentment and shouting, "I have committed no offense against you;

why do you seize me? This illustrates that there is no karmic affinity for the Gate of Exhortation. Although the follower of the Lesser Vehicle may have once developed the Great Mind in the past, it has long been abandoned and forgotten.
Suddenly hearing the Great Teaching, it contradicts his mind; thus he is startled and, not recognizing it, is alarmed. Therefore, it is said: "The impoverished son was startled and alarmed. Small.

To take afflictions as one's enemies and birth-and-death as suffering, yet to be exhorted that "afflictions are themselves bodhi," is like crying out at the top of one’s voice to proclaim an injustice;
to hear that "birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa" is like crying out at the top of one’s voice to proclaim agony. Therefore, it is said:

"I cry out at the top of my voice, protesting my grievance. Since I originally did not seek the Great [Vehicle], for what reason has the Great been used to transform me? Thus it is said: "I do not..."
Regarding the phrase "What is the offense for which you have been seized? Miaole says that "crying out in resentment" refers to what the sutra simply calls "resentment," rather than "suffering.
In the commentary, the term "crying out" (*dàhuàn*) is explained as "painful suffering" (*kūtòng*). Thus, it possesses two meanings:
because encountering an enemy inevitably involves suffering, "crying out" is used as a metaphor for it. △ Second, receiving the aforementioned section on admonitions as a metaphor.
"It is appropriate that there be no [further] opportunity. First, regarding the "simulation of appropriateness":
the messenger grasped him ever more tightly and forcibly dragged him back.

On his collar was written a warning to the gatekeeper; this is the "simulation of appropriateness. As for "grasping him ever more tightly," it clarifies that although he previously encouraged him toward goodness, he still remained [hesitant].
"To predict that I shall preach matters of fear for him" means to urgently admonish him with words of suffering to cause him to distance himself from evil;
since he lacks internal capacity while being externally constrained by the Great Transformation, this is like forcibly dragging him back.
△ Second, lack of capacity.
At that time, the impoverished son thought to himself, "I am innocent... (up to) "...he became even more terrified, fainted, and fell prostrate on the ground.
Regarding the instruction on the gate of leading [others], there is no [innate] capacity [in him]. As for "thinking oneself innocent," "sin" refers to compassion (*karuṇā*).

Because sentient beings have sin, they enter the prison of birth and death; because the Bodhisattva possesses compassion, he likewise enters the prison as one who shares in their sin, as do those of the Two Vehicles.
A person who lacks compassion is called "sinless" [only in name], yet they enter the prison of birth and death; this is precisely what it means to be imprisoned.
Lacking great skillful means, they enter birth and death and will inevitably forever lose the life-force of the wisdom of the Three Vehicles;
therefore, it is said that they are certain to die. Reflecting on such matters, one speaks of becoming even more terrified and compelled to rely on the Great Teaching rather than small wisdom.

Because he understood [the situation], it is said that he fainted; because he would certainly fall into the three miserable realms by immediately giving rise to slander, it is said that he fell to the ground.

△ Third, summarizing the exhortation to cease the Mahāyāna transformation. Part Four: First, reflecting on the cessation of the transformation. Sub-part One: First, knowing that his great resolve was weak.
The father saw him from afar and spoke to his messenger, saying, "There is no need for this man; do not force him to come.

That he saw him from afar is because his small capacity is far removed from the Great Vehicle; thus it is called "afar. That he is called "one who sees" is because he is a child with whom [the Buddha] has established a karmic connection.

As for "he spoke to his messenger," if we speak according to the teaching, the messenger represents fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while what was said represents the wisdom of the teaching (*deśanā-jñāna*). Thus, it is through the wisdom of the teaching that one knows.
The great teaching for non-sentient beings should be brought to rest;

if one considers humans as the recipients of this teaching, then one tells the bodhisattvas that they need not manifest their sublime and wondrous bodies for the two vehicles to see. As stated in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*:
"Withdraw your bodily fragrance so that those sentient beings do not give rise to delusion or attachment. Furthermore, when Samantabhadra enters this Sahā world, he contracts his body...
That they are "small" is precisely the meaning [of this]. Regarding the phrase "do not force them to come":

since they lack the great capacity (*mahā-avakāśa*), if one were to manifest a superior body and preach the Mahāyāna Dharma, it would likely damage their roots of goodness; therefore, it says "do not force them. △ Second, knowing that their small aspirations are firm.
Sprinkle cold water on their faces to cause them to awaken; do not speak with them further.

Sprinkling cold water on the face signifies that they possess limited aspirations and should employ the three types of ash to sever the principle of water and eliminate the heat of view-delusions and afflictive delusions.
"Face" refers to the aversion toward birth and death, which is like turning one's face away from it; "awakening" means [turning toward] Nirvana.
He opens the Lesser Teaching to accommodate those of lesser capacity, enabling them to depart from affliction and confusion and realize the Four Noble Truths.
"Do not speak with him again" means that one must certainly cease the teaching of the Mahāyāna.

Miaole (妙樂) explains that "face" (*mian*) is interpreted as "to turn toward," because there is a faculty that turns away from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and turns toward *nirvāṇa*; thus it is called a "face," which does not mean sprinkling upon that *nirvāṇa*.
Do not speak with him again; such speech is merely instruction. △ Second, explaining the intent behind ceasing the transformation [of others]:
"For what reason? A father knows his son... [but] he does not say to others, 'This is my son.'"
The followers of the Two Vehicles loathe suffering and delight in emptiness; being intimately attached to what is inferior, they lack compassion and thus fear the Great Dharma as difficult to master.
For the time being, their limited aspirations are permitted, which suppresses the Buddha’s original intent and causes him to cease his transformative activity.

However, knowing with certainty that they had previously resolved upon the Great Mind under twenty-two billion Buddhas, he says, "I know for certain that you are my son. Regarding the phrase "by means of skillful expedients," etc.: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.]
In the past, within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, there was "speech according to the intentions of others" (*parapudgalāśayānuvartana-vāk*), a skillful means used for concealment and protection;

it was called "being a Śrāvaka," while "speech according to one's own intentions" (*svapudgalāśayānuvartana-vāk*)—which refers to being a Bodhisattva—was not spoken of. The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states:

"Because it conceals the real and protects the provisional, it is called 'concealment and protection' (*fuhoku*). It is also 'concealing and shielding' (*fuyin jianghu*) so as not to manifest the reality. Thus, prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, apart from the One Reality...

All are termed "speech according to the intentions of others" because, in the past, within the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā, there were still teachings of the Small Vehicle and no statements that one could attain Buddhahood through the Small Vehicle;
thus, both the "milk" and the two types of "ghee" were addressed to those of Small Vehicle capacity, and it was simply said that [the Buddha] did not speak according to his own intention.
△ Third, the actual clarification of the cessation of transformation.
The messenger said to him, "I now release you; go wherever you please.

By saying "I now release you," he recognizes that the great capacity [of the recipient] is weak; by saying "go wherever you please," he recognizes that the small goodness [of the recipient] is strong.
For these two reasons, he ceases his great transformation. △ Fourth, the appropriateness of ceasing the transformation.
The impoverished son, filled with joy at having attained what he had never experienced before, rose from the ground and went to a poor neighborhood to seek food and clothing.
Because he was not coerced by the Great Teaching, he was joyful; because he was spared from the grave sin of slandering it, he was freed from the three miserable realms.

Thus it is said that "from the ground" there arose a small measure of goodness, and thus it is said that he "arose. Furthermore, previously, when he was presented with the suitability for the Great Dharma, he was bewildered and distressed.
Not understanding how to lie upon the ground of ignorance, one now pauses briefly so that awakening may be attained; thus it is said, "rising from the ground.
Because one seeks the Dharma of the Path within the Four Noble Truths, it is said, "going to a poor village to seek food, clothing, and sublime joy.

Since the objects [of the Lesser Vehicle] encompass only a narrow range of dharmas, it is called a "poor village"; yet to aspire toward the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, one must still rely on both the primary and auxiliary practices.
Therefore, it says "food and clothing. △ Second, sending two people to entice [the children]; first, the teaching of the equal invitation;
fourth, receiving the three carts as previously prepared.
At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his sons, established an expedient means.

From this point downward, it concerns the time when he was leading [the disciples] at the Deer Park. Regarding those he intended to attract: since they had ceased from the Great Transformation (mahā-dharma), he could not bear to abandon them alone;
wishing to establish skillful means (upāya), he said "intending to.
He secretly dispatched two men whose appearance was haggard and who lacked majesty.
Initially, "Mahāyāna" was interpreted as: dispatching attendants represents the One True Truth; the Mahāyāna teaching represents the One Bodhisattva person.
Now it is clarified that "concealing the real" constitutes "secrecy," while "pointing to the partial truth" constitutes "dispatching.

In terms of the teachings, concealing the *maṃtra* (full) syllables constitutes "secrecy," while pointing to the *ardha-maṃtra* (half) syllables constitutes "dispatching. In terms of persons, because he secretly maintains the conduct of a bodhisattva within, it is called "secret"; externally... [he acts otherwise].

Because he manifests as a śrāvaka, it is said that "two persons" are dispatched; since the four great disciples each lead their respective divisions and do not involve bodhisattvas, they are referred to as "two persons.
In terms of the Dharma, this refers to dependent origination and the Four Noble Truths; in terms of principle, it refers to the conditioned and the two truths (the conventional and the ultimate);
in terms of persons, it refers to the two vehicles of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Within these teachings, one does not cultivate the marks and signs [of a Buddha], but only speaks of...

Suffering, impermanence, and impurity constitute the emaciation of physical form; internal fear of impermanence is called "emaciated" (jiao), while externally encountering the eight sufferings is called "worn out" (cuì).
Lacking the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses is termed "lacking majestic virtue."
"You may go to him and speak slowly to that impoverished son.
Regarding the phrase "you may go to him," this means employing the Small Teaching (Hīnayāna) for those of small capacity.

Because the Great Teaching clarifies the principle directly and truly, it says "run swiftly" [to seize him]; because the Small Teaching clarifies what is circuitous and obscure, it says "speak slowly."
"In this place where there is work to be done, I shall double your wages.
This "place where there is work to be done" refers to the Path of Seeing and the Path of Cultivation, which are the sites for severing the afflictions of views and thoughts.

"I shall double your wages" means that while the Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Paths merely prevent one from falling into the three miserable realms, the Four Noble Truths and Twelve Links of Dependent Origination can truly deliver one from them.

The three realms constitute the first multiple; furthermore, while the six practices of the non-Buddhists can only suppress afflictions, practicing the Four Noble Truths now can eradicate afflictions and lead to Nirvana—this is the second multiple.

"If the impoverished son consents to come and work for us—[and we say] 'the two of us shall also work together with you'—if the impoverished son consents, it means there is the capacity [for the teaching], and thus the teaching is established;
if there is no capacity, it means he does not consent, and thus the teaching is not established.
Regarding what he wishes to do: those of the Two Vehicles desire only to eliminate the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) and to realize *nirvāṇa*.
Whether it be purifying Buddha-lands or bringing sentient beings to maturity, the reason it is said, "I have hired you to remove the dung;

we two shall also work together with you," is as follows: in terms of principle (*li*), it refers to wisdom and truth mutually supporting one another; in terms of persons, it refers to the person of provisional means (*upāya*) working together with the person of reality (*bhūtatā*) in their cultivation.
Therefore, it is said that "the two of us shall work together with you. △ Second, acknowledging the aforementioned knowledge of the son.
First, the mind [of the father].
At that time, the two messengers sought out the impoverished son;
having found him and ascertained that he possessed the capacity [to receive the teaching], they said, "We have found him. △ Third, accepting the previous praise of the rarity of the carriage.
He related the aforementioned matters in detail, recounting how he had been hired to perform the work of removing filth. △ Fourth, accepting the son’s previous aspiration:
At that time, the impoverished son first took his wages and immediately set about removing the filth; his father saw his son and felt both pity and wonder.
The followers of the Two Vehicles aspire to the fruit by practicing the cause; this is why they first inquire about its value.

Thus it is said that they "first take" [the price], which refers to taking the price for the Path and Cessation, and removing the filth of Suffering and Origination. When the father sees his sons, he feels pity and wonder:
he pities them for their pursuit of Arhatship and wonders why they do not seek the Buddha-way, for what they lose is great while what they gain is meager. Therefore, he says:
It is strange! This passage from the *Fa-pi* (Analogy Chapter) captures the intended meaning; its phrasing is ultimately wondrous. *Miaoyue* says: "Question:

If [the father] feels pity and finds it strange, why does he secretly dispatch [the son] to teach him how to gather the fruit? Answer: Since the son did not come when pursued openly, it was necessary to dispatch him in secret.

Although he was taught to remove filth, this was not the father’s original intention. Because he wished to make his words manifest and entrust [the estate] to him, he first felt pity and then found it strange."
II. Taking the Meaning and Receiving [the Teaching], Also Called "Probing and Receiving. 4.
First, having long desired to provide a provisional accommodation through skillful wisdom, he further saw the son’s body from afar through a window on another day.

Furthermore, "again" (*yòu*) is a term used for emphasis. The four great disciples, intending to explore and lead [others] regarding the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, have long known the capacities of beings—whether great or small—and thus restate the Buddha’s intent by employing the expedient means of the One and the Three; it is for this reason that the chapter is headed with "again.

As for "another day," it refers to how those of the Two Vehicles consider their own *upāya* (expedient means) to be for themselves, rather than regarding the teachings of the Two Vehicles as being for others.
The "other" (*tā*) refers to the provisional Dharma-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). "Day" (*jīr*) refers to time, and it is also wisdom (*prajñā*).

Because one relies on the temporal function of the Dharma-body to employ wisdom and illuminate the capacities of sentient beings, it is called "another day. If one understands according to the teaching, one takes the activities of the Transformation Body as one's own day, and the activities of the Transformation Body as another's day.
If one probes deeper to understand, one takes [the activities] within the Dharma-body as [one's own day].
This is the illumination of capacities. At the time of the Dharmakāya, its function is the skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) that transforms others.

When this wisdom illuminates capacities for which there may be or may not be [an appropriate response], and when it illuminates the provisional matters of whether something is acceptable or not, all of these are what is illuminated by skillful wisdom;
therefore, the phrase "the windows and doors on another day" refers to how partial views are limited, signifying that skillful wisdom illuminates those partial capacities. "Remote" means small.

Because he has departed from the great suspension, he is called "Son of Far-Sighted Vision. As for the term "son," it was because he had previously planted [the seeds of] great renown that he was designated as such;
because he was modeled after the Great [Vehicle], he is called "Vision. Since the windows and doors were partial and narrow, it was not yet appropriate for a great transformation;

therefore, he ceased the great and applied the small. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) says: regarding "windows and doors," the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "That which is in a house is called a *chuāng* (window); that which is in a wall is called a..."
A window is not a door; therefore, the place where light enters is partial and still narrow. Now it is the same here: because it is not central, it is partial;
because it is not pervasive, it is narrow. Thus, on the stage of the Dharma-body, those without great capacity see only what is partial and narrow, because they were previously matured in that way.
This is merely due to the obstruction of the child at the window; how does it concern the fault of the elder’s partial vision? Moreover, this is the elder himself.

Because one seeks to grasp a partial capacity within the Perfect [Teaching], it remains distant; therefore, it is called "remote. △ Second, long-standing knowledge of expedient means is its cherished plaything.
It is emaciated and haggard, defiled by excrement, soil, dust, and impurities.

The Tathāgata first recognizes that those of the two vehicles have minor attachments; that their power of wisdom cultivated through causes is weak, and their power of merit cultivated through causes is emaciated;
that the four abidings are like dung and soil, and ignorance is like dust and grime.
△ Third, having known this for a long time, he must praise the rarity of the three carts.
He immediately removed his necklaces, fine soft upper garments, and ornaments (until he appeared) as if filled with dread.

The removal of the exquisite robes is a metaphor for concealing the *saṃbhogakāya*— its immeasurable merits, the forty-two stages, the precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, *dhāraṇīs*, and so forth— and its adornments,
such as the necklaces of *śāntikṣānti* (patience of cessation), the fine soft upper garments, and the arrays of the major and minor marks of a Buddha.

If he were to possess full robes and ornaments, those who have attained the fruits of the Two Vehicles would be startled and fearful; they are not fit to behold such marks and signs of excellence (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana).

For this reason, he removes them and puts on coarse, tattered garments, manifesting a body sixteen feet tall. "Coarse" refers to the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) regarding ordinary phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*); "tattered" refers to the stage of Patience regarding the Dharma (*dharma-kṣānti*).

His body being covered in dust signifies that he manifests the presence of afflictions (*kleśa*), conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*), and outflows (*āsrava*). His left hand is a metaphor for the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

The right hand is a metaphor for *upāya* (expedient means); because the function of this *upāya* is easy and convenient, one uses these expedient methods to sever the fetters and attain Buddhahood, and further employs these expedient methods to transform others;
thus it is said that the right hand holds a vessel for removing filth. "Appearing fearful" means appearing as if [in fear];
it demonstrates conformity with the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) in its dread of birth and death, as well as the hardships of the cold wind and the horse-barley.

Regarding the "retribution" (vipāka), Miaole states that "patience with sentient beings" (*sattvakṣānti*) and "patience with phenomena" (*dharma-kṣānti*) are as follows: enduring the afflictions caused by sentient beings—such as mosquitoes and gadflies—is called patience with sentient beings;
enduring the afflictions caused by non-sentient things—such as cold, heat, wind, and rain—is called patience with phenomena.

Regarding "the left hand," etc., this refers to the provisional and the real within the small and middle [vehicles]. Furthermore, regarding "cold winds," etc., see the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 9, by the Buddha.
There are nine afflictions: namely, the six years of ascetic practice; the slander by Sundarī; the golden spikes; the horse-barley; the slaughter at Vaiśālī; begging with an empty bowl;
the slander by Ciñcā Māṇavikā; Devadatta’s pushing down of the mountain; the cold wind and the request for clothing;

and the back pain under the twin śāla trees—these constitute ten [if the latter is included]. △ Fourth, regarding the son of the direct teacher (Mahākāśyapa) fulfilling his original vow and practicing the seven [precepts], first is the analogy for the four [aspects].
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness:
speaking to the laborers means that the teaching of the Tripiṭaka which demonstrates the four foundations of mindfulness is the "removal of filth."

Because it is the realm where the vessel severs the fetters, the *Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching* states: "If one constantly relies on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) to practice the Path, one can destroy the four inversions.

This refers to the sharp vigor that accords with one's aspiration within the "burning house," which corresponds to the stage of the ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) characterized by the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
△ Second, the analogy for the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
"You all must apply yourselves diligently and not allow for slackness; by means of such skillful methods, you shall draw near to that Son.
'Not allowing for slackness' means causing them to diligently cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).

If slackness arises, one cannot extinguish the two evils (those already arisen and those yet to arise) nor produce the two virtues (those already arisen and those yet to arise). Through these two forms of diligence, one is able to give rise to *ūṣmagata*."
Fire faces the burning house, and as they push one another aside, they enter the stage of "warmth" (*ūṣmagata*) through cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).

Because of skillful means (*upāya*), they are able to draw near to their child; however, while in the stage of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), they have not yet attained the principle, and though the fire warms their hearts, they remain distant and cannot yet approach.
Now, through the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), having first attained the skillful means of warmth, they can indeed draw near. △ Third, the parable.
The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Later, he again addressed him, saying: "Ho! Man! [and so on] until: "I also have old, worn-out servants; if you need them, I shall provide them.

"Ho" is a term for startling and awakening, and it is also a form of reprimand. Within the context of right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), this agitation is precisely the nature of wisdom (*jñāna-dharma*).
The man represents the masculine (yang) nature, whereas the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are dharmas of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Just as a woman represents the feminine (yin) nature, because one cannot bring them into resonance with true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) through the mere exertion of right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), he is startled, awakened, and reprimanded so that he may abandon distraction and enter stillness;
thus it is said, "O man! "Always act in this way and do not go elsewhere" refers to mindfulness (*smṛti*).

If one dwells in right effort but the movement of the mind is not single-minded, it cannot be called "constant. Among the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), concentration does not differ from its object;
thus, when there is contemplation, there is concentration, and when there is concentration, there is contemplation. Because concentration and contemplation are single-minded, it is said:

"Are you constantly doing this? because there is no distraction or movement. Therefore, it is said: "Do not go elsewhere again. This still remains within the context of mutual exclusion and displacement.
The stage of the "Dharma of the Summit" (*mūrdha-dharma*) is when one should increase your value;

this means that while one cannot yet produce true contemplation within the midst of right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), one can produce the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) within the "contemplation according to wish" (*yathābhiprāya-vipaśyanā*). Therefore, it is said that "the value is increased.

Whatever may be required—whether contaminated or uncontaminated, wholesome, auxiliary to the Path, or the Path itself—all are sought from within this contemplation according to wish; whatever is desired is obtained immediately. (4)

The essence of dhyāna contains its branches and foliage, like a basin or vessel; the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) is coarse, like rice, while the emptiness of dharmas (dharma-śūnyatā) is subtle, like flour.
This is the Noble Path of the sixteen contemplations of the Four Truths: impermanence is like salt, and suffering is like vinegar.
These are the auxiliary paths, like rice and flour which are difficult to eat and must be mixed with salt and vinegar. The Noble Path is difficult to manifest and requires the auxiliary paths.

Regarding the assistance provided, do not harbor doubts or difficulties; this is because the preceding "principal" and "auxiliary" practices are definitively contained within the *yathā-vastu-manasikāra* (contemplation according to reality).
Therefore, one must not doubt, as it is certain that [the goal] can be accomplished. One should regard it as one's own possession and thus say, "do not find it difficult.
If one wishes to directly employ supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) in place of hands and feet—just as one employs servants for labor—the *yathā-vastu-manasikāra* also includes such supernormal powers.
However, because those who are merely capable but inferior and weak are similar to the "old and decrepit," it is said that there are also "old and decrepit" laborers;
even though they are not in their prime, they are still fit for transport and service, hence it is said that those in need shall be provided with them. △ Fourth, the analogy of the five faculties.
"Set your mind at ease; I am like your father, so do not worry further.
"Set your mind at ease" means that you have attained the five faculties, such as faith, which are stable and difficult to destroy.

"I am like your father" means that because you have already attained a semblance of understanding that borders upon the realization of truth—yet this semblance is not yet actual—it is said to be "like a father. This is also [the meaning].
"Be like a son and do not worry further" means to let the mind rest in peace so as to destroy [the afflictions of] views and thoughts.
△ Fifth, the analogy of the five powers.
Why is this? "I am old and advanced in years... from this day forward, you shall be like a son born to me."
"I am old and you are young" means that the Buddha occupies the ultimate stage of the Path because he has already perfected both wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*); thus he is called "old.

You occupy the initial stage of the Path (the stage of the ordinary person within the mundane path), as you do not yet possess wisdom and abandonment; thus you are "young and vigorous. This refers to the stage of the *kṣānti* (receptivity).

Having attained these five powers (*pañca-balāni*), one is free from the five unwholesome qualities: because one attains the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*), one does not deceive; because one attains the power of vigor (*vīrya-bala*)... [and so forth].
Because of the power of diligence, one does not become indolent; because of the power of mindfulness, one does not become angry; because of the power of concentration, one does not harbor resentment;
and because of the power of wisdom, one does not utter complaints. As for the phrase "other practitioners," this refers distantly to those of external paths who seek the truth through various views;
it refers proximately to those in the four stages such as *uṣmagata*, who have not yet escaped the five faults—these are also called "other practitioners. This is the meaning of the text.

The absence of the five faults constitutes the five powers (*pañca-balāni*). From this point forward, for one who is like a newborn child, the duration of the stage of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) still spans sixteen moments (*kṣaṇa*).
Although the stage of "middle patience" (*madhya-kṣānti*) has already contracted its observation, it is not yet a single moment.

As for "upper patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) and the "highest worldly dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), they consist of the final single moment of mind; because it is adjacent to the truth and approaches the state of the noble ones (*ārya*), it is so named.
The stage of being "born as a son of the Tathāgata" refers precisely to the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). Miaole states:

"Regarding the four stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, one should speak of them as the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); the Supreme Mundane Dharma is the stage of the five powers (*pañcabala*), which is free from the five faults.
△ Sixth, the analogy for the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
Immediately, the elder gave him another name, calling him "Son.
Because the Dharma of the Supreme Worldly State (*laukikāgra-dharma*) and the Truth (*satya*) are not far apart, it is said to be "immediate. The *Āgama* speaks of five kinds of sons of the Buddha:

those of the four fruits and the Pratyekabuddha are called "true sons of the Buddha," while the Bodhisattva is the "son whose fetters are not yet severed," as his purpose has not yet been accomplished.
Now, because the followers of the two vehicles have attained the Eightfold Path and entered the Path of Seeing, they are called "children.

Miaole states that the meaning of "son" has not yet been established within the Āgamas; for although the Āgamas also clarify that Bodhisattvas do not sever their afflictions, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* rejects this as a provisional teaching—it does not mean that the [Abhidharma] treatises are entirely non-existent.
As for the claim that it was composed by Kātyāyanīputra, this refers to the treatise he produced and...

How laughable it is that those who calculate [the teachings] claim that the reconciliation of the two [vehicles] merely returns to the *Āgamas*, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* conforms to the old [teachings] of the twelve years prior!
△ Seventh: An analogy for the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter (up to: "for twenty years he constantly had him remove dung"), because the followers of the Two Vehicles have become sons by means of severing the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*), it is said they "rejoice at this encounter";

yet, as their afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-āsrava*) are not yet exhausted, they still dwell in the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*), and since they must still rely on the teachings to practice and exhaust suffering, it is said they "still consider themselves [as such]."

If a lowly laborer who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) becomes weary of the small [vehicle] and delights in the great, and the capacity for the Mahāyāna is aroused, he should immediately be granted the Mahāyāna;

there is no further need to advance toward severing the remaining residual fetters (*anuśaya*). This is precisely because if one does not abandon the small [vehicle], the great capacity will not be aroused.
For this reason, one causes them to exhaust their outflows (*āsrava*) by relying on the teaching; thus it is said, "For this reason, [it is] two."
For ten years, one constantly performs the removal of excrement; for twenty years, through one unimpeded [knowledge] and one liberation, one abandons the view-based fetters (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*);
and through nine unimpeded [knowledges] and nine liberations, one abandons the thought-based fetters (*bhāvanā-āsrava*). Thus it is said that it takes twenty years.
This passage, along with the following verses, mentions "twenty years" three times; the significance of each instance differs, and they should be explained according to their respective contexts.
It is seen. △ Fourth, the analogy of the family estate, in two parts: first, receiving the family estate; second, first, mutual trust in body and mind.
First, clarifying that mutual trust in body and mind:
After this period has passed, they trust one another in body and mind, entering and exiting without difficulty.
The following section marks the period of receiving the Vaipulya [sūtras]. "After this" means after the Three Piṭakas of the Deer Park;
that is, the Vaipulya. "Mutually understanding and believing in the nature of the mind" refers to fathers and sons fully comprehending and faithfully complying with one another;
it means that within the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, they obtained the price of Nirvāṇa. Since this was not false, [the Buddha] now preaches this Great [Vehicle] for the sake of the Bodhisattvas.

The vehicle is likewise not empty; this is the son trusting his father. The Buddha knows that such individuals have already severed their views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and having heard the Great [Vehicle], they do not slander it;
their untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are sharp, so upon hearing [the teaching], they will certainly give rise to faith—this is the father trusting his son.
Regarding "entering and exiting without difficulty": because they behold the *vairocana* (Universal) Body and hear the teachings of the Mahāyāna, this is called "entering. Furthermore...
Although he was rebuked, he still appeared in a sixteen-foot form preaching the Dharma of the Small Vehicle;
this is called "exiting the Great and entering the Small," and there is no doubt or difficulty regarding this. △ Second, remaining in his original position.
Nevertheless, their place of abiding remains as it was before.

Although those of the Two Vehicles encounter no difficulty in entering and emerging from the Great and Small [vehicles], when they hear the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, they claim it is the business of bodhisattvas and not within the scope of their own wisdom;
thus, unwilling to turn away from the Small toward the Great, they still remain in the rank of arhats.
Because it does not say that he will attain Buddhahood in the future, it is said that "the place where he dwells remains as it was.
△ Second, the command to take charge of his affairs, in four parts: first, clarifying the time and occasion.
At that time, World-Honored One, the elder fell ill and knew for himself that he would soon die.

From this point downward, it concerns the time when he received the Buddha’s command to propagate the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. "One who will soon die" means that when there is a karmic affinity (*yǒujī*), one responds by being born;
when the karmic affinity is exhausted, one should pass away, which is death. Now, as his transformation of sentient beings (*huàjī*) is nearing completion, he should pass away before long.
△ Second, he commands him to know the family business.
He says to the impoverished son: "I now possess much [wealth]... (omitted)... you should know all that which ought to be taken or given.

Gold refers to the principle of the Separate Teaching (*biprakāra-śāsana*), while silver refers to the principle of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānya-śāsana*); the True Truth (*satyārtha*) elucidated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* does not go beyond these.
Regarding the statement that there are "many," from a logical standpoint they are not numerous; however, because they are categorized according to various doors, they may also be called many.
For example, while space itself is not eighteenfold, it is termed the "eighteen emptinesses" based on its application to the refutation of eighteen phenomena.
In the "Chapter on Encouraging Study," it is clarified that all dharma-doors are treasuries of jewels; this door of concentration is precisely the storehouse of the one hundred and eight samādhis.

This gate of wisdom is precisely the realm of the eighteen kinds of emptiness. It is the treasury of both the general and specific teachings, encompassing all meditative concentrations and wisdoms without deficiency;
as it is filled within and overflows without, it is said that "it overflows therein.
Regarding the question of "much or little," when speaking of Prajñā, there are two gates: the extensive and the concise. The concise is "little," while the extensive is "much."
Thus, it is for oneself to practice extensively and for others to be transformed that one provides them; as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:

"You should preach [the Dharma] for the sake of bodhisattvas. Therefore, it says, "You know them all. Regarding the statement in the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) that "gold" refers to the principles of the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), a question is raised:

Since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* contains the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*), why does it only say that it does not go beyond the Shared and Separate Teachings? The answer is: first, it is simply speaking in terms of the Shared and Separate Teachings.

The principle already encompasses the other two treatises; however, the teachings that express it must necessarily possess four aspects. For now, following the principle, it is said that they do not transcend these two.
Furthermore, as for the two vehicles reaching this point, they mostly achieve both the general and the specific, which are also mentioned here.
The "general and specific" and the "storehouse" may be understood accordingly. △ Third, the admonition to realize the mind.
"My mind is thus; you should embody this meaning. Why is this? Because now I and you are no different.
Regarding the instruction to "embody my mind," the Buddha takes *prajñā* as his mind; when you now teach in turn, you should speak in accordance with the Buddha's intention.
As for the statement "now I and you are no different," there are three ways to explain this: first, [the empowerment] bestowed...

1. It is taught that [the Buddha's nature] is not different from that of the Buddha; 2. from the perspective of principle (*li*), because all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*), they are not different; 3.

from the perspective of the present time, one first realizes that the father-son relationship is by nature originally non-different, whereas those of the Two Vehicles merely claim that they have been granted a different [status].
△ 4. The command to avoid any loss of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
You should apply yourself with diligence so as not to let it be lost.
Regarding "not letting it be lost," there are two aspects: first, when you preach the teaching of Prajñā for the sake of bodhisattvas, do not let it be lost;
second, from the perspective of principle, this is your own dharma which you shall employ at a later time; therefore, do not let it be lost.
△ Second, receiving the mandate and taking charge of the four [types of property]. First, the formal acceptance and taking charge of knowledge:
At that time, the impoverished son immediately accepted the instructions and took charge of all the goods—the gold, silver, rare treasures, and various storehouses.
△ Second, the mind is free from longing.
There is not even the slightest intention to long for a single morsel of food.
Although Subhūti transmits the teaching and speaks of the Prajñāpāramitā, he says of himself, "This is the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas; I have no share in it."
△ Third, they have not yet abandoned their original station.
Because they still dwell in that place, they have not yet been able to abandon the inferior mind associated with that station.
Thus, those who remain in their original station—though they may aspire to the Great [Vehicle] while abiding in the stage of an Arhat—have not yet definitively resolved to become [a Buddha].

Even for a Bodhisattva who has not yet abandoned the inferior mind, although they may feel shame regarding the small [vehicle], they have not yet definitively resolved to abandon the realization of the Small Vehicle.
△ Fourth, seeking the Great through contempt for the inferior.
After a short time had passed, the father perceived that his son’s mind had gradually become open and serene, that he had achieved great resolve, and that he now looked down upon his former thoughts.
He asked, "When did you say this was 'a short time'? The son replied, "It was when the *Prajñāpāramitā* was finished;

since then, I have been reflecting upon the Mahāyāna Dharma-gates I have received, pondering whether my longing for them constitutes a loss or no loss. Such reflections as these are themselves the Great [Vehicle].

The "occasion" refers to the time when the spiritual capacity [of the audience] is awakened; since at this time they were not far from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said that it would take but a short time.
Furthermore, it was precisely at the time for preaching the *Anantamukhanirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (the *Wuliangyi jing*) that the capacity for the Mahāyāna was awakened. How is this known?

Within the *Anantamukha-sūtra*, it clarifies the seven kinds of skillful means and the immeasurable gradual and sudden teachings arising from a single Dharma. Having heard this teaching, they reflected upon the past.
The three baskets and the three vehicles all arise from this single Dharma; these three vehicles should likewise enter into the One.

When one contemplates in this way, the mind gradually becomes clear and expansive, and the great resolve is immediately awakened; therefore, it is said that "the great aspiration is accomplished. Miaole says:
regarding "lost" and "not lost," if it is lost, there is no share for oneself; if it is not lost, yet one has not yet attained equality with the Bodhi [of the Buddhas].

At the moment when Sadāparibhūta hesitated, it was precisely the time when his great capacity for awakening (*mahā-avakrānti*) was about to arise; its actual emergence occurred at the time of the "three requests.
Next, regarding the *Anantārthika* [Sūtra], it is extremely close in time to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, being the very last stage.

Since one has already heard the principle of "the many arising from the one," one must now gather the many back into the one; as this is the conclusion of the four flavors of teaching, it is said that the gradual [teachings] have already ceased their function.

Because they were previously separated and distinct, it is said that they have now become "penetrating and expansive" (*tōtāi*). Regarding the phrase "gradually through penetration and expansion" (*zen i tōtāi*), the character "with" (*yi*) should be read as "already" (*yi*);
the subsequent verse states, "Gradually already vast and great," and their meaning is identical—this may be examined in detail. △ Second, the actual entrustment of the family estate, in two parts.
First, the entrustment of the estate, in four sections. First, clarifying the time of the entrustment; below this, the fourth and fifth [sections] are combined as one.
The first is the parable of the entrustment.
"When about to pass away" refers to the period after the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and prior to the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. "When about to pass away" clarifies the timing.
The period of his transformative ministry was nearing its end; it was the time when he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for eight years at Vulture Peak and announced his entry into *nirvāṇa*.
△ Second, the command to assemble the multitude for witness:
He commanded his son and summoned all his kinsmen, kings, ministers, *kṣatriyas*, and lay devotees, and they had all gathered together.
Those among the disciples transformed by twenty trillion Buddhas who are called "sons" are the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas of the ten directions who act as their shadows and echoes;
these many followers of shadows and echoes were all former colleagues of Śākyamuni who,
together with the Tathāgata, were jointly transformed and enlightened by those twenty trillion Buddhas, and they are all his uncles and cousins.

Because it acts as such, this [sūtra] serves as the sovereign for those who are kinsmen or kings; among all the gradual and sudden sūtras, there is none that does not extol its subject matter as the "King of Sūtras.

As it benefits sentient beings according to their capacities, its arising and ceasing occur at different times, and each division differs, yet they are all called "kingdoms" and declared to be the foremost, which is precisely what constitutes a king. Now, since this present sūtra synthesizes and unifies all teachings, how could...?

It is not because the kings have assembled; for in the *Anantārthasūtra*, it was previously stated that first the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination were taught, next the Vaipulya and twelve divisions of the scriptures were taught, and finally the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* was taught.
