This [assembly] universally gathers all the sūtras and harmonizes the gradual and sudden teachings, causing them to enter into one another; therefore, this place is named "The Assembly of Realms" (*Huìguó*).
Maitreya and the other great Bodhisattvas are all those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) who serve as ministers;

those from the first to the ninth stages are of the Kṣatriya lineage of Dharma-kings; and those of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten transferences are householders—all of whom have received transformation through Śākyamuni.
The *Myōraku* states: "From 'king' up to this point, they are kings."

The previous section, based on the teachings of the various schools in former times, spoke of the rise and fall for various kings, ranging from the two rises and two falls of the *Avataṃsaka* to the one rise and three falls of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Now, however, all minor kings are abolished and only a single sovereign is established;
therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is called the "King among Kings. Regarding that which was previously collected in the *Anantamukhanirhāra-dhāraṇī*, although it says:
Since "one gives rise to many" implies that the many all belong to the one, it is said that they are "collected.
That text [the *Wuliangyi jing*] subsequently cites the *Wuliangyi jing* to demonstrate the manner in which various sūtras are collected;

since that sūtra states that the immeasurable sūtras all arise from one, it points to the preceding sūtra as being the "immeasurable Four Noble Truths" and the "causes and conditions," which is precisely the Deer Park.
The sequence of the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā is clearly and perfectly preserved here. △ Third, the reconciliation of father and son:
[The Buddha] then declared himself, saying: "Gentlemen, you should know... (up to) this is truly my son, and I am truly his father."
In truth, you have received instruction from me; you are truly my son, born from my understanding and produced by me.
Because I have indeed constantly taught the Great Dharma in the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas, I am truly your father.
Regarding the phrase "in a certain city," the text in the Western lands (India) is extensive, whereas this [Chinese] version is very brief; perhaps it refers to a country by its former name.
The earth is like the causal conditions of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū; now, to simplify the names, I speak directly of a certain city and a certain person.
Because these sentient beings turn their backs on this Mahāyāna, giving rise to the darkness of ignorance and fleeing into birth and death, it is said they "abandoned me and ran away.
Because they have fully experienced the six realms of existence, it is said they have been gone for "more than fifty years. Formerly, in their native city, they harbored...

Regarding the seeker who was sought out with concern: since time immemorial, the Tathāgata has constantly used both provisional and ultimate wisdom within the realm of the Dharma-body to observe and seek those with the capacity for transformation.
Because the resonance between cause and response has finally converged this very day, it is said: "Suddenly today I have encountered and found him.
"He is truly my son; I am truly his father. Thus, their natural affinity is determined, and they are established as father and son.
...Thus it is. △ Fourth, the formal entrustment of the family estate:
"Now, all the wealth and property I possess are yours, my son; what has previously been spent or brought in is known by you, my son."
Because it encompasses all the myriad practices and myriad virtues of the Mahāyāna, it is called "all that exists.

Regarding what was previously brought forth and internalized—that which the son knows—this refers back to the extensive and abbreviated *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings entrusted to him in the past, including both the common (general) and uncommon (specific) dharmas. These are what you know; they are what you possess. Therefore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [it says...]
This clarifies the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, rather than further elaborating on all the various aspects of practice. The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states:
"The Prajñā entrusted [to us] consists of both the common and the uncommon; it does not emerge from cause and effect.

The cause is the myriad practices, and the fruit is the myriad virtues—namely, the virtues such as the Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Eighteen Emptinesses, which are called the Ten Powers and the Four Fearlessnesses."

Since it is said that these qualities of mine, such as the eighteen unique attributes (*āveṇika-dharma*), belong to you as my sons, you should know that you all possess the treasury of the Tathāgata’s cause and fruit;
this is what is meant by the natural affinity between father and son. Thus, one should understand that both knowledge and vision are the inherent possession of all;
for this reason, the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of them collectively as simply "the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."△
Second, they were filled with joy.
At that time, having heard these words from his father, the poor son thought, "Now this treasure has come to me spontaneously.
Each of them mounted a great carriage as described above and attained what they had never experienced before; yet, looking back at themselves, they had no heart or hope for the Buddha-way.

Now, having suddenly heard that one receives the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, it is said that this is "attained spontaneously without seeking. In the Tripitaka, the fundamental mind did not seek;

in the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras), one felt ashamed of the Lesser Vehicle and severed all hope for it, thus there was no seeking; in the Prajñāpāramitā, although one understood [the truth], it was not within one's own capacity, thus there was no seeking.
Although there was no seeking in the past, it is now attained spontaneously. △ Second, the combined parable, part four. First:
This corresponds to the analogy of father and son who have lost each other.
The World-Honored One as the great wealthy elder is the Tathāgata; we are like the sons of the Buddha.
Regarding the correspondence between the father-like Tathāgata and the son-like [disciples], there are two meanings: first, taking those of great capacity as sons from the past.
"Because they have not yet escaped [the cycle] and do not occupy a true stage, remaining instead among the external ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana), they are said to be 'similar' (*sādṛśya*).

Regarding the second point, those of small capacity are called 'sons' because their small capacity resembles the root-nature (*indriya*) of the Mahāyāna; thus they are called 'similar. Since the son has already fled from his father, he is disparaged as 'similar.
As for the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary stating "Since the son... and so forth, it cites the "True Cause" (*samyak-hetu*) by way of analogy.

The treatise states: "If even those who do not resemble their father are considered true sons, how much more so those who do resemble him? Since they have previously established a karmic connection, who is not a true son?
It is because they once ran away that the father temporarily disparages them; it is because their status is low and their delusion deep that he dismisses them as 'resembling' [sons].
△ Second, the analogy of the meeting between father and son.
The Tathāgata has always said that we are his children.

This corresponds to the elder recognizing his son as soon as he sees him. △ Third, the analogy of following the father’s command to pursue and entice [the son], in two parts: first, the correspondence regarding how the bystanders’ pursuit failed to find a responsive capacity for either admonition or exhortation.
First, the correspondence regarding the lack of responsive capacity for both the gates of admonition and exhortation.
“World-Honored One, because of these three types of suffering, we undergo various fevers and afflictions within the cycle of birth and death, remaining deluded and ignorant.

These three sufferings arise from the three feelings: painful feeling gives rise to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); pleasant feeling gives rise to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*);

and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling gives rise to the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). World-Honored One, it is because of these three sufferings that the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) are intensified; for this reason, [the Buddha] exhorts us.”

The admonition for both gates is that there are no beings of great capacity; they are merely fit for minor transformation. Because the five turbidities are pervasive, this constitutes the three types of suffering.
Because they are shrouded by ignorance, this constitutes lack of knowledge. △ Second, regarding the cessation of transformative activity, there are those with minor aspirations.
They take pleasure in and are attached to inferior teachings.
△ Second, combining the two to provide an analogy for the inducement; first, aligning the teaching with the summary of the preceding events.
Today, the World-Honored One has commanded us to contemplate and eliminate the dung of conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena.
The dung of frivolous conceptualization refers to the views and afflictions. △ Second, clearing away the dung together and taking the price:
"We shall apply ourselves with diligent vigor therein" (up to) "because of such diligent vigor, that which is obtained is vast and abundant."
"Our diligent application of effort therein corresponds to the upper [analogy] of immediately seeking and removing the filth to reach nirvāṇa;

the lower [analogy] corresponds to first taking the payment. △ Second, the correspondence regarding the investigation and receipt, in three parts: first, the correspondence regarding the initial intention to act.
However, the World-Honored One had previously known us.
His earlier statement said he saw us from afar; his present statement says he knew us beforehand. △ Second, [the Buddha] combines skillful means with what they prefer:
their minds are attached to base desires and they take pleasure in inferior teachings.

Previously it was said that they were emaciated and haggard; now it is said that their minds are attached to debased desires. △ Third, combining this with what was previously known, he praises the chariot:
"I see that you shall have a share in the treasure-store of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision," and thus he does not make further distinctions.

The previous statement said that he immediately cast off his necklaces and put on coarse, tattered clothes; the present statement says that he was then abandoned and not granted a share of the treasury.

△ Fourth, the analogy of being entrusted with the family estate has two parts: first, the analogy of being entrusted with the family estate; second, the initial part of the analogy of being entrusted with the family estate, which has two sub-parts:
first, the analogy of causing him to realize and believe; second, the initial part of the analogy of causing him to realize and believe.
The World-Honored One, through the power of skillful means, speaks of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Because he teaches the true reality of the Mahāyāna by employing the expedients of the three vehicles, it is said that "through the power of skillful means, he speaks the Mahāyāna dharma before us.
This also accords with the preceding statement that "he enters and emerges without difficulty," for it is through the power of skillful means that he brings forth eloquence.
If those of the Two Vehicles do not personally realize and believe this through the Buddha’s power of wisdom, how could they clarify the Buddha’s insight before me?
△ Second, returning to their original place.
"We have obtained from the Buddha the price of one day’s worth of nirvāṇa," [and so on], "yet we have no aspiration or seeking for this Mahāyāna.
△ Second, the collective command to receive and take up the karma; first, the collective reception and taking up of the karma.
Furthermore, we have been taught and expounded the Tathāgata’s wisdom for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
△ Second, the unification of non-seeking and non-grasping, in two parts: first, the actual unification;
yet we ourselves have no aspiration or resolve regarding this.
"Is it not that those who have no desire to seek and no aspirations are made to speak according to the Buddha’s mind through the Buddha’s manifesting of majestic power?
Therefore, I have no aspiration. △ Second, the explanation of the intent.
Why is this? Because the Buddha knows us [as it is stated in the text], whereas we do not know that we are truly the sons of the Buddha.
The Buddha, through the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), speaks to us according to our capacities;
yet, because we do not recognize his intention in speaking the Dharma of the true nature (*dharmatā*) together with those of the two vehicles, we do not know that we are truly the sons of the Buddha.
...Thus it is. △ Second, the entrustment of the family business in two parts: First, the entrustment of the task; first, clarifying the absence of parsimony.
Now we have finally come to know that the World-Honored One has no stinginess or regret regarding the Buddha’s wisdom.
△ Second, the explanation of being without parsimony.
Why is this so? From our past until now... [the Buddha] has actually taught and transformed us through the Mahāyāna.
Within this sutra, the following passage cites the present to verify the past; since the principle of the present is one and the same, we know that the three vehicles of the past were not real.
It was only because [the disciples] were not yet capable that [the Buddha], before the Great Vehicle, disparaged the small mind, desiring to cause them to abandon the false and adopt the true;
he certainly did not do so out of stinginess, for the Buddha truly used the Mahāyāna to teach and transform them. △ Second, the combined joy.
Therefore, we say that from the beginning there was no mind... (up to) ...that which the sons of the Buddha ought to attain, they have all already attained.
△ Second, the verse summary has two parts: first, seventy-three and a half lines of verse summarizing the prose; second, first, the summary of the Dharma-exposition.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Today we have heard the Buddha’s teaching... [up to] ...this unsurpassed mass of jewels, which we have obtained without seeking."
He does not praise [the father's seeking] but praises only his own attainment. △ Second, the verse on the parable, in two parts: first, the verse opening the parable, in four sections;
first, the verse on the son turning his back and leaving his father, in four parts; first, the direct verse on the son turning his back and leaving his father.
For example, it is like a young boy who, being immature and ignorant, wanders through various countries for more than fifty years.
The "bright" elder in the burning house represents the sovereign of the kingdom; the cities, towns, and villages represent the broad scope of this teaching.
Herein, the "poor son" wandering through the three realms is named "various countries," and the six destinies are named "more than fifty years. △ Second, the actual verse:
Seeking a son but not finding him—Part One: The Verse on Seeking a Son but Not Finding Him.
His father, filled with anxiety and concern, searched for him in all four directions.

Regarding this "searching in all four directions," it differs from what was mentioned above; whereas the former four directions were based on reasoning according to the Four Noble Truths, here [the meaning is different].
"Observing the four directions" means seeking among the four modes of birth for those who are ready to be saved. △ Second, the verse on stopping at one city:
Having grown weary from searching, he stops at one city (up to) "possessing such great wealth and power."

"Building a dwelling" refers to the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) in other lands; "arousing the house of compassion" means relying on the dwelling of the emptiness of nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*).
"The multitudes who come and go" refers to the bodhisattvas from various lands coming and going to hear the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "suddenly stopping at one city," "sudden" (*don*) means "to be exhausted" (*don-pa*), referring to the appearance of manifesting [the Buddha's] traces; its meaning is the same as "exhaustion. Furthermore—

"Ceasing and resting" means not yet practicing cessation; it refers to seeking the capacity of the sons within the land of skillful means. "Building houses and dwellings" refers to the Land of Residual Phenomena (*śeṣabhūmi*), which is not the Land of Quiescent Light (*prabhāsvaraloka*).
It is not that the supreme transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is naturally manifest as the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) from the beginning;

rather, one further exercises compassion based on emptiness therein. Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] builds [houses] and indulges in the five desires; this is not [the case for the ultimate state].
The coarse and base five desires are [actually] the supreme and wondrous five desires. △ Third, the verse transcends [the previous section] to show that his anxiety deepens;
as he grows old, his concern for his son increases (extending to): "What shall become of the storehouses and all my possessions?"
This merely recites the suffering of previously losing one’s son; because there was no one to whom he could entrust [the family], he grieved. *Myōryaku* (The Wondrous Joy) states:
"It merely recites the son turning his back and leaving his father, which is the suffering of losing a son, yet there is no joy of gaining a son.

Since both the loss of suffering and the gain of joy reside within the father’s breast, it must be known that when he lost [his son], he already harbored joy within himself, and that [the son] would surely return at a later time."

This is because of their coming from afar. "To observe the karmic conditions" means that they have not been as long with the Buddha as those who have been there since the early morning and through the night.

"Early morning" (*sù*) refers to rising at dawn; "night" (*yè*) refers to the end of the day. Furthermore, "early morning" signifies the beginning of the transformation, while "night" signifies the end of the transformation; the beginning and end of this great transformation can be understood by analogy with these explanations.
△ Fourth, the verse summarizing the son’s arrival at his father’s city, in two parts: first, the verse on the reasons for approaching his father.
At that time, the impoverished son sought food and clothing... until he became emaciated from hunger and malnutrition, and sores and scabs broke out upon his body.
His journey "from village to village" represents the mutual interaction between the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), which are like the eighteen realms (*dhātu*).

His cultivation of the contaminated virtues (*sāsrava-kuśala*) of the three realms is like having something to be attained; his cultivation of the uncontaminated virtues (*anāsrava-kuśala*) of the two vehicles is like having nothing to be attained, yet he does not attain it.
The Mahāyāna Dharma-food is like one who is starving and lacks great strength, being emaciated due to weakness and lacking great merit;
it is like having sores and scabs because of the arising of views and afflictions regarding existence and non-existence. △ Second, the verse on finally arriving at the father’s city.
Gradually traveling on, he arrived at the city where his father resided.
△ Second, the verse on the meeting between father and son. Part One: The verse on the son seeing his father. Section One: The verse on the cause for seeing his father.
Through successive rounds of hiring labor, he eventually arrived at his father’s house.
II. Verse on the Signs of Seeing His Father:
At that time, the elder was inside his gate (up to) recording the accounts and documents for the assets brought in and sent out.

The previous section clarified that the place where the father was seen was by the side of the gate; the present statement that the elder was "within the gate" indicates that both the visual sign and the location are obtained.
The bestowal of the great jeweled canopy and so forth is precisely the place where the father’s appearance was seen.

The "notes, records, and commentaries" (zhùjì quànshū) refer to the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), clarifying that this constitutes the practice. Zhanran (Zhang’an) said: "This uses the broad to reveal the concise."
Bestowing the prediction [of enlightenment] is the record; the four great vows are the bond; and cultivation of practice is the commentary.

Regarding the statement in the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) that "by means of the extensive, the concise is revealed," it is as in the *Avataṃsaka*, where the physical marks, lands, practices, and vows are explained extensively.

This is because one originally intends to use this extensiveness to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby manifesting the essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Therefore, it is said: "By means of the extensive, the concise is revealed. As for "bestowing the prediction," it refers to the Lotus Sūtra.

The preceding text lacks explicit words regarding the bestowal of prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*); however, the "Prophecy" section as a supplementary discussion within the *Dharmadhātupraveśa-parivarta* may also be termed a "bestowal of prophecy.
Furthermore, his great vows and practices are most detailed therein. Moreover, the vow serves as a contract:

just as one promises to benefit others according to a formal agreement, one repays this debt through practice; as the commentary states, having completed the repayment up until the attainment of *bodhi*.
At the conclusion of this section, it is further noted that within the *Avataṃsaka*, the bodhisattva’s practices and vows frequently clarify matters of numerical calculation and enumeration.
△ Third, the verse on generating a mind of fear and avoidance:
"The impoverished son sees his father’s wealth, nobility, and majesty... [he] inquires after a poor neighborhood, wishing to go there to work as a hired laborer."
△ II. Verse 2: The Father Sees His Son. Part 1: Verse on the Place Where He Sees His Son.
At that time, the elder was seated upon the lion throne.
△ Part 2: Verse on Recognizing His Son Upon Seeing Him.
From afar he saw his son and silently recognized him.
△ Third, the verse on following the father’s command to pursue and entice [the son], in two parts: first, the verse on bystanders pursuing; third, the verse on calling the son who does not come.
He immediately commanded his messengers to pursue and seize him; the impoverished son was startled and cried out.
This verse illustrates that the gate of exhortation finds no responsive capacity [in him]. △ Second, the verse on being called again but not coming:
he falls to the ground in a state of delirium and distress.
This verse admonishes that there is no spiritual capacity [for this teaching] within the gate. △ Third, the verse on immediately relinquishing [the effort]:
"This person clings to a self and will surely be killed" (up to) "he does not believe my words; he does not believe his father."

This general verse exhorts through two gates regarding those who lack the capacity; because they lack the capacity, the transformative activity ceases, which is seen as "killing" and is identical in meaning to the aforementioned "certain death.
II. Verse on the Two Persons Who Induce [Awakening], Part One: Verse on Responding to Actions, which is the Teaching of Equal Accord.
Part One: Verse on Establishing Expedient Means, which is the aforementioned "Adapting to Suitability."
He immediately employs skillful means to dispatch other people [to the site] to remove the filth and excrement, offering them double the wages.

Since the great transformation has ceased, he uses skillful means to preach the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle to entice and lead them. Those with "squinting eyes" are likened to those who perceive only partial emptiness;
their vision is not correct. The "dwarfs" are those who are vertically short, and the "ugly ones" are those who are horizontally narrow—referring to those who perceive only partial emptiness.

Because they cannot fathom the source of the true nature (*dharmatā*), they are like those who are short; because they lack the adornment of the various virtues of the Mahāyāna, they are like those who are ugly;
and because they do not possess the four fearlessnesses, they are called "lacking majesty," and because they do not possess the permanence, bliss, self, and purity, they are called "lacking virtue."
△ Second, accepting the price and removing filth corresponds to the aforementioned fulfillment of the wish.
Upon hearing this, the impoverished son rejoiced and followed along to remove the refuse and cleanse the various rooms.

These "rooms" refer to the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), and the "house" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). △ Second, the verse on the instruction to work as a metaphor, which first probes and leads [the disciple]. Initial section.
In the verse concerning the window:
The elder constantly sees his son from within the window.
△ Second, the verse on emaciation.
Reflecting that his son was foolish and inferior, delighting in base matters.
△ Third, the verse on changing clothes:
Thereupon, the elder put on tattered, filthy garments, took up a dustpan for clearing refuse, and went to where his son was.
△ Fourth, the practice of correct instruction.
This involves using skillful means to approach them with speech that encourages diligent effort (up to the point where it says), as well as using gentle words such as "you are like my own son.
Regarding the seven categories of Dharma-gates in the Elder’s instruction on practice, what is here called "speech" corresponds to the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).

Furthermore, "causing those who practice with diligence" refers to the Four Right Efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*). The line of verse beginning with "having already increased your price" refers to the Four Bases of Psychic Power (*ṛddhi-pāda*).
Just as oil applied to the feet enables one to walk upon deep water, it serves as a metaphor for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

and just as oil can dispel wind, it serves as a metaphor for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Abundant food and drink" refers to the aforementioned rice and flour; "thick and warm mats and bedding" refers to the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
By practicing the four kinds of dhyāna, one is able to eliminate discursive distraction through the cultivation of these concentrations.

Such words of exhortation—"You should apply yourself with diligence"—constitute the second line of the summary verse for the fourth [topic], consolation. This corresponds to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

The fifth [topic], being beyond fault, corresponds to the five powers (*pañcabala*). Once the faculties and powers have been perfected, one is then capable of receiving such words of exhortation. Furthermore, if one uses gentle speech, as in "If it were as I... [the following applies].

The two lines concerning the "son" summarize the sixth stage, "action," which refers to the Eightfold Noble Path; the seventh stage, "causing constant action," refers to the Seven Factors of Enlightenment.

Both of these belong to the stage of the "son. Regarding these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), according to conventional discourse, the Seven Factors of Enlightenment precede the Eightfold Noble Path;
however, here they are arranged according to their sequential order, and thus the Eightfold Noble Path is placed before the Seven Factors of Enlightenment. △

The four verses on entrusting the family business consist of two parts. First, the verse concerning the reason for entrusting the task, which corresponds to the aforementioned "entrusting the family business.
Within this, the first verse concerns the mental state and the essence of faith:
"The elder, possessing wisdom, gradually causes [the son] to enter and exit [the house]."
△ Second, the detailed acceptance of the family business in two verses. Part one: the verse on receiving the command.
For twenty years he managed the household affairs (until) all matters concerning the inflow and outflow of goods were made known to him.
Some say that for twenty years, the teachings of the Two Vehicles were transformed into Mahāyāna teachings to instruct the Bodhisattvas in severing their distinct views and distinct thoughts;
others say that the period of preaching the *Prajñāpāramitā* lasted for a total of twenty years. △ Second, they still remained in their original positions.
He remained outside the gate, lodging in a thatched hut, reflecting on his own poverty: "I lack these things.
Because he had not yet abandoned his inferior mindset, he continued to stay in the thatched hut. △ Third, the realization of the great resolve.
The father knew that his son’s mind had gradually become vast;
as it became increasingly vast, the capacity for the Mahāyāna was activated. △ Second, the verse on entrusting the family estate, in two parts:
first, the verse on the actual entrustment of the estate, in three sections; first, the verse on assembling the kinsmen.
Desiring to bestow wealth and goods, he immediately assembled his kinsmen, the king, ministers, *kṣatriyas*, and householders.
△ Second, the verse on determining the nature of his son:
"In this great assembly, he declared, 'This is my son' (up to) 'having wandered everywhere in search of him, I have finally come here.'"
These words were spoken because the Buddha was moved by the presence of those with the capacities of the two vehicles; thus it says, "Since you first came as my son, twenty years have already passed.
The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "Only these two names are established, and they are designated as 'twenty years. △ Third, the verse on the formal entrustment.
"Whatever houses and people I possess, I entrust them all to him, to be used as he pleases.
△ Second, the verse on the joy of receiving the entrustment:
"The son reflects upon his former poverty and his inferior aspirations... [until] he experiences great joy, having attained what he had never experienced before."
△ Second, the four verses that combine the parables. First, the verse combining the loss of father and son.
"The Buddha is also like this.
*Miaole* says: If one were to combine the meaning of the loss of father and son with only the single phrase "the Buddha is also like this," the intent would still remain incomplete.
The phrase "next, I know that [he] delights in the small" has not yet clearly manifested the meaning of the father and son meeting; nor has it been made clear why this is so.
This is because the preceding phrase relies on the following phrase to establish the knowledge that he delights in the small, and thus their meanings would otherwise be mutually lost.

Furthermore, the subsequent phrase relies on the preceding phrase to establish the Buddha’s knowledge that he delights in the small; thus, they are able to meet. His delight in the small arises from his regression from the Great Vehicle, which is why they meet.
The great loss and regression arise from delighting in the small; this is why they meet one another. △ Second, the verse on the reunion of father and son:
[the son] knows that his father delights in the small.
△ Third, the verse on the father’s command to pursue and entice him, consisting of two parts: first, the verse on the pursuit by bystanders.
Never has it been said, "You shall become Buddhas.
Second, the verse summarizes how the two [leaders] enticed us,
saying that we had attained all outflows-free states and accomplished the stage of the Śrāvaka disciples of the Hīnayāna.

△ Section Four: The Combined Verses on Entrusting the Family Business (2). Part One: The First Verse Combining the Entrustment of the Family Business (2). Part One: The Extended Verse Commanding Acceptance and Knowledge.
The Buddha exhorted us, saying: "I shall preach the supreme path; those who practice this shall attain Buddhahood."
The supreme path is precisely the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*); there is nothing that surpasses it.
△ Second, the actual verse on receiving [the precepts] without seeking or grasping, in two parts: first, the formal acceptance of the life [of the precepts].
"I have received the Buddha's teaching for the sake of the great bodhisattvas" (up to the point where it says) "yet he did not preach this essential truth to me.
The "Son of the Buddha who hears the Dharma and attains realization" refers to one who clearly turns the teaching to benefit others.

At that time, it was said only that he turned the teaching to transform and instruct bodhisattvas, and not specifically for my sake. II. Unifying [the two] to eliminate the desire for gain. Part One: Restating the preceding parable.
Correspondence.
Just as that impoverished son, upon approaching his father, recognizes all the various goods but does not desire to take any of them in his heart.
△ Second, the actual correspondence regarding the absence of desire to take; first, the direct verse on the meaning of the absence of desire to take.
Although we speak of the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha, we ourselves likewise lack such aspiration.

△ Second, because they possess both wisdom and abandonment, there is no seeking or grasping. Part one: the heading. Part two: the detailed explanation. First, the heading: because they possess the virtue of abandonment, there is no seeking or grasping.
We consider our own internal extinction to be sufficient; we understand only this matter and believe there is nothing further.

"Internal extinction" (naimie) means that "internal" refers to the essence of the afflictions; because the afflictions of view and thought within the three realms have been exhausted, it is called "internal extinction.
Therefore, this section is categorized as the mark of the virtue of severance. △ Second, the mark of the virtue of wisdom: being complete, there is no further seeking or grasping.
If we were to hear of purifying Buddha-lands and teaching sentient beings, we would feel no joy at all.

Since it is said "if one hears," hearing and teaching belong to wisdom; therefore, this section is categorized as the heading for the virtue of wisdom. Because they possess only small wisdom, they do not rejoice in great wisdom.
This, along with the preceding heading on the virtue of abandonment, presents the fault of having no delight in the Great [Vehicle], thereby revealing their attachment.
This is the fault of being small-minded. △ Second, the explanation: Why is this so?
From "All dharmas" (until) "one has already repaid the Buddha’s kindness. First, from "Why is this so?
until "does not give rise to joy," this explains the severance [of afflictions]. Next, from "We have for a long night" until "is called... [the explanation continues].

This is the ultimate explanation of the sequence of wisdom (*jñāna*). Following this, we have the long night [of ignorance] leading up to *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which is a re-explanation of the sequence of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
Next, from the Buddha’s teaching up to repaying the Buddha’s kindness, there is a re-explanation of wisdom;

thus, one should know that the first two lines clarify abiding in one's own small-scale abandonment, the next one and a half lines clarify the loss of great wisdom, and the final one and a half lines provide a re-explanation of small-scale abandonment.

Next, the first line explains the statement regarding the loss of great wisdom: "All phenomena are empty and quiescent," etc., means that the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally empty, eternally abiding, equal, pure, and unconditioned.

"The final body" refers to the Arhat. "Nirvana with remainder" means that while the fetters of the "son" (the afflictions) have been exhausted, the fetters of the "fruit" (the aggregates) still remain. Regarding "that which is taught by the Buddha," it is because [they] have attained...
This clarifies the fault: because one lacks great wisdom, there is no aspiration or joy; if one possessed great wisdom, one would give rise to aspiration and joy.
To cultivate this and attain the Way is to repay the Buddha’s kindness. △ Third, the conclusion.
"Although we are sons of the Buddhas... (up to "...we have forever no aspiration for or delight in this Dharma.

This concludes the explanation that [the disciples] themselves have no intention of seeking or grasping [the Dharma]. △ Third, it clarifies that the Buddha’s vision of their relinquishment accords with their lack of aspiration for grasping.
The Teacher, seeing that he had been abandoned [by others] and observing my own mind, did not initially urge me forward or speak of the actual benefit.
△ Second, the verse on the entrustment of the family business, in two parts: first, the verse on the formal entrustment of the business, in which the analogy is cited and applied.
Just as a wealthy elder, knowing his son’s inferior aspirations (up to the point where he finally entrusts him with all his wealth).
△ Second, the actual verse on the entrustment of the task:
The Buddha is likewise; manifesting rare and marvelous events (up to the point where he tames the mind and then teaches great wisdom).
△ Second, the verse on attaining joy through entrustment:
"We have today attained what we never had before" (up to) "...should universally receive offerings therein.
Those who "attain the Way" attain the Way of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*); those who "attain the fruit" partially attain the fruit of practice of the Mahāyāna. This...

"Clarifying the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge" means attaining the pure eye regarding the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) dharmas; this clarifies the opening of the Buddha’s vision, which perceives the principle of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).

Seeing the outflow-free in the past did not fall into the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); seeing the outflow-free today does not fall into the level of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Seeing emptiness with the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) in the past, one now sees the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*) with the pure eye. By upholding the precepts, one attains [this].

To repay the pure conduct and observance of the precepts shared yesterday, which together manifested the outflow-free state, though we have now reduced our bodies to ashes and extinguished our wisdom such that no one receives this karmic retribution, today’s pure conduct can attain the outflow-free state;
this is the meaning of the "enabling cause" (了因) that takes up the fruit.
Observance of the precepts is the meaning of the "conditioning cause" (緣因), and the principle perceived by the pure eye is the meaning of the "true cause" (正因). We are truly Śrāvakas.
"Those who hear" refers to the true stage of the Mahāyāna. During the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), one's voice pervades the three thousandfold world-systems;

this resembles the Way but is not yet the reality. Now, entering the ten abodes (*vihāra*) is precisely that reality. There are three meanings of "true *arhat*," but here only the single meaning of "worthy of offerings" (*dakṣiṇīya*) is cited.
One is called "worthy of offerings" only when they are capable of serving as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for the ten dharma-realms. Furthermore—

It is said that if there is no arising, yet one does not arise through transformation, only then is it called "non-arising. It is also said that "killing the thief" means severing both the general and specific *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* (afflictions of views) and *bhāvanā-āsrava* (afflictions of cultivation) until they are exhausted;

only then is one called a "killer of thieves. *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) states: "Those who partially obtain the fruit of practice of the Mahāyāna" refers to the time of attaining the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*);
because one breaks through one grade of ignorance and thus attains birth [in the Pure Land], it is called the "fruit of practice. △ Second, ten [verses].
Third, praising the Buddha’s profound kindness in three ways.
Regarding the passage from "The World-Honored One’s great kindness is a rare occurrence" to "he taught the Three [Vehicles] according to what was appropriate for the One Vehicle Path," Zhanran says:
"The World-Honored One’s great kindness refers to when the Buddha first established his compassion and made great vows to rescue [sentient beings]."
The suffering of the six realms and the bliss of the four noble ones universally enter the Four Great Vows throughout the ten dharma realms; this is the second aspect of the Tathāgata’s room:
the grace of the Tathāgata’s practice, which teaches the Bodhisattva path and the Mahāyāna. Although one may temporarily forget [the teachings], wisdom and vows are not lost;
this is the third aspect of the Tathāgata’s room: the grace of great compassion that bestows bliss, being both cool and warm. [Furthermore,] sentient beings may regress from the Mahāyāna.
When encountering suffering, the Buddha observes their capacity and opportunity in the interim—like a calf following its mother—to benefit them by practicing the six perfections.
This is because the Tathāgata’s chamber wards off the cold and obstructs the heat, and his great compassion uproots suffering;
thus, although the four Buddhas have attained enlightenment and ought to enjoy the bliss of unconditioned quiescence, they conceal their divine virtues to employ what the poor delight in.
1. At the Deer Park, he first used the five precepts and ten wholesome paths to cause them to leave behind the various veils of desire;
this is the Tathāgata’s robe that wards off the heat and affliction of greed. 2. He manifested as an old bhikṣu to approach them through skillful means and preach the Three Vehicles for them;
this is the Tathāgata’s robe that removes the cold of wrong views and the heat of craving. 3. Regarding the Vaipulya sūtras, he rebuked and censured [them].
7. Being cast out and humiliated, yet feeling shame for one's smallness and aspiring toward greatness—this is the Tathāgata’s robe that conceals ugliness. 8.
Receiving the command to take charge of the family estate, such that all gold, silver, and treasuries are made known—one is the Tathāgata’s robe that bestows adornment upon me. 9.
Attending the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, where kinsmen are confirmed as father and son, and the unsurpassed treasury of jewels is revealed.
Seeking self-attainment is the seat of the Tathāgata; having sat upon this seat, body and mind become serene, and one attains swift peace and stability.

By causing the sound of the Buddha-way to be heard by all, and being universally worthy of receiving offerings therein among all devas and humans, this is the seat of the Tathāgata, which enables me to fulfill my own practice and transform others—this is its grace.
This refers to what is meant by the saying that the Great Benevolence of the World-Honored One cannot be repaid even by bearing it upon both shoulders. *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states:
"As for 'ox-head sandalwood' (*gośīrṣa-candana*), the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says it emerges from Mount Vimala; if used to anoint the body, fire cannot burn it.
The *Saddharma-smṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "In the northern continent there is a mountain named High Mountain (*Ucca*), which has much ox-head [sandalwood]."
As for *Candana*: because the shape of this mountain peak resembles a cow’s head, and *candana* trees grow upon this peak, it is named "Cow-Head" (*Gośīrṣa*).
Alternatively, some say that "Cow-Head Mountain" is its name, and since the fragrance originates from that mountain, it is so called.
*Candana* is explained as in the "Introductory Chapter."
Annotated Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Two;
Annotated Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Collected Commentary on the “Parable of the Medicinal Herbs,” Chapter Five of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, by the mountain-dwelling bhikṣu Yirú of Shang Tianzhu Jangsi.
This chapter is titled specifically after the medicinal herbs among mountains, rivers, clouds, and rain because the earth is that which brings them forth.

The clouds and rain are that which moisten, and the grasses and trees are that which is produced by such moisture; both the moisture and what is produced have utility, yet among them, the medicinal herbs possess a superior efficacy.
Likewise, all conditioned wholesome dharmas (*sāsrava-kuśala*) are capable of eliminating evil, but unconditioned wholesome dharmas (*anāsrava-kuśala*) are supreme.
Among the great disciples within the assembly of those possessing the unconditioned, the four elders understood the Buddha’s teaching through the parable of the impoverished son.

The parable of the burning house deeply accords with the Sage’s intention; now, as the Tathāgata describes their attainment of understanding, he uses this as a metaphor for those individuals, hence it is called the "Chapter on the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.
The *Myōryaku-ki* states: "Question: If this were based on the Buddha’s own narration, one should have spoken of 'grass, trees, the earth, and the rain.
Since this chapter is a text that summarizes and completes [the previous discourse], why does it refer only to the 'grass' among the śrāvakas?"

[Question: "Are you referring to the four great disciples and others? [Answer: "It is indeed as you have asked. Because the words are general while the meaning is specific, the term "medicinal herbs" is used;

though the words are specific, the meaning is general, and for now, it refers specifically to the Śrāvakas. △ Third, in the "Medicinal Herbs" chapter, the Tathāgata provides a summary confirmation in two parts:
first, a brief summary confirmation, which begins with the dual exclamation of "Excellent! (sādhu).
At that time, the World-Honored One [said]: "Excellent! Well-spoken are the true merits of the Tathāgata; it is exactly as you have said.

The double exclamation of "Excellent! is a dual expression: one "Excellent" describes his realization of the reality (*tattva*) in both instances, and one "Excellent" describes his mastery of the provisional (*upāya*) in both instances.
"Well-spoken are the true merits of the Tathāgata" expresses this with refined and elegant phrasing.
Because it is skillful, it is said to be "well-spoken"; because it is all the Buddha-dharma, it is said to be "true.

"True" describes his realization of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-guṇa*), while "real" describes his realization of the provisional means (*upāya*). "Just as you have said" is the intent of the seal of confirmation.
Miaole states that "the two places" refers to the stage of Expedient Means and the Burning House, which are the two cycles of the Dharma and the Parable. △ Second, the realization.
It cannot be fully reached.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits (up to the point where they) cannot be exhausted by description.

While the teachings for the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) stop at leading those of the two vehicles to obtain benefits, they do not concern the paths of humans and devas, nor the *piṭaka*, *ākāra*, and *pratyeka* bodhisattvas.
That Śāriputra attained benefit is what is meant by "beyond the reach of comprehension. *Myōryaku* (The Wondrous Joy) states:

"Regarding 'beyond the reach of comprehension,' this cites Kāśyapa’s inability to comprehend it to reveal that others of his kind likewise possess the capacity [for realization]. Furthermore, the statement that [the Buddha's teaching] cannot be fully exhausted is employed to clarify its inexhaustibility;
if even the Buddha’s own preaching is inexhaustible, how much more so Kāśyapa’s? △ Second, the detailed exposition in two parts.
The first part, the prose exposition, has two sections. The first is the teaching by way of Dharma. The first [sub-section] cites that the Dharma King does not speak in vain:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the king of all dharmas; whatever he speaks is never in vain."
Although the Buddha-dharma is vast, it does not transcend the provisional and the real; beyond the provisional and the real, there is no other dharma.
Yet, as for what was previously stated regarding its "immeasurability," this meaning is difficult to believe; therefore, the Dharma King speaks these words of truth to encourage faith.

△ Second, the exposition of the opening [of the provisional] and the manifestation of the one reality. Part One: Clarifying the opening of the provisional and the manifestation of the real according to the teachings. Sub-part One:
Explaining the opening of the provisional according to the teachings.
"Regarding all dharmas, he expounds them through the skillful means of wisdom."

"All dharmas" refers to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya-dharma*). Although these dharmas are numerous, they are expounded according to the various capacities and voices of beings through the *pāramitā* of expedient means;
there is nothing that does not accord with them. For humans and devas, they preach the precepts and wholesome deeds;

for those of the Two Vehicles, they preach the Truths and the conditions (*satya-pratītyasamutpāda*); for the *Tripiṭaka* Bodhisattvas, they preach the phenomenal *pāramitās*; and for the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Common Teaching) Bodhisattvas, they preach non-arising (*anutpāda*).
The Separate Teaching explains the sequential revelation of the Tathāgatagarbha; this is called describing its realization of the third [opening].
△ Second, describing the manifestation of the ultimate according to the teachings:
"All the dharmas he preaches reach the stage of all-knowledge."
"Earth" (*bhūmi*) refers to the true mark (*dharmatā*). Because it is ultimately non-dual, it is called "one. Because its nature is vast and expansive, it is called "universal.
Because it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, it is called "wisdom. Because it is the foundation of non-abiding that establishes all phenomena, it is called "earth.
Regarding the phrase "ultimately equal" in the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy): this clarifies that all provisional [teachings] ultimately return to the true mark.

Therefore, because the teachings and wisdom of the three vehicles have not yet been unified, they are not called "One. That which is quiescent yet constantly illuminating is the ground upon which wisdom relies and from which all wisdoms are produced;
thus it is called the "Ground of Wisdom" (*jñānabhūmi*). This ground is itself the foundation of non-abiding.
△ Second, clarifying the opening of the provisional and the manifestation of the real by means of wisdom, in two parts: first, describing the opening of the provisional by means of wisdom.
The Tathāgata contemplates and knows the destination of all phenomena, attaining unimpeded penetration.
He contemplates that all destinations are provisional and realizes the ability to illuminate the provisional;
he knows that all destinations are provisional and possesses the wisdom to recognize the medicine; he knows the conduct of the deep mind and possesses the wisdom to diagnose the illness.

Both medicine and illness are provisional teachings (*upāya-dharma*), and each provisional teaching has its own ultimate destination. Precepts, wholesome deeds, and the like are proximate paths leading toward the human and celestial realms;
yet, when they serve as distant conditions, even a single prostration or a raised hand leads far toward the fruit of Buddhahood.

The foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and so forth are proximate paths leading toward *nirvāṇa*; yet, when they serve to adorn merit, the path you all practice is that of a bodhisattva, leading far toward the Jewel.
From the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) down to the specific and general dharmas, the various paths and vehicles—whether proximate or remote—toward which one returns may be understood.

Regarding the practices of the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*), there are two types: if the profound mind is attached to the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*), it gives rise to the ten grave evils that obstruct the vehicle of humans and devas;
if the profound mind is attached to the dharmas as grasped objects (*grāhya-dharma*), it gives rise to the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*) and the three paths (*trayo mārgāḥ*).
One should know that the six obscurations, the four abidings, and the five abidings obstruct the four noble vehicles;

these signs of deep mental illness differ from one another, yet the Tathāgata, by means of his expedient wisdom, illuminates them all with unimpeded penetration. △ Second, describing the manifestation of the ultimate truth based on wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding all phenomena, he exhaustively and clearly understands them, demonstrating to all sentient beings all-encompassing wisdom.
To "exhaustively and clearly understand all phenomena" means that this is true wisdom capable of illuminating reality;

because all provisional dharmas without exception enter into reality, it is called "exhaustive. Because it is what is seen by the Buddha-eye, it is called "clear"; because it is the sphere of true wisdom, it is called "real."
Because it knows, it is called "clear" (*liǎo*). If this wisdom illuminates this medicine and this illness, it does not illuminate that medicine and that illness.
If that wisdom illuminates that, it cannot illuminate this; such distinctions in kind are the illumination of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

When a single wisdom universally illuminates all medicines and all illnesses, this is the illumination of true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*). It can thus demonstrate to sentient beings this perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*).

Because it refers to both objects and wisdom, it is called "all-encompassing wisdom. Furthermore, in the preceding passage on provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), the phrase "unimpeded penetration" discusses the real in terms of the provisional;
whereas in this current passage on real wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*), the phrase "regarding all phenomena" discusses the provisional in terms of the real.
That these two passages manifest each other precisely clarifies that the real is the provisional-real and the provisional is the real-provisional.
One should know that the ultimate is neither provisional nor real, neither differentiated nor non-differentiated;
yet through the skillful means of wisdom, there are provisional differences, while upon reaching the ground of wisdom, there are no differences. △ Second, the illustrative explanation, in two parts:
first, the actual clarification; second, the opening of the analogy. First, the analogy of having distinctions, describing the wisdom of the provisional teachings (6): first, the land.
For example, Kāśyapa, it is like the mountains, rivers, valleys, and terrain of a trichiliocosm.
The trichiliocosm is a metaphor for the world of sentient beings; the mountains, rivers, and valleys are metaphors for the world of the five aggregates.

There is no separate dharma that constitutes the mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands; likewise, there is no separate dharma that constitutes sentient beings, for they are composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Since the lands serve as a general analogy for the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), the mountains, rivers, and valleys serve as analogies for the other four aggregates.
Furthermore, to provide specific analogies: the mountains represent the five aggregates of Bodhisattvas, the rivers represent the five aggregates of Pratyekabuddhas, and the valleys represent...
The five aggregates (*skandha*) of the Śrāvakas are like the "land" (the heavens), while the five aggregates of humans are like the "valleys" below.

Each of these five aggregates possesses both causal conditions of habituation (*vāsanā-hetu*) and fruits of habituation (*vāsanā-phala*); their basis is like mountains and rivers serving as the foundation for the seeds and trunks of grasses and trees.

As for "river" (*kuan*): it means to pierce through (*chuan*). That which can penetrate through by virtue of its great volume of water is called a river; generally, any place where water flows through is termed a river. As for "valley" (*ku*): it is... [text fragment].
(Water flows into the stream; furthermore, a spring that connects to a river is called a *gǔ* [pronounced both as *gǔ* and *yù*]). △ Second, the analogy of herbs and trees:
The various species of herbs, trees, groves, and medicinal plants that grow there differ in their many names and forms.

"Herbs" (*huì*) is the general name for grasses; "trees" (*mù*) is the collective designation for plants. When many grasses form a clump and many trees form a forest, those with superior power and efficacy in treating illnesses are called "medicines" (*yào*).
Just as wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) can all treat evils, the untainted wholesome (*anāsrava-kuśala*) excels in the sense of curing delusions;
therefore, they are likened to medicinal herbs—the seeds of cause and effect for the five vehicles and the seven stages of expedient means.

Because they are not one, it is said that their types are manifold; such various types each have designations, which are name (*nāman*), and each has a physical characteristic, which is form (*rūpa*);
therefore, it is said that name and form are distinct. △ Third, the simile of dense clouds.
Dense clouds spread everywhere, completely covering the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system.

These "dense clouds" are a metaphor for the Buddha’s three mysteries (*triguhyaka*). That the clouds possess form and color is a metaphor for the Buddha appearing in the world, which is the mystery of body (*kāyaguhyaka*).

That the clouds can provide shelter and shade is a metaphor for the Buddha’s compassion, which is the mystery of mind (*manoguhyaka*). In the following passage, the distant rumbling of thunder is a metaphor for the Buddha’s... [speech].

The teaching of the Dharma is the secret of speech; because it permeates the ten dharma-realms through the compassionate influence of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) preaching the Dharma, it is said to be "pervasively spread.
Miaole states: "Whenever the three secrets are mentioned, they necessarily refer to the response and transformation bodies.
If one were to speak of the self-enjoyment reward body or the equal dharma-body, what would there be to call 'secret'? △ Fourth, the analogy of pouring down rain.
They fall equally at once.

This is a metaphor for the Buddha using the eightfold voice and four types of eloquence of his secret speech (*vāgguhya*) to proclaim and pour down the rain of the Dharma, benefiting and nourishing sentient beings.
△ Fifth, the metaphor of receiving the moisture.
Its moisture universally permeates the herbs, trees, and forests—down to their great roots, great stems, great branches, and great leaves.
The rain of Dharma universally moistens the seeds of habitual causes within the mental ground of the seven classes of sentient beings, causing them to sprout;

this is what is meant by "universally permeating the roots, stems, branches, and leaves. Herein, faith is the root, precepts are the stem, meditative concentration is the branch, and wisdom is [the leaf].
Because the leaves assist one another in succession, they are likened to these four [roots]. The small roots, stems, and so forth refer to the faith and precepts of humans and devas;

the medium roots, stems, and so forth refer to the faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom of the two vehicles; and the great roots, stems, and so forth refer to the faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom of the bodhisattvas.
The *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "All five vehicles rely upon these four dharmas; it is only the human vehicle [that possesses them all]."
Lacking meditative concentration and wisdom, these are to be addressed by the mental factors (*caitasika*). △ Sixth, the analogy of growth:
Just as all trees, whether large, medium, or small, grow and develop according to their respective superior, middling, or inferior [conditions], producing flowers, fruits, blossoms, and seeds.
This clarifies that grasses and trees receive moisture according to their respective capacities.

When the two causes—the habitual (*vāsanā*) and the retributive (*vipāka*)—of the seven classes of sentient beings encounter the moisture of the Dharma rain, the two fruits—the habitual and the retributive—each attain growth.

"In accordance with their seed-nature" (*gotra*) clarifies the employment of provisional means (*upāya*): for those of small capacity, it does not exceed their limits; for those of great capacity, it does not diminish. This is precisely [the meaning].

The "seven kinds" refer to the two causes: the habitual cause (*vāsanā-hetu*) and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*). "Flowers, fruits, blossoming, and ripening" refers precisely to the two effects:

the habitual effect (*vāsanā-phala*) and the retributive effect (*vipāka-phala*). *Miaole* states: "Regarding 'flowers, fruits, blossoming, and ripening,' the flowers are like the habitual effect and the fruit is like the retributive effect.

This use of separate characters is for the sake of correspondence, stating that "the flowers blossom and the fruit ripens. △ Second, the analogy of non-differentiation describes the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*).
Regarding the analogy for the first of the three types of wisdom arising from a single stage:

although it arises from a single stage, it is ultimately through the stage of wisdom after the Path that what was previously produced in the stage of mind prior to the Path can finally give rise [to it]. As the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) says:

Regarding the statement that "one who can generate [the path] from the stage of the mind prior to the Way (dao-qian xindi) up to the stage of ultimate wisdom," this refers to the designations of "prior to the Way" and "subsequent to the Way.

These names have both general and specific applications. "Subsequent to the Way" definitely refers to the period after the fruit [of enlightenment]. "Prior to the Way" generally extends down to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);

thus, in the "Chapter on Expedient Means," that which precedes Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) is also termed "prior to the Way. In this context, it must refer to ordinary beings at the level of the broad ground (*bodi*) who lack precepts.

The virtuous take it as the Way before [attaining] the five vehicles; they take it as the Way during the middle stages. Thus, whether before or after the Way, the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) is equal;

its essence is undifferentiated across all stages (bhūmi). Nevertheless, because it is capable of producing [all things], one knows that even before the Way, how could the mind-ground of sentient beings not possess the nature of being able to produce?
That which cannot produce and cannot accomplish [the fruit] is simply due to the absence of conditions.
One must necessarily rely upon the stage of ultimate resultant wisdom (*phala-jñāna-bhūmi*) to cause [the roots of goodness] to arise and to bring them to fulfillment;

from the moment the resolve for awakening (*cittotpāda*) is generated until final consummation, they are all matured by relying upon this stage of wisdom. △ Second, the analogy of the rain falling from a single cloud.

Moistened by a single rain and proclaimed with a single voice, the Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle develops five kinds of roots of goodness within the Path; ultimately, these are the teaching of equality through a single voice.
*Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) states that the five kinds of roots of goodness are the Five Vehicles, all of which are categorized [according to this principle].

Because the Tathāgata speaks from the perspective of the transformative intent, it is said that "in the end there is but one sound. To say "in the end" means that there is ultimately no fixed set of five;

thus it is so called. Although the objects [of the teaching] are fivefold, the transformative intent is singular. From the perspective of provisional expediency, it must be designated as the "four flavors.
△ Third, the analogy of the three types of grass and two types of trees.
Yet each of these grasses and trees has its own distinctions:

small grass represents humans and devas; medium grass represents those of the Two Vehicles; superior grass represents Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka Teaching; small trees represent Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching;
and large trees represent Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching. These three types of grass and two types of tree receive benefit according to their respective capacities.
They personally perceive that the five kinds of roots of goodness have grown according to their respective capacities through the rain of the Buddha-dharma;
yet they do not know that the causes of these five kinds all rely upon the single Buddha-nature, nor do they know that the teachings of the five vehicles are all the Mahāyāna,
nor do they know that they all ultimately return to the Buddha-wisdom— it is only the Tathāgata who can know this.
△ Second, the application of the two analogies. First, the application of the analogy of differentiation. First, the formal application in six parts.
First, the application of the dense clouds: "Kāśyapa, you should know... just as that great cloud completely covers the trichiliocosm."
The preceding section provides the analogy; from here below follows the application of that analogy.
"The Tathāgata likewise appears in the world" is the direct application [of the analogy], signifying the appearance of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) in the world.

"Just as a great cloud arises" is the citation of the analogy used to clarify that the Tathāgata’s great compassion manifests in form to cover and nourish all beings. "With a great voice" refers to...
"Raising the Buddha’s secret speech" refers to the sound produced by the clouds;

"devas, humans, and asuras" specifically enumerates the three virtuous realms who receive the benefit of the secret speech—namely, those of the three vehicles' spiritual capacities. "The thirty sons" specifically receive the benefit of the sound.
"Like that great cloud" is the illustrative metaphor, which corresponds to the sound of the clouds; it completely covers the great trichiliocosm.
This refers collectively to all who are sons of the Buddha, all of whom receive the benefits of the Buddha’s secret speech (*mukha-guhya*).
△ Second, the combined annotation on the rain [of Dharma]. Part one: Establishing the topical headings. Section six: First, the initial proclamation of the ten titles.
In the midst of the great assembly, he proclaimed these words: [up to] "the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
△ Second, he proclaimed the Four Great Vows:
"To deliver those not yet delivered" [up to] "to lead those not yet in nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa."

The *Bie xing xu* (Prolegomena to the Separate Practice), Part II, states: "The great vows are fundamentally perfected through compassion; since compassion takes suffering and pleasure as its objects, the great vows are likewise based upon the Four Noble Truths.
If one perceives the truth of suffering—its oppression, agony, bitterness, and acridity—one gives rise to a vow on this basis;
hence it is said, 'Those not yet crossed over, may they be crossed over. If one perceives the truth of origination—the inverted flow, delusion, and the fetters of birth and death..."
Vast and boundless, it is truly pitiable. Therefore, he made this vow: "I have not yet understood;
may I understand the Way of Purity. Sentient beings do not recognize this; those who practice this Way can transcend birth and death to reach the ground of peace and bliss.
Desiring to show sentient beings and establish them in this Way, he said: "I have not yet attained peace; may I attain peace and extinguish afflictions."

The state is named the "Son of Nirvāṇa"; having severed the bonds of fruit, one attains the two types of nirvāṇa. Because one makes this vow with respect to this [state], it is said that what has not yet been attained shall be attained.
△ Third, the proclamation of the threefold knowledge (*trividyā*).
One knows the present life and future lives as they truly are.

A commentary raises an objection: "Past-life knowledge (*pūrvanivāsa-jñāna*) reaches the past; the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) reaches the future; and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*) reaches the present.
These are the three penetrations (*trividya*), also called the three insights (*tisro vidyāḥ*). △ Fourth, the three knowledges with a single mind.
I am the All-Knowing One.
The All-Knowing One is one who is fully endowed with the three types of knowledge. △ Fifth, proclaiming that he possesses the five eyes:
the All-Seeing One.
"One who possesses all vision" means one who is fully endowed with the five eyes. △ Sixth, the three karmas are conjoined with wisdom:
"one who knows the Way," "one who opens the Way," and "one who speaks the Way.

"One who knows the Way" refers to non-restraint of the mind; "one who opens the Way" refers to non-restraint of the body; and "one who speaks the Way" refers to non-restraint of speech. Truly, these are—

Because the three modes of action (*trikarma*) of the Tathāgata are always conjoined with wisdom and thus free from error, there is no need for him to guard them; this is called the "threefold non-guarding" (*trividha-arakṣa*).
△ Second, the exhortation to listen and receive:
"All you hosts of devas, humans, and asuras should come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma."
He exhorted them to follow the three wholesome paths and encouraged them to go and listen to the Dharma. △ Third, the gathering of the local populace:
At that time, countless thousands of myriads of kotis of sentient beings came to where the Buddha was to listen to the Dharma.

"Those numbering in the hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, and millions" refers to the sentient beings of the ten dharma realms; here, we are specifically speaking of the distinctions among the sentient beings of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*).
The *Myōraku-ki* states: "Although 'hundreds,' 'thousands,' and so forth generally encompass the ten realms, the four miserable destinies (*catur-gati*) do not possess the principle of growth.
△ Fourth, combining [the categories of] herbs and trees.
At that time, the Tathāgata observes the sharpness or dullness of these sentient beings' faculties and their diligence or indolence.

Just as in the preceding analogy there were differences among the herbs and trees in their size and kind, here, in the combined explanation, it is clarified that faculties are either sharp or dull and practices are either diligent or indolent;
this refers precisely to the depth of the causes of cultivation, which corresponds in meaning to the analogy of the herbs and trees. At that time—
If one discusses the gradual beginning, it refers to the time when the Three Vehicles were first taught at the Deer Park.

If one discusses the intermediate period, it can be discussed in various places regarding those who are dull-witted or sharp-witted at that time. If one makes a general judgment: those in the three miserable realms, whose causes are evil and whose fruits are suffering, and who cannot receive the Way, are called "dull-witted.
Those who, through the seven kinds of skillful means, gain benefit upon hearing the teaching, are called "sharp-witted. If one distinguishes them individually...
Regarding the distinction between the dull and the sharp: those among humans and devas who receive only the retribution of their karma and are unwilling to accept the Way are called "dull";

those of the three vehicles' root-nature who sever delusions and transcend the realms are called "sharp. Furthermore, Śrāvakas who contemplate arising and ceasing are called "dull," while Bodhisattvas who contemplate non-arising and non-ceasing are called "sharp.
By discussing the sharp and the dull across the three teachings—Shared, Distinct, and Perfect—one can understand the distinctions in diligence.

Those who are indolent are those who are heedless regarding the three miserable realms; such people are called "indolent. Those among humans and devas who uphold the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths are called "diligent.
Humans and devas who do not weary of suffering are "indolent," while those of the Two Vehicles who fear impermanence are "diligent.

Those of the Two Vehicles who crave realization and do not seek to become Buddhas are "indolent," whereas Bodhisattvas who aspire to the path of Buddhahood are "diligent. Thus it is said in the *Sūtra of Sublime Joy*.
"Time" refers to the time for observing the capacities [of sentient beings]. As for the phrase "if one were to discuss," this sets aside the *Avataṃsaka* for the moment;
thus, the terms "sharp" and "dull" apply generally to the three or four flavors and the ten realms. △ Fifth, the combined reception of moisture.
He preaches the Dharma according to their respective capacities, in various and immeasurable ways, causing them all to rejoice and swiftly obtain wholesome benefits.
"According to their respective capacities" means that he accords with their individual dispositions and needs, free from the fault of either excess or deficiency.

"Rejoicing and obtaining wholesome benefits" means that each receives the nourishment of the Dharma and attains its benefit. Regarding the phrase "free from the fault of excess or deficiency," the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states:

Because they are designated according to the capacities of the five vehicles, there is neither increase nor decrease. For example, when teaching humans, one bestows the ten wholesome actions, which is an "increase";
when teaching devas, one bestows the five precepts, which is a "decrease. This continues in this manner even up to the bodhisattvas, where they relate to one another in the same way.
△ Sixth: Increasing Growth.
When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they gradually enter the Path according to their respective capacities and abilities.

Having heard this Dharma, they increase in accordance with what was mentioned above; being peaceful and secure in the present life is precisely the cause for such increase, while being reborn in a good realm in future lives is the mark of such increase.
The Buddha is like a great cloud that universally covers all things.

Along the way, they likewise obtain moistening and growth; as it is said regarding the Prajñā and Vaipulya sūtras, it is also clarified that those in the hells gain benefit—if the fire is extinguished and the boiling water cools, this is peace and security in the present life;

or if one is reborn among devas or humans, this is a favorable rebirth in a future life; to cultivate the Path amidst devas and humans is to experience joy through the Path. If one is among devas or humans...
Hearing the Dharma and upholding the precepts brings merit that supports the body, such that ghosts and dragons do not cause harm; this is peace and security in the present life.
Alternatively, devas may be reborn as humans, or humans may be reborn as devas, or devas and humans may be reborn interchangeably; this is birth in a favorable realm in future lives.
Being able to awaken to and understand [the truth] is to experience bliss through the Path. When those of the Two Vehicles hear the Dharma, they attain *nirvāṇa* with remainder.

This is to be secure and at ease in the present life by being born in the Land of Expedient Means; it is to be in a good place in future lives by hearing this sutra there, thereby receiving joy through the Way.

If Bodhisattvas of the birth-body hear the Dharma preached by Vairocana Buddha and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), this is to be secure and at ease in the present life by being born in the Land of True Retribution; it is to be in a good place in future lives, receiving [joy] through the Way.
Those who delight in being free from all obstacles will attain peace and security in the present life and, according to their capacity, gradually enter the Path;

thus, they will experience the bliss of the Path and the sublime joy in future lives. Although the sutra speaks only of "good realms," those who take up rebirth in the evil paths do so for two reasons:
first, because [the Buddha] wishes to encompass the ten realms of existence; second, because within the three evil paths there are seven types of sentient beings with wholesome capacities.
Therefore. △ Second, the application [of the analogy].
Just as that great cloud rains upon all (up to) they fully receive its moisture and each attains growth.
"The great cloud" corresponds to the first [benefit], providing both form and sound; "raining upon all" corresponds to the second, the six [senses].
Section Four: The Chapter on the Methods of the Dharma-Gate, titled "The Postscript on the Forests of Flowers and Trees. Section Five:

The Postscript on Receiving Transformation, titled "Sentient Beings of Sharp or Dull Faculties, Lazy or Diligent, and Deep or Shallow Causes of Practice, Receiving Moisture According to Their Seed-Nature. Section Six:

The Postscript on Receiving Moisture and Attaining Benefit, titled "Each Attaining Growth," which concerns the increase of peace and security in the present life. Part Two: The Combined [Postscripts].
The first part on non-differentiation consists of two sections. The intention of non-differentiation corresponds to the preceding [section] regarding "one earth" and "one rain.
The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is of a single characteristic and a single flavor, culminating ultimately in all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Single characteristic" means that the minds of sentient beings share the same characteristic of True Suchness; this is the first stage.
"Single flavor" means that the Dharma of the One Vehicle equally explicates a single principle; this is the single rain.

In the past, the single reality-characteristic was expediently opened into seven characteristics, and within the Dharma of the One Vehicle, it was differentiated and taught as seven teachings. The Buddha knows that this is ultimately the final end.
This returns to the single characteristic and the single flavor. To explain these two—the single characteristic and the single flavor—further:
the nature of the minds of sentient beings is itself the liberation of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), which is the threefold characteristic of detachment, quiescence, and extinction.
