Regarding these: the "characteristic of liberation" means there is no characteristic of birth-and-death; the "characteristic of detachment" means there is no characteristic of nirvana; and the "characteristic of extinction" means there is neither characteristic nor non-characteristic.
Because characteristics possess only the true characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), they are called "one characteristic"; within this one characteristic, there are three characteristics.

When the Tathāgata speaks these three characteristics with a single voice, they are precisely the three samādhis. That which is called the "characteristic of liberation" (*vimukti-lakṣaṇa*) is so named because it is free from the characteristics of the karmic bonds of the two extremes—namely, the fragmented birth-and-death (*saṃvarta-vivarta*) and the transformational birth-and-death (*pariṇāma*).
The "characteristic of detachment" (*vivikta-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the attainment of the wisdom of the Middle Way.
This wisdom is able to distance itself from the two extremes and is free from grasping; therefore, it is called "the characteristic of detachment" (*viveka-lakṣaṇa*).

It is called "the characteristic of cessation" (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) because, through the cessation of the causes of the two extremes, one attains *nirvāṇa* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), and through the cessation of the effects of the two extremes, one attains *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
Within this single flavor (*ekarasa*), these are the three characteristics. These three characteristics then serve as the objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Because one gives rise to the practice of the Middle Way and, upon its completion, attains the fruit of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*), it is said that "one ultimately reaches the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Miaole states: "From 'one mark' to 'one ground' means that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is simply this single Real Mark;
the 'seven marks' are simply the marks of the seven expedient means, which are the marks of practice; the 'seven teachings' are simply..."

These are the teachings on the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*). Regarding the three characteristics (*tri-lakṣaṇa*) below, the text again points to the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) as the objects of cultivation;
because it subsequently raises the characteristics of cultivation, they are called the "practices" (*caryā*), which are the causes.

At the end, the three wisdoms (*tri-jñāna*) of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*) are raised; since these are named after wisdom, they constitute the three wisdoms. First, the nature within the characteristics is explained.
Virtue (*guṇa*) is essentially the characteristic of liberation within the path of karma;

the characteristic of detachment is the characteristic of *prajñā* (wisdom) within afflictions; and the characteristic of quiescence is the characteristic of the *dharmakāya* within the path of suffering.
Since there is no [separate] reliance on the cultivation of birth-and-death and so forth to explain it, and because there is only the concluding summary below, it is called "real" (*satya*).

In the section on the "Three Characteristics" (*trilakṣaṇa*) following the phrase "the Tathāgata’s single voice," regarding the first characteristic: while it was previously stated simply that there is "no characteristic of birth-and-death" (*saṃsāra-lakṣaṇa*), here, in accordance with the teaching (*śāsana*), it is stated that there is "no second death.
This is because the teaching resides in the realm of differentiation (*vibhāga*). Regarding the preceding characteristic:

while it was previously stated simply that one is "detached from characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-vivikta*) and that there is "no characteristic of nirvāṇa" (*nirvāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), here, in accordance with the teaching, it is stated that one "attains the wisdom of the Middle Way" (*madhyamā-prajñā*) and even [reaches] detachment.

This refers to attachment to the two extremes. While the preceding section merely stated that "the markless is also markless," here, in terms of the teaching, it is said that "the causes and effects of the two extremes are extinguished.
This should be understood as the extinction of both the general and specific delusions, as well as the internal and external deaths.
Now, in contrast to the Middle Way—the Middle Way being derived from principle—these causes and effects are termed "separation from the two extremes"; these are the two types of *nirvāṇa*.
The two cessations [of the Lesser Vehicle] are necessarily not simultaneous; herein, these two cessations have no sequence of before and after.
△ Second, the meaning of the distinction, which combines with the five distinctions of grasses and trees above; first, sentient beings are not like them.
There are sentient beings who, upon hearing the Dharma of the Tathāgata, do not realize for themselves the merit they have attained.

Regarding the phrase "there are sentient beings," this refers to those who are unaware; it means that when one hears even a single utterance of the Dharma and upholds or explains it, this clearly demonstrates their lack of realization.
Indeed, while their upholding and explaining differ from those who practice cultivation, they still perform the deeds of humans and devas.
The interpretations of the precepts, the good, the three vehicles, the truths, the conditions, and the perfections differ; since these interpretations are not the same, they constitute distinctions.

That those who have attained merit do not themselves realize this clarifies that although the five groups of people each receive the teaching, they do not know that the Buddha’s teaching is of a single flavor and without distinction.
This is to say they do not recognize the reality, nor do they understand the differences among the seven kinds of skillful means.
To differentiate their teachings and each cling to one's own interpretation as the truth is to be unaware of skillful means; thus it is said, "they do not realize it for themselves.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s ability to know, in four parts: first, knowing by means of the four dharmas.
Why is this so? Because only the Tathāgata knows the lineage, characteristics, and essential nature of these sentient beings.

Regarding "lineage" (*gotra*), it refers to the three paths, which are the seeds of the three virtues. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The host of all afflictions constitutes the lineage of the Tathāgata.
This clarifies that through the path of affliction, there is precisely *prajñā*. Furthermore, it speaks of the five immediate transgressions (*pañcānantarya*).
All give rise to the appearance of liberation; this arises from the unwholesome as the very existence of wholesome dharmas and liberation.
All sentient beings possess the appearance of nirvāṇa and cannot be further extinguished; this is precisely that which is birth-and-death functioning as the Dharma-body.
This is discussed in terms of categories when considering types; if one considers them by way of their nature, all lowering of the head and raising of the hand is entirely liberation.
The seeds of all worldly knowledge and the minds of liberation of the three vehicles are the seeds of *prajñā*. Indeed, those who possess a mind shall all become Buddhas;
these are the seeds of the *dharmakāya*. Although there are various distinctions among these seeds, the Tathāgata knows that all seeds are but one kind—namely, non-differentiation.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata is also able to know that within this non-differentiation there is differentiation, yet even this differentiation is non-existent.
Regarding "differentiation is itself differentiation," the Tathāgata is also able to know its characteristics and essential nature as explained within the ten dharma-realms and the ten suchnesses.
If one discusses differentiation, it refers to the characteristics of the ten dharma-realms; if one discusses non-differentiation, it refers to the characteristic of the single Buddha-realm.
The Tathāgata, who is both differentiated and non-differentiated, knows that differentiation is itself non-differentiation and non-differentiation is itself differentiation.
The Tathāgata is likewise able to know their essential nature; by analogy, this can be understood. △ Second, knowing the three [realms] in relation to the three dharmas.
First, clarifying the objects of the three types of wisdom:
what is recollected, what is contemplated, and what is cultivated?
Hearing, contemplation, and cultivation are called the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*). "Mindfulness" refers to the wisdom of hearing;

"objects" refers to the domain of these three wisdoms—namely, that which is heard, contemplated, and cultivated, such as the dharmas of categories, characteristics, essence, and nature as explained in the teachings below.

The repeated use of the word "what" points to the objects of apprehension; according to the teachings, there are differences between contemplation and cultivation, while in relation to the realms, there are the [three] baskets (*piṭaka*).

Regarding the objects of contemplation, the *xiang* (Shared) and *tong* (Distinct) vehicles take the six realms as their object, while the *bie* (Special) and *yuan* (Perfect) vehicles take the ten realms as their object.

Regarding the method of contemplation, the *xiang* and *tong* vehicles take the partial truth (*bianzhen*) as their contemplation, whereas the *bie* and *yuan* vehicles take the Middle Way (*zhongdao*) as their contemplation. △ Second, clarifying the essence of the three types of wisdom.
What is mindfulness (*smṛti*), what is reflection (*manasikāra*), and what is cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?
Regarding "what is mindfulness": mindfulness is the recording of the Dharma as it has been heard; it is precisely the essence (*tattva*) of mindful wisdom.
In the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy), it says: "That which is called 'essence' refers to the very substance itself. Now, the initial inquiry "what is... points to the agent [of the action].
Since the essence of mindfulness (smṛti) and the cultivation of reflection (cintā-bhāvanā) are likewise so, one knows that these are precisely the three types of wisdom (tri-prajñā).

This very essence is that which can hear, reflect upon, and cultivate; therefore, it is said to "record the dharmas heard," and so forth. △ Third, the causes and conditions of the three types of wisdom.
By what dharma does one recollect? By what dharma does one contemplate? By what dharma does one cultivate?

These are the three types of wisdom that apprehend objects. Hearing the Dharma is their causal condition. Thus, regarding these three vehicles and the three types of wisdom, it was previously said that there are differences because the nature of the objects and their causal conditions differ;
however, upon entering the perfect and subtle [state], the three types of wisdom are then non-existent [as distinct entities].
The Tathāgata is able to know both distinction and non-distinction; furthermore, he is able to know that distinction is itself non-distinction and non-distinction is itself distinction.
As for what is called "taking the object and hearing the Dharma as causes and conditions":
the object taken and the wisdom that takes it are, in essence, identical to gnosis (*jñāna*), and both are termed the cause of hearing the Dharma.
Taking this as a condition, the causes and conditions are able to give rise to the three kinds of wisdom; these are the dharmas that are produced.
One should know that although the objects, the essence, and the causes and conditions of the three kinds of wisdom are threefold, they are actually two: namely, the object and the wisdom.
△ Third, knowing by way of two dharmas.
By what dharma does one obtain what dharma?
By what dharma as the cause does one obtain what dharma as the fruit? The causes of the five vehicles each obtain their respective fruits;
this is "differentiation. That all Buddhas are of one suchness and non-dual is "non-differentiation. △ Four.
Regarding the knowledge of phenomena as a single principle:
sentient beings abide in various stages, which only the Tathāgata perceives as they truly are, with clarity and without obstruction.
Because the seven stages of expedient means involve abiding in seven positions, they are called "various stages"; this refers to the distinctions of the Tathāgata.
When viewed with the eye of a Tathāgata as it truly is— just as when various rivers flow into the ocean and lose their original flavors so that no distinction remains—
the Tathāgata is able to know the distinctions through the speech that accords with the inclinations of others and is expounded by means of wisdom and skillful methods.
Furthermore, regarding all the teachings he proclaims, which reach the ground of omniscience, the Tathāgata is able to know them as being without distinction.
The distinction. △ Third, the inability to know [the distinctions] is illustrated:
just as those herbs, trees, forests, and various medicinal plants do not themselves know their own superior, middling, or inferior natures.
△ Fourth, the preceding point is restated to explain the capacity to know.
The Tathāgata knows that this is a dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor (up to: a character of eternal quiescence that ultimately returns to emptiness).
Regarding the single characteristic and single flavor, as explained previously, the characteristics and flavors—such as liberation, detachment, and cessation—are distinguished through conditions;
yet they are one within the immeasurable, which is ultimate *nirvāṇa*. That which ultimately returns to emptiness is the one within the immeasurable.

This restates the preceding point to re-explain the absence of differentiation. Why? Because if the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) and single flavor (*ekarasa*) of liberation were the essential nature of the Dharma of the Two Vehicles, they would still be differentiated.

Now, it is declared that this constitutes the ultimate *nirvāṇa* of the Mahāyāna, which ultimately returns to emptiness; thus, there is no differentiation. This "ultimate *nirvāṇa*" summarizes all the preceding phrases.
This is not the *sopadhiśeṣa* or *nirupadhiśeṣa* [nirvāṇa] of the two vehicles, but rather ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
It is the mark of eternal quiescence; it summarizes the preceding phrases. This is not the quiescence of the Lesser Vehicle, but rather the eternally abiding quiescence. As stated above:
"All dharmas, from the very beginning, are eternally and spontaneously characterized by quiescence"—this refers precisely to this meaning. "Ultimately returning to emptiness" does not mean...
This emptiness of the severance of ashes is precisely the Middle Way, the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). △ Fifth, resolving various doubts:
The Buddha, having known this, observed the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings (up to... and did not immediately preach the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This is the resolution of a doubt. One might fear that someone will doubt, saying: "If the Buddha already knew from the beginning to the end that all is one, why did he not immediately preach the truth at the Deer Park?
The explanation says: He observed the minds of sentient beings and, wishing to protect them by following the three *siddhāntas*, did not preach it immediately for fear they might slander it.
△ Second, the praise, which has two parts: first, the description of the praise.
"O Kāśyapas, it is truly rare that you are able to understand the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and are able to believe and accept it.

It is truly rare that those of the two vehicles can renounce what they have realized to enter into the ultimate truth; therefore, [the Buddha] first praised them for being able to understand the teaching according to what is appropriate.
By describing their ability to receive it, he [demonstrates] the opening of the three [vehicles]; by describing their ability to believe and accept it, he [demonstrates] their capacity."
This explains the first point: the ability to comprehend and manifest the One. Second, the explanation of the praise. Why is this so?
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; it is difficult to understand and difficult to know.

Although the Buddha speaks of the Three Vehicles within the Single Path—a profound mystery that is difficult to comprehend—you are nonetheless able to believe and accept it; therefore, he praises this as rare and marvelous.

...and so forth. △ Second, the verse summary, which has two parts. First, the verse summary of the Dharma-exposition, which has three parts. First, the verse summary that the Dharma-King does not speak falsely.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The Dharma King who destroys existence appears in the world.
"Existence" refers to that which persists as cause and effect; there are twenty-five [realms], and the twenty-five kings of samādhi destroy these twenty-five existences.
Because the Tathāgata has already destroyed this existence, he is the King among all dharmas, and is thus called the "Dharma King who destroys existence. △
The two verses open [the topic] by revealing three to manifest one. Regarding the first verse, there are two parts: the teaching and its application. First, the verse on the provisional teaching:
it preaches the Dharma in various ways according to the desires of sentient beings;
according to their inclinations and wishes, it employs expedient means to preach the three [vehicles]. Second, the verse on the real teaching.
The Tathāgata honors wisdom that is profound and far-reaching; he has long remained silent on this essential point and does not strive to speak of it hastily.

Because he does not treat what he says lightly, he is said to "honor" it. Having deeply discerned that those of inferior capacity were not yet capable of receiving it, he remained silent for more than forty years without speaking.
Now that the great capacity has been awakened, he speaks for their sake. △ Second, the verse:
Regarding the two types of wisdom, the first verse explains provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*):
"Those with wisdom, upon hearing it, will be able to believe and understand; those without wisdom will doubt and regret, thereby suffering eternal loss.

The *Myōryaku-ki* states: "Question: Since it says 'those with wisdom who hear it,' this must refer to the capacity of the recipient (*tāyin*). How can it be said to belong to the Buddha’s provisional wisdom?"
The commentary states: Since it is said that if one who lacks wisdom were to speak [these words], how could they cause those with wisdom to believe them? Therefore, this belongs to the Buddha.
From the preceding section on "following the desires of sentient beings" up to this point, this verse praises the aforementioned teaching:
"expounding through wisdom and skillful means. 2. The verse explaining ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Therefore, Kāśyapa, he teaches according to their capacities, employing various causes and conditions to enable them to attain right view.

This brings one to the stage of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā-bhūmi). Teaching various doctrines according to various causes and conditions is entirely for the purpose of enabling one to attain the right view of the Mahāyāna;
prior to this, all are termed wrong views. *Miaole* says: "From this point onward..."

Previously, those such as Kāśyapa and the other four great disciples were all termed "those with wrong views" because, prior to hearing this parable, their understanding of the meaning was still that of wrong view and not yet correct.
Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* cites the case of the youth Kāśyapa’s own account as an illustration;
he too, prior to hearing the *Nirvāṇa*, referred to himself as one with wrong views. △ Second, the verse on the parable.
Regarding the explanation of the two [aspects], the first verse provides the opening analogy. First, the six verses on the analogy of differentiation. The first verse concerns the dense clouds:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that it is like a great cloud (up to) hanging low and spreading out so densely that it seems as if one could grasp it."
The clouds are a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body); because the response body acts in accordance with wisdom, it is called a "cloud of wisdom.

Because it is able to possess the teachings of the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it is said to "contain moisture. If the response body were not to preach the Dharma—like Śākyamuni or Prabhūtaratna—this cloud would not contain moisture.
Its body emits great radiance like the flash of lightning, and its mouth shakes the four types of eloquence like...
Because they hear the Dharma with joy amidst the thunderous sound, it is said they are "delighted. Because the ninety-five kinds of heterodox radiances do not appear, it is said they are "obscured.
Because the heat and affliction of the ninety-eight kinds of views and afflictions are removed, it is like the coolness upon the earth.

Although the response-body descends into the world as if identical to the three realms of existence, and one might seem to perceive it with a mind that seeks to grasp it, it is in fact unattainable; therefore, it is said to be "like something that can be [grasped]."
The *Chenglan dalun* (Treatise on the Compilation of Great Discourses) states that the Buddha Susīma did not preach the Dharma at all. △ Second, the verse describes the rain:
"That rain falls equally everywhere, descending and flowing in all four directions; it pours down in immeasurable quantities, saturating the entire land."

The eightfold musical tones and the four types of eloquence proclaim and pour down the rain of Dharma, which is heard simultaneously; therefore it is said that [the rain] falls everywhere at once upon the four quarters.
Since all who possess a mind receive benefit and profit, it is said that the entire realm is saturated. △ Third, the verse on the land.

The mountains, rivers, and steep valleys—this verse describes the aforementioned land, which represents the five aggregates (*skandha*) of sentient beings in the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidhopāya*).
Now, they receive the rain of the Dharma, so that their bodies and speech become supple, just as the soil receives moisture. △ Fourth, the verse on the herbs and trees.
Regarding the herbs, trees, and medicinal plants produced from the deep recesses:
"produced from the deep recesses" is a verse summarizing the aforementioned differences in the habitual causes of sentient beings.

Because the habitual causes planted by sentient beings over a vast period of time are hidden within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), they are said to be in "deep recesses. Now, having encountered the rain of Dharma, they all obtain [their growth].
Because they are brought forth through development, they are said to be "produced. △ Fifth, the verse on receiving moisture:
"The various trees, both great and small, the hundred grains, and the sprouts of crops... (up to) the grasses, trees, and thickets receive moisture according to their respective capacities."
The term "hundred grains" is used generally to refer to the five grains, which serve as a metaphor for the five vehicles being able to produce a hundred virtues.

Sugarcane and grapes are metaphors for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). "Thoroughly moistening dry land" is a metaphor for causing those who have not yet attained faith to believe.

Other metaphors are as explained in the *Wenmiàolè* (Sublime Pleasure). Regarding the phrase "able to produce," this is spoken from the perspective of the fruit; if spoken from the perspective of the cause, it is that the hundred virtues are produced [from them].

Regarding the causes of the five vehicles—both Great and Small Vehicles—how could they exceed the ten wholesome actions? It is because the ten wholesome actions mutually adorn one another that they constitute the ten thousand wholesome actions.
If one cannot cultivate these causes of mutual adornment, they will not be discussed here.

If that is so, since the human vehicle consists of the five precepts, why speak of "a hundred wholesome actions"? [The answer is: the prohibition against alcohol guards the mental ground; this is a general teaching, for it is not that sugarcane does not exist.

Since these two items have been raised, there ought to be a corresponding pairing; let us now attempt to pair them. The substance of the sugarcane is singular and can be used as a metaphor for *samādhi* (concentration);
the many forms of the grape can be used as a metaphor for *prajñā* (wisdom). Wisdom is categorized according to what it dispels, while concentration is categorized according to its object;
thus, they are merely distinguished by being "many" and "one. △ Sixth, the verse on increase.
All trees—whether superior, middling, or inferior—and everything reached by the single rain, all attain a fresh luster.
△ Second, the verse on non-differentiation, part one: the actual verse on non-differentiation.
Just as their essential nature and characteristics differ in magnitude, that which they moisten is one and the same.
The first two lines of the verse describe that which is produced and that which is moistened; the next line describes that which moistens, thereby expressing their lack of distinction.
△ Second, the verse on the ignorance regarding distinctions.
And each flourishes and thrives.

△ Second, the verse on the synthesis of the parable, in two parts. First, the verse on the synthesis of the distinctions, in six parts. First, the verse on the synthesis of the dense clouds, in two parts.
First, the direct synthesis.
The Buddha likewise appears in the world in this same manner.
△ Second, the application [of the analogy]:
It is like a great cloud that universally covers all things.
△ Second, the combined commentary on the two verses. Part one: the heading of the section. Part two: the first verse on the Ten Epithets.
Having appeared in the world for the sake of all sentient beings... [up to] ...having appeared in the world like a great cloud.

The *Myōraku-ki* states: "This verse [summarizes] the text on the Ten Epithets. Its phrasing is concise while its meaning is comprehensive. 'Transcending the world' (*lokottara*) refers to the 'Unsurpassed One' (*anuttarapuruṣadamyasārathi*) and the 'Buddha' (*buddha*).

'For the sake of preaching' refers to the 'Perfectly All-Knowing One' (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) and the 'One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct' (*vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*). 'World-Honored One' (*bhagavat*) is the tenth epithet.

'Among gods and humans' refers to the 'Tamer of Men' (*puruṣadamyasārathi*) and the 'Teacher of Gods and Humans' (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). 'Tathāgata' is the first epithet; it means one who has come from suchness (*tathā-āgata*) and gone well (*sugata*)."
Furthermore, the Sugata has appeared in the world as one who understands the world. △ Second, the verses on the Four Great Vows:
To nourish and moisten all withered sentient beings... [up to] the happiness of the world and the bliss of nirvāṇa.

To thoroughly moisten and nourish all beings is the vow to deliver infinite sentient beings, which means causing them all to be free from suffering—that is, to be free from the suffering of cause and effect;
it is the vow to sever afflictions that are inexhaustible;
it is the vow to study immeasurable Dharma-gates to attain the bliss of peace and security; and it is the vow to accomplish the unsurpassed Buddha-way, which is the bliss of nirvana.
The worldly happiness possessed by all those of the five vehicles shall be made to attain the supreme happiness of Nirvana.
△ Second, the exhortation to listen and receive:
"All you hosts of devas and humans, listen with one mind" (up to) "...constantly acting as the causal conditions for the Mahāyāna."
The *Myōraku-ki* (Record of the Profound Joy) states that within the section on "Exhorting to Listen and Receive," there are further two parts. First, the initial two lines praise the Buddha;
second, for the sake of the great assembly, it praises the excellence of the person who can preach. Because he is honored, the Dharma he preaches is wondrous nectar—the medicine of immortality.
Since hearing this wondrous Dharma now prevents the life of wisdom from being cut short, it is called "pure Dharma. As for that Dharma having a single flavor:

Because the seven types of goodness all ultimately converge in the One Vehicle, [the Buddha] exhorts [beings] to listen to and receive this teaching; by citing the absence of differentiation, he explains away their perceived differences.
△ Third, the verse on the merging of mountains and rivers:
"I observe that all things are universally equal" (up to) "constantly preaching the Dharma of equality for all."

The Buddha preaches the Dharma for the seven types of sentient beings like pouring rain that does not distinguish between valleys and ridges; because the Buddha’s teaching is impartial, there is no distinction of "this" or "that.

Whether one has the capacity [to understand] or lacks it, whether one plants roots of goodness or harbors love and hatred, whether one is favorable or hostile—should there be love and hatred, then there would be "this" and "that.
Those who do not possess the capacity for the Buddha may love other capacities, but they harbor hatred toward this [Buddha-capacity].
Therefore, there is no attachment or limitation.
Just as it is for one person, so it is for many; [it] suffices the world like rain universally moistening it.
Buddha-activity is for oneself, while Mara’s activity is for others; one should respond to those who come first and depart last, entering into reality.
The sitting Buddha manifests as standing Buddhas to observe sentient beings with equanimity; this is precisely the meaning of the "equal rain" falling upon mountains and rivers.
This verse praises the aforementioned countless billions of kinds of sentient beings who come to the Buddha’s presence to listen to the Dharma.
△ Fourth, the verse on the convergence of herbs and trees.

Whether noble or base, high or low, those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them—from [the phrase] "equally raining down the Dharma rain" to "without weariness"—regarding status as noble or base, upholding or violating the precepts, and regarding faculties as sharp or dull according to their practice:
from the noble and base to the sharp and dull, one must also fully traverse the five vehicles and seven good dharmas to explain this in succession. △ Fifth, the Verses.
Regarding the three sections on "receiving moisture," the first provides a general explanation of receiving moisture:
all sentient beings who hear my Dharma receive it according to their capacity and abide in various stages.
△ Second, the specific explanation of receiving moisture has five parts; the first concerns the moisture received by the "small grass" of humans and devas.
Those among humans and devas who are wheel-turning sage-kings, Śakra, or the various Brahmā kings are the small medicinal herbs.
Humans and devas who have not yet severed their afflictions together constitute the minor herbs. △ Among the second [category], the medium herbs are the two vehicles who receive the moisture.
Knowing the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) that can attain *nirvāṇa*—up to attaining the realization of a *pratyekabuddha*—is the middle medicinal herb.

Both of the two vehicles possess wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), which together constitute the middle herbs. The six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), the three insights (*tisro vidyāḥ*), and the explanation of the views are illustrated in the "Simile and Parable" chapter (*Upamā-parivarta*).
△ Third, the superior herbs are the *piṭaka*-bodhisattvas.
Those who seek the state of a World-Honored One and practice the samādhi of diligence with the resolve to become Buddhas are the superior medicinal herbs.
Bodhisattvas of the six perfections who aspire to Buddhahood and transform others are superior to those of the two vehicles; they are the "excellent herbs.

Regarding the *Miaole* (Sublime Joy) commentary’s statement that the "excellent herbs" refer to the six perfections: since it specifies the practice of the samādhi of diligence, this refers specifically to diligence among the six perfections.
Because it is supreme, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Generosity, precepts, and patience are merely the conventional dharmas of the world;

if one wishes to cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom, one must necessarily apply diligence. Moreover, since all five perfections require diligence, citing diligence alone encompasses all six.
△ Fourth, the small tree represents the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching.
Furthermore, those sons of the Buddha who single-mindedly devote themselves to the Buddha-way (up to) being decisive and free from doubt are called "small trees.

The Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śikṣā*) have already severed the delusions common to all [vehicles], yet they vow to sustain their remaining habits while engaging with existence to transform others;
because they are superior to those below but inferior to those above, they are called "small trees. △ Fifth, the "great trees" are the Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śikṣā*).

Abiding securely in supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they turn the wheel of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-cakra*). [From] "Thus, such a bodhisattva is called a great tree" [to the end]. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states:

"Regarding the 'great tree,' since it says 'turning the wheel of non-retrogression,' this refers to the fact that a bodhisattva of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) at the first stage (*bhūmi*) is able to turn the wheel of Dharma; this is the recollection. In this context, the bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching excel in both their own practice and the transformation of others, being preeminent in their loftiness and vastness; therefore, they are called "great trees.

The *Miaole* further explains that within the category of the "great tree," the phrase "turning the wheel of non-retrogression" indicates that a person of the Separate Teaching at the initial stage is capable of turning the wheel of the Dharma. This is the intended meaning.
It is non-retrogressive. △ Third, the conclusion on the moistened and the moister. First, the topical explanation of the moistened:
"The Buddha’s impartial teaching is like a rain of a single flavor... just as the plants and trees that receive it differ from one another."
△ Second, explaining that which can moisten.
The Buddha uses this analogy as a skillful means to reveal [the truth]: [it reaches] up to the point where [the moisture] is like a single drop in the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Because that which can moisten the Buddha’s wisdom is vast, it is like the ocean; whereas the seven kinds of sentient beings moistened by the aforementioned [moisture] are few, like [a single drop].
It is but a single drop from the ocean. △ Sixth, the verse on the combined increase [of merit]. First, the general verse on increase; second, the specific verse on increase.
I rain down the rain of Dharma to fill the world; this Dharma of a single flavor is practiced according to one's capacity.
The "world" refers to the thirty kinds of worlds within the ten dharma-realms.

Since the Dharma is fundamentally of a single flavor, yet cultivation differs according to individual capacity, it is said that one practices "in accordance with one's power. △ Second, the analogy is presented and explained.
Just as the medicinal herbs and various trees in that forest gradually increase in size and flourish in beauty.
△ Second, the specific verses on growth, part one: clarifying the growth of humans and devas.
The Dharma of all Buddhas always employs a single flavor (up to) gradual cultivation so that all may attain the fruits of the Way.
"Universally attaining fullness" refers to the principle of this verse: peace and security in the present world through gradual cultivation;
"in the future world receiving joy through the Way" refers to the latter part of this verse. △ Second, explaining the growth of the two vehicles.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas dwell in mountain forests... [up to] this is called the medicinal herbs each attaining growth.

Regarding those who dwell in their final bodies, there are two interpretations: first, it is said that for the followers of the Two Vehicles, even if they do not encounter a Buddha in this life, this body would not necessarily be their last;

however, because they meet a Buddha, it becomes their final body—this is the meaning of "growth. Second, it is said: *Note: The ellipsis (... indicates the omission of intervening text from the source.*
The two vehicles attain *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and, while dwelling in their final bodies, are ripened by the Buddha through the five flavors of teaching;
eventually, upon hearing the Mahāyāna teachings in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they enter the single reality, at which point it is called the meaning of "increase.

Regarding the statement in the *Myōraku-ki* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) that "the increase of the two vehicles has two different interpretations," the former explanation holds that attaining the exhaustion of birth-and-death in the Lesser Vehicle is termed "ultimate."

Next, in the subsequent explanation of the Mahāyāna, the term "final body" (*paścima-deha*) is used for one who has no further rebirths; this is merely a provisional designation according to the Hīnayāna teachings, meaning "no more," rather than an absolute non-existence.
When one attains the Dharma-body and Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), after one final turning, one enters Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-bodhi*);
it is only then that one is said to be "final. △ Third, the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*samānyayāna*).
If the wisdom of all bodhisattvas is firm and solid—[up to] this is called a small tree that attains growth.

"Firm and solid" refers to the wisdom of the essence of dharmas; "thoroughly penetrating the three realms" refers to the exhaustion of delusions. △ Fourth, explaining the bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching.
Furthermore, there are those who dwell in dhyāna and attain the power of supernatural faculties (up to this point), which is called "the great tree attaining growth.

Hearing that all dharmas are empty refers to the cultivation of emptiness in the Ten Abodes; the light of liberation saving sentient beings refers to the cultivation of the provisional in the Ten Practices.
△ Second, the verse on the non-differentiation of the two [truths], divided into two parts: first, the verse on the differentiation within non-differentiation.
In this way, the Dharma taught by Kāśyapa Buddha [extends] until it moistens the flowers of humanity, each attaining its own fruit.
This is like a great cloud that rains with a single flavor—this verse refers to the lack of distinction;

"moistening the flowers of humanity so that each attains its own fruit" refers to the distinctions mentioned above. ○ Because the flower is used as a metaphor for humanity, it is called the "flower of humanity. △ Second.
The verse explains the non-differentiation within differentiation.
Kāśyapa, you should know that through various causes and conditions (up to) gradually practicing and studying, all shall attain Buddhahood.

The phrase "through various causes and conditions" below clarifies the provisional; this provisional is precisely differentiation, which corresponds to what was previously mentioned as being produced. Now...
I shall explain for you the most ultimate reality: this is the manifestation of true reality, which is non-differentiated and unified within the single stage (*ekabhūmi*).
Those who have not attained extinction (*nirvāṇa*) have not yet transcended the cycle of death and rebirth characterized by transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*).

The reason I speak specifically of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) is that their minds are so strongly fixated on emptiness as a refuge and attached to the Lesser Vehicle. As for humans and devas, they do not regard the fruits [of their merit] as *nirvāṇa*.
Because a Bodhisattva does not realize [the fruit] midway, they speak only of the Two Vehicles.

As for your statement, "What you practice is the Bodhisattva path," even when a Bodhisattva practices the path, they must also sever the pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna-kleśa*). Now, since the Two Vehicles have already severed these afflictions completely, this is precisely the Bodhisattva path;
the path is thus the cause. This is because it is said that the wisdom and abandonment of the Two Vehicles are already [complete].
Since the causes of a bodhisattva are not the same as those of the two vehicles, how could it be appropriate for them to take this wisdom and severance as their fruit?
Therefore, [the Buddha] dismisses them by saying, "This is the path of a bodhisattva," further commanding them to practice so as to shatter ignorance and delusion before they can attain Buddhahood;

thus he says, "By gradually practicing and studying, all shall surely become Buddhas. ○ *Miaole* states: This was translated during the Sui dynasty by Jñānagupta and is titled the *Supplemental Version of the Lotus Sutra*.

Regarding the *Huá* (Flower) edition, all other texts are entirely based on the *Miào* (Wondrous) edition. However, in the original manuscript, there is an additional long prose verse following the gāthās;
this was added after being retranslated. Furthermore, the "Entrusting" chapter (*Zhūlèi pǐn*) was moved from its original position and placed after the "Exhorting to Resolve" chapter (*Quàn fā pǐn*).
Aside from these changes, the remaining portions were not altered from the earlier translations. The phrasing of the retranslation largely resembles that of the original manuscript.

As for the additions: those that first employ the analogy of the sun and moon within the prose to praise the Buddha’s wisdom, as well as those clarifying that within the five destinies there are causes for the three vehicles and so forth, were not translated by Master Kumārajīva because they were redundant with the preceding text.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Six: The Bestowal of Prophecies (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*).
In the Sanskrit language, *vyākaraṇa* is translated here as "bestowal of prophecy" (*shouji*). To speak with holy words is called "bestowal" (*shou*);

to grant a promise to the mind is called "prophecy" (*ji*). However, there are many kinds of prophecies. If it is a general prophecy, as stated at the beginning of the "Dharma Master" chapter: "Upon hearing the Lotus... [and so forth].

"Whoever rejoices in even a single phrase or a single verse of this sutra, or even for a single moment of thought, I bestow upon them all the prediction that they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
As for the specific predictions— such as the prediction following the Dharma-exposition during the first three weeks, the prediction following the parable to Śāriputra,
the prediction following the causes and conditions of the four great disciples, and the prediction of the five hundred disciples and others— if these were based on the true cause alone,"
Regarding prophecies based on the *nimita* (condition), they are as stated in the "Never-Disparaging" chapter: "I do not dare to disparage you; you shall all become Buddhas.

Regarding prophecies based on the *ālambana-nimitta* (causal condition), they are as stated in the "Dharma-Master" chapter: "One who makes offerings with the ten kinds of gifts, such as flowers and incense, should be known as a great Bodhisattva who has accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding prophecies based on the *parijñā-nimitta* (condition of realization), they are as bestowed during the three cycles [of the Lotus Sutra].

Regarding the three types of persons, if they are predicted based on the true cause (*dharmatā-hetu*), the prediction is broad; if based on the conditions or the understanding (*pratyaya* and *pariniṣpanna-hetu*), it is narrow.

Alternatively, the prediction may be delayed, as in the case of the śrāvakas, or swift, as in the case of the dragon girl, or as in this text regarding the Buddha’s own prediction, or as in the prediction for bodhisattvas in the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging" (*Adhyeṣaṇā-parivarta*).

Although there is no fixed determination regarding the kalpas or the lands, such a prediction is nonetheless attained. Furthermore, there is the "remote prediction," such as that of the conjured city (*nirmita-pura*).
Regarding those disciples of the present, this chapter says: "These people should gradually enter the Buddha-way by means of this Dharma.
Regarding disciples of the future, it says: "They shall seek the Buddha-wisdom in that land.
Other sutras merely record the bodhisattvas and not the two vehicles; they merely record the good and not the evil; they merely record men and do not record [women].

Previously, women were recorded only among humans and devas, but not among animals; now, in this sutra, they are all recorded. "Prediction" (授記) is also called "receiving prediction" (受記), "receiving the decision" (受決), or "receiving the decree" (受莂).
"Granting" (授) means to bestow; "receiving" (受) means to obtain; "prediction" (記) means to record events; "decision" (決) means to determine; and "decree" (莂) means to fully explain.
When the four great disciples heard the Dharma during the two cycles of parables, the three vehicles were opened and the One Vehicle was revealed in full.

The commentary on the understanding of the meaning is as follows: Although [the bodhisattvas] know for themselves that they will become Buddhas, the details of the time and circumstances remain uncertain. If they receive the Buddha’s sincere words, which grant them the assurance of their future fruition—including the determination of the kalpa, the land, and the distance of the time—it brings them great joy. One does not destroy external forms nor extinguish the marks of external forms. The reason for this is that the practitioner, in order to enter the second dhyāna of internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), must eliminate the perception of the internal skeleton;
yet, because the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm are difficult to sever, one still contemplates the marks of external impurity.
When practicing the third pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*) through bodily realization, the practitioner removes the marks of external impurity.
However, within meditative concentration, one refines the eightfold radiant light so that it is pure, bright, and clear like the color of a wondrous jewel;
therefore, it is called "realizing the pure body. Furthermore, by means of a mind free from attachment, one experiences the pervasive bodily bliss within the third dhyāna;
therefore, it is called "realizing the body. As for the liberations of the four spheres of infinite space, if one suppresses the form of the fundamental fourth dhyāna:
First, with the mind focused on infinite space, one enters meditative absorption without being attached; this is the liberation through the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Second, having relinquished space, with the mind focused on consciousness, one enters meditative absorption without being attached; this is the liberation through the sphere of nothingness.

Third, having relinquished consciousness, with the mind focused on nothingness, one enters meditative absorption without being attached; this is the liberation through the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

"Transformation" (*hua*) refers to that which is produced by supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). Because it exists through supernatural power, it suddenly appears where there was previously nothing; thus it is called "transformation.
