"O Holy Lord, King among Gods... through the auspicious merit of our past lives, we have now encountered the World-Honored One."
The King among Gods is the Buddha, the Sage of the ultimate fruition who reigns as sovereign over the ten realms;
because he is now praised by all the gods, he is called the "King among Gods. *Kalinga* (迦陵頻伽) is translated here as the "Bird of Wondrous Sound. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Just as when the *kalinga* bird is still within its egg and has not yet emerged, the subtle and wondrous sound it produces is superior to that of all other birds."
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that there is a mountain named Vana-vyūha (the Forested Wilderness), wherein many *kalaviṅka* birds produce wondrous sounds.
Such beautiful voices cannot be equaled by those of devas, humans, or *kiṃnaras*, except for the voice of the Tathāgata;
therefore, it is called the "voice of the *kalaviṅka*. Sentient beings are blind and deluded, having lost [their way].
Because right view does not know the essential way out, the Buddha points it out and leads them forth; therefore, it is said that he acts as the eye for sentient beings.
△ Sixth, requesting the Buddha to preach the Dharma.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, they spoke these verses with one mind and in unison:
"The Great Sage turns the Wheel of Dharma, revealing the characteristics of all phenomena... [and] increases those who possess patience and goodness."

Since it is said that "manifesting the characteristics of the Dharma to deliver sentient beings from suffering" is identical to the aforementioned request in the East for the turning of the "half-words," [the Buddha] remained silent.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
△ Third, regarding the seven [signs] in the southern direction, first one beholds their auspicious omens.
Furthermore, the bhikṣus in the south (up to) each saw their own palaces illuminated by brilliant light.
△ 2. Each was individually struck with amazement;
they experienced unprecedented joy and leaping exultation, giving rise to a sense of rare wonder.
△ 3. They questioned one another to resolve their doubts.
They immediately went to one another and deliberated on this matter (until) they spoke these verses for the sake of the assembly of Brahmās:
"Our various palaces... [have appeared] because a Great Virtuous One has been born as a deity, or because a Buddha has appeared in the world."
△ 4. Seeking Light and Seeing the Buddha.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings (up to) requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
△ 5. Making Offerings through the Three Karmas.
Then the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet (until: with one mind and in unison, they praised him in verse, saying:
“The World-Honored One is most difficult to behold (until: O World-Honored One of great compassion and pity, we only pray that you will graciously accept [our offerings].”
△ 6. Requesting the Buddha to Preach the Dharma.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha in verse, they spoke with one mind and in unison, reciting these verses:
"We pray that the Honored One among Gods and Humans will turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma... [until] you shall now manifest your profound and far-reaching voice."

Since it is said that he "turned the unsurpassed wheel," this corresponds to the request of the Brahmās to turn the Dharma; it clarifies the fulfillment [of the teaching] as contrasted with the partial [teaching], just as the present Buddha now preaches the Vaipulya sūtras.
△ The seven Buddhas silently granted their assent.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently gave his consent.
△ Fourth, a general explanation of the six directions:
from the southwest to the nadir, it was likewise so.
Regarding these six directions—namely the southwest, the west, the northwest, the north, the northeast, and the nadir—it is stated that "it is likewise so.
Thus, this is identical to the previous section on the south, where the request for the turning of the wheel was presented in contrast to the half-illumination versus the full illumination.
△ Second, the six [directions] above: first, beholding the auspicious signs.
At that time, from five million billion lands in the upper direction [up to] their radiance and majestic brilliance.
△ Second, each was struck with alarm;
they experienced unprecedented joy and leaped for joy, giving rise to a sense of wonder.
△ Third, the mutual inquiry and resolution.
That is, they each went to one another and deliberated upon this matter (up to: and spoke these verses for the sake of the assembly of Brahmās:
"By what causes and conditions (up to: has a Great Virtuous One been born among the devas, or has a Buddha appeared in the world?"
△ 4. Seeking Light and Seeing the Buddha.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings (up to) requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
△ 5. Making Offerings through the Three Karmas.
Then the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet (and so forth), and with one mind and in unison, they praised him in verse, saying:
"Excellent! To behold all Buddhas, the Holy Honored Ones who save the world... (and so forth)... may we all together attain the Way of the Buddha."
△ 6. Requesting the Buddha to Preach the Dharma.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings (up to) spoke these verses:
"World-Honored One, turn the wheel of the Dharma; beat the drum of the Dharma of Ambrosia... [up to] the Dharma practiced throughout immeasurable kalpas."

Since it is said that he "beats the Dharma-drum of ambrosia" and further says that he "delivers sentient beings from suffering and affliction," this refers to the occasion when the Brahmās requested him to turn the wheel [of the Dharma], which was half-illuminating yet complete, just as the present Buddha now preaches the *Prajñāpāramitā*. △ Second, the proximate causes, which have two parts:
first, the turning of the wheel of the half-syllable (*ardha-kṣara*) Dharma; third, the Buddha immediately accepts the request.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū... [up to] the request of the sixteen princes.
This formation of the conditions for the connection is due to the immediate cause of the Buddha accepting their invitation to preach the Dharma;
because of this, the sixteen princes later attained the ability to expound the teaching in turn, thereby forming the conditions. △ Second, the actual turning of the wheel of Dharma.
Immediately, he turned the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects.

Herein, first, he turned the Wheel of the Half-Syllables (*ardhakṣaradharmacakra*). Regarding the "three revolutions": these refer to the demonstration, the exhortation, and the realization. Regarding the "demonstration":

it refers to the teaching that "this is suffering" up to "this is the path. Regarding the "exhortation": it refers to the instruction that "suffering should be known" and "the origin [of suffering] should be abandoned."
"Cessation should be realized" means that suffering has already been known by me and need not be known again, up to "the path has already been cultivated by me and need not be cultivated again.
"Showing" refers to demonstrating its characteristics; "exhorting" refers to urging one toward cultivation and realization;
"realizing" refers to leading others to what one has personally realized. For those śrāvakas whose faculties are dull, there are three turnings; for pratyekabuddhas, there are two.
Regarding this, for those with sharp faculties who undergo a second turning, it constitutes a single turning; this is merely a provisional explanation.

Generally speaking, according to the universal principle, all involve three turnings and twelve aspects (*dvādaśākāra*). First, in terms of teaching (*upadeśa*), it means that each of the Four Truths has its own demonstration, exhortation, and realization—this is the twelvefold Wheel of the Dharma-teaching.
Second, in terms of practice (*pratipatti*), it means that the three turnings of the Four Truths all give rise to [realization].

The arising of vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening is the twelvefold wheel of Dharma. This may refer collectively to three types of persons, or it may be considered with respect to a single person.

Here, we follow the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga) for three types of individuals with sharp faculties: the first hears the "turning through demonstration" (*deśanā-pravartana*), the next hears the "turning through exhortation" (*anuśāsana-pravartana*), and the next hears the "turning through realization" (*sākṣātkriyā-pravartana*).
Each gives rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening. Because these three types of persons are mentioned together, it is called the "twelvefold."
Because the practice and the teaching proceed in mutual succession and together are able to crush delusions, it is called a "wheel.
It is that which neither śramaṇas nor brāhmaṇas, nor gods, Māras, or Brahmās, nor any other beings in the world can turn back.
That which cannot be turned: even a śramaṇa who has not heard it cannot know it, let alone turn it;
though a pratyekabuddha may have awakened to it, he cannot speak of it with his mouth; though a brāhmaṇa may hear its name, he does not understand its principle; the same is true for Māra and Brahmā.
As for "turning," it means to turn this Dharma-measure into the minds of others, causing them to attain awakening and to shatter [delusion].
The sixty-two views are what is called the "turning of the wheel of Dharma. Because this meaning does not exist [in other systems], Māra, Brahmā, and others are unable to turn it.
The *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "As for 'śramaṇa,' this refers to those who have left home for the Buddha-dharma;

if they do not even know the name [of these views] because they did not hear them taught by the Buddha, how could they possibly turn the wheel? If even the śramaṇas are thus, how much more so the rest of the multitude? Some say this refers to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Those who have gone forth from the midst [of society] are called śramaṇas. If that is so, why is it said that they cannot even know this?
It is because one uses the correct to illustrate the false;
namely, "this is suffering," "this is the origin of suffering," "this is the cessation of suffering," and "this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
This refers to the Śrāvakas’ initial turning of the Dharma-wheel of the Four Noble Truths of Arising and Ceasing.
Regarding what is called "suffering," the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma-realm) states: "Suffering takes 'oppression' as its meaning;

because all conditioned mental activities are constantly oppressed by the afflictions of impermanence, it is called suffering. To speak briefly, this refers to the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering.

"Of these, that which is within the three realms and the cycle of birth and death across the six destinies constitutes suffering (*duḥkha*). 'Accumulation' (*samudaya*) has the meaning of gathering together;
that is, the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-kleśa*), together with karma, are able to engender birth and death, and are therefore called accumulation.

Accumulation is the cause and suffering is the fruit; since every fruit must have a cause, it is said that this is the accumulation of suffering. This refers to the causes and fruits of the mundane world. Cessation (*nirodha*)."
"Cessation" (nirodha) takes the meaning of extinguishing through non-action (*asamskṛta*). Since afflictions and karma have been exhausted, there is no longer the burden of birth and death;

therefore, it is called the "cessation of suffering. The essence of the Truth of Cessation consists of two types of *nirvāṇa*: if the bonds of the "son" [the aggregates] are exhausted, it is called *nirvāṇa with remainder*;
if the body is reduced to ashes and wisdom is extinguished, it is called *nirvāṇa without remainder*. As for the "Path" (*mārga*), the path is so called because it is able to lead one through.
The Noble Path and its auxiliaries are called the "Path" because these two support one another and can lead to Nirvana;

it is called the "Path" because it can extinguish suffering. Briefly stated, this is the path of morality, concentration, and wisdom; extensively stated, it is the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
The Path is the cause and extinction is the fruit; this is the supramundane cause and effect. As stated in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*:

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is naturally so: it cannot be defiled by *saṃskāra* (formative forces), it cannot be afflicted by suffering (*duḥkha*), it cannot be penetrated by the Path (*mārga*), and it cannot be purified by cessation (*nirodha*).

It is like the moon shrouded by clouds; [the clouds] cannot obstruct or harm it. Once afflictions (*kleśa*) have been removed, one then perceives the nature of phenomena. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states:
"One should know that *duḥkha* and *saṃskāra* are merely able to cover, but not able to afflict or defile; whereas *mārga* and *nirodha* are able to reveal."

Yet the principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally pure; the nature of phenomena is like the moon, while suffering and its accumulation (*duḥkha-samudaya*) are like clouds. The path (*mārga*) is like the clearing away [of the clouds], and cessation (*nirodha*) is like their having been cleared away.

Furthermore, it extensively explains the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), from [ignorance] up to birth as the condition for old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress.
This is the Pratyekabuddha’s turning of the wheel of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
They manifest as causes through successive fruition and serve as conditions through mutual dependence. Regarding "ignorance" (*avidyā*): all afflictions of the past are the substance of ignorance;
its nature is delusion, confusion, and darkness, for it lacks clarity and understanding. Therefore, it is called ignorance, which is to say, it is delusion.
The "formations" (*saṃskāra*) refer to the various karmas created by the practitioner in past lives; because karma is produced through delusion, it is said that "ignorance conditions formations.
These two belong to the causes of the past. "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) has the meaning of discernment and is thus called consciousness;
because it is brought about by karma, it draws one into birth within the three realms, as the deluded thoughts of the mental consciousness enter and take refuge in the mother’s womb.

Therefore it is said that once consciousness (vijñāna) has taken recourse in the mother’s womb through the condition of volitional formations (saṃskāra), there are the three factors of warmth, breath, and consciousness;

these undergo a transformation every seven days, resulting in mind-and-form (nāmarūpa). Because this mind-and-form constitutes the substantial basis, it is said that name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness.

As for the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana): within this womb, the six faculties (indriya) possess the capacity to enter into their respective objects, and thus they are termed "bases" (āyatana). Since...
When mind and form are present, the six sense bases are accomplished; thus it is said that "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases.
As for "contact," from the time after birth until the age of three or four, because the sense organs encounter their objects yet one is unable to discern them, this is called contact;
thus it is said that "the six sense bases condition contact. As for "feeling," the reception [of an object] is called feeling; this lasts from the age of five or six until the age of twelve.
When the three causes—the six sense objects—contact the six sense faculties, one experiences the qualities of the preceding objects, such as their being pleasant or unpleasant;

although this constitutes discernment, it is not yet sufficient to give rise to a mind of craving and attachment. Therefore, it is said that "contact conditions feeling. These five [links] belong to the present result.
As for craving (*tṛṣṇā*), from the ages of fourteen or fifteen until eighteen or nineteen, one becomes greedy for various kinds of superior and wonderful things.
Regarding requisites, forms, desires, and other objects, although one has not yet extensively and universally pursued them, craving arises precisely because of this experience;
therefore, it is said that "feeling is the condition for craving. From the age of twenty onwards, whenever one encounters any object, a mind of grasping arises;
since grasping arises from craving, it is said that "craving is the condition for grasping. This refers to such craving.
Grasping (*upādāna*) is also the cause for future birth and death; it belongs to the category of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Since it arises through attachment to various objects and initiates the accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome karma, it draws forth rebirth within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).

Therefore, it is said that grasping conditions becoming (*bhava*); furthermore, it is the cause for future birth and death and belongs to the category of karma, being similar to past formations (*saṃskāra*).

This refers to taking birth within the six realms of existence. Because one returns from the state of *bhava* (existence) to undergo further birth in future lives, it is said that "conditioned by *bhava* is birth.

As for "conditioned by birth are old age and death," the maturation and decay of the body that has taken birth is called old age and death; thus, it is said that "conditioned by birth are old age and death.
These two belong to the results of the future. At the end of the text, the mention of "sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction" is as [explained] in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The profound clouds [of the sūtras] state that old age and death must inevitably entail sorrow and lamentation.
When ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease—and so on, until when birth ceases, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction cease.

These twelve links of dependent origination are simply a detailed observation of the Four Noble Truths in their specific characteristics; viewed in terms of suffering and its origin, they are either present or absent.
From ignorance up to old age and death, regarding their cessation through the path, there is the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death.
Whether observing in reverse or in direct order, all are rooted in ignorance;
therefore, when ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease, and so on, until birth ceases, whereby old age and death cease. △ Third, attaining the Way upon hearing the Dharma.
The Buddha, amidst the great assembly of devas and humans... [up to] immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.
"One who does not accept any dharmas" refers to one who does not accept various views and has realized the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).

"One who attains liberation" refers to one who is liberated from the two bonds of the fruits of the *puthujjana* and the *śaikṣa*, having attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). "One of profound and wondrous concentration" refers to one who is liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). The "three knowledges" (*trividyā*)...
As explained previously, when the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination were first taught, six hundred trillion nayutas of people attained the Way;
however, during the second, third, and fourth teachings of the Dharma, those who attained realization became even more numerous than before, such that they cannot be counted.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha* (Wondrous Bliss) states that those who are "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) are fully endowed with the practices of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), training (*śikṣā*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The name of this samādhi is "Profound and Sublime. △ Second, the Turning of the Wheel of the *Pūrṇākṣara* (Full-Syllable) Dharma: First, the Prince’s Renunciation.
At that time, the sixteen princes... [until] they sought *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

*Śrāmaṇera* is here translated as "ceasing [evil] and practicing kindness" (*xi ci*), meaning to cease unwholesome conduct and cultivate compassion. "The various faculties" refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).

Because these six faculties are pure, they are said to be "penetrating and sharp. Furthermore, because the six faculties function interchangeably, they are said to "penetrate," and because they reach the realm of the Buddha, they are said to be "sharp.
"Wisdom is clear and lucid" refers to the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering. △ Second, the request to practice and study the Dharma.

They all addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these immeasurable [qualities] up to the mindfulness of the Buddha arising from the profound mind are personally realized and known by the Buddha.
The sixteen sons again requested that he set aside the partial teaching and clarify the full one, just as the present Buddha now teaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

That Buddha first taught the perfect and sudden Mahāyāna, wherein the merits of all the sons were fully complete; yet he further took pity on those who had not yet [attained it] through the various skillful means.
For the sake of ultimate realization, he again entreats the Buddha to reveal the provisional and manifest the real.
The phrase "all śrāvakas have already achieved" clarifies that their hindrances have been removed and the capacity for the Mahāyāna has been awakened; therefore, he makes this request.

The statement "our aspiration is for the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision" means that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* elucidates only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; to be intent solely upon this is the formal entreaty.
The manifestation of the full syllable as the abandonment of the half-syllable is clearly like this. △ Third, those whom he leads forth to leave the household life:
At that time, among the multitude led by the Wheel-Turning Sage King, [those who] also sought to leave the household life were immediately granted permission by the King.
△ Fourth, accepting the invitation to preach the Dharma.
At that time, that Buddha accepted the request of the śrāmaṇera... (up to) ...they all together received, upheld, recited, and mastered it.

After twenty thousand kalpas had passed—having previously preached the teachings on the Truths, Dependent Origination, and so forth for the sake of the three vehicles—he subsequently accepted [the request of] his sons.
Please understand that because he requested the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is known that he could not remain silent or without speaking in the interim;
for within those twenty thousand kalpas, he must have preached the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā. Thus, the subsequent verse states:

"He preached the six pāramitās as well as the matters of various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Prajñā is the practice, while supernormal powers are the phenomena; this is evident now in many of the current Vaipulya sūtras.
Because it discusses the various matters of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), one knows that this is the Vaipulya taught by that Buddha.

Furthermore, because a verse states, "Discriminating the true Dharma," which clarifies the meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Great Perfection of Wisdom) regarding the *bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā* (wisdom of the reality-mark), one knows that this is the *Prajñā* taught by that Buddha.
△ Fifth, the understanding or lack thereof among the assembly.
When this sutra was being preached, from the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras up to the assembly of thousands of millions of beings, all gave rise to doubt and confusion.
While the sixteen śrāmaṇeras and those of the two vehicles immediately attained faith and understanding, the remaining thousands of millions all gave rise to doubt and confusion;
this assembly that did not understand [the meaning] then listened to the sixteen sons as they delivered a re-explanation and finalized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
...the conditions for this. △ Sixth, the duration of the preaching of the sutra:
The Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand kalpas without ever ceasing or resting.
△ Seventh, having finished preaching, he entered meditative absorption.
Having spoken this sutra, he immediately entered a quiet chamber and remained in meditative concentration for eighty-four thousand *kalpas*.
That Buddha, after preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, entered samādhi precisely as a proximate cause for establishing karmic connections;
because those who harbored thousands of millions of various doubts and perplexities had no one to consult, the sixteen śrāmaṇeras [were sent].

Regarding his lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as a cover-lecture, Miaole states: "As for the 'eighty-four thousand kalpas,' one must clearly understand the significance of the duration of time.

How could the Buddhas ever not be accompanied by meditative concentration? It is simply because the capacity of sentient beings was limited to the period of forming karmic connections with the sixteen sons that such a length of time was required.
The *Zhengfahua jing* (Sanskrit version) says: "He entered into meditative concentration and remained there for..."
For three hundred thousand kalpas, one does not know why the number [of verses] translated by Dharmarakṣa suddenly differs [from others].

△ Second, the formal conclusion of the karmic connection (saṃbandha), in two parts: First, the Dharma-exposition on concluding the karmic connection; second, first, clarifying the past shared karmic connection, in four parts: First, knowing that the Buddha had entered meditative concentration.
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha had entered his room and was in silent meditative concentration.
△ Second, the princes resumed the preaching.
Each ascended the Dharma seat and, for eighty-four thousand kalpas, extensively expounded and analyzed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

Because the Buddha had entered meditative absorption, he was able to know that his work of transformation was nearly complete and that there were no longer those among this group who required further ripening;
thus, he caused the prince to form a karmic connection with them.

Furthermore, knowing that these individuals would certainly attain ultimate liberation through the prince, he remained in absorption for a long time without emerging. △ Third, the benefits obtained by the assembly.
Each and every one [of them] was led across [to enlightenment], up to the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because they all gave rise to the bodhicitta, it is said that they were "led across. When they first gave rise to the mind, they vowed to become Buddhas;

having already transcended the mundane world, this is the meaning of having crossed to the other shore of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*). [The number of] sentient beings was *nayuta*.

This refers precisely to the assembly that was previously unable to understand. "Showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening" means: pointing out is "showing"; instructing and admonishing is "teaching";
causing them to obtain benefit is "benefiting"; and rejoicing when others obtain benefit is "gladdening. △ Fourth, the Buddha’s arising from meditative concentration and his praise, in two parts:
first, praising the Bodhisattvas.
The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū passed eighty-four thousand kalpas [until] he revealed and taught it to sentient beings, causing them to enter therein.
△ Second, exhorting others to draw near, in two parts: first, the exhortation to draw near.
"You all should repeatedly draw near to them and make offerings to them.
△ Second, the explanation of the intent of the exhortation:
"Why is this? Whether it be the wisdom of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas... [up to] the Tathāgata’s wisdom of Samyaksaṃbodhi..."
△ Second, clarifying the encounters encountered during the interim.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: [up to] they have encountered forty trillion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and even now this number is not exhausted.
This clarifies that throughout the interim, there are three types of encounters. If one constantly encounters [the teaching] and meets with it, one will always receive the Mahāyāna;
such individuals have already achieved realization during the interim and do not remain so until the present.

If one encounters it but meets with a regression from the Mahāyāna, being instead provided with the Hīnayāna, such individuals have still not reached their end during the interim, though they now obtain the opportunity to hear the Mahāyāna once again.
Regarding the teaching of the *Śrāvakayāna*, it discusses only meeting with the Small Vehicle and does not discuss meeting with the Great Vehicle;

thus, those who were not yet liberated during the intermediate period remain so even until now, and it is only now that they begin to receive the Great Vehicle, continuing until after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa that they attain the Way. Question:

If, as stated above, such a vast number of kalpas—as numerous as motes of dust—have passed and only now have they attained Arhatship, then how can this be consistent with the "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
"How easy it is to ascend! In response to the Great Sage’s skillful means, he speaks thus according to the four *siddhāntas*:

for those who weary of the long duration of the Buddha-way, he speaks of it as short; for those who give rise to thoughts of contempt toward the Buddha-way, he speaks of it as long—this is the *prātipakṣika-siddhānta*.
Or, for the purpose of generating past roots of goodness, he speaks of it as both long and short—this is the *pauruṣeya-siddhānta*.
"Dāna" (giving) may be explained as long or short according to the worldly desires of beings; this is the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint).
Or, if by hearing an explanation of it as long or short one immediately attains entry into the principle, this is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (ultimate standpoint).

One should know that the statement that one only attains arhatship after such-and-such kalpas is a provisional practice (*upāya*) intended to lead those of true practice (*satyavādins*) to enter [the path].
Regarding the statement that there are three ways to encounter the sublime joy of the Dharma: the first two are understandable.

As for the third, since it says "merely encountering [the teaching] in its minor form," this refers to those who, looking back from their current state, originally formed only minor karmic conditions with the Dharma.

This third type of person has never heard the Great Vehicle; they have merely encountered it in its initial, minor form, and thus continue to circulate in saṃsāra. It is precisely because of this initial hearing of the minor [teaching] that they are as they are.
Having first established a connection with the Dharma, and subsequently practicing only the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) during the intervening period, one now encounters the Prince [Maitreya].

At first, upon merely hearing this, a person of small capacity sees that within the entirety of Śākyamuni’s teaching there are some śrāvakas who have not yet resolved their minds for enlightenment, and immediately judges them to be eternally extinguished and incapable of generating the aspiration for awakening.
This is because such a person does not understand the Tathāgata’s long-term transformation of beings. One asks: what is the intent of this sūtra?

The text proceeds to address their delight with a brief response: as stated in the "Dragon Girl Attaining Buddhahood" and the "Dharma Master" chapters, anyone who hears even a single word or a single verse, or even for a single moment rejoices, shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Although there is no fixed duration, it should not be considered distant.
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, this is mostly explained as taking a long time; in the teachings of the Mahāyāna, it is mostly explained as being swift.

[Short. △ Third, explaining that the present teaching is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Part one: Concluding the connection between the past and the present. Sub-part one: Concluding the connection between the teacher’s past and present.
"O bhikṣus, I now tell you... [until] ...he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

The *Akṣobhyavyūha-sūtra* states: "There is a land named Abhirati, and its Buddha is titled Akṣobhya. The commentary explains: "A" means "non-" and "kṣobhya" means "agitation"; thus, it signifies "unshakeable.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Pure Land of Immeasurable Purity and Equal Enlightenment) translates this as "Immeasurable Purity," while the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha-sūtra* (Immeasurable Life) translates it as "Immeasurable Life.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Praise of the Pure Land) states: "In that [land], the World-Honored One..."
He is named Amitāyus (Immeasurable Life) and Amitābha (Immeasurable Light). Śākyamuni: “Śākya” is translated as Nengren (Capable Benevolent One), which is his clan name;
“Muni” is translated as Jimo (Silent Sage), which is his personal name. As a Capable Benevolent One, he benefits sentient beings through compassion;

as a Silent Sage, he penetrates the principle through wisdom. Because he benefits sentient beings, he does not abide in nirvāṇa; because he penetrates the principle, he does not abide in saṃsāra. The names of other Buddhas have not yet been seen.
Regarding the term *Sahā*, which is also called *So-ha*, it means "Endurance" (*Kāṃkṣan*);
this refers to a trichiliocosm as the transformation realm of a single Buddha. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Why is it named Sahā?
Because these sentient beings endure the three poisons and all afflictions; because they can endure such evils, it is called 'Endurance'."
Section on the Earth. △ Second, the assembly of disciples throughout the past and present. Part one: the assembly of present disciples.
Subsection four: the stage of non-retrogression. "O monks, when we were śrāmaṇeras... [up to] ...unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi)."
This statement refers to those who, after the great elements have subsided, do not retreat from their dwelling in the unsurpassed path. △ Second, those who retreat to dwell as śrāvakas:
these sentient beings currently dwell [in this state]... (up to) they should gradually enter the Buddha-way by means of this Dharma.
This means that after having planted the seeds [of the Mahāyāna], they subsequently regressed from the Great Vehicle toward the Small, dwelling in the stage of a Śrāvaka;
the Buddha then taught them through the Mahāyāna so that they may now gradually enter the Buddha-way. △ Third, explaining the intent behind their regression and dwelling.
Why is this so? Because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe in and difficult to understand.

This explains the intent behind those who retreat from and abide in [the Lesser Vehicle]: although they have planted the great seeds [of aspiration], because the Buddha’s wisdom is difficult to believe and understand, they retreat from the Great Vehicle and turn toward the Small.
△ Fourth, the formal conclusion connecting the ancient and the present.
"The immeasurable sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed at that time" refers to you, all you bhikṣus.
"At that time" points to the period when seeds were planted under the Great Penetrating Wisdom Buddha (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū).
II. Gathering Future Disciples. Part One: The Actual Gathering.
"These are none other than my śrāvaka disciples who will appear in future ages after my parinirvāṇa.
△ Second, the resolution of doubts:
"After my parinirvāṇa, there will again be disciples... (up to) "...except for the skillful means used by the Tathāgatas in their preaching of the Dharma."

A doubter asks: "Those in the present who hear the Buddha preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and enter the One Vehicle may indeed be among those with whom [the Buddha] has established a karmic connection;
however, as for those in the future who enter parinirvāṇa without hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, how could such people abandon the Lesser Vehicle to enter the One Vehicle?
The commentary explains: "Even though they have entered parinirvāṇa, I shall become a Buddha in other lands and ultimately [lead them there]."
Those who shall hear this sutra in other lands refer to the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*).
"Except for those Tathāgatas who speak through skillful means" removes doubt; the Three Vehicles are taught as skillful means, for in reality there are not three.
II. Explaining the Preaching of the Lotus Sutra. A. First, the purity of the assembly at the initial time.
If the various bhikṣus know that the Tathāgata himself has realized the dharma of emptiness, entered deeply into meditative concentration, and reached the time for parinirvāṇa— that is,
when the Buddhas' appearance in the world and their work of transforming beings through the Path is about to be completed—
they then preach the Lotus Sūtra. Just as Kāśyapa Buddha, the Buddha Sun-Moon-Lamp, and others appeared in the Pure Land and, having finished preaching the Lotus Sūtra, [entered parinirvāṇa].

Śākyamuni enters nirvāṇa after appearing in this defiled land, having finished preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and proclaimed that he would soon pass away; yet he further preaches the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Those whose assembly has become pure have already obtained the benefit of the Tripiṭaka teachings and are thus spared from the calamities of the five turbidities and the eight sufferings.
Those with firm faith and understanding have, regarding the Vaipulya (Vaipulya) teachings, realized the true nature of the mind through internal conviction. They have attained full comprehension.
When those who practice the Dharma of Emptiness hear the teaching of Prajñā on the Dharma of Emptiness, they attain thorough realization within that very Dharma of Emptiness;
this is the intent behind the transformation of the teaching. △ Second, the formal preaching of the Lotus Sūtra.
"He then gathers the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas" (up to) "only through the single Buddha-vehicle do they attain extinction.
Regarding this, the gathering of the bodhisattvas refers to the assembly of kinsmen, and the assembly of śrāvakas refers to summoning his sons;
thus, the Sons of the Śākya Clan and the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body serve as the retinue of influence and response. When verified by this text, the meaning becomes clear.
Regarding the statement that "there are no two vehicles in the world," according to reason, there is not a single person who should enter extinction forever;
all must ultimately return to the Great Vehicle. △ Third, explaining the intent of the previous opening.
"Monks, you should know that the Tathāgata’s skillful means (upāya) [extends] until such a person hears it and then believes and accepts it.
This follows the meaning of the preceding text. If there were no followers of the Two Vehicles who attained extinction (nirvāṇa), for what reason would the Tathāgata bestow the three [vehicles]?
The explanation states: "Monks, you should know that the Tathāgata, by means of his skillful and provisional wisdom (upāya-kuśala-jñāna), deeply understands sentient beings."
There are those with inferior aspirations who are attached to the five objects of desire and obscured by the five turbidities;

therefore, the Buddha first speaks of the nirvana of the three vehicles to enable them to break through their obscurations and escape their hardships, and subsequently speaks of the One [Vehicle]. △ Second, the illustrative explanation of establishing karmic conditions has two parts: first, the opening of the illustration; second, the specific illustrations.
First, the analogy of the guide has five parts; first, the analogy of the five hundred *yojanas*.
For example, five hundred *yojanas*.
These five hundred *yojanas* represent the abodes of saṃsāra where the multitudes above who have not yet crossed over take pleasure and become attached;

they correspond to the "burning house" in the "Convenient Means" (*Upāya-paṛiccheda*) chapter, where the vast and great threefold world (*triloka*) offers no peace. This stands in contrast to the "Peaceful Abode."
This refers to the sense of peace and security. In terms of the lands (*kṣetra*), the Land of Common Abode of the Three Realms is three hundred;
the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder is four hundred; and the Land of True Reward is five hundred. In terms of afflictions (*kleśa*), the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are one hundred;

the lower-tier delusions (*avarabhāgīya-kleśa*) are two hundred and five; the upper-tier delusions (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-kleśa*) are three hundred; and the delusions as numerous as motes of dust (*rajas-kaṇa*) are [four hundred and five].

Regarding the four hundred *yojanas* of the delusions of ignorance and the five hundred *yojanas*, these are explained according to the perspective of contemplative observation: entering the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) allows one to pass the three hundred;

entering the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*) allows one to pass the four hundred; and entering the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-vipaśyanā*) allows one to pass the five hundred *yojanas*, as explained previously.
△ Second, the analogy of the perilous and evil paths.
A perilous and evil path, vast and desolate, a place of fear where no people dwell.
This perilous and evil path is a metaphor for the heavy defilements of the multitudes who have not yet crossed over;

it corresponds to the fire breaking out within the burning house, as described in the "Expedient Means" chapter, and represents the dharma of insecurity as opposed to security—namely, the two types of suffering: *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence) and *pariṇāmi-bhava* (transformative existence).

The various births and deaths constitute the perilous difficulty of the result; the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the dust-like afflictions (*rajas-kleśa*), and the ignorance (*avidyā*) constitute the perilous difficulty of the cause.
Because of these causes and results, they are called the "evil paths. There are two kinds of paths: first, those that are desolate yet have people upon whom one can rely;

second, those that are desolate and have no people upon whom one can rely. That which has people upon whom one can rely is analogous to [the possibility of liberation] within the midst of birth and death.

There are cases where nirvana exists amidst afflictions and bodhi exists amidst samsara; although these may seem vast and remote, there are people who can rely upon them, and this generally refers to the three teachings of the Mahayana.

If there were no nirvana or bodhi within samsara and afflictions—just as there is no sickness within medicine and no medicine within sickness—then this would be a vast and remote state where no one could rely; such cases mostly pertain to the Tripitaka.
The Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are established on principle as being common to the Two Vehicles of the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-śāsana).
△ Third, the analogy of the many crowds:
"If there are many crowds" is an analogy for the hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of beings converted by the Prince above, who all gave rise to doubt and failed to understand.

"Born" refers to the thirty sons and five hundred people within the burning house; this corresponds to the "Expedient Means" chapter’s understanding of the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings.
△ Fourth is the analogy for the desire to reach the place of treasure.
Desiring to pass beyond this path to reach the place of rare treasures:
because the followers of the Two Vehicles have severed the afflictions of views and thoughts and emerged from the Triple World, it is said they "desire to pass beyond this path";

furthermore, because they seek to sever the dust-like and sand-like afflictions as well as ignorance to attain the unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment, it is said they "seek to reach the place of rare treasures. △ Fifth, there is a guide.
For example, there was a guide who was wise, discerning, and thoroughly understood the characteristics of dangerous paths—both their impassable and passable aspects.
This "guide" refers to the sixteenth prince; his eyes and ears were pure, which is what is meant by being "wise."

"Purity" (*qingjing*) refers to "attainment" (*da*); in summary, this is the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*). "Wisdom" (*hui*) refers to the threefold wisdom of the single mind;

"clarity" (*ming*) refers to being fully endowed with the five eyes as well as the three insights (*trividyā*). Furthermore, the ten powers (*daśabala*) constitute "attainment. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states:

"The purity of the six sense faculties is partially attained at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*); this is the time when the sixteen sons first established a karmic connection, now [manifesting] throughout the eight directions."

Since attaining Buddhahood depends solely upon the ultimate fruit, the *Shi huiming* (Explanation of Wisdom and Clarity) states that this consists of the three knowledges, the five eyes, the three insights, and the ten powers.
Regarding "obstructions and openings": suffering, its origin, the twelve links of dependent origination, the six obscurations, and the sands of ignorance constitute the obstructions;

while the path, its cessation, the wisdom that extinguishes dependent origination, the six perfections, the single mind, and the threefold contemplation constitute the openings. △ Second, the analogy of leading and guiding.
Third, the analogy of the people led at the outset:
it is like leading a multitude of people across this perilous difficulty;
it illustrates those for whom the original karmic conditions were established but who have not yet attained liberation—those whose original conditions remain intact as they are led by the Guide. △
Second, "slackening and retreating midway" is an analogy for the first [of two types] of retreating from the Mahāyāna.
First, regarding "slackening and retreating midway":

the people and crowds being led who slacken and retreat midway are precisely an analogy for those who, encountering [obstacles] along the way, retreat from the Mahāyāna and take up the Hīnayāna. "Midway" refers to the middle stage.

The "road" does not refer to the midpoint of the journey; it is called the "middle road" simply because it begins with the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment and ends with the attainment of Buddhahood.
Because one gives rise to the intention of retreating from the Great Vehicle within these two pillars, it is named the "middle road.
△ Second, addressing the Guide:
They addressed the Guide, saying, "We are utterly exhausted and filled with fear.
Regarding the term "Guide," there is the Guide of Compassion who possesses the direct path, as the text says:
"There was a guide who led a great multitude. There is also the Guide through karmic connection, as the text says: "The people being led..."
The assembly addressed the Guide, saying: "This is so. There is the Guide of Expedient Wisdom (upāya-jñāna), as the text says:
"The Guide possesses many skillful means. There is the Guide of Real Wisdom (bhūta-jñāna), as the text says:
"The Guide knows this multitude of people. Now, when it says "addressing the Guide," it specifically refers to addressing the Guide who establishes karmic connections.
When they regress from the Great [Vehicle], the Great perishes; when they connect with the Small [Vehicle], the Small arises. One birth and one extinction are felt within the Dharma-body.
Calling this "the white prince," it is known that his regression from the Great is because his roots of goodness from hearing were weak and he was obscured by ignorance;
thus, he speaks of being "exhausted" and weary of birth and death, which is termed "fear. This is as stated in the *Miaole* (The Sublime Joy).
Regarding these four guides: the first penetrates both cause and effect; the second pertains only to the cause; and the third and fourth pertain only to the effect.
To say they "penetrate the common way" means they apply to others; to say they "form a karmic connection" means they are specific to my own teacher.

To speak of "expedient wisdom" refers to the time of bestowing the small [vehicle]; to speak of "real wisdom" refers to the time of revealing the expedient. These four differ according to the time, yet the person remains the same.
Both of these princes, from the beginning until now, have spoken of being moved by the *dharmakāya*.

This is because their great capacity (*mahāyāna*) has already ceased and their small capacity (*hīnayāna*) is about to arise; therefore, they have not yet seen the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha, as they are instead moved by the *dharmakāya* in obscurity.
△ Third, they cannot advance further.
"Unable to advance further; the path ahead is still long, and now we wish to turn back.
"Unable to advance further; the path ahead is still long" means that the afflictions of view and thought, the dust-like and sand-like [afflictions], and ignorance are difficult to sever abruptly.

Nevertheless, by employing the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) as a provisional means to lead them, one does not allow them to return immediately to their original state; thus, there is also the sense of "advancing. △ Second.
"Receiving those of the lower fourth stage through many initial expedients":
the Guide possesses many expedient means;
this analogy refers to the immediate reception of the lower stage through appropriate application. △ Second, grieving over the loss of the treasure.
And he formed this thought: "These people are pitiable; why do they wish to turn back and abandon such great treasures?
He grieved for their loss of treasure, which was like knowing of the small while being ignorant of the great. △ Third, the manifestation of a city, in two parts: first, the manifestation itself.
Having formed this thought, by the power of skillful means (upāya), [the Buddha] creates a city at a distance of more than three hundred yojanas.

This is precisely the teaching of skillful means used to transform those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), enabling them to sever the delusions of views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi- and kleśa-āvaraṇa) and escape the suffering of the triple world.

Thus, it is said that they are made to pass beyond three hundred yojanas; because he causes them to provisionally realize true emptiness (śūnyatā) and nirvāṇa, it is said that he "creates" [the city].
One city. △ Second, the description of the transformation:
He addressed the multitude, saying, "Do not be afraid... (up to) if you can proceed forward to the place of treasure, you may also go."
This analogy corresponds to the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma as explained above: "Do not be afraid;

do not retreat" is the turning of exhortation (*pravartana*), which exhorts one to enter the city. "Now, you may dwell in this great city and act as you please" is the turning of demonstration (*darśana*), showing that the city is a place where one may reside.
"If you enter this city, you will swiftly attain peace and security" is the turning of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).
It means that one attains the security of the City of Transformation; one may also proceed to reach the Treasure Place (*ratnasthāna*).
Within the Tripiṭaka teaching, the meaning of "proceeding forward" is not yet discussed. In the Mahāyāna gate, regarding the Treasure Place of the common Bodhisattvas, there are two meanings:
if one employs the ultimate sense, the Treasure Place is taken as the supreme fruit (*phala*). Therefore, the preceding text states: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can [fully realize it]."

To exhaustively investigate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, one enters [the stages] by parts; thus, the initial stage of the resolve for enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādabhūmi*) is taken as the "Jewel Place.
Therefore, the preceding text states: "The unsurpassed mass of jewels is obtained without seeking," and further:
"One has already attained those portions of the Buddha-dharma which are to be attained by a Son of the Buddha. △ Fourth, the Parable of Entering the City.
At that time, the assembly, exhausted to the extreme, felt great joy; (up to: having given rise to the thought of having crossed over, they gave rise to the thought of peace and security.

Their great joy was immediately the stage of wisdom through hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); the unprecedented [experience] was the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*); being freed from the evil realms was the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*);

the swift peace and security was the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*); entering the city ahead was the stage of "Seeing the Truths" (*darśanamārga*); the thought of having crossed over was the stage of "No-more-learning" (*aśaikṣamārga*).
This is the same as the courageous and vigorous pushing of the children out of the burning house to satisfy their wishes.

The thought that they have already been saved is like attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); the thought of peace and security is like attaining the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Furthermore, possessing wisdom and virtue is like having already realized the transcendence [of suffering], while the virtue of cessation is like peace and security.
△ Third, the analogy of leading them to the place of jewels, in two parts: first, knowing they have rested.
Thus it was. At that time, the Guide knew that this multitude of people had already attained rest and were no longer weary.
That they had attained rest and were no longer weary is an analogy for when the time for supreme *nirvāṇa* has arrived and the assembly is furthermore purified.
Thus, having escaped the calamity, the great capacity [for enlightenment] shall be awakened. △ Second, proceeding toward the place of treasure:
immediately the conjured city is extinguished [up to] "The great city you previously saw was merely something I conjured for the sake of providing rest."
This is like the parable of destroying the conjured city to lead [beings] toward the place of jewels. The aforementioned correct teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* reveals the true aspect;
the "place of jewels" being near refers to the great city. The statement "that which I have conjured" serves as a metaphor to discard the provisional and manifest the real. Question:
Regarding the five locations where the three are opened up to reveal the one, what is the difference between them? Answer: Generally speaking, there is none.

The *Vibhaṅga* (Discourse on Distinctions) discusses the provisional means (*upāya*) with differentiation; the "Chapter on Expedient Means" explains the teaching by opening up the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle, stating:

"The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for sentient beings solely by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle; there are neither two nor three. The "Fire House" chapter explains the practice by opening up the three to reveal the one;
"vehicle" (*yāna*) carries the sense of transport, and transport serves as a metaphor for practice. As the text states: "Each mounts a great vehicle."
"Roaming in the four directions" refers to sporting and enjoying themselves. In the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding," the three are opened up and the one is revealed in relation to persons;
the conclusion identifies the hired laborers as being the sons of the elder. The text states: "From of old, we have truly been the sons of the Buddha.
In the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," the provisional and the real are clarified through the distinction between differentiation and non-differentiation, yet this is not definitive.
The process of rejecting and accepting merely clarifies that sentient beings do not know [the truth], which the Buddha intends for them to know.
If one understands the sevenfold distinctions, one knows the provisional; if one realizes they are identical in relying on a single principle without distinction, one knows the real.

Through the non-distinction of distinctions and the distinction of non-distinction, he causes them to understand this meaning. He never says that there is neither one nor many; this is explained from the perspective of the self.
Because the Buddha speaks according to his own intent through the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate truth, it is that which the Buddha knows while sentient beings do not.
Now, the "transformed city" (the *parīttābha* city) is precisely established based on principle to open up the three and reveal the one;

both the transformed city and the treasure site represent the two principles of the Great and Small Vehicles, wherein the principle of transformation for the Two Vehicles is set aside to reveal the true principle of the One Vehicle at the treasure site. As the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) says:

In the fifth section, "Clarifying the Provisional," although each [of the four aspects]—the teaching, the practitioner, the principle, and whether one knows or does not know—is explained according to the general tenor of the text, every single passage must nonetheless fully incorporate all four aspects, such as clarifying whether the Tathāgata knows or does not know, and so forth.
△ Second, combining the parables. Part one: the formal combination. Sub-part one: combining the parable of the guide.
The fifth point, "initially correctly corresponding with the Guide above," means that the Tathāgata is likewise with the bhikṣus.
△ Second, "corresponding with the great multitude of people."
"Now I act as the Great Guide for you all.
*Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) says: "Now I act as the Great Guide for you all" refers to one who accords with a great multitude of people;
this uses that which leads to manifest that which is led. △ Third, the convergence of dangerous and evil paths.
He knows that all births and deaths, afflictions, and evil realms are perilous and difficult,
spanning four hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length and distance.
△ Fifth: Those who are intelligent, wise, and discerning are also fit to reach the place of the most precious jewels;
they should go and they should be delivered.
Those who are superior in intelligence, wisdom, and discernment, and who well know the signs of the dangers, obstructions, and openings on the path, are likewise fit for the aforementioned desire.

This is like passing through a perilous path to reach a place of precious treasures. △ Second, the combined analogy of leading and guiding, in three parts: first, the combination of the people being led.
"If sentient beings... [and so forth].
△ 2. Combining the "Retreat from the Great Path" with the "Connection to the Small Path. First, combining the "Retreat from the Great Path" at the midpoint:
Those who merely hear of the Single Buddha Vehicle are combined with the aforementioned retreat at the midpoint;
this indicates they lack the great capacity for the intent [of the Great Vehicle]. △ 2. Combining the statement addressed to the Teacher:
Consequently, they do not wish to see the Buddha nor wish to draw near him;
together they address the Guide, refusing his exhortations and admonitions. △ Third, being unable to advance further, they think thus:
"The path of the Buddha is long and distant; only after enduring diligent suffering for a long time can it be accomplished."
"Joining [the hands] above and being unable to proceed further signifies the cessation of transformative intent. △ Second, joining and connecting the minor three:
first, joining the skillful means of the Guide.
The Buddha knows this mind.

The meaning of "joining the upper [part] while withdrawing from the middle and returning to the great, then reconnecting with the small" is illustrated by the fact that although there were originally four combinations, there are now only three;
this precisely represents the intention of the Guide’s many skillful means (*upāya*) in adapting to what is appropriate. △ Second, combining these who are to be pitied.
Those who are timid and inferior are, by the power of skillful means, joined with the superior [vehicle];
these pitiable ones are known to possess limited capacities.
△ Third, having manifested the transformation-city midway as a place for rest, two types of nirvana are taught.

The gathering of the multitude and their entry into the city is a parable; yet, to speak of two types of *nirvāṇa* along the way—where the delusions of the triple world are exhausted but the sands-of-samsara ignorance remains unbroken—one distinguishes between *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* at this midpoint.

This is also the *nirvāṇa* of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*. Furthermore, while the death of fragmentation (*pariccheda-maraṇa*) has been exhausted, the death of transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*) has not yet been eliminated; these constitute the two deaths.
Because it is judged as being with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) or without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), it is called the "Middle Way of Sublime Joy.

Regarding this, there are three explanations: first, in terms of afflictions (*kleśa*); second, in terms of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), which refers to wisdom; and third, in terms of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), where the interval between the two deaths is named the Middle Way.
△ Third, combining [the stages] to reach the treasure place, part one: combining the knowledge that breathing has ceased.
If sentient beings abide in two stages, these two stages are themselves the two nirvāṇas.
