In the Vaipulya sutras, manifesting the acceptance of censure is the trace of protecting, upholding, and assisting the proclamation of the Dharma that clarifies the "Full" (Pūrṇa) while being paired with the "Half" (Ardha);
in the Prajñāpāramitā, this is the trace of protecting, upholding, and assisting the proclamation of the Dharma that carries both the "Half" and clarifies the "Full";

in the Lotus Sutra, attaining awakening is the trace of protecting, upholding, and assisting the proclamation of the Dharma that abolishes the "Half" and clarifies the "Full. As the aforementioned text says: "I..."
This refers precisely to the meaning of constantly praising various merits.

While inherently endowed with the merits of both the provisional and the real, he manifests traces within the five flavors to assist the Buddha in maturing those of the true practice; is this not the intent of diligently assisting in the proclamation [of the Dharma]?
Furthermore, his ability to instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly is the discernment of the teachings of the "half-letters," which he possesses in their entirety.

The "Explanators" assist in proclaiming the teachings of the *paripūrṇa* (complete) word; the "Greatly Beneficial Ones" assist the Buddha in benefiting sentient beings of both the *ardha-paripūrṇa* (half-complete) and *paripūrṇa* categories;
and the "Fellow Practitioners of Brahma-conduct" are the disciples of both the half-complete and complete categories who are transformed within these manifested traces.
△ Second, a specific description of the unfathomable merits of the original ground.
Since his renunciation, none except the Tathāgata has been able to exhaust the eloquence of his discourse.
From those who have descended from the Buddha down to the practitioners of the seven stages of expedient means, none can know the eloquence of his original ground.
△ Second, manifesting his original practices by reference to the past.
"You should not think that Pūrṇa (up to) constantly performs the work of a Buddha to transform sentient beings.
It is not merely that Pūrṇa assisted me in proclaiming the teachings of both the Half and the Full [Tripitaka];

he has likewise assisted in proclaiming the teachings of both the Half and the Full at the abodes of Buddhas throughout the distant past. Taking his assistance today as a manifestation of his true origins," [he said].
To take up the past and proclaim it serves to reveal the original source. There are two ways of revealing the original source: first, the remote original; second, the proximate original.
Because the remote original is obscure and distant, it is difficult for people to believe; therefore, we now cite only the ninety billion [aeons] of the proximate original.

Since one possesses the wisdom of recollecting past lives, they are able to know the proximate original. By citing the proximate to verify the remote, one causes others to give rise to faith and to protect and uphold [the teaching].

"Assisting in the proclamation" refers to assisting in the proclamation of the Dharma of the "half-letters. "The Buddha’s True Dharma" refers to assisting in the proclamation of the Dharma that clarifies the "full" in contrast to the "half.
Furthermore, "clearly understanding and penetrating the Dharma of emptiness" refers to assisting in the proclamation of the Dharma that clarifies the "full" while transcending the "half.
"The four unhindered knowledges" refer to the four unhindered eloquences (*pratisaṃvid*), because knowledge resides in speech. (1)
1. The unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) is the thorough and unobstructed comprehension of the meanings of all phenomena. 2.

The unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) is the wisdom that penetrates the names and designations of all phenomena through analysis, without obstruction, for the sake of knowing all meanings. 3.
The unimpeded knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*) refers to the various regional and diverse languages of all sentient beings, whether they be a single word or two words.

Whether it be extensive speech, abbreviated speech, detailed speech, feminine speech, masculine speech, or speech concerning the past, future, and present—through such linguistic expressions, he enables each person to attain understanding.
He possesses unimpeded eloquence such that all who hear him comprehend his discourse.
This is the bodhisattva’s unimpeded knowledge of joyful eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), by which he can expound upon all things within a single syllable.
Within a single syllable or a single phrase, one can expound all phrases; within a single dharma, one can expound all dharmas.

All that is taught is entirely true and provides benefit according to those who are to be saved—namely, the twelve divisions of the scriptures and the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma, which accord with the inclinations of the faculties of all sentient beings regarding the teachings they wish to hear.
He expounded the Dharma for them, and those who heard it were never weary; by virtue of his mastery of supernormal powers, he was able to follow the Buddha’s lifespan in practicing pure conduct.
During the era of that Buddha, as he had not yet revealed his true identity, everyone regarded him as a mere śrāvaka and did not say he was a great bodhisattva.
He transformed immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to establish themselves in *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is precisely to assist in proclaiming the dharma that sets aside the partial and clarifies the full;

such assistance in proclaiming the Buddha-dharma is essentially for the purpose of forming karmic conditions with sentient beings for the Pure Land. If one does not form these conditions with sentient beings, then when the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, the land will be defiled and lack the receptive capacity required for transformation.
△ Third, [the section] concerning the causal practices cultivated by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The bhikṣu Pūrṇa likewise, from the time of the seven Buddhas until now, has constantly and diligently applied himself to teaching and transforming sentient beings.
This also follows the previous examples of assisting in the proclamation of the Dharma of the Half and Full [Teachings], benefiting those of both great and small capacities.
As for the seven Buddhas, according to what appears in various texts: first, Vipaśyin Buddha; second, Śikhin Buddha; third, Viśvabhū Buddha;... [and so forth].
1. Buddha Krakucchanda; 2. Buddha Kanakamuni; 3. Buddha Kāśyapa; 4. Buddha Śākyamuni.

These constitute the seven Buddhas, comprising the final three Buddhas of the Thousand Buddhas of the *Bhadrakalpa* (Auspicious Aeon) and the first four Buddhas of the Thousand Buddhas of the *Vibhadrakalpa* (Present Aeon). According to this present sutra, Śākyamuni himself says:
Now, among those who preach the Dharma under my guidance, he is likewise foremost; thus, by taking the seven Buddhas as the past,
Śākyamuni as the present, and Maitreya and other Buddhas as the future,
one should point to the latter four Buddhas of the *Prabhūtaratna* Kalpa (*Kṛta-yuga*) and the first three Buddhas of the *Bhadrakalpa* as the "seven Buddhas of the past," as found in various texts.
In some instances, Śākyamuni is included with the preceding six Buddhas to constitute the "Seven Buddhas of the Past";
this is likely because the *Jiezhang jing* was compiled after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni, and thus he was also categorized as a Buddha of the past.
△ Second, the bestowal of predictions (vyākaraṇa). Part one: clarifying the perfection of causes.
Gradually, he will fulfill the path of a bodhisattva.
△ Second, the fulfillment of the fruit:
After immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he shall become a Buddha, a World-Honored One and Teacher of Gods and Humans, in this very land.
△ Third, the Pure Land of the Country of Threefold Clarity (Samvidyā). First, the Great Adornment and Purity of that Land of Clarity:
its Buddha is like the sands of the Ganges [as previously described], until humans and devas meet and are able to see one another.

Regarding the phrase "the ground is as level as a palm," the sutra simply says "as a palm" and does not specify "the palm of a hand. Since the palm of a hand is not level, this cannot be what is being cited;
rather, there is a stone at the bottom of the ocean called "Palm" (Kara), which does not have even a speck of dust's worth of unevenness—it must be like this "ocean-palm.
Furthermore, the *Bhadrakalpika Sūtra* clearly explains it as being like the palm of a Buddha’s hand; it is not a citation from that source.
Tongren (Companionship) is the palm of the hand. △ Second, it clarifies that this is purely a path of goodness.
There are no evil paths, nor are there women; all sentient beings are born by transformation and are free from lustful desire.

Regarding those realms where there are no evil destinies (*apāya*), there are likewise distinctions and differences among them: some are places where, in the absence of women, there are certainly no evil destinies;
others are places where, even though women exist, there are no evil destinies—such as the land of Akṣobhya Buddha, where although women exist, there is no female activity;
and the land of Amitāyus Buddha, where both [the presence of women and the existence of evil destinies] are entirely absent. △ Third, the explanation of merit and wisdom.
Fully endowed [with these], he attains great supernormal powers and his body emits radiance. (Up to: First, the food of dharma-joy; second, the food of dhyāna-delight.
The ninth chapter of the *Candragarbha-sūtra*, "The Sūtra on the Food of Dharma, the Food of Joy, and the Food of Dhyāna," states in its general summary: "Dharma-joy and dhyāna..."
Regarding the distinct categories of joy, there should be three kinds of sublime delights. What is called "Dharma-food" refers to hearing the Dharma;
as in the realm of Sukhāvatī, those born there of inferior grade constantly hear the Dharma being preached by Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara.
"Joy-food" refers to the joy experienced upon hearing the Dharma: while actually hearing it belongs to Dharma-food, the joy that arises after having heard it is Joy-food. As for "Meditation-food":
This means that he sustains himself through the dharma of dhyāna and does not require material food; alternatively, the dharma itself is joy.
△ Fourth, it clarifies that his disciples are numerous:

there are immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* thousands of myriads of koṭis [of them], up to those possessing the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the three knowledges (*trividyā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
△ Fifth, the accomplishment of the merit of the five precepts.
The Buddha-land is adorned and accomplished with such immeasurable merits as these.
The *Candragarbha-sūtra*, fascicle 5, clarifies that each of the ten wholesome actions possesses ten merits; first, by not killing, one obtains ten merits.
First, one attains fearlessness toward all sentient beings; second, one attains a mind of great compassion for sentient beings;
third, one severs evil habitual karma; fourth, one has few illnesses; fifth, one enjoys a long life; sixth, one is protected by non-human beings;
seventh, one has no bad dreams; eighth, one has no enemies; ninth, one does not fear the evil realms; and tenth, after death, one is reborn in a good realm, and later, when becoming a Buddha—
The country shall be free from weapons of harm, and its inhabitants shall enjoy longevity; furthermore, by the tenth [vow], through the attainment of right view, they shall obtain ten merits:
first, a nature that is single-minded, gentle, and virtuous, up to the tenth, being reborn in the good realms at death.
When one becomes a Buddha, the people of the country shall possess correct faith—this is the adornment of immeasurable merit. △ Fourth, the name of the eon of the land.
The kalpa was named Treasure Radiance (*Ratnaprabhāsa*), and the land was named Well-Purified (*Suvimala*).
△ Fifth, the Buddha’s lifespan:
that Buddha’s life span lasted for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
△ The six dharmas shall endure for a long time;
the Dharma shall endure for a very long time.
△ Seventh, making offerings to the śarīra.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, stupas made of the seven treasures will arise and fill his country.
△ Second, the verse summary has two parts: first, the verse summary of the revelation of origins; second, the general revelation of the origins of all śrāvakas, which has five parts.
First, the heading indicating the inconceivable Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O bhikṣus, listen attentively! The path traversed by the Son of the Buddha, through his skillful mastery of expedient means, is inconceivable."
This indicates that once the disciples have completed their inconceivable practice, they attain the method of manifesting traces. △ Second, explaining the reason for manifesting traces:
Knowing that the multitudes delight in inferior teachings and fear great wisdom, the bodhisattvas accordingly manifest as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
△ The third [section]: The manifestation of traces for the benefit of others.
By means of countless skillful expedients (*upāya*), he transforms all classes of sentient beings (until) gradually causing them to become Buddhas.

To those with small desires, he demonstrates the seeking of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); to those who are indolent, he demonstrates the retrogression from the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). This is accomplished through the exercise of skillful means.
This leads those who practice according to reality and transforms all sentient beings, gradually causing them to become Buddhas. △ Fourth, explaining the inner concealment and outer manifestation:
"Inner concealment of Bodhisattva practices, outer manifestation as a Śrāvaka" (up to) "using skillful means to deliver sentient beings."
It is not only that he manifests as a śrāvaka; he also manifests as a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) and as an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) of the three poisons.
Śāriputra’s manifestation of anger, Nanda’s manifestation of greed, and Devadatta’s manifestation of delusion are all of this same category. △ Fifth, a brief indication to suppress the extensive.
If I were to fully describe the various manifestations of my transformations, sentient beings who hear them would harbor doubts and confusion.
△ Second, the distinct manifestation of the traces of fulfilling vows, consisting of two parts: first, a verse revealing the past origin.
Now this Pūrṇa, from the time of a thousand billion Buddhas in the past (until now), has purified his own Buddha-field.
△ Second, the verse on the causes of practice throughout the three periods of time:
In the future as well, he will make offerings to immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas (until now) and achieve all-encompassing wisdom.
△ Second, the prediction in verse, in four parts: First, the perfection of causes.
Making offerings to all Tathāgatas and upholding the treasury of the Dharma-jewel.
△ Second, the fulfillment of the fruit.
Thereafter, he attained Buddhahood, and his name was called Dharmaprabhāsa (Dharma-Illumination).
△ Third, the names of the eon and the land:
that land was named Sunirmala (Excellently Pure), composed of the seven precious jewels; the eon was named Ratnaprabhāsa (Jewel-Illumination).
△ Four verses on the purity of the land.
From "The assembly of bodhisattvas is exceedingly numerous, their count being immeasurable billions" (up to) "I now speak only briefly.
△ Second, the bestowal of predictions upon the twelve hundred; first, the initial request for instruction.
At that time, [the thought occurred to] the twelve hundred arhats: "Would it not be wonderful if we were like the other great disciples?
These twelve hundred persons had all already attained the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle; because they were no longer afflicted by the delusions of views and thought, their minds were autonomous.
Having heard the Dharma preached during the three turnings of the wheel and having seen the prediction of enlightenment for Pūrṇa, they were filled with joy and desired [to attain the same].
Please take note. △ Second, granting the prediction (vyākaraṇa), in two parts: First, the prose section, in three parts; first, the general prediction for the twelve hundred.
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in their minds... [up to] the prediction of *samyaksambodhi*.
△ Second, the specific bestowal of the prediction upon Kauṇḍinya.
[The text states: "Among this assembly, my great disciple... (up to) the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Because Kauṇḍinya was the first to realize the Way and occupied the position of the foremost elder, he is specifically granted this prediction. *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) asks: If...

Question: Why is the first cycle of teaching not recorded at the very beginning? Answer: If we consider the distinction between the actual practice (*samyak-pratipatti*) and the provisional practice (*upāya-caryā*), the two beginnings differ.
In the case of actual practice, because Śāriputra was the first to establish the great connection (*mahā-saṃbandha*), he attained realization first during the first cycle;

because Cunda was the first to establish the small connection (*hīna-saṃbandha*), he attained realization first in the Deer Park. If we consider the provisional practice intended to lead sentient beings toward aspiration, there are two [beginnings].
Since the intentions of each are different, the methods for manifesting traces cannot be standardized. △ Third, the individual bestowal upon the five hundred people:
those five hundred arhats (up to) all share the same title, named Puming (Universal Radiance).
Kālodāyin—here translated as "Black Radiance" (Heigu) or "Coarse Black"—is so called because his complexion was black yet radiant.

Cūḍapanthaka—alternatively called Zhouli—is here translated as "Born by the Side of the Great Road. The *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sutra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha) states that his mother followed her husband to another country;
after a long time she became pregnant, and as her delivery drew near, she thought of returning home. While traveling halfway there, she gave birth.
In this manner, the son gave birth to two children twice;
he distinguished them by their size—the elder being Cūḍapanthaka and the younger being Śāradvatīputra (also called Panthaka or Panthaka). [The disciple] asked:
"I previously saw the Buddha grant sequential predictions to one thousand two hundred disciples; why now does he grant a prediction only for five hundred?"
The "one thousand two hundred who receive the prediction" refers to these five hundred being included within the number one thousand two hundred;
for in the final verse of the gāthā, "Kāśyapa, you already know," etc., one and a half lines collectively grant the prediction to seven hundred, thus making it one thousand two hundred.
△ Second, the verses in praise, which have two parts: first, the prediction for Cunda and the five hundred.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya... [and so forth] ...the duration of his lifespan in kalpas shall be as described above."
△ Second, the general bestowal of predictions upon all the śrāvakas.
"Kāśyapa, you already know the five hundred masters... (up to) "...you should proclaim it for them.
The first two lines conclude the previous section on the five hundred who have received their predictions; the following two lines are a verse summarizing the seven hundred.

It says that the rest of the assembly of śrāvakas shall likewise be so; furthermore, the next two lines are intended for those not present in this assembly, so that Kāśyapa may proclaim [the teaching] on their behalf, hence it says: "For those who are not in this assembly, you should proclaim it for them.
Later, in the *Dhāraṇī-parivarta*, it says: "I have previously spoken in general that all śrāvakas have already received their predictions."
This specifically indicates that the current one and a half verses are not merely intended for the instruction of the seven hundred śrāvakas.

△ Third, the acceptance and understanding [of the teaching], in two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. First, the scriptural narrator describes their joy, in two parts: first, rejoicing at having attained understanding now, thus being joyful;
first, clarifying the inner heart’s rejoicing.
At that time, the five hundred arhats, having received their predictions in the presence of the Buddha, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
Part Two: Manifesting Reverence through External Form.
They immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, and prostrated themselves, touching their heads to his feet.
△ Second, reproaching oneself for not having understood previously.
This is the repentance and self-reproach.
△ Second, personally recounting one's realization. Part One: The Dharma-exposition. Sub-part One: Repenting of being satisfied with minor attainments.
“World-Honored One, we have always harbored this thought, believing that we had already attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

This was our remorseful confession for having been deluded in the past, being content with a minor attainment and failing to seek the Great [Vehicle]. △ Second, reproaching their dull faculties for the difficulty of awakening.
Now I have come to know it.

This reproof for my dull faculties shows that my initial awakening was not early enough; I now realize that what was previously known as "small" is not ultimate, while the "great" is the true reality.
△ Second, the illustrative explanation has two parts: first, the brief illustration; second, the initial brief citation of the analogy.
They are like those who lack wisdom.
△ Second, explaining the meaning of "lack of wisdom":
Why is this? We ought to attain the wisdom of a Tathāgata, yet we instead consider our own meager wisdom to be sufficient.
△ Second, the actual parable, in two parts. First, the opening of the parable. First, the analogy of the poor man intoxicated with wine.
First, the analogy of the kinsman tying the jewel in his garment. "World-Honored One, it is as if there were a person (up to) who tied it inside his garment and departed."
The parable of the tied jewel illustrates the Prince’s formation of karmic affinity. "Suppose there were a person" refers to those of the Two Vehicles (the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*).
"A close friend" is the Sixteenth Prince from former times. "The house" refers to the Mahāyāna teaching as one's home.

"Drunk and lying down" signifies that at that time, the great capacity [for enlightenment] was temporarily aroused and ignorance was temporarily suppressed, thereby attaining [a state of realization].
Upon hearing the sutra, there is a slight internal understanding, like arriving at the home of a close friend;
yet because ignorance is heavy, one again loses this way, like falling asleep after drinking wine. This "intoxication" has two meanings: first, heavy intoxication, where one is entirely unaware;

second, light intoxication, where one perceives slightly but soon forgets—this too is called non-awakening. Although there are these two meanings, it ultimately results in the binding of the pearl, which is like poison.
"Beating the drum for official business that ought to be carried out" means that when the Prince perceives opportunities arising elsewhere, he approaches and responds to those conditions;
thus it is said "it ought to be carried out. To propagate the Dharma and transform others is not a private matter, hence it is called "official business.

"The priceless jewel" refers to the jewel of the wisdom of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the real mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle. "Tying it within his garment" refers to the patience of enduring shame and disgrace.
That which can obstruct ugliness and anger, as well as prevent external evils, is the outer garment; the mind of faith and joy that internally enwraps the roots of goodness is the inner garment.
At that time, hearing the Dharma and giving rise to a slight faith and joy is the "understanding cause" (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*), which is the seed of wisdom and aspiration.

Regarding the statement in the *Wu miao le* (The Sublime Joy) that "the jewel of true suchness-wisdom" is mentioned, this refers to the teaching according to the stages (*yijiao*); it is by means of the understanding cause...

Because this teaching for binding the jewel elucidates the principle, it is called the "Teaching of True Suchness" (*tathatā*); because it is the functional application of wisdom, it is called the "Jewel of Wisdom.
△ Second, the analogy of being drunk and lying down without awareness:
That person, intoxicated and lying down, was entirely unaware of anything.
This refers to being weary and regressing midway through the journey, failing to receive the Great Dharma;
to lie drunk and unaware is for the mind of ignorance to be heavy, such that one subsequently fails to remember. △ Third, the analogy of rising and wandering about.
Having arisen, they travel on to other lands; upon obtaining even a small amount, they consider it sufficient.

This refers to those who, having received the intermediate teaching, are subsequently led by the minor teachings of the Three Vehicles. Because their roots of goodness are about to sprout and they grow weary of suffering while seeking happiness, it is said that "having arisen, they travel on.
Yet, being shrouded by ignorance, they do not know how to turn back toward the source to seek the Great [Vehicle].
Because of clothing and food, it is said that one goes to another country to seek the clothing and food of the Hīnayāna.
If one regards the Buddha and Māra in relation to each other, the realm of birth and death (saṃsāra) is the "other country" and the Dharma of the Buddha is one's own country.

Regarding the Great and Small Vehicles, the Hīnayāna has not yet escaped birth and death and thus remains an "other country," whereas the Mahāyāna eternally escapes birth and death and is therefore one's own country.
This illustrates that one has ultimately returned to the source of one’s own country, yet is clearly seen as having turned one’s back on the land of the Mahāyāna to go to a land of the Hīnayāna;
unaware that one could obtain what is needed from the jewel, one instead seeks to support oneself through hired labor, and upon receiving a day’s wage, considers it sufficient for its meagerness.
△ Second, the analogy of being awakened by a close friend, which has three parts: first, the reprimand.
Later, a relative encounters him and asks: "What are you doing for food and clothing? and so forth, even to this point.
This reprimand serves as an analogy for the aforementioned movement of attachment and the arising of doubt. △ Second, showing the jewel.
"In the past, I wished to enable you to attain peace and happiness... (until) to seek one's livelihood [thereby] is truly foolish.
This indicates the analogy of the jewel as the causal conditions from a previous life. "In such-and-such a year, month, and day" refers to the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
△ Third, the exhortation to trade.
"You may now trade this jewel for whatever you require; it shall always fulfill your wishes, and you will never lack for anything.
This analogy of trading encourages one who has received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states:

"Although the pearl is worth countless riches, it must be traded before its utility can be realized; likewise, although internal understanding is ultimately perfected, it must rely on past seeds [of cultivation]."
It is easy to manifest [the results] because understanding one thing in the past leads to understanding all things, and practicing one action now leads to practicing all actions;
yet, as the essence of the jewel is inexhaustible and its manifestations are infinite, one must listen further and cultivate further to reveal the jewel’s functional power.
As it says in the *Avataṃsaka*, one obtains the maṇi-jewel, but only after ten kinds of polishing can it rain down treasures.

Only when one's understanding and practice correspond can one be worthy of the Buddha’s prediction; from this point onward, one possesses the robe of *śānti-kṣānti* (the patience of tranquility), the food of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, and the immeasurable jewels of self-cultivation and the transformation of others, reaching a state of effortless spontaneity where both self and others are inexhaustible.
△ Second, the combined analogy, in two parts: First, the combined analogy for the poor man drinking wine, in three parts: First, the combined analogy for the relative and friend binding [him].
The analogy of the jewel:
The Buddha was likewise like this when he was a bodhisattva, teaching and transforming us so that we might give rise to the mind of omniscience.
△ Second, the combined analogy of being intoxicated and unaware.
Yet they soon fall into forgetfulness, unaware and unconscious of it.
△ Third, the analogy of rising together and wandering forth:
Having attained the path of Arhatship, they consider themselves to have reached extinction (*nirvāṇa*); yet their livelihood is difficult, and they are content with what little they obtain.
△ Second, the analogy of awakening a close friend. Part one: the application of the reprimand.
"The vow for omniscience still remains and has not been lost... what you have attained is not ultimate cessation."
△ 2. Combined demonstration of the jewel:
"I have long caused you all to plant the roots of goodness for Buddhahood... yet you believed that you had truly attained extinction.
△ 3. Combined exhortation to trade:
“World-Honored One, it is only now that I truly know [you] to be a bodhisattva... [I am] filled with great joy at having attained what I never had before.
△ Second, the verses in praise, which are twofold: first, the verses praising the internal attainment of understanding; second, the verses celebrating the joy. First, the verses celebrating the joy.
At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Having heard the voice of the unsurpassed, peaceful prediction of our own enlightenment, we experience a joy never before known; we pay homage to the Buddha of immeasurable wisdom."
△ Second, the verses on repentance and reproach:
Now, before the World-Honored One, he personally repents of all his transgressions.
△ Second, the verses on personally recounting his realization, divided into two parts; first, the verses on the Dharma-exposition.
Regarding the attainment of a small portion of nirvana within the immeasurable Buddha-treasure:

this verse summarizes the aforementioned "being satisfied with a small attainment. II. The second part, the verse on the parable, has two sections: first, the verse briefly presenting the parable; second, the verse briefly presenting the illustrative analogy.
(First, the verse briefly presenting the parable:)
Like ignorant and foolish people.
△ Second, a verse explaining the meaning of ignorance:
they then consider themselves sufficient.
△ Second, the two verses that correctly present the parable. Part one: the verse that opens the parable. Part one: the verse on losing the jewel without knowing it.
For example, a poor person goes to the house of a kinsman... [and finds] a priceless jewel.

The "delicacies" (yāṃshàn) are likened to what was first heard from the Buddha of Great Pervasion regarding skillful means; the "tying of the jewel" is likened to the prince’s secret recitation, which subsequently establishes the wondrous and joyful great conditions.
It says: "One should know that the poor man was originally already intoxicated, and further received the delicacies;
having consumed them, he lay down. The aids to the Path of the Three Teachings are like the delicacies, which further employ diverse skillful means to assist in manifesting the [Fourth] Stage.

*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Ten: "The Dharma-Teacher."
This chapter clarifies five kinds of Dharma-preachers: first, those who receive and uphold; second, those who read; third, those who recite;

fourth, those who explain and interpret; and fifth, those who transcribe. The *Mahā-śāstra* clarifies six kinds of Dharma-preachers: first, receiving through the power of faith; second, upholding through the power of mindfulness;

third, reading by examining the text; fourth, reciting so as not to forget; fifth, proclaiming for others as explanation; and sixth, [upholding] the scriptures of the sages, which are difficult [to master].
Regarding the explanation: the combined practice of receiving and upholding (*udgrahaṇa*) constitutes one; the combined explanation (*vyākhyāna*) constitutes one;

recitation (*vācana*) constitutes two; and writing (*lekhana*) constitutes five. In a specific sense, "receiving and upholding" and "writing" refer to one's own practice (*sva-pratipatti*), while "explaining" refers to transforming others (*para-pariṇāmana*).
In a general sense, if one follows these five dharmas as one's own standard, then all five are one's own practice; if one teaches them to others, they constitute the transformation of others.

The five categories of Dharma are all for the purpose of transforming others and serving as one's own guide; thus they are collectively termed "disciples. Because they transform others, they are collectively termed "Dharma-teachers" (*dharmabhāṇaka*).
Following this general sense, it is called the "Chapter on the Dharma-Teacher. "Dharma" refers to a standard or rule; "teacher" (*śāstṛ*) refers to an instructor or craftsman.
Although the Dharma provides a standard, its essence does not propagate itself; it depends upon people. Therefore, these five categories all transmit the Sūtras.

All [of these] are called "masters" because they uphold the Dharma to perfect their own practice; since they take the wondrous Dharma as their master and have achieved mastery over that wondrous Dharma and its sublime practice, they are called "Dharma-masters.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of persons who can instruct and mold others with the wondrous Dharma;
because they uphold the Dharma and look to it as their master, they are called "Dharma-masters. All these various interpretations are based on the teaching of the Perfect (Yuan) Vehicle.

This refers to *nirvāṇa*. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts, various explanations—whether gradual or sudden—are all accompanied by skillful means (*upāya*) so that they may be easily accepted with faith.
In the *Anantamukha-sūtra*, the one gives rise to the immeasurable, and the immeasurable returns to the one; this too is easy to believe.

Now, in the *Dharmaparyāya* [the Lotus Sutra], regarding the Dharma, all distinctions are integrated and unified into one; regarding the persons, both teacher and disciple, as well as their original and manifested forms, are likewise unified.
Because all these people and dharmas have long since become entirely different from those of the past, they are difficult to believe and understand.

When faced with such formidable matters, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has already been preached; since the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* follows after it, it can then be believed. The *Myōraku-ki* states:

"Being at the vanguard" means that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is like a great army that is difficult to break through, while the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is like the remaining forces that are not so difficult. At the beginning, one must first face the vanguard.
This is not easy to do.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, this sutra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas; it must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others.
That which is called the "secret and essential treasury" is "secret" because it is hidden and not spoken of, and it is "essential" because it encompasses all dharmas as True Suchness (tathatā).

The true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is a treasury that encompasses all things and cannot be distributed; its Dharma is subtle and difficult to believe, and it can only be transmitted to those of profound wisdom.
Those without wisdom do not believe and instead slander it, thereby incurring sin; therefore, it must not be spoken of recklessly.
That which has been protected by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, has never been revealed since ancient times.

As for that which has never been revealed since ancient times: it is not taught within the Tripiṭaka that those of the Two Vehicles can attain Buddhahood, nor is the relationship between teacher and disciple, or their original and manifested traces, clarified therein.
Although the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras do speak of the treasury of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), they have likewise not [yet revealed this].
The teaching that the five vehicles attain Buddhahood has not yet revealed their origins or manifested their fundamental nature;

because the various sutras concerning the sudden and gradual teachings have not yet been harmonized, they are called "secret. This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* fully expounds the Dharma previously kept secret;
it is thus the opening of the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*), and it is itself the secret treasury. This secret treasury was guarded from of old, and is now finally revealed and proclaimed.
Furthermore, regarding this sutra, even while the Tathāgata is currently present in the world, there are many who harbor resentment and jealousy; how much more so after his parinirvāṇa?
Although the Tathāgata has been in the world for over forty years—during which time there have been many who harbor resentment and jealousy—he has not yet preached it immediately. Now, although...
When [the Buddha] was about to preach, five thousand [monks] immediately withdrew from their seats. If this was so even during the Buddha’s own lifetime, how much more so will it be in the future?
The principle is that those who are difficult to transform [will not remain]. *Miaole* says: "The Tathāgata addresses resentment and jealousy as follows:

harboring past evils is called 'resentment' (*yuan*); disparaging present goodness is called 'jealousy' (*ji*). Those whose obstructions have not yet been removed are termed 'resentful,' while those who do not rejoice in hearing [the teaching] are termed 'jealous. Now, this is discussed comprehensively."
In the Trace Gate (Jimen), the five thousand [monks] who departed out of dull-wittedness and envy toward the two vehicles and bodhisattvas are not yet sufficient grounds for reproach;

however, in the Root Gate (Benmen), those among the bodhisattvas who delight in proximity to [the Buddha’s] realization act as envious rivals, and since the entire assembly does not recognize this, how can it not be considered strange?
Now, while remaining within the scope of the Trace, the underlying intent can be discerned: the principle lies in clarifying that those who are difficult to transform [are the ones in question].
The intent of this principle is to make known that sentient beings are difficult to transform. △ Second, praising by way of persons:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa... [they] shall have their heads stroked by the hand of the Tathāgata."
This is a praise based on the person. When this Dharma resides in a person, that person becomes noble and honored.

"Clothed by the Tathāgata" means that if one can uphold and expound this sutra, one is practicing and studying the Great Patience; this constitutes being "clothed by the Tathāgata," which corresponds to what was stated above regarding the "Tathāgata’s adornment.
"Protected by the Buddha's mindfulness" means that true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is the Buddha, and true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*) is [the Buddha].
If you revere the true reality (*dharmatā*) and give rise to true wisdom, you will be protected and remembered by all Buddhas.

The four kinds of faith constitute the power of faith (namely, faith in the Three Jewels and the precepts); the four great vows constitute the power of aspiration; and great wisdom constitutes the power of roots of goodness.

As for faith, one believes in the principle, and this principle is the Dharma-body. Aspiration is the establishment of practice, and this practice is liberation. When the roots of goodness are firm, they are difficult to uproot.
To move this is itself Prajñā; one should know that these three powers are the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
When a beginner dwells herein, they are no different from a Buddha; therefore, it is called "dwelling together with the Tathāgata.

As for "rubbing the head," it means that this person, through the power of their vows, the power of goodness, and their own practice of the provisional and the real, acts as the stimulus and response. This "stimulus and response" is what is meant by the "head."

Coming now, by means of the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate for the sake of transforming others, he uses his hands to open up the heads of those before him—the heads representing their own practice of the provisional and ultimate—so that the resonance between teacher and disciple may meet;
thus it is said, "rubbing the head" (*mōtóu*), which is precisely the bestowing of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). The *Myōraku* [Commentary] states:

"Those who, with the initial mind, dwell herein," etc.; this refers to what is symbolized as previously explained regarding the "bearing of the burden. Were it not so, it would merely be the physical body.
What benefit is there in principle for sharing a lodging or even massaging one's head with impure substances?
△ Third, praising by way of location: "Wherever the Medicine King [is], he is close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
This is a praise based on location. This Dharma exists in specific places; indeed, those locations are noble.

Whether it be the place where the Buddha was born, attained enlightenment, turned the wheel of the Dharma, or entered *nirvāṇa*—any place where the Dharma King has traveled should have a stūpa erected.

This sutra is the birthplace of the Dharma-body, the site where the Way was attained, the very essence of the turning of the wheel of the Dharma, and the cave of Great *Nirvāṇa*. Wherever this sutra resides...

Regarding the statement that one need only perform offerings at the stūpa without needing to enshrine śarīra, the *Śāstra* (Vyākhyā) says: "Crushed bone is the śarīra of the birth-body (*janma-kāya*);
a scripture is the śarīra of the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*). This sutra is the śarīra of the dharma-body; there is no need to further enshrine the śarīra of the birth-body.
Both the birth-body and the dharma-body have both complete and crushed forms, as can be understood from the *Myōraku-ki* (Record of Wondrous Joy).
The "fragmented physical body" refers to that of Śākyamuni, which was eight *hu* and four *dou*;

the "complete physical body" refers to that of Prabhūtaratna, whose entire body remains within the jeweled stupa. The "fragmented Dharma-body" refers to the various provisional teachings; the "complete Dharma-body" refers to the single reality (*eka-tattva*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The detailed distinctions among the four teachings and five periods may be seen therein. △ Fourth, [the classification] by way of cause.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, there are many, whether householders or renunciants, who are able to skillfully practice the bodhisattva path.

This praises [the practitioner] in terms of the cause. If one has not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path, having received the three preceding teachings, one is unable to deliver others with skill;
however, if such a person hears this sutra, they immediately enter the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), which is called "skillful delivery. Skillful delivery constitutes skillful practice.

Furthermore, Miaole (Wondrous Joy) states that "skillful deliverance" is as explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation), which cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding the analogy of the two physicians, the skillful and the unskillful. It says:
"Using needles and medicinal herbs is called 'unskillful deliverance,' while employing incantations and arts is called 'skillful deliverance.

The Śrāvakas' transformation of people through ascetic practices (*dhūta*) and so forth is called 'unskillful deliverance'; the Bodhisattvas' transformation of people through contemplating all... [the passage continues].

The reality of the Dharma is truly skillful in delivering others; while the great treatises generally regard the Mahāyāna approach as skillful, here it is specifically designated as "skillful" by virtue of its single reality.
△ Fifth, praising the five fruits: first, clarifying the proximate.

If there are sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way (up to) attaining proximity to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you should know that those who will certainly attain proximity to the fruit of *saṃbodhi* are called "proximate stages" (*upaniṣad*) within the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukha-caryā*).
This fruit of *bodhi* has as its essence the sphere of knowledge and vision of the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom; it is of two kinds: first, the initial...
The Bodhicitta of the mind is the first stage (Prathama-bhūmi), while the Bodhicitta of the subsequent mind is the state of wondrous enlightenment (Sudurjaya-bhūmi).
What is here called "near" refers precisely to being near the Bodhicitta of the first stage. △ Second, the opening of the analogy.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is like a person who, parched with thirst, requires water [and so forth]. His mind becomes resolute, knowing that water must be near. This has two explanations:
first, according to the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); second, according to the gate of teaching (*deśanā*). Regarding the gate of contemplation:

the minds of sentient beings are possessed of all afflictions (*kleśa*), which is likened to a high plateau. Cultivating the wisdom of contemplation is likened to digging; only then does one realize the flavor of principle (*tattva-rasa*). As for...

If one attains pure water, it is like relying on general contemplation (*sāmānyālambana*) of the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*): just as when dry earth is seen to become moist soil and mud, one knows that water must be near;

seeing the Truth (*satyadarśana*) is like attaining pure water. If one relies on specific contemplation (*viśeṣālambana*), first entering from the conventional into emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one sees only emptiness and does not see non-emptiness;
this severs the delusions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*), which is like digging into dry earth where the water is still far off.
Next, emerging from emptiness (*śūnyatā*) through the provisional (*prajñapti*), one first realized it was not provisional and now realizes it is not empty.

By means of these two contemplations, one enters the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), whereby one can suppress ignorance (*avidyā*). Turning the vision toward the moist soil, the water is near; the attainment of clear water represents the first stage (*bhūmi*).

If one relies on the perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*), the Middle Way is neither empty nor provisional, yet it illuminates both emptiness and the provisional as they gradually approach [realization].
Having exhausted the four stages of the moist mud and having subdued ignorance, one attains a semblance of the perfect understanding of the Middle Way;

thus it is said to be "like mud. If one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), awakening to the true understanding of the Middle Way, one then shatters ignorance, just as when the mud settles and clarifies, the Middle Way becomes visible like clear water.
Next, regarding the gate of doctrinal teaching (*yāna*): "earth" is a metaphor for the scriptures and teachings, while "water" serves as a simile.
The Middle Way teachings explain the Middle Way like soil containing water; the Tripitaka teachings have not yet explained the Middle Way, being like dry soil.
The *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings, accompanied by skillful means, speak of the meaning of the Middle Way like seeing moist soil.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* teachings directly and openly reveal the Unsurpassed Way, like seeing mud. Because of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* teachings, hearing arises.
Contemplation and cultivation are themselves the realization of the Middle Way; it is like obtaining pure water and wondrous joy.

Regarding this analogy, one must employ both teaching and contemplation in tandem to fully exhaust its principle. Teaching and contemplation are cultivated together to mutually manifest their subtlety; if either teaching or contemplation is biased, both will lack power.
First, regarding contemplation: first, there is a general clarification of contemplation. Although the words apply broadly to all meanings, they pertain here specifically to the Perfect [Teaching].

Relying on supernormal powers, one contemplates the lower stages and traverses the teachings to clarify that the principles of contemplating and analyzing the essence are identical; therefore, the three baskets (Tripitaka) are omitted.
△ Third, the combined analogy: "The Bodhisattva is also like this" [up to] "one must know that they have drawn near to Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."
To obtain hearing, reflection, and cultivation within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes the perfect contemplation of the three wisdoms, which alone can approach the fruit;
this is not the case for the hearing, reflection, and cultivation found within the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, Vaipulya, or Prajñāpāramitā. △ Fourth, the explanation of "approaching."
Why is this? (Up to: "Now, the Buddha’s teaching transforms and brings to fulfillment the bodhisattvas, revealing it to them.
This explains the meaning of "attaining proximity. "All bodhisattvas" clarifies that within all teachings, they represent the provisional cause;
"triple awakening" (*tri-sambodhi*) clarifies that what all bodhisattvas attain is the provisional fruit. Both this provisional cause and provisional fruit...
To "be subsumed under this sutra" means that just as all soil, whether dry or moist, depends upon water, so too is it said to be subsumed.

Regarding the "opening of the gate of skillful means": in the past, for the sake of the ultimate truth (the Real), provisional means were employed; because people did not know that these means were expedient, the gate of skillful means was closed.
Now, all are opened, for they are themselves the true nature of reality (the Real). Thus, the gate of skillful means is opened. Previously, all things were taught...
"How could worldly livelihoods and occupations ever have been skillful means? Now they are all opened up as being the true reality (*dharmatā*), without contradiction.
Previously, it was taught that the skillful means of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and its fruits were not even the gate of true reality;
how much less so could the skillful means of the Lesser Vehicle be this gate? Now they are all opened up as being the true reality, you."

That which they practice is the Bodhisattva path; their definitive understanding of the Śrāvaka Dharma is the king of all sūtras, causing all sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Not a single form or scent is not the Buddha-Dharma.
Had it not been opened, it would have remained deep, firm, profound, and remote, such that no one could reach it; now that it is opened, one immediately attains the vision.
Water has no dry soil. △ Fifth, the exclusion of those who are not [suitable vessels]:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are bodhisattvas who hear this Lotus Sūtra... (up to) you should know that these are persons of overweening pride."
If bodhisattvas or śrāvakas hear this teaching and become startled or doubtful, they are all like dry soil—not even moist soil, let alone water.
△ Second, showing the method and practice, in two parts: first, showing the method, in three parts; first, the heading.
“Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are good sons (or good daughters) [as far as] they should then extensively expound this sutra for the fourfold assembly.

The room, the robe, and the seat—these three are called the three guidelines. To propagate this sutra in the final age, one must necessarily rely on these three as one's own guidelines to guide others;
thus one will obtain great benefit. Cultivating unconditional compassion is entering the Tathāgata’s room; cultivating the patience of cessation is...”
To don the robe of the Tathāgata and cultivate emptiness within is to sit upon the seat of the Tathāgata. △ Second, the explanation:
"The chamber of the Tathāgata" refers to [all sentient beings]... up to "the seat of the Tathāgata," which is the emptiness of all phenomena.
The mind of compassion is the chamber of the Tathāgata. Because compassion covers all beings while returning the benefit to oneself, it is called a "chamber.
This means that through pity (*karuṇā*), one extracts all suffering—that is, the suffering of the four realms of existence, the three worlds, the two vehicles, and even bodhisattvas;
and through love (*maitrī*), one bestows all happiness—that is, the happiness of humans, devas, nirvāṇa, and eternal abiding. Therefore, compassion is the Tathāgata.
The chamber is the mind of gentle forbearance; this is the Tathāgata’s robe.

It is called a "robe" because it covers those evil obstructions and one's own ugliness—specifically, it covers the ugliness of the four abodes, ignorance, and nescience; thus, gentle forbearance is the Tathāgata’s robe.
Emptiness of phenomena is the Tathāgata’s seat: only by settling the mind in emptiness can one settle others; by settling others, one settles oneself.

It is called the "seat" because emptiness can extinguish all marks—namely, the extinction of the marks of existence in the triple world, the marklessness of the Two Vehicles, and the state of the Bodhisattva who is neither with marks nor without marks. Thus, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) is the Tathāgata’s seat.

Therefore, in benefiting sentient beings, compassion is primary; in engaging with the realm of existence, patience is the foundation; and in preaching the Dharma, it is through the extinction [of marks].
I have proclaimed and propagated the Great Teaching of the Three Dharmas for the sake of fundamental practice;
because it is the reliance of the world, one is called a Dharma Master. Question: For what reason is one called a Dharma Master by reference to these three dharmas? Answer:

To discuss this in terms of actual conduct, one must ascend the hall, adjust one’s robes, and take one’s seat before one can propagate the teaching; therefore, it refers to these three. Furthermore, compassion gives rise to all that is wholesome.
Gentle and mild, they ward off all unwholesome dharmas and empty away all marks. △ Third, the exhortation to practice:
Abiding therein, one should then, with a mind free from indolence, extensively proclaim this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The five kinds of Dharma-preachers employ these three methods as their own internal discipline; thus it is said they "abide therein. They employ them to transform others;
thus it is said, "thereafter, with a mind free from indolence," and so forth—this is an exhortation to practice.
Cultivating the Tathāgata’s chamber is great compassion. If considered from the perspective of identical essence, it is the Dharmakāya; if it covers sentient beings, it is liberation.
To be able to cause sentient beings to realize their identity with the same essence is precisely the cultivation of Prajñā. Regarding the Tathāgata’s robe:
if one considers that which is covered, it is the Dharmakāya; if one considers that which covers and adorns the body, it is the Patience of Quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*), which is Prajñā;
if one considers the harmonizing with light to benefit all beings, it is Vimukti (Liberation). Regarding the Tathāgata’s seat: if one considers...

That which is able to sit is *prajñā* (wisdom); that which is the seat upon which one sits is the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body); the harmonious union of body and seat is *vimukti* (liberation). As Miaole says:
"When these three dharmas are compared with one another, each possesses all three. Although they each possess them, they are merely a single 'three.
Since even this 'three' is not truly three, how could it be divided into nine? Thus, the bodhisattva constantly contemplates *nirvāṇa*."

Therefore, I exhort those who propagate the sutras to propagate it through contemplation; for without contemplating the mind that propagates, one cannot understand the principle of what is being propagated.
Thus, the Buddha allows such a person to enter my chamber, wear my robes, and sit upon my seat. If these three dharmas are absent, how can it be called "propagating the sutra"?

The stupa made of the seven treasures serves to symbolize the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and the seven noble riches (*saptadhanāni*).
As for "stupa" (*tā*), it refers to the realm of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), the locus upon which the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) relies.

Its height of five hundred *yojana*—equivalent to twenty thousand *li*—is intended to represent vertically the ten thousand practices of the causal stage and the ten thousand virtues of the resultant stage; thus, its height signifies the relationship from cause toward fruit.
That which is two hundred and fifty *yojana* wide is precisely ten thousand *li*; its horizontal manifestation of the adornment of myriad virtues is the broad meaning.
"Earth" refers to the ground of the mind of ignorance (*avidyā*). By means of that which has nothing to shatter, one shatters ignorance;

Regarding the "exquisite adornment," the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states that it explains the non-excess of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) in contrast to darkness and distraction;

The banners and streamers represent the supreme marks of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), while the hanging jeweled necklaces signify the merit of the forty stages (*bhūmi*).
The virtue above adorns the Dharma-body, while below it reaches out to sentient beings. The "ten billion jeweled bells" represent the eight tones and four types of eloquence.
The "fragrance emanating from all four sides" signifies that the wind of the Path of the Four Truths blows the fragrance of the four virtues.

Its height reaching as far as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings indicates the thorough exhaustion of the principles of the Four Truths. As the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states regarding the "hanging jewels" and so forth: these are the fruits resulting from the causal stage.
All virtues rely upon the myriad practices within the causal stage; because they are adorned, one is able to transform those below, just as ornaments hang down from a headpiece.

Sitting and relinquishing objective conditions is *dāna*; not transgressing by relinquishing objective conditions is *śīla*;
not allowing afflictions to arise within the sphere of experience is *kṣānti*; not abandoning the practice of non-attachment is *vīrya*; being heedful regarding all matters is *dhyāna*;
and the non-arising of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is *prajñā*. Furthermore, relinquishing the aggregates (*skandha*) is *dāna*... [not]... the aggregates.
To contemplate the aggregates (*skandha*) as such is *śīla*; to have no notion of a self within the aggregates is *kṣānti*; to give rise to the thought of enmity toward the aggregates is *vīrya*;
not being inflamed by the aggregates is *dhyāna*; and the ultimate abandonment of the aggregates is *prajñā*.

Furthermore, relinquishing the elements (*dhātu*) is *dāna*; not being disturbed or turbid regarding the elements is *śīla*; relinquishing the causes and conditions within the elements is *kṣānti*; and [the discernment of] the enumerations of the elements is...
Numerically relinquishing these is progress toward the *dhātu*; not giving rise to them is *dhyāna* within the *dhātu*; viewing them as like an illusion is *prajñā*.
Such as these are called the profound essential dharma of the ultimate skillful means (*paramārtha-upāya-kauśalya*) that can fulfill the six *pāramitās*;

There are three kinds of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*): first, the external protector; second, the fellow practitioner; and third, the instructor of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Regarding the external protector:

one does not discriminate between the "black" and the "white," but simply provides whatever is required for one's needs. Like a mother nourishing her child, or like a tigress carrying her cub, they manage these matters so that all is properly attended to.
Only those who have long practiced the Way are capable of acting as such; this is called the spiritual friend as external protector.
Regarding the second type of companion on the path: they encourage and inspire one another so that there is no dullness or distraction, and they advance daily with renewed vigor.

Regarding the term "external protection" (*bāhya-parigraha*): one's own body and mind are considered "internal," while the body and mind of others are considered "external";
because one is protected by these external factors, it is called "external protection. Regarding "practicing together" (*sahacara*): self and other mutually assist one another.
Because they initiate others and their conduct is identical, it is called "identical practice" (*samāna-pratipatti*).

As for "instruction" (*avavāda*), the proclamation of the sacred word is termed "teaching" (*śāsana*), while the guidance and admonition directed toward oneself is termed "instruction" (*avavāda*). The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Do not associate with evil friends or engage in affairs with fools; you should instead cultivate intimacy with virtuous friends and the wise. If...
Human beings are originally without evil; yet by associating with evil people, they will inevitably become evil themselves, and their ill repute will spread throughout the world.
A spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is the opposite of this; therefore, one should associate with them.

Those called the "four immeasurable minds" (*catur-apramāṇa*)—namely, loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—derive their names from their objects. Because the sentient beings who are the objects of focus are immeasurable, the mind that focuses upon them is likewise immeasurable.
Because it accords with infinite objects, it is called the "infinite mind" (*apramāṇa-citta*). First, regarding the infinite mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*):

the mind capable of bestowing happiness upon others is called the "mind of loving-kindness. When it is free from ill-will, resentment, and malice, and is vast, immeasurable, and pervades the ten directions, it is termed the "infinite mind of loving-kindness.
Second, regarding the infinite mind of compassion (*karuṇā-apramāṇa*): it is the mind capable of extracting the suffering of others.
The mind that is called compassion (*karuṇā*)—free from anger, resentment, and malice, vast and immeasurable, pervading the ten directions—is termed the "immeasurable mind of compassion.
As for the immeasurable mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā*): it is the state of rejoicing and generating a heart of gladness upon seeing others obtain happiness;
being free from anger, resentment, and malice, vast and immeasurable, it pervades the ten directions. This is termed [the immeasurable mind of sympathetic joy].

Regarding the four immeasurable minds of joy and equanimity: when one directs a mind toward others that is free from both hatred and attachment, it is called the "mind of equanimity" (*upekṣā-citta*).

When this state is free from anger, resentment, and affliction, and is vast, immeasurable, and pervades the ten directions, it is called the "immeasurable mind of equanimity" (*upekṣā-apramāṇa-citta*).
These four are also termed the "four immeasurable concentrations" (*catvāry apramāṇa-samādhayaḥ*). △ Second, clarifying the perfection of the fruit.

Through the gathering by the three types of beneficial conduct, the Bodhisattva gives rise to actions of body, speech, and mind as appropriate, enabling all sentient beings to each receive benefit.
Fourth is the gathering through common purpose (*samānārthatā*); herein, the Bodhisattva employs the clarity of the Dharma-eye.

this inconceivable mountain and sea remain exactly as they were, yet the assembly does not see them. It is simply a transformation of perception.
This does not mean that the substance itself is altered; for since Mañjuśrī did not depart for that land, it was simultaneously defiled and purified.

The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, Chapter Fourteen: The Practices Leading to Peaceful Abiding.
The explanation of this chapter has three parts: first, based on the matter; second, following the text; and third, the dharma-gate. Regarding the explanation based on the matter:
because the body is free from danger, the mind is at peace; because the mind is free from sorrow and affliction, there is joy. When the body and mind are peaceful and joyful, one is able to progress;

therefore, it is called "Peaceful and Joyful Practice" (*anurakṣita-caryā*). Regarding the explanation following the text: by donning the robe of the Tathāgata, the Dharma-body is settled and enters [into realization].
The "Tathāgata’s chamber" refers to the liberation of the mind; "sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat" refers to advancing with the guidance of *prajñā*.
This is merely an explanation based on the text of the "Chapter on the Dharma Master. If one were to base it on the text of this specific chapter:
because he dwells in the ground of patience, his body is at peace and not violent; because he contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena with a joyful mind, his practice advances.
Regarding the explanation of the Dharma-door of "Peaceful and Joyful Practice" (*Anraku-gyō*): "Peace" (*an*) means immovability; "Joy" (*raku*) means non-reception;

"Practice" (*gyō*) means non-action. As for "peace" being immovability: it refers to abiding correctly in the Middle Way, such that one cannot be moved by the two extremes—the duality of birth-and-death within the six realms, or the emptiness of the two vehicles' *nirvāṇa*.
As for "joy" being non-reception: non-reception is precisely non-attachment.

Regarding "receiving": The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Characteristics of Practice," states: "One does not receive even practice" (for the practitioner practices *prajñā*, and because the nature of *prajñā* is empty, one does not receive anything).
One does not receive non-practice; one does not receive both practice and non-practice; one does not receive neither practice nor non-practice.
One does not even receive this "non-receiving. If there is receiving, there is suffering; if there is no receiving, there is no suffering.
The absence of suffering and pleasure is called the practice of great bliss; it is called the practice of non-practice. If there is that which is received, there is that which is practiced;

if there is no reception, there is no practice. Because one does not practice the conduct of ordinary beings and does not practice the conduct of noble ones, it is said that one practices through non-practice.
This is the Middle Way; therefore, it is called "practice. This explains the "Peaceful and Blissful Practice" (Anrakugyō) by way of its doctrinal principles.
Furthermore, this chapter represents the fourth intention regarding the dissemination of the Trace Gate.

As for those in the "Chapter on Entrusting," the twenty thousand and eighty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas who receive the mandate to propagate the sutra possess a profound understanding of the provisional and the real, a broad knowledge of the gradual and the sudden, and a mastery of expedient means and spiritual powers.

For those who first rely [on this teaching]—namely, those at the stage of the five ranks and ten levels of faith—who initially desire to cultivate the perfect practice, yet find themselves in a turbid world where they propagate the sutra and are afflicted by its defilements;

whose own practice does not stand firm and who lack the power to transform others—for such people as these, it is necessary to demonstrate the method and clarify the "Peaceful and Blissful Practices," which is why this chapter is taught.
There are also those who speak of the four practices of peaceful bliss (*catur-śukla-karman*): namely, conduct of body, speech, and mind guided by *śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, and compassion;

and the practice of the vow. Because there is *śamatha* in the bodily action, one is free from coarse physical karma; because there is *vipaśyanā*, one neither perceives a self nor perceives bodily action;
because there is compassion, one diligently cultivates bodily action to extensively benefit all beings; and because there is the practice of *śamatha*, one adheres to patience.
Because the robes possess contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), one sits upon the Tathāgata’s seat; because they possess compassion (*karuṇā*), one enters the Tathāgata’s chamber.

When conduct is stilled and free from transgression, the merit of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) is perfected; when contemplative practice is unattached, the merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) is perfected;

and when compassion benefits others, the merit of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*) is perfected. This is called the "peaceful practice of body. The other three peaceful practices—of speech, mind, and vow—are likewise [to be understood].
Regarding this wondrous joy, what is meant by "initially relying on the beginning mind"? The beginning mind refers to the initial stage of the five grades;

although it is not yet the rank of preaching the Dharma, one must propagate the sutra according to one's capacity and require these four practices. Upon reaching the third grade, one is precisely at the stage of preaching the Dharma to support one's own practice;
"preaching" here means propagating the principle, and one requires this grade as the method for doing so. △
