The stage of abiding refers to the ultimate reality (*tattva*). To abide therein is practice; that is, to give rise to practice based upon reality. Regarding "practice and non-practice":

although reality itself is devoid of practice, one practices by relying upon reality. When practice attains reality and comes to rest, it is termed "non-practice. As for its being the foundation for all:

this also refers to the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*) as the foundation of all, because by abiding in the single stage of patience, one possesses the three qualities such as gentleness (*mārdava*), and so forth—just as all things depend upon the earth.
Thus, one gives rise [to virtue] by using this as an analogy for how all practices attain principle and achieve completion.
If one attains the fundamental principle, it lies in being able to be gentle when firm, compliant when confronted with opposition, governing when amidst turbulence, and peaceful when amidst alarm.

From this ground of the Middle Way, immeasurable merit arises; yet this ground has no arising (referring to the aforementioned true principle), while merit (such as gentleness and flexibility) arises from it. This is precisely "non-practice" as practice.
"Practice in accordance with the above" means entering the Tathāgata’s chamber. (One who does not practice according to the principle practices by practicing within non-practice.

"Universally non-discriminating" means that one does not discriminate between the characteristics of non-practice and practice; because the nature and characteristics of practice and non-practice are non-dual, seeing the reality of all phenomena is called "non-discrimination.
There is no non-discrimination that is not itself discrimination, and even this name is neither practiced nor not practiced.

"Discrimination is itself neither practice nor non-practice," which accords with the "Tathāgata’s Seat" mentioned above. The *Nanyue Anlexing Yi* (The Meaning of the Peaceful Practice of Nanyue) states:
"To neither practice nor discriminate means that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are neither one nor different;

because ordinary beings and Buddhas are non-dual within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they cannot be discriminated. Furthermore, because one does not perceive even this non-duality, it is said [to be neither practice nor non-practice]."
Because one practices non-discrimination and the characteristics of non-discrimination are unattainable (text), there are no three practices, yet they are called "three practices";
because they are identical to the single ultimate truth, they are called "abodes. This explanation of practice and abode based on a single dharma clarifies the method for propagating the sutra.
Second, regarding the two dharmas: this refers to the two types of patience, namely patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) and patience toward birth (*janmakṣānti*). These two patiences...

If one analyzes the text by expanding the two emptinesses of phenomena and persons (*dharma-pudgala-śūnyatā*) into four patiences (*kṣānti*): the two characters "gentle" (*mṛdu*) and "pliant" (*sūrata*) constitute the Patience of Subjugation (*adhimukti-kṣānti*);

the two characters "well-conforming" (*anuloma*) and "compliance" (*anuvartana*) constitute the Patience of Conformity (*anulomika-kṣānti*); furthermore, regarding "equality of phenomena" (*dharmasamatā*) and so forth, it is the Patience of Non-arising (*anutpatti-kṣānti*);

and "non-practice" (*apracāra*) and so forth is the Patience of Cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*). (Combined, the former two patiences pertain to persons, while the latter two pertain to phenomena. If one classifies the four patiences according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), [the following applies].
From the initial generation of the bodhicitta until reaching the Vajra-peak [of the path], the complete subduing of the afflictions of the five abodes is termed "Patience of Subduing" (kṣānti);

because from beginning to end it never contradicts the true nature (dharmatā), it is termed "Patience of Accordance" (anuloma-kṣānti); because from beginning to end the mind does not give rise to the two extremes of emptiness and existence, it is termed "Patience of Non-arising" (anutpāda-kṣānti);
and because from beginning to end all manifold practices come to rest, it is termed "Patience of Quiescence" (nirvāṇa-kṣānti). This is due to the mind...

Abiding on the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), upon hearing of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), one does not suddenly become terrified by suffering; and upon hearing of nirvāṇa, one does not suddenly seek to realize pleasure.

For this reason, it is said that one is "not impetuous. Furthermore, whether hearing that the Buddha is eternal or impermanent, that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are different or not different, or that the Buddha-way is long or short, difficult or easy, or neither long nor short, neither difficult nor easy—regarding all such things, one is never startled.

Because of fearlessness, it is said that the mind is not startled. One who practices this path, from beginning to end, endures all phenomena through the principle of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*).
This is to don the Tathāgata’s robe; to abide securely in the principle of the two emptinesses is to sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat;
and to have compassion for all sentient beings is to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber. The two emptinesses and the four patiences (*catur-kṣānti*) are called the practice of the principle. Thus it is.
Regarding this, the explanation based on two dharmas concerns the "sphere of practice" (*caryā-viṣaya*), which is the method for propagating the sutra.
Third, regarding the explanation based on three dharmas, these are the inconceivable three truths (*tri-satya*). "Abiding in the ground of patience" refers generally to the three truths;
only when one has a ground to rely upon can one truly exercise patience. "Gentle, compliant, and harmonious" means being able to accord with the truth of reality (*tathatā-satya*).
Because one endures false views, craving, cold, heat, and so forth, it is said that one is "well-accommodated.

That the mind is not impetuous and does not tremble means that one is at peace within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Because one endures the conditions of the various faculties and accords with their specific capacities, one is not impetuous;
because one physically endures both adverse and favorable objects, the mind does not tremble. Regarding the phrase "there is no practice toward phenomena," it is as follows:
Because one is at ease within the Middle Truth and is able to endure the two extremes, it is said that there is "no place of practice. One correctly abides in the Middle Way;
since the Middle Way is itself the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is said that one "contemplates all dharmas as they truly are.

Furthermore, because even this "reality" cannot be apprehended therein, it is said that one "neither practices nor discriminates. This, then, is called "patience in the locus" (*sthānakṣānti*) based on the ground of the Three Truths.

The humiliation of the five abodes constitutes the practice of practice, which is also threefold: the practice of cessation (*śamatha*) is "practice that is not practice," corresponding to the Tathāgata’s robe;
the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is "neither practice nor non-practice," corresponding to the Tathāgata’s seat;
and the practice of compassion is "non-practice that is practice," corresponding to the Tathāgata’s chamber. This explains the locus of practice by means of these three dharmas.
This is the method for propagating the sutra. △ Second, the explanation of the "near places" has three parts. First, discussing the "near" by means of the "far," in ten sections.
First, distancing oneself from power and influence. It asks:
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s place of close association (upaniṣad), [extending] to ministers and high officials?
The following section explains the "near spheres" (*upasthāna*) by clarifying that the ten afflictions of mental disturbance are "near" despite being distant;

this is also an adjunct to the gate of precepts that assists meditative contemplation. (The "sphere of practice" refers to the primary practice, while the "near sphere" refers to the auxiliary practice; here, one establishes contemplations regarding the ten afflictions and other such matters to assist the primary contemplation that illuminates the principle.

Above, one directly took the principle as an object and dwelt in the stage of patience; now, within the gate of precepts, the various conditions for humiliation are extensively set forth, and one should accordingly cultivate [contemplation].
To remain far removed means not to use weapons or staves for self-defense as ordinary people do, nor to abandon observation like those of the Two Vehicles;

rather, one remains far removed by means of right wisdom. Because this involves distancing oneself from what is distant and approaching what is near, it is called "the place of close proximity. This first point refers to distancing oneself from power and influence;
thus it says, "do not be intimate with kings and the like. The *Myōraku* commentary states: "One fears that by relying on or attaching to such persons, one will lose the Right Path."
Therefore, what appears to be a slight benefit at first results in great harm over time. △ Second, distancing oneself from heterodox persons and teachings:
not associating with various non-Buddhist practitioners such as brahmins, Nirgranthas, and so forth, up to those who follow the Lokāyata.
This is the second [point]: distancing oneself from the teachings of heterodox persons. When people are defiled by heterodox teachings, they become deluded regarding correct principles;
until right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) is established, one must urgently strive to prevent and sever such influences.

Because they do not receive the internal teaching, they are called *bāhiraka* (outsiders) or *brahmacarin* (those of pure conduct); this is also translated as "pure lineage. As for their kind, they claim to have been born from the mouth of Brahmā.
Those who dwell at home and serve Brahmā are called *brahmins* (*brāhmaṇa*). Those who have left the household life among the non-Buddhist outsiders are collectively termed *nirgrantha*;

"nirgrantha" here means "one who has severed ties. Regarding the terms "wen" (文) and "bi" (筆): "wen" refers to the genre of songs and poetry, while "bi" refers to the category of inscriptions and rhapsodies.
"Zan" (讚) and "ying" (詠) refer to those who praise and extol: "zan" denotes manifesting virtue, while "ying" denotes expressing one's sentiments. *Lokāyata* is translated here as "evil."
The *Śāstra* also states: "The 'contrary *Lokāyata*' refers to arguments that oppose one's sovereign or father;
furthermore, *Lokāyata* is called 'virtuous discourse' when it refers to a teacher refuting a disciple, while it is called 'evil discourse' when it refers to a disciple refuting a teacher.
Master Ci'en Ji says: "*Lokāyata* is translated here as 'evil response'; the 'contrary *Lokāyata*' [refers to]..."

This is called the "bad omen" inquiry. Although it now requires that Bodhisattvas distance themselves from the teachings of heterodox persons and do not study external scriptures, if one wishes to ward off external insults, it does not hinder studying and mastering them;
however, one must not forget or abandon one's own fundamental school by becoming single-mindedly addicted to them.
△ Third, distancing oneself from violent and dangerous games.
Nor does one associate with various violent games (up to) and the *nara*-type performances of various transformations.
This is the third [precept]: staying far from violent games. "Mutual boxing and wrestling" refers to violent games;
*nara* here means "strength," which refers to the game of wrestling or the display of physical prowess. The commentary states: "As for *Nārāyaṇa*..."
"Superior entertainers" (shàngjìxì) refers to those who paint their bodies with colorful designs to create various extraordinary appearances;

it also refers to those who perform such feats as climbing poles and performing acrobatic flips. The *Miaoyue* states that those who engage in such violent spectacles are feared because they may lead to dissipation and negligence.
○ *Chā* (initial sound chū jiā; meaning "to strike") and *pò* (pronounced báo; meaning "to push," or alternatively pronounced pǔ bǔ; meaning "a light blow"). △ Fourth, the distant Caṇḍālas.
Furthermore, one does not associate with *caṇḍālas* (down to the point where they preach the Dharma to them) without harboring any expectation of reward;
this is the fourth [point on] distancing oneself from *caṇḍālas*. *Caṇḍāla* here is translated as "butcher" (*túzhě*) or "fierce and blazing" (*yánchì*).
This means that they adorn themselves with fiercely burning evil karma. If one associates with them, it causes people to lack... [virtue].
Those who compassionately raise pigs, sheep, chickens, and dogs, or those who hunt, stalk, and fish, all possess a mind of killing and are thus termed "those of evil discipline" (*akuśala-saṃvara*).
When such people come, one should skillfully preach the Dharma for them to turn their minds away from killing;
one must not harbor any expectation of gain [from them]. Regarding hunters, they do so to eliminate pests from the fields.
"Tián" (田) refers to hunting; it means to seize swiftly. The *Báihùtōng* (白虎通) states: "The hunting conducted during the four seasons is collectively termed 'liè' (獵).

"Tián" may also be written as "tiàn" (佃). The *Yì* (易) says: "By means of tián [one hunts], and by means of yú [one fishes]," with the commentary noting: "Taking wild beasts is called tián; taking fish is called yú.
△ Fifth, distancing oneself from the assembly of the Two Vehicles.
Furthermore, one does not associate with *śrāvaka* bhikṣus (up to those who preach the Dharma according to circumstances without seeking anything for themselves).

This is the fifth [reason] for distancing oneself from those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Because people of the Two Vehicles stagnate in emptiness and quiescence and are unable to give rise to the bodhicitta, they must be kept at a distance.
The *Myōryaku-ki* states: "Associating with those of the Two Vehicles causes people to distance themselves from Bodhi."

Because [the West] is a place where the people of the three vehicles do not dwell in confusion, it is said that even if they come, since they have not yet received the Great Transformation (Mahāyāna), it does not hinder [the Buddha] from preaching in accordance with their lesser aspirations; thus it is called "preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
Furthermore, one must not harbor a mind of seeking [for such things]. △ Sixth, the characteristic of the desire for distant objects.

Mañjuśrī, furthermore, from the bodhisattva [up to] not conversing with young girls, virgins, widows, and so forth—this is the sixth [aspect of] distancing oneself from thoughts of desire (*kāmasaṃjñā*).
Since thoughts of desire can destroy the bodhicitta, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says:
"Regarding 'thoughts of desire,' this is intended to deeply prevent the faults and afflictions of desire; one does not even give rise to such thoughts, much less physical contact."
In some cases of sexual intercourse, one may become stained by the other's physical appearance, gestures, speech, laughter, or deportment;

even their turning, moving, bowing, or rising can all give rise to thoughts of desire. This must be remedied through the contemplation of the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*). As for the "virgin" (*kanyā*), this refers to a girl living at home who has not yet married.
The "widow" (*vidhavā*) is one who has no husband. The *Āgama* Sūtra states that a certain heterodox practitioner asked:
"Bakkula, have you ever engaged in sexual desire within this True Dharma? He replied, "Do not speak such words.

For eighty years, I have never given rise to a thought of desire, never looked upon the face of a woman, never entered a bhikṣuṇī’s quarters, and never exchanged greetings with a bhikṣuṇī; even on the road, I did not speak with one."
Those who propagate the Dharma should observe this as a mirror of reflection; how could they not be cautious? △ Seventh, regarding those who are not men:
one should likewise neither associate with nor form close intimacies with the five kinds of persons who are not men.
This seventh [category] is the "distant impotent" (*puruṣa-dauṣthulya*). The *Myōraku-ki* states: "The impotent corrupt the resolve for bodhi. Regarding the five types of impotence:

they are the "born," the "severed," the "jealous," the "transformed," and the "half. "Born" means that from birth one has been without male organs. "Severed" means having one's virility removed by means of a blade.
"Jealous" means that one only develops a mind of jealousy upon seeing another person engage in sexual intercourse; at that moment, the desire for sexual union arises.
Regarding "arising transformations," this refers to those born in this life who undergo transformations; "half" means being a male for half a month and a non-male for half a month.
There are also five kinds of "non-females," namely: the conch, the tendon, the drum, the horn, and the vessel. △ Eighth: Keeping Harmful Influences at a Distance.

When meeting one another, do not converse; you should instead concentrate your mind on the Buddha. △ Ninth, matters concerning distant censure and suspicion:
If one preaches the Dharma for a woman, one must not smile with bared teeth (up to: ...), yet even this is not considered intimate or close, let alone other matters.
This is the ninth [point regarding] avoiding censure and suspicion: one should avoid exposing the teeth when smiling or revealing the chest, as these increase the unwholesome thoughts of others.
When preaching the Dharma to women, one must avoid such censure; it is not even appropriate to be intimate with them, let alone engage in other matters.
△ Tenth, distancing oneself from maintaining [disciples].
One does not delight in maintaining young disciples, śrāmaṇeras, or children, nor does one delight in having them share the same teacher.

This is the tenth [point on] distancing oneself from maintaining [disciples]. *Śrāmaṇera* is translated here as "one who rests in kindness" (*xi-ci*), meaning a person who has stilled worldly defilements.
It is for the sake of saving all sentient beings through compassion. It is also said that when first entering the Buddha-dharma, one often retains worldly sentiments;
therefore, one must cease evil and practice compassion. Furthermore, raising young children hinders the cultivation of the true path, and thus they must be distanced.
From the initial distancing of the powerful and influential to this distancing of raising children, these ten kinds of disturbances are divided into two extremes; nine of them pertain to birth.
Death is one [aspect] and Nirvana is the other; both are equally remote, being merely different names for quiescence (*śānti*).
Such is the nature of all dharmas across all teachings, though they differ slightly from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) teachings.

This is because the present work is a scripture for the propagation and universal dissemination of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), which is uniquely sublime; therefore, one must remain far removed from the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This refers to those of the Hīnayāna. △ Second, discussing the proximate by means of the proximate:
"Always delighting in sitting meditation, dwelling in a secluded place to cultivate and collect the mind" (up to) "this is called the first proximate station."

Now, cultivating the gathering of the mind is discussed in terms of what is proximate; this is also an auxiliary to the gate of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that supports insight (*vipaśyanā*).

Previously, distancing oneself from the ten kinds of disturbances was the cultivation of ethical discipline (*śīla*); now, constantly delighting in sitting meditation is the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi*);
next, contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*) is the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*). Within this present cultivation of concentration, there are three intentions.

The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states that the "three meanings" refer to the concentration of mind, the concentration of place, and the concentration of gate. "Mind" refers to the mind capable of aspiration;
aspiring to shatter hindrances and manifest principle is precisely the cultivation and gathering of the mind. "Place" refers to dwelling in a quiet location among the five conditions;
this is being in a secluded place now. "Gate" refers to the essential gate for practicing meditative concentration, which is among the five matters.
To balance the mind so that it neither sinks nor floats is precisely what is meant by "always delighting in sitting meditation.

Since there is no time to provide a definitive analysis here, I have merely listed two names from among the twenty-five expedient means according to their necessity. One should cultivate all three of these dharmas through close association.
△ Third, the Discussion on Neither Distance nor Proximity. Part One: A General Indication of Object and Wisdom.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates that all phenomena are empty.
This contemplation that all phenomena are empty is neither distant nor near; yet, when discussing proximity, it is likewise an entry through the gate of wisdom.
This serves to assist contemplation. First, the character "contemplation" (guān) indicates wisdom; it is the contemplative wisdom of the Middle Way that performs the observation.
In the middle, the three characters "all dharmas" (yīqièfǎ) indicate the object; it is the realm of the ten dharma-realms that is the object of observation.
Finally, the character "emptiness" (kōng) merely concludes the relationship between wisdom and its object: both the wisdom that contemplates and the object contemplated are ultimately unattainable.
Both object and wisdom are empty. △ Second, the specific explanation of object and wisdom:
as the true mark (*tathatā*), it is non-erroneous (up to) immeasurable, boundless, unobstructed, and unimpeded.
The three characters "yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa" (the reality as it is) provide a distinct explanation of the object. The two extremes of emptiness and the provisional correspond to the Middle Way;

they are neither identical nor different, and are not merely provisional names for the seven stages of expedient means. Because the real is taken as the characteristic, it is called "yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa.

The various phrases such as "not inverted" provide a distinct explanation of the contemplation. Regarding "not inverted," [it refers to] the ordinary person’s [view of] the two aspects of the environment and its inhabitants.
The nature of retribution is fundamentally impermanent, yet ordinary beings perversely cling to it as permanent; it is fundamentally suffering, yet they perversely cling to it as pleasure;
it is fundamentally selfless, yet they perversely cling to it as a self; it is fundamentally impure, yet they perversely cling to it as pure—these are the four perversions of ordinary beings.
The followers of the Two Vehicles, conversely, perversely cling to the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity as being suffering, impermanent, selfless, and impure.
These two vehicles possess four inversions; because Bodhisattvas lack these eight inversions, they are said to be "non-inverted.
"Immovable" means they are not moved by the two types of birth-and-death: the fragmented (*paricchinna*) and the transformative (*pariṇāma*).

"Non-retrogressive" means they accord with the principle of cessation; moment by moment their minds are quiescent, entering the ocean of *sarvajñā* (here translated as "all-knowledge," which is the wisdom of fruition).
"Non-transmigration" means not transmigrating through birth and death like ordinary beings, nor transforming from the state of an ordinary being into a sage like the Two Vehicles.
"Like empty space" means that empty space exists only as a name, and this name cannot be found when sought;
likewise, the wisdom of the Middle Way contemplation exists only as a name and cannot be found when sought. Miaole said: "It exists only as a name."
"Nature is empty" means that even names are non-existent; "characteristics are empty" refers to the nature of non-existence.
This means that one realizes all phenomena are devoid of the grasping at the four natures—self, other, both, or neither. This is the characteristic of the emptiness of nature.
"All paths of language are cut off" means that speech and thought are severed; this is the characteristic of the emptiness of characteristics. "Non-arising" refers to that which is to be negated.
The wisdom that can destroy these delusions accords entirely with principle, and therefore neither arises nor issues forth.

That which does not issue forth is because the entire body of what the Tathāgata treats as his domain is itself such; there is nothing from which to emerge. That which does not arise is because one has entered into principle;
thus, all skillful means, principles, and teachings are utterly quiescent. This principle of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) cannot be named, and therefore its nature is empty.

Because characteristics cannot characterize [themselves] and because characteristics are empty, it is said that they are "nameless and signless. This reiterates the previous statement regarding "non-existence" and so forth.
"Non-existent" is a further praise of the essence of the Middle Way contemplative wisdom, which lacks existence on either of the two extremes.
"Immeasurable" means that it is not among the numerical categories of the aggregates, elements, or sense bases. "Boundless" means that it is not like the partial [realms].
Because it is a phenomenon with limited dimensions, it is "unobstructed"; because it universally enters all phenomena, it is "unimpeded," meaning there is nothing capable of blocking it.
Although these are many phrases, they merely refer to the ability of the contemplator to unite with the object through signlessness (*animitta*) and non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*);
they are simply called "universal emptiness" in contrast to all phenomena. △ Third, the conclusion establishing the object and wisdom.
"Existence solely by way of causes and conditions" (up to this point) is called the second station of intimacy for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"Existence solely by way of causes and conditions" is a summary of all the preceding phrases, indicating that there is nothing that is not a matter of causes and conditions.

Above, it directly clarified the wisdom of the Middle Way contemplation, which is neither understanding nor delusion, severing the characteristics of the two extremes; now, it clarifies the simultaneous illumination of both extremes.
Birth and death arise from the causal conditions of delusion; nirvana arises from the causal conditions of liberation.

This explains how the single phrase "causal conditions" opens up two distinct realms. Furthermore, when causal conditions exist within nirvana—because one illuminates that which is produced by conditions and thus sees that it is empty, this emptiness is called nirvana—it is shown that what arises from inversion gives rise to birth and death.
This, then, is the manifestation of the meaning of the dual illumination of permanence and bliss.
"Contemplating such dharmas as these" refers to the dharmas of the Three Truths and so forth.

Furthermore, "that which arises from conditions due to inversion" concludes the inconceivable realm of the Three Truths (all dharmas of inversion arising from causes and conditions are the essence of the wondrous realm).
Therefore, "the teaching" refers to the inconceivable teaching. "Constantly delighting in contemplation" concludes the inconceivable threefold contemplation. △
The two verses are divided into three parts; the first verse sets forth the heading.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If there are bodhisattvas who, in the evil world of the future, desire to preach this sutra with a mind free from fear."

The preceding verse states that one who wishes to expound this sutra should abide in four dharmas; because one abides in the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*) and the mind is not startled or terrified, it is said to be "a mind free from fear.
△ Second, the verse on the cultivation of practice has two parts; first, the verse on the distance and proximity of the matter.
One should enter the spheres of practice and the spheres of association (up to) those who are attached to the study of the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna.
From "one should oneself enter the spheres of practice" onwards, fourteen verses describe the distancing from ten afflictive matters; this is a discussion of the near based on the distant.

Regarding "those with overweening pride" (*adhimāna*): it refers to giving rise to arrogance and contempt toward the supreme human dharmas; that is, to claim [attainment] when one has not yet attained it.
Regarding those who have attained [the Dharma], as for the Three Piṭakas:
the Buddha first taught the Sūtra Piṭaka to the five disciples, including Cunda, at Vārāṇasī; he first taught the Vinaya Piṭaka to Sunakṣatra at Rājagṛha;
and he first taught the Abhidharma Piṭaka to the son of the Vaṅgas at the side of the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.
The Abhidharma-piṭaka refers to the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna; because associating with the Hīnayāna hinders the propagation of the Great Dharma, one must distance oneself from it.
One should not associate with those who break the precepts—even those who bear the name of Arhat—nor with any of the upāsikās.
Those called "Arhats by name" refer to those who are nominally Arhats but have not attained it in reality;

because they seek extinction in the present life, they are close to the Lesser Vehicle and are not vessels for the Great Dharma. Therefore, one who propagates the Mahāyāna sūtras must not associate with them.
If such persons come with sincere hearts, one should not associate with them or treat them as close friends.
To have no expectations means, as the Venerable Zuo Xi did, never to speak a single word of Dharma for the sake of profit, nor ever to accept even a hair’s breadth of wealth on account of the Dharma;
only by maintaining such a mind can one be said to be without expectation. Furthermore...
Those who are not male are called *paṇḍaka*; this is translated as "eunuch" (*huángmén*). A eunuch possesses both male and female forms but is incapable of either sexual function.
Furthermore, do not associate with butchers, executioners, or those of similar repute; one must not associate with such persons at all.
Slaughter refers to the carving of meat; "tu-kuai" (屠膾) means finely slicing meat. To peddle is to buy at a low price and sell at a high price;
to "huan" (衒) is to advertise oneself for sale. Since these activities are all not pure deeds, one should distance oneself from them.
Regarding the various playful performances of the fierce and dangerous *sumō* (wrestling), [the text continues] up to: "By means of these two places, one can preach with ease and comfort.

As for entering a village to beg for alms, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: "There was once a sheep that went to a dung heap, ate its fill, and returned to the flock with an air of self-importance, thinking, 'I have obtained excellent food.
Monks are also like this; having received the fourfold offerings, they become conceited."
Attached to perceptions and ignorant of the way out, he treats the bhikṣus with arrogance and disparages others, saying, "I have attained what they have not attained.
This is the sheep-like bhikṣu who goes on almsround. A lion king, upon encountering a large beast, devours it without savoring or attachment;
upon encountering a small beast, it devours it without contempt or disdain. The bhikṣu is also like this. When he obtains [alms], he accepts them...
Having made offerings of the four requisites, one should not give rise to thoughts of attachment, knowing for oneself the path of transcendence with a mind free from increase or decrease;
this is the alms-round of the Lion King Bhikṣu. Furthermore, before a bhikṣu has obtained food while on his alms-round, he should reflect:
"For the sake of cultivating the Path, I must mend the wound of hunger by practicing alms-gathering. Once he has obtained food, it is for the purpose of repaying the kindness of the donors.
"Maintaining mindfulness of the Way without ceasing. The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states: "When begging for food, divide it into four parts: one part to offer to fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring;
one part to give to a single beggar; one part to bestow upon spirits and deities; and one part to eat oneself. △ Second, the verse on neither far nor near.
Furthermore, not practicing the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas—this is what is called the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice (*caryā-viṣaya*).

Regarding the superior, middling, and inferior dharmas: in terms of the teachings (*śāsana*), the distinct teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*) is superior, the common teaching (*sāmānyavyavahāra*) is middling, and the treasury teaching (*pitaka*) is inferior.
In terms of persons, this may refer to the three vehicles or to bodhisattvas of the three teachings. Here, however, it refers to the setting aside of the provisional (*prajñapti-tyāga*).

Regarding the statement "not practicing conditioned phenomena, etc.," conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are mundane dharmas and are therefore unreal; unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are supramundane dharmas and are therefore real.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "also not discriminating, etc.," the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Meaning of Avalokiteśvara) uses male and female as symbols for concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), where wisdom is symbolized by the male and concentration by the female. It correctly cites these two phrases to clarify concentration.
Because the dharma-nature of wisdom is fundamentally beyond words and cannot be differentiated, it is stated below that "one does not apprehend all dharmas," and so forth.
All dharmas are empty and non-existent; [this state] up to being eternally abiding in a single characteristic is called the "near station."
This verse summarizes the preceding passages concerning his constant fondness for sitting in meditation and contemplating the emptiness of all dharmas; this may be seen in the text.
△ Third, the verse clarifies the accomplishment of practice in three parts.
First, the heading: "If there be a bhikṣu who, after my parinirvāṇa... shall preach this sutra at that time without any timidity."
This indicates that when practice is perfected, external conduct is free from error; when principle is perfected, the internal mind is free from obstruction.
Therefore, when preaching the sutras, there is no timidity or weakness. △ Second, the explanation.
At times, the Bodhisattva enters a quiet chamber (until) his mind is at peace and free from timidity.

This explains the cause of his bliss: because he enters a quiet chamber to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he ceases transgressions and evils and attains the realization of the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
Furthermore, because he relies on right mindfulness to cultivate wisdom, he remains undisturbed by external factors and becomes detached from all grasping and attachment.
Having attained the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and being free from internal inversion, the mind is neither timid nor weak;
this lack of timidity is called peace and bliss. △ Third, the conclusion:
Mañjuśrī, this is called a bodhisattva abiding in the first dharma, who is able to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in future ages.
This verse summarizes the initial method in the prose section, which refers to the "peaceful practice of the body. II. Peaceful Practice of Speech:
A. The Prose Section: 1. The Statement of the Chapter.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the period of the Final Dharma (up to the point where it says) "one should abide in the Practice of Peaceful Conduct.
This concludes the second section: the Oral Practice of Peaceful Conduct; now the chapter title is presented. △ Second, the Practices of the Dharma, in two parts.
First, the Practice of Quiescence, in four parts. First, not speaking of faults.
Whether speaking aloud or reading the scriptures, one should not take pleasure in speaking of the faults of others or of the sūtras.
This explains the practice of tranquility for the mouth; within this practice of tranquility, there are both the practices of cessation (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).

Here, regarding the first point—taking no pleasure in speaking of the faults of those who listen or the sūtras being listened to—this refers to the seven stages of expedient means prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This provisional teaching is the Buddha’s discourse spoken in accordance with the capacities and intentions of others; it is called "of incomplete meaning" (*neyārtha*).

If people listen to and accept it, there may be the fault of delighting in the partial and lesser vehicle. If this teaching is merely a discourse adapted to specific circumstances, what fault could there be?
To claim that the Dharma itself possesses a fault would be to disturb those who hear and receive it, rather than bringing peace and happiness to their speech.
This is the characteristic of its practice. △ Second, not being arrogant:
one should likewise not treat other Dharma masters with contempt.
This means that those who propagate the sutra must not rely upon the perfection of the *Lotus Sūtra* they propagate to despise those who teach the partial teachings.

Master Miaole said that even when the Buddha was in the world, he already employed various provisional expedients (*upāya*) and other profound teachings to assist the true path of the perfect reality (*pariniṣpanna*).
How could later students, following the teachings, rigidly oppose them?

One must conform to the Buddha’s intention to protect the capacities of sentient beings. [The questioner asks: When the Buddha observed the capacities of beings in his world, fearing they would fall into suffering, he first...
Question: Is it necessarily the case that those who propagate the Dharma in the final age must exclusively employ the *p'ien* (partial) teachings? Answer:

I fear that those who propagate the sutras may rely on the *yüan* (perfect) teachings and hold the *p'ien* in contempt, thus making such a claim. However, a propagator of the sutras should act according to the depth or shallowness of their own practice and stage;
if a person at the initial stage of propagating the sutras encounters a seeker of the Dharma, they should explain it to them using only the Mahāyāna.
This is the response given in brief. As for those in deep stages who propagate the sutras, they must propagate the Dharma from beginning to end;
only through the three divisions of the Tripiṭaka and the three methods can the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching] be revealed. △ Third, neither praising nor disparaging.
One does not speak of the good or evil, the long or the short of others (up to: nor does one praise their excellence by mentioning their names.
From the outset, one does not speak of all people, nor does one specifically single out and raise one's voice to mention śrāvakas;
one does not speak of the long or the short of others because people loathe hearing of their faults, and one does not praise them because those who are fond of reputation will surely slander them.

Because people are long-lived, the *Sūryagarbha-sūtra* states that during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, one should diminish sleep, apply oneself with diligence to seated meditation, recite the sūtras, and cultivate the Way.
One should turn one's back on birth and death and head toward the path of Nirvāṇa. One should not speak of the shortcomings of others nor boast of one’s own virtues.
Regarding those such as the Śrāvakas: since the spiritual faculties (*indriya*) of Śrāvakas are not fixed, if one praises the Two Vehicles, it may cause them...

To regress from the Great [Vehicle] and adopt the Small, or to disparage the Two Vehicles, or to cause them to lose both the Great and the Small—therefore, both disparagement and praise are inappropriate.
The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which says: "Self-praise and self-disparagement;
praising others and disparaging others—these four practices are not undertaken by the wise. Why is this? One who praises themselves is like a person of delusion."
Those who disparage others are those who delude people with demonic charms; those who praise others are sycophants; those who slander others are backbiting thieves.
The wise should employ the four *siddhāntas* to deliberate and thereby protect both themselves and others. △ Fourth, not harboring resentment or dislike.
Furthermore, one should not give rise to thoughts of resentment or aversion.
If one thinks that the person from whom one received [the teaching] or the Dharma one has inherited obstructs one's own path, this is a mind of resentment;
if one thinks that such a person or their Dharma is base and inferior, this is a mind of aversion. As soon as the mental faculty stirs, speech follows immediately.
Because one has severed the source of transgressions, resentment and aversion do not arise. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states: "When resentment is removed, it diminishes harm to oneself;

when it opposes one's feelings, it is called 'aversion' (*xián*). If even those who practice for peace and happiness still eliminate joy that accords with their own desires, how much more so should they avoid harboring the hatred of resentment?
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says: 'In a past age, there was a rākṣasa king in Kuru...'"
In the Buddha-dharma, he left the household life and gave rise to the bodhicitta, reciting and upholding eighty-four thousand collections of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.
However, because he harbored resentment in his mind toward a *dhūta* bhikṣu who did not recite the sūtras—viewing him as being like a stump—he fell into hell and suffered there.
After emerging from hell, he took birth as a rākṣasa; at the end of this Bhadrakalpa, he will become the Buddha Ruci.
Even ordinary people are thus when they are about to be freed from the bodies of *rākṣasas* by the Buddha; how much more so for one who practices the conduct of peace and happiness!
To propagate the Great Dharma and protect minor practices, one must abandon both resentment and aversion; only then can it be called right practice.

Regarding what is said here in the "Peaceful Conduct of Speech," as for the mind of resentment and aversion: when the mind moves, it manifests in speech. Therefore, to restrain the mind is itself to restrain the mouth.
△ Second, the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Because one has skillfully cultivated such a mind of peace and bliss... [up to] ...one explains it for them so that they may attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Having already contemplated that all phenomena are empty of self-nature as described above, one abides in the principle of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) without any grasping or attachment.
One does not cling to the great while disparaging the small, but rather accords with the dispositions of sentient beings without contradicting the characteristics of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
If there is a difficult question, one does not speak of the Hīnayāna but answers solely with the Mahāyāna;

this has two intentions: first, if one perceives that the person lacks the capacity for the Great Vehicle, one speaks of the Small Vehicle merely to provide them with the provisional benefit of the small.
If one does not perceive the absence of a great capacity [in a being] and yet teaches them the Lesser Vehicle, it obstructs their connection to the Great Vehicle;

therefore, by teaching only the Great Vehicle, one avoids the fault of duality. Regarding "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is explained as before. As for "increased cultivation," it means to accord with the dispositions of beings so as not to oppose their intentions;
one does not even cause them to follow the Dharma at the expense of violating their worldly inclinations. Furthermore, one does not...

If one permits seeing the absence of greatness yet explains it as being small, this obstructs the conditions for that greatness; how much more so when one violates the characteristics of the Dharma and further turns away from the capacities of the audience?
How much more so when one clings to the Great while disparaging the Small, causing both the Great and the Small to be lost? △ Second, the verse summary has three parts;
first, the verse summarizes the headings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva always delights in preaching the Dharma for peace and security... [omitted] ...wearing new, clean robes, being pure both within and without."
These two verses constitute the initial formal heading within the "Practice of Peaceful Abiding" (*sukha-vihāra*) mentioned above. Previously, it was stated generally that one "should abide";
now, in these verses, the specific characteristics (*ākāra*) of that practice are set forth. There are three such characteristics:

first, the first half-verse intends for those present to attain the path and fruit of peace (*kṣema-mārga-phala*—the peaceful path being *nirvāṇa* and the fruit being the result of *nirvāṇa*), which corresponds to the meaning of "entering the Tathāgata’s chamber. Next...
The first half of the verse signifies the meaning of sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat; the latter half of the verse signifies the meaning of donning the Tathāgata’s robe.
Guiding one's verbal karma through these three dharmas is called "Peaceful Conduct. △ Second, the verses on the methods of practice, in two parts.
First, the verses on the practice of cessation (śamatha), in four parts. First, the verses on not being contemptuous.
Seated securely upon the Dharma-seat, he expounds the teaching according to the questions asked.
The following five lines and a half of verse concern the practice of stillness (*śamatha*). Now, this half-line of verse concerns not being disrespectful;
for if one were disrespectful, one would not expound the teaching according to the questions asked. △ Second, not speaking of long or short [faults].
If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs (up to and including) those who pose difficult questions, one should answer according to the meaning.
One should speak solely in reliance upon the sublime meaning and not discuss the likes or dislikes of people. Regarding answering difficult questions according to the meaning, there are two types:
those that may be answered and those that may not be answered. If one engages in mutual interrogation and debate regarding questions and answers, one will know for oneself [the outcome].
"This is the speech of the wise; if one asks while being self-indulgent and insolent, and there is anyone who dares to oppose him, he shall execute them—this is the speech of the king;
if one knows nothing of long or short, right or wrong, and seeks only his own victory—this is the speech of the fool.
Miaole said: "The speech of the wise may be answered; the speech of the king and the speech of the fool may not be answered."
Answer: △ Third, not speaking of others' faults.
By means of causes, conditions, parables, and detailed explanations, one gradually increases [their merit] until they enter the Buddha-way.
If one were to speak of others' faults, it would give rise to poisonous thoughts in people; because I do not speak of their faults now, I cause them to resolve their minds and enter [the path].
The Buddha-way, the Buddha-way, arises from joy. △ Fourth, the verse on being free from resentment and dislike:
"Eliminating slothful intentions and thoughts of indolence, one leaves behind all grief and affliction, preaching the Dharma with a compassionate mind."

When a mind of resentment and aversion arises, one becomes indolent, weary, and distressed; now, by preaching the Dharma with a mind of loving-kindness, there is no resentment or aversion, for one is diligent and free from distress.
The preceding prose section was entirely based on the goodness of cessation (*śamatha*), whereas the verses herein are all based on the goodness of cultivation (*vipaśyanā*).
△ Second, the verses on contemplative practice.
Day and night, he constantly expounds the unsurpassed Way of the Buddha (up to) "this is the great benefit, peace, and bliss of making offerings.

These four lines of verse constitute the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*). In the preceding prose section it says, "He answers solely by means of the Mahāyāna," whereas here in the verse it says, "He expounds the unsurpassed Way.
In the preceding section it says, "Causing them to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)," whereas here in the verse it says, "May they become Buddhas."
"To cause the multitude to likewise attain the Way" means to cause others also to achieve the Buddha-way. **Three:
Verses on the Accomplishment of Practice.** First, a verse designating the accomplishment of practice:
"After my parinirvāṇa, if there be bhikṣus who are able to expound this wondrous *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*..."
This single line marks the completion of the "Peaceful Practice of Speech. △ Second, the removal of faults and difficulties:
"The mind is free from envy, anger, and all afflictive hindrances" (extending to) "and there is no expulsion, because one dwells in patience."
These two lines clarify that if there are no faults within, external difficulties will not arise; it is like flies not coming to a place where there is no foul odor.
△ Third, the accomplishment of wholesome conduct:
A wise person who thus skillfully cultivates their mind can abide in peace and happiness, as I have explained above.
Within this, there are wholesome dharmas by which practice is perfected. △ Fourth, the evaluation of merit:
The merit of such a person cannot be exhausted even by calculation, enumeration, or analogy throughout thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.
△ Third, the Practice of Peaceful Abiding in Mind (Suyāna-caryā). Part One: The Long Exposition (Prose). Sub-part One: The Statement of the Chapter.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... [up to] those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra.
The following is the third [section], the Practice of Mental Tranquility; here the heading is presented. △ Second, the Practice of the Dharma, in two parts.
First, the practice of cessation, in four parts. First, freedom from envy and flattery:
one should harbor no mind of jealousy, flattery, or deception.
Now, those of the Two Vehicles seek to transcend birth and death, and thus first eliminate craving and desire. Bodhisattvas seek to transform others, and thus first eliminate anger, views, and envy.
Envy is a defilement of anger; flattery is a defilement of views. Envy violates the mind of compassion and is not the method for transforming others;
flattery and deception deviate from the path of wisdom and are not the method for one's own practice. If there is wisdom...
If one is obstructed, how can one seek the Buddha-way above? If compassion is hindered, how can one transform sentient beings below?
Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to cultivate the practice of mental peace and bliss must most certainly abandon [such conduct]. △ Second, not slighting or reviling others.
Furthermore, do not disparage or revile those who study the Buddha-way by seeking out their shortcomings.

Regarding the phrase "do not disparage," this precept means that a Bodhisattva person should not, relying on their own practice of the Perfect Teaching (yuan-xing), reproach practitioners of the Separate Teaching (bie-jiao) who study the Buddha-way;
nor should they, relying on the excellence of the Perfect Teaching, seek [to find fault].
Regarding the shortcomings of the provisional teachings, those who understand the underlying intent should criticize them; however, do not revile those who lack such understanding.

If one were to reprimand or revile them, there is the possibility that it might cause their roots of goodness to regress; therefore, it says "do not [revile]" and so forth. △ Third, not causing disturbance.

If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī [says], "You are a person of negligence, for you are indolent regarding the Path," this refers to the four assemblies of bhikṣus and others who all possess the potential for the Three Vehicles;
thus it says "seeking śrāvakas" and so forth. This precept should not be used to reprimand those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) who follow the Three Vehicles of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
Their fundamental nature lacks the great potential [of the Perfect Teaching], yet one forcibly uses the Perfect Teaching to reprimand them.

To act contrary to one's own mind leads to affliction; to be rebuked by the Shared [Teaching] while the Perfect [Teaching] remains unresolved results in both prior doubt and subsequent regret, causing one to lose both the Great and the Small.
Thus, the path to Buddhahood becomes circuitous and exceedingly remote. This affliction pertains specifically to practitioners of the Separate Teaching.

Although the present text speaks of rebuking the Shared Teaching, this is because within the Shared Teaching there are also those with the capacities of the Separate Teaching. If one were to hastily seek realization, one would sink...
To remain stagnant in emptiness and stillness, unable to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), is an affliction that pervades practitioners of the Shared Teaching;

it is termed "indolence" (*kausīdya*) because one loathes birth-and-death and is lazy in guiding and transforming others. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* clarifies that those of the Lesser Vehicle are indolent.
△ Fourth, non-contention.
Furthermore, one should not engage in frivolous speculation regarding phenomena or contend with others;
for such mocking discourse obstructs the practice of peaceful abiding and must therefore be restrained. The *Śālistamba Sūtra* (Sutra on the Bequeathed Teaching) says:
"If one engages in various forms of frivolous speculation, the mind becomes distracted; though one has left the household life, one still cannot attain liberation. Therefore, monks, you should..."
One must likewise abandon this mindset. △ Second, regarding the four aspects of contemplative practice:
First, as for giving rise to great compassion in opposition to envy and flattery, one should conceive thoughts of great compassion toward all sentient beings.

The following four sections clarify the practice of contemplative cultivation (*guanxing*), specifically concerning how to initiate virtuous conduct in response to the aforementioned four types of evil.
△ Second, giving rise to the mind of a compassionate father when encountering insults and abuse.
One should conceive of all Tathāgatas as one's compassionate father.

Anyone who seeks the Buddha-way is a student; they should be revered and studied as Buddhas, and must not be slighted or reviled—this applies to those of the three periods of time, for these are indeed the future Tathāgatas.
△ Third, one should conceive of them as Great Teachers and avoid causing them distress or disorder.
One should regard all bodhisattvas as great teachers (up to: one should always, with a profound mind, pay them respect and prostrate). One should examine this through reasoning:
the three vehicles are all possessed of the virtue of transforming and instructing bodhisattvas; they are all teachers of sentient beings.
One should conceive of them as teachers and not speak of their shortcomings. △ Fourth, preaching the Dharma with equanimity and avoiding contention.
Treatise:
He preaches the Dharma with equality toward all sentient beings (up to: nor does he preach excessively.
Because the Dharma is fundamentally equal in its impartial destruction of biased attachments, it is said that he does not preach excessively because he accords with the Dharma.
"Not few" refers to measuring the sharpness or dullness of their faculties. △ Third, the conclusion:
first, because they have ceased evil, evil cannot be added to them.
When Mañjuśrī, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva... [preaches] this Dharma, none are able to disturb or confuse him.

This refers to the peaceful practice of mental composure (*manas-karma-śānta-caryā*); because one ceases evil, evil cannot be inflicted upon them, and thus it is said that "none can disturb or vex them.
△ Second, because of the excellence of their contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), people gather around them.
One obtains good spiritual friends with whom to read and recite this sutra (up to) making offerings to the scroll of the sutra and reverently honoring and praising it.
Because of the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), superior persons gather, and one obtains good spiritual friends. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts:
first, the summary of the method of practice; second, the summary of the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*). Fourth, the summary of freedom from envy and flattery.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to preach this sutra, one should abandon jealousy, anger, pride, flattery, deceit, and a false mind; one should always cultivate a straightforward and honest conduct."
△ Second, two verses on not disparaging or reviling others.
△ Third, three verses on not engaging in contention or rivalry.
Nor does one engage in frivolous speculation regarding the Dharma.
△ Fourth, the verse on not causing disturbance:
one does not cause others to doubt or regret by saying, "You shall not attain Buddhahood."
△ Second, the four verses on the contemplative practice: The first verse concerns the arousal of great compassion toward all beings.
These children of the Buddha, when preaching the Dharma, are always gentle and capable of forbearance; with compassion for all, they never give rise to a mind of indolence.
△ Second, the verse on conceiving the thought of the Great Master toward Bodhisattvas:
"The great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions practice the Path out of compassion for sentient beings; one should give rise to a mind of reverence, thinking, 'These are my Great Masters.'"
△ Three verses on conceiving of the Tathāgata as a compassionate father and generating the thought of the Buddha-Bhagavāns as one’s unsurpassed father.
△ Four verses on preaching the Dharma with equanimity to still contentious disputes.
Having destroyed the mind of pride, he preaches the Dharma without obstruction.
△ Second, the verse on the accomplishment of practice:
"The third dharma is such that the wise person should protect it; with a single mind, they practice the conduct of peace and bliss, and are revered by immeasurable multitudes."
△ Fourth, the Four Vows on Peaceful Conduct. Part One: The Long Exposition. Sub-part One: Clarifying the Practice of the Dharma. Section One: Indicating the Chapter.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... (up to) "there are those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
Below this is the fourth, the practice of peaceful conduct through vows.

To act with body, speech, and mind in conjunction with compassion is the practice of peaceful conduct through vows, as it involves making a vow to propagate this sutra. △ Second, the methods of practice, in three parts:
first, designating the objects of the vow; second, the object of the vow of loving-kindness.
One gives rise to great compassion toward both householders and those who have left the home life.
This includes all who have previously developed the mind of skillful means but have not yet transcended the triple world; these are called householders.

Those who have exhausted the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃjñā-kleśa*) and have transcended the triple world are called those who have left the home life. This encompasses the two vehicles of the Two Teachings and the Bodhisattvas of the Three Teachings.
Since these individuals all possess ignorance and sufferings that can be uprooted, they should also be objects of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

However, because they have all previously given rise to partial or limited minds (*hīnayāna-citta*) that correspond to vows of benevolence (*maitrī*), one must provide them with the bliss of the perfect path and perfect fruit;
therefore, it is said that "one gives rise to a mind of great benevolence," for benevolence is able to bestow bliss. △ Second, Compassion (*karuṇā*).
The object of the vow:
to give rise to great compassion toward those who are not bodhisattvas.
Here, "those who are not bodhisattvas" refers generally to those who have not yet generated the mind of skillful means; this category includes all beings within the three realms.

Since these individuals have never once given rise to the provisional mind of the Hīnayāna, let alone the true mind of the Mahāyāna, it is known that they are all members of those who transmigrate within the realm of birth and death;
they must also be granted happiness. However, as their transmigration is boundless, it accords precisely with the vow of compassion that one should uproot the causes of their suffering.
Because it is the fruit of suffering, one speaks of giving rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*); this is because compassion is able to uproot suffering.
△ Second, the arising of vows, which has two parts: first, the reason for giving rise to the vow of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
One should reflect thus: "Such a person has suffered a great loss regarding the Tathāgata’s skillful means of preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
This is the reason for giving rise to compassion. "Such a person" refers to those who previously gave rise to the mind of skillful means;

because they delight in the Small [Vehicle], they cling to the Buddha’s skillful means as being ultimate reality and fail to realize the Perfect Path. Therefore, it is said that their loss is "great."
To lose this is the reason for the vow of great compassion. △ Second, the reason for the vow of great pity:
not hearing, not knowing, not perceiving, not inquiring, not believing, and not understanding.
Those who have not yet given rise to the mind of either the partial or the perfect within their fingers do so because they have not yet given rise to such a mind;

because they have not heard of the two paths—the partial and the perfect, they lack the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) regarding the partial path; because they do not know the partial path, they lack the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);
and because they do not realize the partial path, they lack the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Furthermore, they lack the three perfect wisdoms. Why? Because they do not inquire.
Because they do not hear the Perfect Path, they do not believe in the Perfect Path; because they do not hear the Perfect Path, they do not contemplate or understand the Perfect Path;

because they do not hear the Perfect Path, they do not cultivate the three types of wisdom—partial or perfect, provisional or real. They are truly pitiable, and this is precisely why one gives rise to compassion. In the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy), it asks:
"How can we know that the first three are provisional and the latter three are real? The answer is: "It accords with the *Zhengfa* (Correct Arising)."
The text of the vow cites only the latter three [stages] as constituting this sutra; therefore, it says: "Even though such a person does not inquire about, believe in, or understand this sutra.
△ Third, the formal establishment of the vow.
"Although that person does not inquire about, believe in, or understand this sutra" (up to) "leading them so that they may abide within this Dharma"—this is precisely the formulation of the vow.
Although that person does not inquire or believe, the Bodhisattva does not formulate the vow based on the two paths of the partial and the perfect;
rather, desiring to grant them the three types of wisdom of the perfect path, he says, "although they do not inquire."
Those who do not believe or understand this sutra, I shall lead them to enter the attainment of *sambodhi*.
Whether it be their vows, their *bodhi*, their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), or their wisdom—all are obtained through the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukha-vihāra*).
The two powers of supernormal power and wisdom are precisely the two adornments of merit and wisdom; because one deeply contemplates the seat of the Tathāgata, one obtains the power of wisdom.

The four analytical knowledges (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ) serve as adornments that can uproot [defilements] through wisdom. One deeply contemplates the Tathāgata’s dwelling and the Tathāgata’s robe, attaining the power of great sublime tranquility;
without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), one manifests various majestic demeanors, supernatural powers, and the adornment of merit.
First, one moves others by means of meditative concentration. △ Third, the conclusion in three parts: first, a general summary showing the absence of faults.
Mañjuśrī, when this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva—up to the point where he says these teachings—speaks this Dharma, there is no fault.
This concludes the vow for peaceful conduct (*sukha-vihāra*). Now, to summarize that there is no fault:
since there is no fault, his practice is perfected. How is it perfected? Because he has established the great vow, he immediately enters the state of a Tathāgata.
Because Śikṣānanda had realized the fourfold assembly’s failure to attain the perfect path, he sat upon the Tathāgata’s seat.
Because Hengxing had vowed to restrain his mind without indolence, he donned the Tathāgata’s robe.
Because Hengxing had established the three types of conduct, he was said to be free from fault; because his compassion was perfected, he was free from the stain of anger.
Because the robes have been completed, there is no loss through indolence; because the Tathāgata’s seat has been completed, there is no loss through deceit.
Since this fourth vow-practice has been accomplished, there are no such faults. △ Second, the specific conclusion on the accomplishment of compassion.
"Constantly acting as a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī (up to) being able to cause all listeners to attain joy.

This concludes the separate summary of the accomplishment of the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*). Because it is accomplished through loving-kindness, one receives the offerings of the fourfold assembly and of devas and humans;

because the vow to listen to the Dharma is fulfilled, one evokes the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) of the Buddha and the protection of the various devas; thus, the seat of the Tathāgata is established.
Because they do not cling to dharmas, the listeners rejoice. △ Third, the explanation of the fulfillment of the vow and practice.
Why is this so? Because this sutra is protected by the spiritual power of all past (up to) Buddhas.
This explains that because the practice of the vow has been perfected, even the Buddhas of the three periods of time all provide protection, let alone the devas.
△ Second, praising the excellence of the sutra, in two parts: first, the dharma-exposition; second, first, what was not previously revealed.
Mañjuśrī, as for this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—up to and including its very name—it could not even be heard.
Because it had never been revealed or preached in the past, it was not obtained in the past. △ Second, it is now finally obtained.
How much more so for those who obtain the sight [of it], receive, uphold, read, and recite it!
△ Second, the explanation by way of analogy, which has two parts: First, the analogy of not giving the jewel, concerning what was never previously revealed;
second, the opening of the analogy in six parts, the first of which is "subduing all kingdoms through majestic power."

Mañjuśrī, it is like a powerful universal monarch (cakravartin) who, wishing to subdue various kingdoms by his majestic power, appears when the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa reaches eighty thousand years.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states in its *Fan-yi-ming-yi*: "When the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa reaches eighty thousand years, a universal monarch is born;
when the lifespan decreases from eighty thousand years and various evils gradually increase, no such wheel [of sovereignty] exists."
A king who, by means of the wheel’s revolution, leads and subdues all through his majestic power is called a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).

To speak of them in their full enumeration, there are four types of Wheel-Turning Kings—namely, those with wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron—but because the golden wheel is the most excellent, the Sūtra speaks only of the Golden-Wheel King, stating:
"If a king is born into the Kṣatriya caste, succeeds to the position of consecration, and on the fifteenth day receives..."
While he was observing the fast and precepts, a precious golden wheel suddenly appeared in the eastern direction;
its thousand spokes were complete, and its hub and rim radiated wondrous light as it came to attend upon the king. This king must certainly be a Wheel-Turning King of Gold.
A King of Gold leads the four continents, a King of Silver leads three continents, a King of Copper leads two continents, and a King of Iron leads one.

Regarding the differences in how the four types of wheel-turning kings (cakravartin) bring the various directions under their majestic authority over a single continent: Ci'en states that those with the golden wheel convert others by the mere sound of their reputation;

those with the silver wheel subdue them by sending envoys; those with the copper wheel bring them into submission by manifesting their majesty; and those with the iron wheel must first brandish their halberds to establish order.
Now, the wheel-turning king is used as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s transformation of the world; his subduing of various kingdoms is analogous to [the Buddha’s] subduing [of sentient beings].
The five aggregates (*skandha*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) constitute the various objects. △ Second, the minor kings do not obey:

the various minor kings who do not comply with his commands are likened to the various afflictions (*kleśa*) that have not yet been subdued by untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*); this is termed "not obeying his commands."
△ Third, mobilizing the army to go forth and wage war.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King raises various kinds of troops to go and subdue [the enemy].
The raising of various kinds of troops is a metaphor for the methods cultivated among the Seven Sages; the *srotāpanna* serves as the vanguard.
The methods cultivated within the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin constitute the vanguard army; the methods cultivated within the stages of Anāgāmin and Arhat constitute the rear guard army.
That which is destroyed by this [vanguard] refers to the eighty-four thousand crown-thieves of the three poisons in equal measure.
That which is able to destroy them refers to the officers and soldiers of the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates. As it says in the *Myōryaku* (Sukhāvatīvyūha): "Eighty..."
The "ten thousand" and so forth refer merely to the eighty thousand [dharmas] of the Hīnayāna. △ Fourth, joy at meritorious achievement:
when the king sees that his troops have achieved merit in battle, he immediately feels great joy.
△ 5. Bestowing Rewards According to Merit.
Bestowing rewards according to merit may consist of granting fields, houses, villages, cities, and even slaves and subjects.

"Fields" refers to *samādhi*; "houses" refer to wisdom; "villages" refer to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*); "towns" refer to the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*); and "cities" refer to the third fruit (*anāgāmin*).
The city is the *nirvāṇa* of the four fruits; the clothing is the wholesome dharmas of shame and patience; the ornaments for the body are the wholesome dharmas that assist the path;
the various kinds of seven treasures are the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and so forth;

the elephants, horses, and carriages are the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) of the two vehicles; and the male and female servants are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the acquisition of contaminated wholesome dharmas, just as in the case of a person.
"The 'people' refers to the rank of the Seven Sages. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Part Six, Lower Section, states:

'Bestowing rewards according to merit' means that because of their respective functions of diligence, when the Buddha as a Wheel-Turning King sees those in the Small Vehicle who have slightly succeeded in destroying the thieves of views and afflictions, he bestows upon them the fields and houses of mundane dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava) realm;
if he sees a Great Being who should destroy great delusions and has achieved great merit..."
He immediately bestowed upon him the bright pearl from within his topknot. △ Sixth, he did not give him the pearl;
specifically, he did not give him the bright pearl from within his topknot (until) the King and all his retinue were greatly astonished and marveled.

The topknot is a metaphor for the provisional (upāya) and the jewel is a metaphor for the real (tattva). To say that the bright pearl within the topknot is "the real hidden by the provisional" means that what is situated upon the crown represents the ultimate goal of the teaching.
For those with the capacity to transcend birth-and-death within the realms of form and desire, this constitutes a minor achievement;

for those with the capacity to transcend birth-and-death within the realm of subtle transformation (nirmāṇa-kāya), this constitutes a great achievement. Those who are "startled and amazed" are those who have not yet attained greatness.
When the King suddenly bestowed the topknot jewel upon his attendants, all the ministers were filled with doubt and wonder;

this is like the Great Vehicle’s profound capacity remaining unmoved while the Buddha suddenly preaches this sutra, causing those of the Two Vehicles to be perplexed and the Bodhisattvas to be struck with amazement. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Volume 6, Part 2, states:

"Upon the summit of the true Dharma-realm, he opens the topknot of provisional truth that is identical in essence to reality, bestowing the bright pearl of the true mark and receiving the prediction of becoming a Dharma King. △ Second, the synthesis.
Just as the six [kings] first united and subdued all nations, so too is it with the Tathāgata Mañjuśrī;
having attained his own kingdom, he reigns as king over the three realms.
The following six sections correspond to the preceding analogies. △ Second, the analogy for the minor kings who do not submit;
this corresponds to how the various māra kings refuse to yield or submit.
△ Third, the analogy for mobilizing troops to go forth and attack; this corresponds to [the Buddha] sending forth his army.
The Tathāgata and the various noble generals fight alongside them.
△ Fourth, rejoicing in shared merit:
those who have achieved merit also rejoice in their hearts.
△ Fifth, bestowing rewards in accordance with merit.
Among the fourfold assembly, he preaches various sūtras (up to) guiding their minds so that they all rejoice.

As for the faculties and powers (*indriya* and *bala*), these refer to the five faculties and five powers within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*). One cultivates these faculties and powers.
Because one does not fall into the cycle of birth and death within the six realms of existence, these are called the "untainted faculties and powers" (*anāsrava-indriya-bala*).
"Nirvāṇa" is here translated as "extinction and deliverance" (*mie-du*); this refers specifically to the *śūnyatā-nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle.

Because this *śūnyatā-nirvāṇa* can prevent the errors of view-delusion and thought-delusion, and repel the enemy of birth and death, it is called the "City of Nirvāṇa. △ Sixth: Harmonizing with yet not being attached to.
The jewel.
Yet he did not preach this Lotus Sūtra for him.
△ Second, the analogy of giving the jewel, which illustrates hearing [this teaching] today. First, opening the analogy. First, there is the prior merit.
Mañjuśrī, it is like a Wheel-Turning King who, seeing among his troops those who have achieved great merit, feels profound joy.
△ Second, the giving of the jewel:
because this jewel so difficult to believe in had long remained within his topknot and was not given to others indiscriminately, he now bestows it upon him.

The jewel within the topknot is indeed covered by the provisional; untying the topknot immediately reveals the provisional, and the jewel is manifested, which serves as an analogy for the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation of the real through the opening of the provisional.
Because it was kept secret and not spoken of for more than forty years, it is said that "it was not given to others recklessly.
△ Second, the combined analogy, in two parts: first, combining [the analogy] with the one who has performed meritorious service.

The Tathāgata is also like this within the triple world... at that time, the Tathāgata was also greatly rejoiced. Regarding the "noble ones and sages" as clarified above, the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states: "Knowing suffering destroys the demon of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*);

severing the origin [of suffering] leaves one free from the demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*); realizing cessation leaves one free from the demon of death (*mṛtyumāra*); and practicing the path destroys the demon of the gods (*devaputramāra*). Regarding the phrase "seeing the noble ones and sages," the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* says: "Knowing suffering destroys the aggregate-demon; severing the origin leaves one free from the affliction-demon; realizing cessation leaves one free from the death-demon; and practicing the path destroys..."

Regarding the statement "the celestial lord Māra is not now called the celestial lord Māra": this is because those of the Hīnayāna have largely severed the three *māras*, yet they have not destroyed the celestial lord Māra;
nevertheless, since the sense of having destroyed him exists—because one must subdue Māra upon attaining the Way—it is so stated. Regarding "possessing great meritorious achievements" and so forth:

the Tathāgata sees that these worthy ones of the Hīnayāna have already eliminated the suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) within the realms, as well as the [defilements associated with] the aggregates (*skandha*).
When one reaches the Prajñāpāramitā and subsequently destroys ignorance (*avidyā*) to emerge from the *nirmāṇa-bhava* (transformation-existence), this is called a "great meritorious achievement.
