Therefore, the three poisons (*triviṣa*) and so forth are, for the time being, explained within the context of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). Regarding these three poisons—greed (*lobha*), anger (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*)—when they exist within the afflictions of views (*darśana-heya-kleśa*), they are called the "perverse three poisons";

when they exist within the afflictions of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), they are called the "genuine three poisons. Thus, it is known that the three poisons do not transcend the two categories of views and mental cultivation.
The deluded perceive that the Tathāgata has already severed both views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), transcended the three realms, and is no longer ensnared by the net of Māra;
they know that before long he will surely shatter the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*) and emerge from the suffering of the *pariṇāmi-ka* (transformation) birth-and-death.

Therefore, it is universally called "Joy. Regarding the term "Lord of Māras" (*māra-devendra*): according to the *Mingyi* (Exposition of Names), this refers to the Lord of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Attached to...
One who delights in false views and harbors hatred and envy toward all sages, arhats, the path to nirvāṇa, and the Dharma is called the Heavenly Lord Māra.
△ Second, the bestowing of the jewel:
"This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* can cause sentient beings... (up to)... therefore I entrust it to you all and shall expound it."

The "Omniscient One" (sarvajña) refers to one who can know and understand all internal phenomena (adhyātmika-dharma) and internal names, and can also know and understand all external phenomena (bāhya-dharma) and external names;
however, because they cannot give rise to all aspects (sarvākāra) through every path, they are not designated as "Omniscient.
The commentary states that "internal phenomena and internal names" refers to the characteristics of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa) as expounded within the [Buddhist] tradition.
Regarding "the names that express phenomena external to the self" and "phenomena and names expressed apart from principle":

when the contemplation of the emptiness of both the characteristics of the phenomena expressed and the names that express them is accomplished, one is able to realize the essence of these names and characteristics.

As for "having many enemies," this refers to those such as the five thousand who withdrew from their seats; it is as the saying goes: "Even while the Tathāgata was present, there were still many who were envious and hostile. This refers to those who find it difficult to believe.
This refers to those of middling and inferior faculties who are only able to achieve faith and understanding after two cycles of parables and causal conditions.
Regarding the phrase "the foremost among all teachings," it is because this sutra is the most supreme among those already taught, currently being taught, and yet to be taught.

As for the "bright pearl": "bright" is a metaphor for the wisdom of the Middle Way, and the "pearl" is a metaphor for the perfect and substantial principle; it is capable of leading one to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Wisdom is the name for the fruit; the beginning of practice is the cause, and the end of practice is the fruit—this practice is one.

This first point is the oneness of the teaching; the secret treasury is the oneness of the principle. Placing all sons within the secret treasury, I myself shall also before long abide therein—this also includes the oneness of the person.

II. Verses (in two parts): First, the verses. [The verse follows: "The Buddha’s wisdom is profound and subtle, difficult to understand and difficult to enter... [and so forth]. (Note: The provided text fragment ends with the heading for the second section of the verses. The full versified portion would follow this structural marker.)
Regarding the first of the two parts on the practice of the Dharma, this verse summarizes the accomplishment of that practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"By constantly practicing patience and showing compassion for all beings, one is able to expound the sutras praised by the Buddha."

The following four lines of verse concern the accomplishment of practice. While the preceding prose section explained the accomplishment of practice in general, these verses now manifest it specifically:
"Constantly practicing patience" (verse) refers to the accomplishment of wearing the robe of patience;

"having compassion for all" (verse) refers to the accomplishment of entering the chamber of loving-kindness and compassion; and "being able to expound [the Dharma]" (verse) refers to the accomplishment of sitting upon the seat of the emptiness of phenomena. △
Second, the verse on the method for following [the teaching]. First, the verse on the object of the vow:
in the final age, one should generate compassion toward those who uphold this sutra—whether they be householders, renunciants, or even those who are not bodhisattvas.
△ 2. The reason for the vow:
It would be a great loss if these people were not to hear or believe this sutra.
△ 3. The formal establishment of the vow.
When I attain the Way of the Buddha, I shall use various skillful means to preach this Dharma for them, so that they may abide within it.

△ Second, the verse praising the sutra has two parts: first, the verse illustrating the analogy; second, the verse on the analogy of not giving the jewel. First, the verse on the analogy of not giving the jewel.
For example, it is like a powerful Wheel-Turning King who joyfully bestows upon [a subject] female attendants, wealth, and possessions.
△ Second, the verse on the analogy of the crest-jewel:
It is as if there were a valiant hero capable of performing difficult deeds, and the King untied the bright pearl from within his topknot and bestowed it upon him.
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Volume 6, Part 2, states: "Because his power enables him to advance toward the reality, he is called 'valiant and courageous.

Because he gives rise to the practice of diligence based on principle, he is said to 'be able to perform difficult tasks. Now, the Buddha as a Wheel-Turning King understands the provisional and bestows the real;
therefore, it says 'the King unties the topknot,' and so forth. △ Second, the verse that combines the parables, in two parts: first, the verse combining the part about not giving the jewel.
The Tathāgata is likewise the King of all dharmas; (up to: by means of great skillful expedients, he has preached these various sūtras.
△ Second, the verse on the analogy of the jewel:
Having known that sentient beings have obtained its power, (up to: now is precisely the time for me to speak it for you.
The preceding section, comprising ten and a half verses beginning with "For example, like one of great strength," is a praise of the sutra.
"His power" refers to the power of *vīrya* (diligence). "Not revealing [the truth] falsely" means that the great capacity [of the disciples] has not yet matured.

"Now is precisely the time" means it is precisely the time to reveal the provisional (*upāya*) and manifest the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*). △ Third, the summary of the characteristics of the accomplishment of practice, in three parts; first, the summary.
The exhortation on the four practices:
"After my parinirvāṇa, those who seek the Buddha-way (up to) should draw near to these four dharmas.
The following twenty-three lines constitute the third summary, which describes the signs of the attainment of practice and the resulting responses, serving as an exhortation.
The practice now concludes with the exhortation to bind the body, speech, and mind through the four vows.

△ Second, citing the three retributions to provide exhortation, also called the purification of the three obstacles: first, the obstacle of retribution is transformed, whereby the present retribution is turned away.
Those who read this sutra will always be free from sorrow and affliction, and shall likewise be free from illness, their complexions bright and pure.
Hereafter, three types of retribution are presented to encourage the upholding of this sutra; this present instance concerns the transformation of karmic obstacles in the present life.

By extinguishing the sorrows and afflictions of the present world, the retribution of painful sensations is eliminated; this is the transformation of the mind regarding present-life retribution. There is no [further suffering].

The fact that the color of their illness is bright white is the manifestation of the retribution of the present life. △ Second, the transformation of karmic obstacles results in the non-arising of the retribution of future lives;
one will not be born into poverty, low status, or ugliness.

This refers to the transformation of evil karma. Because the causes of evil karma ought to result in evil fruits, by the power of upholding this sutra, one transforms the evil cause to obtain a good fruit;
this is the transformation of retribution in a future birth. "Non-arising" means that there is no arising of evil;

by upholding the sutra in the present, one does not create the karma for poverty, and thus will not be born into a lowly or base state in a future life. △ Third, the obstacle of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa).

Regarding the second part of the subsequent retribution, there are two sections. First, the specific explanation of the transformation of the three afflictive hindrances. First, the specific explanation of the transformation of the hindrance of greed:
sentient beings delight in beholding [the practitioner] as if yearning for a noble sage; celestial youths serve as his attendants.

These three lines—“this sentient being delights in being seen,” “down to the lowest [realms] like the sun’s illumination”—specifically clarify the transformation of the three afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Now, first, it clarifies the transformation of the hindrance of greed: those with excessive desire are treated with contempt by others, and this also hinders birth in the Brahma heavens;
now that the hindrance of greed has been transformed, sentient beings delight in seeing them, people no longer treat them with contempt, and they become like celestial youths (*devakumāra*).
Having attendants does not obstruct birth in the Brahma heavens. △ Second, specifically clarifying the transformation of the obstacle of anger:
weapons and staves cannot be applied, poisons cannot cause harm, and one wanders without fear like a lion king.

This clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of anger (*dveṣa*). By abandoning anger, one removes the internal sword and arrows; thus, when entering the fray, external blades cannot wound one. Therefore, it is said that "swords and staves do not strike.
Anger is the poisonous drug that harms loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*); if there is already loving-kindness and compassion within, external poisons cannot cause harm.
Anger is the internal organ of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*); if there is no anger within, then [harsh words] enter the mouth [but do not take root].
Because they are obstructed and unable to utter abusive speech, and because others do not harm them with abuse, they have no fear or apprehension in places where they travel.
△ Third, a specific explanation of the transformation of the obstacle of delusion.
The light of wisdom shines like the sun.
This signifies the transformation of the obscuration of ignorance.

Since ignorance can obstruct wisdom, once the obscuration of ignorance has been transformed, the light of wisdom shines like the sun. △ Second, a general explanation of the transformation of all afflictions (six points).
First, the dream of entering the ten stages of faith; second, first, the explicit explanation of the retribution of compassion.
If, within the dream, one sees only wondrous things (up to) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, paying homage with palms joined.
The following sixteen lines collectively clarify that the transformation of all afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is also a transformation of future retribution (*paścātpākaphala*).

Because the merit of the four practices—body, speech, mind, and vow—has been perfected, and because the power of propagating the sutra has caused the merit of conversion to accrue to oneself, the signs of fruition first manifest;
thus, the various things seen within dreams are all future retributions.
The marks [of Buddhahood] manifest the events of hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas within a single thought-moment; this serves to illustrate that the wondrous Dharma is inconceivable.
Within the one there are the immeasurable, and within the immeasurable there is the one. These marks appear before us, and in the future they shall surely bear fruit.
From the initial stage of the ten faiths up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment, the attainment of Buddhahood through the eight signs is entirely adorned by the adornments of the Tathāgata.
"Vigor" is the retribution for patience; these two and a half lines specifically refer to the retribution for compassion.
△ Second, "right view" is the retribution for non-delusion:
he sees his own body and preaches the Dharma for it.
Because there is no false delusion, one attains right view; because of right view, there is wisdom;
and because there is wisdom, one is able to preach the Dharma. Therefore, these two phrases are categorized as the retribution of right view and freedom from delusion.
From the previous categorization up to this point—wherein one preaches the Dharma even within a dream—it all constitutes entering the stage of the Ten Faiths of the Perfect Teaching.
...Furthermore, he sees the physical marks of the various Buddhas as golden (up to) "there are also the fourfold assemblies with palms joined listening to the Dharma.

These six lines and a half of verse clarify the dream-entry into the ten abodes (*bhūmi*). Since it is said within the abodes that one "sees the Buddha," this represents [the realization] within oneself.
This is because upon attaining the first stage of the eightfold marks, one immediately shatters one grade of ignorance and manifests as a Buddha throughout the hundred worlds.
"Seeing the body abide in the center" signifies entering the Middle Way of the true mark (*dharmatā*);

"hearing the Dharma with joy" signifies the first stage of the Bodhisattva path, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*), for seeing the Middle Way is equal to the initial Joyful Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Thus, it is also called the *Prāmodya-dhāraṇī*.

"Cloud" (dhāraṇī) means "able to hold": it refers to the ability to collect various wholesome dharmas and maintain them so that they are neither dispersed nor lost. It is also translated as "total retention" (saṃgraha-dhāraṇī), meaning to retain the wholesome without loss and to prevent the unwholesome from arising. It is also translated as "obstructive retention" (vighna-dhāraṇī), meaning to obstruct the evils of the two extremes and to maintain the goodness of the Middle Way. What is now called "attaining the dhāraṇī" consists of three aspects: 1. Retention of hearing (śruta-dhāraṇī): retaining all that has been heard without forgetting. 2. Retention of dharma (dharma-dhāraṇī): retaining all the teachings of the Buddhas without forgetting. 3. Retention of meaning (artha-dhāraṇī): retaining the meanings of all dharmas without forgetting. These three types of dhāraṇī are collectively termed the "Dhāraṇī of Non-forgetfulness. Furthermore, there are four kinds of dhāraṇī: first, the dhāraṇī of the letters; second, the dhāraṇī of the words; third, the dhāraṇī of the phrases; and fourth, the dhāraṇī of the meanings. Among these, the dhāraṇī of the letters refers to the forty-two letters, such as A, Ā, and so forth. The dhāraṇī of the words refers to the names of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, such as Akṣobhya, Vairocana, and others. The dhāraṇī of the phrases refers to the various sūtras and treatises, such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and others. The dhāraṇī of the meanings refers to the realization of the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing, which is the true nature of all dharmas. By attaining these four kinds of dhāraṇī, one is able to uphold the Buddha's teachings and benefit sentient beings. This is what is meant by "attaining the dhāraṇī. Furthermore, there are five kinds of dhāraṇī: first, the dhāraṇī of the letters; second, the dhāraṇī of the words; third, the dhāraṇī of the phrases; fourth, the dhāraṇī of the meanings; and fifth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the seal (mudrā). The dhāraṇī of the power of the seal refers to the attainment of the samādhi of the seal of non-arising, whereby one can manifest various transformations to subdue sentient beings and cause them to enter the path of the Dharma. By attaining these five kinds of dhāraṇī, one is able to fulfill the great vows of a Bodhisattva and attain supreme enlightenment. This is what is meant by "attaining the dhāraṇī. Furthermore, there are six kinds of dhāraṇī: first, the dhāraṇī of the letters; second, the dhāraṇī of the words; third, the dhāraṇī of the phrases; fourth, the dhāraṇī of the meanings; fifth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the seal; and sixth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the mantra. The dhāraṇī of the power of the mantra refers to the recitation of mantras and dhāraṇīs, which can eliminate obstacles and bring about auspiciousness. By attaining these six kinds of dhāraṇī, one is able to overcome all difficulties and achieve all merits. This is what is meant by "attaining the dhāraṇī. Furthermore, there are seven kinds of dhāraṇī: first, the dhāraṇī of the letters; second, the dhāraṇī of the words; third, the dhāraṇī of the phrases; fourth, the dhāraṇī of the meanings; fifth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the seal; sixth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the mantra; and seventh, the dhāraṇī of the power of the samādhi. The dhāraṇī of the power of the samādhi refers to the attainment of various profound samādhis, such as the Lion’s Roar Samādhi, the Moon-Light Samādhi, and others, whereby one can manifest various spiritual powers to transform sentient beings. By attaining these seven kinds of dhāraṇī, one is able to perfect the path of a Bodhisattva and attain the fruit of Buddhahood. This is what is meant by "attaining the dhāraṇī. Furthermore, there are eight kinds of dhāraṇī: first, the dhāraṇī of the letters; second, the dhāraṇī of the words; third, the dhāraṇī of the phrases; fourth, the dhāraṇī of the meanings; fifth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the seal; sixth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the mantra; seventh, the dhāraṇī of the power of the samādhi; and eighth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the vow. The dhāraṇī of the power of the vow refers to the power of the original vows made by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, whereby they can respond to the needs of sentient beings and deliver them according to their capacities. By attaining these eight kinds of dhāraṇī, one is able to fulfill the great compassionate vows and universally benefit all beings. This is what is meant by "attaining the dhāraṇī. Furthermore, there are nine kinds of dhāraṇī: first, the dhāraṇī of the letters; second, the dhāraṇī of the words; third, the dhāraṇī of the phrases; fourth, the dhāraṇī of the meanings; fifth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the seal; sixth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the mantra; seventh, the dhāraṇī of the power of the samādhi; eighth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the vow; and ninth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the merit. The dhāraṇī of the power of the merit refers to the power derived from the accumulation of vast merit over many kalpas, whereby one can spontaneously manifest various transformations to benefit sentient beings. By attaining these nine kinds of dhāraṇī, one is able to transcend the mundane world and enter the realm of the Buddhas. This is what is meant by "attaining the dhāraṇī. Furthermore, there are ten kinds of dhāraṇī: first, the dhāraṇī of the letters; second, the dhāraṇī of the words; third, the dhāraṇī of the phrases; fourth, the dhāraṇī of the meanings; fifth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the seal; sixth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the mantra; seventh, the dhāraṇī of the power of the samādhi; eighth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the vow; ninth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the merit; and tenth, the dhāraṇī of the power of the wisdom. The dhāraṇī of the power of the wisdom refers to the power of the wisdom of the non-arising of all dharmas, whereby one can clearly perceive the true nature of all things and attain liberation. By attaining these ten kinds of dhāraṇī, one is able to realize the ultimate truth and become a true vessel for the Dharma. This is what is meant by "attaining the dhāraṇī. Thus, the term "dhāraṇī" encompasses these various meanings and functions. One who attains them is truly a Mahāsattva who upholds the treasury of the Buddhas. This concludes the explanation of the dhāraṇī. Now, regarding the specific dhāraṇī mentioned here, it is the "Dhāraṇī of the Seal of Non-arising," which is the most profound and essential among all

Regarding the *Sūtra-dhāraṇī* (Revolution Dhāraṇī), the *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* explains the "Dhāraṇī of Two Hundred Thousand Myriad Koṭis of Revolutions" and the "Dhāraṇī of Skillful Means of the Three Dharma-Sounds" as follows:
"Revolution" (*xuan*) means to turn. It refers to turning from the conventional into emptiness to realize the True Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
"Two hundred thousand myriad koṭis" refers to turning from emptiness into the conventional, revolving through analytical discernment to shatter the delusions that are as numerous as motes of dust.

The "expedient means of the Dharma-sound that manifests the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" refers precisely to entering the Middle Way through the expedient means of the two contemplations.
"Non-retrogressive wisdom" refers to the three types of non-retrogression, as explained at the beginning of the Introduction Chapter (*Nidāna-parivarta*).

Since it is stated that one who realizes non-retrogressive wisdom is conferred with a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), one should know that upon entering the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), one attains the prediction of non-arising (*anutpāda-vyākaraṇa*).
This is the stage [of the ten abodes]. △ Third, dreaming of practicing the ten practices:
again, one sees oneself practicing wholesome dharmas within mountains and forests.
Since it is stated that after dreaming of entering the ten abodes, "one again sees oneself in the mountains and forests," etc., it is known that this refers to the ten [practices].
"Practice" (*xing*) refers to the cultivation of wholesome dharmas. Miaole states: "Regarding 'cultivation' and 'practice,' it is not that there was no practice prior to this;
rather, it is because one attains the specific designation of 'practice' most fully upon reaching this stage. △ Fourth, the dream-awakening of the ten transferences.
"Realizing all true realities.
Since it says "realizing all true realities," this refers to the stage of the Middle Way within the correct contemplation of the Ten Stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*).
The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "'Realizing all'—the word 'all' precisely indicates the severing of the thirty grades of ignorance. △ Five: Entering a Dream.
The Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*).

Deeply entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), the Buddhas of the ten directions—those who have deeply entered meditative concentration—are, within the tenth ground, in the stainless samādhi (*vimala-samādhi*) and enter the diamond-like concentration (*vajra-samādhi*). All Buddhas [are thus].

All [the Buddhas] appear to touch their heads with their hands (mōding) and confer their offices. Miaole says: "Regarding the term 'stainless' (wugou), it is already attained at the first stage (prathamabhūmi).
To accord with the Great Sutra, the stainless samādhi is correlated with the first stage; therefore, for now, we speak from the perspective of the first stage.

If one speaks of entering the diamond-like concentration (vajropamasamādhi), that refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi); however, Equal Enlightenment is properly included within the ten stages."
△ Sixth, the dream of entering wondrous enlightenment.
[The text continues: "The bodies of all Buddhas are golden, adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings... (up to) "...like a lamp extinguished when the smoke has vanished.
Since one dreams of performing the eight phases of a Buddha’s life, one knows this is a dream of entering wondrous enlightenment; this may refer to the initial stage.
The state of abiding in the eight aspects of attaining Buddhahood is merely a provisional discussion of the ultimate fruit based on the preceding stages.

Dreaming of becoming a king represents the three phases of descending from Tuṣita, entering the womb, and being born. Leaving the palace, abandoning the five desires, and proceeding to the site of enlightenment represent the phase of renunciation.
Attaining the Unsurpassed Way necessarily involves subduing Māra, which represents the phase of attaining enlightenment.

The two phases of attaining enlightenment and subduing Māra, and the two phases of turning the wheel of Dharma and entering nirvana, are as described in the text. "The smoke ends and the lamp is extinguished":
smoke is a metaphor for the capacity [of the recipient], and the lamp is a metaphor for the response [of the teacher].

The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states that since "peaceful bliss" (*anle*) is the practice of the Tathāgata, those who propagate the sutra prefigure the attainment of the fruit. Thus, we know that the power of the merit of propagation is not small. △ Three: General Summary.
The practice is thus established.
If, in future evil ages, one speaks of this supreme Dharma, that person will obtain great benefit and the aforementioned merits.
This concludes the establishment of the practice.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Fifteen: The Emergence from the Earth.

The Teacher is venerable and the Way is august; bowing in reverent service, they obey a single command of the Tathāgata, rushing forth from all quarters. Hence it is called "The Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth.
This is an explanation according to the *loka-nirukti* (worldly standpoint). Their guidance and transformation throughout the three periods of time bring benefit and profit without end.
"A single month contains ten thousand shadows; who can fathom this? He summons the past to manifest to the present and propagates the wondrous sutra to benefit those of the future;
therefore it is called the 'Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth. This is an explanation according to the *puruṣa-saṃvṛti-satya* (the standpoint of human convention).
Space is serene and still, without beginning or end, yet those who are deluded cling to its traces and remain dark regarding its source; thus he summons the past to reveal [the truth]."

Now, because it refutes the near to reveal the far, it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth"; this is an explanation according to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic antidotes).

Because the young father at the site of tranquility and the old child in the land of tranquil light manifest the power of their medicine so that all may come to know it, it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth";
this is an explanation according to the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth). [The following is] from the *Miaole* (The Joyful Explanation) itself.

Because one ascends to this, it is the world; it summons the person and manifests the person, causing the person to manifest and giving rise to goodness in that person, enabling them to propagate and manifest the sutra so that they may give rise to goodness in their future lives—therefore, it is called "the person. Regarding "space and so forth," this refers to what is symbolized:

space is the principle (*li*), while the fundamental and the manifested (*honjaku*) are the phenomena (*ji*); within phenomena there are the fundamental and the manifested, and within principle there are likewise the fundamental and the manifested.

There is no distinction between early and late; however, those who are deluded are confused about the principle and obscure the relationship between the fundamental and the manifest. Thus, they cling to the near manifest and lose sight of the distant fundamental.
To summon the past and reveal the present, and to shatter the evil of clinging to the near, this is the application of remedial treatment (*pratipakṣa*).

At the site of tranquility (*śītavana*), Śākyamuni manifests his initial attainment of Buddhahood, and thus he is like a young father. In the realm of tranquil light (*sukhāvatī*), the Bodhisattva’s practice has long been established, and thus he is like an aged son. This is likened to the power of medicine.
The father has long since taken the elixir of the seed of wisdom that restores youth;

though he is old, he appears as if young. The son has also long received the method of eternal non-death; though he is young, he appears as if old. Therefore, this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Section Two:

At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas [up to] "to protect, uphold, read, recite, and extensively expound this sutra.
The Tathāgata’s prohibition of this has three general meanings: first, the bodhisattvas from other lands each have their own specific duties;
second, if they were to remain in this land, they would neglect the benefits for those lands; and third, the bodhisattvas from other lands have shallow karmic connections with this land.

Although one might wish to proclaim and transmit [the teaching], there would necessarily be no great benefit; furthermore, if it were permitted, the Bodhisattvas from the lower regions could not be summoned. If the Bodhisattvas from the lower regions did not come here, the immediate traces (近迹) could not be destroyed and the distant root (遠本) could not be revealed. For these three reasons, the Tathāgata refrained from doing so. There are also three reasons for summoning those from the lower regions to come. It is as follows: 1. My disciples should propagate my Dharma; because its conditions are profound and vast, it can benefit this land universally and also benefit other lands afar.
Furthermore, it opens up the near to reveal the far; for this reason, they remain there while summoning those below. △ Third, the emergence from below the earth, in two parts:
first, the narrative by the sūtra compiler describing the signs, in five parts; first, the emergence.
When the Buddha spoke these words, [the beings] from the Sahā world up to the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas simultaneously surged forth.
*Miaole* (The Wondrous Joy) says: "As for 'the earth splitting,' it refers to the earth covering its original retinue, as when a footprint conceals its source;
now, by opening the provisional to reveal the fundamental, the earth splits to symbolize this. △ Second, the physical marks.
The bodies of these bodhisattvas are all golden in color, endowed with the thirty-two marks and immeasurable radiance.
△ Third, their dwelling places:
they originally all resided beneath this Sahā world, in the void of space within this realm.
The "dwelling place" is the Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-śānta-prabhā*). "Constant" refers to the virtue of permanence; "quiescent" refers to the virtue of bliss;
and "light" refers to the two virtues of purity and self. This secret treasury of the four virtues is the dwelling place.

Because it dwells within the secret treasury by means of the dharma of non-dwelling, and because it is the abyssal bottom of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) and the ultimate stage of the profound principle (*paramārtha*), it is called the "lower direction."
"Not belonging to this below, not belonging to that above, neither that nor this—this is the Middle Way.
Furthermore, "emerging from here, not remaining above, nor remaining here below; dwelling in the midst of space—this too is the Middle Way. The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states:
"The abyssal depths of the *dharmatā* explain the term 'below' (*shaka*); it is the ultimate limit of the profound principle (*xuanzong*)."

The "Earth" (bhūmi) explains the direction; it is called the "Mysterious Ultimate" (*xuánzōng*) because it is the source of profound principles. "Ultimate" (*zōng*) refers to the final goal, that which is expected when attaining the fruit.
These various Bodhisattvas have reached their respective expected goals and are thus said to be at the "Ultimate Stage.

Those who do not belong here are situated below, for they are in the void and do not belong to this realm (the void below is called the "lower void"). Those who do not belong there reside within the void.
Because they are in the air below, they do not belong to that realm; since they have emerged from here and do not remain above, they are not of the upper realm.
Since they do not remain here below, it is said they are in the air of this very realm. As the Sūtra says:
"Having emerged from the earth, each went into the void. △ Fourth, hearing the command.
These bodhisattvas heard the sounds spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha emanating from below.
As for the reasons for their coming: they came because they had received the summons; they came to propagate the Dharma; they came to shatter attachments;
and they came to reveal the fundamental nature—all as described above. △ Five: The Retinue.
Each and every bodhisattva is a leader at the head of a great assembly (up to the point where they are beyond what can be known).

As for the retinues they lead: if one were to judge by common human standards, leading six or five *koṭis* of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands] would be considered many, while leading three, two, or one would be considered few;
those who are alone are solitary and single. If one were to seek this according to the literal text:
Sixty thousand and fifty thousand are few; those who are alone are many. Therefore, the verse below says: "Those who dwell alone and solitary are even more numerous than that.
If one relies on the Dharma-gate, each and every one is a teacher capable of leading the multitude to the place of treasure.
One should know that "one" does not mean only sixty thousand, nor does "many" mean only fifty thousand.
1. That is the single path of purity; 2. These two are concentration and wisdom; 3. These three are precepts, concentration, and wisdom; 4. These four are the Four Noble Truths;

5. These five are the Five Eyes; 6. These six are the Six Perfections. Each perfection encompasses the ten dharma-realms, and as each realm mutually encompasses the others, they form one hundred dharma-realms.
Within each realm, the ten suchnesses are present, thus forming one thousand suchnesses. Within each suchness, the ten wholesome acts are present, thereby forming ten thousand wholesome acts.
Once one possesses the ten thousand and six perfections, these constitute sixty thousand dharma-gates; many are not considered many, and one is not considered few.

It is neither many nor few, yet it is both many and few (many is the emptiness of non-multiplicity; one is the conventionality of non-solitude; the dual negation and dual illumination are the Middle Way).

Herein, the distinctness of the six perfections is clarified—not according to the common teaching of the six perfections being mutually adorned—but rather based on the discussion of the six perfections from the perspective of the wondrous realm.
The "Ears of Wondrous Joy" (Ear-miao-yueyun) refers to the practice of relying on wondrous objects to transform and perfect the ten thousand [senses]. △ Second, the assembly’s inquiry:
Part one of three, the offering of the three karmas.
These bodhisattvas, having emerged from the earth... (up to) ...joyfully gazed up at the two World-Honored Ones.
The seats beneath the trees are those upon which the various emanated Buddhas sit; to bow around them is the body [of worship], to praise the Dharma is the mouth, and to gaze up at them is the mind.
From the moment these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first surged forth until they caused the great assembly to perceive it as being only half a day.
Fifty minor kalpas are said to be like half a day; the fourfold assembly perceives this universally.
This is achieved by concealing the long and manifesting the short, employing his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to make the narrow appear broad. Both of these are inconceivable.
That fifty minor kalpas and half a day are identical in duration is an inconceivability regarding time as perceived by the Tathāgata.
Not perceiving them through dualistic marks, he constantly faces and extols the Bodhisattvas of the lower stages; the Tathāgata silently accepts these praises.
To those who understand, what is short is made long—meaning fifty small kalpas; to those who are deluded, what is long is made short—meaning half a day.
This serves as an introductory lead-in for the primary and the manifested traces. If the Tathāgata had not yet spoken, they would have remained ignorant of the fundamental reality.
If one who adheres to the traces of the Buddha reveals and clarifies [the truth], they will awaken to the near and reach the far, realizing that the inconceivable is one.
*Miaole* says: "Fifty minor kalpas are made to seem like half a day.

This clarifies the Tathāgata’s inconceivable power of extending and contracting time, manifesting the sovereign power of the Tathāgata. Since it is said, "He causes the great assembly to perceive... [as if it were half a day].
Just as half a day is shortened for them so that they perceive it as brief, it is said that "the long is concealed";

the same applies to length and breadth. This statement means that what is long is short; the fourfold assembly sees it everywhere (referring to the passage below concerning the fourfold assembly seeing the Bodhisattva).
This statement means that what is narrow is broad. Some say (this refers to Master Daosheng): "The resolve to hear the Dharma causes one to forget its length," or it is also said: [the same].
That both length and shortness are lost, yet length and shortness are preserved—this is to gain the stimulus while losing the response.
How can this suppress the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata? Regarding what the Tathāgata perceives as equal: when viewed with the Buddha-eye, length and shortness are non-dual;

when viewed with the four eyes, length and shortness are not absent. Therefore, he accords with the capacities of beings regarding length and shortness, causing them to see things as not being one and the same.
At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, the fourfold assembly likewise [saw] the empty space of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands.
That the fourfold assembly saw Bodhisattvas everywhere is the Tathāgata lending his supernatural power to cause them to see the vast within the narrow;
this too is inconceivable. Indeed, what is seen by the fleshly eye and the divine eye does not extend far, yet now—

Seeing that [the realm] fills the void, one knows that since the marks and signs of a Bodhisattva are so numerous, they must have simultaneously realized the true principle that pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
*Myōryaku* (The Wondrous Joy) states: "With the two eyes—the fleshly and the divine—one sees according to their own power, yet not beyond a certain distance.
Now, suddenly seeing what is far away, one knows it is not by one's own power; thus one knows that the Tathāgata has manifested this supernatural transformation. It must be so.
He preached the sublime Dharma. △ Second, the presentation of words of inquiry, in two parts: First, the designation of the four guides.
Among this assembly of bodhisattvas, there were four guides (up to) who were the most eminent leaders and preceptors.
The reason only four persons are mentioned is intended to illustrate the forty stages of "opening, showing, awakening, and entering.

This is similar to how the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* mentions only Dharmamati, Guṇakāra, Suvarṇadhvaja, and Suvarṇagarbha to explain these forty stages. Miaole states that "ni" (擬) means "to compare" or "to correspond," as in the *Avataṃsaka*.
The passage below cites this to show the correspondence between the two; since the Buddha-wisdom of those [in the *Avataṃsaka*] is identical to that of humans, [the analogy holds].

When viewed from the perspective of the Dharma, they are also equal; however, that [the former] is the trace while this [the latter] is the source. That is both [source and trace], whereas this is only the source.

Although source and trace differ, both "this" and "that" consist of the four [assemblies], and as both serve as leaders, they may be treated analogously. Regarding the term "Changdao" (Leader of the Invocation), the supplementary note states:

"To initiate and awaken others to the Dharma-gates is called 'Chang' (Invocation); to guide and receive those with the capacities of sentient beings is called 'Dao' (Leading). 2. The actual presentation of the questions.
Section Two: The Prose Exposition. Part One: Questioning the Tathāgata’s Well-being.
[The assembly] stood before the Tathāgata, each joining their palms together, and asked: "Are you free from illness and affliction, and are you dwelling in peace and happiness?"
△ Second, the question regarding the ease with which sentient beings may be delivered:
"Are those who should be delivered easy to instruct, such that it does not cause the World-Honored One weariness?
△ Second, the verse summary, in two parts: first, the verse summarizing the inquiry as to whether the Tathāgata is at ease.
At that time, the four great bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
"World-Honored One, you are at ease, with little illness and little affliction; you teach and transform sentient beings without ever experiencing weariness.

World-Honored One, you have already transcended the worldly outflows and the five aggregates; how could you have illness or affliction? It is merely that you wish to manifest yourself as being like ordinary humans."
Since the Dharma accords with the constant norms of this land, one must inquire, saying, "I am afflicted by illness. △ Second, the verse asks whether sentient beings are easy to deliver:
"Furthermore, are sentient beings easy to transform, so as not to cause the World-Honored One weariness?"
△ Third, the Buddha’s response regarding his well-being. First, the response concerning his well-being:
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly of bodhisattvas... [until] the Tathāgata is at ease, with little illness and little affliction.
This answers the question posed in the first verse above. △ Second, answering the question regarding the ease of deliverance:

First, those with sharp faculties and abundant merit—“All such sentient beings are easily transformed and delivered” (up to) “they all immediately believe and accept, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata.”

This answers the question posed in the preceding verse. There are two types of those who are easily delivered: first, those with sharp faculties and profound merit who, throughout successive lifetimes, have constantly received the Great Transformation;
upon first beholding my body, they immediately receive the *Avataṃsaka* teachings and enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Because their fruit has ripened, it falls easily—such a class of sentient beings is easily delivered. Second, those with dull faculties and meager merit.
Excepting those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna (up to the point where they hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom)—
among those easily delivered, there are those of dull faculties and meager virtue who, from lifetime to lifetime, have not received the Great Transformation;
for the sake of such people, it was necessary to open up the Sudden teaching and explain the Gradual, including the Tripiṭaka, Vaipulya, and Prajñāpāramitā, in order to discipline them.
It also causes this person, now hearing the Lotus Sūtra, to enter the Buddha-wisdom; compared to what preceded it, although it is difficult, for the Buddha it is exceedingly easy.
Whether their faculties are sharp or dull, that which they enter is the same. In the commentary, ten points are briefly raised to explain this:
first, from "first seeing" to "now seeing," up to the tenth, where those of sharp faculties who have first matured enter the Buddha-wisdom, while those of dull faculties do so later.

Consider that those who have now entered the Buddha’s wisdom must have had different conditions; briefly, there are ten such differences. Because the *sarvajñajñāna* (all-encompassing wisdom) and the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) are without distinction, this sutra states:
"As soon as they see my body and hear what I teach, they all believe and accept it, entering the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
This excludes those who previously practiced and studied the *hīnayāna*, who only now enter the Buddha’s wisdom upon hearing this sutra.

The clear evidence is right here; there is no need for doubt. Formerly it was said that the *Avataṃsaka* is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), complete (*pūrṇa*), and eternally abiding, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is of non-definitive meaning, incomplete, and not eternal.
Now, by comparing them through this text: if what one first entered was of definitive meaning, then what one enters now is of non-definitive meaning;
if what one first entered was the Buddha’s wisdom, then what one enters now is not the Buddha’s wisdom. If...
The Buddha’s wisdom is already perfected, and the definitive meaning is likewise fully complete; the eternal presence of the full letters is entirely thus.
△ Fourth, the verses on sympathetic joy. At that time, the great Bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
"Excellent, excellent, Great Hero, World-Honored One! [and so on] up to "having heard this, we believe and practice it; we rejoice.
The one who asks is none other than the four great bodhisattvas in the *Avataṃsaka* and Śāriputra’s three requests in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
both are capable questioners. That which is asked is precisely the wisdom of the Buddha. *Miaole* says: "Having heard..."
"Those who practice with faith" refers to the people being transformed by the various bodhisattvas who are able to practice with faith after hearing the bodhisattvas' teachings;

"we rejoice" refers to those such as Śreṣṭhadatta who rejoice in the great benefit initiated by the questioning bodhisattvas and rejoice in the people being transformed by those bodhisattvas. △ Five, the Tathāgata’s Response.
[The Buddha] sighed with approval. At that time, the World-Honored One praised the leaders [up to] those who were able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) toward the Tathāgata.
How does the Tathāgata’s expression of praise differ from the previous [passage]? It is because in the preceding text, those who were able to ask questions with sympathetic joy were all...
When these bodhisattvas and those they have transformed hear this and practice it with faith, they are in fact generating a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) toward the bodhisattvas and others.
Now, why does the Tathāgata, in his praise, instead say, "You all are able to generate a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata"?
This is because those who are able to ask such questions are all ancient Buddhas; that you are able to rejoice in accord is itself to follow [the path].
The Tathāgata *Prīti* (Joy) is the Tathāgata who rejoices in the traces of the bodhisattva and praises his original foundation;

this also secretly indicates the wondrous bliss of the lifespan (*āyus-pramāṇa*). Regarding "secretly indicating the lifespan": here, by praising the bodhisattva as already being an ancient Buddha, it secretly indicates that the present Buddha was not newly accomplished in the present.
Since he was not newly accomplished in the present, there must necessarily be a remote origin from which he has not yet [fully] attained [manifestation].

Because it is manifest and clear, it is called the "Secret Manifestation. △ Second, the section on doubts, which has two parts. First, the doubts of the bodhisattvas of this land, which begins with the prose narrative of their reflections:
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, along with eight thousand Ganges-sands [of bodhisattvas]... (omitted)... and wished to resolve their own doubts.
The following is the second introductory section of the inquiry. As for why Maitreya and the various bodhisattvas raise this inquiry:

from the time the *Avataṃsaka* was first preached at the site of enlightenment until now, when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is being taught on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, although the great beings from the ten directions who have come to this assembly are beyond limit, I—by means of the power of my wisdom as one in his final birth (*caramabhavika*)—see and know them all.

Yet among this assembly, there is not a single person he recognizes. Although I have traveled and transformed beings throughout the ten directions, paying homage to the Buddhas, and am well known to the great assemblies of those Buddhas, even when I trace him back to the places where he has journeyed, he still does not recognize me.
Furthermore, while those other Great Beings were advanced scholars who had gone before, Maitreya is a junior student from a later generation.

Because they were unaware of what preceded, they did not recognize him; furthermore, as these Great Beings are fundamentally the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), their manifestations throughout the ten directions—whether as *nirmāṇakāya* or *sambhogakāya*—are beyond the sphere of Maitreya’s perception, and thus he did not recognize them.

Moreover, the Buddha entrusted the propagation of the sutra by summoning these Great Beings to secretly reveal the *Tathāgatāyuṣpramāṇa*; since this was not something known to the assembly at that time, it is said that they did not recognize him. The above.

The various explanations by Śāriputra are based on the intent of the four *siddhāntas*. The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "First, it refers to the coming; second, it refers to the place of departure.
Because coming and departing are different, consciousness does not distinguish them. Because there is no such distinction, there is no benefit for the world (*loka-siddhānta*).

If Maitreya did not know the joy of advancing forward, his own goodness would not arise; thus, there is no benefit for the person (*pudgala-siddhānta*). This is the fundamental purpose of transforming sentient beings."
If Maitreya does not know how to treat the ailments of sentient beings, he would lack the path of benefiting others; thus, failing to recognize the ailment, there would be no benefit from the remedy.
That the "Secret Opening of the Lifespan" (*Guhyakālaṃkāra*) is the ultimate truth is precisely the most extreme principle of this single section;
is it not, therefore, the foremost? Since the assembly at that time did not know this, they lacked the benefit of the ultimate truth. This is so.
It is because Maitreya initiated the assembly and merely said that he did not recognize or know [the Buddha]. △ Second, the verses praising the formal inquiry (five parts):
first, asking from where he has come.
With palms joined toward the Buddha, he asked in verse:
"Immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of the great assembly of bodhisattvas... from where have they come?
"Those with two feet" refers to those who are fully endowed with the two kinds of adornments: merit and wisdom. △ Second, the question of for what reason they have come.
For what causes and conditions have they assembled with such massive bodies and great supernormal powers (up to: from where have they come)?
△ Third, describing their number:
the various retinues led by each of these bodhisattvas (up to: cannot be fully known).
△ 4. He asks whose teacher they are, and what Buddha-way these bodhisattvas of great majesty and diligence have cultivated.
△ 5. Maitreya’s summary request, first summarizing and praising their supernormal power.
Such is the great power of the supernormal knowledges and wisdom of these bodhisattvas.
△ Second, the request for an answer regarding their place of origin:
"The earth in the four directions split open, and [they] all emerged from within" (up to) "I have never before seen such a multitude."
△ Third, the request for an explanation of the circumstances of his appearance:
"In this assembly, I do not recognize a single person; yet suddenly one has emerged from the earth. I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions thereof.
△ Fourth, the joint request of the great assembly.
In this great assembly today, [the World-Honored One has explained] the causal conditions from beginning to end for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions [of beings].
△ Fifth, the request for the Master to provide an answer:
"O World-Honored One of Immeasurable Virtue, we pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly."
The commentary states: "Regarding 'requesting an answer from the Master,' this refers to requesting an answer as to who it was that preached the Dharma for him, and so forth. **2.
The Doubts of the Bodhisattvas from Other Lands.** At that time, the various Buddhas who were emanations of Śākyamuni... (up to)... "you yourselves shall hear it through this."

This was the doubt of the bodhisattvas from other lands. Their respective Buddhas’ attendants were actually bodhisattvas from other directions—emanated members of their retinues stationed throughout the ten directions—who shared the same doubt as Maitreya and likewise did not know that the Tathāgata had attained Buddhahood in his original ground long ago.
Thereupon, each of them presented their doubts to their own Buddha, and all those Buddhas suppressed them and bided their time until Maitreya’s arrival.
Therefore, it is said: "Maitreya has already asked about this matter; you yourselves shall, by means of this, hear the sublime joy.

Why does it say, "waiting for Maitreya"? It is because the various Buddhas who are emanations of the body consider that the benefit of answering the question does not lie with them, and thus they do not answer.
Furthermore, it is because [the Buddha] waits for Śākyamuni to answer Maitreya’s question; hence it says, "waiting for Maitreya" only. What [else could it mean]?
The matters inquired about by Maitreya are no trivial ones; throughout the entire career of Śākyamuni Buddha’s one lifetime, they have never been explicitly taught.

It is because of this inquiry that [the Buddha] has extensively revealed the long life [of the Tathāgata]. This profound mystery of the present lifetime was kept secret until the Buddha himself opened it;
you shall hear it for yourself, and I should not have answered [otherwise]. [The Prologue of the Essential Gate is concluded. II. From this half-chapter up to the speech of Maitreya.
The Verses conclude the section on the Correct Exposition of the Fundamental Gate, Part Two: Initial Admonition and Permission, Subsection One: Prose Exposition, Part One:
Admonition, Subsection One: Eulogy.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha... [up to] ...is thus able to question the Buddha regarding such a great matter.
From here below begins the main exposition of the fundamental teaching. Ajita—here translated as "Invincible"—is the clan name of Maitreya.
△ Second, the formal admonition:
"You all should together with one mind don the armor of diligence and resolve upon a firm intention."
Exhort them with single-mindedness not to let their armor be disarrayed; exhort them not to be indolent, but to remain firm; exhort them not to retreat.
△ Second, the granting [of the teaching], in two parts. First, indicating the fruit of wisdom:
"The Tathāgata now wishes to manifest and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas."
△ Section 2–3: Teaching through Transformation and Enlightenment.
From "The sovereign power of the supernatural penetrations of all Buddhas" (up to) "the majestic power of the great might of all Buddhas.

The topical outline states: "Teaching through transformation and enlightenment" refers to the proclamation [of the Dharma]; "sovereign supernatural power" refers to the benefiting of beings in the past.
"Leaping like a lion" refers to the present benefit of sentient beings at the locations where the emanated bodies throughout the ten directions appear.
"Majestic and fierce power" refers to the future benefit of sentient beings. Master Zhanran privately comments: "The sovereignty of the Tathāgata" is the virtue of self;
"supernormal powers" are the virtue of bliss; and "leaping like a lion," which leaps to remove defilements, is the virtue of purity.
The Great Power, the Majestic and Fierce, is the virtue of eternally benefiting sentient beings in the future. *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states:

"Because supernatural powers are the playful sport (*vikrīḍita*) of a Bodhisattva, they are called 'joy'; because they benefit beings until the end of the future, they attain this 'eternity'. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts;
first, the summary of the admonition.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"You should be diligent and single-minded; I wish to speak of this matter, so do not harbor any doubt or regret."
△ Second, the two verses on the granting [of the teaching]. First, the verse on the fruit of wisdom:
The Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable.
△ Second, the verse on the transformations throughout the three periods of time.
"Now, exerting the power of faith and abiding in the goodness of patience... (until) you all listen with a single mind.

Regarding the verse on the "Three Times" by Miaole: the previous [verse] concerning the lion and others clarifies the three times, yet within that text there is no explicit mention of the "three times";
it is simply through the force of the meaning that it corresponds to the three times. This current verse is likewise; it refers directly to the Buddha.

The passage "There is no non-true speech," etc., is used as a half-verse to provide a general explanation; since the words are not false, one knows that the benefits throughout the three periods of time are also real and true.
△ Second, the actual exposition has two parts: first, the first one and a half chapters properly open up the near and reveal the far;
second, at the end of this chapter, there is a brief opening of the near and revealing of the far, which moves fixed attachments and gives rise to doubt. First, the brief opening:
Regarding the two [sections] on revealing the near and the distant, first is the prose section; within that, first is the double response. First, the response concerning the teacher and disciple:
At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses... [until] ...he tamed their minds and caused them to resolve upon the Way.
This concludes the "Chapter on the Full Lifespan," which now opens by revealing the near while manifesting the far. △ Second, the answer regarding their location:
These bodhisattvas all dwell beneath this Sahā world, in the space of this realm.

This realm refers to the lower direction. Regarding those who dwell in the space of the lower direction, the *Śāstra* clarifies that there are four explanations concerning the *tiras-karaṇa-samādhi* (the samādhi of passing through):

first, "existence" (*asti*) refers to the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*); second, "bottom" (*tira*) refers to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naiva-saṃjñā-nāsaṃjñāyatana*), which is called the "bottom" because it is profound and supreme;

third, "existence" (*asti*) refers to names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*); and fourth, "bottom" (*tira*) refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is called the "bottom" because it is empty and quiescent.
Regarding "having a bottom," there are two conventional [interpretations]. "Bottom" (*di*) refers to the fulfillment of ultimate wisdom; thus, it is called the "bottom.
Now, this sutra states that the void of the lower direction is the bottom. It is neither the upper realm nor the lower realm, but represents the Middle Way as the bottom.

This is a distinction made according to the teachings. As the *Miaole* (The Wondrous Joy) says: "Regarding 'having a bottom' in the sense of 'dispersed,' 'bottom' (*di*) means 'downward' (*xia*). In the sense of being dispersed, it is called the "bottom."
This refers to emptiness; this merely dissolves names. If one were to produce its essential substance and characteristics, it would be as explained according to the teachings (*yàojiào*).

That which is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is the bottom of the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) realm; emptiness is the bottom of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); and the knowledge of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-jñāna*) is the bottom of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*). All of these are explained by way of the ultimate.
Since it says "distinguishing according to the teachings," the first [category] is the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and the second is the *Vaipulya* (Shared).
The next one is distinct; this present sutra is Perfect (Yuan), taking the Middle Way as its foundation.

Among the four types of exegesis, it simply says "having a foundation" (*di*) and does not say "dispersed" (*san*), because the foundation is itself the dispersion. II. A dual explanation of the two [masters]: first, the explanation of teacher and disciple. A.
First, the dual cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
Regarding the various sūtras, one reads, recites, masters them, contemplates, analyzes, and maintains right mindfulness.

The teacher knows that the disciple cultivates the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*); in the analysis of the sūtras, this is the cultivation of wisdom and right mindfulness, while this is the cultivation of abandonment.
△ Second, the dual realization of wisdom and abandonment.
Ajita, these sons of good family (up to) practice with diligent vigor without ever resting.
Their lack of delight in being amidst the crowd is the realization of the virtue of abandonment; their diligent practice of vigor is the realization of the virtue of wisdom.
△ Third, the explanation of the locus.
Nor does one dwell depending upon humans or devas (up to: with single-minded diligence seeking unsurpassed wisdom).
"Not dwelling depending upon humans or devas" is the explanation of the locus; it means not abiding in and not clinging to the two extremes of humans and devas.
"One of profound, unimpeded wisdom" refers to relying on inconceivable wisdom. "Delighting in the Buddha-dharma" means delighting in [the Dharma].
This is the inconceivable realm; the profundity and subtlety of this realm and its wisdom mean that it is not for Bodhisattvas of shallow practice.
Miaole (妙樂) says: "Not relying on humans or devas" means that while one dwells in empty space, one does not rely at all upon those above [the heavens] or those below [humans].
He further states that "humans and devas" refer to the two extremes (*anta*), explaining them in terms of what they represent: most people are stuck in attachment, as these terms represent existence.
The "Heaven at the Edge" (Biantian) dwells in pure blessings to symbolize abiding at the edge of emptiness; by dwelling within this emptiness, it symbolizes the Middle Way.
△ Second, the verse summary has two parts: first, the summary of the dual response; second, the initial response concerning master and disciple.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Ajita, you should know that these great bodhisattvas... [have come] for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way."
△ Second, the answer concerning the location, which has two parts: first, the direct answer regarding the location;
[it] dwells in the space below the Sahā world.
△ Second, praising the virtues of the Bodhisattvas.
The power of his resolve and mindfulness is firm and steadfast; he constantly and diligently seeks wisdom and preaches various sublime dharmas with a mind free from fear.
△ Second, the verse provides a dual explanation in two parts: first, the explanation of the teacher and disciple.
I sat beneath the Bodhi tree in the city of Gayā... (until) you all believe with one mind.
△ Second, the explanation of the location:
From long ago, I have been teaching and transforming these multitudes.
The *Kō* (Commentary) states: "Regarding the 'place' (*sthāna*), Miaole says that the sutra does not mention a place but only speaks of 'teaching for a long time.
This is because it has already been stated in the preceding prose section of the direct answer that [the Buddha] resides in the space beneath this Sahā world;
therefore, it explains the 'place' solely by means of time. For what location was he teaching when, in the distant past, he transformed beings and caused them to enter [the Way]?"
Reality is precisely emptiness. △ Second, further inquiry due to doubt, in two parts: first, the prose section; second, the initial doubt.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva... (omitted)... causing them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Having heard the two accounts—that Maitreya and others were first taught under the Bodhi tree and have now all reached the stage of non-retrogression, and that I myself have been teaching this assembly for a vast period of time—they were shaken by their attachments and gave rise to doubt. II.
The Request [for Clarification] (in two parts): A. The Explanatory Discourse (in three parts): 1. Clinging to the recent and doubting the distant.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [he] shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This doubt arises because he perceives that his attainment of the Way is near and the beings he will transform are very numerous; thus, grasping at what is near, he doubts what is far.

Gayā—this is translated as "Mountain City"—is approximately twenty *li* from the site of the Bodhi-maṇḍala. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that the city was extremely steep and fortified.
Five or six *li* to the southwest of the city, one reaches Gayāśīrṣa Mountain, where the valleys and gorges are profound and dark, and the peaks and ridges are perilous;

according to the local custom of the Indian kingdom, it is called "The Holy Mountain" (*Rishiyue Shan*). Regarding the forty-odd years [of his ministry], the *Fashu song* (Verses on the Exposition of the Dharma) states:

"Twelve years for the *Āgamas*, eight for the *Vaipulya*, twenty-two years for the *Prajñāpāramitā*. As for the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it occurs after the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Thus, it is said that the *Lotus Sūtra* was preached subsequent to the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
It is said to be more than forty years. △ Second, resolving doubts regarding the distance [of time]:
"World-Honored One, this assembly of great bodhisattvas... has accomplished the bodhisattva path and constantly cultivated pure conduct."

These beings to be converted have already practiced for many eons and their stages are profound and subtle; yet they cling to what is distant while doubting what is near. The *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary says: "Question:
Since Maitreya does not know their number nor recognize even a single person, how can he know that they have long planted roots of goodness?
Answer: Precisely because he does not know them and does not recognize them—and furthermore, because the Buddha has praised the virtues and deeds of their dwelling place as being manifold."
Maitreya, being deeply perplexed, wondered whether these bodhisattvas could possibly have been transformed by a Buddha who had recently attained enlightenment.
△ Third, the conclusion of the request based on the difficulty of belief:
"World-Honored One, such a matter as this is difficult for the world to believe."

The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) states: "In the section on the invitation, only those who find it difficult to believe are cited; by using objects as a pretext for their disbelief and rejection, they strike at the Buddha so that He must inevitably provide an answer.
△ Second, the illustrative explanation has two parts. First, the opening of the analogy has three parts. First, the analogy regarding the intent of the proximity to attaining enlightenment.
For example, suppose there is a man with a handsome appearance and black hair, twenty-five years of age.
△ Second, the analogy for the many dispositions of those to be converted:
pointing to a hundred-year-old man and saying, "He is my son," [and so on], down to saying, "He is my father who begot and raised us."
△ Third, the summary of the parable regarding the difficulty of belief:
This matter is difficult to believe.

That one possesses beautiful complexion and black hair is generally characteristic of youth; thus, the analogy that the Tathāgata is one’s father corresponds to the sense that his attainment of enlightenment was recent.
This also refers to the hundred-year-old man; comparing him to the Bodhisattvas who emerge from the earth illustrates the vast number of those transformed.

The various masters of the region north of the Huai River explain this analogy as follows: the father takes an elixir that reverses aging, so his appearance matches that of a twenty-five-year-old (though old, he is young);
the son does not take the medicine, so his form remains like that of a hundred-year-old (though young, he is old). If one knows the power of the medicine...
Those who doubt that the father knows [the son] find it strange; now the household unites this analogy: the Tathāgata administers the medicine of manifesting traces, showing that he was born in Gayā;
yet for the various bodhisattvas, he speaks directly of their original ground, where they have long since resolved upon the Way and now abide in non-retrogression.
If the Buddha and the Buddhas clearly know these matters, those below cannot reach them; thus, one has no choice but to accept this.

Because of these doubts, the text concludes by stating: "This matter is difficult to believe. *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) comments: "Since it says 'if the Buddha and the Buddha,' this reveals that Maitreya does not know [the full extent].
Speaking of the Tathāgata’s horizontal administration of medicines for downward-reaching responses: the wisdom that accords with profound principles arises from vertical administration;

the medicine of the True Truth benefits beings everywhere, while the medicine of horizontal administration for downward-reaching responses arises precisely because of that vertical administration of the medicine of the True Truth."

Regarding the medicine of the truths: because the provisional is identical to emptiness, the skillful means is identical to the ultimate, and one's own practice is in profound accord with reality. Regarding the medicine of manifested response:
because emptiness is identical to the provisional, the ultimate is identical to the skillful means, and transformation for others arises. △ Second, the combined analogy, in three parts:
first, combining the proximate analogy.
The Buddha is also like this; since he attained the Way, it has actually not been long.
△ Second, the combined distant analogy:
"Yet this great assembly of bodhisattvas and others... (up to)... all the world finds them most rare."
This Bodhisattva has long planted roots of goodness; it is not merely by generating the aspiration at Gayā that one enters, emerges from, and abides in them well.

"Entering well" refers to the nine successive concentrations (the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling). "Emerging well" refers to the Lion’s Rush Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*). "Abiding well" refers to the Leap-over Samādhi (*vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*).
This concludes the two teachings of the *Kō* (Vaipulya/Shared) and *Tō* (Distinct/Separate); [this applies] from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth.
The stage of the name "Skillfully Entering the Ten Grounds" and "Entering the Gate of the Profound Mystery" while again practicing the affairs of an ordinary person is called "skillful entry";

the stage of the name "Skillfully Exiting" and "the Wondrous Enlightenment Pervading All" is called "skillful exit. This is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao). The stage of the name "Ultimate Dharma-nature Samādhi" is called "skillful entry";

the stage of the name "Śūraṅgama Samādhi" is called "skillful exit"; the stage of the name "King Samādhi" is called "skillful abiding. This is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao) in its sequential order.
Those who practice all wholesome dharmas are "good" by virtue of their cause; those who enter well into the wholesome are "good" by virtue of their fruit.

Those who answer difficult questions are endowed with the two kinds of adornment: merit and wisdom. Because they are the most honored among the seven stages of skillful means (*saptopāya*), they are called "jewels among men.
The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states that the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) are the "good entry," for one enters from dhyāna to dhyāna without interruption.

Therefore, "exertion" (*prāgalbhyam*) refers to those who skillfully emerge; from one dhyāna to another, they pass through the distracted mind, and thus it is called "emerging" by virtue of that distraction.
"Transcendence" (*abhibhava*) refers to those who skillfully abide; although they pass through transcending distractions, they abide in dhyāna with perfect clarity.

"Ultimacy" (*paryanta*) refers to those who skillfully enter; "ultimacy" means exhaustion. Because they exhaust the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is able to manifest majestic deportment.
Regarding the "King-like Samādhi," it is so called because it is like a king who secures his kingdom. △ Third, the combined request and response, in three parts: first, citing the Buddha’s words:
"Today, the World-Honored One has only now said that when he attained the Way of the Buddha... [he] was able to perform such a great meritorious deed."
△ Second, explaining the intent of the request, in two parts. First, for the sake of those in the present:
"Although we have faith in the Buddha’s teachings spoken according to his suitability [to the capacities of beings], we have fully mastered everything that the Buddha knows."
Maitreya said of himself: "I personally see and hear this in the present; although I have not yet attained [realization], I believe it to be so. △ Second, for the sake of those in the future:

"However, there will be bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa... [will] give rise to the karmic causes and conditions of the sin of destroying the Dharma."
The reason for my present request is precisely this: for those of future generations who practice shallowly and have newly resolved their minds, joy may give way to slander;
through slander, they fall into the evil realms. Even those who do not regress may be able to believe without slandering, yet they cannot increase their progress on the Path.

If I were to explain by making distinctions, it would cause those who slander to develop faith, and those who already have faith to increase their progress on the Path. △ Third, the Proper [Exposition].
Please answer these two points first to dispel our doubts.
"Certainly, World-Honored One; we pray that you will explain this for us to dispel our doubts.
△ Third, dispelling doubts regarding the future.
Furthermore, when good sons of future generations hear this matter, they too shall not give rise to doubt.
△ Second, the verse summary has two parts; first, the summary of the prose explanation has three parts; first, the summary of clinging to the near.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past, the Buddha left the Śākya clan for homelessness and sat beneath the Bodhi tree near Gayā; not much time has passed since then."
△ Second, two verses expressing doubt regarding the distance [of the assembly].
These sons of the Buddha, their number being immeasurable... (up to)... this matter is difficult to conceive.
△ Third, one verse concluding the request.
How can it be believed that the Buddha attained the Way so recently? [The text proceeds] to explain this through a detailed analysis according to reality.
△ Second, the verses on the parable, which has two parts; first, the verse that introduces the parable.
For example, it is like a person in the prime of youth, aged twenty-five (up to) something that the whole world does not believe.
△ Second, the verse that combines the parable, in three parts: first, the verse that combines the proximate [parables].
The World-Honored One is likewise; it has been but a very short time since he attained the Way.
△ Second, the verse on the convergence of the distant:
These bodhisattvas, their resolve firm and free from cowardice... (extending to) they dwell in the space below.
△ Third, the combined request in three verses:
"We have heard this matter from the Buddha and have no doubt... (up to) "...abiding in the stage of non-retrogression.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Sixteen: "The Tathāgata’s Lifespan."
"Tathāgata" is the general designation for all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time—the two Buddhas, the three Buddhas, the fundamental Buddha, and the trace Buddha.

"Life-span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*) means to measure and evaluate; it refers to measuring and evaluating the merits of the two Buddhas, the three Buddhas, the fundamental Buddha, and the trace Buddha of the ten directions and three periods of time.
Since this passage specifically evaluates the merits of the three fundamental Buddhas of the original ground, it says:
In the "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata," the meaning of *tathāgata* is manifold; here, two or three aspects will be clarified, while other examples may be understood by extension.

Regarding these two aspects of the *tathāgata*, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Because one comes (*āgata*) to achieve perfect enlightenment by means of the path of reality (*tathatā*), one is called a *tathāgata*.

Here, "path" refers to the wisdom that accords with suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*), and "reality" refers to the object that is suchness (*tathatā-viṣaya*). When object and wisdom are in union, [the state of a *tathāgata*] exists.
The path of cause is awakening as the cause; the path of result is the realization of that awakening.
When this meaning is established, one comes by means of the path of reality to achieve perfect awakening; this is the Dharmakāya Tathāgata.

That which, by means of the wisdom of reality, comes by the path of reality to be born within the triple world and manifests the attainment of perfect awakening, is the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata. These are the three Tathāgatas.
The Dharma as suchness (dharmatā-tathatā) is neither cause nor fruit; whether a Buddha appears or not, its essential nature remains eternally so, pervading all places without variation.
It is "such" because it is immovable, yet it "arrives"; thus, this Dharma-body Tathāgata is so named.
