The wisdom of the Dharma as suchness, riding upon the true path of suchness, arrives to achieve perfect enlightenment; from the perspective of principle, it is so called.

Just as one comes from the name "Wisdom" to this Reward Body Tathāgata (*sambhogakāya-tathāgata*), because the object and wisdom of suchness (*tathatā*) are united, he is able to manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment, the eightfold path of enlightenment, and the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma in every place;
this is the Response Body Tathāgata (*nirmāṇakāya-tathāgata*). The Dharmakāya Tathāgata is named Vairocana, which translates as "Pervading All Places"; [this is] the Reward Body.
The Tathāgata named Vairocana is translated as "Pure and Full"; the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) Tathāgata named Śākyamuni is translated as "Able Benevolent One" and "Tranquil Silence.
These three Tathāgatas are such that one necessarily possesses all three, and the three are identical to the one;
they are neither one nor different, neither vertical nor horizontal. They are the provisional names for the Tathāgata who perfectly contemplates these three dharmas. Next, the lifespan is explained.
"Measure" (*pramāṇa*) refers to the lifespan of the aforementioned three Tathāgatas; "lifespan" (*āyus*) has the meaning of "receiving. "Measure" means "discriminative measurement.
Because True Suchness is not separated from all phenomena, it is called "receiving" this discriminative measurement.
The Dharmakāya Tathāgata takes suchness as its life-force; since its nature and characteristics are eternally thus—neither arising nor ceasing—the Sūtra says it is "not real."
Neither non-existent nor identical, yet not different from this—such is the lifespan of the Dharmakāya.
Because the object and wisdom are in correspondence, it is called "receiving" [this measure]; thus, the Sambhogakāya Tathāgata takes wisdom as its life-force.

Just as the wisdom of suchness accords with the object of suchness, and since that object is immeasurable, boundless, eternally abiding, and indestructible, so too is the wisdom. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
It is said: "The power of my wisdom is such that, through the insight obtained from long-cultivated practice, its light illumines immeasurable lifespans over countless kalpas.
This refers to the lifespan of the *saṃbhogakāya*. If one period of retribution lasts for a hundred years without interruption, it is called "receiving" [this span].
By this measure, the *nirmāṇakāya* Tathāgata should likewise accord with the conditions of sentient beings; as the conditions for his life are long, he remains long.
Because the conditions that prompt [the manifestation] are limited, the Sūtra says, "frequently manifesting birth and frequently manifesting extinction," and so forth;
this refers to the lifespan of the Nirmāṇakāya (Response Body). Furthermore, one must know that the Dharmakāya is neither measurable nor immeasurable.

Regarding the Saṃbhogakāya (Enjoyment Body), it is measurable prior to the Vajra stage and immeasurable thereafter. As for the Nirmāṇakāya, it is measurable according to conditions; its application is not fixed.
When severed, they are immeasurable; thus, each of the three bodies possesses both measurable and immeasurable, permanent and impermanent meanings.
Regarding this, various masters of old have explained permanence by means of the immeasurable and impermanence by means of the measurable.

According to our school’s interpretation based on the meaning of the sūtras, there should be four explanations: first, that which is actually measurable yet spoken of as immeasurable, as in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

Regarding the statement that the Buddha’s lifespan is seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas: since there is already the numerical figure of seven hundred, is it not the case that there is actually a finite limit?
Although there is such a limit, because humans and devas cannot calculate it, it is called "immeasurable lifespan.

This is the lifespan of the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata, which corresponds to the length of the causes [of his vow]. Second, although it is truly immeasurable, it is spoken of as having a measure such as this.
Although this chapter’s analytical exposition generally clarifies all three bodies (*trikāya*), from a specific perspective it primarily concerns the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*). As the Sūtra says:
"Since I attained Buddhahood, an exceedingly long time has passed," which implies that it is truly immeasurable; yet the title of the chapter simply refers to it as the "Life Span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the four Buddhas spoke these verses to the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa: [The verses follow]
The number of drops in the ocean, the weight of Mount Sumeru, the dust motes upon the earth, and the dimensions of space may all be known;

yet no one can know the lifespan of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the title of that chapter merely says "Lifespan" (*āyuṣ-pramāṇa*), which refers to the lifespan of the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) Tathāgata.
Thirdly, although it is truly immeasurable, it is called "immeasurable"; as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* also states: "Only a Buddha and..."
The Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable; this is the lifespan of the Dharmakāya Tathāgata.
Fourth, although there is actually a measure, it is spoken of as having a measure—such as the present Śākyamuni proclaiming his extinction at eighty years;

this is the lifespan of the Nirmāṇakāya, which accords with the brevity of conditions. One should know that a single Buddha-body is itself endowed with all bodies, and its lifespans and merits follow accordingly.
The four propositions regarding the differences in perceived length based on conditions have already clarified their meaning through analysis;

for those who remain unenlightened, they are further distinguished by the four propositions of permanence and so forth. That which is neither permanent nor impermanent represents the ultimate limit of principle, which is the Dharmakāya.
That which is permanent—because perfect wisdom is complete and is neither born nor extinguished—is the Sambhogakāya, and it is likewise permanent.
Regarding "also impermanent," it should be understood as employing inexhaustibility as its permanence; even chanting the name of *nirvāṇa* as impermanent refers to the *nirmāṇakāya*.

As for "impermanence," from the stage prior to the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) through the progression of wisdom and function, up to the arising and ceasing of birth and death among ordinary beings—all these are impermanent.
This is explained according to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). If explained according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), however:

Each and every Tathāgata is fully endowed with the four phrases, as clearly explained in detail in the commentary; how could one possibly interpret this by focusing exclusively on "permanent" versus "impermanent" or "measurable" versus "immeasurable"?
Furthermore, one should know that the Buddha fundamentally has no body, no lifespan, and no measure;
it is only in accordance with worldly convention that the three bodies (trikāya) are discussed, and it is likewise in accordance with worldly convention that they are so described.

The primary intent of this chapter on the Three Lifespans (*trisāyuṣya*), although it discusses the lifespan and wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya*, is that the meaning of the three bodies (*trikāya*) is fully realized through their upper correspondence with the ultimate and lower harmony with the conventional.
All such various merits of the three bodies were already accomplished long ago at the site of the Bodhi tree during the primordial time;
they are therefore called "original. It was only in the interim, today, at the site of the Path of Quiescence (*śāntimārga*), [that they were manifested].
The realized one is called the "trace" (*jiji*); yet there would be no trace without a basis, and there would be no way to manifest the basis without the trace.
Although the basis and the trace differ, they are inconceivably one. The *Miaole* says: Question: The Dharma-body and Reward-body are the basis, while the Response-body belongs to the trace.
Why, then, do you speak of the three Buddhas of the original ground? Answer: If that [distinction] were not yet opened, the Dharma-body and Reward-body would not be the trace.

If one reveals the remote [past], there are three aspects each for both the original and the manifested. △ Second, in the "Chapter on Lifespan," there is a broad opening of the near to reveal the remote, which severs delusions and engenders faith;
this has two parts. First, the admonition to believe, which has four sections. Third, the initial admonition.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas (up to): "You all should believe and understand the Tathāgata’s words of truth.
This is because he intends to reveal the immediate traces (*pratyutpanna-vyañjana*) in order to manifest the distant origin (*dūramūla*). Therefore, he first exhorts belief in the Buddha’s intent.

A solemn admonition is used as the warning for the various capacities of the assembly, while their receptive acceptance constitutes "belief. If the section on the traces (*vyañjana-mukha*) contains three requests and one admonition—as at the beginning of the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*—then this follows that pattern.
After the third request, he merely exhorted them, saying: "Now listen attentively and reflect upon this well.

In this present Gate, there are three exhortations and three requests; with these repeated requests and repeated exhortations, there are five exhortations and seven requests in total, signifying a most extraordinary, momentous, and earnestly solemn matter.
When he exhorted them, saying, "You all should believe and understand," it refers to the non-doubting realization of the near-perfect state.
It is said that "faith" (*śraddhā*) means clarity regarding the distant origin; "understanding" (*adhimukti*) means sincerity; "loyalty" (*bhakti*) means being faithful;

and "truthfulness" (*satya*) means being thorough and real, not deceiving others, so that one's words reach the ultimate reality. Previously, when one was a person of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*), whatever was spoken was all speech according to the intentions of others, not a declaration of sincere truth.
Now, the teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*—pure, perfect, and fully revealed—is precisely speech according to one’s own [realization].

The mind and speech demonstrate this through its essentials; thus, it is called "truthful. Having received these sincere admonitions, the Bodhisattva dares not harbor doubt and, upon hearing them, must take them as faith—this is the acceptance of truthful words.

The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states that since it says, "Having thus made these three requests," and then further says, "I only pray that you will speak of it," this constitutes the fourth request. Regarding the Buddha’s response to these three requests:
Thereafter, it says again: "You all, listen attentively. This is the fourth solemn admonition; its gravity is to be explained as previously stated.
△ Second and Third Requests.
At that time, the great assembly of Bodhisattvas, with Maitreya at their head... (up to) having thus made these three requests.
Once the Tathāgata had bestowed the three admonitions, the assembly of disciples then extended their three requests.
Regarding these three successive requests, they spoke again, saying: "We only pray that you will expound it; we shall faithfully accept the Buddha’s words."
After having already extended three requests, he further said, "I only pray that you will explain it," thus constituting four requests. △ Fourth, the repeated admonition:
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the Bodhisattvas would not cease their threefold request, addressed them, saying, "Listen attentively, all of you."
After having bestowed the three admonitions, he further declared, "Listen attentively," thereby forming four admonitions. △ Second, the direct answer, in two parts:
First, the prose exposition; second, first, the teaching by Dharma; second, first, benefiting beings across the three periods of time;
first, benefiting beings in the past; first, exposing attachment to narrow-minded sentiments; first, exposing the dharmas that cause delusion.
The Tathāgata’s power of secret supernormal faculties.
△ Second, identifying those who are deluded:
all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras.
△ Third, the departure from delusion regarding distance:
This refers to the common view that Śākyamuni Buddha attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* only recently.
The preceding two sections explain this together; as for the "secret," it means that the single body is itself the three bodies, which is termed "secret."
The three bodies (*trikāya*) being one body is called "mystery" (*guhya*); that which was not previously taught is called "secret" (*rahasya*);
and that which is known only by the Buddha himself is called "mystery. As for the power of spiritual penetration (*abhijñā*), it is the function of the three bodies.

"Spirit" (*shen*) is the principle of natural immovability, which is the Dharma-nature body (*dharmakāya*). "Penetration" (*tong*) is unobstructed, inconceivable wisdom, which is the Reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Furthermore, power is the functional activity; being sovereign is the *nirmāṇakāya*. The Buddha possesses these three bodies equally throughout the three periods of time.

Because they are kept secret and not transmitted within the various teachings, all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—all believe that the present Buddha has only now attained these three bodies at the Bodhi tree.
Thus, clinging to the recent, they doubt the distant. This is the Fundamental Gate.
In the discourse on the Dharma, there is no further mention of the two vehicles; rather, it addresses only Bodhisattvas.

Since Bodhisattvas are subsumed within the three wholesome realms of existence—gods, humans, and asuras—and because those in the remaining three evil destinies have heavy karmic offenses, dull faculties, and little wisdom and thus do not understand [the teaching], the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The Mahāyāna excels over gods, humans, and asuras," yet it does not say so explicitly.
The three evil realms. There are three kinds of Bodhisattvas who dwell in the lower regions of other directions; these are the ones who have long resided there.

"Lower regions" refers to those whom he originally transformed in his previous life, and thus they are free from attachment to what is near. Regarding those who dwell in other directions, there are two types:

first, those who manifest from the Dharmakāya; these were either those who attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in past lives, or those who had already previously...

Regarding the hearing of the revelation of the original ground from the manifested trace: even those who have not yet attained the exhaustion of retribution and receive the Dharma-nature body will naturally hear this teaching of the long and distant within the stage of the Dharma-body;
therefore, one should give rise to the Bodhisattva’s great non-attachment. "Near" refers to two types:

first, those who have now for the first time attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*); and second, those who have not yet attained it, all of whom harbor this notion of "nearness."
The underlying principle is that because people believe the present Buddha first attained these three bodies at the Bodhi tree, they cling to what is near and doubt what is far.
△ Second, refuting the near to reveal the far, in two parts: first, revealing the far through dharma and parable; second, first, revealing the far through a dharma-exposition.
"However, son of good family, it has indeed been hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas since I truly attained Buddhahood.
From this point downward, the text clarifies the refutation of attachments and the dispelling of delusions to reveal the primordial origin from long ago;

the aforementioned "sincere and truthful admonition" refers precisely to this. Now, to clearly manifest the distant antiquity: since the Tathāgata has stated that his attainment of Buddhahood is exceedingly remote and ancient.
Thus, it is said that the attachment to the notion that [the Buddha] attained enlightenment near Gayā is immediately shattered.

There are briefly ten meanings for shattering the "near" to reveal the "far," as fully set forth in the ninth fascicle of the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra). This text correctly employs two meanings: shattering the near to reveal the far (*po jin xian yuan*) and abolishing the near to reveal the far (*fei jin xian yuan*).
"Shattering the near" refers to shattering the attachments of emotional clinging; "abolishing the near" refers to abolishing the provisional teachings of the present day. △ Second.
The first part of the analogy for comparison consists of three sections; here, the analogy is presented as a question:
"Suppose there were five hundred thousand million billion [sands]... would one be able to contemplate and calculate and know their number?
Other sutras clarify large numbers by using metaphors such as unspeakable numbers of dust motes and sands of the Ganges; this is done in order to compare that [magnitude] with the present case.

This is indeed much; for what reason? If even the realms that have been reached by particles falling directly downward from a world of immeasurable lifespan cannot be described, how much less so those realms where no particles have fallen—how could they possibly be described?

Since even the realms where particles have fallen and those where they have not are already indescribable, how could the particles within those worlds where particles have neither fallen nor not fallen ever be described?
Moreover, as the subsequent text states: "Furthermore, beyond this, how could it even be described?
*Nayuta* is translated here as "ten billion," and *asaṃkhyeya* is translated as "innumerable. △ Second, the answer to not knowing.
Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others all addressed the Buddha, saying... [up to] "...these various worlds are immeasurable and boundless.
In the answer, three individuals are cited as being unaware [of this]. *Avivartya* is also called *Abhibhūti*;
this is translated as "non-retrogression," which has already been explained previously. △ Third, the combined manifestation of the distant.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of great bodhisattvas... [up to] "a hundred thousand million nayuta asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
This collectively reveals the vast duration of time. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy), citing the *Monastic Biographies*, states:

"According to the old translation by Kumārajīva, the four characters 'one speck of dust, one kalpa' (*yī chén yī jié*) were absent; there was a Qi-era eminent monk named Tánfù who, while reciting the sutra, experienced a dream and said that one [phrase] was missing."

The result following the phrase is obtained as follows: as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states, "While the number of drops in all the oceans of the world may be known, there is no one who can know the lifespan of the Tathāgata.
This also clarifies that it refers to future lifespan, not past.
To cite this as scriptural evidence [for a different point] would be entirely inconsistent. II. What is Appropriate for Benefiting Beings. A. First, the place where beings are benefited.
"From that time until now, I have constantly remained here in this Sahā world (until) guiding and benefiting sentient beings.
Regarding the necessity of clarifying the locations where he benefited beings in the past— since it was stated in the preceding analogies that he attained Buddhahood a very long time ago,
yet it was not specified where he had resided for so long— it is said that he has "constantly been in this land and other foreign lands."
Regarding the statement that "performing Buddha-works brings marvelous joy and benefits sentient beings," this Sahā world is precisely the land where the original response-body (hon-jin) resides.
Today, the manifested trace-body (shaku-jin) dwells therein without departing from its original site; it is merely that the times of past and present differ.

Those who see it as being consumed by fire perceive only what is near, whereas those who realize the fundamental reality penetrate the far-reaching truth. Thus, the Sūtra says: "When the great fires burn, my land remains peaceful."
The Hidden One is always present on Vulture Peak and in all other dwelling places; how could one seek the eternally quiescent apart from Gayā?
Is there a Sahā world existing outside the Land of Eternal Quiescence and Light? △ Second, clearing away doubts regarding the traces above.
"Good sons, within this interval—up to this point—all these have been distinguished through skillful means.
Previously, seeing that the causes for practice taught in various places were inconsistent was a cause for doubt;

furthermore, seeing that the predictions of attainment (*vyākaraṇa*) received in various places were inconsistent was a cause for doubt regarding the fruit. Such explanations concerning the causes of practice and the attainment of prediction are all [unreliable]."

Because one knows these are skillful means (*upāya*) subsequent to the fruit, doubt arises; now, to sweep away this doubt, he points to the causal practices performed at the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, thereby sweeping away doubt regarding the cause.
Furthermore, by pointing to the receiving of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) and entering *nirvāṇa* at the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he sweeps away doubt regarding the fruit.
Thus, these causes and fruits are not merely single paths; they all constitute skillful means.

Because it is a statement of reality, it is called "dispelling doubt. Furthermore, the word "that" (其) refers precisely to that which was employed as a provisional manifestation during the intermediate period.
This is because when the Buddha was formerly a bodhisattva under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he entered nirvāṇa himself;
thus, one cannot say it was the nirvāṇa of Dīpaṃkara. The *Myōraku* commentary states: "The scriptural text first presents the facts and concludes [the section]."
To say that all these are skillful means (*upāya*) is precisely what is meant by "brushing away" [doubts].

Although one may have seen differences among the various teachings and thus give rise to doubt, this was because one did not know that they were skillful means manifested after the attainment of fruition, nor the intended meaning behind such demonstrations of distinctions—namely, that [the Buddha] met Dīpaṃkara and entered *nirvāṇa* during the time of Dīpaṃkara. △ Third, the actual clarification.
Section Two: Initial Response and Resonance.
"Good sons, if there are sentient beings... [from] ...whether their faculties are sharp or dull, they are saved according to their capacity.
Those who come to my presence are precisely sentient beings of the past whose gradual and sudden capacities have silently struck against the Dharma-body."
To observe with the Buddha-eye is the function of one who has long since attained Buddhahood; to discern and illuminate with the Buddha-eye leaves nothing unperceived or erroneous.
When intending to manifest the two types of response—the superior and the inferior—to benefit beings according to their virtuous capacities, there are two powers:
first, to elicit the flowery rewards of the human and celestial realms; second, to elicit the karmic fruits of the Buddha-way. If one observes and knows sentient beings with the Dharma-eye...

The myriad roots of goodness, according to their respective gravity or lightness, each receive their intermediate rewards; yet one cannot ultimately know that they will finally attain the fruit of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
If, however, one uses the Buddha-eye to perfectly illumine the myriad roots of goodness of sentient beings, one can then know their initial causes and final fruits.
This sutra exclusively clarifies that through the observation and knowledge of the Buddha-eye, one knows that the myriad roots of goodness of sentient beings ultimately result in Buddhahood.
The primary intent for appearing in the world is this one great matter. The various faculties, such as faith, refer to the five faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
The faculty of wisdom is the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*), while the remaining faculties are the "contributing causes" (*pratyaya-hetu*).

These two roots of goodness each possess both sharp and dull capacities, encompassing the conditions of both sudden and gradual vehicles. Within the sudden vehicle, the distinctions between sharp and dull capacities correspond to the two teachings of the Perfect (*Vimalakīrti*) and the Distinct (*Śrīmālā*).
The gradual [practitioners] with sharp or dull faculties are those of the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Vaipulya) teachings.

Furthermore, those with Small Vehicle roots are called "dull," while those with Great Vehicle roots are called "sharp. Moreover, those with Small Vehicle roots are called "sharp," while those with the roots of humans and devas are called "dull.
All the good roots—whether sharp or dull—of sentient beings within the ten dharma realms are used as the "faculty" (*indriya*); evil dharmas and evil faculties are not so used.

This is because it does not depend on the two causes of *ālambana* (object-condition) and *vijñapti* (cognition). The Tathāgata fully illuminates the wholesome capacities (*kuśala-mūla*) within the ten realms;

according to what is required for deliverance, he manifests forms and sounds to provide benefit. The *Myōryaku-ki* states: "Question: Since the Buddha-fruit is already ultimate, how can it also be said to arise in response to the capacities of sentient beings?
Answer: This discussion concerns the capacities of beings and distinguishes between those who are sharp and dull; therefore, the Buddha-dharma realm is not yet [the final state]."
Because it concerns the fruit of Buddhahood, the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) discusses the mutual interaction of the ten realms regarding the conditions for the capacity [of beings];
this is because the capacity for the fruit-Buddha universally extends across all ten realms. △ Second, the bestowing of transformation has two parts: first, the dual benefit of form and voice;
second, the benefit of form has two parts: first, manifesting birth where there is no birth.
In various places, he speaks of his own names being different and his ages being greater or smaller.
"In various places" refers, when discussed vertically, to the various lands where causes were cultivated in the past;
when discussed horizontally, it refers to the lands of the ten directions in former times. Regarding "names being different," once the physical form is manifested, there is a name.
Names are used to invoke the essence through appellations, and there are distinctions between the capacities of beings and the excellence or inferiority of their forms.
The "inferior" refers to the body of the Inferior Response (lièyìng), which consists of the thirty-two marks and is intended for the capacities of those following the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings.

The "superior" refers to the body of the Superior Response (shèngyìng), which consists of eighty-four thousand marks and secondary characteristics and is intended for the capacities of those following the Distinct and Perfect Teachings. This concerns the manifestation of the Buddha-dharma.

Regarding the differences in the names and forms of the nine dharma-realms: if the names and forms of the manifested bodies of the nine dharma-realms are diverse and immeasurable and boundless, they can be understood through the mind.

As for the magnitude of their ages, this clarifies the length of their lifespans: "great" refers to the superior response-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), while "small" refers to the inferior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The lifespan manifested by the inferior response-body is finite, whereas the lifespan manifested by the superior response-body is infinite. All of these...
He manifests his body and the length of his life according to those who are to be saved. Second, though he does not actually pass away, he manifests passing away;
furthermore, he declares that he shall enter *nirvāṇa*.
Those who are to be delivered through parinirvāṇa, he manifests parinirvāṇa to them, causing them to feel longing and reverence so that they may attain liberation.
△ Second, benefit through sound:
Furthermore, by means of various skillful expedients, he preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
That they possess small bodies and short lifespans refers to the teaching of gradual instruction; thus it is said that there are "various skillful means.

That they possess large bodies and long lifespans refers to the teaching of sudden instruction; thus it is said that they "expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma. △ Second, the joy derived from attaining benefits.
It can cause sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy;
although it employs gradual means at the outset, it ultimately leads them into the Great [Vehicle], and for this reason it is said that it "can cause joy.

This very joy is precisely the benefit obtained through the Buddha’s transformative teaching, wherein the Buddha, relying on the four *siddhāntas*, bestows both physical and vocal benefits, and sentient beings thereby obtain [these gains].

Regarding the four benefits: when [the teaching] accords with the capacity [of the recipient], there is joy; when it deviates from the capacity, there is distress. Now, since it accords with the capacity and brings about benefit, there is rejoicing.
△ Second, benefiting beings in the present, in two parts: first, clarifying the resonance of the capacity.

"O sons of good family, when the Tathāgata sees sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings (*hīna-dharma*), whose merit is meager and whose defilements are heavy—this 'seeing' by the Tathāgata is the illumination of the Buddha-eye.
These sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings are the 'capacities' (*indriya*) that are thus perceived.
Master Nanyue said: "Those who delight in the inferior are not people of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*); rather, they are those who delight in what is near [to them]."
What has been said thus far is but a brief explanation; now I shall provide a comprehensive account.

That which is called "craving for the twenty-five realms of existence" refers to the capacity of those in the human and heavenly realms who crave and cling to nirvana, seeking their own liberation—this is the capacity of the followers of the Two Vehicles.

Those who delight in the gradual and circuitous path of the Buddha-way are the capacity of the Bodhisattvas of the Three Teachings. When these various capacities arrive, [the teaching is accordingly revealed].

"All that I possess" refers to those who delight in the Lesser Dharma (*hīnayāna*). "Those of meager virtue" means that their application of the two types of goodness—the causal and the realized—is weak and inferior.
"Those with heavy defilements" means that the two delusions of views and thought have not yet been eliminated. This is explained in terms of the Trace Gate (*jiamen*);

if explained in terms of the Origin Gate (*benmen*, *mūlamukha*), it refers to those who take pleasure in hearing about the minor events of his departure from the palace of the Śākya clan and his recent attainment of enlightenment, rather than desiring to hear of the Great Vehicle.

Because they have heard [the teachings] for a long time and have long since accomplished the Great, it is said that they "delight in the Small. Such small-mindedness is not something that begins only today;

if they had previously delighted in the Great, the Buddha would not have taught the beginning of accomplishment. Those who teach the beginning of accomplishment do so only for the sake of those who delight in the Small Dharma.
The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) states: "Those of meager virtue and heavy defilement possess neither of the two causes for the True Teaching."
...Thus it is. △ Second, explaining the manifested transformation [body] has two parts: first, manifesting birth where there is no birth; second, the actual explanation. First, manifesting birth:
for the sake of these people, I say, "I left home at a young age and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

The text here states that "manifesting in birth" means the traces manifest within the realm of birth. Previously, it was clarified that those of sharp and dull capacities come to evoke the Dharma-body;

now, it is shown that two types of responses—superior and inferior—are manifested. The inferior response corresponds to those of dull faculties, while the superior response corresponds to those of sharp faculties.
These two responses both possess the two bodies of birth and dharma. Regarding the inferior response, the body of birth is manifested; as for this "birth," it is by means of the [True] Reality...
The one who enters the womb through wisdom, takes seven steps at birth, and undergoes six years of ascetic practice until his return is this [Nirmāṇakāya].
The inferior *saṃbhogakāya* born as a Dharma-body is that which is attained when the fetters and habitual tendencies are exhausted through the thirty-four moments of mind;
the superior *saṃbhogakāya* born as a body of manifestation is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other scriptures, where he dwells together with all the Bodhisattvas.

While dwelling in the womb of Māyā, he constantly preached the Mahāyāna Dharma; upon his birth, he took seven steps in each of the ten directions. This refers to the manifestation of the Supreme Response Body (saṃbhogakāya).

As for the manifestation of the Dharma Body (dharmakāya), at the site of the Path of Quiescence (śāntimārga-maṇḍala), through the final moment of the Vajra Mind, he severed the delusions of ignorance;

having exhausted them, he attained the wisdom corresponding to Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). His penetrating illumination reached the limit of the Dharma-nature, and his Perfectly Bright Universal Wisdom of the Seeds of Myriad Virtues was fully realized.

This is what is meant by "preparation. For those who leave the household life, the inferior response consists of leaving behind the *pariccheda-maraṇa* (birth-and-death of limited duration), while the superior response consists of leaving behind both the *pariccheda-maraṇa* and the *pariṇāma-maraṇa* (birth-and-death of transformation).

Regarding the attainment of *bodhi*: the inferior response is to possess the untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) produced by the four noble truths with their conditioned aspects;
this is called *bodhi*. The superior response is the illumination of the three truths [and the truth of the path].
The Way of Reality takes all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) as its bodhi. Miaole states:

"If one examines the characteristics established in these two locations, it is clear that the bodies of the Tripitaka and the Shared [teachings] are the inferior response-bodies, while the bodies of the Distinct and the Perfect [teachings] are the superior response-bodies.

Although it is said that each of these two types of response-bodies possesses both a birth-body and a dharma-body, the meaning of the fivefold dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*) resides within the superior response-body.
Although it is said that the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body) is superior to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), they are identical in meaning to the *dharmakāya*. The supplementary note states:
"The teachings of the Hīnayāna do not discuss permanence; since the fivefold *dharmakāya* ultimately returns to extinction, their meaning is identical to that of the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Since the Mahāyāna discusses permanence, [the emanation body] must arise from the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature); as the *dharmatā* is indestructible, the emanation body is likewise [indestructible]."

Because he is eternally abiding, his birth in the royal palace was not a true birth, but a manifestation of birth; his tranquil spirit at the Śāla Grove was not a true extinction, but a manifestation of extinction.
Therefore, in meaning, they are identical to the Dharmakāya. △ Second, [the section on] non-birth.
"However, the fact that I have truly attained Buddhahood has been for as long as this; (up to) causing them to enter the Buddha-way, I speak thus.
This passage states that "not born" means not having been born at the very beginning. Yet, from "I have truly attained" onwards, it clarifies that the fundamental reality is that there was no birth.
Nevertheless, devas, humans, and asuras perceive these two kinds of birth-phenomena and two bodies, and thus say: [they speak thus].
It is not so that this [birth] occurs for the first time; rather, I have long since attained this dharma of birth of the two bodies (*dvikāya*).
Today’s birth is not a real birth; therefore it is said to be "as long as this, as long as this," meaning its duration is as vast as the analogies mentioned above.
It is only through skillful means (*upāya*)—to clarify below that although it is not a real birth, why does he manifest birth? It is solely for the sake of benefiting [sentient beings].
Furthermore, because those who delight in the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle have meager virtue and heavy defilements, [the Buddha] enables them to attain the Way of the Buddha;
therefore it is said that he teaches and transforms sentient beings solely through skillful means (*upāya*). Since these are not actual births but manifestations of birth, he speaks in this manner.
△ Second, the benefit [of the teaching], which has two parts: first, the benefit of form and voice.

"O sons of good family, regarding the various sutras expounded by the Tathāgata—from [the passage] 'or manifesting his own affairs' to 'or manifesting the affairs of others'—this clarifies that he benefits sentient beings through the manifestation of form and voice in this present life.
'Expounding' refers to the teaching of voice; 'manifesting' refers to the regulation of form. Form and voice do not arise apart from self and other:
if one speaks of the *dharmakāya*, it is speaking of one's own body; if one speaks of the *nirmāṇakāya*, it is [speaking of the body of another]."
To speak of another’s body as having met Dīpaṃkara Buddha is to speak of one’s own body; to say that Dīpaṃkara Buddha was one’s teacher is to speak of another’s body.
Speech according to one’s own intention is to speak of one’s own body; speech according to another’s intention is to speak of another’s body.
To manifest the primary retribution (vipāka) is to show one’s own affairs; to manifest the secondary environment (niśraya) is to show another’s affairs. △
Second, explaining that [the teaching] is not false. First, the heading:
"That which is spoken is all true and not false.

Although the statement that speech is not false primarily relies on the benefit of sound, since sound necessarily accompanies form, it must be explained in both respects. Thus, it says "speech" (yan).
The "empty" refers to the fact that the two types of capacities—gradual and sudden—receive these two superior and inferior responses; thus, the benefit of form and voice is not in vain.

If one discusses the empty and the real according to the two gates of the provisional trace and the fundamental reality: in the past, when the practice of skillful means had not yet attained the benefit of the true path, this was the emptiness of the cause;
and because one clung to the near traces without yet attaining the benefit of the true reality of the original ground, this was [the emptiness of] the result.
The fruit was previously empty; now, hearing the teaching of the Trace Gate, one enters equally into the true aspect (*dharmatā*) and immediately obtains the real benefit within the causal stage.
Hearing the teaching of the Origin Gate, one eliminates the attachment to the near and obtains the real benefit of the long-term fruit-ground.
Because these two realities now contrast with the two previous emptinesses, it is said that all is real and not false. △ Second, explaining "not false."
Second, the initial illumination of principle is not in vain.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the three realms as they truly are.

From here below, there is a general explanation of how benefiting sentient beings is not in vain; first, we shall explain here that the benefit through physical form is not in vain, consisting of six phrases.
It is revealed that the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) is not separate from the *dharmakāya* (dharma body); the *dharmakāya* is formless and likewise has no arising or ceasing.

Yet, when sentient beings possess the conditions for arising and ceasing, they evoke a response from the *dharmakāya*. Through the power of the Tathāgata’s vows, [the *saṃbhogakāya*] appears to arise and cease in accordance with them.
Since this perception of arising and ceasing originates from sentient beings, these various phrases are explained by way of the three realms. As for "knowing and seeing as it truly is":
This refers to true wisdom illuminating the reality of the triple world according to principle; yet in that reality, there are no causal marks of the triple world.

*Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) states: "The six phrases herein clarify that the present response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is none other than the eternally perfected dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), for they are inconceivably one.
Thus it says, "illuminating principle, etc., without causal marks. If one follows the subsequent phrase, [it means] "without..."
Regarding the two types of death, it should be said that there are no causal characteristics of the two kinds of triple-world realms.
There is no birth-and-death;
there are no fruits of suffering consisting of the two kinds of birth-and-death: the fragmented and the transformative.

"Whether regressing or departing," there are five abidings and accumulations called "regression," and two fruits of death called "departure. Regarding the phrase "the causes and conditions of the household of the two deaths do not exist above the fetters":
this refers to the first clause when the Tathāgata arrives here.
Furthermore, there is neither one who remains in the world nor one who has entered extinction;
nor is there one who remains in the world of birth and death nor one who enters the extinction of nirvāṇa.
Because both of these are extinguished, it is said that "there is neither," and so forth. This is the second phrase.
Neither real nor unreal;
it is not the reality of extinction (nirvāṇa), nor is it the unreality of saṃsāra—this is the third phrase.
Neither like nor different.
It is not that there is difference within the mundane world, nor is it that there is suchness within the supramundane.
This is because sentient beings of the six realms perceive the three realms as being different, while those of the two vehicles perceive the three realms as suchness—that is, emptiness itself.
The Buddha perceives the three realms as neither suchness nor different; this simultaneous illumination of both suchness and difference—these four phrases above clarify the Middle Way.
"It is not as the three realms perceive the three realms.
"It is not as the two kinds of sentient beings in the three realms perceive the characteristics of the three realms" means that what is called "not as" (不如) refers to "not being like" (不如三界者，如者同也).
The Buddha possesses both provisional and ultimate wisdom; he must certainly not be the same as those two kinds [of beings].

Regarding the two kinds of threefold realms—the characteristics of cause and effect within the two extremes as perceived by sentient beings of the three realms—there are two types of "threefold realms.

The name "threefold realm" applies universally to both the internal and external realms. As for establishing the designation of "threefold realm" with respect to the external [realms], it is because the external is modeled upon the internal.
Because the Middle Way has not yet been fully realized, this is termed "delusion through views" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), which pervades all three realms even within the *parināmika* (transformation) lands.

The five excellent and wondrous sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are called the objects of desire (*kāmadhātu*), while inconceivable mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are called the objects of the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*).
The *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Pure Name) details their characteristics; this constitutes the fifth phrase.
The Tathāgata perceives such matters clearly and without error.
Because only the Buddha internally possesses the function of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), he exhaustively and accurately illuminates the reality of the triple world.

This is both speech according to his own intention (*svātman-tantra-vacana*) and also speech concerning his own person. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Within this there is no conceptual discrimination. Although the Tathāgata’s true wisdom is without discrimination, it does not hinder the use of expedient wisdom to know and see the characteristics of the triple world according to their measure;
thus, it accords with the views of the sentient beings within the triple world.

Although he is free from the two kinds of death, he manifests bodies subject to the two deaths in accordance with the intentions of others; thus, he speaks of the existence of the two deaths. Although he neither regresses nor emerges [from the world],...

In accordance with the intentions of others, he speaks of there being those who withdraw; yet although there are none who remain in the world or enter parinirvāṇa, he accords with the intentions of others by manifesting birth in the world and manifesting entry into nirvāṇa. He says there are those who remain in the world and those who attain extinction;
though these do not exist in reality, he speaks of the reality of nirvāṇa, and though that is not empty, he speaks of the emptiness of the triple world. Though the three [realms] do not exist...
The world differs, and thus its explanations differ; although there is no such thing as an ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there are explanations that accord with it.

Within the three realms, all that is perceived within the three realms is speech according to the intentions of others, termed "explaining the affairs of another's body" or "showing the affairs of another's body.
Because the Tathāgata’s two types of wisdom clearly and precisely discern the two truths, his physical form and voice both provide benefit, and both are real.

It is not in vain. *Miaole* (The Wondrous Joy) says: Since it is stated generally that "viewing as such" integrates what was previously illuminated into a single vision, all five preceding phrases of reality are restated together to form the characteristics of the two wisdoms of provisional and real.

While the preceding real wisdom illuminates only the realm of reality, the addition of provisional wisdom here allows one to perceive the provisional according to the capacities of beings; this clarifies that seeing is not seeing, yet it is seeing.
The two wisdoms are non-dual. △ Second, [the teaching] accords with capacities and is not in vain. Part one:
the stimulus of sentient beings. Because all sentient beings possess various natures (up to) various recollections, conceptions, and discriminations.
Because the faculties of sentient beings differ— being either sharp or dull, gradual or sudden— and because their dispositions, inclinations, practices, and wisdoms vary in manifold ways,
[the Buddha] taught the doctrines concerning himself and others, as well as non-futile causes, conditions, and parables, in order to cause their various roots of goodness to increase.
Regarding "nature," since there are various types of both gradual and sudden root-natures, it is necessary to employ the *puruṣapudgala-siddhānta* (the teaching for individuals).
Regarding all roots of goodness, even those who possess the disposition for such roots— whether of gradual or sudden capacity— if their various desires and inclinations differ,
one must employ the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint) to cause them all to rejoice according to their respective inclinations.
As the practitioner cultivates various practices according to their inclinations, one must employ the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (standpoint of the person) to generate their latent wholesome seeds.
If, in the course of practice, one has many attachments that cause hindrances, one must employ the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic method) to destroy these manifest evil conceptualizations;

this is wisdom, which is a semblance-understanding. For those of both gradual and sudden capacities who abide in the stages of the outer and inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), because they possess various roots of goodness, they desire and delight [in the path];
because they desire and delight, they practice; and because they practice, they attain the signs.

To understand this, one must employ the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint). According to whatever conceptual understanding one has attained, one further explains the Dharma so that they may enter into the principle.
This continues until, at the stage of the first ground (*bhūmi*), there is the desire to practice;

at the time of the second ground, one likewise conceptualizes the realm of the second ground—this is "recollection and thought" (*smṛti-saṃjñā*). If a true understanding of the second ground then arises, then...

This contemplation of mental conceptions removes the phenomena of verbal expression; from their cessation up to the fruit of wondrous enlightenment, only when one attains Buddhahood does one finally achieve ultimate liberation from recollection and thought, obtaining the wondrous joy of eternal, quiescent illumination.
*Wenmiaole* asks: "One should speak of the 'First Abode' (Prathamābhūmi); why then do you say 'First Ground' (Prathamabhūmi)? Answer:
This is spoken in accordance with the gradual and sudden approaches, merely using the schema of grounds as a provisional reference. △ Second, the manifestation of transformation.
Desiring to cause various roots of goodness to arise— up until the point where the Buddha-activities he performs are never for a moment neglected—

he manifests various deeds of himself and others through various sounds of benefit for himself and others; this is precisely because he wishes to cause those with gradual and sudden capacities to produce various roots of goodness,
and thus he appears in various forms of himself and others, with various sounds of teaching for himself and others, and through various causes and conditions.
This is by way of analogy: for those of gradual capacity, there are the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) and four gates with various causes, conditions, and parables;
within each of these gates, there are likewise further varieties of the four gates of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

For those of sudden capacity, it is the same for the Distinct and Complete Teachings (*bhūta-yāna*), each having its own four gates and various kinds of methods, such as those employed by the thirty-two bodhisattvas in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.

Each [teaching] speaks of entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality; the various types of practices and their characteristics within the *Avataṃsaka* are all expedient teachings employing various parables and expressions, bestowed according to the capacities of those with distinct or perfect roots.

That "the Buddha-work performed has never for a moment ceased" is a summary concluding that these are not in vain. As stated above, these various forms and sounds—whether pertaining to oneself or others—cause all beings...
Because they enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision from the very beginning and do not concern the limited matters of humans, devas, or the two vehicles, it is called "Buddha-work.
If one person alone were to attain extinction while others did not, the Buddha-work performed would be rendered deficient;

if it were deficient, sentient beings would not receive true benefit. How, then, could it be said that all is real and not false? Now, those of the seven stages of expedient means are all... [The text continues: ...included.

Entering into the single reality allows one to say that all things are real and not false, and that the Buddha’s work is never abandoned. △ Second, [the section on] "Non-extinction yet manifesting extinction," which has two parts:
first, the formal explanation; second, the first part, clarifying that the fundamental reality is not extinguished, which further has two parts: first, clarifying the permanence of the fruit-stage.
"In this way, since my attainment of Buddhahood has been for a very long time" (up to) "it abides eternally and does not perish.
Attaining Buddhahood is the fruit; because it has been for a very long time and so forth, it is eternal and thus does not perish.

Since it does not perish, its benefit extends into the future; therefore, these four characters are employed to clarify that the great power and majesty of the future abide eternally and provide benefit.
It is a matter of fact. △ Second, citing the cause to illustrate the result:

"O sons of good family, when I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path... [as previously stated] ...even now it is not yet exhausted; furthermore, it shall be doubled from the aforementioned number."

This passage cites the cause to illustrate the fruit in order to clarify eternal permanence. For when a Buddha cultivates the perfect cause and attains the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), he has already obtained an eternal life that cannot be exhausted;
this already exceeds the measure of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas mentioned above—how much more so, then, is the life of the fruit?
It is like a crown prince whose stipend is already inexhaustible while still a prince, let alone when he ascends to the pinnacle of sovereignty.

"How could it ever be exhausted? This refers to the "wondrous bliss. To cite the cause as an illustration for the fruit means that when the Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path in his past lives, even the causal lifespan he attained through those practices was not yet exhausted; how much more so, then, would the resultant lifespan be?
Thus, we know that by using the inexhaustible causal lifespan to illustrate the inexhaustible resultant lifespan, it is shown that both cause and fruit are eternal. △ Second, the explanation.
Within the traces [of his manifestation], he proclaims extinction;
yet now, though there is no actual parinirvāṇa, he nevertheless proclaims that he shall attain extinction.

Within the traces, all three bodies possess the principle of proclaiming extinction where there is no extinction. Regarding the Dharma-body, which is not subject to extinction, it proclaims extinction as follows:

As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Because phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, there is nothing that can be extinguished; this is the meaning of the Dharmakāya as non-extinction. It further states:
"This is the meaning of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*)," which refers to the proclamation of extinction. Regarding the Sambhogakāya, it is not subject to extinction.

As for the one who proclaims extinction—who possesses wisdom and who possesses afflictions? To say that wisdom is able to destroy [afflictions] is precisely the meaning of the Sambhogakāya being non-extinguishable.

If sentient beings who have not yet realized the meaning hear this, they will immediately claim that they themselves are Buddhas, giving rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, and no longer cultivate the Way.
Therefore, it is further proclaimed that "the Way can extinguish delusions," which is itself the proclamation of extinction. The Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not subject to extinction;

thus, the one who proclaims extinction must be the function of the Response, Reward, and Dharma bodies. Since their essence is without extinction, how could their function ever be exhausted? This is precisely the Response Body.
The body does not possess the meaning of extinction; however, for the sake of sentient beings, if they were to see the Buddha constantly, they would give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence.
Therefore, he proclaims, "Tonight I shall enter parinirvāṇa," which is precisely the proclamation of extinction. △ Second, the benefits, in two parts:
first, the harm caused by non-extinction for sentient beings; second, the harm caused by non-extinction. First, the harm caused by non-extinction.
The Tathāgata uses these skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings (up to) entering the net of conceptualization and false views.

This section states that "not extinguishing [them] causes harm," meaning that those who, like people of inferior capacity who delight in the small vehicle, see the Buddha as eternally present, fail to plant roots of goodness;
being impoverished and lowly, they do not give rise to the two kinds of goodness—true and middle—and thus there is no benefit, yet their views are not severed.

The two evils of volitional ignorance (*saṃkalpa-avidyā*) result in the impairment of the five desires, which correspond to the afflictions of thought (*saṃyojana*), while recollective conceptualization corresponds to the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Because the defilements of sentient beings are thus heavy, it is necessary to proclaim "cessation" (*nirodha*);
if cessation were not proclaimed, the two evils would arise without being extinguished, and the two virtues would be impaired without arising. △ Second, the detailed explanation of non-extinction.
If one sees the Tathāgata as eternally present and imperishable [up to] being unable to give rise to the thought that he is difficult to encounter or a heart of reverence;
if, seeing the Buddha always remaining in the world, one gives rise to arrogance and indolence— thereby causing harm because reverence is not produced—

and if, due to such arrogance and self-indulgence, views-afflictions increase and due to weariness and indolence, thought-afflictions arise, one will fail to produce the thought that he is difficult to encounter.
Because one cannot give rise to the realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*), one cannot sever the view of non-reverence;

because one cannot give rise to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one cannot sever [the afflictions] of thought. For this reason, it is appropriate that [the Buddha] should manifest extinction.

Furthermore, if one hears that the three Buddhas do not enter extinction, there arises the sense of pride and self-indulgence; if one hears that the Dharma-body does not enter extinction, one then [misconceives] the assembly as...
The birth [of the Tathāgata] is like that of Maitreya; it is one suchness, not two suchnesses. From this, pride arises in the mind, and conceit is born, thinking:
"Since all afflictions are fundamentally unborn from the beginning and now likewise do not cease, what need is there to cultivate the path?
Thereupon, they indulge their desires and become dissolute, proclaiming: "The Dharma-body has the meaning of quiescent extinction," while hearing that the Reward-body is imperishable.
They then claim that all sentient beings are the very mark of nirvāṇa, and that the mark of nirvāṇa is identical to the mark of afflictions.
Consequently, they give rise once more to arrogance and self-indulgence, no longer cultivating goodness, becoming indolent and negligent. To justify this, they proclaim:

"The wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) can extinguish afflictions, whereas the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) does not extinguish them; it merely manifests extinction for the sake of easy understanding by sentient beings. Upon hearing this proclamation, [the deluded] follow it.
Upon his parinirvāṇa, one gives rise to the thought that a Buddha is difficult to encounter regarding these three [aspects], thereby engendering a mind of reverence.
△ Second, the proclamation of the parinirvāṇa is beneficial to sentient beings, in two parts: first, praising the difficulty of encountering a Buddha.
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks by means of skillful expedients, saying that bhikṣus should know that the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is difficult to encounter.
It is difficult for the three Buddhas to appear simultaneously, and sentient beings delight in and are attached to inferior dharmas;

with their afflictions of views and thoughts heavy, they do not cultivate the Path upon hearing that the three bodies are imperishable, and thus it is difficult for them to achieve union with the Buddha. △ Second, explaining the meaning of "difficult to encounter."
Why is this? Because those people of meager merit—though there has been no actual cessation—speak of "nirvāṇa.
If one sees the three Buddhas, that person possesses much goodness and little evil; for such a person, I do not proclaim cessation, as they see the Buddha constantly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Or, if one does not see the Buddha, it is because their obstructions are heavy and their goodness is slight; for them, I speak of the three [vehicles].
When sentient beings hear that the Buddhas are difficult to encounter, they immediately think:

"Although the three Buddhas are neither born nor extinguished, one must necessarily give rise to goodness and eliminate evil to attain realization and vision; since this matter is not easy to achieve, it is said to be 'difficult to meet.

Regarding the phrase "the heart harbors longing and admiration," etc., this clarifies that although [the Buddha] manifests extinction, there is no impairment; because he does not impair [the eradication of] views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), it is called "unimpaired."
Planting roots of goodness is called being beneficial. △ Second, a summary showing that [the teaching] is not in vain. Third, first clarifying the sequence from near to far:
Furthermore, son of good family, the Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is always thus.

This clarifies that when the Buddhas appear in the five turbidities, they necessarily manifest first the three [vehicles] and later the one [vehicle], and first those who are near and later those who are far. △ Second,
it clarifies acting for the sake of transforming sentient beings and delivering sentient beings.
△ The three knowledges are all not false;
they are all real and not deceptive.

△ Second, the explanation by way of analogy, in two parts: First, the opening of the analogy; second, the analogy of the skilled physician treating his son, which illustrates the aforementioned three periods of time.

Regarding the three initial analogies for responding to and transforming according to what is appropriate: first, the analogy of the physician traveling afar illustrates the benefit of beings in the past. Within this, there are two parts:
first, the analogy for responding and transforming. First, the direct analogy for responding and transforming:
It is like a skilled physician who is wise and discerning, proficient in formulating medicines, and adept at curing all manner of illnesses.

This surpasses the previous analogy; with my Buddha-eye, I observe that there exists the wisdom capable of responding [to the needs of beings]. "Excellent physician" means one who is virtuous and skillful;
it is a metaphor for the Buddha, who internally possesses the three types of penetration (*trividyā*) and the five eyes—that is, the eight arts—and thus perfectly masters the nature of the medicine.
Externally, he recognizes the root causes from which the illnesses of all sentient beings arise. "Wisdom" refers to the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate, which are profound.
He knows the two truths; the wise and penetrating one uses the five eyes to discern the capacities of beings for the sudden and gradual teachings without error.
The principles and texts of the twelve divisions of the teaching are profoundly deep, like clearly refined prescriptions and medicines.

Relying on the four *siddhāntas*, he universally understands the diseases of the afflictions of sentient beings according to their sudden or gradual [dispositions], like a skilled physician who treats all manner of ailments. There are ten kinds of physicians; the first is the physician who treats diseases.

The illness increases without diminishing, or at times it leads to death; this is like the non-Buddhist heretics who hold views of emptiness, acting willfully in evil and teaching others to give rise to false views and sever the roots of goodness—once the Dharma-body has perished, the life of wisdom also dies. Second, the illness neither increases nor diminishes;
this is like the non-Buddhist ascetics who hold views of existence, practicing good through austerities such as throwing themselves from cliffs or leaping into fire.
First, attaining meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) yet being unable to sever the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) is neither decrease nor increase;
second, being unable to sever even wholesome states is likewise neither increase nor decrease.
Third, curing illness through decrease without increase refers to those who practice worldly meditation and sever the fetters—namely, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Fourth, curing illness...
First, it can cause a cure such that the illness does not recur;

yet, its treatment is not universal, as those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) treat only one or two types of beings with whom they have a karmic connection, unable to treat all universally. Fifth, although it may be both comprehensive and universal, it lacks skillful means in the application of treatment for suffering;
the *Śāstra* calls this "clumsy deliverance" (*duḥkhapāramitā*), which refers to the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) of the Tripiṭaka Teaching.
The Bodhisattva’s great compassion is a broad healing. Sixth, regarding the wondrous art of healing diseases:

it heals those who suffer pain and affliction, yet it cannot heal those destined for certain death—this is like the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching who employ the emptiness of the essence of phenomena to treat only those with reversible conditions, while failing to treat the "burnt seeds" of ordinary beings and the Two Vehicles.
Seventh, although they treat diseases that are difficult to cure, yet...
8. Being unable to treat all illnesses simultaneously is the stage of a Bodhisattva prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) in the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).
9. Being able to treat all illnesses simultaneously yet being unable to restore them to their original state is the initial stage of the Ten Faiths (*shixin*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
10. Being able to treat all illnesses universally and also being able to restore them to their original state...
That which is fundamental yet cannot cause one to transcend that fundamentality is precisely the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) through to the *vajra-citta* of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Tenth, to treat all illnesses at once and thereby enable their restoration, while also causing them to transcend the fundamental, is the Tathāgata.
Of these, the first three are the "old physicians," while the latter seven are all "guest physicians. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states that the former...

These three types are also called "physicians" because, before the Buddha appeared in the world, all non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) claimed for themselves the status of renunciants and each led their own followers;
thus, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Tathāgata alone is contrasted with those non-Buddhists and designated as the "new physician.
Furthermore, prior to the appearance of the Buddha in the world, a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) who governed the world through the ten wholesome paths was also so called.
The former physicians were originally the masters and those who came later were called guests; thus they are termed "guest physicians. The *Wuliangyi jing* (Sutra of Innumerable Meanings) states:
"Among the great physicians and king-like physicians, the eighth and ninth may both be called 'kings,' but only the tenth physician alone is called the 'Great King.
△ Second, the analogy for the resonance between the capacity and the response.
That person has many sons—perhaps ten, twenty, or even up to a hundred.
This person is a metaphor for the Buddha; "many sons" refers to those such as the ten śrāvakas, the twenty pratyekabuddhas, and the hundred bodhisattvas.
Setting aside the two vehicles for a moment, let us specifically clarify the sons of the bodhisattva, of whom there are many.

Regarding the meaning of the three types of seeds: first, as for the seed of the direct cause, because all sentient beings possess the three causes of Buddha-nature through correct conditions and are thus the children of the Buddha, it is said that "the sentient beings therein are all my children," and the present text further states, "there are many children.
If categorized according to the ten mental factors (*caitasika*), there are one hundred "children," with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) being the father.

The wisdom that constitutes the true cause Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) is the revealing cause Buddha-nature (*vijñapti-hetu*); the remaining nine factors that support and give rise to it belong to the conditional cause Buddha-nature (*pratyaya-hetu*).
When one factor arises, the other nine provide assistance; thus, they together constitute the hundred [factors].

Although all sentient beings possess these three causes, because the revealing cause has never yet given rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and the conditional cause has never yet applied itself through spiritual practice (*prayoga*), they all remain within the state of the true cause.

Because they are children of the Buddha, there are two types of conditions: the "condition as cause" (en-in) and the "child of the cause. For example, when the sixteen princes gave a re-exposition of the *Lotus Sūtra*, those who heard the Dharma developed even a slight understanding;
this immediately constituted the "nature as the cause of fulfillment" (jō-in-shō). In the past, their slight ability to practice served as the "nature as the condition" (en-in-shō).
While the "true nature as the cause" (shō-in-shō) is the fundamental basis, although there are thus three natures of cause, we shall here focus on the conditions established in the past.

Because they all belong to the category of conditional causes (*pratyaya-hetu*) that stimulate today’s realization of the single reality, they are able to form a karmic connection and become sons of the Buddha.

Regarding the meaning of "a hundred sons": this refers to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*); when one stage of faith arises, it already contains the remaining nine, and thus there are a hundred instances of faith, which are called the "hundred sons.
The third, the sons of the causal factor of completion (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*), are those who today hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Abiding within true wisdom, I shall certainly become a Buddha; born from the Buddha’s own mouth and having obtained a portion of the Buddha-dharma, I am called a true son.
This also has three causes: now that the Buddha-nature is clearly manifested and seen, these all belong to the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*).
As for the meaning of the "hundred sons" of the Buddha-sons, the hundred [stages] that correspond to the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) are further brought into the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).
This refers to the hundred names and hundred sons of partial realization. Now, the "hundred sons" in this text do not signify the "sons of understanding";

rather, they belong to the category of those who have not yet lost their minds, as clarified within the section on "Taking Medicine. The subtle joy therein is called "understanding" (*liǎo*) because it marks entry into the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*).
From the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) up until the stage prior to the [ten] abidings (*vihāra*), all are termed "conditions" (*yuán*). △
The second analogy illustrates the manifestation of parinirvāṇa.
It is like having a matter requiring one's presence that necessitates traveling far to another country;

this illustrates the manifestation of parinirvāṇa within the past responsive transformations, because the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) for this land has already matured while the conditions (*pratyaya*) for that other region have ripened.

"The view that should be extinguished and the view that should arise are called 'reaching a distant foreign land. △ Second, the analogy of returning and departing again illustrates the present response to transformation.
Part one: the analogy for the stirring of conditions.
Later, the sons drank another person’s poisonous medicine; when the medicine took effect, they became dazed and disoriented, rolling about on the ground.

This section below is an analogy for the present manifestation of the Buddha’s transformative benefit of sentient beings; it specifically illustrates those of superior capacity whose response is harmonized with the teaching.
It says "drank" because sentient beings of meager virtue and heavy defilements, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, take pleasure in and become attached to the teachings of false teachers.
Because he is ignorant of the essential path for transcending the world, he is said to be "confused and agitated" as he wanders through the various realms of existence.

Because he falls within the triple world (*tridhātu*), he is said to be "rolling on the ground. *Miaole* (妙樂) states that it is called "ground" merely because one is looking toward the dharma of world-transcendence.
△ Second, the analogy for the response-body and transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Part One: Manifesting birth where there is no birth. Part One: The analogy for the benefit of form and sound.
The first analogy illustrates the benefit of the physical form.
At that time, his father returns home and [says], "I wish to be healed and granted a renewed lifespan.

The following section illustrates that which is not born appearing as born; the current analogy of the benefit of the physical form—where the father returns home—illustrates the Buddha’s re-manifestation.
To be born in this land and yet believe and accept the teachings of false teachers is called "drinking poison and losing one's mind.

This refers to those who are greedily attached to the five desires of the triple world and lose the roots of goodness previously planted for the three vehicles, thereby failing to manifest the karmic response of the Great or Small Vehicles.

It is for such people that the Buddha speaks of extinction; it is not that he proclaims extinction when it has already occurred. Furthermore, there are those who, though attached to the five desires, do not lose the [roots of goodness].

Riding upon their roots of goodness, there are differences in the magnitude of their capacities; it is for the sake of such beings that the Buddha manifests birth, though he has not actually been born.
As for "seeing from afar," this clarifies that when the Buddha appears in the world, sentient beings likewise see the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*);

however, because they are obstructed by the five hindrances and the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), they are unable to personally attend upon the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and thus it is called "seeing from afar. All who see or hear of the Buddha’s appearance experience joy.
Because they paid respect to this matter, the sutra text says, "All were greatly rejoiced," and so forth; examples such as the Brahma King’s request are likewise expressions of seeking salvation.
△ Second, the analogy for the benefit of the sound, in two parts: first, the analogy for the Buddha accepting the request and turning the Dharma wheel of the Two Truths.

The father, seeing his sons suffering in this manner, [prepared a medicine] by pounding and sifting the ingredients, mixing them together, and gave it to his sons to take. The *Kē* (Commentary) states:

"When turning the wheel of the Two Truths (*dvaya-satya*), one should speak of the Three Truths (*tri-satya*). While the names "Two Truths" and "Three Truths" are mutually inclusive, they differ in their specific application;

here, setting aside the specific to follow the general, we refer to the Two Truths within the Sudden Teaching (*tun*). The "various scriptures" (*fang*) mentioned therein refers to the twelve divisions of the canon (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).
"Teaching" refers to the eighty thousand dharma-gates elucidated within the teachings;

the twelve divisions of the sutras that emerge from the Buddha represent the "sudden medicinal herbs," while the nine divisions of the sūtras that emerge from the Buddha represent the "gradual medicinal herbs.
"Color" is a metaphor for the precepts, for the phenomena of body and speech are restrained and their characteristics are clearly manifested, just as color and fragrance [are manifest].

"Form" (*rūpa*) is a metaphor for the merit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which perfumes all things with its wondrous fragrance. "Taste" (*rasa*) is a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*), which is able to attain the flavor of principle.
Furthermore, form is the color of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) clearly illuminated by *prajñā*, being distinct and unimpeded.

Fragrance is liberation (*vimukti*), the quality of abandonment that is free from foul odors. Taste is the flavor of principle within the *dharmakāya*. These three dharmas are neither sequential nor... [repeated text] ...sequential.

The horizontal name is "Secret Treasury" (Guhyakośa); by practicing according to the teachings, one attains entry into this treasury. Both gradual and sudden approaches equally possess precepts, concentration, and wisdom;
however, in this text, we follow the specific [classification] and attribute it to the Perfect-Sudden (Yuan-dun).

If the gradual teaching speaks of the three vehicles, the power of the samādhi of emptiness is like pounding with a pestle, the samādhi of signlessness is like sifting through a sieve, and the samādhi of wishlessness is like blending the ingredients—one for each.
The three contemplations—emptiness, like pounding; the provisional, like sifting; and the middle, like blending—are each inseparable from precept, concentration, and wisdom.
Because this Dharma is given to sentient beings of both gradual and sudden capacities for their practice, it is called "causing them to take medicine.
△ Second, the analogy of the Buddha using these two gates of admonition and exhortation to transform [beings]. First, the gate of exhortation.
And he spoke these words: "This great and excellent medicine is fully endowed with color, fragrance, and delicious flavor; you should take it.
Second, the section on admonition:
