'It will swiftly eliminate suffering and affliction, so that you shall no longer have any further ailments.'"
The Buddha intends to exhort and instruct through two teachings so that all sentient beings may take the medicinal medicine of the Dharma. △ Second, the analogy for the non-futility of the benefit:
Among those sons, those who had not lost their minds (up to) immediately took it, and their illnesses were completely eliminated and they were healed.
"These various sons" refers to the son of the internal cause (*nidāna*) among the three sons explained above.

That he does not lose his mind and his illness is cured by taking the medicine is a metaphor for what was stated above: that all is real and not false. **II. The Non-extinction and Manifestation of Extinction.** **A.
The Parable of the Impending Death.** **1. The Parable of the Reasons for Announcing the Death.**
Other who have lost their minds see their father come, yet they are unwilling to take such excellent medicine.

This is a metaphor for the reason why [the Buddha] manifests extinction: it is precisely because sentient beings lack merit that, though they see the Buddha as ever-present, they only increase their arrogance and self-indulgence without practicing;
this is precisely what is meant by being unwilling to take the medicine. △ Second, the formal proclamation of the analogy of impending death.
Second, the analogy of first intending to depart or remain:
"I shall now employ skillful means to cause them to take this medicine.

This is analogous to the aforementioned case where remaining in the world causes harm, while manifesting extinction brings benefit; thus, one should employ skillful means and immediately intend [to depart]. △
Second is the parable of announcing the impending death, which states:
"You should know... [the messenger] was sent back to inform your father that he had already died.
This precisely illustrates that the period for the manifestation of nirvāṇa is nearing its end; therefore, it says, "When the time of old age and death has arrived, one shall enter [nirvāṇa]."
Regarding *nirvāṇa*: although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, he leaves behind the sūtras and teachings in the world; therefore, it is said that these are "excellent medicines.
That they now remain here and will subsequently go to other lands means that he manifests extinction in this region while manifesting birth in other regions.

As for "sending messengers" and so forth, this refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Four Reliances speaking to sentient beings, saying: "The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa; he has left behind only this [teaching]."

"I shall now proclaim and propagate the Dharma; you should receive and practice it. In the future, if sentient beings lack the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) for the transmission and exposition of the sūtras and the Dharma, how could they know for themselves that the Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa? Therefore, the four reliances are the guides for people."
△ Second, the parable of the sons’ awakening, in two parts. First, the benefit of manifesting death:
At that time, the sons heard that their father had passed away (up to: "Now he has abandoned us and died far away in another land."
Sentient beings must first know of their father’s passing before they can awaken; likewise, it is only when the Tathāgata manifests his parinirvāṇa that sentient beings are able to practice.
△ Second, the response of future capacities.
Reflecting upon myself, I am orphaned and exposed, with no one left to rely upon... (up to)... I immediately took [the medicine] and wore it; my grievous illness was completely cured.

This is truly because, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, sentient beings have awakened and taken this medicine to practice as a causal condition, thereby being able to respond to and transform others in the future, just as the *Śāstram Upadeśam* says:
"Those who have not yet been delivered, all have already been brought to completion."
The conditions for deliverance are also experienced through present manifestations; it is not only Śākyamuni who appears, as the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* states:

"Through diligent effort and reaching the limit of suffering, one may behold the emanations of Śākyamuni, the many treasures (Prabhūtaratna), the Eastern Virtuous Deity (*Śubhavyūha*), and the World-Honored Ones of the Seven Buddhas.
△ Third, the analogy of seeking and later returning illustrates the future response and transformation.
When the father heard that his sons had all recovered, he immediately returned and allowed them all to see him.
This is an analogy for the future benefit of sentient beings: when the "father" hears that the "sons" have recovered, it immediately becomes the responsive capacity that enables all to see him;
this gives rise to the future response, which will subsequently provide both physical and vocal benefits. *Miaole* says: "They have recovered."

These words do not mean that delusion is entirely severed; rather, for those with the capacities of the three vehicles who are capable of meeting [the teaching], whether their delusions are severed or not, they are all said to have "recovered.
△ Second, the analogy of treating a child’s actual illness illustrates that the benefits conferred upon beings throughout the three periods of time are not in vain.
"What do you think, sons of good family? [The sons of good family replied: "No, World-Honored One.
△ Second, the combined analogy, in three parts. First, combining with the benefit of beings in the past.
The Buddha said: "I am also like this; since I attained Buddhahood, for the sake of sentient beings, [it has been] incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas."
△ 2. Second, combining [the past and future] to benefit beings in the present:
by the power of skillful means, he declares that he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
△ 3. Third, combining [the past and future] to show that benefiting beings is not in vain.
Furthermore, there is no one capable of rightfully accusing me of the fault of falsehood.
△ Second, the verse summary has three parts; first, the verse summary of the Dharma-exposition; second, the verse summary of benefiting beings throughout the three periods of time;
third, the verse summary of the past [has three parts]; first, the verse summary that enlightenment was attained long ago.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Since I attained Buddhahood, the number of kalpas that have passed is immeasurable—hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya years."

The supplementary note states: "A hundred births, a thousand births, ten thousand births, a hundred million births, a billion births, a ten-billion births, a hundred-billion births, a trillion births, a ten-trillion births, a hundred-trillion births, a quadrillion births, a ten-quadrillion births, a hundred-quadrillion births, a quintillion births, a ten-quintillion births, a hundred-quintillion births, a sextillion births, a ten-sextillion births, a hundred-sextillion births, a septillion births, a ten-septillion births, a hundred-septillion births.
△ Second, the verse on benefiting beings during the intermediate period.
He constantly preaches the Dharma, transforming and teaching countless billions of sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way for immeasurable kalpas.
△ Third, a verse on his constant dwelling in this place;
for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he employs skillful means to manifest parinirvāṇa (up to: though near, they do not see him).
△ Second, two verses concerning the present; the first verse concerns the non-arising of what appears to arise:
"The multitude sees me enter parinirvāṇa and extensively makes offerings to my relics... [omitted] ...all emerge from Vulture Peak Mountain."
△ Second, two verses clarify that there is no extinction, yet an appearance of extinction occurs.
"I am always present among sentient beings and do not perish" (up to) "but it is said that I have entered parinirvāṇa.
△ Third, three verses concern the future; the first verse concerns the awakening of the capacity of future beings.
"I see all sentient beings submerged in suffering and affliction... (until) I emerge to preach the Dharma for them.

From this point downward, the verse praises the future while the preceding prose merely mentions the four characters "permanently abiding and not perishing. Now, this verse expands that text into four sections;
this one and a half lines clarify the future response of those with karmic capacity. △ Second, the verse on permanence.

Abiding in non-extinction, his supernormal powers are such that throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he scatters [flowers] upon the Buddha and the great assembly while always remaining on Vulture Peak Mountain;
this is called the Land of True Reward (*vipākabhūmi*). As for "other various abodes," this refers to the various directions.

"There are other lands" refers to the meaning of the aforementioned other countries. "Filled with devas and humans" means that those at the stages of abiding, practice, and heading toward [enlightenment]—the thirty minds—are the humans, and those at the ten bhūmis are the devas.
"Beating the celestial drum" symbolizes the Buddha’s spontaneous preaching without being questioned.
"Raining down māndārava flowers" symbolizes the exposition of the ranks and positions of the worthy and the sage. *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) says: "If one follows the other [traditions]..."
Regarding "land," if it refers to that which possesses residual territory, the retributive land must be identified as the *paranirmita-vashavartin* (other-enjoyment) land;

however, according to the phrase "constantly abiding," it belongs to the *svasaṃbhoga* (self-enjoyment) land. If one follows the verse’s mention of "jewel adornments," it refers to the original *paranirmita-vashavartin* land.
As for "other-enjoyment," this is the land inhabited by the *paranirmita-vashavartin* body of recompense.
The Name-Realization Reward Land (*nāma-vipākakṣetra*) pertains to phenomena; it belongs to the Other-Realization [Land], which is the Supreme Response Body (*sambhogakāya*).
Because it is seen according to the karmic resonance of sentient beings, it is called "Other-Realization. The Self-Enjoyment Land is the land inhabited by the Self-Response Body;

it is named the "Eternally Quiescent Light" (*nitya-praśānta-prabhā*) and pertains to principle. The Self-Response Body is wisdom. As the Sūtra says: "That which is obtained through long-cultivated practice is the light of wisdom that illuminates immeasurably."
This is so. △ Third, explaining the causes and conditions for not seeing it:
My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitude perceives it as being utterly consumed by fire... (up to) ...they do not even hear the names of the Triple Gem.
△ Fourth, the causes and conditions for attaining the vision [of the Buddha].
"All those who cultivate merit, who are gentle and upright" (up to) "...attained through long-cultivated practice.
Miaole explains: "The phrase 'all those who cultivate merit' and so forth refers to those who are fully endowed with the two causes of conditions and fulfillment."
"Furthermore, all see my body" refers to seeing the body of true recompense (*sambhogakāya*) within the land of true recompense;

"or at times for these multitudes" likewise refers to those at the first stage (*bhūmi*) or the first dwelling (*vihāra*). "Only after a long time do they see the Buddha" specifically indicates those for whom the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) are heavy.
"Such is the power of my wisdom" summarizes the great majesty [of the Buddha]. △ Second, the verse on how all is real and not false.

"You who possess wisdom, do not harbor doubts regarding this; you should sever them so that they are forever exhausted. The Buddha’s words are real and not false. △ Second, the verse on the parable, in two parts:
first, the verse on the opening of the parable, in three parts; first, the verse on the past.
It is like a physician who employs skillful means.
△ Second, the verse on the present:
in order to cure his mad son, he speaks of being dead while actually remaining alive.
△ Three verses show that [the Buddha's words] are not false;
none can speak what is deceptive.
△ Two verses combine the analogy. Part three: The first verse combines the past.
I am also the Father of the World who rescues all those afflicted by suffering.
These two verses together concern the present;
for the sake of ordinary beings who, due to their inversions, claim that what truly exists has ceased, I preach various dharmas.
△ The three verses combined show that [the teaching] is not in vain.
Each time he forms this intention: "By what means can I cause sentient beings to enter the unsurpassed wisdom and swiftly achieve the Buddha-body?
Opening the three to reveal the one, and opening the near to reveal the far—desiring to cause sentient beings to swiftly attain the Buddha-way, this matter is certain.
It is not in vain.
From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter Seventeen, "Distinguishing Merit":
When the Buddha spoke of his lifespan, the past disciples who emerged from the earth and the present disciples on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa attained the planting of [roots of goodness].
Because it brings about various benefits, it is called "merit" (*guṇa*); because its depth and shallowness differ, it is called the "Chapter on Distinctions.

This passage constitutes the second section of the "Root Gate," the Bestowal of Prophecy. Although, according to the merit of hearing the sutra, it would merely belong to the "residual" category, based on the statement that one shall "attain bodhi in the future," it is equivalent to the bestowal of prophecy.
According to the *Dharmapada-sūtra-śāstra*, this passage possesses the power of the Dharma.
Regarding the power of cultivation and the power of the Dharma: because they are accomplished through the Dharma, they are called "powers. There are five aspects:
first, realization, which refers to six hundred and eighty trillion beings attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) up to those who attain *bodhi* in a single lifetime;
second, faith, which refers to bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); third, making offerings.
That is to say: first, when it is said that this bodhisattva attains great benefit of the Dharma, celestial flowers rain down from the void, as described in the third chapter;
second, as in the present chapter; fourth, hearing the Dharma, as in the "Chapter on Rejoicing" (Anumodanā-parivarta);

fifth, reading, reciting, upholding, and explaining—reading and reciting as in the "Chapter on the Merits of a Dharma Master" (Dharmabhāṇaka-guṇa-parivarta), and upholding as referring back to the "Dharma Master’s Peaceful Practice" (Dharmabhāṇaka-sukha-vihāra) which encourages upholding the three [practices].

Regarding the exposition of the chapters: the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" and the "Chapter on Entrustment" illustrate the power of instruction; the "Chapter on the King of Medicine" illustrates the power of ascetic practice;
the "Chapter on Wondrous Sound" illustrates the power of conversion; the two chapters on Avalokiteśvara and the Dhāraṇī illustrate the protection against difficulties;
the "Chapter on the King of Sublime Adornment" illustrates the manifestation of merit; and the "Chapter on Samantabhadra" illustrates the protection of the Dharma. II. Differentiation of Merit.
Preface to the Chapter on Merits, Part One: Receiving the Prediction Concerning the Dharma-body. First, the general introduction by the Sūtra compiler:
At that time, the great assembly heard the Buddha speak of the lifespan and the vast number of kalpas in this manner (up to), and they attained great benefit.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s detailed exposition.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... [up to] "attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The commentary states: "The term 'detailed exposition' (fenbie) refers to the meaning of differences in depth and shallowness, as noted in the sub-commentary beneath the title of the superior grade."
The Buddha’s words are perfect and subtle (referring to the two gates of the Trace and the Source); thus, one must not use provisional stages to explain the sutra.

Therefore, in the preceding Gate of the Trace, the opening, showing, awakening, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision were explained; now, in the Gate of the Source, the various bodhisattvas’ increase in the Path and decrease of births are all explained according to the perfect stages.
Those who attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas enter the stage of the ten abidings of the Perfect Teaching; thus [it is said in] the *Huayan*...
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "In the first stage, the Abiding in Initial Resolve, one gives rise to all at once;

one attains the Tathāgata’s single body that is an infinite body, the pure and wondrous Dharma-body, which is profoundly still yet responds to all things. This is precisely the meaning [of this passage]. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another, nor from both, nor without a cause; therefore, it is said that they are unarisen."
Furthermore, the *Huayan shu* states: "The syllable 'A' signifies entry into the meaning of non-arising. The principle of non-arising universally encompasses all phenomena;
when a Bodhisattva attains this non-arising, they realize the emptiness of all dharmas and sever all obstacles."
Furthermore, there are a thousandfold more bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who attain the *dhāraṇī* gate of hearing and retaining.
Having attained the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining, they enter the stage of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*). As clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three *dhāraṇīs*:
first, the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining; one who attains this *dhāraṇī* [perceives] all speech and all phenomena with their ears.

That those who hear it do not forget or lose it is precisely what is called "retention" (dhāraṇī). There are three types: first, the dhāraṇī of analytical knowledge; second, the dhāraṇī of entering sounds;
and third, the dhāraṇī of possessing vision. This concludes the translation of the meanings of the names.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in another world-system who attained the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).
Regarding those who attained such joyful speech and so forth, they have entered the stage of the Ten Dedications; as the "Dedication" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The Bodhisattva attains the inexhaustible treasury of decisive eloquence and expounds the equal Dharma of all Buddhas."
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in another world-system who attained the *apramāṇāvarta-dhāraṇī*.
By attaining the *apramāṇāvarta-dhāraṇī*, they entered the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "Avarta means 'to revolve.
This refers to revolving analytical discernment to shatter the afflictions as numerous as grains of sand, thereby manifesting the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as grains of sand."
Furthermore, there were bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world systems who were able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
The meaning of "irreversible" is as seen previously; this refers to their entry into the second stage (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, there were bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms in two thousand middle-sized world-systems who were able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma;
these had entered the third stage.
Furthermore, there were [bodhisattvas] numbering as many as the atoms in a small thousand-world system who would attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after eight births.
Those who enter the fourth bhūmi after eight births, the fifth bhūmi after seven births, the sixth bhūmi after six births,
and the seventh bhūmi after five births;
furthermore, there are those who, after four, three, two, or one birth within the four continents, shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
In four births, one enters the eighth stage.
Furthermore, after three [births] among the three sets of four continents, one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
In three births, he enters the ninth stage.
Furthermore, [after passing through] two sets of four continents, in two births he shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The second birth is the entry into the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
Furthermore, from one four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*) up to [the point where] in one birth they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Throughout one's life, one enters the Vajra-mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). From the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to this position of Equal Enlightenment, one successively destroys one grade of ignorance at each stage, totaling forty-one grades.
By further destroying one final grade of subtle ignorance, one enters the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*suviśuddha-bodhi*).

If one discusses the increase of the Path and the decrease of birth at each stage, these refer to the increase of wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*); the decrease of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) is discussed separately.

The treatise discusses decrease and increase, which refers to the arising of the Dharmakāya and the cessation of ignorance; "increase" refers to the perfect and wondrous Way, while "decrease" refers to birth through transformation (*pariṇāmiki-jāti*).
However, the attainment of the Way in this Root Chapter exceeds that of all other sutras by several multiples; not only is the number of beings great, but their cultivation has been long-standing.
Since the original source manifested traces everywhere to guide and lead them, they have encountered [the teaching] repeatedly during the interim and have reached maturity time and again.
In this world, the five flavors are each tamed, gathered, collected, and brought together in the Lotus Sūtra.
It is like a farming family that sows and plants in spring, grows and weeds in summer, harvests in autumn, and stores in winter; all are reaped at once.

After the Lotus Sūtra, those who attain the Way are like those who gather what has been left behind. The *Myōryaku* (Exquisite Joy) states: "Gathering what is left behind is like [the attainment in] the *Nirvāṇa*."

It is said that eight thousand śrāvakas received their predictions within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; like the harvest in autumn followed by storage in winter, there is nothing further to be done.

Thus we know that the great harvest must occur in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. (The term *jun* [first tone] refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which reveals and clarifies the truth like a great harvest;
*Nirvāṇa* is like the gathering of remaining stalks, as the term "gathering" (*jun*) refers to picking up the leftover ears after the main harvest.)
Furthermore, there are sentient beings numbering as many as the atoms in eight worlds who [give rise to] the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Those who resolve their minds in eight worlds are persons whose six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) have become pure, entering for the first time into the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Thus, the *Ratna-rāja-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva of the Ten Good Deeds resolves his great mind and forever parts from the ocean of the suffering wheel of the triple world"—this refers precisely to this.
Regarding the meaning, Miaole states: "The 'Bodhisattvas of the Ten Good Deeds' clarifies that each of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) fully possesses the ten good deeds;
it does not mean that the human and celestial [precepts], such as non-killing and non-stealing, are specifically matched one-to-one with the ten stages of faith.
△ Third, the assembly makes offerings.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas sang immeasurable verses in praise of the Buddhas.

At that time, the assembly, having heard this profound and far-reaching Dharma, attained great benefit; desiring to repay the Buddha’s kindness, they made offerings, which were likewise symbolic acts expressing their understanding and realization.
Thus, the Gate of the Superior Trace opened the provisional to reveal the real, and the bodhisattvas also attained awakening.
Since the Great Matter has not yet been concluded, he does not present offerings here, but rather expresses his realization.

Now that the opening of the proximate and the revelation of the remote in the Present Gate have been completed, Maitreya offers a comprehensive expression of his realization; thus, he uses offerings to represent this.

As for the bodhisattvas holding banners and canopies and ascending in succession up to the Brahma Heaven: "banner" (dhvaja) signifies the sense of turning [the wheel of Dharma], while "canopy" (chattra) signifies...
The meaning of "covering" (*pi*) refers to the beginning; "Brahma" (*brahman*) means purity. Wisdom and severance proceed sequentially, while compassion covers each stage in turn.

High and low, deep and shallow, do not lose their proper order. Reaching up to the Brahma Heaven, this represents all Bodhisattvas increasing the Path and diminishing birth, approaching the state of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and reaching the ultimate purity. △ Second, Maitreya articulates his understanding and realization (3).
When the first verse was recited, the assembly attained understanding.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat (and proceeded until) joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"The Buddha has preached a rare Dharma, never heard before... (and so on until) "...joy pervades my entire body."
△ Second, the verses on the Tathāgata’s differentiation:
[They] either abide in the stage of non-retrogression or have attained dhāraṇī... up to "as boundless as space.

Regarding those who attain Buddhahood according to their number of births, these verses describe Bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms of the four continents, who shall attain it after four more births.
From the stage of Bodhi up to the point where Bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms within two continents, shall attain Bodhi after two more births and become omniscient ones;
and the wisdom of the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment attained after one final birth—these constitute the attainment of immeasurable, untainted, and pure retributive fruits.
This is stated in order to distinguish them from the limited fruits of the Two Vehicles.
Because it is produced by immeasurable and wondrous causes, it is called "pure"; because it is free from obstacles, it is called "retribution.
This distinguishes it from the non-retribution of the two vehicles. △ Third, verses on the offerings of the assembly at that time.
"Raining down *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* [flowers] to assist the unsurpassed mind.
From this verse until the end of the sutra, there are eleven chapters and a half, all belonging to the section on the Propagation (Prasāraṇa). This is divided into two parts:
first, from here down to the "Chapter on Never-Despising" (*Anupalipta*), there are three chapters and a half that clarify the profound merit of propagating the sutra.
Regarding the exhortation for circulation, there are two parts from the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (*Shenli pin*) downward, comprising eight chapters in total.

This section is further divided into two, each containing three sub-sections. The first three are as follows: this half-chapter and the "Chapter on Rejoicing" (*Suixi pin*) clarify the merits of the causes within the first stage of the five stages (*wupin*), thereby exhorting circulation;
second, from the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" (*Fashi gongde pin*), it clarifies the five stages.

Regarding the first section, the "Chapter on the Merit of the Fruit" encourages circulation in three ways: first, the "Chapter on Not Disparaging" cites the offenses for slandering faith and the blessings of merit as evidence to encourage circulation;
second, the two chapters beginning with "Supernatural Powers" and "Entrustment" concern the entrustment of circulation;

third, the five chapters beginning with "Bhaiṣajyarāja" encourage circulation by means of transforming others; and fourth, the "Samantabhadra" chapter encourages circulation by means of one's own practice.

Regarding the eleven chapters and a half on the sequence of arising (*utpatti-krama*) in general: as stated above, one gains the benefit of both the genuine and the semblance understanding by hearing the sutra in the present.
Furthermore, if one merely hears a single phrase and gives rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodana*), its merit is comparable to that of the "Fourfold Faith" of the present;
for fear that people might doubt the merit is small after the Buddha has passed away when no Buddha exists, it is said [to be equal] after his parinirvāṇa.
Within the five grades of practice (*pañca-varga*), the merit is subtle and hidden, not yet as manifest as the merit of the fruition;

therefore, the "Chapter on the Merit of the Dharma Master" speaks of both cause and effect together. It does not yet provide as clear a citation of scriptural evidence as the "Chapter on Never-Despising" (*Adhimātra-pūjā*).
Although that chapter mentions people of the past, it does not yet manifest their supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) as clearly as the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers. Although...
Demonstrating supernatural powers is not as significant as the bestowing of the crown of the head and the entrustment; therefore, the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*) is taught.

Although this constitutes a general entrustment, it is not as profound as revealing the essential method of discarding the body to preserve the Way; therefore, the "Chapter on Bhaiṣajyarāja" (*Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*) is taught.

Although this admonishes those who transform others, it is not as profound as admonishing those who are transformed to give rise to the perception of the Buddha wherever they hear the Dharma; therefore, the "Chapter on Gadgadasvara and Avalokiteśvara" (*Gadgadasvara-avalokiteśvara-parivarta*) is taught.
Regarding the two chapters on Sound: since those who first resolve to propagate the sutra lack supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), they must rely on internal prohibitions;

thus, the "Dhāraṇī" chapter is taught. Furthermore, as external protection is required, the two chapters on King Śubhavyūha and Samantabhadra are taught in succession and with great emphasis, so that the Great Dharma may be widely propagated.
From this verse to the end of the chapter, the long prose section is divided into two major parts.

Regarding the statement that "there is one [type of person] in the present with four kinds of faith, and two types after the extinction [of the Buddha] with five grades in the future, while there are none when no Buddha exists," this was said because one might suspect that propagating the sutra after the Tathāgata’s extinction could not possibly equal the abundance of merit found in the four kinds of faith; hence it is said that the merit is small.
△ 3. From here downward, through eleven chapters and a half, belongs to the section on the circulation of the "Root Chapter" (Honmon). Part 2:
First, from here downward through three chapters and a half, it clarifies the profound merit of propagating the sutra and exhorts its circulation. Part 3:

First, from here downward until the chapter on "Rejoicing," it clarifies the exhortation to circulate the merit of the causes of the first chapter. Part 4: First, the four types of faith in the present. Part 5: First, faith for a single thought-moment.
The first part of the explanation consists of three sections; the first is the introductory prose. First, the person is identified:
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... up to "those who are able to give rise to even a single thought of faith and understanding."
One should know that proceeding from this constitutes the characteristic of profound faith and understanding (*adhimukti*). Regarding the four types of faith and understanding present now:

first, faith and understanding in each individual thought-moment, which cannot yet be fully articulated; second, a concise explanation of the verbal expressions; third, explaining them extensively for others;

and fourth, the accomplishment of profound faith through contemplation. As for "faith and understanding in each individual thought-moment," it refers to the sudden, expansive opening of realization at whatever point one hears the teaching.
Clearly following awakening, one enters without obstruction; one believes that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma, and further believes that the Buddha-dharma is not separate from any dharma.
One realizes that the Buddha-dharma cannot be attained apart from all dharmas, nor can all dharmas be attained apart from the Buddha-dharma.
Thus, seeing all dharmas is seeing the Buddha-dharma—being one yet three, being three yet one—just like a path leading forward through a gate.

To penetrate all directions—east, west, south, and north—without obstruction, such that the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, in whatever they encounter, are likewise free from doubt, is called "faith" (*śraddhā*);
to be clearly aware of this is called "understanding" (*adhimukti*). This is the mind of faith and understanding in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-śraddhādhimukti-citta*).
Such faith and understanding is termed the stage of the Iron Wheel (*ayaścakra-bhūmi*). According to another interpretation, this is not yet [the final stage].

Being "fully endowed with the iron wheel" refers to the initial stage of the ten levels of faith; because that person has not yet attained the purity of the six sense organs, it is not yet the formal rank of the iron wheel.
△ Second, clarifying its merits, in two parts: first, a general discussion of their immeasurability.
The merit thus obtained is without limit.
△ Second, the comparative measurement of the quantity [of merit], in two parts: First, citing the five perfections as the basis for comparison.
"If there were good sons or good daughters... (up to) excluding the Prajñāpāramitā."
Prajñā is precisely the correct wisdom that now serves as the standard for measuring the five perfections; therefore, it is said that [the other perfections] are excluded when Prajñā is present.
△ Second, the formal comparison of their relative quantities shows they fall short:
"By comparing these merits with the former merits... [they are] such that they cannot be known even by calculation or analogy."
△ Third, non-retrogression in practice.
If a son or daughter of good family possesses such merit (up to) "it is impossible," then upon hearing of the merit of the lifespan at the initial stage of the ten faiths of the Perfect Teaching,
they will be externally sustained and inwardly accord with the perfect understanding of faith.

Because one is internally perfumed, one does not regress; thus, the stage of "wondrous joy" is called the non-regression of position and the non-regression of practice. Regarding the textual analysis:

because those who have attained the four levels of faith are established as being within the ten levels of faith, from the first faith through the seventh faith constitutes non-regression of position, while from the eighth faith onward constitutes non-regression of practice.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that for Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śikṣā*), there is regression when Māras are present, and no regression when Māras are absent.

In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), even a beginner cannot be taken advantage of by Māra, let alone one who has attained the stage of non-retrogression; therefore, it is said that such a thing is impossible.
△ Second, the verse summary in three parts: first, the comparison of quantity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If a person seeks the Buddha’s wisdom... [and] practices all these merits as described above."
△ Second, the verse summarizing the characteristics of persons:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who hear me speak of the lifespan... their merit shall be such as this.
△ Third, non-retrogression in practice and stage.
"Those bodhisattvas who have practiced the path for immeasurable kalpas—up to this point—they have no doubt regarding this.
'Practicing the path for immeasurable kalpas' means having long cultivated the various *pāramitās*. 'May I, in the future... and so forth, expresses the arising of vows of compassion and pity.
Having already heard the vow for long life, one should now likewise [aspire] to it; having now first heard this sutra, even for a single thought-moment..."
"Faith and understanding equal the merit of long practice, yet even this surpasses it; the wondrous joy is such that speech cannot describe it.

Regarding the phrase "lifespan is also like this," it means that when one speaks of eternal lifespan, if one attains such eternal life, one will surely exceed this [present duration] throughout the future. Why is it merely like this?
It is because the Tathāgata’s lifespan is here spoken of according to conventional truth; thus, for the time being, it is permitted to be so. As for "the profound mind and so forth":
"Profound" means exhausting the principle of non-duality; "direct" means that from beginning to end the method is one and the same.

One who has no doubt regarding this possesses five qualities within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanmen) of the Original Ground (*mūlabhūmi*), and only then can they sever their doubts: first, generating faith upon hearing the distant [teaching];
second, the profound mind; third, the direct mind; fourth, the mind of extensive learning; and fifth, the mind of explaining it for others.
This constitutes the five dharmas. △ Second, the brief explanation of the meaning of the words, in two parts. First, the description of the person's characteristics:
"Furthermore, Ajita, if there are those who hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching and understand the meaning of these words..."
△ Second, the formal evaluation:
The merit obtained by this person is limitless and can give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of a Tathāgata.
This is the second concise explanation of the meaning of faith; whereas previously one only had faith and understanding and was unable to elaborate upon it, here the explanation proceeds.
One must be well-versed in terminology and dialects; since these are now complete, it is said that one "understands their meaning.

This refers to explaining them for the sake of others, and by the power of such explanation, one is able to give rise to unsurpassed wisdom in both oneself and others. △ Third, extensively explaining them to others, in two parts:
first, identifying the characteristics of the person.
How much more so for one who extensively hears this sutra, or teaches others to hear it, up to making offerings to its physical scrolls.
II. The actual comparison:
The merit of such a person is immeasurable and boundless, capable of giving rise to all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).

△ Fourth, the accomplishment of the contemplation of deep faith.

This is the fourth: the accomplishment of the contemplation of deep faith, which means that by adding the cultivation of contemplative practice to the three aforementioned faiths, one enters [the stage].
In the application of dhyāna, through the conceptualization of wisdom, one gives rise to the marks [of the two lands] and is able to see their appearances:
seeing the Buddha together with the assembly of bhikṣus constantly residing on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is the mark of the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*);

furthermore, seeing the Sahā world consisting purely of bodhisattvas is the mark of the Land of True Retribution (*vipāka-bhūmi*). The first two stages of faith are the stage of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*). This is extensive.

Hearing this extensive explanation constitutes the stage of wisdom through reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); the accomplishment of the mental image of contemplative practice constitutes the stage of wisdom through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Progressing from the shallow to the deep, one achieves the purity of the six faculties at the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "Regarding 'the accomplishment of the mental image and the arising of the signs':

the principle inherently contains these signs; based on this principle, the mental image arises. Therefore, when this image is accomplished, one immediately perceives these signs. From the very beginning of practicing contemplation, however..."

Because the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) based on the perception of names is shallow, one relies solely on this perception; as it gradually deepens and matures, one enters the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), where one spontaneously and universally perceives all things with unimpeded application.
Question: Since one gives rise to perceptions in accordance with principle, why is it necessary to employ the perception of lands?

Is it not sufficient simply to contemplate the wondrous principle within a single thought-moment? Answer: In the three previous teachings, the application of contemplation requires the breaking of the aggregates (*skandha*). Only in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*) is this not required.
The teaching is precisely this: to contemplate that within a single thought-moment (ekacitta-kṣaṇa), the three thousand realms and the three truths are fully present.
This means that within one mind are all minds; within one body are all bodies; and within one land are all lands.

Therefore, when contemplation is perfected, one mind perceives all minds, one body perceives all bodies, and one land perceives all lands, manifesting within the bodies of all Buddhas of the ten directions.
Therefore, within the constant tranquil light of one’s own mind, one universally perceives all bodies and lands of the ten directions;
this is just as the Great Master Tiantai personally beheld the assembly on Vulture Peak as if it were still present without dispersing.

From the beginning of this first chapter up to this point, if the contemplation of principle (*li*) has matured, external affairs will not hinder internal cultivation;

"One merely contemplates principle and has not yet had leisure to engage with affairs; now that correct contemplation is somewhat clear, one may simultaneously assist and benefit others. Thus, one is able to...
Even if one gives a small gift, it is made equal to space and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), causing all dharmas to incline toward *dāna*, with *dāna* itself being the dharma-realm;
the same applies to the other five perfections (*pāramitā*). Although the actual phenomena (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*) are few, the mental resolve (*citta-udāra*) is exceedingly vast.

This indicates the characteristics of the person.

If a person reads, recites, receives, and upholds this sutra—[continuing until] they possess sharp faculties, wisdom, and are skilled in answering difficult questions—the *Miaoxuan* states that by the fifth stage, the complete contemplation (*yuan guan*) has become somewhat mature;
principle and phenomena (*li-shi*) are about to merge, such that engaging with phenomena does not hinder [the practice].
Since principle is not separated from phenomena, one fully practices the six perfections. When practicing generosity, one is free from the attachments of the two extremes;
regarding the ten dharma realms and their environments and inhabitants, one gives all—giving away wealth, body, and life—and performs the giving of fearlessness.
When observing precepts, there is no distinction between what is inherently grave and what is subject to censure; one does not touch upon the five categories of heavy or light offenses.
Regarding the transgressions: when practicing patience, one gives rise to the patience of the cessation of phenomena (*dharmas*) and so forth, bearing and enduring with composure;

when practicing diligence, both body and mind are pure, uninterrupted, and without retreat; when practicing meditation, one enters the various *dhyānas*, where stillness and distraction do not hinder one another;
and when cultivating wisdom, one thoroughly investigates and penetrates both provisional and ultimate knowledge, even extending to worldly wisdom for managing livelihood.
All the practices are not in contradiction with the true nature (*dharmatā*);

they fully explain the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*), and because they augment the fire of right contemplation (*samyak-pratyavekṣā*) like adding fuel to a flame, it is said that the correct practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) constitutes the fifth chapter.

Regarding the six perfections, the reason *dāna* (giving) is not specifically mentioned is that explaining them for others is inherently the meaning of the "Dharma-gift" (*dharma-dāna*), which necessarily encompasses all of them.

Among the five grades, the first three persons are at the stage of wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); those who practice the six perfections concurrently are at the stage of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);
and those who are correctly practicing the six perfections are at the stage of wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). All of these precede the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Alternatively, it is said that the first "Grade of Rejoicing" (*anumodana*) is the stage of entering the mind of faith; dividing this one grade into two minds, the five grades constitute the ten minds of faith.
This is the stage of the purification of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) of the Iron Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*). The *Myōraku-ki* states: "Question:

Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Eighteen: "The Merit of Rejoicing.
"Rejoicing" means to accord with both principle and phenomenon as being non-dual and without distinction; "rejoicing" is to celebrate oneself and others upon hearing the profound [Dharma].

The "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing" is so called because it explains the convergence of the provisional and the real, wisdom and severance: the merit of conforming to principle through the profound Dharma is the merit of reality;
the merit of conforming to phenomena through expedient means is the merit of skillful means; rejoicing in oneself is wisdom; rejoicing in others is compassion.

This is an explanation according to the *lokasaṃvṛti-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint). Furthermore, "conforming to principle" refers to hearing that the Buddha’s original ground is profound and far-reaching.
Believing and complying without opposition, one is free from even a hair’s breadth of doubt or stagnation.

Those who follow the phenomena hear that the Buddha benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, pervading all places both vertically and horizontally, yet they too are free from even a hair’s breadth of doubt or stagnation.

Thus, through extensive phenomena one reaches profound principle, and through profound principle one reaches extensive phenomena. Though non-dual, they appear as two; though not distinct, they are distinct—yet even as two, they remain one.
Although they are distinct, there is neither duality nor difference; such faith and understanding is called "conforming to the Tathāgata.

For more than forty years since his appearance in the world, he did not reveal the ultimate reality, nor did he speak the truth regarding the seven stages of expedient means. Now, this sutra reveals and clarifies it, bringing joy to myself and others.
With the minds of ordinary beings, we shall become equal to what the Buddha knows; with the eyes produced through this practice, we shall be identical to the Tathāgata.
Seeing such things and knowing that the vision of the ultimate Dharma-realm is unsurpassed—this is called "rejoicing. The Buddha now speaks of this;
because I have heard it, it is named the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing. This is an explanation according to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic antidotes).
As for the fiftieth person, they are at the initial stage of the first "Rejoicing" chapter within the five ranks (*pañca-vastu*). However—

If there is one who attains understanding in a single thought-moment, rejoicing for themselves and for others, yet has not yet engaged in actual practice so that their grace does not extend to others, the merit they obtain—as illustrated by the Tathāgata’s skillful parables—is such that it surpasses even those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);

how much more so for those who hear this at the assembly for the first time, and how much more so for those who have heard it for the second, third, fourth, or fifth time. The Tathāgata speaks of this profound and wondrous merit.

Because virtue inspires admiration in others, this is called the "Chapter on Rejoicing in Merit" (*Anumodanā-puṇya-parivarta*); this is an explanation according to the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint for the benefit of individuals).

When the merits of upholding the sutra were extolled during the preceding "Chapter on the Dharma Master," the "Chapter on Retention," and the "Chapter on the Analysis of Merit"—specifically regarding the four levels of faith and the five grades of practitioners—the assembly could not fathom the greatness of the merit of those with the initial resolve, and they all assumed that these individuals had already attained [the stage of] *srotāpanna*.
Because this is the stage of the true cause, it now demonstrates that while his practice was shallow, its merit was profound, thereby revealing the power of the sutra;

thus, doubts regarding its insignificance are resolved, and it is called the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing. This is an explanation according to the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint).

Miaole states: "In the initial explanation of 'rejoicing,' the phenomena and principle are merely different names for the provisional and the real; once these provisional and real aspects are understood, they are not [separate]."
Because the provisional and the real are non-dual and without distinction, this accords with the principle of "opening the provisional to reveal the real.
When the provisional and the real are spoken of in conjunction with wisdom and severance, they are combined with the joy resulting from the severance of both wisdom and practice;

furthermore, because one rejoices in the principles and events concerning oneself and others, this belongs to the World-Understanding (loka-vyavahāra) *siddhānta*. Regarding the "profound and remote original ground," it refers to the profundity of the principle and the remoteness of the time.

Furthermore, for those who have extensively practiced and attained profound understanding, the manifestation of the traces of the teaching reveals the near events as pointing toward the distant fundamental principle.

"The Buddha now," and so forth, concludes the title of the chapter; because it removes doubts regarding phenomena and principle, it belongs to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remediation).
"The Tathāgata’s skillful parables" refers to the passage below concerning four hundred million *koṭis*, and so on. "The Tathāgata," and so forth, concludes the intent of the scripture’s exhortation.

The title of this chapter is established because it enables one to advance toward the principle, enter the stages, and generate wholesome dharmas; therefore, it belongs to the *puruṣapudgala-siddhānta* (the standpoint for individuals).

The holy words personally praise [this stage] to encourage the attribution of merit and eliminate doubt; thus, the "releasing and clarifying" (*śithilīkaraṇa*) is cited to represent the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth).
Among the five ranks, the latter four persons are discussed in the final section at the end of the preceding "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit."

The section on comparative evaluation concludes here; however, regarding the text of the first chapter, "Rejoicing," it merely indicates the characteristics of the individuals involved and does not yet provide a comparative evaluation.
Consequently, Maitreya seizes the opportunity to prompt the Buddha to extensively evaluate the first chapter, so that one may know the merit of the latter four chapters is great.
This is why this present chapter has come into being. △ Second, the chapter on rejoicing evaluates the merit of the first chapter.
Second, the initial inquiry:

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (up to) asked, "How much merit does one obtain who, after the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, hears this sutra and is able to rejoice in it? He then spoke in verse:
"How much merit does one obtain who, after the World-Honored One has entered Parinirvāṇa, hears this sutra and is able to rejoice in it?"
△ Second, the response, which has two parts: first, the prose section; second, the initial response concerning those who inwardly rejoice, which has five parts.
First, the successive instruction: At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... [continuing] thus, successively transmitted until the fiftieth person.
The two schools of the Northeast explain that fifty people do not understand the intent of the sutras; their current explanation divides them into two categories:

first, a horizontal classification across the various teachings and the fourfold assembly; second, a direct classification according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Regarding the horizontal classification across the various teachings:
for example, within the Tripiṭaka there are four gates, and each gate contains the four groups of the assembly—bhikṣus and so forth—with further distinctions made for śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs.

Combining six people at each of the four gates results in twenty-four people; further including those of the stages of faith-practice (*śraddhā-carita*) and dharma-practice (*dharma-carita*), there are forty-eight people.
Including the first and last [stages], this totals fifty people. This applies equally to the four gates of both the distinct (*vyavasthita*) and the perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) teachings.
If one calculates directly according to the perfect gate alone, the method of counting consists of seven small sevens, seven large sevens, and seven times seven, which makes forty-nine.
Nineteen of these are instances where master and disciple successively instructed one another, all possessing the virtue of both self-cultivation and the transformation of others;
only the final individual merely possessed self-understanding without the virtue of teaching others, and thus he is ranked below to highlight those above.
The *Myōraku* states: "This is because ancient masters interpreted this as the fifty stages, from the Ten Grounds down to the Ten Faiths."
Because the text is damaged and the reasoning lost, I now assist it by temporarily relying on the gates of the teachings to establish the number of people.

Regarding the two interpretations: the first is based on the meaning of the three teachings, wherein there were fifty people according to the former teachings who have now heard the Perfect [Teaching];

the second is that those from the present time again constitute fifty, all of whom, having been opened and revealed, are entirely perfected as Perfect persons. Therefore, the number is cited according to the Perfect [Teaching].
There is nothing by which they can be distinguished; furthermore, they are designated by the numerical method, ceasing at one and seven.
Within these seven, because the "great" is taken first, there are forty-nine, and including the final person, they total fifty.

The supplementary note states that those who are both teacher and disciple receive the instruction of their predecessor as disciples and then instruct subsequent persons as teachers; thus, the number is complete. There is no [other] round number.
That which can be analyzed refers to the first three teachings, which may be distinguished by way of persons or gates;
as for the fifty individuals [of the Lotus Sutra], this present sutra reveals that they have no further differences, so how could they be analyzed by number as was done above?
Therefore, we provisionally rely on the seven great assemblies to establish the number of the sutra’s chapters. △ Second, the comparative evaluation of the original.
Ānanda, those fifty good men (up to the point mentioned) all attained mastery and were endowed with the eight liberations.

the merit of all people throughout Jambudvīpa does not equal the merit of a single person in Aparagoyānī, the merit of all people in Aparagoyānī does not equal the merit of a single person in Pūrvavideha,
and the merit of all people in these three continents does not equal the merit of a single person in Uttarakuru.
The merit of all people filling the four continents does not equal that of a single Cāturmahārājika deva; the merit of the four Cāturmahārājas does not equal that of a single Śakra;

and so on, up to the merit of the sixth heaven (the Paranirmita-vaśavartin) does not equal that of a single Brahmā. The merit filling the Brahma-heavens does not equal the merit of the noble ones of the Tripitaka (Tripiṭaka) teachings of the Three Vehicles;

the merit of the Tripiṭaka does not equal that of the Shared (Sādhāraṇa) teaching; the Shared does not equal that of the Distinct (Pratyekabuddha) teaching; and the Distinct does not equal the hearing of the Perfect (Pūrṇa) teaching.

Why is the merit of the "Chapter on Initial Rejoicing" (*Anumodanā-parivarta*) in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* [superior]? It is because those three preceding teachings are the vehicles of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), not the Buddha-vehicle;
they are provisional and not ultimate; they are partial and not perfect (*pariniṣpanna*). Thus, although one may abide in the final fruition [of those paths], it does not equal my initial resolve.
Such is the meaning. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "Now, having heard this wondrous sūtra, one rejoices in the initial resolve."
If this surpasses even those later sages, how much more so the original sages?
Were it not for the solemn intent of our Buddha, the Great Sage, who could believe such a rare wonder as this? △ Second, directly clarifying those who hear the Dharma externally;
first, going there oneself to listen.
Furthermore, Ajita, if someone, for the sake of this sutra, goes to a monastery (and so forth) or even boards a celestial palace,
they shall share half the seat. Or again,
if someone sits in a place where the Dharma is being preached (and so forth), or in a place where a Wheel-Turning Sage King sits, [they shall likewise share half the seat].
△ Third, exhorting others to listen:
"Ajita, if there is another person... [up to] ...who sees the Buddha, hears the Dharma, and faithfully accepts his teachings.
Zhan’an says: "This passage also concerns the merit of the six sense organs; keen faculties and wisdom are the merit of the mind organ."
Not being mute is the merit of the tongue; the nose being well-cultivated, high, and straight is the merit of the nose;

seeing the Buddha is the merit of the eyes; hearing the Dharma is the merit of the ears; the remaining [features] are the merits of the body. The preceding [section] concerns the merits of the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*);
the present [section] concerns the merits prior to the stage of semblance. As for the *Miaole* (Sublime Joy), it states that the preceding [section] concerns the merits of the stage of semblance.

Regarding "virtues and so forth," this refers to what was stated previously in the *Pinfen Gongde Pin* (Chapter on Distinguishing Merits), which says that after [the Buddha's] parinirvāṇa, there are five grades.

Based on the *Puxian Guan Jing* (Sutra on the Contemplation of Samantabhadra), some judge that these five grades of practice are contained within the six faculties; hence they are called "resemblance.
Here, in the calculation of the initial grade, it is further the first person among fifty. It is possible that those who heard the Dharma at the first assembly belong to this initial grade.
The fiftieth person must be among those at the beginning of the "Chapter on Rejoicing" (Suixi-pin).
However, although the title of the chapter is "Rejoicing," it does not strictly limit itself to the first person alone, but applies generally to all fifty individuals.
