How much more so for one who listens with a single-minded focus, explains its meaning and intent, and practices according to those teachings; their merit would be beyond measure.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter Nineteen, "The Merits of the Dharma-Preacher," the meaning of "dharma-preacher" is as explained in the preceding chapter. As for "merit," it refers to the merit of sympathetic joy mentioned in the previous chapter.
Among the five grades, the initial grade precedes the stage of semblance (*sādharmya*).

The present grade concerns the merit of the Dharma-preacher, which refers to the merit of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) above the five grades; this is precisely the stage of semblance within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
By means of this merit, one is adorned internally and externally; the purity of the five faculties is called "external adornment," while the mind is the internal.
The purity of the sense faculties (*indriya-viśuddhi*) is called "inner adornment" (*adhyātma-alaṃkāra*).
Furthermore, that all forms and images, from those of the hells up to those of a Buddha, manifest entirely within one's own body is called "inner adornment.

That all forms and images, from the hells up to a Buddha, transform others through external manifestation by means of the Samādhi of Universal Manifestation (*samanta-prabhāsa-samādhi*) is called "outer adornment" (*bahirdhā-alaṃkāra*). Since it is thus with the faculty of the body, so it is with the remaining five.
The same applies to the faculties (*indriya*): if reciting and chanting results in the purification of the six faculties, so too does receiving, upholding, explaining, and transcribing [the text].
Just as the first of the five stages (*pañca-varga*) results in the purification of the six faculties, so do the subsequent four stages;

and just as the semblance (*sādharmya*) purification of the six faculties is thus, the true (*bhūta-tattva*) purification is twice as great. This is explained according to the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint).

When the practitioner hears this explanation of its meritorious benefits, they experience such joy that they cannot contain themselves; they seek it with tireless diligence, and their faith and progress increase manifold—this is an explanation according to the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of the person).
To clearly recognize that the Mahāyāna possesses great power and to resolve all nets of doubt—this is an explanation according to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedy).
This marks the very beginning of "semblance-understanding," surpassing the initial stage of the *śrāvaka* vehicle.
"Exceedingly, exceedingly, by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, from the initial indication to the final manifestation, there is ultimate liberation;

this is the inconceivable ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This is an explanation according to the *paramārtha-siddhānta*. What is elucidated in this chapter fully encompasses these four meanings;
because it concerns the merits of the Dharma-preacher (*dharma-bhāṇaka*), it is called the 'Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma-preacher. Miaole says: 'Dharma...'"

Since the designation "Teacher" (Śāstr) is used generally and does not exclude those at the four stages of faith or the five grades of practice, this text refers to that passage to explain the titles of the chapters.
Question: Why does copying [the scripture] purify the six sense organs? Answer: Because it equally supports correct understanding;

thus, for the four grades, it is added that the "Manifestation of Resolve" (Pratibhāna) is indeterminate, beginning from the first stage of "Rejoicing" (Anumodanā) and extending through to the fifth stage of "Correct Practice" (Samyak-pratipatti), wherein the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) are all practiced.

Regarding the arousal of the purity of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriyaviśuddhi*), why must one necessarily pass through the five stages (*pañcaprakāra*) before entering the stage of semblance (*pratirūpaka*)?
To say that this is so is because, when comparing the beginning to the end, the beginning is already able to enter; yet the latter four stages include the former semblance-understanding.

As for the "beginning of beginnings," according to the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra*, after having rejoiced (*anumodana*), one should be at the head of the semblance-understanding; furthermore, the fiftieth person is again situated within the initial act of rejoicing.
Because this is the beginning of the chapter, it is called "the first of the firsts. Regarding "the ultimate of the two vehicles": the Arhat has already reached the ultimate and is free from doubt;

because they are also ultimate, it is called "the ultimate of the ultimate. Even though they are free from doubt, they cannot equal the person who rejoices at the very beginning by even a hundred-thousand-millionth part, as calculated previously.
To point to the beginning in order to reveal the end means that by taking the initial act of rejoicing, one reveals the state of wondrous enlightenment.
The end. △ Third, in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma-Master," the merits of the fruit from the first chapter are clarified to encourage the circulation [of the text].
Part one: A general enumeration of the expansion and contraction of the merits of the six sense organs.
At that time, the Buddha told Constantly Diligent (up to) “adorn the six sense faculties and cause them all to be pure.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: “Because form is pure, Prajñā is pure; because Prajñā is pure, form is pure. Because form is pure, the five faculties are pure;
because Prajñā is pure, the mental faculty is pure. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that it is fully endowed with six thousand merits.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata, by means of a single faculty, is able to see forms, hear sounds, smell fragrances, distinguish tastes, perceive tangibles, and know dharmas.

In this present sūtra, the purification of the six faculties is the same as in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*. This adornment of the six faculties through such merit is the same as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Regarding the nose seeing forms, hearing sounds, and perceiving [dharmas], it is the same as in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, as noted in the commentary.

Although this serves to refute the biased interpretations of other masters—which are improper—and to align with the intent of the three sutras, its primary purpose is to clarify that the six sense organs, and so forth, possess one thousand merits.
If one were to clarify the number of six thousand merits, according to the "Peaceful Practices of the Three Karmas," there are the ten wholesome actions;
since each wholesome action has ten aspects, there are one hundred wholesome actions, and within each of these one hundred wholesome actions...
There are ten suchnesses, which constitute one thousand virtues; when categorized according to self-cultivation and the transformation of others, they become two thousand.

When further categorized according to the Tathāgata’s chamber, the Tathāgata’s robe, and the Tathāgata’s seat, they become six thousand. The five kinds of Dharma-preachers all possess the purity of the six sense organs;
each individual organ possesses one thousand merits (this refers to the one thousand [virtues] clarified through the methods for propagating the sutra). Furthermore, first...
Within the mind, the ten dharma realms are fully present; each realm possesses the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), thus forming one hundred.

When a single faculty universally apprehends the six sense objects, there are six hundred. By combining these with the two adornments of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they become one thousand two hundred.

Since every faculty is fully endowed with the adornments of concentration and wisdom, there are one thousand two hundred for each. (This is calculated according to the principle of the objective realm and so forth.)
If one discusses the purity of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*), then that purity is not described in terms of whether its merit is great or small.
If one speaks of their adornment, they can be expanded and contracted, yet they can also be made equal; this "equal adornment" means six thousand [qualities] for each organ.
If one speaks of twelve hundred, it manifests their capacity for expansion; if one speaks of eight hundred, it manifests their capacity for contraction; if one speaks of...
"Pure, without increase or decrease, and without equal; the six faculties function interchangeably because the faculties are sovereign;

this is the inconceivable wondrous bliss. It is said that by now relying on the "Peaceful Practices" (*Anrakugyō*) to clarify the three karmas as being correct, the Dharma Master—by following the proper method for propagating the sutra—causes the purification of the six faculties to be attained. Furthermore, it says: "The three karmas herein are..."
Because these are the six sense organs, they do not further correspond [to objects]; when the merit of the three karmas is perfected, the six sense organs become pure.

If one speaks of "twelve hundred" and so forth, it next distinguishes between expansion and contraction; this refers specifically to the current sutra’s discussion of expansion and contraction based on what was previously equalized.

If one speaks of "purity," this cites the previous passage from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* regarding the mutual functioning of the six sense organs; this cites the previous passage from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.

The commentary challenges [the view] based on Mount Gushan’s interpretation of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*, which explains the threefold transformation of the flow as being intended to awaken the beginner's mind and cause them to know the locus of inversion;

thus, it demonstrates the superior and inferior functions of the six sense-faculties of ordinary beings, with the underlying intent for Ānanda to select the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) as the ground for cultivation and realization. Now, regarding the circulation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*...

The attainment of the purity of the six sense organs at the stage of "similarity" within the ten faiths, where their mutual functions operate without obstruction, cannot be equated with this [present case].
△ Second, the six chapters are separately composed; they shall now be explained in detail. Part Six: The Eye Organ. Section One:
The Prose Exposition.
These sons and daughters of good family (up to) will see and know all the places where the fruits of their retribution arise.
△ Second, the verse summary.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
If, within a great assembly, one possesses a mind free from fear... [the power of] the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is thus.
That which is born of one's parents is called the fleshly eye; its ability to see both the interior and exterior of a trichiliocosm is what is meant by "seeing.
This exceeds the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) obtained as a karmic reward by the Brahmā King, who sees throughout his own realm; [this fleshly eye] sees throughout the entire trichiliocosm.
Externally, there is a wind-circle that acts as an obstruction for the eye, preventing one from seeing what is outside;

if one is in another realm, one does not see the entire great trichiliocosm, because it is not under one's governance. A minor arhat sees a small trichiliocosm, while a major arhat sees a great trichiliocosm;
a pratyekabuddha sees a hundred buddha-worlds. For them, the wind-circle does not constitute an obstruction, nor do they have the distinction between "one's own" and "another's" realms.

Separated from the present by the power of the sutras and treatises, the eye is able to see the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm; this should be the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), yet it is still called the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*).

This is because within the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-avasthā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), although there is the superior function of the faculties due to the power of the sutras, true reality has not yet been manifested, and thus it cannot be termed the divine eye.
Although it is called the fleshly eye, it possesses the functions of the five eyes and sees the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm.
The function of the *cakṣus* (eye) is to see all sentient beings; the function of the *dharmacakṣus* (dharma-eye) is that its eyes are exceedingly pure;

the function of the *prajñācakṣus* (wisdom-eye) is to see the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm simultaneously, seeing karma and seeing purity, and furthermore, to completely subdue the delusions of ignorance regarding the Middle Way within the obstructions.
As for the function of the *buddhacakṣus* (Buddha-eye), the Great Sūtra states: "Though one possesses only the fleshly eye, it is called the Buddha-eye."
Because the eye is the Buddha-eye, it is called "pure," for it possesses the five eyes; thus it is said to be "adorned.

Because it can expand and contract, it is called the "function of the supreme faculties" (indriya-viśeṣa), and is termed "mastery over the faculties" (indriya-vaśitā). How could one interpret this merely as eight hundred or twelve hundred [kalpas]? The *Myōraku* states:

"Within the initial faculty of the eye, there is no discussion yet of cultivating and manifesting the true divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and so forth; it refers directly to the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*)."
Because it is able to see the great trichiliocosm, it is said to be "produced by one's parents. However, if one discusses its function, it has already surpassed the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*);
therefore, it should now be called the "resemblance to the Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakṣur-nirbhāsa*), and even the "resemblance to the five eyes.

Furthermore, it should also be said that it sees the two vehicles, bodhisattvas, Buddhas, and so forth, for according to the scriptural texts concerning the ears and nose, such [passages] must necessarily exist here as well. Thus, it sees the Great.
Regarding the "thousandfold internal and external" as the *divyacakṣus* (heavenly eye): it refers to seeing coarse and subtle forms; seeing the boundaries of karma and seeing the purity [of karma].
Since there is a distinction in the karma seen but no distinction in the purity [seen], seeing both objects simultaneously represents the *madhyamajñāna* (middle wisdom).

Furthermore, because it can perfectly subdue [all things], it is the *buddhacakṣus* (Buddha-eye). The *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Names and Meanings) states: Some say that *Mīlū* translates as...
"Radiant Light" refers to the seven golden mountains, so called because they possess a golden radiance.
According to the *Paramārtha-dharmavijaya-sūtra*, it states that Mount Sumeru is [referred to as] Mīlu; thus, "Mīlu" is an archaic translation for Sumeru.
This indicates that there are differences in the Sanskrit pronunciation. According to the present sutra, however, it speaks of the "inner and outer Mīlu Mountains."
Sumeru and Cakravāḍa are the names of two mountains whose essential natures are distinct. △ Second, the faculty of hearing, in two parts:
first, the prose section.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence... [up to] ...various sounds without damaging the faculty of hearing.
△ Second, the verses in praise.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The ears born of one's parents are pure, free from turbidity and defilement... [omitted] ...the merits are already thus."

The faculty of the ear also possesses the functions of the five ears; therefore, it is able to universally hear the sounds of the ten dharma-realms, both internal and external, throughout the great trichiliocosm.
Hearing the sounds of the six realms of existence is through the two ears of flesh and heaven; hearing the sounds of the two vehicles is through the ear of wisdom;
hearing the sounds of the bodhisattvas is through the ear of dharma; and hearing the sounds of the Buddhas is through the Buddha-ear. Furthermore, that which is produced by one's parents is...

The fleshly ear can hear both the internal and external; this is the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*). Hearing without attachment is the wisdom ear (*prajñā-śrotra*), which is fully capable of discernment;
this is the Dharma ear (*dharma-śrotra*). Hearing simultaneously and interchangeably is the Buddha ear (*buddha-śrotra*).

By analogy with the ear, the eye is also thus: seeing humans and devas is the fleshly eye and the divine eye; seeing the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*) is the wisdom eye; seeing Bodhisattvas is the Dharma eye.
"Seeing the Buddha with the eyes" refers to the Buddha-eye. A supplementary note states that *kalaviṅka* translates as "bird of beautiful voice.
This bird’s song within its egg surpasses that of all other birds. Regarding the *jīvajīvaka*, the *Ratnakoṣa-sūtra* states:

"On the Snowy Mountains there is a bird named 'Shared Life' (*sahajīva*), which has one body and two heads; while their consciousnesses are distinct, their life-force is shared, and thus it is called 'Life-Life' (*jīvajīvaka*)."

The *Shorter Amitābha Sūtra* refers to it as the "co-life bird" (*saṃjīva*), the *Suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā Sūtra* refers to it as the "life-giving bird," and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* refers to it as the "jīvaka-jīvaka";
all these are names for this same bird. The "Radiant Sound" (*Ābhāsvara*) is the third heaven within the Second Dhyāna;
the "Universal Purity" (*Śubhakṛtsna*) is the third heaven within the Third Dhyāna; and the "Summit of Existence" (*Bhavāgra*) is the ultimate heaven of the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*). △
Third, the faculty of the nose. Part one: the initial prose section.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence (up to): "If one wishes to analyze [the teachings] and explain them to others, one should maintain mindfulness without error.
△ Second, the verse summary.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The nose of this person is pure within this world... (omitted)... first attaining this mark of the nose."
The faculty of the nose likewise possesses five functions: the fleshly nose born of one’s parents;
the celestial nose that perceives all fragrances within and without the great trichiliocosm; the wisdom nose that is untainted and unattached; the dharma nose that discerns without error;
and the Buddha nose that employs these faculties simultaneously. Regarding the mutual functioning of the faculties, the nose knows the good and the bad and distinguishes the noble from the base.

When a person of low station beholds the magnificent adornments of the celestial palaces, the nose possesses the function of the eye; when reading scriptures or preaching the Dharma, one can discern fragrances, thus the nose possesses the function of the ear;
when cognizing the scents of various flowers, fruits, and essences such as ghee and oil, the nose possesses the function of the tongue;

and upon entering or emerging from dhyāna—wherein there are the eight tactile sensations (aṣṭasparśa) and the play of the five desires—all these are likewise the phenomena of touch, which are heard [by the sense-faculties].

If the nose can cognize fragrance, it possesses the function of the body; if it also cognizes a mind of attachment, desire, delusion, or anger, as well as the cultivation of wholesome states and so forth, then the nose possesses the function of the mind.
The sovereign and superior function of the nose faculty is such that, by this analogy, the other five faculties are also like this.

Miaole says: "The *Nasendriya-vibhūti-parivarta-sūtra* (Sutra on the Clarity of the Mutual Functions of the Nose Faculty) is most detailed; taking this as a model, the same should apply to the remaining faculties."
Thus, this is merely an abbreviated text regarding the eight tactile sensations: movement, itching, lightness, heaviness, cold, warmth, roughness, and smoothness. Regarding "stopping and observing":
it is said that if one enters meditative concentration for a month without distraction, the eight tactile sensations will immediately arise and touch the body.
*Sumana* (seen before by Jāti) is translated here as *jinqianhua* (golden coin flower). *Mallikā* is also called *moli*; it is translated as *manhua* (garland flower).
Because these flowers are suitable for making garlands, they are called *pārala* (translated as "reborn"); *tamālapatra* (translated as "nature-stainless");
and *tagara* (translated as "root"). The *Mahā-śāstra* states that it is a tree of wood fragrance (*kāṣṭha-gandha*).
The *pārijātaka* (translated as "round-born" tree) has roots, stems, branches, and leaves whose fragrance wafts fifty *yojanas* even against the wind.
A hundred yojanas downwind is the Kūṭāgāra, here translated as "Great Play," a magnificent hall of the Dharma where Śakra dwells.
This "Miao Fa" (Wonderful Dharma) is also called "Shan Fa" (Good Dharma).
On the four fast days, Śakra and the various devas assemble in this hall to deliberate upon whether the affairs of the human world accord with the Dharma or not. △ Four.
The first part of the two sections on the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) is the prose explanation.

Furthermore, from "Again, Constantly Diligent" up to "is also able to produce the sounds of profound and wondrous Dharma," it is stated that the tongue-faculty also possesses the functions of the five tongues and can produce the speech of the six realms; specifically, the two tongues—the fleshly tongue and the celestial tongue—are able to [perform these functions].

To speak the language of the Two Vehicles is the tongue of wisdom; to speak the language of Bodhisattvas is the tongue of Dharma; to employ them simultaneously and interchangeably is the Buddha-tongue.
Regarding the "Seven Jewels," the supplementary note states: when a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, the Seven Jewels manifest spontaneously:
first, the wheel; second, the jewel; third, the elephant; fourth, the horse; fifth, the minister of war; sixth, the [minister of] wealth; [seventh, the queen].
The Seven Jade Maidens of the Treasury Minister. △ Second, the Verse Summary.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The tongue-faculty of such a person is pure, and they shall never again experience foul tastes... (omitted)... or at times he manifests his body."
"Vasavartin" refers to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), which resides at the summit of the Desire Realm and is the abode of the Demon King (*māra*).
"Mahādeva" refers to Maheśvara, the deity at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

These explanations follow the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra) and differ from those listed previously among the assembly. △ Fifth, the Body-faculty: Part One, the Prose Exposition.
Furthermore, from "Constantly Diligent" up to "all manifest their forms and images within the body":
the five functions of the body are manifested within the body; all that exists in the world is manifested within the body as the function of the physical body.

From the highest point of existence (bhavāgra) downward, the celestial bodies are manifested within the body as the function of the celestial body. The bodies of the Two Vehicles are likewise manifested within the body.
The function of the body of wisdom: the Bodhisattva manifests the function of the Dharma-body within his own body; the Buddha manifests the function of the Buddha-body within his own body.
They are manifested perfectly at once, mutually functioning at once, without error at once, and without attachment at once.

"Without error" refers to the provisional (the aspect of wondrous bliss); "without attachment" refers to the empty (the aspect of reality). To illumine both simultaneously is called the Middle Way. II. Verses.
Verse. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one upholds the Lotus Sutra, their body will be exceedingly pure... [and so forth] ...all things appear within it."
△ Sixth, the Faculty of Mind (manas-indriya), Part Two: First, the prose section.

The three Buddha-natures are as follows: reciting and chanting the sutras is the *nirvedhabhāga* (the nature of the cause of realization); practicing all the bodhisattva paths is the *pratyaya-bhāga* (the nature of the causal condition);

To respect persons and respect the Dharma without giving rise to contention is the mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). Furthermore, this profound respect of the "Not-Disparaging" [Samantabhadra] is the seat of the Tathāgata; it is patience.
To endure being struck and reviled is the robe of the Tathāgata; to constantly practice with a mind of compassion without ceasing is the chamber of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, to deeply respect this mental karma (*manas-karman*) and not speak lightly of others is verbal karma (*vāk-karman*); thus, going to pay homage is physical karma (*kāya-karman*).

Furthermore, where a phrase is set as a separate clause, it is simply because the fourfold assembly lacks the *upāsikā* (laywoman);

however, if one later encounters a *bhikṣuṇī* (nun) and considers that the name of the Buddha has a specific source [for her], then it is not necessary to set it as a separate clause. △ Second, citing the contrary to provide an exhortation.

"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you should know that regarding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—up to the point of reading, reciting, explaining, and copying this sūtra—this is an instance of citing the contrary to manifest the compliant, and an exhortation to uphold [the sūtra] to prohibit its disparagement. This sūtra possesses great power and will ultimately bring about great fruits;

one must therefore diligently practice the five kinds of conduct. Regarding the "five kinds of conduct," the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states that these are the five types [of practitioners].
The Dharma Master proceeds. △ Second, the verses in praise consist of two parts; first, the verses on the causes and effects of faith and slander.
First, a general summary of the fundamental matter.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
In the past, there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (up to: ...), who was honored by devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits.
△ Second, the specific verses on the primary narrative (pūrvayoga), part three: first, verses that jointly designate the two individuals.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma is about to perish, the fourfold assembly will become attached to the Dharma.

Those who are attached to the Dharma cannot be shown the Dharma; if one definitively asserts that it exists, this is attachment to the Dharma, and even definitively asserting that it is neither existent nor non-existent is likewise called attachment to the Dharma. The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states: "The wheel of swords brings harm."
The faults of the people of Jambudvīpa are still relatively few; those who claim to have attained realization while preaching the Mahāyāna commit sins far greater than theirs.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "To contend over existence and non-existence, or even to contend over neither-existence-nor-non-existence and existence-and-non-existence, is like a cowhide rope and a dragon-cane rope—neither can escape the affliction.
The *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* states: "The Buddhas taught the Dharma of emptiness as the very foundation..."

Those who are attached to existence cannot be transformed by the Buddhas, nor can those who are attached to emptiness. To definitively state that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent is called a discourse of delusion.
If one loses the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*, whether acting for oneself or transforming others, one is attached to phenomena.
If one attains the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*, both self and other are free from attachment. — *Miaole* (The Wondrous Joy).

The phrase "If one is fixed in [the view that]... and so forth means that this is not a definitive judgment regarding the heterodox, the Buddha’s provisional or ultimate teachings, or the attachments;

rather, it is because clinging with a mind of attachment to the teaching of non-attachment—like being bound by dragon-whiskers and entering water only to find the pain intensify, or like having an ox-hide tied around one's body which becomes more rigid when exposed to the sun—one loses the True Dharma as if one's own body were being damaged. Therefore, one must receive the instruction according to the method.

Thus, even those who merely provide instruction at the stage of the outer ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana) cannot entirely avoid the charge of slander. II. Verse 2: A Verse Pair Clarifying Both Gain and Loss.
A. First, the verse on what is gained:
The Bodhisattva Asaṃkīrṇa went to their place [and said]: "You all practice the Way; you shall all become Buddhas."
△ Second, the verses describe their faults:
Having heard this, people despise, revile, and abuse them.
△ Third, it further clarifies the attainment.
The Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging was able to endure it.
△ Third, the summary of those who believe and those who slander, consisting of two parts; first, the retribution:
"When their offenses have been exhausted, at the time of their death... (until) they gradually fulfill their merits and swiftly attain the Buddha-way."
This passage sets forth the retributions for faith and slander, as well as the correlation between the ancient and the present. The supplementary note states:

"When his offenses were completed" refers to the Bodhisattva Constantly Not Disparaging (*Sadāparibhūta*). Because the fourfold assembly treated him with contempt, he was given the name "Not Disparaging";
furthermore, because he was able to endure being struck and pelted with tiles and stones, all his karmic offenses were thereby exhausted. Therefore, when he...
In the end, having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* preached by the Buddha Prabhūtaratna (Viyinwang), he immediately attained the purity of the six sense faculties.

This is identical to what is said in the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: "If this person’s karmic offenses from previous lives should have caused them to fall into the evil realms, because they are now slighted and despised by others in this life, their karmic offenses from previous lives are immediately extinguished. △ Second, the summary and correlation.
"At that time, 'Not Disparaging' was none other than my own self... (up to) life after life I upheld such a sutra as this.
△ Second, the verse on the fruit of upholding [the sutra]:
"For billions of billions of kalpas, up to the inconceivable... (up to) "life after life encountering Buddhas and swiftly attaining the Buddha-way."
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-one: The Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers.

The meaning of "Tathāgata" is as explained above in the Chapter on the Lifespan. Regarding "supernatural powers" (*ṛddhi*): "supernatural" (*shen*) means unfathomable, and "power" (*li*) refers to efficacious function.
Unfathomable signifies the profoundness of the natural body; efficacious function signifies the greatness of the power of transformation. This...
Because this section involves the entrustment of the profound Dharma and the manifestation of ten kinds of great functions, it is titled the "Chapter on Spiritual Power" (*Ṛddhi-viṣaya*).

From this chapter downward, there are eight chapters in total, all of which concern the entrustment and circulation [of the teaching]. This present chapter clarifies how the Bodhisattvas receive their mandate to propagate the sutra;

the following chapter concerns the Tathāgata’s bestowal of his hand upon their heads as an act of entrustment. Regarding the term "spiritual power" (*ṛddhi*) mentioned by Miaole: "Spirit" (*shen*) resides in...

The "internal" refers to the essence and substance; "power" (li) is named the "trunk," which refers to function. The Buddha’s exposition of the power and function of the oral wheel regarding the fundamental and the manifested has already concluded previously.
Now, he further manifests this supreme function through the physical wheel to cause the teachings on the fundamental and the manifested to circulate among the masses;
therefore, it is said that "the essence is profound and the power is great. △ Second, from the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (Shenli Pin) downward, eight chapters clarify the entrustment.
The Entrustment for Circulation has three parts: first, the entrustment through supernatural power; second, the explanation of the entrustment and circulation in the [next] chapter.

Regarding the first, the Chapter on Supernatural Power, which clarifies how the bodhisattvas receive their mandate to propagate the sutra, there are two parts: first, the prose section; within this, first, the bodhisattvas receiving their mandate;
within this, first, the narrative by the sūtra compiler describing the ritual proceedings.
At that time, bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within a thousand worlds (up to) joined their palms with single-minded devotion and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance.
△ Second, the vow to propagate the sutra; Part Three: First, the time.

They addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, after the extinction of the Buddha, we shall go to the lands and places of nirvana where the World-Honored One’s divided bodies reside. (2) The Locations.
△ Third, the Vows.
Why is it that this sutra shall be explained extensively? (Up to: "One shall explain, transcribe, and make offerings to it.
It is not merely that one obeys the command to benefit others; one also vows for oneself to attain this truly pure Great Dharma, thereby providing salvation for both self and others.
It is excellent. △ Second, the Buddha manifests his supernatural powers. Part one: the assembly present.
At that time, the World-Honored One was before Mañjuśrī and others, including all the assemblies of humans and non-humans.

Regarding "Mañjuśrī and others," these are the assembly of those to be converted within the traces [of the Buddha's manifestation]. Regarding "the long-resident ones," these are the original assembly of those to be converted from the lower direction.

Regarding "the entire assembly," this includes those who have come from other directions, those who have come following the emanation-bodies of the Buddhas, as well as the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings—all of them are included.
△ Second, the actual manifestation of supernatural power, in ten parts: first, exhaling a long breath.
The mark of the tongue:
manifesting great supernormal power, he extends his broad and long tongue upward as far as the Brahma-world.
This is the first supernormal power. Regarding the manifestation of the tongue-mark, that which is expounded in the present sutra reveals the three to disclose the one.
The benefits bestowed upon beings in the near and distant past, as well as throughout the three periods of time, are all true and not false. The tongues of those with merit reach their nostrils;
the tongue of the Buddha of the Tripitaka reaches the hairline; now it reaches the Brahma Heaven, transcending both the ordinary and the sages, extending to the very summit of the Pure Heavens.
Since his physical marks are thus extraordinary, his teachings are even more worthy of trust. △ Second, light radiates from his entire body.
From every pore, he emits immeasurable and innumerable rays of light of various colors (continuing until) for a full hundred thousand years.
This is the second supernatural power. Light is emitted from the pores of his entire body and all over his frame, pervading the ten directions so that there is nowhere it does not illuminate.
This signifies that the principle of the two gates is one, and the realm of wisdom is ultimate. Above, in the Gate of Traces, the white tuft of hair emits [light].

The radiance first appeared in the east, signifying the initial insight into the single principle at the beginning of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*). Now that the present *mūlaparivarta* (Root Chapter) has concluded, it emits all-encompassing light that illuminates all lands;
this enables those at the stage of the causal path with their initial resolve to reach the ultimate wisdom of a Buddha at the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samayaksaṃbodhi*).
The emanated Buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*) are also like this. Regarding the phrase "emanated bodies and so forth" in the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy), this refers to these characteristics.
Since they are identical, the benefit bestowed within each respective land is likewise so. △ Third, the sound of clearing the throat:
thereupon, he withdraws his tongue-mark and clears his throat all at once.
This is the third supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). "Clearing the throat" is the manner of about to speak, and it is also a sign of thorough clarity.
The teaching of the two gates has now been fully expounded, which is itself the teaching of the One;
that which was hidden and secret for over forty years is now revealed without obstruction or residue. This great matter of world-transcendence is now thoroughly clarified.
Therefore, he clears his throat, wishing to entrust this Dharma to the bodhisattvas so that they may guide and benefit sentient beings in future generations, and thus speaks these words.
For this reason, there is the clearing of the throat; the clearing of the throat possesses two meanings: first, to signal that the matter is concluded;
second, to entrust [the matter] to another. △ Fourth, the sound of snapping fingers:
everyone snaps their fingers together.

This is the fourth supernatural power. To snap one's fingers is to express sympathetic joy (*anumodana*). It is to rejoice that those on the seven stages of expedient means enter together into the Perfect Path;
to rejoice that the Perfect Path increases wisdom and diminishes birth; to rejoice that all Bodhisattvas uphold the Great Dharma of True Purity;

and to rejoice that future generations shall obtain the Unsurpassed Treasure. This single snap of the fingers penetrates vertically through the three periods of time and extends horizontally across all realms.
The manifestation of the ten directions through the two gates of entry into reality constitutes the first [aspect] of the teaching. △ Fifth, the sixfold earthquake:
this second sound pervades the worlds of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, such that the earth everywhere quakes in six ways.
This is the fifth supernatural power. Regarding the "two sounds," these refer to clearing one's throat and snapping the fingers.

As for the earth shaking in six ways, this symbolizes the stages of abiding, practice, and penetration (*caryā-bhūmi*, *pratipatti-bhūmi*, and *prativedha-bhūmi*), as well as the sixfold subtle movements.

Since the delusions of ignorance have already been shaken off, the fact that it now shakes again signifies that the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) of all people are made pure; it symbolizes the breaking [of obstacles] through the two gates.
Delusion is identical to formative action (saṃskāra). △ Sixth, the Universal Vision of the Great Assembly:
Among them, the sentient beings—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth—all experienced great joy, attaining what they had never before.
This is the sixth supernatural power. That the entire great assembly is seen universally signifies that the Way of all Buddhas is identical.

From this day forward, it shall likewise be so. As for the five thousand who withdrew earlier and were moved elsewhere by the three transformations—having lost their original resolve and being unable to receive benefit in the present—they shall attain it through the extinction of what is not actually extinguished, by means of the Bodhisattvas propagating the sutra.
The Way enters the Buddha-wisdom just as it does in this assembly, without difference; it likewise manifests for those with the capacity [for enlightenment] in the future.

Regarding the statement that "those who have departed, those who were moved away, and those who lost their minds" constitute three types of people, these three examples refer to those who obtain benefit after the [Buddha’s] extinction.
As for the phrase "the capacity is one," the meaning of "capacity" (機) should be understood as being comprehensive, encompassing all [who possess it] even in the future.
This is because of the "four and one"; that is, one obtains the benefit of these four and one. △ Seventh, the proclamation in the void:
At that moment, the various devas in the void [until] they shall likewise pay homage and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.
This is the seventh supernatural power. As for the voice proclaiming from the air, it signifies that in the future there shall be the teaching (the first).
△ Eighth, all take refuge.
After those sentient beings heard the voice from the void (up to) "Namo Śākyamuni Buddha."
This is the eighth supernatural power. *Namo* (in the language of the South) means "I take refuge";
it signifies that among future beings there shall be those who become disciples of the Buddha. △ Ninth: Scattering various objects from afar.
With various flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, and canopies, [they] completely cover all the Buddhas here.
This is the ninth supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). That various objects are scattered from afar and arrive like gathering clouds signifies that there will be practice in the future;
this is the first [point]. △ Tenth, the single Buddha-field.
At that time, the worlds of the ten directions were unimpededly accessible as if they were a single Buddha-land.
This is the tenth supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). That the ten directions are universally identical to a single Buddha-land signifies the oneness of principle (*li-yi*).

Question: By what means is it known that the ten marks represent the fourfold oneness of the present, and furthermore, that they also represent the fourfold oneness of the future? Answer: [As stated] below.

The text states: "If I were to use this supernatural power to explain the merits of this sutra for the sake of entrustment throughout immeasurable kalpas, I would still be unable to fully express or manifest its meaning.
This clearly illustrates the significance of the passage. Miaole (Wenxiu) comments:

"Regarding the ten supernatural powers, the first five specifically clarify the present circulation of the *honji-suijaku* (original and trace manifestations), while the latter five collectively represent the future."

Furthermore, it is said that the four subsequent marks separately represent the future; while one of these four is simply called "one," the distinction between the original and the trace is not mentioned because they pertain to the future.
Since they have not yet entered into reality, who would discuss their origin? If one perceives reality, one also perceives its origin.
△ Third, the summary and exhortation to uphold [the teaching], in four parts: first, the praise and entrustment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, including Upāriṣṭa and others... [until] ...even so they could not exhaust it.
△ Second, the summary and entrustment:
To speak in brief, all that the Tathāgata has [taught]... is all proclaimed and clearly expounded within this sutra.
The essential points of this binding consist of four phrases: "All dharmas" means that all things are the Buddha-dharma;
this binding is the name for the fact that all are wondrous. "All powers" means penetrating without obstruction and possessing the eight masteries;
this binding is the wondrous function. "All secret treasuries" means that everywhere is the true reality (*dharmatā*); this binding is the wondrous essence.
Regarding the phrase "matters that are exceedingly profound," cause and effect are these profound matters; this concludes the wondrous thesis (*miào zōng*).

The statement "all are proclaimed and clearly expounded in this sutra" summarizes the entire scripture as consisting of only four [sections], grasping its essential pivot and transmitting it so that it may circulate.
Miaole says: "The conclusion must have four phrases" refers to the two gates of the original (*ben*) and the trace (*ji*).

Each has its own principle and function—“principle” (zōng) referring to the provisional cause and provisional fruit, as well as the fundamental cause and fundamental fruit; “function” (yòng) referring to the severing of doubts regarding the provisional and the arising of true faith, and the severing of doubts regarding the near and the arising of faith regarding the distant.

The essence of these two gates does not differ in the two locations [the Lotus Sūtra and the *Fahua Xuanyi*]. This title encompasses these three and summarizes the essentials of the entire three-part work; how could the core importance exceed this?
Therefore, they are gathered together to form a statement for the circulation [of the teaching]. It is said: “Since the revelation and manifestation are complete, it is now concluded.”
To state the essential point: that which is referred to as the "Tathāgata" is an expression of the fruit [of enlightenment] and the ultimate word;
that which is called "all" encompasses both awakening and delusion—it is the wondrous Dharma of inconceivable mystery. Furthermore, regarding the designation of the "wondrous" for all phenomena:

these are the dharmas of the inherent nature and virtue possessed by sentient beings from the beginning, and they are also the dharmas perfected through the Tathāgata’s long-term cultivation; this remains so even while [these dharmas] are within the bonds of saṃsāra.

Differing from those who have merely emerged from the entanglements, the essence of this Dharma is truly pure, harmonious, subtle, and utterly transcendent; thus it is called the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma), which is its name.
As for the wondrous function of all powers and fetters, sentient beings possess them yet remain deluded, while the Tathāgata realizes them and never ceases his activity.

By means of the power of mastery, he establishes transformations through the three wheels to startle and move the hearts of sentient beings; it is for the purpose of expounding this Dharma that [he appears].
Next, the function is explained by name: "The wondrous essence that binds all secret treasuries" refers to this body of true reality (*dharmatā*) which the Tathāgata has already attained;
he now preaches the Dharma for it and causes sentient beings to likewise attain this essence—thus, through the function, the essence is revealed.
"The wondrous principle that binds all profound matters" refers to the fundamental dharma of cause and effect; since the Buddha...

Since the cultivation and realization of sentient beings are likewise so, the core tenet is concluded immediately following the essence. This follows the sequence in which the Tathāgata gave rise to his teachings;
thus, first the names, then the functions, then the essence, and finally the core tenet.

Therefore, the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning), fascicle one, cites this conclusion of the essentials to verify the sequential order of the five chapters on the "Approximate Teaching. △ Third, the exhortation and entrustment.
Therefore, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, you all should build stupas at these locations and make offerings to them.
△ Fourth, the explanation of the intent behind the entrustment:
Why is this so? You should know that these places are where all Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa.
The aforementioned passage states that wherever this sutra volume is located, a stupa should be erected there. The essential teachings within the sutra are summarized in four matters:

the explanation of the profound matter regarding the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); the explanation of the attainment of Bodhi; the explanation of the secret treasury regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
and the explanation of the entry into Nirvāṇa through all dharmas by means of supernatural power (ṛddhibala). These four essentials encompass the entire text of the sutra.
Because they are all exhausted, one should erect stupas for them all. What is essential is this: attaining *bodhi* is the *dharmakāya*;

turning the wheel of the Dharma is *prajñā*; entering *nirvāṇa* is *vimukti*. These three dharmas constitute the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*), and the Buddha abiding within it is the meaning of a stupa.
The *Āgama Sūtra* says: "When a Buddha appears in the world, stupas are erected at only four places."

The place where he attained the Way, the place where he turned the wheel of Dharma, the place where he entered *nirvāṇa*, and the place where he sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)—these are the birthplaces of the *dharmakāya*.
All other matters are as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "the site of enlightenment explains the profound matter" from the *Miaole*:

"matter" refers to cause and effect; here, the site of enlightenment is the effect, and every effect must have a cause. As for explaining the "treasury" (*garbha*) by means of *bodhi* (enlightenment): *bodhi* is...
The wisdom capable of accords with reality must have an object that it illuminates; this object is the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*), for the subject reveals the object.

Regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*) as an explanation of all phenomena: there must be a Dharma that is turned, and such Dharma necessarily possesses a name. Regarding the explanation of power and function (*prabhāva*) through *nirvāṇa*:

the fulfillment of principle explains the provisional (*upāya*), while the proclamation of extinction (*nirvāṇa*) explains the near doubt regarding the ultimate essence (*tattva*). Although these are categorized as near and far, [they are ultimately one].

Regarding the statement that "the cause and effect of the same name are no longer distinguished," the citation of the *Āgama* borrows from the Small Vehicle to testify to the Great; that [citation] does so from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*).
Now, borrowing it to testify to the Perfect [Vehicle], the Small is opened as the Great, and thus it may serve as proof. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts:
first, the summary of the manifestation of the ten spiritual powers.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas, the saviors of the world, abide in great supernormal powers... (omitted)... manifesting immeasurable spiritual powers."
The *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states that among the ten supernatural powers described in the verse, only five are mentioned because the latter five are omitted.

Of the former five, those currently manifest are retained for their essential importance; the distinction between the former and latter sets of five lies simply in their being present or future. Since the future can be inferred from the present, they are abbreviated.
△ Second, the verse on the summary and the entrustment has three parts. First, a general verse on the four dharmas.
Because he entrusts this sutra, he praises those who receive and uphold it (up to) "its limit cannot be found.
Miaole says: "The general verse on the four dharmas only mentions 'entrusting' up to 'reaching the limit,' yet it fully contains the four meanings;
for all four meanings are themselves boundless. △ Second, the individual verses on the four dharmas. First, the verse on "all."
The Dharma.
One who is able to uphold this sutra has already seen me (up to: ...and) has taught and transformed all bodhisattvas.
To uphold the Dharma is to uphold the wondrous bliss of the Buddha-body. It is said that all dharmas do not transcend the transformer and the realized one.
This is because they are those to be transformed. △ Second, the verse on sovereign spiritual power:
"May those who can uphold this sutra cause me and my emanated bodies (up to: 'and also cause them') to attain joy."

The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: Regarding the verse on supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), since it says "rejoicing," this refers to the full manifestation of sovereign function (*vaśitā-vibhūti*).
△ Third, the verse on the secret treasury:
"The secret essential dharma attained by all Buddhas when seated at the site of enlightenment—those who can uphold this sutra shall also attain it before long."
△ Four verses on the profound matter:
"One who can uphold this sutra [attains] the meaning of all dharmas... ultimately abiding in the One Vehicle.
To preach the Dharma, destroy darkness, and enter the One Vehicle is the profound matter of the Buddha. *Myōryaku* (The Wonderful Joy) states: "These verses [expound] the profundity."

"Phenomena" (vastu) refers to the teaching and transformation of all bodhisattvas so that they ultimately abide in the Single Vehicle; this is cause and effect, for cause and effect pertain to phenomena.
△ Third, the summary verse concludes the meaning.
Therefore, those with wisdom who hear these benefits of merit will reach a state of certainty and have no doubt.
*Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states that this verse summarizes the four dharmas, saying: "If one can uphold these four dharmas..."

In the twenty-second chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "Entrusting the Teaching" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*), both the former masters Ci'en Ji and An-guo She proposed moving this chapter to follow the "Encouraging the Resolve" (*Saṃcodana*) chapter.
However, if it were placed there, there would be eight contradictions and ten untenable points. Thus, the Venerable Jingxi, in his *Commentary* (*Ji*), [addressed this].
Each point in the text has been explained and refuted in detail; as it would be too cumbersome to record them all here, I shall now provide the direct exegesis.

"Entrustment" (*zhù*) refers to that which the Buddha has committed to others, while "bequeathing" (*lèi*) refers to the task of propagating it. Because this [title] derives its name from the Sage’s command, it is called "entrustment.

Furthermore, "entrustment" signifies receiving it upon one's head with reverence, while "bequeathing" signifies doing so with joy rather than weariness. Because this [title] derives its name from the Bodhisattva’s respectful compliance, it is called "bequeathing."

Therefore, it is said "entrustment" (*parindanā*). Furthermore, "entrustment" refers to that which was entrusted by the golden mouth of the Tathāgata, while "receiving" refers to the Bodhisattva’s sincere heart bearing this upon his crown.
Since these aspects of giving and receiving are discussed together, it is called "entrustment.

Moreover, the Tathāgata rose from his seat in person, extended his hand, and stroked [the Bodhisattva’s] head, bestowing upon him the Dharma that is difficult to obtain; the great assembly bowed their bodies and joined their palms, as if before the World-Honored One himself.
The decree [to] "fully and reverently practice" and the earnest entrustment constitute what is called the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Nyorui-hon*).

*Myōryaku* states that within the formal explanation of this chapter, the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) are also fully present. First, regarding the derivation of its name, the explanation of how the chapter acquires its title is distinct;
this is the *loka-siddhānta*. Furthermore, "entrustment" (*ru*) means to extend or involve. "I trouble you" (*nan-ni*)—here, "you" (*ni*) refers to "thou. It means to involve you.
That later generations might be burdened by this is the Tathāgata’s timely transformation, wherein he displayed humble words;
furthermore, it ensures that the transmission of the Dharma remains uninterrupted throughout the three periods of time. These three periods, though distinct, likewise constitute the world.

Moreover, when Bodhisattvas respectfully comply with future generations and proclaim the goodness of living beings, they act for the benefit of humanity. This is what was entrusted by the Golden Mouth.
The Bodhisattva bears this mandate upon his head so that future generations shall not lose it; to rectify their failings and evils is the "counteractive" (pratipakṣa).

Furthermore, by earnestly transmitting and receiving [the teaching], he causes people of later ages to receive the intent and enter into its realization; entering therein and realizing the truth is the "Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha).

△ Second, the Entrustment Chapter (Parīndanā-parivarta) clarifies the Tathāgata’s conferral of the mandate through touching the crown of the head. Part One: The Proper Clarification of the Entrustment.
II. The Initial Entrustment by the Tathāgata. A. The Actual Entrustment.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha... [omitted] ...causing all sentient beings everywhere to hear and know it.
Because he simultaneously and universally strokes the crowns of the heads of all bodhisattvas with one hand, he is called the Buddha of Great Supernatural Power (*mahā-ṛddhibala*).

Because the Tathāgata uses the skillful hand of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) to stroke the crowns of the heads of the bodhisattvas of true wisdom— who fill the void of three thousand three hundred *nayuta* lands—
he is called the Hand of Expedient Wisdom, for the Tathāgata bestows the Way and transforms others through this means.
Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva himself practices and receives the Way, it is called the "Crown of Real Wisdom" (*bhūta-jñāna-śīrṣa*).
To stroke the crown with an outstretched hand is the entrustment of the body; the provisional wisdom approaching the real wisdom is the entrustment of the mind;
and to speak these words is the entrustment of the mouth. These texts contain the four *siddhāntas*. For immeasurable kalpas, I have cultivated this which is difficult to obtain.
This Dharma was received and studied from previous Buddhas and is now entrusted to you; you shall transmit it to those who succeed through the three generations.
This is the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint). Its single-minded dissemination is the *pudgala-siddhānta* (individual standpoint).
Causing it to increase extensively is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (remedial standpoint). That which benefits is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (ultimate standpoint). It is wondrous.
Regarding the statement that the Tathāgata manifests great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*):

although he has already manifested ten kinds of supernormal powers to complete the fourfold benefit for the future and the present, his current manifestation of supernormal powers specifically symbolizes the entrustment of the three—body, speech, and mind.
In the *Siming Jiaoxing Lu*, it is recorded that a Japanese monk asked: "To what does [the text] refer?"

Regarding the statement that there are "three thousand three hundred nayutas" of world-systems, some say this refers to the three transformed pure lands, while others claim it refers to the eight directions each being further transformed into two hundred trillion nayutas of worlds; if one follows this latter meaning, one may indeed say "three thousand three hundred.
Is this explanation correct? Answer: According to the principle, it must refer to the three transformed pure lands. This is so because...
The middle [section] should not take a great trichiliocosm as a single land; it likely refers to a single four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*) as one land.
Since "Sahā" is the name for a great trichiliocosm, it could suffice to constitute three thousand times three hundred [worlds].
However, even a great trichiliocosm seems insufficient to reach one hundred million *nayuta* four-continent world systems; this is likely an increase based on a large-scale approximation.
Regarding the Great Trichiliocosm, what are the small numbers? A small number consists of ten tens making one hundred; a large number consists of one hundred hundreds making one thousand;

and so on, with one thousand thousands making ten thousand, and so forth. Thus, in the first transformation, the Sahā world-system becomes one hundred nayutas; in the second and third transformations, there are two hundred nayutas each.
Therefore, in one direction there are four hundred nayutas, and for all eight directions combined, [there are three thousand two hundred nayutas].
Three thousand two hundred [worlds] together with the one hundred of the Sahā world make three thousand three hundred. △ Second, the explanation of the entrustment. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata possesses great compassion... (up to)... do not give rise to stinginess regarding the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Possessing great compassion is the chamber of the Tathāgata; being free from stinginess is the robe of the Tathāgata;
and being without fear is the seat of the Tathāgata. The wisdom of the Buddha is the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*);
the wisdom of the Tathāgata is the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*); and natural wisdom is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Regarding the Tathāgata...
Within the chamber, one can bestow upon sentient beings the three kinds of wisdom; it is likewise so within the seat.

This means that the robe, the seat, and the chamber each possess the three wisdoms. By means of these three things, one propagates the sutra to benefit others, enabling them each to attain the function of the three wisdoms at the stage of fruition.
Thus we know that if the chamber lacked the two great vows, its benefit would not be universal, nor would the robe.
If there are no two [aspects], the Dharma-body will not fill the seats; if there are no two [types of] delusions, the destruction [of them] will not be universal.
Thus, when a donor lacks none of these three dharmas, both self and others are not left empty. You should study the Tathāgata’s three dharmas in this way and propagate them.
With these three sets of three, you should bestow them upon all; you yourselves are the great leaders of sentient beings.
The donor is said to be one who explains the Buddha’s intention and receives the entrustment. *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) states:
"The Buddha’s wisdom" and so forth refers to the aspect of awakening and illumination, which belongs to the all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) and vision;

"the Tathāgata’s ultimate emptiness wisdom" and so forth refers to obtaining the name of the path-knowledge (*mārgajñatā*) from cause to fruit. Thus, regarding "the donor" and below, it concludes the discussion on the one who practices giving.
Because the mind is the donor, it possesses great compassion; because it has already entered the chamber itself, it causes others to enter the chamber;

because it is free from stinginess, it has already donned the robes itself and causes others to don the robes; because it is free from fear, it has already sat upon the seat itself and causes others to sit upon the seat.
Alternatively, it may be said that because it is free from stinginess, it bestows these three dharmas, and because it is free from fear, it speaks of them.
If one possesses compassion when either bestowing or expounding the Three Dharmas, this constitutes the "Three Dharmas for Entering the Chamber. △ Second, the injunction of entrustment:
"In future ages, if there are good sons (up to) then it shall be as if they have already repaid the debt of gratitude to all Buddhas."
If their roots are deep and their wisdom sharp, one should explain the Buddha’s wisdom directly.

If they are not yet capable of this, one should instruct, benefit, and gladden them within other profound dharmas so that they may realize the Buddha’s wisdom. This Buddha’s wisdom is profound, whereas the other six skillful means are "other" rather than profound;
the distinct teaching (biejiao) and the gradual teaching (cidi) are both "other" and profound. You are able to assist in proclaiming the Buddha’s wisdom by means of these other profound dharmas.

This refers to skillfully repaying the Buddha’s kindness; it is called the "Instruction and Entrustment. Regarding "showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening," the *Soyōki* (Record of Essential Points) states:
"Directing and instructing is called 'showing' (*śāsanā*); commanding is called 'teaching' (*anuśāsanā*); providing benefit is called 'benefiting' (*anugraha*);
and causing joy is named 'gladdening' (*saṃharṣaṇā*). △ Second, the Bodhisattvas’ Acceptance.
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas [from "up to"] replied, "So be it, World-Honored One; we pray that you have no further concern.

The Buddha entrusted [the matter] to the bodhisattvas through the three modes of action (trikarma), and the bodhisattvas likewise received it through the three modes of action with joy: they received it mentally by being delighted in their intent;
they received it physically by bowing their bodies and lowering their heads; and they received it verbally by raising their voices together, saying, "As the World-Honored One has commanded."
The command "Receive [this]" signifies the intention of entering the Tathāgata’s chamber as the Great Benefactor; one should practice it with full devotion.
The command "Observe [this]" signifies the intention of donning the Tathāgata’s robe, being free from all stinginess and attachment.

The command "Do not have any anxiety" signifies the intention of sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat, being without fear. Since the Buddha thus entrusted [the teaching] three times, the Bodhisattva likewise responded three times.
The procedures for receiving [the offerings] are all as stated in the text. △ Third, when the affairs are concluded, the dispersal is announced.
At that time, from Śākyamuni Buddha (until) the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha shall return to its former state.
Because Prabhūtaratna has come to bear witness to this sutra, the two gates of the trace and the origin have already been concluded;

therefore, he must subtly depart and close [the stupa] as before. He manifested his divided bodies in order to open the stupa, and now that the task of opening it is finished, he causes each of those divided bodies to return to their own lands.
Since the stupa cannot be opened again, the divided bodies depart and do not appear, yet the stupa continues to hear the Dharma.
Therefore, it was closed because [the teaching] had already been realized;
yet it remained open for the purpose of listening to its circulation. △ Second, the assembly rejoiced.
When these words were spoken, the immeasurable [beings] of the ten directions (up to) who heard what the Buddha taught all rejoiced greatly.
The Buddhas rejoice because their work for the sake of transforming others has been accomplished; the Bodhisattvas rejoice because they have attained the Dharma for their own practice;
furthermore, they rejoice because the person who can preach it is pure—this refers to the Buddha—and they rejoice because they have heard the pure Dharma, which is subtle and wondrous.

This refers to the sutra itself; furthermore, it refers to those who, having heard the Dharma, have attained realization and thus rejoice, as well as those who will benefit in the present and the future—those who possess these three things experience great joy.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Twenty-Three: "The Past Deeds of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja."
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states: "In the past, when he was named Jyotīrasa, he heard the Venerable Sūryagarbha preach the wisdom of the Buddha.
He offered medicinal herbs from the Snow Mountains to the assembly of monks, vowing, 'May I, in the future, be able to cure the two ailments of body and mind for all sentient beings.
The entire world rejoiced and called him Bhaiṣajyarāja. Now, this sūtra clarifies that [the Bodhisattva] Sarvasattvapriyadarśana suddenly..."

Having sacrificed one body and further burned both arms, he regarded his life lightly while valuing the Dharma; though his life ended, the Way remained. To illustrate the past and manifest it in the present, it is called the "Chapter on Past Deeds.
The five chapters below are all for the purpose of transforming others and circulating [the teaching], as fully detailed above.

Now, having completed the explanation of the "Chapter on Expedient Means," which opens the three vehicles to reveal the One and clarifies the perfect cause, the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" elucidates...

The explanation of the Dharma of mounting the vehicle, clarifying the fruit of the vehicle, is hereby concluded. In the following section of this chapter, the person who mounts the vehicle is clarified;
thus, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* states: "The Great Vehicle is that which is mounted by great beings such as Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī;
it is the vehicle mounted by Bhaiṣajyarāja through ascetic practice, and by Gadgadasvara and Avalokiteśvara through samādhi and dhāraṇī."

One rides the vehicle of *dhāraṇī* to achieve wondrous adornment; one rides the vehicle of vows to [attain] Samantabhadra; and one rides the vehicle of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to perform this interpretation.
For one who understands it thus, it is convenient for the purpose of transforming others and circulating [the teaching]. Miaole (妙樂) says:

"From the section on Bhaiṣajyarāja until the section on the convenience of circulation" means that after the Buddha’s entrustment (*parindanā*), the great task is completed; therefore, [the teaching] proceeds according to the preferences of sentient beings. Thus, it is called a "vehicle."
The various vehicles differ, yet the true suchness (tathatā) as the ultimate reality is the essence of that which is mounted; the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle are the matters mounted upon;

and ascetic practices and the like are the conditions for mounting the vehicle. Because these are adapted to the capacities of sentient beings, the propagators of the teaching differ according to circumstances;
thus, the essence of what is mounted is in every case the wondrous Dharma, for it is established upon the one reality as the basis for cause and fruit.
Because one rides upon that which is ridden for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, it is called "the vehicle of vehicles" (yānayāna).

△ Second, from the "Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter downward, five chapters concern the exhortation to circulate [the teaching] by means of transforming others. First, the "Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva" chapter clarifies the exhortation for the teacher who transforms others:
"I only pray that the Great Dharma may be widely proclaimed and that great vows may bring great benefit to sentient beings. Thus, [he] exhausts himself...

Exhausting his supernatural powers throughout his entire life, with profound and earnest devotion, his will remained undaunted; he hoped to cause his disciples to revere the Dharma as they did their teacher.
"I transmit this clarity to you, and you shall again transmit it to others; let this clarity be passed on endlessly"—this was the teacher's resolve.
Thus we know that this chapter exhorts teachers who propagate the Dharma. Next, the two chapters on "Wondrous Sound" (Ghoṣadatta) and "Avalokiteśvara" clarify [the practice].

Furthermore, the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas), having received their mandate, propagate this sutra and universally manifest forms; their physical appearances have no fixed standard and cannot be perceived with the eyes of cattle or sheep, nor can they be fathomed by the consciousness of the ordinary and ignorant. Regarding what is heard, one must not give rise to thoughts of disparagement, for if such thoughts arise, the Dharma will not permeate the mind. Thus, we know that these two sections exhort the disciples who receive the Dharma.
