Throughout the entire night, Da continued to call upon the name and recite the scriptures, still hoping for a single response. Toward dawn, the Qiang came to take him.
Suddenly, a tiger emerged from the grass and roared; the Qiang tribesmen scattered and fled. The tiger then bit through the palisade, making a hole, and departed.
Da escaped with his young son by fleeing and defecting, thus avoiding death. Furthermore, Pei Anqi defected from the captives and returned south;
reaching the riverbank, he was unable to cross. Seeing the pursuing cavalry behind him, he was on the verge of death in an instant.
Thereupon, as he invoked Avalokiteśvara, he suddenly saw a white wolf spring up, seize him, and toss him across to the southern bank;

immediately, the wolf was lost. The pursuing riders remained together on the northern bank, gazing at him and sighing with boundless lamentation. Regarding the interpretation of this account, there are also three views:
first, the theory of karmic retribution, which holds that the hostile bandits were beings who had come from the hells up to the sixth heaven.

There are always conflicts and disputes, as stated in the Āgama Sūtras: "In the war between the Trāyastriṃśa devas and the Asuras, when the devas were defeated and sought assistance, they reached as far as the sixth heaven.
When such enemies meet, if one can invoke [the Buddha's] name, one will immediately attain liberation.

Second, regarding the treatise on the two evil karmas, concerning "enemies and bandits": when one cultivates goodness, evil is often like an enemy; it is like ice and fire. One should invoke [the Buddha's] name.
The waning of evil and the accomplishment of wholesome karma are like the extinction of darkness and the arising of light. The three afflictions act as enemies and robbers;
all afflictions are the enemies of those who have transcended the world. The mind-king is the caravan leader, and the mental factors (*caitasika*) are the merchants.

Right contemplation and wisdom are the precious treasures, while unwholesome applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) are the enemies and robbers. Alternatively, *prajñā* (wisdom) is the caravan leader. (5)
The crossing over of the myriad practices is the merchant's dharma; the true mark of the dharma-nature is the precious treasure; the six hindrances are the hostile bandits.
If one can single-mindedly invoke the name, one shall immediately attain liberation. △ Second, the conclusion regarding the supernatural power.
Such is the majestic and sublime power of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Infinite Intent.
Since the power of Avalokiteśvara is so great and his protective grace so vast, how could it be limited to merely seven perils?
One should know that he is able to rescue and protect throughout the entire Dharma-realm; thus, the term "majestic and sublime" is repeated to emphasize the height and accumulation of his excellence.

It is also clarified that the power of Avalokiteśvara transcends the realm of shared existence and the stage of segmented birth, responding vertically to the two lands of Expedient Means and True Reward;
thus it is said "repeatedly clarifying. Because one is repeatedly bathed in his divine response, it is said "highly accumulated.
For these reasons, it is described as "lofty and majestic" (*weiwei*). △ Second, the response to the mental faculties, in two parts: first, clarifying the three poisons.
If there are sentient beings who have an abundance of lust (up to) they will thereby attain freedom from delusion.

This is an explanation of the faculties of mental karma (*manas-karma*) based on the three poisons. It is divided into two parts: first, the literal commentary (*pian-wen*); second, the contemplative interpretation (*guan-jie*).

Regarding the literal commentary, each of the three poisons has three aspects: first, clarifying the presence of suffering; second, silently contemplating these two [aspects], which constitutes the clarification.

The three types of knowledge (*vidyā*) are the illumination that is free from these [afflictions]; these three are collectively termed "poisons" (*viṣa*) because they can harm the practitioner, being compared to poison.
There are both single and compound forms: if one speaks of greed, anger, and delusion, these three are single;
now, following the compound form, they are called lustful desire, hatred, and ignorance. Furthermore, loving oneself is [called] desire for self, while loving others is... [desire for others].

Lust directed toward oneself is called "anger" (恚); anger directed toward others is called "hatred" (瞋); delusion directed toward oneself is called "ignorance" (愚); and delusion directed toward others is called "folly" (癡).

Here, it is clarified that even those with a preponderance of the three poisons can, by recollecting Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s spiritual power, be made to leave them behind—how much more so those with fewer afflictions?
This is an instance of using the "many" to illustrate the "few. Furthermore, those with excessive lust do not distinguish between humans and beasts.

One may avoid the perils of high walls and wide moats, yet fail to reckon with the calamities of ill repute and the loss of virtue; such a person brings ruin to their family, destruction to their state, and extinction to their clan, with the disaster extending even to their own person.

The *Nettippakaraṇa* (Pure Abiding Sūtra) and the *Dhyāna-sūtra* clarify that those with many desires are infested by "desire-insects," and further state that desire-demons harass and agitate their minds, causing them to give rise to inverted delusions. As for those with much anger, [the consequences manifest] in this very life.
People do not like to see anger, for it is like a thirsty horse guarding its water or a lioness protecting her cub. Therefore, the *Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching* states:
"No thief of merit across the kalpas exceeds anger. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The arising of a single thought of anger obstructs the Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "If one gives rise to a single thought of anger, all demons and ghosts will find an opportunity; such ignorance is great."
Those who engage in perverse views, deny cause and effect, and slander the Mahāyāna suffer from such afflictions as the three poisons;
yet if one can single-mindedly maintain mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara, one shall immediately be freed from them.

As for the contemplative understanding (*guanjie*), one does not grasp at the characteristics of the three poisons within the realm of conditioned existence (*dhātu*), but rather speaks of them from the perspective beyond the realm (*dhātu-bāhya*) in terms of both the favorable and the adverse. Regarding the favorable explanation, it is found in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
It is said that the aspiration for all wholesome dharmas is their root. To desire and delight in *nirvāṇa* as do those of the Two Vehicles is called greed;

to loathe and abhor *saṃsāra* is called hatred; and to fail to realize this principle is called ignorance. For a Bodhisattva, to greedily seek the Buddha-dharma is called greed; to despise the Two Vehicles is called hatred;
and to have an unclear vision of the Buddha-nature is called ignorance. One desires to eliminate these three afflictions.
Therefore, if one constantly recollects and contemplates Avalokiteśvara, who responds according to the capacities of beings, one will immediately attain eternal liberation. To speak contrarily:

all sentient beings are said to have few desires; yet why is this? It is because those who cease hatred seek to avoid the suffering of the three miserable realms and desire the joy of humans and devas, while those of the Two Vehicles cease hatred to avoid the suffering of birth and death and desire to attain the joy of Nirvana. All [of these] are...
To be called a "lesser bodhisattva" is not so; rather, to seek everywhere for all the unspeakable Buddha-dharmas is called greed.
Not only to refuse saṃsāra, but also to refuse nirvāṇa, is called hatred. For the delusion of final ignorance to still persist is called delusion.
These three poisons constitute three dharma-gates: first, grasping; second, rejecting; and third, neither grasping nor rejecting.

Not abandoning great loving-kindness and great compassion, the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), purifying the buddha-fields, and transforming and delivering sentient beings is called the "gate of grasping," which is itself great greed.

That all phenomena are empty, non-existent, non-abiding, non-attached, without attainment, and without realization is called the "gate of relinquishing," which is itself great hatred. The Middle Way is neither grasping nor relinquishing; it is without aversion.
Because it is neither attachment nor abandonment, neither eternal nor annihilated, neither arising nor ceasing, and because it excludes the two extremes, it cannot be expressed in words;
this is called the gate of non-grasping and non-rejection, which is precisely Great Ignorance (mahāmoha). Thus, Mañjuśrī said:
"I am the śrī of desire, the śrī of hatred, and the śrī of false views. This is clear evidence that one wishes to fulfill these three dharmas.
If one constantly recollects and contemplates Avalokiteśvara at the gates, one shall immediately attain their wishes.

Since there is no practice for the realization of self or the transformation of others by any sage that does not enter through these three gates, the *Wuxing jing* (Sutra on Non-action) states: "Lust is itself the Way; anger and delusion are likewise so.
Within these three dharmas, all Buddha-dharmas are complete. These three dharma-gates cannot be fully expressed in words.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, [the Buddha] may provide teachings that accord with their dispositions or those that oppose them, involving mutual inclusion or exclusion;
this is precisely the intent of the four *siddhāntas*, benefiting others by responding to their specific conditions. The *Yishu ji* (Commentary on the Meaning) states:

"To constantly contemplate seeking liberation from the three afflictions is called 'teaching in accordance' (*shun-shuo*); to constantly contemplate seeking fulfillment through the three dharma-gates is called 'teaching in opposition' (*ni-shuo*). Fulfillment refers to the fulfillment of the three gates of liberation.
The distinction between accepting and rejecting [the two] is made solely from the perspective of the *siddhānta* (established tenet). △ Second, the conclusion on the benefits:
"Ajita, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva... therefore, sentient beings should always keep him in mind."

△ III. The Response of the Three Bodies to the Capacities [of Sentient Beings]. Part Two: First, clarifying the two types of seeking. Part One: Seeking a male child. Sub-part One: Establishing the vow.
"If there is a woman who wishes to seek a male child...

From here below, it clarifies that physical action serves as the capacity (*kāraṇa*). This also has two parts: first, the literal application of the text; second, the contemplative interpretation. Regarding the literal application of the text:
The text states: "If a woman seeks a son and yet remains childless, the lineage will be extinguished;
if she has a son, both parents rejoice. Why, then, does it single out only the woman seeking a son? It is because for a woman, being childless is a source of suffering:
she is abandoned by her husband, despised by her fellow wives, and ridiculed by others. Furthermore, regarding the seven faults of a wife, six of them are still tolerable.

Lack of patience, childlessness, extreme severity, an ugly appearance, a malicious nature, jealousy, inability to serve one's parents-in-law, gluttony, and incompetence—because these hardships stem from childlessness, they are specifically cited as the afflictions of women.
The contemplative understanding of this is found below. △ Second, the practice.
One pays homage and makes offerings to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
△ Third, regarding meritorious deeds:
one will then give birth to a son endowed with merit and wisdom.
Regarding "merit and so forth," this clarifies that among the hundred practices of a noble person, wisdom occupies the foremost place.

If one possesses only wisdom but lacks merit, then one’s status will be low and one’s wealth meager, meeting with obstacles and pitfalls at every turn. When wisdom and merit are combined, they mutually support and manifest one another:
through merit, one’s wealth and rank rise high; through wisdom, one’s reputation becomes vast and far-reaching. Therefore, it is said that "merit and wisdom are produced."
This refers to the man. △ Second, seeking a wife, in two parts: first, establishing the vow.
If one wishes to seek a wife, the text for seeking a wife clarifies only the vows and virtuous deeds, and does not clarify the practice; the practice is identical to that of prostration.
Therefore, since vows and merit differ, they must be discussed separately. II. Merit and Action:
She immediately gave birth to a daughter of upright appearance and auspicious marks, who had planted roots of virtue in past lives and was loved and respected by all.

Physical beauty is the foremost of the seven virtues of a woman; yet, if one possesses beauty without the auspicious marks (*lakṣaṇa*), she may become orphaned early or widowed in youth, as her fortune and merit are not favorable.
Now, when appearance and marks support one another, their virtues are made even more manifest.
Beauty brings forth favor and love, while the marks bring forth honor and respect for one's fortune. Therefore, the text says: "The multitude loves and respects her," as explained above.
If one seeks a son, a son endowed with merit and wisdom shall be born; if one seeks a daughter, a daughter of upright appearance shall be born.
This is because the holy power of Avalokiteśvara is so great that there is nothing it does not bestow, enabling those who possessed merit and wisdom in previous lives to take rebirth.
Even if one did not plant roots of goodness in former lives, this power can still cause them to cultivate merit within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

This meaning is derived from the *Antarābhava-sūtra*. Regarding the contemplation and understanding of male and female, there are two parts. First, clarifying those who seek male and female as a result of karmic retribution:
as the *Āgama-sūtra* states, from the realm of hell up to the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all suffer the pain of childlessness;
by prostrating and making prayers, one’s heart’s desires can be fulfilled. Second, clarifying the cultivation of causes regarding males.
Regarding the "female," first is the Dharma-gate of Discernment, followed by the Dharma-gate of Bestowing Vows. Ignorance is the father and craving is the mother;
the six sense-faculties are the males and the six sense-objects are the females, with consciousness acting as the matchmaker to give birth to the countless descendants of afflictions.
These males and females do not need to labor through vows or seeking; they spontaneously form a kinship. If one proceeds from the perspective of the Buddha...
The King’s teachings give birth to all Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Buddhas;
skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) is their father, and the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is their mother. There are no Great Teachers who are not born from these.

Furthermore, compassion (*karuṇā*) is their daughter, and the virtuous mind is their son; or, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and its subtle stillness are the daughter, while discerning insight (*vipaśyanā*) is the son.
The male represents those of the Two Vehicles who possess much concentration and little wisdom, while the Bodhisattva possesses little concentration and much wisdom.

Here, worldly men and women are borrowed to symbolize the Dharma-gates: although concentration is stillness and wisdom is illumination—thus forming two parts—they are not separate from the *dharmatā*.
To speak of concentration is already to have wisdom; to speak of wisdom is already to have concentration. It is like a woman having a left hand, or likewise a man.

Just as a son possesses both his right hand and wisdom, so it is here: great compassion is endowed with the wisdom of correct contemplation, and through meditative concentration, it is designated as the "Middle Way" and the "Knowledge of All Modes.
Great compassion is established through meditative concentration, yet it is characterized by wisdom. How could this be merely a matter of principle?
The present text is likewise so; as the text says, "a son of merit and wisdom is born," these words inherently encompass both.
Regarding these two dharma-gates, why trouble yourself with doubt by referring to them as "men"? The text says: "One immediately gives birth to a beautiful girl of auspicious marks.

Beauty implies the absence of depravity and ugliness; this represents the Middle Way and Right Contemplation, which is free from the ugliness of the two extremes—this is the meaning of *prajñā* (wisdom).
"Marks" refers to the thirty-two marks produced by the cultivation of a compassionate mind; this represents the meaning of *samādhi* (concentration). Although...

Since one is called "woman" despite possessing both [qualities], we know that if this passage is interpreted as having two aspects—male and female—it expresses that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are non-dual yet dual;
if it is interpreted as being non-dual, it expresses that concentration and wisdom are dual yet non-dual.
In reality, they are neither dual nor non-dual; appearing as dual or non-dual in accordance with conditions is precisely what expresses the dharma-gate of duality.
The meaning of the text lies herein. Next, we clarify "fulfilling vows," which refers to fulfilling vows in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.

Fulfillment through karmic retribution has been explained previously. Regarding fulfillment through the cultivation of causes: if we discuss the practice of the five precepts, not killing is benevolence (*ren*) and not stealing is integrity (*lian*);
these two belong to the female principle and represent the dharma of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Not speaking falsely is sincerity and straightforwardness (*zhizhi*).
Abstaining from sexual misconduct is being virtuous; abstaining from intoxicants is being free from delusion and depravity. These three pertain to men and manifest the dharma of wisdom.
If one does not obtain these five precepts, both men and women will lose the paths of humans and devas, falling into poverty, solitude, and the three miserable realms.
If one takes refuge and seeks salvation, and the five precepts remain unimpaired, then the wishes of both men and women will be fulfilled. [The same applies to] the ten wholesome actions.

False speech is subsumed under the four [precepts] of the mouth; intoxicants are the three [precepts] of the mind, both belonging to wisdom and pertaining to the male body—these three examples can be understood as explained in the discourse on the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*).
If one discusses them in terms of cultivating worldly meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), each of the four dhyānas and four concentrations has its own cultivation and realization.
To take the first dhyāna as an example: five factors constitute the cultivation, and five limbs constitute the realization. Among these five factors, there are desire (*chanda*) and effort (*vīrya*).
Advancing in skillful wisdom, these three skillful means are distinguished as follows: mindfulness and one-pointedness of mind constitute the male;

within the five factors [of dhyāna], the three factors of vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), and prīti (joy) constitute the male; the two factors of sukha (bliss) and citta-ekāgratā (one-pointedness of mind) constitute the female.

Next, to clarify the male and female aspects of the śrāvaka, among the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthiti-citta*), the use of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) serves to counteract hatred, while the use of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) serves to counteract distraction; these two [are the male].

Those belonging to concentration are female: they employ the contemplation of impurity to treat greed, dependent origination to treat delusion, and mindfulness of the Buddha to treat obstacles to the Path;

these three belong to wisdom and are male. If one does not obtain these "male" and "female" [faculties], one will immediately fall into the state of an ordinary person and be burned and harmed by the house on fire.
If one is graced by the descent of the response [of the Buddhas], the male and female of the five *sthāpanā-cittas* arise, and one immediately attains entry into the Truth.
One no longer fears the twenty-five states of existence. Next, to clarify the male and female Pratyekabuddhas:

when first cultivating the signs of the seeds of merit, if one gives rise to the contemplation of compassion through the path of skillful means, it is called the "female" contemplation; if one gives rise to the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination through wisdom, it is the "male.
Once these male and female [contemplations] are attained, one transcends the triple world, and all that is sought and wished for is fulfilled with tranquility.

Next, regarding the Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) who are male and female: those who possess compassion (*karuṇā*) yet do not sever their afflictions (*kleśa*), remaining within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to benefit sentient beings, are called "female" [Bodhisattvas].

Those who practice the Six Perfections through skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are called "male. Furthermore, those who transform people before them must also cultivate the Six Perfections.
If a person previously cultivated five of the perfections, they are born as a female; if they previously cultivated [all six], they are born as a male.
Wisdom is the birth of a son; if the meanings of wisdom and concentration are not established as male and female respectively, then the bodhisattva practice cannot be established.
Therefore, by seeking Avalokiteśvara, one’s vows are fulfilled. Next, regarding the male and female aspects of Bodhisattvas in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao):

since the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching have severed the afflictions, they possess the wisdom of severance and the wisdom that contemplates the principle of the Truths (satya); this constitutes the "male" aspect. As for the "female" aspect, it supports [the former].
Those with residual habits who enter the triple world are called "women"; if they do not seek and pray to Avalokiteśvara, their vows will not be fulfilled.
Next, to clarify the male and female bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*):

Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Ten Faiths (*shixin*) who cultivate the adornment of merit and virtue through the five *pāramitās* are "women," while those from the first and second grounds who possess the adornment of wisdom are "men" at the stage of the Ten Abidings (*shizhu*).
The ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*) and the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*)—these thirty mental states are called the place where male and female unite.

In the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), the Middle Way and correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) are developed; this is called the birth of a male. The mind of unconditional compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*) is developed; this is called the birth of a female.
These two essentials are attained for the first time in the first stage; they are also called the simultaneous birth of male and female, and these are the male and female born therein.
Because one gives rise to great joy, it is called the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Next, regarding the male and female of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*):
by means of unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*), one plants the karma for the thirty-two marks; this is also called "female. This female is upright and possesses these marks.
Taking the wisdom of the Middle Way as "male," this male is straightforward and possesses merit. Through the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) become pure.

This is called "Abiding in the Womb. At the initial stage of abiding in compassion and wisdom, sons and daughters are born together; that is, the two desires for both male and female are fully satisfied.
Furthermore, from the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths up to the sixth heaven, there is no fixed dhyāna (meditative concentration).
All stages are exclusively the dharmas of scattered-mind wisdom; because they possess wisdom without concentration, they are like "mad men. [In contrast,] the various [stages of] the four dhyānas...
Since the "limbs" (aṅga) correspond to concentration and wisdom, they are called "male and female," signifying the fullness of both merit and wisdom.

Furthermore, within the three dhyānas, concentration and wisdom lack the functional utility of "movement" and "emergence. Why is this? Because the male lacks the power to destroy delusions, while the female lacks the strength to give rise to and produce the outflow-free (anāsrava) state;
these are the "male and female" that are functionally useless. [This applies] from the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha stages through the Shared Teaching Bodhisattva...

If wisdom possesses the function of severing delusions and concentration possesses the virtue of generating the outflow-free (anāsrava), then these are men and women who are effective in accomplishing the essential task.
Yet, if these men and women are separated—meaning that wisdom lacks the function of being "effective"—one cannot destroy ignorance and see the Buddha-nature;
though one may be male, one is effectively female. Likewise, if concentration lacks the capacity to "conceive," one cannot give birth to the child of the Middle Way.
It is like a barren woman; although she is a woman, she is male because she lacks the capacity for birth.

Thus, the Great Sūtra states that those of the Two Vehicles possess fixed concentration but little wisdom, and thus do not see the Buddha-nature. Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching possess much wisdom but little concentration, and they too do not see the Buddha-nature.
Only when those of the Distinct Teaching reach the first stage (*bhūmi*) does true, luminous wisdom arise and unconditioned great compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*) be perfected; this is...

This is called the true and correct state where, upon attaining the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching and perceiving the Middle Way, one is endowed with both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and the characteristics of both male and female are fully perfected;

only then does one accord with the scriptural text. Since the male represents merit and virtue while the female represents physical excellence, we know that these worldly matters are used to symbolize the Dharma, and their meaning is as profound and vast as this.
If one were to restrict it merely to worldly affairs of seeking a son or a daughter, [the significance would be lost].
Thus, it is not that the tenfold benefits of Avalokiteśvara’s salvific power are not manifest, pervasive, and universal. Fearing excessive prolixity, I have recorded them here in full;
may all who read this take care to reflect upon them. △ Second, the conclusion that [the benefits] are not in vain.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Infinite Intent possesses such power (up to) that merit is not in vain.
If there is one who prostrates, their merit is not in vain. This concludes the discussion on the conditions for the formation of bodily karma; it also serves the purpose of resolving doubts.
To explain how this conclusion resolves doubts: if one says that the fulfillment of vows comes through prostration itself, then prostration is already present [as a cause].
If one does not receive the fulfillment of their vows, how can it be said that [the practice] is not in vain? "In vain" (*táng*) means empty; "vainly discarded" (*tuánjiān*) means abandoned.
Because the mind lacks resolve, the vow remains unfulfilled; yet the merit of prostration is secretly sustained and not lost. This is the resolution of the doubt.
△ Third, the exhortation to uphold the Name, which has three parts: first, the exhortation to uphold.
Therefore, all sentient beings should receive and uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

Previously, the causes and conditions for Avalokiteśvara’s receiving his name were explained; since his power is vast and great, and neither his physical form nor substance was analyzed, but rather his name was recounted and his virtues discussed, those who wish to take refuge in and honor him should reverently uphold his name. Thus, the exhortation is made by citing the upholding of the name.
△ 2. Evaluation.
If there is anyone, Akṣayamati, who upholds [this teaching]—[up to] it cannot be exhausted even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
Sixty-two billion [beings] are cited for the abundance of their field of merit; "as long as life lasts" is cited for the abundance of the duration; the four requisites are fully provided.
"Offering many seeds and reciting many names"—these four "many" instances are cited as the basis for comparison.
"What do you think? is the question; "The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati replied" introduces the answer. "If there were another person...
begins the formal comparison. Within this formal comparison, four "few" instances are again cited to compare with the four "many" merits.
The Virtuous One asked with perfect equanimity, "With what intention do you bring the few to the many? The Buddha replied, "When measured by the Buddha-eye, there is neither increase nor decrease;
the fourfold layers of merit are perfectly equal. When weighed according to this standard, there is not even a hair's breadth of error.

This is because the nature of 'one' and 'many' cannot be apprehended; they lack dual characteristics. That which is one is not one, and that which is many is not many; they both enter into the same reality."
It is like the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and the true mark (dharmatā), perfectly equal and without difference. △ Third, the concluding praise:
"Ajita, by receiving and upholding [this], Avalokiteśvara... one shall obtain such immeasurable and boundless benefits of merit."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the merit of reciting the name even for a single moment is inexhaustible; it says that if one scatters a single flower into the air, its merit will not be exhausted until the end of suffering (*niṣṭhā-duḥkha*).
The *Yìshùjì* (Commentary on the Meaning) explains: "Offering a single flower to the Buddha is used as an analogy for the act of holding the name of Avalokiteśvara for a single moment.
'Until the end of suffering' refers to the exhaustion of the two deaths [birth and death]. This implies that the merit of scattering flowers to become a Buddha is still [inexhaustible]."
Not finished. △ Second Round of Question and Answer, Part One: The Initial Question, Section Three: The First Question Concerning the Body.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... how does he travel through this Sahā world?"

The previous question asked: "By what cause is the name 'Buddha' obtained? The answer was: "When the three karmas of sentient beings manifest as the capacity for awakening (the objective condition), the spiritual wisdom of the Dharma-body responds mysteriously to that object.
Due to these causes and conditions between object and wisdom, he is named Avalokiteśvara. This meaning is now concluded. The current question asks:
"How does he roam this Sahā world? The Buddha answers: "By means of the Universal Gate, he manifests his three karmas to respond to sentient beings."
"How does one move within the profound mechanism of arising? asks regarding the body-karma (*kāyakarman*). "How does one speak?

asks regarding the mouth-karma (*vākkarman*). "What are the skillful means? asks regarding the mind-karma (*manaskarman*). These are the three karmas of the Sage, which respond universally to all things without deliberation;
they are also called the "inconceivable transformations of the three wheels. The *Yishu ji* (Record of the Commentary) states: "Sentient beings invoke the Name, constantly mindful of it..."

Because the three karmas of body, speech, and mind are manifested in prostration, it is called "manifesting the capacity. The spiritual wisdom of the Dharmakāya is the true body formed by the union of the two types of awakening—the original and the initial.
Because this wisdom responds in secret to uproot suffering, it is called "secret response.

Now, the following questions clarify the meaning of Avalokiteśvara’s mental karma in discerning capacities, his physical karma in manifesting forms, and his verbal karma in preaching the Dharma, so as to cause [beings to attain liberation].
Because sentient beings perceive through cognition and see through hearing, it is called "manifest response" (*xiansheng*);

yet, because the characteristics of the three karmas practiced by sentient beings are not explicitly described, this arises from past goodness lying latent within the heart, thereby enabling such an evocation, and is thus called "latent capacity" (*mingji*).
△ 2. Question concerning speech:
How does one preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?
△ 3. Question concerning mind:
What is the nature of the power of skillful means (*upāya*)?
The *Yishu ji* states: "The meaning of the question regarding skillful means does not refer to the skillful means for apprehending principle prior to the Path;
rather, it refers precisely to the skillful means for discerning the capacities [of beings] subsequent to realization. △ Second, the answer, in three parts: first, the specific answer.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati (up to the point where he) immediately manifested the body of a Buddha and preached the Dharma for him.
This is a specific answer that returns to the three questions. The phrase "should employ" is the answer to the question regarding the power of his skillful means and his mental karma (*manas-karma*).
How is this known to be so? It is because the mental ground observes the capacities of beings and perceives what is appropriate; it is to show what is suitable for them.
Since one should preach whatever Dharma is appropriate to transform beings accordingly, it is known that this is the intended meaning of the response.

Manifesting the body is the answer regarding bodily action (*kāyakarma*), and preaching the Dharma is the answer regarding verbal action (*vākkarma*); thus, this constitutes a complete answer to the three questions.

Within these individual answers, thirty-three bodies are manifested and nineteen [instances of] preaching the Dharma are shown; when condensed, these constitute ten realms of bodies, though one is missing.
Regarding the Bodhisattvas in the two realms of hell: logically, Bodhisattvas ought to exist there; however, the text is merely abbreviated.

Although there is no separate answer for the hell realm as a whole, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) section states: "They travel through various lands in manifold forms. How can it be said that they do not exist there?
Regarding the thirty-three bodies, the text is divided into eight sections: first, the noble body (*āryakāya*); second, the celestial body (*devakāya*).
Regarding the bodies of the three [kinds of] persons, the fourfold assembly, the five kinds of women, the six types of children, the seven classes of beings, and the eight vajra-bodies:
among these sacred bodies, first to clarify the Buddha-body—does this refer to the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) or the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body)?
It is because the Sage, in responding to sentient beings, possesses both meanings; if he appears suddenly at one time, it is as an emanation (*nirmāṇa*).

The names for the beginning and the end should likewise be consistent; thus, the Buddha has two aspects: first, the Superior Response-body (*abhisambodhi-nirmāṇakāya*), and second, the Inferior Response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇakāya*).

The Superior Response-body responds to those with the capacities of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings, while the Inferior Response-body is directed toward the multitudes of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings.

If one responds within the Real Reward Land (*samyag-vipāka-kṣetra*), one manifests only the Superior Response-body, its marks of perfection like an ocean and its radiance immeasurable, as taught in the forty-first stage.
Regarding the Dharma of the true, ultimate, and correct reality, all these bodhisattvas have already entered the stages (*bhūmi*) accordingly;

they cannot manifest in the bodies of other realms, nor can they manifest in the bodies of other Buddhas. If they manifest in a land of skillful means and are able to cultivate Madhyamaka to subdue ignorance, their vision of marks is superior;
however, if they remain within the two [coarse] observations and have not yet subdued ignorance, [their vision is inferior].
Those who perceive [the Buddha] through marks see him as inferior; yet though the marks may be superior or inferior, they are but one single *rūpakāya*.

Therefore, it is not a "combined body" (*saṃbhogakāya*), but merely a teaching of two types of Mahāyāna dharma: the sequential and the non-sequential. Consequently, there is no need for other bodies or other methods of transformation.
Whether responding to those in the realm where ordinary beings and sages dwell—also called the realm of purity and impurity coexisting—it refers to the Pure Land.
This is because in each defiled land, ordinary beings and sages dwell together. Within these defiled lands, there are two types of capacities: the great and the small.
For those of small capacity, he manifests the body of a Buddha of the Tripitaka and teaches the gradual Dharma; this is called the "inferior response.
For those of great capacity, he manifests the body of Śākyamuni (Sāṃbhogakāya) and teaches the sudden Dharma; this is called the "superior response. Thus it is said of the defiled lands.

Since the [Saha] world is thus, the Pure Land is likewise. Since there are two types of capacities—the sharp and the dull—how could one not employ both the sudden and gradual teachings to clarify the manifestation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and its preaching of the Dharma?
Question: The sutra only mentions wandering through the Sahā world; it does not mention the Real Reward (*vipākaphala*) or Expedient Means (*upāya*) lands.
Answer: In the general response, it says "wandering through all lands. The word "all" refers to the fact that they are not one and the same.
How could this teaching pertain solely to the Sahā world? Furthermore, as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya* Sūtra:
"If one can deeply contemplate and see me on Vulture Peak together with the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas," this very Sahā world is thus a skillful means (*upāya*).
The sūtra further states: "One also sees the Sahā world, its ground made of lapis lazuli, and so forth, all completely composed of jewels."

The assembly of bodhisattvas all dwell therein; since it is said that they see [the Pure Land] again, it cannot be the same location as before. Furthermore, it is stated that there are "exclusively bodhisattvas, with no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
From this, one can verify that the Sahā world is itself the land of true recompense (*sambhoga-kṣetra*).

These passages all pertain to the four kinds of faith (the present fourfold faith). Through wondrous contemplation, one perceives these two lands within the Saha world—this is the vision of Avalokiteśvara.
How could one of profound wisdom wandering in the Sahā world allow for himself alone to dwell in this defiled land?
To those who are to be saved by the body of a pratyekabuddha, he manifests the body of a pratyekabuddha and preaches the Dharma for them.
This is like Mañjuśrī, who for twenty trillion kalpas acted as a pratyekabuddha to transform sentient beings, manifesting his body to preach the Dharma.
To those who should be delivered by means of the body of a śrāvaka, he manifests the body of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.

Sometimes he manifests as a Śrāvaka of the *Āgama* or *Vaipulya* teachings, or as a Śrāvaka who transforms according to the five flavors, secretly concealing his inner realization while appearing outwardly to guide sentient beings.
To those who are to be saved by the body of a Brahmā King, he immediately manifests as a Brahmā King and preaches the Dharma for them.
The Brahma King is the Lord of the Heaven of Form (Rūpadhātu); his name is Śikhin, which here is translated as "Topknot and Necklace.
The *Śrī-mālā-sūtra* clarifies that each of the four dhyānas has its own king. This mention of "Brahma" likely refers to the summit of the first dhyāna;

because he still possesses vitarka and vicāra (applied and sustained thought), he is able to serve as the lord of a trichiliocosm. This is to say that Avalokiteśvara cultivated the White-Colored Samādhi.

Because he neither grasps nor abandons what is not to be grasped, he is not reborn through the power of dhyāna; because he does not abandon [sentient beings], he should expound the discourse on transcending desire for the sake of the Brahma King, using skillful means to lead them toward the ultimate reality.
To those who should be delivered by the body of Śakra, he manifests the body of Śakra and preaches the Dharma for them.
Śakra is the Lord of the Earth-dwelling Devas; his full name is Śakradevendra.
"Śakra" means "able," "deva" means "heaven," and "indra" means "lord.
Because he is able to act as the Lord of Heaven, he is now referred to by the abbreviated title "Diśì" (Śakra). The Bodhisattva cultivates the white samādhi.
Neither grasping nor abandoning, he expounds various superior discourses to lead [beings] from the provisional to the ultimate.
To those who should be saved by the body of Maheśvara, he manifests the body of Maheśvara and preaches the Dharma for them.
Īśvara is the summit of the desire realm; in Sanskrit he is called Vaśavartin, which translates as "Mastery over Others' Transformations.
By utilizing the transformations wrought by others to achieve his own pleasure, he is none other than the Māra King. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:
"Mostly these are Bodhisattvas of inconceivable liberation who dwell in the Crimson Samādhi; neither grasping nor rejecting, they should manifest as Māras."
The King commanded that the realms of all māras are themselves the realm of the Buddha;

furthermore, he manifested various bodies below to demonstrate that all are bodhisattvas dwelling in samādhi, using these skillful means to lead toward the ultimate reality—let it be known by this analogy.
For those who are to be delivered by means of the body of Maheśvara, [the Buddha] preaches the Dharma to them.
Maheśvara is Mahesvara at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*); the *Loutan jing* (Kāraṇḍavyūha-sūtra) calls him Akaniṣṭha, while the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* refers to him as Akaniṣṭha;
the commentary states that Maheśvara is translated here as "Great" (*Mahā*).
He rides freely upon a white ox, possesses eight arms and three eyes; these celestial generals do not yet know that he is of the same name as they.
Pointing directly to this deity as their general, he preaches the Dharma to those who are to be saved by means of the body of a Great Celestial General.
In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Saṃjñeya is designated as the Great General. This great scripture states that among the eight *kṣatriya* gods, he is a powerful warrior;
he is also called Kumāra, which means "Boy," who rides upon a peacock, holds a rooster, carries a rattle-drum (*ghaṇṭā*), and grasps a red banner.
Furthermore, Viṣṇu—translated as "Pervasive Hearing"—has four arms, holding a conch shell and a discus, and rides upon a golden-winged bird (*garuḍa*).
These are all great generals of the devas.
To those who should be liberated by means of the body of Vaiśravaṇa, he manifests the body of Vaiśravaṇa and preaches the Dharma for them. "Vaiśravaṇa" is translated here as "Much-Hearing" (Duowen);
the *Suo-yin* [commentary] states that it is called so because his fame for merit and virtue is heard in the four directions. Thus says the sub-commentary (*shu*).
The *Bushi yishu ji* (Notes on the Commentary on the Meaning) states that the explanation for Vaiśravaṇa is missing because he is visible.
Those who are to be saved by the body of a minor king (*kṣudrarāja*) are immediately manifested as a minor king and taught the Dharma.

Some say that the Heavenly Kings (Devarāja) are the great and the Human Kings (Manuṣyarāja) are the small; yet among human kings themselves, there are four types of Wheel-turning Kings (Cakravartin)—of gold, silver, copper, and iron—who naturally have their own degrees of greatness and smallness.
Those who are not among these four types of Wheel-turning Kings are called "Scattered Grain" (Khaṇḍaka) Kings, who likewise have their own degrees of greatness and smallness.

When viewed in successive succession, those of the central kingdom are called "great," while the subordinate vassals are called "small"; it is in this sense of relative comparison that they are now referred to as "small."
If one performs even minor acts for their sake, how much more so for great ones?
To those who are to be saved by the body of a householder (*gṛhapati*), he immediately manifests the body of a householder and preaches the Dharma for them.
Because they possess the virtues of a householder, they are called "householders. The *Daben shu* (Great Commentary) states: "A householder of the world is fully..."
There are ten virtues that accord with ten kinds of merit, as explained in the "Parable" chapter.
To those who are to be liberated by means of the body of a householder, he manifests in the body of a householder and preaches the Dharma for them.
Accumulating vast wealth and possessing abundant property, yet dwelling in the Way through these means, he is thus named.
To those who are to be delivered by the form of a high official, he manifests as a high official and preaches the Dharma for them.

"Minister" (*zhài*) carries the meaning of "principle," while "official" (*guān*) carries the meaning of "function. This means that the Three Dukes, by virtue of their function, are able to assist the ruler in governing;
thus they are called "ministerial officials. Districts and counties are also referred to as "ministerial offices" because those in charge are able to govern the people below them.
To those who are to be liberated by means of a Brahmin body, he immediately manifests in the form of a Brahmin and preaches the Dharma for them.

"Brahmin" (婆羅門) is here translated as "Pure Conduct" (淨行). Because they were the first lineage at the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*) and lived in seclusion among the mountains and wilds, people called them "of Pure Conduct.
Alternatively, they are named "Brahmacārin" (梵志), which is the same.
One should preach the Dharma by manifesting the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās;
this has already been explained as before.
One should preach the Dharma by manifesting the bodies of elders, lay devotees, and officials, even manifesting the body of a woman.
As for the women of the minor kings, because they were confined within the royal palace and forbidden from wandering about, it was difficult to transform them;
therefore, [the text] does not mention it. If it were like the case of Gadgadasvara, it would simply state that he transformed himself into the form of a woman within the king's harem.
Those who are to be delivered by means of a young boy or a young girl [should be taught] and for them he preaches the Dharma.
As for these young boys and girls, they include the two sons of King Subhavyūha, Śreṣṭha and Puṣyaśrī,
as well as the children playing with sand and counting beads, and others like them.
He should manifest as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth, up to [the various forms mentioned], and preach the Dharma to them.
As seen in the Introduction Chapter,
he manifests as the Vajrapāṇi deity for those who are to be saved by the Vajrapāṇi deity, and preaches the Dharma to them.
Regarding the Sanskrit name Vajrapāṇi: *vajra* means "diamond" (or "thunderbolt") and *pāṇi* means "hand.
Thus, he is named for holding a vajra in his hand. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"In the past, there was a king whose queen gave birth to a thousand sons. Desiring to test the order in which they would attain Buddhahood in the future, [the Buddha] K Krakucchanda..."
The Buddha drew the first tally, and so on until Loushi (Lokiteśvara) drew the thousandth tally. Second, the second wife gave birth to two sons:
one vowed to become a Brahmā King and invite his elder brother to preach the Dharma; the other vowed to become a Vajra Protector and guard his elder brother’s teachings.
△ Second, the general response.
"Akṣayamati, this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara... travels through various lands to deliver sentient beings.
The phrase "accomplishing such meritorious virtues" constitutes the specific answer to the preceding question. The statement "travels through various lands in various forms" is the general answer.
His manifold names are not uniform: horizontally, they pervade the ten directions; vertically, they encompass all time.
The three lands manifest according to conditions; how could the manifestation of thirty-three bodies through transformation and response be limited merely to the Sahā world?
By means of various forms, it generally clarifies the manifestation of the body; by traveling extensively through all lands, it generally clarifies the places where beings are transformed;

and by extensively delivering and liberating sentient beings, it generally clarifies those who receive benefit. Although these words are brief compared to what precedes them, they encompass the full scope.
Since the meaning is broader than what preceded, it is called a "comprehensive answer. Miaole states: Question: This sutra reconciles the three vehicles;

why then does it say, "One should [teach] by means of the three vehicles," and so forth? Answer: Because while their forms differ, the Dharma is one. Thus, the *Myōon-hin* (Chapter on the Wonderful Sound) says:
"The various transformations through which this sutra is preached are not seen by people; those who claim it teaches the three vehicles are in error. Question:

Why is it that in the "Chapter on the Exquisite Voice" (Ghoṣadatta-parivarta), the four vehicles (*catur-yāna*) appear at the end, whereas in the "Universal Gate Chapter" (Samantamukha-parivarta), the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*) appear at the beginning?
Furthermore, there is no mention of a bodhisattva providing the response; in general, there is nothing that is not a bodhisattva, yet for specific purposes, they must manifest distinct forms.

This is merely a matter of textual abbreviation. Moreover, as for the thirty-three bodies, they respond immediately according to the needs of those who perceive them—how could there be any sequence? It is simply a difference between these two texts.

In the individual answers, the text is extensive while the meaning is narrow; "extensive text" refers to the separation of many phrases, whereas "narrow meaning" refers to manifesting only thirty-three bodies.
In the general answer, the text is narrow while the meaning is broad;
"narrow text" refers to using only twelve characters such as "various" (zhongzhong), while "broad meaning" implies that since it says "various," what could it not encompass?
△ Third, the exhortation to make offerings, in two parts. First, the formal exhortation:
"Therefore, you all should with one mind... (up to) "...all shall be called 'Bestowers of Fearlessness'.

The Buddha’s response to the previous question proceeds from the general to the specific; at the end, he exhorts [the assembly] to receive and uphold [this teaching], because sentient beings look up to and rely upon it.

The true body (*dharmakāya*) of the Bodhisattva benefits beings secretly and can only be sustained by upholding its name and maintaining its characters; therefore, it exhorts one to receive and uphold it.
In answering the latter part of the question, the Buddha first treats the specific cases and then the general principle.

Finally, he exhorts them to make offerings because sentient beings have already received the manifest benefits of the Bodhisattva’s three karmas—seeing his form and hearing his voice—and thus he exhorts them to make offerings. Therefore, as for "you all," etc., [the text] first...

To praise [the name] is also to express the intent of making offerings to Avalokiteśvara; it is precisely because he can bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings that he receives his name from this virtue.
Sentient beings are liberated from their fears, and for this reason, this name was established.

If one examines the fourteen kinds of merit of fearlessness clarified in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, they consist of rescuing from the seven calamities, responding to the two requests, and escaping the three poisons.

Regarding the bestowal of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*), since this chapter follows the second round of question and answer, it clarifies that the bestowal of fearlessness appears to consist in manifesting one's body and preaching the Dharma.

However, according to the text stating that "one can bestow fearlessness amidst terrors and urgent calamities," it may also comprehensively encompass the preceding rounds of question and answer; thus, it is both real and responsive.
Both bodies are capable of bestowing both hidden and manifest benefits, and both attain fearlessness. △ Second, receiving the command, in six parts:
first, accepting the mandate.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: ... "O Benevolent One, please accept this precious necklace as a gift of Dharma."
Regarding "various jewels" (*nānā-ratna*) and so forth: it means that various jewels interspersed with pearls together constitute the adornment.

If one follows the *Sūtra of the Necklaces* (*Yingluo jing*), there are necklaces of copper-jewels from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the necklaces of *maṇi*-jewels at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Since the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati has now entered a high stage, his necklaces ought to be made of priceless jewels; how could they be worth only a hundred thousand taels?
The Golden One replied: "The mention of 'hundreds of thousands' is a brief citation of a large number, similar to how one speaks of 'the common people' or 'the myriad subjects';
how could it be restricted merely to one hundred ten thousand? If we distinguish them by their status as *ratna-avalambana* (necklaces), they must be priceless.

If we approach this from the perspective of contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*), using phenomena to manifest principle—how can one interpret this solely as a literal matter? 'Neck' (*jing*) symbolizes the single reality of the Middle Way."
The principle is adorned with numerous non-attached dharma-gates, like a necklace upon the neck;

"loosening" (*jie*) signifies that the Bodhisattva practices constant relinquishment, for they do not dwell in nor cling to any merit of vows and practices, up to and including Buddha-wisdom, bodhi, and nirvana—hence it is called "loosening.
"Hundred thousand" (*baiqian*) refers to one hundred thousand; this symbolizes...
The first bhūmi possesses ten thousand merits; the tenth bhūmi thus possesses one hundred thousand. As for the giving of Dharma (*dharmadāna*), it is the giving according to the Dharma.
It is precisely because wealth penetrates the Dharma that wealth is called "Dharma-wealth.

This Dharma-wealth is the dharmas produced by causes and conditions, which are simultaneously emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—these three truths complete within a single mind. What is equal regarding the Dharma is also equal regarding wealth.
Giving in this manner is itself the gift of Dharma. △ Second, not accepting.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was unwilling to accept it.
As for his unwillingness to accept: "I have not yet received the command to receive offerings from Akṣayamati; why do you suddenly accept them on your own authority?"

Furthermore, this matter requires humility and deference; if one considers it from the perspective of contemplative understanding, because the vast function of samādhi is not received, there is nothing to receive. △ Third, the repetition:
Ajita (Endless Meaning) again addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying... [up to] ...accepting these necklaces.
Again, he said: "Those who take pity on me may do so because they request that the superior show compassion to the inferior; or perhaps because our status is equal and thus we pity one another;
or perhaps because I act for the sake of the fourfold assembly, and you, out of benevolence toward the fourfold assembly, accept [my offering].
You accept these various receptions by means of non-reception. △ Fourth, the Buddha’s exhortation.
At that time, the Buddha said to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva... [omitted] ...therefore he accepted this necklace from humans, non-humans, and others.
The Buddha’s exhortation to have compassion means to have compassion for all sentient beings as well as the fourfold assembly.
It is precisely because the Bodhisattva acts for the sake of beings that he gives for the sake of beings and accepts for the sake of beings. △ Five: Acceptance.
At that moment, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly... [up to] ...offered one portion to the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
The two portions symbolize the two causes of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*); by offering them to the two Buddhas, he intends to lead these two causes toward their two fruits.
The *Yi-shu-ji* states: "With a single necklace..."
The "two parts" signify that within a single line, two causes must necessarily be present: in principle, they are the direct cause (*hetu*); in fact, they are the contributing condition (*pratyaya*).
The non-duality of principle and fact is termed the "wondrous cause," which is capable of producing the fruits of the *dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya*.

As for not discussing the *nirmāṇakāya*, it is because when the person attains the fruit, the two bodies—the *dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya*—are collectively manifested; once these are established, the functional application (*nirmāṇakāya*) arises spontaneously. △ Six: General Summary.
[The section on] "The Vows" [ends]. From "The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Inexhaustible Intent" up to "wandering in the Sahā world"—
this refers to the manifestation of the thirty-three bodies through the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*) to preach the Dharma by means of such sovereign spiritual powers.
...also. △ Second, the verse summary, in three parts: first, the double verse summary of the two questions; second, the initial praise of virtues.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati asked in verse:

The *Yishu* (Commentary) and *Ji* (Record) state that regarding the verses repeated at the end of the text, Master Kumārajīva did not translate them; all masters maintain that they were present in the Sanskrit original.
The Venerable Jingxi said, "This also does not fathom Master Kumārajīva’s profound intent. The *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* states that this verse was translated by Jñānagupta;
since this verse had not yet circulated when Zhiyi appeared, there was nothing [Zhiyi] could have explained.

Furthermore, Jingxi also cited the passage from the *Fuxing ji* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) stating, "It returns and attaches itself to the original person"; thus we know [this to be the case].

There is no contradiction in providing a detailed commentary; furthermore, the Dharma Master Shishi of a nearby Indian monastery has divided the text into sections, wherein the two types of question-and-answer correspond to the prose like two halves of a tally.
I shall now briefly explain these verses according to his topical outline.
The World-Honored One is endowed with wondrous marks.
That the World-Honored One possesses these marks is truly due to the adornment of myriad virtues; therefore, to praise his marks is to praise his sublime virtues.
△ Second, the double inquiry, which first contains the two preceding questions.
I now ask him again:

this single line contains the two preceding questions. In the prose section, he first asked about the causes and conditions for obtaining the name, and next asked about the manner of his travels and transformations through the three karmas;
since these are now restated in verse, how could the latter question be omitted? Thus, we know that within this sentence, he asks those two things.
The title also encompasses the subsequent question. △ Second, the separate verses on the first question:
"O Son of the Buddha, by what causes and conditions is he named Avalokiteśvara?
△ Second, the double verses on the two answers. Part one: The sūtra narrator’s account.
The Honored One, endowed with the wondrous marks, answered Ajita in verse.

While the words of the scribe recording the compilation ought to have been stated directly, the fact that they are here in verse may be because the compiler took the opportunity to versify them, or because Kumārajīva translated them into verse;
whether they follow the prose or are interspersed is of no consequence. △ Second, the verses.
The Buddha’s response has two parts; first, he adds a general praise of the practices and vows:
"Listen to the practices of Avalokiteśvara, which respond skillfully to all places... until... they give rise to great pure vows.

The two characters "Listen" (rǔ tīng) command careful attention. Regarding the "practices of Avalokiteśvara," this refers to the contemplation of those beings through the threefold wisdom of the one mind.
Causing immeasurable suffering to be liberated all at once by means of sound is precisely the fulfillment of the practice of benefiting others.
Manifesting forms in the three worlds while remaining unmoving from the true mind is called "skillfully responding" because one appears everywhere as needed; thus it is said, "in all directions.
These two lines collectively praise the two bodies—the True and the Responsive—which have been attained. Next, there is a general discussion of the practices and vows that bring them about. First:

The "Clarifying the Initial Mind" section explains the four universal vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*) in detail; it further demonstrates that one practices throughout immeasurable eons because the vows are profound, and thus one does not regress over such a long duration.
Because the time is so vast, one encounters many Buddhas, and by acting in accordance with each Buddha, one is truly called a "servant of the Buddhas" as one cultivates the practices of all Buddhas.
At each and every Buddha-field, one generates pure vows; these are the subsequent and specific vows.
If it were not so, how could one obtain true wisdom to universally uproot all sufferings, and how could one manifest response-bodies to universally deliver all beings?
II. Specific Verses on the Two-Part Response. A. Verses on the First Response: Explaining the Origin of Avalokiteśvara’s Name.
1. Verses on the General Response.
I shall briefly explain for you that hearing the name, seeing the body, and mindful recollection are not empty or in vain, as they can extinguish all suffering within the realms of existence.
To state the essentials, I say "briefly explained": hearing the name refers to the stimulus of the vocal karma; seeing the body refers to the stimulus of the bodily karma;
and mental recollection is precisely the stimulus of the mental karma. Hearing the name is a response from the unseen realm.
The body is the perfection of both the manifest response and the two types of responsive manifestations; it may also be seen as the body of wondrous wisdom, which is the hidden response.
"All existences" refers to the twenty-five realms of existence. △ Second, the verse provides specific answers to the two [sections];
first, the verse provides answers to the seven difficulties. (12) First, the verse directly addresses the first difficulty: being burned by fire.
Suppose one were to give rise to a harmful intent and push another into a great pit of fire; by the power of mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara, that pit of fire would transform into a pool. Question:

In the prose section, it is said that "to seek liberation from the three poisons, one must constantly mindfully recollect Avalokiteśvara. The commentary (*shū*) states that "constant mindfulness" is the essence of right mindfulness, wherein one realizes that afflictions are themselves the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), being neither an agent nor an object.

Why, then, does this verse say "mindfulness of him"? Answer: [This refers to] the mindfulness directed toward that [Bodhisattva]. It is not that one is mindful of the afflictions themselves as the limit of reality; rather, it is through mindfulness of the Bodhisattva that one attains such realization. Thus, the verse says "mindfulness of him."

Since "Avalokiteśvara" and "that one" are thus distinguished, how could the subject-object duality be forgotten? To answer: the Perfect and Wondrous Teaching cannot be sought through ordinary sentiment;
it appears somewhat contradictory, yet its meaning ultimately converges on a single principle. Now, the text states that this meaning applies to both directions:

if we consider the Buddha’s perspective, taking Avalokiteśvara as "that one," they are distinguished as teacher and disciple; if we consider the perspective of sentient beings who recollect "that one," [the same distinction applies].

Avalokiteśvara, this is a matter of resonance and response that distinguishes between teacher and disciple; yet the subtle teaching that elucidates this resonance is entirely the Dharma-realm, wherein each and every thing is perfectly interfused.
Sentient beings are the resonance within the mind, while those Buddhas respond from within the mind.
Once sentient beings have attained realization, Avalokiteśvara is present through mindfulness; thus, both the one who contemplates and the object of contemplation are themselves the Dharma.
Since the realms have no subject or object, although they are distinguished as "this" and "that," both subject and object are utterly transcended;

therefore, although the verse speaks of "recalling that," it is entirely not in contradiction with the aforementioned right mindfulness. △ Second, the actual verse on the second difficulty of being swept away by water.
Or if drifting upon the vast ocean, amidst the perils of dragons, fish, and various ghosts, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one cannot be submerged by the waves.
△ Third, an added verse on the peril of falling from Mount Sumeru.
Or if one is on the peak of Mount Sumeru and is pushed over by someone, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one will abide in the sky like the sun.
△ Fourth, the verse added regarding the peril of falling from a mountain of diamond.
Or if pursued by evil men and falling down Mount Vajra, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, not even a single hair can be harmed.
△ Fifth, this verse transcends [the previous section] and addresses the seventh difficulty: that of hostile bandits.

Or if one encounters hostile bandits surrounding them, each wielding a blade to inflict harm, by virtue of mindfulness of the power of Avalokiteśvara, they will all immediately give rise to a compassionate heart.
△ Sixth, this is a retrospective verse on the fourth peril: the danger of blades and staves.
Or if one encounters the suffering of royal punishment and faces execution at the end of life, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, the blade shall instantly break into pieces.
△ Seventh, a summary verse on the sixth difficulty: the hardship of shackles and fetters.
Or if one is imprisoned and shackled, with hands and feet bound by cangues and fetters, through the power of that Avalokiteśvara, one shall be released and attain liberation.
△ Eighth: An added verse on the perils of curses and poisonous drugs.
Regarding curses and various poisonous drugs intended to harm one’s body: by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they will return to the person who sent them.
That they return to the sender means that when one employs demonic arts with poisonous drugs to harm another, it is only through the other's own perverse thoughts that they receive the suffering;
if the person maintains right mindfulness, [the curse] returns to the sender. As stated in the *Dṛṣṭāntaparyāya-sūtra*: [text follows].
There was a lay follower who had initially observed the five precepts, but later, as he grew old, he frequently forgot them.
At that time, a thirsty brahmin in the mountains begged him for a drink; being busy with his farming work, the lay follower did not have the leisure to attend to him and departed in resentment.
The brahmin was able to raise corpses and command spirits; he summoned a murderous spirit and commanded it, saying: "He insulted me—go!"
While he was being killed, an arhat in the mountains perceived this and went to the farmer’s house, saying:

"Tonight, light a lamp early; diligently recite the Three Refuges and chant this verse: 'Guard the mouth and do not let the body transgress. Cultivate thoughts of compassion for all sentient beings, and you shall attain peace and security.
The host followed these instructions throughout the night, mindfully reciting the Buddha's name and chanting the precepts; thus, the ghosts and spirits were unable to harm him.

The master ordered him to kill [the Brahmin], and he was about to do so; however, because that Brahmin possessed the virtue of being "unslayable," the law required that the executioner be killed instead.
When the ghost sent by the master became enraged and sought to harm the Brahmin, the latter used his supernatural powers to shield himself so that the ghost could not see him.
Upon realizing the truth of the Way, the Brahmin was saved. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) cites this passage, stating: "This is precisely contemplation (*vipaśyanā*)."
The text of the *Śīla-sūtra* returns to the original wording of the scripture itself. △ Ninth, a retrospective verse on the third peril of rākṣasas:
"If one encounters evil rākṣasas, venomous dragons, various ghosts, and the like, by recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, they shall all dare not cause harm."
△ Tenth Verse: The Difficulty of Being Encircled by Fierce Beasts.
If one is encircled by fierce beasts with terrifying sharp teeth and claws, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they will flee swiftly to the boundless directions.
△ Eleven: Additional Difficulties from Vipers, Snakes, Vipers, and Scorpions.
The poisonous vapors of vipers, snakes, vipers, and scorpions blaze like fire; yet by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they turn back of their own accord upon hearing his voice.
△ Twelfth, the calamity of clouds, thunder, hail, and rain:
When clouds gather and thunder rolls, lightning flashes, and hail falls with torrential rain, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall be dispersed and vanished at that very moment.
Including the introductory verses and the main verses, there are seven difficulties, totaling twelve;

each must be fully explained according to the fruit-retribution, evil karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), the six realms of existence, and the four teachings. As for what they symbolize, it does not exceed six types:
Mount Sumeru and the diamond (*vajra*) belong to the earth element; clouds and thunder belong to water; and beasts, snakes, and curses are all sentient beings.

All these represent the seeds of the Bodhisattva’s causes; having cultivated the distinct and perfect contemplations (*bipāka* and *pariniṣpanna*) regarding these six kinds [of objects] during the causal stage, he now abides at the juncture of the six kinds of reality-as-it-is (*yathābhūta*).
Therefore, throughout the entire Dharma-realm, he rescues all from suffering and affliction. To state the essential point:
all things, both the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*), are the wondrous form and wondrous mind of Avalokiteśvara. All sentient beings, within this sacred form and mind...
Because one's own difficulty and the seeking for rescue through the three karmas are themselves Avalokiteśvara, the conditions are fulfilled and the response is immediate;
therefore, one should contemplate this meaning in every thought-moment. What concern is there that it would not be identical to Avalokiteśvara’s benefiting of sentient beings?
The six elements are earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness. The two [sets of] three poisons and the two seekings.
Sentient beings are trapped in distress, their bodies oppressed by immeasurable suffering; yet through the wondrous power of wisdom, Avalokiteśvara can rescue the world from its pain.
Most sentient beings, within the realms, are afflicted by greed, anger, and false views, as well as the delusions of the three poisons outside those realms;
externally, they lack the retribution-born status of male or female, while internally, they are deficient in meditative concentration and wisdom—thus do they bring about [their own bondage].
The two kinds of birth-and-death and their entanglements are therefore called "immeasurable oppression by suffering.
The preceding prose commentary’s exposition on the three poisons and the two pursuits already encompasses all meanings; this subsequent verse section leaves nothing further unaddressed.
II. The second part: Verses responding to the universal manifestation. A. First, the direct verses on the manifestation. 1. First, the anticipatory verse providing a general response.

Endowed with the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*) and having extensively cultivated the skillful means of wisdom (*prajñopāya*), there is no land in the worlds of the ten directions where he does not manifest his body.
The prose section answers in general terms by stating that he wanders through various lands in diverse forms to deliver sentient beings;

now, the verse discusses the underlying cause for such responsive manifestations: it is through the power of supernormal faculties and the skillful means of wisdom. Were it not for his entire being being the thousand suchnesses (*tathatā*), [such manifestation would be impossible].
The application of these [powers] is not termed "the power of fully perfected supernatural faculties" (*abhijñā*).

Although these faculties are inherently possessed by nature, they are further manifested through the cultivation of vast, wondrous wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*), which illuminate that nature to bring forth the faculties. Thus, one attains the sovereign manifestation of the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*), pervading all lands throughout the ten directions without limit.
The three lands are not external to oneself; they do not depart from the single mind as it universally responds to all realms. △ Second, a verse summarizing the specific answers.
Third, the first verse concerns the universal response of bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
It gradually causes all the various sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death within the evil destinies—the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—to be completely extinguished.
In the preceding prose section, the various bodies were listed individually, each consisting of the three types of action; now, in this verse, the three are specifically demonstrated once again.

That every single karma is all-pervasive is the artistry of the *geya* (versified) verses. Now, while the single line of the separate verses refers to the body-karma universally responding to and encompassing the ten realms, it only indicates the three miserable states (*durgati*).
This is because by showing the lower, one may infer the higher. Furthermore, the various evil destinies collectively refer to the nine realms;
from the perspective of the Buddha, all nine realms are termed "evil. Next, the three miserable states are specifically singled out as the ultimate [representatives].

This is because they are evil. Within the nine realms and the two types of death, there are all four marks [of conditioned existence] which must be gradually extinguished and eliminated so as to return to eternal tranquility.
This is also the gate of the Dharma for Avalokiteśvara to realize evil; being sovereign over evil, he is able to spontaneously eliminate the sufferings of the various evil destinies.
△ Second, the verse on the universal contemplation of mental karma, in two parts: first, clarifying the compassion of the fundamental contemplation.

The Contemplation of Reality, the Contemplation of Purity, the Contemplation of Vast Wisdom, the Contemplation of Compassion, and the Contemplation of Loving-kindness—these should always be aspired to and constantly looked up to.

All five characters for these contemplations are pronounced with the departing tone (go-shō), which fully clarifies the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) as well as compassion and loving-kindness. The Contemplation of Reality is emptiness (*śūnyatā*);

the Contemplation of Purity is the provisional (*prajñapti*). Because the provisional arises from emptiness and is free from the defilements of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), it is called "pure. "Vast" refers to the Great [Vehicle].
In the contemplation of wisdom, both the negation and the illumination are simultaneous—neither partial nor dependent; this is precisely the Great Wisdom of Equality.

Regarding why both compassion and mercy are termed "contemplation" (*guan*), there are two intentions: first, Guanyin observes sentient beings through unconditioned compassion, which is thus called the "Contemplation of Compassion and Mercy";
second, the dharma of compassion and mercy must necessarily employ the Three Contemplations.
It is because the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) can accomplish all practices;

they are called the "contemplation of compassion" (*karuṇā-vipaśyanā*) because one uses the three contemplations to uproot suffering, and the "contemplation of loving-kindness" (*maitrī-vipaśyanā*) because one uses the three contemplations to bestow happiness. Although there are these two interpretations, their essence is one.

From the beginning until reaching the ultimate stage, the Bodhisattva’s three contemplations and compassionate thoughts never depart from mindfulness; therefore, they cause sentient beings to always aspire to practice them.
I constantly look up to this contemplation. △ Second, the wisdom-light shines universally:
The stainless, pure light of the sun of wisdom shatters all darkness; it can subdue the winds and fires of calamity, shining everywhere throughout the world.
